senses.definition: A part of the human body, such as an eye, hand or tongue.

senses.label: Members as instruments of action
senses.definition: The body's parts as the means through which a person serves sin or righteousness, and where sinful passions operate.

senses.label: Members of Christ's body
senses.definition: Believers as parts of the one body of Christ, each with a function and belonging to one another.
senses.note: Believers' bodies are 'members of Christ', not to be joined to a prostitute (1CO 6:15).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul develops the image of the church as Christ's body with many members, each needed, and uses the same word for the bodily members believers must present to God.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James singles out the tongue as a small member able to set the whole body on fire, and locates conflicts in passions waging war 'in your members'.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Jesus' warning that it is better to lose one member than the whole body uses deliberate hyperbole about decisive action against sin.

study.translationNote: Older versions use 'member(s)' throughout; many modern versions say 'part (of the body)' (NIV, MSB in Rom 6:13; 1 Cor 12:27) because 'member' now suggests club membership. That can obscure the link between the body's members in Rom 6 and the church's members in Rom 12 and 1 Cor 12.

background.note: In early Greek the word occurs only in the plural, 'limbs'.
Herodotus uses κατὰ μέλη for cutting a body 'limb by limb'.
2 Maccabees describes enemies being cut limb from limb.
A complainant reports being beaten 'on every limb of my body'.

study.exegesisTip: Track Paul's move from literal members (Rom 6:13) to the members of Christ's body (Rom 12:4–5); both stress that the whole person belongs to God and to others.
study.caution: In Col 3:5 ('put to death your members which are on earth') interpreters differ on whether 'members' are bodily members used for sin, or whether the listed vices themselves are called 'members' of the old self.

study.summary: To repent: to change one's mind and direction, above all to turn from sin back to God; once (Luke 17:3–4) to regret a wrong done to a fellow believer.

senses.label: Turn to God at his summons
senses.definition: A decisive reorientation of the whole person toward God in response to the announcement of his kingdom, often paired with believing, being baptized or 'turning'.
senses.note: Usually absolute, without stating what one repents of.

senses.label: Repent of specific sins
senses.definition: To renounce particular wrongdoing, with the sin marked by ἀπό ('from'), ἐκ ('out of') or ἐπί ('over').
senses.note: The construction with ἐκ mirrors the Hebrew 'turn from' (šûb min).

senses.label: Repentance as the response God seeks
senses.definition: The penitent response that God's works and warnings should evoke and that heaven rejoices over; its absence brings judgment.
senses.note: Sometimes pictured with visible mourning: 'in sackcloth and ashes' (MAT 11:21; LUK 10:13).

senses.label: A church returning to its first ways
senses.definition: Addressed to believers and congregations: to recognise their lapse and return to former devotion and works.

senses.label: Regret a wrong done to another
senses.definition: Within the community, to express sorrow for an offence against a brother, which calls for forgiveness.
senses.note: Here the focus is interpersonal rather than conversion.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the verb most (14×), joining repentance to forgiveness, baptism and 'turning' to God, and stressing God's joy over one sinner who repents and his call to all nations.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: The verb never occurs in John's Gospel or letters; all 12 Johannine uses are in Revelation, where the risen Christ calls the churches to repent and the world's refusal to repent is underlined.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb only once, of Corinthian believers who have not repented of immorality; he normally expresses conversion in terms of faith and of dying and rising with Christ.

study.translationNote: Most versions say 'repent'. The Latin Vulgate's paenitentiam agite became 'do penance' in the Douay–Rheims version, which Reformation scholars contested as implying a sacramental act. Some modern versions paraphrase to bring out the reorientation involved, e.g. 'change your hearts and lives' (CEB) or 'turn from your sins'.

background.note: In classical Greek the verb commonly means simply to change one's mind or purpose, without moral overtones.
In the Septuagint it mostly renders Hebrew nāḥam ni., often of God relenting or not relenting from a declared action; the human 'turning' of the prophets is usually rendered by ἐπιστρέφω.
A 3rd-century letter plays repentance against persistence: 'if you persist in your folly, I congratulate you; if you repent, you only know'.

study.exegesisTip: Note what the repentance is from (ἀπό, ἐκ, ἐπί) and what accompanies it (believing, baptism, turning, fruits), since these define its content in each context.
study.caution: Popular appeals to etymology ('after-mind', so merely 'change of mind') understate the word; New Testament usage, shaped by the prophets' call to turn back to God, describes a reorientation of life, though theologians debate how its mental, emotional and behavioural sides relate.

study.summary: Covenant: an arrangement settled by one party (above all God) that others accept, defining a relationship with promises and obligations; in ordinary Greek also a last will and testament.

senses.label: God's covenant with the fathers
senses.definition: The gracious arrangements God made with Abraham and Israel's ancestors, carrying his promises.
senses.note: The plural 'covenants' (ROM 9:4; EPH 2:12) gathers Israel's successive covenants.

senses.label: The Sinai (old) covenant
senses.definition: The covenant given through Moses at Sinai, with its law, tablets and ritual, called 'first' or 'old' in contrast to the new.
senses.note: 'The reading of the old covenant' (2CO 3:14) refers to the Scriptures of Moses read in the synagogue; 'ark of the covenant' (HEB 9:4) is the chest holding its tablets.

senses.label: The new covenant in Christ
senses.definition: The covenant promised in Jeremiah 31 and inaugurated by Christ's death, bringing forgiveness and the law written on the heart.
senses.note: Hebrews calls it 'better' and 'eternal' (HEB 7:22; HEB 13:20).

senses.label: Will, testament
senses.definition: A legal disposition of property taking effect at the testator's death, the standard sense in contemporary Greek.
senses.note: Whether these verses mean 'will' or 'covenant' is disputed (see caution).

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the word 17 times, quoting Jeremiah's new-covenant promise in full and presenting Jesus as guarantor and mediator of a better covenant that supersedes the first.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul sets the covenant of promise with Abraham before and above the law, contrasts the 'old covenant' of the letter with the 'new covenant' of the Spirit, and allegorises two covenants in Hagar and Sarah.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke roots the gospel in God's remembered covenant with Abraham, and alone among the Synoptics records 'the new covenant in my blood'.

study.translationNote: The KJV often says 'testament' (whence 'New Testament', via Latin testamentum), modern versions 'covenant'. In Heb 9:16–17 the NIV and ESV switch to 'will', judging that the writer plays on the everyday legal sense, while others keep 'covenant' throughout; Gal 3:15 shows a similar split ('covenant' vs 'will').

background.note: In Attic Greek the normal meaning is a will disposing of property.
Aristophanes uses it once of a compact between parties, showing a wider sense 'arrangement' was available.
Papyri and inscriptions use the word for 'will' with complete consistency; King Attalus of Pergamum bequeathed his kingdom to Rome by such a διαθήκη.
The Septuagint chose διαθήκη, not συνθήκη ('agreement between equals'), for Hebrew bĕrît; Aquila's later version substituted συνθήκη here.

study.exegesisTip: Read διαθήκη as an arrangement God sovereignly sets up and offers, not a contract negotiated between equals, and let the context (Sinai, Abraham, Jeremiah 31, the Supper) say which covenant is meant.
study.caution: Whether Heb 9:16–17 and Gal 3:15 shift to the sense 'will' (requiring the testator's death) or keep 'covenant' (with death referring to covenant sacrifice) is a long-standing debate among commentators.

study.summary: Wine: the fermented drink of everyday Mediterranean life, used at meals, celebrations and as medicine, abused in drunkenness, and in Revelation a vivid image of seduction and God's wrath.

senses.label: Wine as ordinary drink
senses.definition: The common fermented grape drink of meals and festivities, whose abundance signals joy.
senses.note: Abstaining from it (LUK 1:15) recalls the Nazirite vow.

senses.label: New wine in new wineskins
senses.definition: Freshly fermenting wine that would burst old, stiff skins, Jesus' image for the newness of his ministry that old forms cannot contain.

senses.label: Wine as medicine or sedative
senses.definition: Wine used to cleanse wounds, aid digestion, or, mixed with myrrh, to dull pain.

senses.label: Wine in excess
senses.definition: Wine as a source of drunkenness and dependence, which church leaders and believers must avoid.

senses.label: Figurative: wine of passion and wrath
senses.definition: An image for the intoxicating seduction of Babylon and for the cup of God's judgment that the nations must drink.
senses.note: Drawn from prophetic images of the cup of wrath.

senses.label: Wine as a commodity or crop
senses.definition: Wine as an article of trade or, by metonymy, the vineyard crop.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's Gospel features wine only at Cana, where water becomes abundant 'good wine' kept until last, a sign of the messianic age; Revelation uses wine as an image of Babylon's seduction and God's wrath.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's letters treat wine as permissible but subject to love for weaker believers and to self-control, especially for leaders.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke contrasts John the Baptist's abstinence with Jesus' freedom to eat and drink, and alone has the Samaritan's use of oil and wine on wounds.

background.note: Homer already praises 'old' wine as the best, the assumption behind Luke 5:39.
An ostracon contrasts οἶνος καινός ('new wine') with old wine, using καινός rather than νέος.
Letters mention 'a quantity of quite thin wine', reflecting everyday trade and quality grades.

study.exegesisTip: In Revelation look at the genitives attached to 'wine' (of passion, of immorality, of God's wrath) to see whose influence or judgment is pictured.
study.caution: Some have argued that biblical 'wine' could mean unfermented grape juice; the lexical evidence and passages warning against drunkenness (EPH 5:18) or mentioning it (JOH 2:10) indicate ordinary fermented wine, commonly mixed with water.

study.summary: Cup: a drinking vessel or its contents, the cup of the Lord's Supper, and, following Old Testament imagery, the portion God appoints, whether Christ's suffering or divine judgment.

senses.label: Drinking vessel
senses.definition: An ordinary cup, often of wine, as an object to be washed or held.
senses.note: The Pharisees' cleaning of cups becomes an image of outward purity hiding inner greed.

senses.label: A cupful; the contents
senses.definition: The drink in the cup, as in a cup of water given to a disciple.

senses.label: The cup of the Lord's Supper
senses.definition: The cup Jesus gave at the Last Supper and the cup of blessing shared at the Lord's Table, signifying the new covenant in his blood.
senses.note: Paul contrasts 'the cup of the Lord' with 'the cup of demons' (1CO 10:21).

senses.label: Cup of suffering appointed by God
senses.definition: The suffering and death the Father assigns to Jesus, which he prays may pass yet accepts, and which his disciples will share.

senses.label: Cup of divine wrath
senses.definition: God's judgment poured out to be drunk by the wicked, from the prophets' image of the cup of his anger.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul alone calls it 'the cup of blessing', a 'participation' in Christ's blood that excludes 'the cup of demons' and must not be drunk unworthily.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's Gospel has no Gethsemane prayer about the cup, only Jesus' resolute question at his arrest; Revelation turns the cup into the cup of God's wrath.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke mentions a cup both before and after the bread at the Supper.

background.note: Herodotus reports that Egyptian priests drink from bronze cups which they scour daily.
The prophets picture God's judgment as a cup of wrath that his people or the nations must drink, the source of Gospel and Revelation imagery.
Temple inventories list 'bowls and cups' among sacred vessels.
A letter asks for 'a little cup for little Theonas', showing the everyday word.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether 'cup' means the vessel, what is in it, or a God-given portion (blessing, suffering or wrath), as in Old Testament imagery.
study.caution: The longer form of Luke's Supper account, ending with the second cup at LUK 22:20, is absent from a few Western manuscripts; most textual critics accept it, but the order of cup and bread in Luke is discussed. Whether Jesus' 'cup' in Gethsemane implies bearing God's wrath or chiefly suffering and death is also debated.

study.summary: Poor: properly a destitute beggar; in the NT the needy without resources, the oppressed poor to whom the gospel is announced, the 'poor in spirit', and figuratively what is worthless.

senses.label: Beggar, destitute person
senses.definition: Someone with nothing who depends on others' charity for survival.
senses.note: Lazarus lies at the rich man's gate.

senses.label: Materially poor, needy
senses.definition: Lacking money and goods, opposite of rich; often the recipients of alms.
senses.note: The widow's two coins were 'all she had'.

senses.label: The poor as heirs of the good news
senses.definition: The afflicted and lowly whom God champions, who receive the gospel and the kingdom, echoing Isaiah's 'poor'.
senses.note: Material poverty and dependence on God are bound together here.

senses.label: Poor in spirit; spiritually poor
senses.definition: Aware of one's spiritual destitution before God, or, negatively, spiritually bankrupt without realising it.
senses.note: Paul's 'poor, yet making many rich' (2CO 6:10) plays on material and spiritual wealth.

senses.label: Worthless, impotent
senses.definition: Of things: miserably inadequate, with nothing to give.
senses.note: Of the 'elemental principles' to which the Galatians were returning.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke (10×, all in the Gospel) highlights the poor: Jesus' Nazareth manifesto, the plain blessing 'you who are poor', banquet invitations, Lazarus and Zacchaeus' restitution.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James condemns favouritism toward the rich in the assembly, reminding readers that God chose the poor of the world to be rich in faith.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's concern for 'the poor' is tied to the collection for the Jerusalem believers, which he was eager to fulfil.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew's beatitude speaks of 'the poor in spirit', making explicit the inward humility that Luke's 'you who are poor' assumes.

study.translationNote: In Gal 4:9 the KJV's 'beggarly elements' preserves the root sense, while modern versions give the effect: 'worthless' (ESV) or 'miserable' (NIV). Matthew's 'poor in spirit' and Luke's 'you who are poor' render different wordings of the beatitude and should not be harmonised in translation.

background.note: In Homer the πτωχός is a wandering beggar, protected by Zeus along with strangers.
Aristophanes distinguishes the πτωχός, who has nothing, from the πένης, who lives frugally by work.
The word appears in Ptolemaic papyri, though rarely; in secular use it had a contemptuous ring until the Gospels gave it honour.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether a passage stresses economic need, social helplessness or humble dependence on God; Luke 4:18 quotes Isaiah 61, where these belong together.
study.caution: Interpreters debate whether Jesus' blessing of 'the poor' concerns material poverty, spiritual humility (Matthew's 'in spirit'), or the pious, oppressed poor of the Psalms and Isaiah who look to God.

study.summary: To read written words, privately or, very often, aloud to others; Jesus' 'Have you not read?' implies reading Scripture with understanding.

senses.label: Read a written text
senses.definition: To read words written on a scroll, letter or notice.
senses.note: Ancient reading was normally audible, which is why Philip could hear the eunuch reading (ACT 8:30).

senses.label: Read aloud in worship
senses.definition: Public reading of Scripture in the synagogue or of apostolic letters and prophecy to the gathered church.
senses.note: The blessing on 'the one who reads' (REV 1:3) addresses a public reader.

senses.label: Read Scripture with understanding
senses.definition: To know what Scripture says and grasp its point; Jesus' 'Have you not read?' rebukes failure to perceive what was plainly there.

senses.label: Read and grasp a letter
senses.definition: Reading apostolic writing as the way to understand the writer's mind.
senses.note: In 2CO 1:13 Paul plays on ἀναγινώσκω and ἐπιγινώσκω ('read' and 'understand').

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew repeats Jesus' challenge 'Have you never read?' to opponents who knew the text but missed its meaning.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke shows the reading of Scripture as the setting for proclamation: Jesus in Nazareth, Moses and the prophets read every Sabbath, and the Ethiopian reading Isaiah.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul expects his letters to be read aloud to whole churches and exchanged, and speaks of the veil that remains whenever Moses is read.

study.translationNote: Most versions simply say 'read', but where the setting is public the NIV and ESV say 'reads aloud' (Rev 1:3), bringing out that one reader voices the text for listening hearers.

background.note: Papyri use the verb for the reading aloud of a petition in an official hearing.
A private letter: 'I received the letter from the Arab and read it and was grieved', of reading to oneself.
A 2nd-century letter puns on ἀναγνοῖς and καταγνοῖς, much as Paul does with two γινώσκω compounds.
ἀνέγνων ('I have read') served as an authenticating official signature.

study.exegesisTip: Picture a listening congregation when the NT speaks of reading: Scripture and apostolic letters were mainly heard, read aloud by one person to many.
study.caution: In 'let the reader understand' (MAT 24:15; MAR 13:14), it is debated whether the reader is the individual reading the Gospel, the public reader in worship, or the reader of Daniel.

study.summary: A great number or multitude of things or people; with the article, the whole body of a group, such as a city's populace, a council, or the assembled church.

senses.label: Large quantity of things
senses.definition: A great amount or number of non-personal things, such as fish, sticks or sins.
senses.note: 'Cover a multitude of sins' (JAM 5:20; 1PE 4:8) reflects a proverb on love's forgiving power.

senses.label: Large crowd of people
senses.definition: A great number of people, often with 'great' (πολύ) or a genitive of who they are.
senses.note: Also of angels: 'a multitude of the heavenly host' (LUK 2:13).

senses.label: The whole people or populace
senses.definition: With the article, the entire population or crowd of a place, sometimes an excited mob.

senses.label: A council as a body
senses.definition: The full membership of a ruling body acting together.

senses.label: The church community assembled
senses.definition: The whole body of believers or disciples, especially when gathered for decisions.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke accounts for 25 of about 31 uses and characteristically uses τὸ πλῆθος for the whole community of believers acting together, as when choosing the Seven or receiving the Jerusalem decision.

study.translationNote: Renderings vary widely ('number', 'multitude', 'crowd', 'whole', 'assembly', 'congregation') because the word covers both an indefinite large number and, with the article, the whole membership of a group; 'multitude' can mislead where a definite body such as the Jerusalem church (Acts 15:12) is meant.

background.note: From Homer on it means a great number, especially of people.
Classical writers use τὸ πλῆθος for the mass of ordinary citizens, the populace.
Papyri use it of amounts of goods and of an organised body, 'the corporation of priests'.

study.exegesisTip: Watch the article: πλῆθος alone usually means 'a large number', while τὸ πλῆθος (often with πᾶν, 'all') means 'the whole body' of a group.
study.caution: Some scholars compare Luke's τὸ πλῆθος for the church's decision-making assembly with the Dead Sea community's term 'the Many'; how far this is a technical term rather than ordinary Greek usage is debated.

study.summary: Darkness: physical absence of light, and by extension ignorance, sin, the realm of Satan's power, and the 'outer darkness' of final exclusion.

senses.label: Physical darkness
senses.definition: Literal absence of light, as at the crucifixion, in cosmic signs, or in sudden blindness.
senses.note: 2CO 4:6 recalls creation: 'Let light shine out of darkness'.

senses.label: Ignorance and lostness
senses.definition: The condition of people without God's revealing light, needing illumination and rescue.
senses.note: An inner darkness can also afflict one who thinks he has light (MAT 6:23; LUK 11:35).

senses.label: Moral evil
senses.definition: Sinful conduct and the sphere of wrongdoing, set against the 'light' of righteousness.
senses.note: 'Things hidden in darkness' (1CO 4:5) are secret motives God will expose.

senses.label: The realm and power of evil
senses.definition: The domain under Satan's rule, opposed to God's kingdom, from which believers are rescued.

senses.label: Darkness of final judgment
senses.definition: The place or state of final exclusion and punishment.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Only Matthew uses 'the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth', of those cast out from the kingdom banquet.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul frames conversion as transfer from darkness to light: believers once were darkness, are rescued from its dominion, and must lay aside its works.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses σκότος only twice, preferring the related σκοτία, but sharpens the moral contrast: people loved darkness rather than light.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter describes conversion as being called out of darkness into God's light; 2 Peter, like Jude, speaks of 'the gloom of darkness' reserved for false teachers.

background.note: In Homer darkness covering the eyes is a standard image of death; tragedians speak of dying in darkness.
Classical writers set darkness against light, with the gloom of night.
A magical papyrus invokes the deity 'who created light and darkness', echoing Genesis-style language.

study.exegesisTip: Note the paired opposite (light, day) and the genitive phrases ('works of', 'power of', 'sons of' darkness) to see whether ignorance, sin or hostile power is in view.
study.caution: Whether the 'outer darkness' and the images of fire describe the same reality, or are complementary metaphors for exclusion from God's presence, is discussed by interpreters.

study.summary: Conscience: inward moral awareness that bears witness to and judges one's conduct; occasionally simply consciousness or awareness of something.

senses.label: Awareness, consciousness of something
senses.definition: Knowledge or awareness of a fact or person, without a strictly moral-judging sense.
senses.note: 'Consciousness of sins' (HEB 10:2); 'mindful of God' (1PE 2:19).

senses.label: Conscience as inner witness
senses.definition: The faculty that testifies to and judges one's own conduct, accusing or excusing.
senses.note: Also the motive for obedience: 'for the sake of conscience' (ROM 13:5).

senses.label: A good or clear conscience
senses.definition: The settled state of knowing oneself blameless before God and people, expected of believers and leaders.

senses.label: A weak or scrupulous conscience
senses.definition: A conscience not yet free to accept what is permitted, easily wounded and to be respected by others.
senses.note: In 1CO 10:29 it is the other person's conscience that limits one's freedom.

senses.label: A defiled conscience needing cleansing
senses.definition: A conscience corrupted, seared or burdened by guilt, which only Christ's sacrifice can purify.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (21×) makes conscience a witness alongside God's law even among Gentiles, protects the 'weak conscience' at Corinth, and in the Pastorals joins a good conscience with faith.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews argues that the old sacrifices could not perfect the worshipper's conscience, whereas Christ's blood purifies it for service to the living God.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter urges a good conscience before slanderers and links baptism to the response of a good conscience toward God.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: In Acts the word appears only in Paul's defence speeches, as his claim of a clear conscience before God and men.

study.translationNote: 'Conscience' is standard, but where the sense is mere awareness modern versions vary: Heb 10:2 'consciousness of sins' or 'felt guilty' (NIV); 1 Pet 2:19 'conscience toward God' (KJV) versus 'mindful of God' (ESV) or 'conscious of God' (NIV). In 1 Cor 8:7 manuscripts differ between συνειδήσει ('conscience of the idol') and συνηθείᾳ ('being accustomed to the idol').

background.note: Democritus speaks of the consciousness of one's wrongdoing, an early moral use.
The only Hebrew-based LXX use means inner thought: do not curse the king even in your thoughts.
A woman is described as 'oppressed by the consciousness' of what she had appropriated, a guilty awareness.
A Menandrian maxim says 'for all of us conscience is a god'.

study.exegesisTip: Note the qualifying adjective (good, pure, clear, weak, seared, evil) and whose conscience is meant, since Paul distinguishes one's own from another's.
study.caution: How far Paul's use derives from popular Greek moral philosophy (it is absent from Epictetus) and whether in 1 Cor 8–10 the word denotes a judging faculty or simply moral self-awareness are debated; the NT does not treat conscience as infallible.

study.summary: To come together: to assemble or gather, especially of the church meeting; to accompany someone on a journey; and of marriage, to come together as husband and wife.

senses.label: Assemble, gather
senses.definition: Of crowds, councils or groups coming together in one place.
senses.note: Also of the Sanhedrin convening (MAR 14:53; ACT 22:30).

senses.label: The church's meeting
senses.definition: Believers assembling as the church for worship and the Lord's Supper.

senses.label: Accompany, go with
senses.definition: To travel or go along with someone, with the dative or σύν.

senses.label: Come together in marriage
senses.definition: Of husband and wife, to begin married life together or to resume sexual relations.
senses.note: In 1CO 7:5 the verb appears in some manuscripts only.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke alone uses the later sense 'accompany', especially of believers travelling with Peter or Paul.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In 1 Corinthians the verb almost becomes a term for the church assembly: Paul's critique of divisions and the Supper repeatedly begins 'when you come together'.

study.translationNote: In Matt 1:18 'before they came together' keeps the Greek ambiguity; some versions make it explicit as the marriage taking place (NLT) or living together, since the verb was used both of setting up a married home and of sexual union.

background.note: Herodotus uses it of people coming together to assemble.
Marriage contracts state that a couple 'have come together with one another for marriage'.
A letter asks the recipient to 'accompany Ailourion who conveys this letter', the sense found in Luke–Acts.
An order to 'assemble to-day at the accustomed place'.

study.exegesisTip: In 1 Cor 11 and 14 notice how 'when you come together' marks the gathered church as the setting where Paul's instructions apply.

study.summary: To buy or purchase, originally 'to do business in the market'; in the NT both ordinary shopping and, figuratively, God's acquiring of people as his own at the cost of Christ's blood.

senses.label: Buy, purchase
senses.definition: To acquire goods, food or property by paying for them; the everyday market sense, often paired with 'sell' (πωλέω).
senses.note: The price can be expressed by a genitive or ἐκ ('with the money'), as in MAT 27:7.

senses.label: Trade, do business
senses.definition: Used absolutely or with 'sell' for commercial activity in general, the ordinary buying and selling of economic life.
senses.note: In Revelation the ability to buy and sell becomes a test of allegiance (REV 13:17).

senses.label: Acquire people as owner
senses.definition: Figuratively, to purchase persons so that they belong to a new master: believers are 'bought' by God or Christ, the price being Christ's death.
senses.note: The emphasis is on transfer of ownership: those bought are no longer their own (1CO 6:20).

senses.label: Obtain spiritual goods
senses.definition: Metaphorically, to secure what is needed for spiritual life, using the image of buying from a seller.
senses.note: In REV 3:18 the risen Christ invites the self-satisfied Laodiceans to 'buy' from him what money cannot provide.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul twice says 'you were bought at a price' (τιμῆς), drawing the ethical conclusion that believers must honour God with their bodies and not become slaves of men.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: The Gospel uses the word only for buying food or supplies, while Revelation celebrates the Lamb who by his blood bought people from every tribe for God.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 2 Peter makes the false teachers' guilt sharper: they deny the very Master (δεσπότης) who bought them, the language of a slave-owner.

study.translationNote: Most passages are simply 'buy'. In the theological passages the KJV has 'redeemed' (Rev 5:9; 14:3–4), while modern versions prefer 'purchased' or 'ransomed', keeping the commercial image. 'Redeem' is better kept for related words such as the compound ἐξαγοράζω or λυτρόω.

background.note: The basic classical sense is to frequent or spend time in the ἀγορά, the market-place; 'buy' develops from this.
The verb is common in Egyptian deeds of sale, recording what someone bought from whom.
It is used of buying slaves, e.g. a request to buy a slave named Sarapion from his owner — a close parallel to 'you were bought at a price'.

study.exegesisTip: In the figurative uses look for the price (τιμῆς, 'by your blood') and the new owner: the image is a change of master, with obligations that follow from it.
study.caution: Deissmann linked 'bought at a price' to sacral manumission, where a slave was fictitiously sold to a god; many scholars now think the ordinary slave-market sale fits Paul's wording better. The NT never says to whom the price was paid.

study.summary: Unclean, impure: ritually defiled under the Mosaic law, morally impure, and above all in the Gospels describing evil spirits as 'unclean spirits', opposed to God's holiness.

senses.label: Ritually unclean things
senses.definition: Defiled or forbidden according to the purity laws, especially food and animals that an observant Jew may not eat or touch.
senses.note: Often paired with κοινός ('common, profane') in Peter's vision.

senses.label: Unclean persons
senses.definition: People regarded as outside the sphere of holiness, whether Gentiles under Jewish purity rules or children not set apart for God.
senses.note: God's lesson to Peter is that no person is to be called unclean (ACT 10:28).

senses.label: Morally impure
senses.definition: Defiled in conduct, especially by sexual immorality, so as to be unfit for God's kingdom.

senses.label: Unclean (evil) spirits
senses.definition: With πνεῦμα, a demon: a spirit that is defiling and hostile to God's holiness, which Jesus and his followers cast out.
senses.note: In the Gospels the word always has this sense, interchangeable with δαιμόνιον ('demon').

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark (11 uses) favours 'unclean spirit' for demons, and his scenes stress uncleanness — a man among tombs, a herd of pigs, a Gentile woman's daughter.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke has the unique 'spirit of an unclean demon', and in Acts Peter's vision overturns the clean/unclean distinction as a barrier between Jew and Gentile.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word for ritual-style separation applied to the church, for the status of believers' children, and for the morally impure person.

study.translationNote: Most versions keep 'unclean spirit'. The NIV (2011) has 'impure spirit' and the NLT 'evil spirit', which makes the moral sense clear but loses the link with the purity laws; the KJV sometimes has 'foul spirit' (Mark 9:25; Rev 18:2).

background.note: The Septuagint uses it constantly for ceremonial impurity in the Law, translating Hebrew ṭāmēʾ.
The phrase 'unclean spirit' already appears in Zechariah's promise that God will remove it from the land.
Plato already uses it of the morally impure soul.
A Lycian dedication forbids anyone 'unclean' to approach a shrine without purification from garlic, pork and women — plainly ritual impurity.

study.exegesisTip: Ask what kind of uncleanness is meant — ritual, moral or demonic — and notice how the NT moves the weight from food and contact to the heart and to spiritual powers.
study.caution: The sense of 'otherwise your children would be unclean' (1 Cor 7:14) is debated: whether it concerns the children's covenant status, their legitimacy, or simply their being set within a believing household.

study.summary: Wind, the moving air of weather and storm; also an image of instability, and in the plural 'four winds' the four points of the compass, i.e. the whole earth.

senses.label: Wind as natural force
senses.definition: Moving air, usually strong or contrary wind at sea or in a storm.

senses.label: Winds obeying Christ
senses.definition: Storm winds as forces of creation that Jesus rebukes and silences, revealing his divine authority.
senses.note: The disciples' question 'Who then is this?' turns on the wind's obedience.

senses.label: Image of instability
senses.definition: Figuratively, what pushes something weak or unanchored about: a reed, a ship, rainless clouds, or shifting teaching.
senses.note: 'Every wind of teaching' (EPH 4:14) pictures immature believers blown about by doctrinal fashion.

senses.label: Four winds: all directions
senses.definition: 'The four winds' means the four quarters of the earth, the whole world from end to end.
senses.note: In REV 7:1 the four winds are also destructive forces held back by angels.

senses.label: Winds in apocalyptic imagery
senses.definition: Wind as an agent in end-time visions, shaking the cosmos under God's control.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke's account of Paul's voyage uses ἄνεμος with nautical precision for contrary winds and the north-easter that drove the ship.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses the plural 'winds' in the parable of the two builders and in the stilling of the storm, and adds Peter's fear of the wind when walking on the water.

background.note: Homer uses it for the wind's blast, e.g. something flying on the breath of the wind.
Land documents describe neighbours 'from the four winds', i.e. on all four sides — the same idiom as 'the four winds' in the Gospels.
A land-sale declaration refers to boundaries 'by wind', meaning the plot's bounds on each side.

study.exegesisTip: ἄνεμος is ordinary wind; the Spirit-related word πνεῦμα (also 'breath, wind') is a different term, so do not read 'wind' passages here as references to the Spirit.

study.summary: To say no: deny a statement as untrue, and especially disown or repudiate a person (above all Christ), or renounce a belief or way of life, by word or by conduct.

senses.label: Deny a fact, say no
senses.definition: To declare that something is not so or to refuse to admit it; the opposite of affirming or confessing.
senses.note: John 'confessed and did not deny' (JOH 1:20): the Hebraic pairing of positive and negative for emphasis.

senses.label: Disown a person
senses.definition: To refuse to acknowledge or to repudiate someone with whom one should stand, especially Jesus before others.
senses.note: Said of God too: Christ 'cannot deny himself', i.e. cannot be untrue to his own character (2TI 2:13).

senses.label: Deny the faith by conduct
senses.definition: To abandon or contradict the Christian faith, either openly under pressure or by a life that belies one's profession.

senses.label: Renounce, refuse
senses.definition: To say no to something or someone, turning it down deliberately: oneself, worldly desires, or a privileged status.
senses.note: Here the 'no' is commended: self-denial in discipleship and Moses' refusal of Egyptian rank.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In the Gospel the word frames Peter's denials and the Baptist's honest testimony; in 1 John denial becomes doctrinal — denying that Jesus is the Christ, which means losing the Father as well.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: In Peter's and Stephen's speeches Israel 'denied' (rejected) the Holy and Righteous One, as their fathers rejected Moses.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: The Pastoral Letters stress denial by behaviour — neglecting one's family, ungodly works, a form of godliness without power — and the warning 'if we deny him, he will deny us'.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 2 Peter describes false teachers as denying the Master who bought them, close to Jude's language about those who deny Christ.

study.translationNote: 'Deny' is standard, but with a personal object versions also use 'disown' (NIV, Matt 10:33) or 'reject' (Acts 3:14; 7:35), and with an abstract object 'renounce' or 'say no to' (Tit 2:12). 'Deny' with a person can sound like denying the person exists; the meaning is refusing to acknowledge them.

background.note: From Homer on it means to deny or disown, e.g. to go back on one's word.
Sarah 'denied' having laughed, out of fear — the word's only use in the Hebrew-based Septuagint.
A letter of Augustus speaks of a man who 'persisted in his denial'.
In a legal record a man repudiated (renounced) his father's inheritance.

study.exegesisTip: Read ἀρνέομαι against its opposite ὁμολογέω ('confess, acknowledge'): the issue is public loyalty, whether expressed in words or in a way of life.
study.caution: Whether 'if we deny him, he will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful' (2 Tim 2:12–13) is purely a warning or ends in reassurance is debated, as is how persistent the denial must be.

study.summary: To show: point out or exhibit something to be seen, make known or reveal (especially divine revelation), and demonstrate or prove by evidence such as deeds.

senses.label: Show, point out
senses.definition: To cause someone to see something physically present, pointing it out or displaying it.

senses.label: Present oneself for inspection
senses.definition: With a reflexive pronoun, to go and present oneself to an official, as a healed leper to the priest.
senses.note: The priest's inspection was the legal confirmation of cleansing (Lev 13–14).

senses.label: Reveal by vision
senses.definition: Of God or an angel, to disclose heavenly realities or future events, often in a vision.

senses.label: Make known, teach
senses.definition: To make something clear by explanation or instruction, so that it is understood.
senses.note: 'Show us the Father' (JOH 14:8) asks for a revelation, answered by Jesus himself.

senses.label: Prove, demonstrate
senses.definition: To give evidence that something is real or true, as faith is shown by deeds or authority by a sign.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In the Gospel the Father 'shows' the Son all he does, and the Son shows the Father to those who see him; in Revelation the verb frames the whole book as things God 'showed' his servants through an angel.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James uses it for proof: genuine faith and wisdom are demonstrated by works and good conduct, not claimed in words.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews cites the pattern 'shown' to Moses on the mountain, making the earthly tabernacle a copy of a heavenly reality.

study.translationNote: Almost always 'show'. In MAT 16:21 ('Jesus began to show his disciples that he must suffer') modern versions often have 'explain' or 'point out', since the showing is by teaching rather than display.

background.note: Used in the plain sense of exhibiting, e.g. 'showing signs'.
An imperial rescript of Caracalla says a person's way of life 'shows' (reveals) his character — close to the sense of proof in James.
A later Christian prayer asks God, 'Show your power', echoing 'show us the Father'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the 'showing' is display to the eyes, revelation from God, explanation, or proof — and who is the source of what is shown.

study.summary: Freedom of speech: plain, open speaking without riddles; fearless boldness in proclaiming; openness in public; and the confidence with which believers approach God or others.

senses.label: Plainness of speech
senses.definition: Speaking clearly and directly, without figures or veiled language; παρρησίᾳ often means 'plainly'.
senses.note: In JOH 16:25 it is the opposite of speaking 'in figures' (παροιμίαι).

senses.label: Boldness in speaking
senses.definition: Courageous, unintimidated freedom to speak the message openly, even before hostile authorities.
senses.note: In Acts it is a gift prayed for and given by the Spirit (ACT 4:29, ACT 4:31).

senses.label: Openness, in public
senses.definition: Being or acting openly before people rather than in secret.

senses.label: Confident access to God
senses.definition: The assurance with which believers come before God in prayer and will stand before him at Christ's coming, without fear or shame.

senses.label: Confidence, courage before others
senses.definition: Assured confidence or freedom in relation to people or circumstances, including courage that faces even death.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the word most (13×): in the Gospel for Jesus speaking plainly and acting publicly; in 1 John for confidence before God in prayer and at judgement.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts makes παρρησία a mark of Spirit-filled witness: from Pentecost to the book's final words Paul preaches 'with all boldness, unhindered'.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses it for the confidence believers must hold fast and the access they have into the sanctuary through Jesus' blood.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul links it to the open, unveiled ministry of the new covenant and to his courage in prison, and asks prayer that he may speak boldly.

study.translationNote: English versions divide one word among 'boldness', 'confidence', 'plainly', 'openly' and 'publicly', depending on whether the context concerns speech, public visibility, or inner assurance; the Greek reader hears one idea — the freedom of a person with nothing to hide or fear.

background.note: In Athens παρρησία was the prized right of free citizens to speak their mind.
Plato describes the democratic city as 'full of freedom and παρρησία'.
God says he brought Israel out of Egypt so that they walked 'with παρρησία', upright as free people rather than slaves.
Already in a 2nd-century BC letter the word passes from frank speech toward general confidence.

study.exegesisTip: Watch the construction: dative παρρησίᾳ usually means 'plainly/openly', μετὰ παρρησίας 'boldly', and ἔχειν παρρησίαν 'to have confidence'.
study.caution: In some verses the sense is disputed: COL 2:15 may mean Christ exposed the powers 'publicly' or 'boldly', and 2 Cor 3:12 may stress bold speech or the openness that contrasts with Moses' veil.

study.summary: To call someone to oneself, summon: used of Jesus calling disciples or crowds, of officials and masters summoning people, and of God's call to salvation or mission.

senses.label: Call to oneself
senses.definition: To bring people near by calling them, especially Jesus calling disciples or crowds in order to teach or commission them.
senses.note: The middle voice stresses that the caller summons people to himself.

senses.label: Summon officially
senses.definition: To send for or call in someone under one's authority, as an official, master, or church leaders.
senses.note: In JAM 5:14 the sick person takes the initiative to 'call for' the elders.

senses.label: God's call
senses.definition: Of God or the Holy Spirit calling people to himself in salvation or to a particular task.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark repeatedly uses the participle προσκαλεσάμενος ('having called to him') to introduce a significant saying or teaching of Jesus.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts uses it for the divine summons: the promise is for all whom God calls, and the Spirit calls Barnabas and Saul and leads Paul into Macedonia.

background.note: Ptolemaic papyri use the middle exactly as in the NT, of an official calling someone to himself.
The passive is used of being summoned to appear before officials.

study.exegesisTip: When Jesus 'calls to himself' disciples or a crowd, expect an important commission or teaching to follow; the verb marks the moment.

study.summary: Active: to shine or give light. Passive: to appear, become visible, be seen, or seem — what something looks like, sometimes in contrast with what it really is.

senses.label: Shine, give light
senses.definition: Active and intransitive: to emit light, of a lamp, the sun, or the light of God's revelation.

senses.label: Appear, become visible
senses.definition: Passive: to come into view or be seen, of a star, crops, a sign, mist, or anything that becomes visible.
senses.note: In 1PE 4:18 'where will the sinner appear?' means 'what will become of him?' at judgement.

senses.label: Appear to someone
senses.definition: Of heavenly beings or the risen Jesus, to make oneself seen to a person, often in a dream or vision.

senses.label: Appear as, seem
senses.definition: To be seen as or give the appearance of something, often contrasting outward appearance with inner reality.

senses.label: Seem in judgement
senses.definition: To seem so to someone's mind, i.e. how a matter strikes them: 'what do you think?'
senses.note: Equivalent to δοκεῖ ('it seems').

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses the word most: for the angel appearing to Joseph in dreams, and for hypocrites who aim to 'appear' righteous before people while God sees in secret.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the active 'shine' for the light of God's revelation in Christ that darkness cannot overcome and that is already shining.

study.translationNote: PHP 2:15 (φαίνεσθε) is rendered either 'you shine as lights' (KJV, ESV, NIV) or 'you appear as lights' (NASB), because the passive/middle form can mean either 'shine' or 'appear'.
study.exegesisTip: Check voice: active φαίνω means 'shine'; passive φαίνομαι means 'appear' or 'seem', and the context decides whether the appearance is real or only outward.

study.summary: To flee or run away from danger; to escape; and figuratively to shun what is morally dangerous — or, of things, to vanish.

senses.label: Flee from danger
senses.definition: To run away in order to save oneself from a threat such as persecution, war, or a ruler's violence.
senses.note: Even the devil 'will flee' from those who resist him (JAM 4:7).

senses.label: Run off, scatter
senses.definition: To run away suddenly through fear or alarm, often abandoning a post or companions.

senses.label: Escape
senses.definition: To get away successfully from a danger or penalty, with the danger as object or with ἀπό.
senses.note: 'Flee from the coming wrath' means to escape God's judgement.

senses.label: Shun, avoid
senses.definition: Figuratively, to keep well away from sins that endanger the soul, such as sexual immorality, idolatry or greed.
senses.note: Usually paired with διώκω ('pursue') the opposite virtues.

senses.label: Vanish, disappear
senses.definition: Of things, to vanish from sight or elude someone, in apocalyptic imagery.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's imperatives 'flee!' (sexual immorality, idolatry, the love of money, youthful passions) are matched by the command to 'pursue' righteousness, faith and love.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses flight as a mark of crisis — the holy family's flight to Egypt, flight from persecution and from the coming tribulation — and of the impossibility of escaping judgement.

study.translationNote: Versions render the same verb 'flee', 'run away/run off' or 'escape' according to context; with a sin as object it is often 'flee from' or 'shun' (KJV 'flee fornication').

background.note: Common from Homer for flight in battle; classical Greek also used it for going into exile and for being a defendant in a lawsuit.
A private letter reports that a man came and 'has fled'.
A Christian amulet commands, 'Flee, hateful spirit! Christ pursues you' — compare James' promise that the devil will flee.

study.exegesisTip: Look for the partner verb: φεύγω answered by διώκω ('pursue') shows the Christian life as decisive avoidance of one thing and active pursuit of another.

study.summary: A tribe: a group bound by common descent, chiefly one of the twelve tribes of Israel; extended to the peoples or clans of the whole earth.

senses.label: A tribe of Israel
senses.definition: One of the twelve divisions of Israel descended from Jacob's sons, used to state someone's ancestry.

senses.label: The twelve tribes: all Israel
senses.definition: 'The twelve tribes' as the complete people of God, whether historic Israel or Israel restored and judged in the age to come.

senses.label: Peoples of the earth
senses.definition: The families, clans or peoples of all humanity, often in lists with 'tongue', 'people' and 'nation'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation has 21 of the 31 uses: the tribal roll of the sealed in chapter 7, and a fourfold formula — tribe, tongue, people, nation — for the whole human race.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews argues that Jesus, from the tribe of Judah rather than Levi, holds a different priesthood, after the order of Melchizedek.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul names his tribe, Benjamin, as part of his credentials as a true Israelite.

study.translationNote: In 'all the tribes of the earth will mourn' (Matt 24:30; Rev 1:7) some versions have 'peoples' or 'nations', and the KJV 'kindreds' (Rev 1:7; 5:9). The Greek γῆ can also mean 'land', so some take these 'tribes' to be those of Israel's land rather than the whole world.

background.note: Classical writers use φυλή for the hereditary tribes of Greek cities, such as the Dorian and Ionian tribes.
In Egypt priests were organised in numbered 'tribes'; a priest 'of the fifth tribe' registers his son's birth.
Claudius' letter to the Alexandrians mentions a civic tribe named after the emperor.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether 'tribe' refers to Israel's tribes or to humanity's peoples; the phrase 'of the earth' and lists with 'tongue' and 'nation' usually signal the universal sense.
study.caution: Whether 'the twelve tribes' in James 1:1 and the sealed tribes of Rev 7:4–8 mean ethnic Israel or the church as the renewed Israel is much debated.

study.summary: A lamb; in the NT used once of Christ's flock and otherwise by Revelation as its chief title for Christ: the slain yet living Lamb who rules, judges, shepherds and is worshipped with God.

senses.label: Lamb of the flock
senses.definition: A young sheep, used figuratively of the believers Peter is to feed and care for.
senses.note: Originally a diminutive ('little lamb'), but by NT times ἀρνίον simply means 'lamb'.

senses.label: The slain Lamb
senses.definition: Christ as the sacrificial Lamb whose death redeems people, standing alive though bearing the marks of slaughter; his blood washes and conquers.
senses.note: 'Standing as though slain' (Rev 5:6) joins death and resurrection in one image.

senses.label: The enthroned, worshipped Lamb
senses.definition: Christ sharing God's throne and receiving the worship given to God, often paired with 'the One seated on the throne'.

senses.label: The Lamb as ruler and judge
senses.definition: The Lamb who opens the seals of history, whose wrath the wicked fear, and who conquers the hostile kings as Lord of lords.
senses.note: The paradox of a lamb's 'wrath' (Rev 6:16) is deliberate.

senses.label: Shepherd and bridegroom
senses.definition: The Lamb who leads his people to springs of living water, whom they follow, and whose marriage to his bride, the church, is celebrated.

senses.label: Counterfeit lamb
senses.definition: The second beast has 'two horns like a lamb' but speaks like a dragon: a deceptive imitation of the true Lamb.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Every NT use is Johannine. Revelation uses ἀρνίον about 28 times as its main title for Christ, while John's Gospel uses it only of the flock Peter must feed (a different word, ἀμνός, stands in the Gospel's 'Lamb of God').

background.note: In classical Greek ἀρνίον is a diminutive of ἀρήν, 'a little lamb'; it can also mean a sheepskin or fleece.
Jeremiah compares himself to an innocent lamb led to the slaughter, one of the OT images behind the slain Lamb.
Everyday documents list ἀρνία among livestock with no diminutive force, simply 'lambs'.

study.exegesisTip: In Revelation, read each 'Lamb' passage alongside Rev 5:6: the one who conquers, judges and reigns does so as the slain Lamb.
study.caution: Scholars debate the main background of Revelation's Lamb: the Passover lamb, the suffering servant 'like a lamb' (Isa 53), Jeremiah's lamb led to slaughter, or the horned ram-leader of Jewish apocalyptic; many see the author fusing several of these.

study.summary: One who serves: a household or table servant, an agent acting on another's behalf, a minister of God or the gospel, and in some letters a recognised church officer, a 'deacon'.

senses.label: Household or table servant
senses.definition: An attendant who waits at table or carries out a master's orders in a household or royal court.
senses.note: At Cana the διάκονοι are the waiters who draw the water.

senses.label: Servant as pattern of greatness
senses.definition: In Jesus' teaching, the humble role disciples must take if they wish to be great or first.

senses.label: Agent of a higher power
senses.definition: One who acts on behalf of, or furthers the cause of, another: the ruling authority as God's agent, Christ as 'servant' of the circumcision, Satan's agents.
senses.note: Here the stress is on agency and commission rather than menial status.

senses.label: Minister of God or the gospel
senses.definition: A person commissioned to serve God, Christ, the new covenant or the gospel, especially Paul and his co-workers.
senses.note: Also used of trusted co-workers such as Tychicus (Eph 6:21; Col 4:7) and Timothy (1 Tim 4:6).

senses.label: Church officer, deacon
senses.definition: A recognised office-holder in a local church, named alongside overseers and given qualifications.
senses.note: Whether Phoebe (Rom 16:1) held such an office is debated.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (22 uses) applies the word chiefly to himself and his co-workers as God's commissioned agents of the new covenant and the gospel, and in Philippians and 1 Timothy to an emerging church office.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the word both for the servants at Cana and for the disciple who follows Jesus and will be where he is.

study.translationNote: English versions choose 'servant', 'minister' or 'deacon' depending on whether they read an office in the context. Rom 16:1 is the main test case: Phoebe is 'servant' (KJV, NIV text, MSB), 'deaconess' (RSV) or 'deacon' (NRSV, NIV 2011 footnote, CSB), since the masculine form διάκονος can be used of a woman and the phrase 'διάκονος of the church in Cenchreae' may name a recognised role.

background.note: Herodotus uses the word for servants; tragedians also use it of a messenger.
In Esther the διάκονοι are the attendants of the Persian king.
Before Christianity, inscriptions use διάκονοι for officials of temples and religious guilds, including a female διάκονος beside priests.
Christian papyri of the fourth century greet 'presbyters and deacons' as church officers.

study.exegesisTip: Note the genitive that follows: 'διάκονος of God', 'of Christ', 'of the gospel' or 'of the church' tells you on whose behalf the person serves.
study.caution: Since J. N. Collins (1990) some scholars argue that διάκονος mainly means a commissioned go-between or agent rather than a humble table servant; others hold that lowly service remains central, especially in Jesus' sayings. Whether Rom 16:1 denotes an office is also disputed.

study.summary: Teaching: either the content taught (a body of instruction, especially Jesus' or the apostles') or the activity of teaching; used also of rival and false teachings.

senses.label: Jesus' authoritative teaching
senses.definition: What Jesus taught, which astonished hearers by its authority and which he says comes from the Father.
senses.note: The crowd's astonishment 'at his teaching' is a recurring Gospel motif.

senses.label: Apostolic, Christian teaching
senses.definition: The received body of Christian instruction that believers hold to and by which other teaching is tested.
senses.note: Hebrews speaks of elementary instruction about washings (Heb 6:2).

senses.label: New or rival teaching
senses.definition: A teaching as it strikes outsiders or opponents, whether as novel, threatening, or false.
senses.note: Revelation warns against 'the teaching of Balaam' and of the Nicolaitans.

senses.label: The act of teaching
senses.definition: Instruction as an activity, or a piece of teaching contributed in worship.
senses.note: 'In his teaching' (Mark 12:38) means 'in the course of his instruction'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John's Gospel Jesus insists his teaching is not his own but the Sender's; 2 John makes 'remaining in the teaching of Christ' a test of having God, and Revelation exposes rival teachings in the churches.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark links Jesus' teaching closely with his authority over demons: a 'new teaching with authority'.

study.translationNote: The KJV usually has 'doctrine'; modern versions prefer 'teaching'. 'Doctrine' now suggests a fixed system of beliefs, whereas διδαχή can mean either the content taught or the act of teaching, and in the Gospels often includes ethical instruction.

background.note: In classical prose the word means teaching or instruction in general.
An imperial letter of Hadrian's time uses it for soldiers' military training or discipline.
A fragment of an uncanonical gospel asks what 'new teaching' Jesus teaches, echoing Mark 1:27.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the word names content (what is taught) or activity (teaching as it happens); Acts 2:42 and 1 Cor 14:26 read differently depending on the answer.
study.caution: C. H. Dodd's sharp distinction between κήρυγμα (proclamation to outsiders) and διδαχή (instruction of converts) has been widely questioned as too neat; the 'pattern of teaching' in Rom 6:17 is also variously read as baptismal instruction or as the gospel itself shaping believers.

study.summary: To make clean: to cleanse objects, heal leprosy, declare or make ritually clean, purify by sacrifice, and cleanse people morally from sin.

senses.label: Heal leprosy
senses.definition: To cure someone of a skin disease that made them ritually unclean, restoring both health and fitness for community and worship.
senses.note: 'Cleanse' rather than 'heal' keeps the ritual dimension of leprosy.

senses.label: Clean an object
senses.definition: To wash or clean something physical, used in Jesus' critique of cleaning only the outside of cup and dish.

senses.label: Declare clean
senses.definition: To pronounce something ritually clean or acceptable, so that it may no longer be called impure.

senses.label: Purify by sacrifice
senses.definition: To make ritually pure by sacrificial blood, of the old sanctuary and, supremely, of the conscience by Christ's blood.

senses.label: Cleanse from sin
senses.definition: To free people inwardly and morally from sin and defilement, by God's action or by their own repentance.
senses.note: 'Cleanse your hands, you sinners' (Jas 4:8) applies ritual language to repentance.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke has the most uses: healings of lepers (including the ten in Luke 17), and Peter's vision where what God has cleansed must not be called common, extended to God cleansing Gentile hearts by faith.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the verb in a cultic frame: almost everything was purified with blood under the law, but Christ's blood purifies the conscience.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: 1 John promises that Jesus' blood cleanses from all sin and that God cleanses those who confess.

study.translationNote: In Mark 7:19 the participle 'cleansing (all foods)' is taken by most modern versions (ESV, NIV, NRSV) as Mark's comment: '(Thus he declared all foods clean)'. The KJV, following a different construal, makes it part of the digestive process: 'purging all meats'.

background.note: The Septuagint, mainly for Hebrew ṭāhēr, uses it for cleansing the altar and for ritual purification.
Sirach already uses it of purifying the heart from sin, the ethical sense found in the NT.
In farm documents the verb means cleaning grain, pruning vines and clearing ground of weeds.
The mystery inscription of Andania uses it for ritual purification 'from' things, the construction of 2 Cor 7:1.

study.exegesisTip: Identify the kind of uncleanness in view (disease, ritual, or moral) before deciding what 'cleanse' means in the verse.

study.summary: To give an order or instruction with authority: Jesus instructing disciples and healed people, authorities issuing orders, apostles charging churches, and God commanding all people to repent.

senses.label: Jesus' instructions and orders
senses.definition: Directions Jesus gives his followers, crowds or people he has healed, often with a prohibition such as 'tell no one'.

senses.label: Command to a spirit
senses.definition: An authoritative order to an unclean spirit to leave a person.
senses.note: Paul's command is given 'in the name of Jesus Christ' (Acts 16:18).

senses.label: Official order or ban
senses.definition: An order issued by an authority such as the Sanhedrin or Roman officials, often forbidding speech or directing custody.

senses.label: Apostolic charge
senses.definition: Binding instruction an apostle or church leader gives believers, carrying the Lord's authority.
senses.note: In 1 Cor 7:10 Paul says the charge is 'not I, but the Lord'.

senses.label: Divine command or commission
senses.definition: God's command to all people everywhere to repent, or Christ's commission to the apostles to preach.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the verb for Jesus' commands and for the Jewish authorities' repeated orders not to speak in Jesus' name, setting human bans against divine commission.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In the Thessalonian letters and 1 Timothy the verb marks firm pastoral directives, sometimes given 'in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ'.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'command', 'order', 'instruct' and 'charge' (KJV and ESV often 'charge' in 1 Timothy). The verb covers both a superior's order and solemn pastoral instruction, so the strength of the English should follow the speaker and setting.

background.note: Its earliest sense is to pass a message along, as of a beacon fire relaying news.
In classical prose it is the usual word for a general giving the word of command.
Ptolemaic papyri use it for an official summons to appear before a court.
In a private letter it softens to 'I bid you', a request between family members.

study.exegesisTip: Note who gives the instruction and on whose authority; in Paul the charge often rests explicitly on the Lord.

study.summary: To trip someone up spiritually: to cause to sin or fall away; passive, to be caused to stumble, desert the faith, or take offence (especially at Jesus).

senses.label: Lead into sin
senses.definition: Of something within oneself (eye, hand, foot) that entices a person into sin.

senses.label: Cause another to stumble
senses.definition: To bring about another believer's spiritual fall, especially the 'little ones' or the weak brother.

senses.label: Fall away (passive)
senses.definition: To abandon faith or loyalty to Jesus under pressure, persecution or fear.
senses.note: The disciples' falling away at the arrest was followed by restoration.

senses.label: Take offence at Jesus
senses.definition: To be repelled or shocked by Jesus or his teaching so as to reject him.

senses.label: Give needless offence
senses.definition: To offend people unnecessarily, which Jesus avoids by paying the temple tax.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew (14 uses) uses it most, stressing radical self-discipline, care for 'little ones', and the danger that many will fall away.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses it in the ethics of the strong and the weak: freedom must give way rather than cause a brother to fall.

study.translationNote: The KJV's 'offend' now sounds like hurting feelings. Modern versions distinguish 'cause to sin' (Matt 5:29), 'cause to stumble' (1 Cor 8:13), 'fall away' (Matt 26:31) and 'take offence' (Matt 13:57) because the verb covers enticement to sin, apostasy and indignant rejection.

background.note: The verb is almost exclusively biblical; Sirach warns not to gaze at a virgin lest one 'be made to stumble'.
The related noun σκανδάληθρον was the trigger-stick of a trap; Aristophanes speaks of setting 'word-traps'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the subject is the one ensnared (passive, 'fall away' or 'take offence') or the one ensnaring (active, 'cause to sin'), and what the trap is.
study.caution: Some (e.g. Moulton–Milligan) stress the image of a baited trap rather than an obstacle one trips over. Interpreters also differ on whether 'falling away' denotes final apostasy or a recoverable failure, since the disciples who 'fell away' (Matt 26:31) were restored.

study.summary: Friend: someone bound by affection and loyalty, from personal friends and social circles to Jesus' disciples, a political title ('friend of Caesar'), and 'friend of God'.

senses.label: Friendly (adjective)
senses.definition: Well-disposed, friendly towards someone.
senses.note: Of the Asiarchs who were friendly to Paul.

senses.label: Personal friend, neighbour
senses.definition: A person in a close or neighbourly relationship who can be called on and shares joy.
senses.note: Luke 15:9 has the feminine 'friends'.

senses.label: Social circle of friends
senses.definition: The network of friends and associates with whom one exchanges hospitality and favours.
senses.note: Jesus challenges reciprocity: invite those who cannot repay (Luke 14:12).

senses.label: Jesus' friends
senses.definition: Those Jesus treats as intimate friends rather than servants, for whom he lays down his life; also Jesus as 'friend of sinners'.

senses.label: Friend as a role or title
senses.definition: A defined relationship of loyalty: the bridegroom's friend, or 'friend of Caesar' as a loyal ally of the emperor.

senses.label: Friend of God or of the world
senses.definition: Allegiance as friendship: Abraham as God's friend, versus friendship with the world that makes one God's enemy.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke (18 uses) features friends in parables and in the economy of hospitality and reciprocity, which Jesus reshapes.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John makes friendship a theological category: Jesus calls disciples friends, not servants, and dies for them; the Baptist is the bridegroom's friend.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James contrasts Abraham, 'friend of God', with whoever chooses to be 'a friend of the world'.

study.translationNote: Most versions translate 'friend', but John 3:29 is sometimes rendered by its social role ('best man'), and John 19:12 'friend of Caesar' may be read as a quasi-title or as 'loyal to Caesar'.

background.note: Private letters routinely send greetings to 'the friends' and use friends to deliver goods.
In Ptolemaic Egypt 'the first friends' was a court rank of royal favourites.
Inscriptions attest the honorific 'friend of Caesar', the phrase in John 19:12.

study.exegesisTip: Look for what binds the friendship: affection, patronage, political loyalty or covenant allegiance; each changes the force of the word.
study.caution: Whether 'friend of Caesar' in John 19:12 alludes to the formal title amicus Caesaris or simply means a loyal subject is debated.

study.summary: To guard: to keep watch over, protect from harm, preserve what is entrusted, and observe commands; middle, to be on one's guard against something.

senses.label: Keep watch, guard a prisoner
senses.definition: To watch over people or things, especially to keep prisoners in custody.

senses.label: Protect, keep safe
senses.definition: To protect someone from harm or loss, often of God or Christ keeping believers.

senses.label: Guard a deposit
senses.definition: To keep intact what has been entrusted, especially the apostolic gospel.

senses.label: Observe commands
senses.definition: To keep or obey laws, commandments, decisions or the word of God.
senses.note: The middle in the rich man's 'all these I have kept' (Mark 10:20) follows Septuagint idiom.

senses.label: Be on guard, beware
senses.definition: Middle or reflexive: to protect oneself against a danger, avoid it.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke (14 uses) uses the verb for shepherds keeping watch, soldiers guarding Paul, and keeping the law and the apostles' decisions.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: The Pastoral Letters make 'guarding the deposit' a key charge to Timothy, with confidence that God also guards it.

study.translationNote: English 'keep' covers both φυλάσσω and τηρέω, and versions switch between 'keep', 'guard', 'observe' and 'obey'; in commands it means faithful observance, in protection it means keeping safe.

background.note: From Homer on the verb means to keep watch, as sentries at night.
The Septuagint uses it hundreds of times for Hebrew šāmar, especially of keeping God's statutes.
An amulet prays that a god will guard and protect a woman from fever.
Marriage contracts require spouses to 'keep the rights of marriage', i.e. observe its duties.

study.exegesisTip: Check the object and voice: a person or place (guard), something entrusted (preserve), a command (observe), or middle with ἀπό (beware of).
study.caution: In 2 Tim 1:12 'my deposit' may be what Paul has entrusted to God (his life, his work) or what God has entrusted to Paul (the gospel, as in 1:14); both readings have strong support.

study.summary: To make or treat as holy: to consecrate things or persons for God, make people God's holy people, purify, and 'hallow' God's name.

senses.label: Consecrate a thing
senses.definition: To set something apart as holy or fit for God's use, such as a gift on the altar, an offering or food.

senses.label: Christ set apart
senses.definition: The Father's setting apart of the Son for his mission, and the Son's consecrating himself for his self-offering.

senses.label: Make God's holy people
senses.definition: God's act, through Christ's sacrifice and the Spirit, of making people his own holy people; often perfect participle 'the sanctified'.
senses.note: Of an unbelieving spouse in a mixed marriage (1 Cor 7:14) in a special, derived sense.

senses.label: Growth in holiness
senses.definition: Making believers holy in character and life, a work God carries to completion.

senses.label: Ritual purification
senses.definition: Levitical cleansing that restores outward, bodily purity.

senses.label: Treat as holy, hallow
senses.definition: To honour or reverence as holy what already is holy, God's name or Christ as Lord.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses it in a sacrificial setting: Jesus sanctifies the people by his own blood, once for all, bringing them into God's family.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John, Jesus is the one the Father sanctified and sent; he sanctifies himself so that the disciples may be sanctified in the truth.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul can speak of believers as already sanctified in Christ and pray that God will sanctify them completely.

study.translationNote: The same verb is rendered 'hallowed' in the Lord's Prayer, 'sanctify' in most other places, and 'honour' or 'revere' (e.g. 1 Pet 3:15 'in your hearts honour Christ the Lord as holy' ESV). The variety reflects whether the object is made holy or recognised as holy.

background.note: The verb is a Jewish-Greek coinage; the Septuagint uses it for Hebrew qādaš, as when God sanctified the seventh day.
Philo also uses the verb, but no clear pagan use is known; pagan religion used ἁγίζω instead.

study.exegesisTip: Note the tense: aorists and perfects often state a completed setting-apart (1 Cor 6:11; Heb 10:10), while presents can describe an ongoing process (Heb 10:14).
study.caution: Theologians debate how far NT 'sanctify' is definitive (a status given at conversion) or progressive (growth in holiness); Heb 10:14 'those being sanctified' and the sense of 1 Cor 7:14 for an unbelieving spouse are especially contested.

study.summary: Knowledge: especially knowing God and his truth, God's own knowledge, a Spirit-given gift of insight, and practical understanding; Paul warns that knowledge without love puffs up.

senses.label: Knowledge of God, Christ, salvation
senses.definition: Personal, saving acquaintance with God or Christ, or with God's saving work.

senses.label: God's own knowledge
senses.definition: The unsearchable knowledge belonging to God, hidden in Christ.

senses.label: Knowledge given in the law
senses.definition: Knowledge of God's will and truth available through the Scriptures and their teachers.
senses.note: 'The key of knowledge' (Luke 11:52) is withheld by the lawyers.

senses.label: Spirit-given insight
senses.definition: Understanding of spiritual truth as a gift of grace, exercised for the church and destined to pass away.

senses.label: Claimed or self-important knowledge
senses.definition: Theological insight that inflates its holder or harms others, or that is falsely so called.

senses.label: Practical understanding
senses.definition: Moral and practical insight that shapes conduct, listed among Christian virtues.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (23 uses, mostly in Corinthians) prizes knowledge of God in Christ above all, yet insists that knowledge must serve love and that it is partial and temporary.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: In 2 Peter knowledge is a step in the ladder of Christian virtues and something to grow in; 1 Peter applies it to husbands' considerate conduct.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses it for 'knowledge of salvation' through forgiveness and the 'key of knowledge' the lawyers withhold.

study.translationNote: In 1 Pet 3:7 'according to knowledge' (KJV) becomes 'in an understanding way' (ESV) or 'considerate' (NIV), since the phrase means acting with insight. In 1 Tim 6:20 versions vary between 'science' (KJV) and 'knowledge' falsely so called.

background.note: In Attic orators γνῶσις can be a judicial inquiry or investigation.
Hannah's song calls the Lord 'a God of knowledge', rendering Hebrew daʿat.
Papyri use it for the decision of a lawsuit.
A decree praises a citizen who advanced to personal 'acquaintance' with the emperors, a sense some see in Phil 3:8.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether γνῶσις is relational (knowing God), informational (knowing truths), or charismatic (a gift), and whether love governs it (1 Cor 8:1).
study.caution: Scholars debate whether the 'knowledge' of the Corinthians and 'falsely called knowledge' (1 Tim 6:20) reflect an early form of Gnosticism or Jewish and Hellenistic speculation, and whether Phil 3:8 echoes mystical language or simply personal acquaintance with Christ.

study.summary: Daughter: a female child, and by Hebrew idiom a female descendant, a woman addressed with kindness, the inhabitants of a city ('daughter of Zion'), and God's people as his daughters.

senses.label: Female child
senses.definition: A person's own daughter, whether a young girl or a grown woman.
senses.note: Includes 'Pharaoh's daughter' (Acts 7:21; Heb 11:24) and Philip's four prophesying daughters (Acts 21:9).

senses.label: Tender form of address
senses.definition: Used in the vocative by Jesus to a woman not his relative, expressing warmth and acceptance, much like 'my dear'.
senses.note: Compare Boaz addressing Ruth as 'my daughter' (Ruth 2:2, 22).

senses.label: Female descendant of an ancestor
senses.definition: By Hebrew idiom, a woman belonging to a family line or people, however distant the ancestor.
senses.note: 'Daughter of Abraham' (Luke 13:16) affirms that the crippled woman is a full member of God's covenant people.

senses.label: Inhabitants of a city
senses.definition: A city or its people personified as a woman: 'daughter of Zion', 'daughters of Jerusalem'.
senses.note: From the prophets (Isa 1:8; Zech 9:9).

senses.label: Daughters of God
senses.definition: Believers, women as well as men, as members of God's family.
senses.note: Paul adapts the promise of 2 Sam 7:14, adding 'and daughters' (cf. Isa 43:6).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
