authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word most (12×), often to show women's place in God's people: Anna the prophetess, the 'daughter of Abraham' set free, the 'daughters of Jerusalem', and daughters who prophesy as Joel foretold.

study.translationNote: Most versions keep 'daughter', but for the city idiom some modern versions say 'Daughter Zion' (NIV 2011) or paraphrase as 'people of Jerusalem/Zion' (NLT), which is clearer but loses the poetic picture of the city as a beloved young woman.

background.note: The ordinary word for daughter from Homer on; poets could even call mules 'daughters of horses'.
The Septuagint renders Hebrew bat, including its idioms for a city ('daughter of Zion') and for kindly address.
Inscriptions record adoption of a girl 'by daughter-making', the female counterpart of adoption as a son.

study.exegesisTip: When Jesus calls a woman 'daughter' or 'daughter of Abraham', read it as a public word of belonging and restoration, not merely a polite address.

study.summary: Sacrifice: an offering presented to God (or a god), especially the animal and grain offerings of the Law; in the NT also Christ's self-offering and, figuratively, believers' lives, praise and gifts.

senses.label: Sacrificial worship as institution
senses.definition: Sacrifice as a form of religious practice, often contrasted with what God values more (mercy, love, obedience).
senses.note: 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice' (Hos 6:6).

senses.label: An offering presented
senses.definition: The animal or other gift actually offered on an altar, to God or to idols.
senses.note: Those who 'eat the sacrifices' share in the altar (1 Cor 10:18).

senses.label: Levitical sacrifices, repeated
senses.definition: The regular offerings of the old covenant priesthood, which could not cleanse the conscience or remove sin.
senses.note: Often paired: 'gifts and sacrifices'.

senses.label: Christ's self-offering
senses.definition: Christ's death understood as the one, final sacrifice for sin.
senses.note: Note the contrast of many repeated sacrifices with 'one sacrifice' (Heb 10:11–12).

senses.label: Spiritual sacrifice of believers
senses.definition: Figuratively, the self-giving, praise, good deeds and generosity that Christians offer to God.
senses.note: Bodies (Rom 12:1), faith (Phil 2:17), gifts (Phil 4:18), praise and sharing (Heb 13:15–16).

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews has over half the NT uses: the endlessly repeated sacrifices of the Law are set against Christ's single sacrifice of himself, after which no other sacrifice for sin remains; believers now offer praise and good works.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul transfers temple language to Christian life: bodies presented as a living sacrifice, the Philippians' faith and gifts as offerings, and Christ's death as a fragrant offering.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: Believers as a holy priesthood offer 'spiritual sacrifices' through Jesus Christ.

study.translationNote: In Rom 12:1 the Greek has a singular 'sacrifice' with plural 'bodies'; ESV and KJV keep 'a living sacrifice', while NIV and some others say 'living sacrifices'. The singular may suggest the church offering itself together, though it can also be a distributive idiom.

background.note: Herodotus uses the word for sacrifices by which people sought to win a god's favour.
The Septuagint names the 'sacrifice of peace' and 'sacrifice of praise', the latter echoed in Heb 13:15.
During the Decian persecution, certificates were addressed to officials 'chosen to oversee the sacrifices' that Christians were ordered to perform.
A temple inscription warns that if anyone uses force, 'the sacrifice is unacceptable to the god'—compare 'an acceptable sacrifice' in Phil 4:18.

study.exegesisTip: In Hebrews watch the number: plural 'sacrifices' marks the old, repeated system, while singular 'one sacrifice' marks Christ's finished work.
study.caution: The second half of Mark 9:49 ('and every sacrifice will be salted with salt') is found in the Byzantine text but omitted by many early manuscripts and modern critical editions.

study.summary: Sword: a short sword or long knife; hence armed violence and violent death, the state's power to punish, and figuratively conflict and the penetrating word of God.

senses.label: Short sword as weapon
senses.definition: A literal sword or dagger carried and drawn, as at Jesus' arrest.
senses.note: 'All who draw the sword will perish by the sword' (Matt 26:52).

senses.label: Violent death, killing
senses.definition: The sword as the means of execution or slaughter, and so violent death itself; 'mouth (edge) of the sword' is a Hebrew idiom.

senses.label: Authority to punish
senses.definition: The sword borne by the civil ruler as a sign of God-given power to punish wrongdoers.

senses.label: War, division, strife
senses.definition: Figuratively, conflict and the breaking of peace, whether war on earth or division within families.
senses.note: In Matt 10:34 the sword is the opposite of 'peace': loyalty to Jesus divides households.

senses.label: God's word as a sword
senses.definition: A metaphor for the word of God, sharp and penetrating, the weapon the Spirit gives.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews pictures God's word as sharper than any double-edged sword, cutting to the inner person, and lists death by the sword among the trials of the faithful.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's three uses cover the range: the sword as a threat that cannot separate believers from Christ's love, the ruler's sword of justice, and the Spirit's sword, the word of God.

study.translationNote: English versions use 'sword' almost everywhere, but μάχαιρα originally meant a large knife and in the NT period usually a short sword or dagger, distinct from the long ῥομφαία. In Luke 22:36–38 some have suggested 'knives' as an alternative rendering.

background.note: In Homer it is a large knife carried beside the sword-sheath, also used as a carving or sacrificial knife.
The knife Abraham took to sacrifice Isaac; elsewhere it chiefly translates Hebrew ḥereb, 'sword'.
Papyri speak of a man 'armed with a sword' and of a youth deprived of the soldier's sword he had inherited from his father.
Egyptian documents mention 'sword-bearers', a kind of armed police, illustrating the ruler's sword of Rom 13:4.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the sword is literal, a figure for violent death or state power, or a metaphor; in Matt 10:34 and Eph 6:17 a literal reading misleads.
study.caution: Jesus' instruction to buy a sword and his reply 'It is enough' (Luke 22:36–38) are debated: a literal call to self-defence, a figurative warning of coming hostility, or a rebuke of the disciples' misunderstanding.

study.summary: Wages, pay earned by work; more broadly, reward or recompense, especially God's reward of the faithful, but also the 'wages' that wrongdoing earns.

senses.label: Wages, pay for work
senses.definition: Money owed to a hired worker for labour done.
senses.note: 'The worker is worthy of his wages' (Luke 10:7; 1 Tim 5:18).

senses.label: What is owed, not given
senses.definition: Payment as a debt due, contrasted with a free gift of grace.
senses.note: Paul's point: justification is not a wage earned.

senses.label: God's reward
senses.definition: The recompense God gives, now or at the last day, to those who serve him faithfully.
senses.note: Also 'full reward' (2 John 8) and the reward of prophets and saints at the judgment (Rev 11:18).

senses.label: Human recognition as reward
senses.definition: The praise of people sought by religious display, which is all the reward such acts receive.
senses.note: 'They have their reward in full' (Matt 6:2).

senses.label: Wages of wrongdoing
senses.definition: Gain from evil, or the just recompense that wickedness brings.
senses.note: Judas's payment and Balaam's love of 'the wages of unrighteousness'.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew has a third of the NT uses, mostly in the Sermon on the Mount: a great reward in heaven for the persecuted, and no reward from the Father for piety done to be seen.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul contrasts wages with grace in justification, yet speaks of each worker receiving a reward according to his labour, and of his own 'reward' as preaching free of charge.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 2 Peter uses the word ironically of false teachers who, like Balaam, love the 'wages of unrighteousness' and will be paid accordingly.

study.translationNote: The same word is rendered 'wages' (Rom 4:4; Jas 5:4) and 'reward' (Matt 5:12; 6:1). English 'reward' can sound like a bonus, while μισθός keeps the idea of fitting recompense. In 2 Pet 2:13 versions differ ('receive the wages of unrighteousness' KJV; 'suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing' ESV) because of a textual variant in the verb.

background.note: From Homer on, the word means hire or fixed wages for service, including soldiers' pay.
Papyri speak of a labourer's 'daily wage'.
A slave is apprenticed to a shorthand-writer for an agreed salary.

study.exegesisTip: Check whether the context sets μισθός against grace (Rom 4:4) or simply promises God's faithful recompense (1 Cor 3:14); the word does not by itself imply earning salvation.
study.caution: How NT talk of 'reward' relates to salvation by grace, and whether it implies different degrees of reward, is debated among interpreters.

study.summary: A calling alongside: an earnest appeal, exhortation that urges people on, encouragement that strengthens, and comfort in sorrow, including Israel's longed-for messianic 'consolation'.

senses.label: Appeal, earnest request
senses.definition: An urgent plea or request made to someone.

senses.label: Exhortation, urging address
senses.definition: Speech that urges hearers to act, especially preaching that applies Scripture.
senses.note: 'Word of exhortation' (Acts 13:15; Heb 13:22) seems to describe a sermon.

senses.label: Encouragement, heartening
senses.definition: That which strengthens and cheers others in faith and hope.

senses.label: Comfort in affliction
senses.definition: Consolation given in suffering, above all by God, which the comforted then pass on.
senses.note: Also ironically: the rich have already received their 'comfort' (Luke 6:24).

senses.label: Messianic consolation of Israel
senses.definition: The comfort God promised to bring his people through the coming of the Messiah.
senses.note: Echoes Isaiah's 'Comfort, comfort my people' (Isa 40:1).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul accounts for two thirds of the uses. In 2 Corinthians the word clusters (2 Cor 1:3–7) around God, 'the God of all comfort', who comforts in suffering so that believers can comfort others.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke ties the word to the messianic hope ('the consolation of Israel'), to the Spirit's work in the growing church, and to Barnabas, 'son of encouragement'.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews calls itself a 'word of exhortation' and speaks of the strong encouragement given by God's oath.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'comfort', 'consolation', 'encouragement', 'exhortation' and 'appeal' because the Greek covers all of these: it is a word for coming alongside someone with speech, whether to plead, urge, hearten or console. The context decides, and translators sometimes disagree (e.g. Rom 12:8; 1 Cor 14:3; Phil 2:1).

background.note: In classical Greek it means summoning help or an earnest appeal; Thucydides uses it of imploring.
In the Septuagint it renders Hebrew words for comfort, as in God's promise to restore comfort to his people.
A papyrus speaks of appeals made on behalf of soldiers, illustrating the sense 'appeal' (2 Cor 8:4).

study.exegesisTip: Read the context: in hardship the word usually means comfort, in teaching or preaching it means exhortation, and in requests it means appeal; the verb παρακαλέω nearby is often a clue.
study.caution: Whether 'son of encouragement' (Acts 4:36) is a true etymology of 'Barnabas' is doubted, and some take 'the comfort of the Holy Spirit' (Acts 9:31) as 'exhortation' or 'invocation' rather than comfort.

study.summary: To go past: pass by a person or place; of time, elapse; of trouble, be averted; of the world or things, pass away; figuratively, pass over (neglect); and occasionally, come up or arrive.

senses.label: Pass by, go past
senses.definition: Of people moving past someone or something, or travelling past a place.

senses.label: Elapse (of time)
senses.definition: Of time going by or being already past.

senses.label: Be averted, pass from
senses.definition: Of suffering or a destined trial passing away from someone without striking him.
senses.note: Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane that the 'cup' or 'hour' might pass.

senses.label: Pass away, come to an end
senses.definition: Of things ceasing to exist or losing validity: heaven and earth, a generation, the old order, the rich.
senses.note: Contrast: Jesus' words will 'never pass away' (Matt 24:35).

senses.label: Pass over, neglect
senses.definition: To disregard or transgress a duty or command.

senses.label: Come up, come forward
senses.definition: To come to someone; used with another verb almost as 'come and…'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke alone uses the verb for neglecting God's justice or a father's command, and for a master who 'comes and serves' his servants.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew frames Jesus' teaching with the contrast between what passes away and what endures: not one stroke of the Law, and none of Jesus' words, will pass away.

study.translationNote: The verb has several English equivalents ('pass by', 'pass away', 'neglect', 'disobey', 'come'), so readers may miss that the same word links, for example, the transience of heaven and earth with the permanence of Jesus' words. In Luke 15:29 versions vary between 'never disobeyed' and 'never transgressed' your command.

background.note: In Homer it is used of a ship going past; Demosthenes says a danger 'passed away like a cloud'.
A letter tells of many loaded boats sailing past, as in 'Jesus of Nazareth is passing by'.
Documents use the participle of time already gone by.

study.exegesisTip: Note what is passing: a person (pass by), time (elapse), a trial (be averted), the created order (pass away) or a command (neglect).
study.caution: What 'this generation will not pass away' (Matt 24:34; Mark 13:30) refers to depends on the meaning of 'generation' and of 'all these things', and is much debated.

study.summary: To think, have an opinion; more characteristically, to have a settled mindset or orientation — to set one's mind on, care about, be like-minded with others, or observe a day.

senses.label: Think, hold a view
senses.definition: To have a particular opinion or way of thinking.

senses.label: Assess oneself
senses.definition: To think about oneself in a certain way, rightly or arrogantly.
senses.note: Wordplay in Rom 12:3: not to 'over-think' but to think soberly.

senses.label: Be of one mind
senses.definition: To share the same outlook and purpose with others, especially in τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν.

senses.label: Set one's mind on
senses.definition: To be oriented toward, preoccupied with or devoted to something; a direction of life, not just an idea.
senses.note: Paired opposites: things of God / of men; of the Spirit / of the flesh; above / on earth.

senses.label: Care for, be concerned
senses.definition: To feel and show practical concern for someone.

senses.label: Observe, regard a day
senses.definition: To treat a day as special in honour of the Lord.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Almost all uses are Paul's, ten in Philippians alone, where a shared Christ-shaped mindset is the remedy for rivalry and the mark of maturity.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Jesus rebukes Peter for having in mind 'the things of men' rather than 'the things of God' — an orientation, not a single mistaken thought (so also Matthew).

study.translationNote: Renderings range from 'think' and 'have in mind' to 'set the mind on', 'be like-minded', 'have this attitude' or 'mindset' (e.g. Phil 2:5: 'have this mind among yourselves' ESV; 'have the same mindset' NIV 2011). The verb concerns the direction of one's thinking and will, which 'think' alone can understate.

background.note: Homer praises men 'best both in battle and in counsel', using the verb for having understanding.
Moses laments that Israel did not 'have understanding' to perceive their end.
A complaint says a woman 'thought otherwise' (became disaffected) and left — the verb of a settled change of attitude.
An epitaph says of a married couple that they went to Hades 'saying the same things, thinking the same things', illustrating Phil 2:2.

study.exegesisTip: Ask what the mind is set on (its object), not only what is thought; Paul's commands with this verb aim at reshaping outlook and loyalties.
study.caution: Phil 2:5 is elliptical: it may mean 'have the attitude that was in Christ Jesus' (Christ as example) or 'have the attitude that is yours in Christ Jesus' (union with Christ); scholars are divided.

study.summary: To marry: of a man taking a wife, of a woman marrying, and of marriage in general as part of ordinary life; in Paul, marrying as a legitimate but not obligatory choice.

senses.label: Take a wife (of a man)
senses.definition: A man marries a woman, often with an object ('marry her').
senses.note: Several are in Jesus' teaching on divorce and remarriage.

senses.label: Marry (of a woman)
senses.definition: A woman marries a husband; in Koine the active form is used of women too.

senses.label: Marriage as ordinary life
senses.definition: Marrying as part of normal human life in this age, alongside eating and drinking.
senses.note: In the resurrection people 'neither marry nor are given in marriage'.

senses.label: Marrying vs remaining single
senses.definition: Whether to marry, as a choice weighed against singleness and devotion to the Lord.
senses.note: Forbidding marriage is a mark of false teaching (1 Tim 4:3).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (11×) treats marriage as good and no sin, yet commends singleness for undivided service; he advises younger widows to marry and condemns those who forbid it.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew records Jesus' rulings on remarriage after divorce and the disciples' startled reply that it may be better not to marry.

study.translationNote: Most versions simply say 'marry'. The pairing 'marrying and giving in marriage' (Matt 24:38; Luke 17:27) reflects two verbs: γαμέω for the couple marrying, and a related verb for parents giving a daughter in marriage.

background.note: From Homer on, the active is used of a man taking a wife.
One of its very rare Septuagint uses.
A man asks an oracle of Zeus-Helios-Sarapis, 'Is it granted me to marry?'
A will of 285–284 BC provides for sons who marry and are later divorced, using the verb of a man taking a wife.

study.exegesisTip: Notice who is the subject and whether the verb is active or passive (1 Cor 7:39 'to be married'); it shows how Koine had begun using the same active verb for husband and wife.
study.caution: In 1 Cor 7:36–38 it is debated whether the man is a fiancé deciding whether to marry his betrothed, or a father deciding whether to give his virgin daughter in marriage.

study.summary: Clean or pure: physically clean or unmixed, ritually clean, morally pure in heart and conscience, cleansed by Christ's word, and innocent of guilt.

senses.label: Physically clean
senses.definition: Free of dirt or stain, as washed water, cloth or vessels.

senses.label: Pure, unmixed, clear
senses.definition: Free of admixture: refined gold, clear water, bright linen.
senses.note: In Rev 19:8 the 'bright and pure' linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.

senses.label: Ritually clean
senses.definition: Acceptable under purity rules, especially of food; Jesus and Paul declare all foods clean.

senses.label: Morally pure, sincere
senses.definition: Inwardly pure and undivided in heart, conscience or religion before God.
senses.note: 'Pure heart' and 'clean conscience' are frequent pairings.

senses.label: Cleansed by Christ
senses.definition: Made clean by Christ's washing and word, so belonging to him.

senses.label: Innocent, free of guilt
senses.definition: Not responsible for another's fate; 'clean from' their blood.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John's Gospel the disciples are 'clean' through Jesus' washing and word; in Revelation the word describes the pure linen, gold and river of the new creation.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul declares all foods clean, yet stresses inward purity: a pure heart and a clean conscience are the source of love and faith.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses καθαρὸς ἀπό ('clean from') for Paul's innocence of his hearers' blood, in the language of Ezekiel's watchman.

study.translationNote: Versions alternate between 'clean' and 'pure' (and 'innocent' in Acts 18:6; 20:26). 'Clean' suits ritual and washing contexts, 'pure' moral and material ones, but it is the same word. In John 15:2–3 'clean' also plays on the related verb for pruning a vine.

background.note: In Homer it describes clean clothes; Herodotus uses it of clear river water.
The Septuagint speaks of 'pure living water' used in a ritual of the Law.
Contracts use 'clean from' for property free of public dues, showing the construction is ordinary Greek, not a Hebraism.
A temple inscription requires worshippers to have 'hands and mind pure and healthy', then lists outward purity rules — compare Matt 23:26.

study.exegesisTip: Identify the kind of purity in view — physical, ritual, moral or relational — since NT writers deliberately move from outward to inward cleanness (Matt 23:26; Titus 1:15).

study.summary: Judgment: a decision or verdict, especially God's; very often an adverse verdict, condemnation or punishment; also the right to judge and a legal case.

senses.label: Judgment passed by people
senses.definition: The decision or standard by which people judge others, or a legal sentence.
senses.note: 'Sentence of death' (Luke 24:20).

senses.label: God's judgment, decisions
senses.definition: God's act or decisions as judge, including his inscrutable ways and the coming final judgment.
senses.note: Also judgment beginning 'with the household of God' (1 Pet 4:17).

senses.label: Condemnation, penalty
senses.definition: An adverse verdict and the punishment it brings.
senses.note: Often with 'receive', 'bear' or 'have' (Gal 5:10; 1 Tim 5:12).

senses.label: Authority to judge
senses.definition: The right or power of passing judgment, given to the saints.

senses.label: Lawsuit, legal case
senses.definition: A matter brought before a court.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul warns that careless eating of the Lord's Supper brings judgment, that resisting authorities incurs it, and that God's judgments are unsearchable.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Jesus says he came 'for judgment', a judgment that reverses who sees and who is blind.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: Teachers will receive a stricter judgment.

study.translationNote: Versions differ between 'judgment' and 'condemnation' (and KJV 'damnation', e.g. 1 Cor 11:29; Rom 13:2). The word means a verdict, but in context the verdict is often negative; 'damnation' overstates, while 'judgment' can sound neutral.

background.note: A later word (Hellenistic) for a decision or judgment, used by Polybius.
In the Septuagint it renders Hebrew mishpat, God's 'judgments' or ordinances, especially in Psalm 119.
Papyri use it for official legal decisions on taxes.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the context makes the verdict neutral (a decision), positive, or adverse; the word does not by itself mean eternal damnation.
study.caution: Whether the 'judgment' of 1 Cor 11:29 is temporal discipline (illness and death, vv. 30–32) or final condemnation is debated, as is how far the warnings of Rom 13:2 apply.

study.summary: The basic Greek connective: 'and' joining words and clauses, but also 'and so', 'and yet', 'namely', 'both…and', and adverbially 'also, even'. Context decides which.

senses.label: And: joining words
senses.definition: Links nouns, names or phrases of equal standing; repeated, καὶ… καί means 'both… and'.
senses.note: Repeated καί in a list (Rom 7:12, 'holy and righteous and good') gives each item weight.

senses.label: And: linking clauses, narrative
senses.definition: Joins sentences in a simple chain, often opening a new sentence in narrative ('and', 'then').
senses.note: Includes the Hebrew-flavoured transition καὶ ἐγένετο, 'and it came to pass' (MAR 1:9).

senses.label: And so: result
senses.definition: Introduces what follows as a consequence, especially after a command: 'and so', 'and then'.
senses.note: 'Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men' (MAT 4:19).

senses.label: And yet: contrast
senses.definition: Joins two statements that stand in tension, where English needs 'and yet' or 'but'.
senses.note: 'The world was made through him, and [yet] the world did not know him' (JOH 1:10).

senses.label: That is: explanatory
senses.definition: Adds a phrase that explains or specifies what precedes: 'and indeed', 'namely'.
senses.note: 'The hope and resurrection' (ACT 23:6) = the hope, namely the resurrection.

senses.label: Also, even (adverb)
senses.definition: Not a connective but an adverb adding emphasis or inclusion: 'also', 'even', 'too'.
senses.note: ὁ καί with a name means 'who is also called' (ACT 13:9, 'Saul, also called Paul').

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark strings episodes together with sentence-opening Καί, giving his narrative its brisk, oral feel.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John favours short clauses chained by καί, sometimes carrying contrast ('and yet') rather than simple addition.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke imitates Septuagint narrative style with καὶ ἐγένετο and with καί opening the main clause after a time clause ('then').

study.translationNote: Because καί is so frequent, modern versions (NIV, MSB) often drop sentence-opening 'and' (e.g. MAR 1:5) or render it 'then', 'so', 'but' or 'even', while the KJV keeps 'and' throughout. The adverbial 'also/even' and the explanatory 'namely' are easily missed if every καί is read as 'and'.

background.note: From Homer on, καί both joins words and sentences ('and') and works as an adverb ('even, also').
A dream account from the Serapeum chains short clauses with καί just as John and Mark do, showing that such parataxis was ordinary popular Greek, though Septuagint usage also shaped it.
The pleonastic 'with also' (μετὰ καί) of Phil 4:3 has a parallel in a fourth-century papyrus.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether καί simply adds ('and'), draws a result ('and so'), sets up tension ('and yet'), explains ('namely') or emphasizes ('even, also').
study.caution: Whether καί is additive or explanatory is debated in key verses: GAL 6:16 ('and upon the Israel of God' or 'even the Israel of God') and TIT 2:13 ('our great God and Savior' as one person or two).

study.summary: Intensive 'self' (he himself), emphatic 'he', the ordinary third-person pronoun 'him, her, it, them' in oblique cases, and with the article 'the same'.

senses.label: Self, himself (intensive)
senses.definition: Emphasizes a person or thing as distinct from others: 'he himself', 'I myself', 'the very'.
senses.note: αὐτὸς ὁ… with a noun = 'the … himself' (1TH 3:11, 'God himself').

senses.label: He (emphatic subject)
senses.definition: In the nominative, where Greek needs no subject pronoun, αὐτός stresses the person: 'he and no other'.
senses.note: 'He will save his people' (MAT 1:21): he, Jesus, not another.

senses.label: Him, her, it, them
senses.definition: In oblique cases the ordinary unemphatic third-person pronoun; the genitive serves as possessive 'his, her, its, their'.
senses.note: English capitals ('Him', 'His') for God or Christ are translators' interpretation, not in the Greek.

senses.label: Resumptive after relative
senses.definition: Repeats a pronoun already implied by a relative clause ('whose daughter of her'), a Semitic-style redundancy left untranslated.
senses.note: Mirrors Hebrew 'ăšer… lô; common in Revelation.

senses.label: The same
senses.definition: With the article (ὁ αὐτός, τὸ αὐτό) it means 'the same', as in 'to think the same thing'.

senses.label: Together (ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό)
senses.definition: The phrase ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό means 'together, in the same place', and by extension 'in all'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke often uses καὶ αὐτός as a weak narrative 'and he', and αὐτῇ τῇ ὥρᾳ for 'that very hour', blurring the classical difference between αὐτός ὁ and ὁ αὐτός.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses αὐτὸ τοῦτο 'this very thing' and calls for believers to 'think the same thing' (τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν).

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews applies ὁ αὐτός to the Son's changelessness: 'you are the same'; 'Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever'.

study.translationNote: English cannot show when αὐτός is emphatic, so 'he' may stand for a stressed 'he himself' or a plain pronoun; versions differ in how often they add 'himself'. Capitalized 'He/Him' (MSB, NASB) reflects a decision about the referent, which can be debated in some verses.

background.note: In Homer αὐτός can mark a person's true self, even the soul as opposed to the body.
In official documents αὐτός often means little more than 'the said' person, close to ἐκεῖνος.
ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό is used arithmetically for a total ('in all'), which may illuminate Acts 2:47.
A marriage contract uses κατὰ ταὐτό for living together, illustrating 'together' in Acts 14:1.

study.exegesisTip: A nominative αὐτός is usually deliberate, since Greek verbs already contain their subject; ask what contrast or emphasis it creates.
study.caution: Whether ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό in ACT 2:47 means 'together' (of the gathered church) or 'in all, to the total' is debated, as is how far αὐτός has lost its emphasis in Luke's narrative.

study.summary: Second-person pronoun 'you': singular σύ (thou) and plural ὑμεῖς (you all), with genitive 'your'. The nominative is often emphatic or contrastive.

senses.label: You (singular)
senses.definition: Addresses one person: 'you, thee' (σύ, σοῦ, σοί, σέ).

senses.label: You (plural)
senses.definition: Addresses a group: 'you all' (ὑμεῖς, ὑμῶν, ὑμῖν, ὑμᾶς), the normal form in letters to churches.
senses.note: The plural in 1CO 3:16 makes the congregation God's temple; in LUK 22:31–32 Satan sifts 'you' (plural) but Jesus prays for 'you' (singular), Peter.

senses.label: Emphatic 'you'
senses.definition: The nominative, not needed by the verb, stresses or contrasts the person addressed: 'you yourself', 'but you'.
senses.note: Also before a vocative in solemn address (MAT 2:6; LUK 1:76). Not every nominative is emphatic: 'You are my Son' (HEB 1:5) follows Hebrew idiom.

senses.label: Your (possessive)
senses.definition: The genitive marks possession or relation: 'your'; placed before its noun it can be emphatic.

senses.label: Idiomatic expressions
senses.definition: Set phrases such as σὺ εἶπας 'you have said it' and τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί 'what have I to do with you?'

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's dialogues are full of contrastive pronouns ('Who are you?', 'You testify about yourself'), sharpening the clash between Jesus and his hearers.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In Romans Paul switches to the singular σύ to address an imagined dialogue partner in diatribe style ('who are you to judge?').

study.translationNote: The KJV's 'thou/thee' versus 'ye/you' preserved the singular–plural difference that modern English 'you' hides, so readers may miss that much of Paul is addressed to the whole church. σὺ εἶπας is rendered variously: 'You have said so' (ESV), 'You have said it', or 'Yes, it is as you say' (NIV).

background.note: The Septuagint renders Hebrew 'attâ; 'You are my Son' (Ps 2:7) keeps a Hebrew pronoun pattern quoted in Acts and Hebrews.
Vernacular letters show irregular forms such as ἐσοῦ for σοῦ ('all those with you').
The personal pronoun can stand for the reflexive ('with you yourself').

study.exegesisTip: Check whether 'you' is singular or plural: many promises and commands in the letters are addressed to the community as a whole.
study.caution: Whether σὺ εἶπας (MAT 26:64) is a clear 'yes' or a reserved, qualified affirmation ('the word is yours') is debated.

study.summary: A postpositive connective marking a new step: mild contrast ('but'), continuation ('and, then'), transition or background ('now'), and emphatic addition ('even'). Often left untranslated.

senses.label: But: contrast
senses.definition: Sets a statement against what precedes, often answering μέν: 'but', 'on the other hand'.
senses.note: μὲν… δέ = 'on the one hand… on the other'.

senses.label: And, then: continuation
senses.definition: Moves to the next item or event with little or no contrast: 'and', 'then'.
senses.note: In Matthew's genealogy each new link begins with δέ.

senses.label: Now: new section or topic
senses.definition: Signals a transition to a new episode or subject: 'now'.

senses.label: Now: background, explanation
senses.definition: Introduces a parenthesis or explanatory aside: 'now (it was the Sabbath)', 'what I mean is'.

senses.label: Change of speaker or subject
senses.definition: With the article or a pronoun (ὁ δέ, ὑμεῖς δέ) it marks a switch of actor: 'and he', 'but you'.

senses.label: Even, indeed: emphatic addition
senses.definition: Picks up a word to intensify it, or with καί means 'and also': 'even', 'indeed'.
senses.note: 'Obedient to death, even death on a cross' (PHP 2:8).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses δέ far more than καί to move the story on, including the formula ἐγένετο δέ.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In 1 Corinthians περὶ δέ ('now concerning') introduces each topic raised in the church's letter.

study.translationNote: Versions render δέ as 'but', 'and', 'now', 'then' or leave it out, and the KJV's frequent 'but' can create contrasts the Greek does not intend. Its force is usually weaker than ἀλλά.

background.note: In classical prose δέ classically answers a preceding μέν, balancing two clauses ('once called…, but now…').

study.exegesisTip: Before reading δέ as 'but', ask whether there is a real contrast or simply a new step, speaker or explanation.

study.summary: Preposition with the accusative: motion 'into, to', and by extension goal, purpose, result, relation ('toward, against'), time ('until, for'), and in Koine sometimes simple location ('in').

senses.label: Into, to: motion
senses.definition: Movement into or toward a place: 'into', 'to', 'among'.

senses.label: In, at: location
senses.definition: In Koine εἰς can overlap with ἐν and mark position without motion: 'in', 'at'.
senses.note: Sometimes 'pregnant', implying a prior movement ('went and settled in').

senses.label: Until, for: time
senses.definition: Extends to a point or through a period: 'until (the day)', 'for ever'.
senses.note: εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας = 'for ever'.

senses.label: Into: change, result
senses.definition: After verbs of turning or becoming, marks what something becomes: 'into', 'so as to be'.
senses.note: 'The two shall become one flesh' (εἰς σάρκα μίαν, MAT 19:5).

senses.label: For, in order to: purpose
senses.definition: Marks goal or purpose; εἰς τό with infinitive = 'so that, in order to'.

senses.label: Toward, against: relation
senses.definition: Direction of an attitude or act toward someone, friendly or hostile: 'toward', 'for', 'against'.

senses.label: Into: faith and union
senses.definition: Believing or being baptized 'into' someone expresses trust in, allegiance to, or union with that person.
senses.note: 'Baptized into Moses' (1CO 10:2) shows the sense of belonging to a leader.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's characteristic πιστεύειν εἰς ('believe into') presents faith as personal commitment to Jesus.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul often uses εἰς τό with an infinitive to state the purpose or result of God's action.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses εἰς τὸ διηνεκές ('for all time') for the permanence of Christ's priesthood and sacrifice.

study.translationNote: Because εἰς covers motion, purpose, result and relation, versions differ: εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν (ACT 2:38) is 'for the forgiveness' (most) or 'so that your sins may be forgiven'; baptism εἰς τὸ ὄνομα (MAT 28:19) is 'in the name' in most versions but literally 'into the name'.

background.note: The older form ἐς was usual in Ionic and Thucydides; εἰς became standard in Attic inscriptions from the fourth century BC.
Papyri use εἰς with verbs of rest ('I shall stay at the inn'), matching NT cases where εἰς = ἐν.
A letter from Alexandria uses ἐν and εἰς Ἀλεξάνδρειαν side by side for the same location.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether εἰς marks place, goal, result or relationship; 'into' can express purpose as readily as motion.
study.caution: In ACT 2:38 most scholars read εἰς as purpose ('for, with a view to forgiveness'); a causal sense ('because of') has been argued but is not well supported. In JOH 1:18 it is debated whether εἰς τὸν κόλπον is static ('in the bosom') or dynamic ('toward').

study.summary: The negative of fact, 'not, no', used mainly with the indicative; in questions it expects 'yes'; with μή (οὐ μή) it is the strongest denial, 'never'.

senses.label: Not: denial of fact
senses.definition: Negates a statement as a matter of fact, usually with an indicative verb.
senses.note: πᾶς… οὐ = 'no one, nothing' (LUK 1:37; EPH 5:5).

senses.label: Not… but: antithesis
senses.definition: οὐκ… ἀλλά denies one thing in order to assert another: 'not this, but that'.

senses.label: Question expecting 'yes'
senses.definition: Introducing a question, οὐ anticipates agreement: 'Do you not…?', 'Surely…'.

senses.label: No! (standalone answer)
senses.definition: Used alone as a flat refusal or denial: 'No'.
senses.note: 'Let your yes be yes and your no, no' (JAM 5:12).

senses.label: Shall not: solemn prohibition
senses.definition: With a future verb it forms a categorical command, following the Hebrew style of the Law: 'You shall not'.

senses.label: Never: οὐ μή
senses.definition: Combined with μή and an aorist subjunctive or future, the most emphatic negation: 'never, by no means'.

senses.label: Not a little: understatement
senses.definition: Negating an opposite to affirm strongly (litotes): 'no small' = 'great'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts is fond of litotes such as οὐκ ὀλίγος ('no small'), a cultivated Greek touch.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's Gospel concentrates Jesus' οὐ μή promises: the believer will never hunger, never be cast out, never die.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul repeatedly frames his gospel with οὐ… ἀλλά antitheses.

study.translationNote: Questions with οὐ expect 'yes', so versions often turn them into statements ('Surely…', 'You know that…'). οὐ μή is rendered 'never', 'certainly not' or 'by no means', and some versions flatten it to a simple 'not'.

background.note: Papyri use οὐ with participles stating facts ('being unable through sickness'), not only with the indicative.
The formula 'we determined not to record' supports reading 1 Cor 2:2 as 'I resolved to know nothing'.
οὐ μή is rare in the papyri, but a petulant boy's letter uses it: 'I won't eat, I won't drink'.

study.exegesisTip: Note which negative is used: οὐ denies facts and in questions expects 'yes'; μή negates wishes, commands and hypotheses and expects 'no'.
study.caution: In 1CO 2:2 (οὐ γὰρ ἔκρινά τι εἰδέναι) the negative grammatically goes with 'decided', and some read 'I did not decide to know anything'; most take it as 'I resolved to know nothing'.

study.summary: The near demonstrative 'this, these': pointing to what is present or just mentioned, or ahead to what follows; as a pronoun 'this one, he', sometimes contemptuous ('this fellow').

senses.label: This (near, present)
senses.definition: Points to a person or thing at hand: 'this, these'.
senses.note: 'These hands' (ACT 20:34), with a gesture.

senses.label: This one, he (pronoun)
senses.definition: Used alone for a person: 'this man', 'he', often in identifications.
senses.note: 'This is my beloved Son' (MAT 3:17).

senses.label: This fellow (contempt)
senses.definition: Pointing at someone with scorn or dismissal.
senses.note: 'This son of yours' (LUK 15:30) distances the speaker.

senses.label: Referring back
senses.definition: Resumes a person or thing just described: 'he (is the one)', 'these things'.

senses.label: Pointing forward
senses.definition: Anticipates a following ὅτι, ἵνα or ἐάν clause: 'this: that…'.

senses.label: Idiomatic phrases
senses.definition: διὰ τοῦτο 'therefore', μετὰ ταῦτα 'after this', ἐκ τούτου 'from then on / for this reason', καὶ τοῦτο 'and that too'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John repeatedly uses forward-pointing ἐν τούτῳ and αὕτη ἐστίν… ἵνα/ὅτι to define life, love and knowledge, and μετὰ ταῦτα to open new episodes.

study.translationNote: Contemptuous οὗτος is often rendered neutrally ('this man'), whereas the KJV's 'this fellow' (MAT 12:24) catches the tone. In 1 John, versions differ over whether ἐν τούτῳ ('by this') points back or forward.

background.note: ἐκ τούτου 'for this reason' appears in a son's letter to his father, as in John 6:66.
A literary parallel shows ταῦτα with a gesture of both hands, as Paul's 'these hands' in Acts 20:34.
An abrupt ταῦτα ('there now!', 'that's that') closes a boy's threat in a letter.

study.exegesisTip: Locate what οὗτος points to: backward to what was said, forward to a following clause, or to a person present, perhaps with scorn.
study.caution: In EPH 2:8 the neuter τοῦτο ('and this is not your own doing') does not match feminine 'faith' or 'grace'; whether it refers to faith, grace, or the whole of salvation is debated.

study.summary: Postpositive particle giving the reason or explanation for what precedes ('for, because'), adding background, advancing an argument, and in questions or exclamations 'why, what!'.

senses.label: For, because: reason
senses.definition: Supplies the cause or ground of a preceding statement or command.
senses.note: Often grounds a command: 'for those who sought the child's life are dead' (MAT 2:20; also COL 3:3).

senses.label: Explanatory aside
senses.definition: Introduces background information needed to understand the narrative: 'for, you see'.
senses.note: 'For they were fishermen' (MAR 1:16).

senses.label: Developing an argument
senses.definition: Introduces an elaboration, proof or illustration that unpacks a previous claim.

senses.label: Why, what!: in questions
senses.definition: In questions, answers and exclamations it adds liveliness: 'why', 'what then', 'indeed'.
senses.note: 'Why, what evil has he done?' (MAT 27:23).

senses.label: For indeed (καὶ γάρ)
senses.definition: καὶ γάρ means 'for also, for even' or simply 'for indeed'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Nearly half of all NT uses are Paul's: chains of γάρ clauses (e.g. Rom 1:16–18) carry the logic of his arguments.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark uses γάρ for explanatory asides to his readers, and his Gospel's best-attested ending closes on ἐφοβοῦντο γάρ ('for they were afraid').

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews builds its case from Scripture with γάρ, introducing quotations and proofs.

study.translationNote: The KJV, ESV and NASB usually keep 'for', while freer versions (NIV, MSB) often omit γάρ or use 'because', which can hide how a sentence supports the one before it (e.g. GAL 5:14, LUK 9:26).

background.note: From Homer on, γάρ gives the reason or explains what is implied in the preceding clause.
A third-century BC letter shows ascensive καὶ γάρ ('for in addition'), as in Rom 11:1.
Papyri also show γάρ ending a clause, as in Mark 16:8.

study.exegesisTip: Trace each γάρ back to the statement it supports; this reveals the structure of an argument, especially in Paul and Hebrews.
study.caution: Whether Mark deliberately ended his Gospel at 16:8 with ἐφοβοῦντο γάρ is debated; that a sentence (and a book) can end in γάρ is grammatically possible, but some think the original ending was lost.

study.summary: The negative of will and thought: 'not' with commands, wishes, purposes, conditions, infinitives and participles; as a conjunction 'lest'; in questions it expects 'no'.

senses.label: Do not: prohibition
senses.definition: Forbids an action, with imperative or aorist subjunctive: 'do not'.

senses.label: Not: conditions, infinitives, participles
senses.definition: Negates hypothetical or non-factual ideas: after 'if', with infinitives, and with participles describing a type of person.
senses.note: ὁ μὴ πιστεύων = 'whoever does not believe' (JOH 3:18).

senses.label: Lest: purpose and fear
senses.definition: With ἵνα or alone, 'so that not'; after verbs of fearing or watching, 'lest, that… not'.
senses.note: 'See that no one deceives you' (MAT 24:4).

senses.label: Question expecting 'no'
senses.definition: Introduces a question anticipating a negative answer: 'Surely not…?', '… is he?'.

senses.label: May it not be: wishes
senses.definition: With the optative it negates a wish, above all μὴ γένοιτο, 'may it never be!'.

senses.label: Never: οὐ μή
senses.definition: After οὐ it forms the emphatic denial 'certainly not, never'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul answers false inferences from his gospel with μὴ γένοιτο, 'by no means!'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses μή-questions ironically: speakers expect 'no' where the reader knows the answer is 'yes'.

study.translationNote: μὴ γένοιτο is 'God forbid' (KJV), 'By no means' (ESV, NIV) or 'May it never be' (NASB). Questions with μή are often rendered 'You are not…, are you?' to show the expected 'no'.

background.note: From Homer on μή is the negative of will and command: 'do not provoke me'.
Letters use μή with the aorist subjunctive for future prohibitions: 'Do not forget me'.
μή with the present imperative can bid someone stop what they are doing: 'do not molest him'.

study.exegesisTip: When a question opens with μή, the speaker expects 'no' (JOH 4:12, 'You are not greater than our father Jacob, are you?').
study.caution: The rule that μή with a present imperative means 'stop doing' and with an aorist subjunctive 'do not start' is a tendency, not a law; context must decide.

study.summary: Preposition, nearly always with the accusative: motion or speech 'to, toward'; presence 'with'; attitude 'toward, against'; purpose 'for'; reference or comparison 'with regard to'; time 'for a while'.

senses.label: To, toward: motion and speech
senses.definition: Movement toward a person or place, or words addressed to someone: 'to'.

senses.label: With, at: presence
senses.definition: Being in someone's company or near something: 'with', 'at', 'by'.
senses.note: With the dative, 'near, at' (MAR 5:11).

senses.label: Toward, against: relationship
senses.definition: Attitude or dealings with someone, friendly or hostile: 'toward', 'with', 'against'.

senses.label: For, in order to: purpose
senses.definition: Goal or purpose; πρὸς τό with infinitive = 'in order to'.
senses.note: The one NT genitive use means 'for (your survival)' (ACT 27:34).

senses.label: Regarding, according to, compared with
senses.definition: Reference or standard: 'with regard to', 'in accordance with', 'in comparison with'.
senses.note: 'Not worth comparing with the glory' (ROM 8:18).

senses.label: For a while: time
senses.definition: Duration, usually limited: 'for a time', 'for an hour'; or 'toward (evening)'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke (about 300 uses) habitually writes 'said to' with πρός rather than a simple dative.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses πρός for the Word's and the life's being 'with God/the Father', and for Christ as advocate 'with the Father'.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark uses πρός for being 'with' people ('are not his sisters here with us?').

study.translationNote: In JOH 1:1 nearly all versions read 'with God'; some commentators and paraphrases press 'toward God' or 'face to face with God' to bring out relationship. Elsewhere πρός may be rendered 'to', 'with', 'for', 'against' or 'compared with' depending on context.

background.note: Classical πρός takes genitive, dative and accusative; Homer uses the genitive only rarely, and the NT almost only the accusative.
πρὸς ὀλίγον 'for a short time' is attested in a papyrus, as in James 4:14.
πρός of accountability toward someone ('the account will be to you') parallels Heb 4:13.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether πρός expresses movement, presence, attitude, purpose or comparison; in ROM 8:18 it means 'compared with'.
study.caution: Whether πρὸς τὸν θεόν in JOH 1:1 implies an active, face-to-face relationship or simply means 'with' (possibly reflecting Aramaic idiom) is debated.

study.summary: Preposition 'through': with the genitive, passage through space or time and the agent or means by which something happens; with the accusative, the reason or purpose — 'because of, for the sake of'.

senses.label: Through (place or medium)
senses.definition: With the genitive, motion through a place or medium from one side to the other; figuratively, the state or circumstance through which one passes.
senses.note: Figuratively of attendant circumstance: 'we walk by faith, not by sight' (2CO 5:7).

senses.label: Through, during (time)
senses.definition: With the genitive, throughout a period, within a span of time, or after an interval has passed.
senses.note: διὰ παντός means 'continually, always' (HEB 13:15); διὰ νυκτός 'by night' (ACT 5:19).

senses.label: Agent or intermediary
senses.definition: With the genitive of a person, the one through whom an action is carried out, often distinguished from the ultimate source (ὑπό or ἐκ).
senses.note: 'Spoken by (ὑπό) the Lord through (διά) the prophet' (MAT 1:22): God speaks, the prophet mediates.

senses.label: Means or instrument
senses.definition: With the genitive of a thing, the means, channel or instrument by which something is accomplished.

senses.label: Because of (reason)
senses.definition: With the accusative, the cause or ground of an action: 'because of, on account of'.
senses.note: διὰ τοῦτο 'for this reason, therefore' (REV 18:8); διὰ τό with an infinitive gives a reason (JAM 4:2).

senses.label: For the sake of
senses.definition: With the accusative, the person or goal for whose benefit something exists or is done.
senses.note: 'The Sabbath was made for man' (MAR 2:27).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul repeatedly speaks of God acting 'through Christ' — the mediator of peace, reconciliation and creation — while all things are 'from' and 'to' God.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews presents the Son as the one through whom the ages were made, and stresses that he entered the sanctuary 'through his own blood' and opened a way 'through the veil'.

study.translationNote: English 'through', 'by' and 'because of' overlap, so versions vary: 1 Thess 4:2 is 'through the Lord Jesus' (ESV) or 'by the authority of the Lord Jesus' (NIV); in Rom 4:25 'raised for our justification' or 'because of our justification' reflects different readings of διά with the accusative.

background.note: In Homer the root sense is 'right through', often of a spear passing through shield and breastplate.
Commercial documents constantly use διὰ χειρός of money paid 'by hand', directly — the vernacular phrase behind biblical 'by the hand of'.
διὰ νυκτός means 'by night', under cover of darkness, as of a man breaking into a farmstead.
διὰ παντός 'always' is common in letters, replacing the obsolescent ἀεί.

study.exegesisTip: Check the case: genitive διά gives the route, agent or means ('through'), accusative διά gives the reason or purpose ('because of, for the sake of').
study.caution: In Rom 4:25 ('handed over because of our trespasses and raised because of/for our justification') interpreters debate whether the second διά is retrospective (because justification was secured) or prospective (in order to bring about justification).

study.summary: Preposition with the genitive meaning 'from': separation or motion away, deliverance from danger or sin, the starting point in place or time, origin and source, and in Koine also cause.

senses.label: Away from (separation)
senses.definition: Motion away from a place or person, removal, or distance from something.
senses.note: Also partitive, 'some of': 'kept back part of the price' (ACT 5:2).

senses.label: Rescue or cleansing from
senses.definition: After verbs of saving, fleeing, cleansing or cutting off: freed or separated from sin, danger or wrath.

senses.label: Since, from (time)
senses.definition: The point in time from which something begins or continues: 'from, since'.
senses.note: ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν 'from now on' (LUK 1:48); ἀπὸ τότε 'from then on' (MAT 4:17).

senses.label: Origin; starting point of range
senses.definition: Place of origin or home town, and the first term of a series or range ('from… to').
senses.note: 'Jesus from Nazareth' identifies his home town (MAT 21:11).

senses.label: Source or giver
senses.definition: The person from whom something is received, learned or sent.

senses.label: Cause; on one's own
senses.definition: The cause or means of something ('because of, by'); with a reflexive, acting 'from oneself', on one's own initiative or authority.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John repeatedly says the Son does and speaks nothing 'from himself' (ἀπ᾽ ἐμαυτοῦ), stressing his dependence on and unity with the Father; the Spirit too will not speak 'from himself'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's greeting names 'God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ' together after a single ἀπό, as one source of grace and peace.

background.note: The partitive use ('some of') is well attested in papyri, as in a will freeing certain of one's slaves.
A letter warns 'beware of the Jews' with βλέπε… ἀπό, showing that the NT 'beware of' idiom (Mark 8:15) is ordinary vernacular, not only Semitic.
Titles with ἀπό meant 'ex-' (a former official), and ἀπό alone could mean 'free from', as 'blameless'.
The Hebraic phrase ἀπὸ προσώπου ('from the face of') reflects Hebrew mippĕnê.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether ἀπό marks separation, origin, time or cause; in Koine it overlaps with ἐκ ('out of') and ὑπό ('by'), so the verb and context decide.
study.caution: In 2 Thess 1:9 ('destruction away from the presence of the Lord'), scholars debate whether ἀπό means separation from his presence or punishment that comes from his presence.

study.summary: Adversative conjunction 'but', stronger than δέ: it replaces a preceding negative ('not this but that'), marks contrast, objection or transition, introduces commands, and after a condition means 'yet, at least'.

senses.label: Not this, but that
senses.definition: After a negative, introduces the correct alternative that replaces what was denied.
senses.note: οὐ μόνον… ἀλλὰ καί 'not only… but also' (EPH 1:21).

senses.label: Not so much… as
senses.definition: A rhetorical antithesis in which the first member is not wholly denied but subordinated to the second.

senses.label: Except, only
senses.definition: Equivalent to εἰ μή after a negative, 'except, but only'; ἀλλ᾽ ἤ 'save, except'.

senses.label: Contrast, objection, transition
senses.definition: Without a preceding negative, marks a contrast, an objection, a turn in the argument, or introduces a command or request.
senses.note: Before commands: 'but get up and go' (ACT 10:20).

senses.label: Yet, at least
senses.definition: In the main clause after a condition or concession: 'yet, still, at least'.

senses.label: Indeed, yes even
senses.definition: Adds an emphatic, heightening statement.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (about half of all uses) builds his argument on sharp 'not… but' antitheses that set the gospel against human alternatives.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John often uses an elliptical ἀλλ᾽ ἵνα ('but this happened so that…') to state the divine purpose behind an event.

study.translationNote: Usually 'but'; where the second clause replaces the first, versions use 'instead', 'rather' or 'only'. In idioms such as Mark 9:37 ('not me but the one who sent me') the Greek can mean 'not so much me as…', which a bare 'but' may obscure.

background.note: Classical Greek uses ἀλλά in simple corrections after a negative: 'not bad, but good'.
ἀλλ᾽ ἤ means 'except': 'there is no one left here except ourselves' — the idiom of 2 Cor 1:13.
ἀλλά alone can mean 'except': a marriage contract forbids taking 'any other wife but Apollonia'.

study.exegesisTip: When ἀλλά follows a negative, read both halves together: the author is replacing one idea with another, and the weight falls on what follows ἀλλά.
study.caution: Whether a 'not… but' antithesis is absolute or relative ('not so much… as') is sometimes debated, e.g. 1 Cor 1:17 ('Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel').

study.summary: Interrogative pronoun 'who? what? which?', in direct and indirect questions; the neuter τί also means 'why?', and rhetorical questions with τίς often amount to a strong denial.

senses.label: Who?
senses.definition: Asks the identity of a person, in direct or indirect questions.

senses.label: What? which?
senses.definition: Asks about a thing, its nature or kind; as an adjective, 'what…?'; sometimes 'which of the two?'.
senses.note: Standing for 'which of two' (MAT 27:17; LUK 22:27).

senses.label: Why?
senses.definition: The neuter τί, alone or in διὰ τί, ἵνα τί, asks the reason for something.
senses.note: κατὰ τί 'by what?, how?' (LUK 1:18).

senses.label: Rhetorical question, implying denial
senses.definition: A question expecting the answer 'no one' or 'nothing', functioning as an emphatic negation.
senses.note: τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί, 'what do you and I have in common?', politely or sharply distances the speaker (MAR 1:24; JOH 2:4).

senses.label: Whatever, what (relative)
senses.definition: In Koine τίς sometimes stands for a relative pronoun: 'what, that which'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's diatribe style uses τί οὖν; ('What then?') and chains of rhetorical 'who…?' questions to press his argument.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke often opens Jesus' parables with 'Which of you…?' (τίς ἐξ ὑμῶν), inviting hearers to judge from ordinary life.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark's Gospel turns on the question of Jesus' identity: 'Who then is this?' and 'Who do people say that I am?'.

study.translationNote: The idiom τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί (John 2:4) is rendered 'What have I to do with thee?' (KJV), 'What does this have to do with me?' (ESV) or 'Why do you involve me?' (NIV): it is a Semitic expression of distance whose tone is debated.

background.note: In exclamations τί renders Hebrew mah, 'how!': 'Lord, how many are my foes!'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the question is real or rhetorical: many τίς-questions in Paul and Hebrews ('Who will separate us…?') are emphatic denials.
study.caution: In Luke 12:49 τί θέλω εἰ ἤδη ἀνήφθη may be an exclamation ('how I wish it were already kindled!') or a question ('what do I want, if it is already kindled?'); interpreters differ.

study.summary: Enclitic indefinite pronoun 'someone, anyone, something'; as adjective 'a certain, some'. It introduces unnamed persons, frames general conditions ('if anyone…'), and in 'to be something' means 'somebody important'.

senses.label: A certain (person)
senses.definition: Introduces an individual not yet named or not important to name: 'a certain man, a priest'.

senses.label: Some, certain people
senses.definition: In the plural, an unspecified group, often left deliberately vague.
senses.note: Frequently a veiled reference to opponents (GAL 1:7; JUD 1:4).

senses.label: Anyone, anything
senses.definition: Indefinite and general, especially in conditions 'if anyone, whoever'.

senses.label: No one, nothing (negated)
senses.definition: With a negative or in warnings with μή: 'no one, nothing, lest anyone'.

senses.label: Somebody, something significant
senses.definition: εἶναί τι / τινα: to be someone of importance, or something real.

senses.label: A kind of; about
senses.definition: Softens or approximates a word: 'a sort of', 'some'; with numerals 'about, some'.
senses.note: 'A kind of firstfruits' (JAM 1:18).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul frames general principles with εἴ τις ('if anyone') and refers to opponents as unnamed 'some' (τινες).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke characteristically introduces new characters with τις: 'a certain man', 'a certain disciple'.

study.translationNote: Because the word is unemphatic, versions supply 'a', 'a certain', 'someone', 'anyone' or 'some', or leave it untranslated; where it points to opponents ('certain people'), the vagueness of the Greek is often deliberate.
study.exegesisTip: Notice whether τις is vague by necessity or by design: Paul's unnamed 'some' (GAL 1:7; 2CO 10:12) often points at known troublemakers he declines to name.
study.caution: Phil 2:1 εἴ τις σπλάγχνα combines a singular masculine/feminine τις with a plural neuter noun; scholars debate whether to read εἴ τι ('if there is anything') or accept a colloquial indeclinable usage.

study.summary: Postpositive particle 'therefore, then, so': it draws an inference or exhortation from what precedes, sharpens questions, and in narrative — especially John — simply marks the next step or resumes the story.

senses.label: Therefore (inference)
senses.definition: Draws a logical conclusion from what has been said.
senses.note: With a participle, 'since, then' (ROM 5:1; 2CO 7:1).

senses.label: So then (exhortation)
senses.definition: Introduces a command or appeal grounded in the preceding teaching.

senses.label: Then (in questions)
senses.definition: In questions, presses the implication of what precedes: 'What then?', 'Why then?'.

senses.label: So, then (narrative sequence)
senses.definition: Continues or resumes a narrative, marking the next event with little or no causal force.
senses.note: Also resumes a topic after a digression (1CO 8:4).

senses.label: So then (ἄρα οὖν)
senses.definition: Combined with ἄρα, a strong concluding summary: 'so then, consequently'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John (about 200 uses) employs οὖν chiefly as a narrative link — 'so, then' — moving from scene to scene rather than signalling strict logic.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul often uses οὖν at the hinge from teaching to exhortation: what God has done grounds how believers must live.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts frequently opens a new section with μὲν οὖν ('So then…'), linking the story's stages.

study.translationNote: Since οὖν ranges from a strong 'therefore' to a light 'so' or 'then', versions differ widely, especially in John, where it is often left untranslated as a mere connective; whether a given οὖν signals logic or sequence can change how a passage is read.

background.note: In early Greek οὖν was confirmatory, 'really, in fact', and in Homer occurs only combined with other particles.
Letters use οὖν for 'therefore': 'it is well with me; I beg you therefore, father, write me a letter'.
A looser use simply continues the narrative or instructions: 'having received it, then, let me know'.
In requests οὖν adds urgency: 'take care, then, that action is taken'.

study.exegesisTip: When 'therefore' opens an exhortation, trace it back to the argument it rests on; in narrative, do not read a logical cause into a simple 'so' or 'then'.
study.caution: Some grammarians (notably J. R. Mantey) argued that οὖν sometimes carries an emphatic or responsive force ('indeed, certainly') rather than an inferential one; how often this applies in the NT is disputed.

study.summary: Conjunction 'if': introduces conditions (assumed, contrary-to-fact or merely possible) and indirect questions ('whether'); with other particles, εἰ μή 'except', εἰ καί 'although', and in Hebraic oaths a solemn denial.

senses.label: If (condition)
senses.definition: Introduces a condition, usually with the indicative, stated as assumed for the sake of argument; context shows whether the speaker thinks it true.
senses.note: Some conditions are clearly true ('if you have been raised with Christ', COL 3:1), others false (1CO 15:13).

senses.label: If… would have (unreal)
senses.definition: With past tenses of the indicative and ἄν, a condition contrary to fact.

senses.label: Whether (question)
senses.definition: Introduces an indirect question after verbs of asking, seeing or knowing.
senses.note: Following Hebrew usage, εἰ can introduce a direct question (LUK 13:23).

senses.label: Except, unless (εἰ μή)
senses.definition: With μή, 'if not, unless, except, but only'.
senses.note: εἰ δὲ μή 'otherwise' (JOH 14:11).

senses.label: Although, even if (εἰ καί)
senses.definition: With καί, a concession: 'although, even if'.

senses.label: Oath: surely not
senses.definition: Following Hebrew idiom, εἰ with an unexpressed curse forms a solemn oath meaning 'they shall certainly not…'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul argues in chains of conditions, often from the lesser to the greater ('if… how much more').

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews repeats the oath of Psalm 95, 'if they shall enter my rest' (= they shall never enter), as a warning.

study.translationNote: Greek εἰ with the indicative presents a condition as assumed for the argument, not necessarily true; some popular teaching renders it 'since', which suits some passages (Col 3:1) but not others (Matt 4:3; 1 Cor 15:13). Hebraic oaths (Heb 3:11, KJV 'if they shall enter') appear in modern versions as 'they shall never enter'.

background.note: The Septuagint renders Hebrew oath formulas with εἰ and a suppressed curse — the source of the NT idiom.
εἰ also translates the Hebrew interrogative particle, giving direct questions introduced by 'if'.
The line between εἰ and ἐάν blurs in Koine, so εἰ occasionally takes the subjunctive.
εἰ μή can mean simply 'but', as in Gal 1:7.

study.exegesisTip: Identify the type of condition and any particle joined to εἰ: εἰ μή means 'except', εἰ καί 'although', and εἰ in an oath means 'certainly not'.
study.caution: In Gal 1:19 ('I saw none of the other apostles except James') scholars debate whether εἰ μή counts James as an apostle or means 'but only' (James was not one of them).

study.summary: Preposition, originally 'down': with the genitive 'down from', 'throughout', 'against', and 'by' in oaths; with the accusative 'according to', 'throughout, at', distributive 'each', and 'with respect to'.

senses.label: Down; throughout (gen.)
senses.definition: With the genitive, motion down from or down over something; in Luke–Acts, 'throughout' a whole region.

senses.label: Against (gen.)
senses.definition: With the genitive of a person or thing, hostile direction: speaking, plotting, fighting or witnessing against.
senses.note: In oaths, 'by': he 'swore by himself' (HEB 6:13; HEB 6:16).

senses.label: According to (standard)
senses.definition: With the accusative, the norm or pattern in keeping with which something happens: 'according to, in line with'.

senses.label: Throughout; at (place, time)
senses.definition: With the accusative, extension through a place, location 'at, in', or a point or period of time.
senses.note: κατ᾽ οἶκον 'in the house, at home' (1CO 16:19); κατ᾽ ὄναρ 'in a dream' (MAT 1:20).

senses.label: Each, one by one
senses.definition: Distributive: 'place by place, city by city, year by year, one by one'.

senses.label: With respect to
senses.definition: With the accusative, the respect in which something is true: 'as regards, in relation to'.
senses.note: καθ᾽ ἑαυτήν 'by itself' (JAM 2:17).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses κατά to name the standard of life or knowledge — 'according to the flesh' versus 'according to the Spirit', 'according to grace' versus 'according to debt', 'according to his purpose'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke alone uses καθ᾽ ὅλης ('throughout all…'), and describes the church's life 'daily' and 'from house to house' with distributive κατά.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews' argument turns on a priest 'according to the order of Melchizedek', 'according to the power of an indestructible life', not 'according to' the law.

study.translationNote: κατὰ σάρκα is rendered 'according to the flesh' (ESV, NASB), 'as to his earthly life' or 'by human descent' (Rom 1:3), or 'from a worldly point of view' (2 Cor 5:16 NIV): κατά expresses a standard or a sphere, and the context decides which.

background.note: Homer uses κατά with the genitive for motion 'down from' a height, as from the peaks of Olympus.
Legal documents use κατά with the genitive for charges brought 'against' someone, a usage common throughout the Koine.
Oaths are sworn 'by' (κατά) the gods and the kings, as in Heb 6:13–16.
κατά with the genitive can mean 'throughout' an area, a sense in the NT confined to Luke.

study.exegesisTip: Check the case: with the genitive κατά is usually hostile ('against') or local ('down'); with the accusative it most often supplies a standard ('according to') or a distribution ('each').
study.caution: In 2 Cor 5:16 ('even if we have known Christ according to the flesh') scholars debate whether κατὰ σάρκα qualifies the knowing (a worldly way of evaluating him) or Christ himself (the earthly Jesus).

study.summary: Preposition: with the genitive 'with, among' — company, association, divine presence, accompanying manner, even conflict ('fight with'); with the accusative 'after', mostly of time, once of place ('behind').

senses.label: With, in company of
senses.definition: With the genitive, accompaniment or association with persons.

senses.label: Among, amid
senses.definition: With the genitive, in the midst of a group or set of circumstances.
senses.note: 'Why do you seek the living among the dead?' (LUK 24:5).

senses.label: God with (presence, help)
senses.definition: God or Christ being 'with' someone: his active presence, help and guidance.

senses.label: With (manner, accompaniment)
senses.definition: With the genitive of a thing, the attitude, emotion or circumstance accompanying an action, or what something is mixed with.

senses.label: Partnership or conflict with
senses.definition: Shared relationship with someone, or, in Hebraic idiom, conflict: 'fight with' = against.

senses.label: After (time)
senses.definition: With the accusative, subsequent in time; μετὰ ταῦτα 'after these things'.
senses.note: Once of place, 'behind' the second curtain (HEB 9:3).

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew frames his Gospel with 'God with us' (Immanuel) and the risen Jesus' promise 'I am with you always'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John marks transitions with μετὰ ταῦτα and stresses abiding fellowship: the Spirit remains 'with you', and Jesus desires his own to be 'with me'.

background.note: From Homer on, μετά with the genitive meant 'among, in the midst of'; it gradually displaced σύν for 'with'.
Letters close with wishes for someone's health 'with (μετά) your children' — the ordinary 'together with'.
μετά expresses manner, as a prisoner pleading 'with prayer and supplication'.
'Fight with' (πολεμεῖν μετά) imitates Hebrew 'fight with' = fight against.

study.exegesisTip: Watch the case: μετά with the genitive ('with') speaks of presence or association, with the accusative ('after') of sequence; 'the Lord is with you' is a biblical idiom for active help.

study.summary: Preposition: with the genitive 'about, concerning' and 'for, on account of' (especially of sin and of prayer); with the accusative 'around' in place, 'about' in approximate time, and 'occupied with, regarding'.

senses.label: About, concerning
senses.definition: With the genitive, the subject of speaking, thinking, asking or caring.
senses.note: τὰ περί τινος 'one's affairs, news about someone' (EPH 6:22).

senses.label: Now concerning (new topic)
senses.definition: περὶ δέ at the start of a sentence introduces a new subject: 'as for, now about'.

senses.label: For (sins), on account of
senses.definition: With the genitive, the occasion or cause of an offering or sacrifice: 'for, on account of sins'.
senses.note: περὶ ἁμαρτίας is the Septuagint term for the 'sin offering' (HEB 10:6).

senses.label: For, on behalf of
senses.definition: With the genitive, especially in prayer and thanksgiving: 'for, on behalf of'.

senses.label: Around (place, time)
senses.definition: With the accusative, 'around' a place or person; οἱ περί τινα 'someone's companions'; of time, 'about' an hour.
senses.note: οἱ περὶ τὸν Παῦλον 'Paul and his companions' (ACT 13:13).

senses.label: Occupied with, regarding
senses.definition: With the accusative, figuratively, the matter one is busy with or concerned about.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In 1 Corinthians, περὶ δέ ('Now concerning…') marks the successive topics Paul takes up — marriage, virgins, food offered to idols, spiritual gifts, the collection, Apollos.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John repeatedly speaks of testimony 'about' Jesus — from the Baptist, the Scriptures, Moses, his works and the Spirit.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses περί in sacrificial language: offerings 'for sins' and 'for sin'.

study.translationNote: In Rom 8:3 καὶ περὶ ἁμαρτίας is rendered 'and for sin' (ESV text), 'to be a sin offering' (NIV) or 'as an offering for sin' (NASB): the phrase can mean simply 'concerning sin' or be the Septuagint term for the sin offering.

background.note: The root sense is 'round about'; with the genitive of place it is mainly poetic.
Letters constantly use περί for 'concerning': 'you wrote to me about the land'.
περί opening a clause marks a heading or topic, as in an inscription's section titles — compare 1 Cor 7:1.
περί overlaps with ὑπέρ in prayers 'for' someone's welfare.

study.exegesisTip: In 1 Corinthians, each 'Now concerning' (περὶ δέ) likely signals Paul taking up the next matter, possibly one raised in the Corinthians' letter (1CO 7:1).
study.caution: Whether every περὶ δέ in 1 Corinthians answers a question from the Corinthians' letter, or simply marks a new topic, is debated.

study.summary: Demonstrative adverb 'thus, so, in this way': it points back to what precedes or ahead to what follows, sets up comparisons ('as… so'), states how things stand, and occasionally intensifies ('so great').

senses.label: Referring back: in this way
senses.definition: Sums up a manner or situation just described, 'so, thus, in this way'; with οὖν it can draw a conclusion ('so then').
senses.note: It can also resume a preceding participle: 'and so he departed' (ACT 20:11; ACT 27:17).

senses.label: Pointing ahead: as follows
senses.definition: Introduces what comes next — an account, a prayer, or a Scripture quotation ('thus it is written').

senses.label: In comparisons: as… so
senses.definition: Paired with ὡς, καθώς, ὥσπερ or καθάπερ to draw an analogy between two events or persons.
senses.note: Acts 1:11: Jesus will return 'in the same way' (οὕτως… ὃν τρόπον) as he was seen going.

senses.label: Predicate: so it is
senses.definition: Used with 'be' or 'have' to state how a matter stands: 'it is so', 'so shall it be', 'is this so?'.
senses.note: In JOH 4:6 ἐκαθέζετο οὕτως probably means Jesus sat down 'just as he was', tired from the journey.

senses.label: Intensive: so very
senses.definition: With an adjective or adverb it marks degree: 'so terrifying', 'so great', 'so quickly'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul repeatedly builds arguments on the correspondence 'as… so also' (οὕτως καί), especially in the Adam–Christ contrast and in applying Christ's death and life to believers.

study.translationNote: In John 3:16 most traditional versions read 'God so loved the world', which many readers take as degree ('so much'). Several recent versions render it as manner — 'this is how God loved the world' (CSB, NET) — because οὕτως normally means 'in this way' and here points to the giving of the Son.

background.note: The everyday Greek of the papyri uses the same correlative 'as… so' pattern, as in a letter declaring that as the gods had not spared the writer, so neither would he spare the gods.
'This being so' (τούτων δὲ οὕτως ἐχόντων) was a standard phrase in official documents, like the predicate use in Acts 7:1.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether οὕτως looks back or ahead, and look for a correlative (ὡς, καθώς, ὥσπερ) — together these show exactly what 'so' refers to.
study.caution: In Rom 11:26 ('and so all Israel will be saved') scholars debate whether οὕτως means 'in this manner' (through the process just described) or has a temporal sense ('and then'); most lexicons favour manner. John 3:16 is similarly debated between manner and degree.

study.summary: Enclitic connective 'and', binding more closely than καί. Paired as τε… καί or τε… τε it means 'both… and', presenting items as a unit. Over two-thirds of NT uses are in Acts.

senses.label: And (closely connecting)
senses.definition: Used alone, τε joins words or clauses that belong closely together, often adding the next step in a narrative ('and so').
senses.note: Being enclitic, it never stands first in its clause.

senses.label: Both… and (τε… καί)
senses.definition: With a following καί it pairs two items as a matched set: 'both Jews and Greeks', 'both to do and to teach'.

senses.label: Whether… or (τε… τε)
senses.definition: Repeated τε correlates two parallel clauses, 'whether… or', 'both… and'.
senses.note: In Rom 1:26–27 τε γάρ… ὁμοίως δὲ καί sets women's and men's conduct side by side.

senses.label: Binding a series
senses.definition: Placed after the first of several items to tie a whole list together as one group.
senses.note: In 1 Cor 1:30 the τε… καί… καί suggests righteousness, holiness and redemption together spell out the 'wisdom from God'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke, especially in Acts, uses τε far more than any other writer, a mark of his more literary Greek; it often links successive actions in a narrative.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews, the most polished Greek in the NT, uses τε frequently for balanced pairs.

background.note: Legal papyri use τε… καί in fixed pairings, e.g. a property sold free 'of every debt, both public and private'.
τε is one of many particles that faded from the spoken language and does not survive in modern Greek, so its NT use reflects a somewhat literary register.

study.exegesisTip: τε… καί presents two items as a pair belonging together (Jews and Greeks, doing and teaching) rather than as a mere list.
