study.summary: Preposition whose root idea is 'beside'. With the genitive, 'from (the side of)'; with the dative, 'beside, with, in the sight of'; with the accusative, 'alongside', and figuratively 'beyond, contrary to, more than'.

senses.label: From, from the side of (gen.)
senses.definition: With the genitive of a person it marks source or origin: receiving, hearing or coming from someone; also the agent ('from the Lord').
senses.note: Idioms: τὰ παρ' αὐτῆς 'her means' (MAR 5:26; LUK 10:7); οἱ παρ' αὐτοῦ 'his people' (MAR 3:21).

senses.label: Beside, with, among (dat.)
senses.definition: With the dative of a person, location in someone's presence or home; with plurals, 'among'.
senses.note: JOH 19:25 ('by the cross') is a rare dative of a thing.

senses.label: In the judgment of (dat.)
senses.definition: Figuratively, 'before, in the estimation of': what is possible, right or favoured from God's standpoint.

senses.label: Beside, along (acc.)
senses.definition: With the accusative, of place: beside or along something, after verbs of motion or rest.

senses.label: Beyond, contrary to (acc.)
senses.definition: Figuratively, going past a boundary: 'against' nature, law or teaching; 'beyond' hope; 'less' one.
senses.note: 2 Cor 11:24: 'forty less one' lashes.

senses.label: Compared with, more than (acc.)
senses.definition: In comparisons, 'more than, above, rather than'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses παρά to frame Jesus' origin and destiny: he is 'from the Father' (genitive) and shared glory 'with' the Father (dative) before the world existed.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses comparative παρά to argue Christ's superiority to angels, Moses and the old sacrifices.

study.translationNote: Comparative παρά can mean 'more than' or 'rather than, instead of'. In Rom 1:25 the KJV says people served the creature 'more than the Creator', while most modern versions read 'rather than', implying exclusion rather than mere preference.

background.note: From Homer onward παρά with the genitive denotes motion 'from beside' a place or person.
Receipts use παρά with the genitive exactly as in the NT: 'I have received from you'.
οἱ παρ' αὐτοῦ commonly means a person's agents, representatives or associates.

study.exegesisTip: Identify the case after παρά first: genitive = from, dative = beside/with, accusative = alongside, beyond or contrary to.
study.caution: In Mark 3:21 οἱ παρ' αὐτοῦ is usually taken as Jesus' family (cf. 3:31), but because the phrase in Koine can denote friends or associates, some interpreters prefer 'his followers' or 'those around him'.

study.summary: Postpositive particle, usually untranslatable, that marks its word or clause as the first of a contrast completed by δέ ('on the one hand… on the other'); alone it can concede ('indeed') or, with οὖν, move a narrative on.

senses.label: Contrast: μέν… δέ
senses.definition: Sets up a contrast or balance with a following δέ (or ἀλλά); the weight usually falls on the second member.
senses.note: Usually best left untranslated; 'indeed… but' over-emphasizes it.

senses.label: One… another; some… others
senses.definition: With pronouns or articles in distributions: ὃς μὲν… ὃς δέ 'one… another', οἱ μὲν… οἱ δέ 'some… others'.
senses.note: τοῦτο μὲν… τοῦτο δέ 'partly… partly' (HEB 10:33).

senses.label: First (πρῶτον μέν)
senses.definition: Introduces the first item of a series, even when no 'second' follows.

senses.label: Concessive: indeed, to be sure
senses.definition: Without a correlative, it grants a point before a contrast that is implied or follows loosely.
senses.note: Col 2:23: such rules 'indeed have an appearance of wisdom' — but no real value.

senses.label: So then (μὲν οὖν)
senses.definition: In narrative μὲν οὖν sums up what precedes or opens a new section: 'so then, now'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts uses μὲν οὖν as a transitional marker to close one episode and open the next, often summarizing the church's growth.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses μέν… δέ to set the old order against the new: angels and the Son, Moses and Christ, mortal priests and the living one.

study.translationNote: Older versions often render μέν as 'indeed', 'verily' or 'truly' ('I indeed baptize you', KJV); most modern versions leave it untranslated and let the following 'but' carry the contrast.

background.note: Letters open πρὸ μὲν πάντων 'first of all' or πρῶτον μέν without a second item following, like Rom 1:8.
μὲν οὖν in papyrus letters likewise sums up or moves on to a new matter.

study.exegesisTip: When you meet μέν, look ahead for the δέ (or other contrast) that completes the thought; the emphasis usually falls on that second member.

study.summary: Comparative conjunction 'just as, even as': it compares, cites a standard ('as it is written'), measures degree ('according as'), and sometimes grounds a statement ('since, inasmuch as').

senses.label: Just as (comparison)
senses.definition: Likens one action or state to another: 'be merciful, just as your Father is merciful'.

senses.label: As… so (correlative)
senses.definition: Followed by οὕτως or καί to build an analogy between two parallel realities.

senses.label: In accordance with (a word)
senses.definition: Marks that something happened as Scripture or a speaker said: 'as it is written', 'just as he said'.

senses.label: Since, inasmuch as (ground)
senses.definition: Gives the basis or reason for what is said, shading from comparison into cause.

senses.label: According as (degree)
senses.definition: Marks proportion or measure: 'as they were able', 'as he wills', 'as each has decided'.

senses.label: How; when
senses.definition: Less often it introduces content ('how God first visited') or, once, time ('as the time drew near').

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John repeatedly grounds the disciples' life in the Father–Son relationship with 'just as… so I/you' (καθώς… κἀγώ).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses καθὼς γέγραπται 'as it is written' to anchor arguments in Scripture, and καθὼς οἴδατε 'as you know' to appeal to readers' experience.

study.translationNote: Because καθώς can compare or give a reason, versions differ: Eph 1:4 is 'even as he chose us' (ESV) or 'just as he chose us' (NASB), but 'For he chose us' (NIV), which reads it as a ground.

background.note: καθώς is Hellenistic, replacing classical καθά, and was condemned by Atticist grammarians.
A letter's 'do as I told you about the knives and the pepper' closely parallels the construction of 1 Tim 1:3.
Official oaths say 'as aforesaid' (καθὼς πρόκειται), a formal appeal to a written standard like 'as it is written'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether καθώς only compares ('just as') or also gives a reason ('since'), especially in John's 'as I have loved you' sayings and Eph 1:4.
study.caution: In sayings like John 13:34 and 17:21–23 interpreters debate whether καθώς is mainly comparative (a pattern to copy) or causal (the love received is the ground and source); many hold that both are present.

study.summary: Modal particle, usually untranslatable, that makes a statement contingent: 'would' in unreal conditions, '-ever' with relatives and conjunctions ('whoever, until'), and a potential or tentative force with the optative.

senses.label: Would (have): unreal conditions
senses.definition: With a past indicative in the main clause it states what would be or would have been if a condition (not met) were true.
senses.note: The 'if' clause may be implied: 'I would have collected it with interest' (LUK 19:23; MAT 25:27).

senses.label: -ever: indefinite relatives
senses.definition: With relative pronouns and the subjunctive it generalizes: 'whoever', 'whatever', 'as many as'.

senses.label: Until; as soon as
senses.definition: With ἕως it means 'until', with ὡς 'as soon as', leaving the time open.

senses.label: Potential with the optative
senses.definition: Softens a question, wish or indirect question: 'how could I?', 'I would pray', 'what he might want'.

senses.label: Repeated past action
senses.definition: With a past indicative it marks what happened whenever an occasion arose.
senses.note: Acts 2:45: they distributed 'as anyone had need', i.e. whenever need arose.

senses.label: Softening idioms
senses.definition: In set phrases: ὡς ἄν 'as it were' and εἰ μήτι ἄν 'unless perhaps'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's dialogues often turn on unreal conditions with ἄν, exposing what hearers would have known or done had they recognized Jesus.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew frames many sayings as general rules with ὃς ἄν 'whoever'.

background.note: ἄν was fading in everyday Koine: ἐάν increasingly replaced it after relatives, but ὡς ἄν 'as soon as' stayed common in letters, as in 1 Cor 11:34 and Phil 2:23.
Unreal conditions with ἄν appear in ordinary letters: 'if the bronze donkey had been for sale… I would have sent it'.

study.exegesisTip: ἄν rarely translates as a word; ask what it does to its construction — making a statement unreal, indefinite ('-ever'), repeated, or tentative.

study.summary: Demonstrative adverb of time, 'then, at that time': of a past or future moment, of the next event in a sequence ('thereupon'), and as the answer to 'when' (ὅτε/ὅταν… τότε).

senses.label: At that time (past)
senses.definition: Refers to a past period, often contrasted with 'now'; attributively 'the world of that time'.

senses.label: Then, next (sequence)
senses.definition: Introduces the next event in a narrative: 'then, thereupon'.

senses.label: Then (future)
senses.definition: Points to a future moment, especially in prophecies of the end.
senses.note: 1 Cor 13:12 sets 'now' (ἄρτι) against 'then' (τότε).

senses.label: When… then
senses.definition: Answers a ὅτε/ὅταν clause, stressing that one thing follows on the other.
senses.note: 2 Cor 12:10: 'when I am weak, then I am strong'.

senses.label: From then on (ἀπὸ τότε)
senses.definition: Marks the start of a new phase that continues: 'from that time'.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew accounts for over half of NT uses; 'then' is his favourite narrative link, and ἀπὸ τότε ἤρξατο marks turning points in Jesus' ministry.

background.note: From Homer onward τότε usually refers to past time in contrast to νῦν, but can also point forward.
The attributive use 'of that time' (2 Pet 3:6) has papyrus parallels such as 'the valuation that will then be made'.
τότε could weaken to little more than a connecting particle, as often in Matthew.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether τότε marks the same time ('at that time') or the next step ('then, next'); in Matthew it often simply moves the story forward.
study.caution: Some scholars treat Matthew's two ἀπὸ τότε ἤρξατο statements (4:17; 16:21) as the main structural divisions of the Gospel; others see them as important transitions within a different outline.

study.summary: Hebrew loanword meaning 'firm, sure'. In the NT: Jesus' solemn 'truly' introducing his own sayings, the hearer's 'so be it' after prayer or praise, and once a title of Christ, 'the Amen'.

senses.label: Truly (introducing Jesus' words)
senses.definition: Placed before a saying ('Amen I say to you') to guarantee its truth and authority; found only in Jesus' speech.

senses.label: So be it (response of assent)
senses.definition: Said by hearers to affirm another's prayer, thanksgiving or praise as their own.
senses.note: 1 Cor 14:16 implies the congregation's spoken 'the Amen'.

senses.label: Closing a doxology or blessing
senses.definition: Ends one's own prayer, doxology or benediction, sealing it as sure.

senses.label: Title: Christ the Amen
senses.definition: Christ is 'the Amen', the faithful and true witness in whom God's promises are confirmed.
senses.note: Echoes Isa 65:16, 'the God of amen'; in 2 Cor 1:20 the church's Amen is spoken through Christ.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John's Gospel Jesus' 'amen' is always doubled ('Amen, amen'), heightening the solemnity; Revelation uses it liturgically and as a name of Christ.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul closes doxologies and benedictions with 'Amen', inviting readers' assent.

study.translationNote: Jesus' introductory ἀμήν is rendered 'Verily' (KJV), 'Truly' (ESV, NIV 2011), 'I tell you the truth' (NIV 1984) or 'Very truly' for the doubled form in John (NRSV, NIV 2011). At the end of prayers versions simply transliterate 'Amen'.

background.note: The Septuagint usually translates Hebrew 'āmēn as γένοιτο 'may it be', transliterating it only rarely, as in the people's response in Nehemiah.
In the curses of Deuteronomy the people answer each one with γένοιτο, the response NT congregations voiced as 'Amen'.
Christian papyri end prayers with 'Amen', sometimes written as the numeral 99 (the sum of its letters).

study.exegesisTip: An 'Amen' at the start of a saying is Jesus affirming his own words in advance, not responding to another's — a mark of authoritative, solemn pronouncement.
study.caution: Many closing 'Amens' found in later manuscripts (e.g. MAT 28:20; PHP 4:23) are absent from the earliest witnesses. Scholars also debate how unique Jesus' introductory 'Amen' was in Judaism, though it is widely seen as characteristic of him.

study.summary: Adverb 'now': the present moment, the present age as against past or future, phrases like 'from now on' and 'until now', and, logically, 'but as it is' (νῦν δέ).

senses.label: Now, at this moment
senses.definition: The immediate present: something to be done or seen right now.

senses.label: Now (in contrast to then)
senses.definition: Sets the present against a past state, often of conversion: 'once… but now'.

senses.label: The present (age, time)
senses.definition: With the article, as an adjective: 'the present age', 'the present time', 'present-day Jerusalem'.

senses.label: From now on; until now
senses.definition: In phrases ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν 'henceforth' and ἄχρι/ἕως τοῦ νῦν 'until now'.

senses.label: But as it is (logical)
senses.definition: Marks the actual situation in contrast to a supposed one, or moves an argument on: 'but in fact', 'and now'.
senses.note: τὰ νῦν 'as for now' (ACT 5:38).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: For Paul 'now' is the time of salvation that has dawned in Christ: justification, freedom from condemnation and the day of salvation are present realities.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John stresses that the awaited 'hour' is 'now': true worship, life-giving, judgment and glorification arrive in Jesus' ministry and passion.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: The classical phrase τὰ νῦν 'and now' is confined in the NT to Acts.

study.translationNote: νῦν δέ can be temporal ('but now') or logical ('but as it is'). Older versions keep 'now' (KJV, John 18:36: 'but now is my kingdom not from hence'), while many modern ones read 'but as it is' or 'but in fact' (ESV, NIV).

background.note: Homer already speaks of 'mortals as they now are', the attributive use behind 'the present age'.
ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν 'henceforth' is common in legal papyri, e.g. a request that someone be registered 'henceforth' at a house.
τὰ νῦν 'and now' appears in everyday letters, as in Acts.

study.exegesisTip: In 'νῦν δέ', ask whether 'now' contrasts before and after (temporal) or the real case with an unreal one (logical, 'but as it is').

study.summary: Adverb originally 'back', then mainly 'again, once more'; it also links sayings or Scripture quotations ('again, furthermore') and can mark a counterpoint ('on the other hand').

senses.label: Back (return)
senses.definition: Movement back to a former place or state, often with verbs of going or returning.
senses.note: Often pleonastic with 'return' (GAL 1:17).

senses.label: Again, once more
senses.definition: Repetition of an earlier action or state: 'again', 'a second time'.
senses.note: Spiritual relapse or renewal: GAL 4:9; GAL 5:1; HEB 6:6.

senses.label: Furthermore (adding sayings)
senses.definition: Introduces a further parable, saying or Scripture quotation in a series: 'again, moreover'.

senses.label: On the other hand, in turn
senses.definition: Marks a contrasting or complementary point.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark uses 'again' to link episodes, tying new scenes to earlier ones beside the sea, in Capernaum or with the crowd.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews strings Old Testament quotations together with καὶ πάλιν 'and again'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul likewise chains Scripture citations with πάλιν.

study.translationNote: In Mark 15:13 the crowd 'cried out again' (KJV, ESV), though no earlier shout is recorded; some versions render 'shouted back' or omit 'again', taking πάλιν in a looser sense 'in response, thereupon'.

background.note: In early epic the dominant sense is 'back', as in 'give back'.
By the Koine period 'again' prevails, as in 'until I… write to you again'.

study.exegesisTip: When πάλιν introduces a quotation or saying it adds a further item ('again, moreover') rather than repeating an action.
study.caution: In Heb 1:6 scholars debate whether πάλιν simply introduces another quotation ('and again') or modifies 'brings in' ('when he again brings the firstborn'), pointing to Christ's return or exaltation.

study.summary: Negative particle: as a conjunction 'and not, nor, neither', continuing or adding a negation; as an adverb 'not even', often emphatic (οὐδὲ εἷς 'not a single one').

senses.label: 'Nor, or' continuing a negative
senses.definition: Joins a further item or clause to a preceding negative, so that the negation carries over: 'not … nor/or'.
senses.note: English after a negative often uses plain 'or' (Matt 6:26 'do not sow or reap').

senses.label: 'Neither' opening a new negation
senses.definition: Introduces a fresh negative statement that matches or answers a previous one: 'neither will I', 'and not'.
senses.note: Luke 20:8: Jesus answers their refusal with his own: 'Neither will I tell you'.

senses.label: 'Not even' (emphatic)
senses.definition: Used adverbially to heighten a negation, singling out the least likely case: 'not even'.
senses.note: Mark 13:32: not even the angels, nor the Son, know the day.

senses.label: 'Not a single one'
senses.definition: With εἷς/ἕν it means 'not even one', an absolute denial.
senses.note: John 1:3: 'not even one thing' came into being apart from the Word.

senses.label: In indignant questions
senses.definition: Opens a reproachful question expecting assent: 'Have you not even read …?', 'Do you not even fear God?'.

study.translationNote: Because οὐδέ can be a conjunction ('nor') or an adverb ('not even'), versions sometimes differ: in Mark 13:32 and Luke 7:9 'not even' brings out an emphasis that a simple 'nor' or 'not' loses.

background.note: Classical Greek already uses οὐδέ both as 'but not / and not' and, without a preceding negative, simply to add a negation.
Everyday letters use adverbial οὐδέ 'not even', exactly as in Mark 6:31 and 1 Cor 5:1: 'you have not even written'.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether οὐδέ simply links negatives ('nor') or intensifies ('not even'); the second often carries the rhetorical point, as in Gal 6:13.

study.summary: Preposition with the dative, 'with, together with': company, partnership, shared experience or fate, help, and addition ('besides'); in Paul, believers' union and destiny 'with Christ'.

senses.label: In the company of
senses.definition: Being or going together with someone: accompaniment, staying, eating or travelling with others.

senses.label: Companions, colleagues ('those with him')
senses.definition: οἱ σύν τινι denotes someone's attendants, associates or party.
senses.note: Acts 4:13 may imply partisanship: they had been 'with Jesus'.

senses.label: Sharing the same action or fate
senses.definition: Joined with others in a common experience, especially suffering, death or blessing.
senses.note: Gal 3:9: believers are blessed together with faithful Abraham.

senses.label: Union with Christ
senses.definition: Believers' participation in Christ's death and life, and their future being with him at his coming.
senses.note: Paul also forms many σύν-compounds (συζάω, συσταυρόω) to express the same idea.

senses.label: Assistance: 'with' as helping
senses.definition: The presence of a helping power working alongside someone.
senses.note: 'Not I, but the grace of God with me' (1 Cor 15:10).

senses.label: Addition: 'together with, besides'
senses.definition: Adds one thing to another, almost equivalent to 'and' or 'in addition to'.
senses.note: Luke 24:21 σὺν πᾶσι τούτοις 'besides all this'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses σύν far more than any other writer (about 75 times), often for travelling companions and associates.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul makes 'with Christ' a theological formula: believers died with Christ, will live with him, and will be 'with the Lord' for ever.

background.note: Papyri use οἱ σὺν αὐτῷ for those sharing the same office or work, as in the Gospels and Acts.
The phrase σὺν θεῷ, 'with God's help, God willing', is common, and appears in a Christian letter of the late third century.

study.exegesisTip: Where Paul writes 'with Christ', ask whether the reference is to a past participation (died with him), a present reality, or the future hope of being with him.
study.caution: How Paul's 'with Christ' (σύν) relates to his 'in Christ' (ἐν) language, and what 'to be with Christ' at death implies (Phil 1:23), are debated.

study.summary: Interrogative adverb 'how?': asks about manner or means, often in rhetorical questions implying impossibility or reproach; also introduces indirect questions ('how') and exclamations ('how hard!').

senses.label: Direct question of manner
senses.definition: Asks in what way or by what means something happens or can happen.
senses.note: Acts 8:31 'How could I (understand), unless someone guides me?'

senses.label: Rhetorical: 'how could …?'
senses.definition: A question that implies the thing is impossible or absurd, often in argument.
senses.note: With the subjunctive it becomes deliberative: 'how are they to …?' (Rom 10:14; Matt 23:33).

senses.label: Reproachful: 'how is it that …?'
senses.definition: Expresses surprise or rebuke at someone's failure or behaviour.

senses.label: Indirect question: 'how'
senses.definition: After verbs of seeing, knowing, telling or considering, it introduces the manner of something.
senses.note: Eph 5:15: 'watch carefully how you walk'.

senses.label: Exclamation: 'how …!'
senses.definition: Expresses strong feeling about the degree of something.
senses.note: John 11:36: 'See how he loved him!'

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John πῶς often voices misunderstanding of Jesus' words ('How can a man be born when he is old?'), which Jesus then corrects.

background.note: In Attic drama πῶς is often used to express displeasure, astonishment or doubt rather than a neutral question.
A husband writes to his wife 'How can I forget you?', a rhetorical πῶς like those in the Gospels.
Letters also use πῶς in indirect questions, 'write me how …', 'you know how I esteem and love you'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether a 'how?' seeks information or is rhetorical; many of Jesus' and Paul's 'how' questions are arguments that something cannot be so.
study.caution: In later Greek πῶς can weaken to little more than 'that' (ὅτι); whether some NT indirect uses (e.g. 1 Thess 1:9) still stress manner or simply mean 'that' is disputed.

study.summary: Reciprocal pronoun 'one another, each other' (no nominative): actions exchanged within a group, especially the mutual love, service and peace commanded of believers, but also mutual hostility.

senses.label: Reciprocal action within a group
senses.definition: Members of a group do the same thing to each other, e.g. speak, look or reason among themselves.
senses.note: Often with πρός: 'said to one another'.

senses.label: Mutual duty among believers
senses.definition: Commands to love, serve, bear with and care for one another as members of Christ's people.

senses.label: Mutual hostility or sin
senses.definition: The same reciprocity turned to harm: hating, betraying, devouring, slandering or lying to one another.

senses.label: Mutual belonging or separation
senses.definition: Expresses how persons are related to each other, as members of one body or as parted from one another.
senses.note: 'Members of one another' (Rom 12:5).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John repeatedly frames Jesus' 'new commandment' as loving one another, the mark of discipleship.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's letters are full of 'one another' exhortations that shape the life of the congregation.

background.note: From Homer on the word means 'of/to one another', used for all three persons, often with prepositions.
The Septuagint uses it of the halves of Abraham's covenant animals laid opposite one another.

study.exegesisTip: Note that 'one another' commands address the community as a whole: the obligation runs in every direction, not only from leaders to members.

study.summary: Negative connective 'and not, nor'; mostly paired (οὔτε … οὔτε) 'neither … nor' to deny two or more alternatives together; occasionally 'not even'.

senses.label: 'Neither … nor' (paired)
senses.definition: Repeated οὔτε denies each item in a series, so that none of the alternatives holds.
senses.note: Can run to long lists, as in Rom 8:38–39.

senses.label: 'Or, nor' after another negative
senses.definition: Continues a negation begun by οὐ, οὐδείς or οὐδέ; English often uses 'or'.

senses.label: 'Not even'
senses.definition: Used alone with intensifying force, singling out an extreme case.
senses.note: Luke 7:9: 'not even in Israel have I found such faith'.

senses.label: 'Not … and' (paired with καί)
senses.definition: A negative clause is matched by a positive one joined with καί.
senses.note: John 4:11: 'you have no bucket, and the well is deep'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses οὔτε … οὔτε in sweeping lists and in declaring outward distinctions void in Christ.

study.translationNote: After a negative, English idiom prefers 'or' to 'nor' (Rev 5:3 'no one … or on earth'), so the same Greek appears as 'neither/nor', 'or', or 'not even' in different versions.

background.note: Classically οὔτε is rare singly; it is mostly repeated, 'neither … nor', like Latin neque … neque.
A schoolboy threatens his father that he will not write to him, 'or speak to you, or wish you health', with a chain of οὔτε.
A letter complains 'you neither answered nor came'.

study.exegesisTip: In a paired οὔτε … οὔτε, the items are usually being set on the same level; notice what single reality Paul or Jesus sets above them all (e.g. Gal 5:6).

study.summary: Adverb 'immediately, at once, straightway': marks an action following without delay, the instant effect of Jesus' word, or (rarely) 'soon'; characteristic of the Gospel narratives, above all Mark.

senses.label: At once, without delay
senses.definition: An action follows immediately on what precedes, often prompt response or obedience.
senses.note: The disciples' immediate leaving of nets and family stresses the authority of Jesus' call.

senses.label: Instant effect of healing
senses.definition: The result of Jesus' word or touch takes place on the spot.

senses.label: 'As soon as'
senses.definition: Marks one event following straight on another, almost equivalent to a temporal clause.

senses.label: Quickly, without depth
senses.definition: Describes a hasty response that does not last, as of seed springing up and falling away.

senses.label: Soon, shortly
senses.definition: Of the near future: 'soon'.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark uses 'immediately' far more than any other writer, giving his narrative its rapid, urgent pace; it often functions as a vivid narrative link.

study.translationNote: In Mark the Byzantine text often reads εὐθέως where other editions read εὐθύς; in either case versions vary between 'immediately', 'at once', 'just then' or simply 'and', depending on whether they treat the word as strictly temporal or as a stylistic connective.

background.note: In the Septuagint the word renders Hebrew 'suddenly'.
The common Hellenistic form of 'straightway', used in letters: 'straightway when I entered Misenum, I received my travelling money'.
Business letters urge 'send the animals at once'.

study.exegesisTip: In Mark, ask whether 'immediately' marks real temporal haste or mainly drives the story forward; either way it highlights the urgency of Jesus' ministry.
study.caution: Scholars debate how far Mark's frequent 'immediately' keeps its full temporal force and how far it is a weakened connective ('then, and so').

study.summary: Comparative adverb of μάλα: 'more, to a greater degree', 'more than'; 'how much more' in a fortiori arguments; and 'rather, instead', expressing preference or correction.

senses.label: More, all the more
senses.definition: Increase in degree or intensity: something happens more, or still more.
senses.note: ἔτι μᾶλλον καὶ μᾶλλον 'more and more' (Phil 1:9).

senses.label: More than (comparison)
senses.definition: Compares two things, usually with ἤ or a genitive: 'more than'.

senses.label: How much more (a fortiori)
senses.definition: With πόσῳ or πολλῷ, argues from a lesser case to a greater: if this is true, how much more that.
senses.note: A standard form of Jewish argument (qal wahomer).

senses.label: Rather than (preference)
senses.definition: Prefers one thing over another: 'rather than'.
senses.note: 'Lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God' (2 Tim 3:4).

senses.label: Rather, instead (correction)
senses.definition: After a negative or a wrong course, introduces the right alternative: 'but rather, instead'.

senses.label: 'Or rather' (self-correction)
senses.definition: μᾶλλον δέ corrects or heightens what has just been said.
senses.note: Gal 4:9: 'you know God, or rather are known by God'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (over half the NT uses) builds key arguments with 'much more', especially on the surpassing grace of Christ over Adam's sin and the new covenant over the old.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses 'how much more' to argue from the old order to the greater reality in Christ.

background.note: The Septuagint uses μᾶλλον ἤ to render the Hebrew comparative 'more than'.
Official documents speak of acting 'in defiance of rather than in obedience to' proclamations.
A fourth-century Christian letter has ἔτι μᾶλλον, 'still more', as in Phil 1:9.

study.exegesisTip: Identify whether μᾶλλον compares, intensifies, argues a fortiori or corrects; the 'how much more' arguments of Romans 5 and Hebrews carry the weight of the passage.
study.caution: In 1 Cor 7:21 μᾶλλον χρῆσαι is famously ambiguous: 'rather make use of (freedom)' or 'rather make use of (your present slavery)'.

study.summary: Crasis of καί + ἐγώ (also κἀμοί, κἀμέ): 'and I', 'I also, I too', 'even I'; frequently expressing correspondence ('so I in turn'), especially in John's sayings of mutual relationship.

senses.label: 'And I' (connective)
senses.definition: Simply links a statement about the speaker to what precedes: 'and I'.

senses.label: 'I also, I too' (additive)
senses.definition: The speaker joins himself to others in the same action or claim.
senses.note: κἀμοί 'to me also' (Luke 1:3; Acts 8:19).

senses.label: 'I in turn' (correspondence)
senses.definition: Expresses a matching or reciprocal response: as you/the Father do, so I do.

senses.label: Emphatic 'I' in contrast
senses.definition: Sets the speaker over against another person: 'I for my part', 'even I'.
senses.note: John 1:31: 'I myself did not know him'.

senses.label: 'Both me and …'
senses.definition: κἀμέ … καί means 'both me and …'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses κἀγώ in reciprocal formulas binding the Father, the Son and the disciples: as the Father … so I; you in me and I in you.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses 'I too' to set himself alongside his opponents' claims, notably in his 'fool's speech'.

study.translationNote: Because the καί may mean 'and' or 'also/even', versions differ in emphasis: e.g. 'I knew him not' (KJV) vs 'I myself did not know him' (John 1:31).

background.note: The crasis is common in everyday letters: 'since I also am coming up to the city'.
Already in a third-century B.C. letter: 'that I also may know'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether κἀγώ simply adds 'and I' or stresses 'I too / I in turn'; in John the reciprocity is often the theological point.

study.summary: Adverb (neuter of μόνος) 'only, alone, merely': restricts a statement; 'just' with commands; above all in οὐ μόνον … ἀλλὰ καί 'not only … but also', and as a clause-opening 'only' introducing a single proviso.

senses.label: Only, merely (restrictive)
senses.definition: Limits a statement to a single person, thing or sphere: 'only, alone'.
senses.note: 1 Cor 15:19: hope in Christ 'for this life only'.

senses.label: 'Just' with commands and conditions
senses.definition: Reduces what is required to one simple act: 'just believe', 'if only I touch'.

senses.label: 'Not only … but also'
senses.definition: οὐ μόνον … ἀλλὰ καί adds a further, usually weightier, element to a first one.

senses.label: 'And not only that' (elliptical)
senses.definition: οὐ μόνον δέ, with the verb understood, carries an argument to a further step: 'and not only this, but …'.

senses.label: Clause-opening 'only' (proviso)
senses.definition: At the head of a clause it singles out the one thing that matters: 'only (let it be that) …'.
senses.note: Phil 1:27: 'Only conduct yourselves worthily of the gospel'.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James presses that hearing or believing 'only' is not enough without doing.

study.translationNote: English versions place 'only/alone' differently, which can shift its scope; e.g. James 2:24 'not by faith alone' (ESV) vs 'not by faith only' (KJV).
study.exegesisTip: Check exactly what μόνον limits: a word, a phrase, or the whole clause; in οὐ μόνον … ἀλλὰ καί the emphasis usually falls on the second member.
study.caution: James 2:24 ('not by faith only') and its relation to Paul's teaching on justification by faith is a long-standing debate; many argue the two use 'faith' and 'works' in different senses.

study.summary: Conjunction (εἰ + τε), usually repeated: 'whether … or', setting alternatives side by side as equally possible or equally covered; also 'if it is …' in lists, and 'whether' in indirect questions.

senses.label: 'Whether … or' (indifferent alternatives)
senses.definition: Two or more possibilities are named, and the main statement holds in either case.
senses.note: 1 Thess 5:10: 'whether awake or asleep' we live with him.

senses.label: Comprehensive: 'all, whether …'
senses.definition: Spells out the full range of a 'whole' or 'all': nothing is excluded.
senses.note: Col 1:16, 20: all things, whether in heaven or on earth.

senses.label: 'If it is …' in lists
senses.definition: Introduces each item of a list with the verb understood, often with an instruction for each case.
senses.note: In Rom 12:6–8 translators supply 'if it is'.

senses.label: Conditional: 'if … if'
senses.definition: Each member states a condition with its own consequence.
senses.note: 2 Cor 1:6: if afflicted … if comforted, it is for your sake.

senses.label: 'Whether' in indirect questions
senses.definition: After a verb of knowing, it presents open alternatives: 'whether … or … I do not know'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Almost all uses are Paul's: he uses εἴτε to show that life or death, presence or absence, and every gift and status alike stand under Christ.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: Peter applies it to submission to every human authority, 'whether to the king … or to governors'.

study.translationNote: Because εἴτε clauses often lack a verb, versions supply different words ('whether', 'if it is', 'or'), especially in Romans 12:6–8 and 2 Corinthians 8:23.

background.note: Classical Greek uses εἴτε … εἴτε, like Latin sive … sive, to put two cases as equally possible; it can be repeated three times.

study.exegesisTip: Look for what the 'whether … or' alternatives have in common: the point is usually that the main statement holds in every case.

study.summary: Demonstrative of quality, 'such, of this kind': it points to a kind or class rather than an individual, used as adjective, as correlative with οἷος/ὁποῖος, and as a noun ('such a person', 'such things').

senses.label: Such, of this kind
senses.definition: Qualifies a noun by its kind or degree: 'such signs', 'such a high priest', 'such hostility'.
senses.note: Can stress degree: 'such great authority' (MAT 9:8), 'such confidence' (2CO 3:4).

senses.label: Correlative: such as
senses.definition: Paired with οἷος, ὁποῖος or ὡς to compare: 'as is the one ... so are the others'.

senses.label: Such a person
senses.definition: With the article as a noun, ὁ τοιοῦτος 'such a one', referring back to someone just characterized, often an offender.
senses.note: The person is identified by conduct or character, not named.

senses.label: People like these
senses.definition: Plural noun for a class of people sharing the trait just described, e.g. those like children to whom the kingdom belongs.

senses.label: Such things, such cases
senses.definition: Neuter plural for a category of acts or matters, often summing up a vice list: 'those who practice such things'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (33 uses) closes vice lists with 'those who practice such things' and uses ὁ τοιοῦτος for the disciplined offender, avoiding his name.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses 'such a high priest' to sum up the qualities of Christ's priesthood just described.

study.translationNote: In 'of such is the kingdom' (KJV) versus 'belongs to such as these' (ESV, NIV) the sense is the same: the kingdom belongs to people of the children's kind, not to children only.

background.note: The neuter with the article is used as a noun, 'those who have acted in this way'.
An official edict forbids 'such knavery', showing the same pointing-back use.

study.exegesisTip: Find what the context has just described, since τοιοῦτος always refers back to that kind or quality.

study.summary: Adverb 'first': earlier in a sequence ('first ... then'), first in a list of points, first in priority, and first in God's appointed order of salvation and of end-time events.

senses.label: First, before something else
senses.definition: Marks the earlier of two actions, often answered by τότε or εἶτα 'then'.

senses.label: First of all (enumerating)
senses.definition: Introduces the first item in an argument or letter, often with μέν, even when no 'second' follows.

senses.label: First in priority
senses.definition: What must take precedence in importance or loyalty.

senses.label: Appointed prior stage
senses.definition: An event that must come first in God's plan before another: Elijah's coming, the gospel to the nations, suffering, apostasy.

senses.label: To the Jew first
senses.definition: The priority of Israel in the offer of the gospel and in judgment.

senses.label: At first, originally
senses.definition: τὸ πρῶτον, 'at the first, formerly', of an earlier time contrasted with later.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses πρῶτον for Israel's priority ('to the Jew first') and to open a series of points.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew's Jesus repeatedly sets what must come first: reconciliation, the kingdom, removing one's own beam, cleansing the inside.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether 'first' marks sequence (then something follows), rank, or a list item; MAT 6:33 and ROM 1:16 read differently depending on the choice.
study.caution: In ROM 1:16 and 2:9–10 scholars debate whether 'first' is mainly historical sequence (the gospel went to Jews before Gentiles) or an abiding covenant priority of Israel.

study.summary: Negative connective 'and not, nor', the μή-counterpart of οὐδέ, continuing prohibitions and other non-factual negations; also 'not even'.

senses.label: Nor, and do not
senses.definition: Continues a prohibition begun with μή, adding a further thing not to do.
senses.note: English often simply repeats 'do not' or uses 'or'.

senses.label: Nor, in dependent clauses
senses.definition: Continues a negation in purpose clauses, participles or infinitives, where μή rather than οὐ is used.

senses.label: Neither ... nor
senses.definition: Repeated in a series to exclude each item in turn.

senses.label: Not even
senses.definition: Strengthens a negation to exclude even the least case.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul strings prohibitions with μηδέ in exhortation, as in the warnings drawn from Israel in the wilderness.

study.translationNote: In EPH 5:3 μηδέ ('not even') is rendered 'must not even be named' (ESV) or 'not even a hint' (NIV): the first keeps the wording, the second paraphrases the force.

background.note: Used from Homer onward as a conjunction continuing a prohibition.
A wife complains her husband has 'neither thought of returning nor spared a look' for their plight.

study.exegesisTip: Read a μηδέ clause with the prohibition before it: it adds a parallel command or heightens it ('not even').
study.caution: In MAR 8:26 the Byzantine text has two μηδέ clauses ('do not go into the village or tell anyone'), while modern critical texts read a shorter form.

study.summary: Strengthened form of οὐ, 'not, no': an emphatic 'No!' in reply, an emphatic negation, and most often a question expecting 'yes' ('Is it not ...?').

senses.label: Emphatic 'No!'
senses.definition: A standalone denial or correction, often followed by ἀλλά or 'I tell you'.

senses.label: Not (emphatic negation)
senses.definition: Negates a statement or word with emphasis: 'not all of you are clean'.

senses.label: Question expecting 'yes'
senses.definition: Opens a question whose answer is assumed to be affirmative, like Latin nonne: 'Do not even tax collectors do the same?'.

senses.label: How much more (a fortiori)
senses.definition: In 'how will he not ...?' or 'why not rather ...?', argues from the greater to the lesser.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses οὐχί in argumentative questions that draw the reader into agreement.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke has Jesus' emphatic 'No, I tell you' answering mistaken assumptions.

background.note: Used in a rhetorical question in a love-lament: 'to what end else have we friends?'.
Also used non-interrogatively by a farm steward: 'we are not able to supply'.

study.exegesisTip: When οὐχί opens a question, the speaker presents the answer 'yes' as obvious and builds on it.

study.summary: Inferential conjunction (from δι᾽ ὅ) 'therefore, for this reason, that is why', drawing a consequence or exhortation from what precedes; διὸ καί 'and so also'; διὸ λέγει introduces Scripture.

senses.label: Therefore (exhortation)
senses.definition: Draws a practical appeal from what has been said.

senses.label: That is why (result)
senses.definition: States a fact or event as the consequence of what precedes.

senses.label: And so also
senses.definition: διὸ καί stresses that the result follows naturally from its cause.

senses.label: Therefore it says
senses.definition: Introduces a Scripture quotation as support for, or consequence of, a statement.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses διό to turn exposition into exhortation and to introduce Scripture.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul often marks a theological consequence with διό: God's giving people over, Christ's exaltation.

background.note: Common in official and legal documents: 'execute the deed therefore, as is fitting'.
διὸ καί also appears in papyrus petitions.

study.exegesisTip: Always trace διό back to its ground: the exhortation or result depends on what precedes.
study.caution: In PHP 2:9 interpreters debate whether διό presents Christ's exaltation as a reward for obedience or as God's vindication flowing from it.

study.summary: Preposition and conjunction 'until, as far as': a limit in time ('until now'), in space ('as far as'), in degree ('even to death'), and as conjunction 'until' (ἄχρι οὗ) or 'while'.

senses.label: Until (time)
senses.definition: With the genitive, the point in time up to which something lasts.
senses.note: Fixed phrases: ἄχρι τοῦ νῦν 'until now', ἄχρι ἧς ἡμέρας 'until the day'.

senses.label: As far as (place)
senses.definition: The spatial limit reached.

senses.label: Even to the point of
senses.definition: Degree or measure: to the extreme of death.

senses.label: Until (conjunction)
senses.definition: Introduces a clause naming the event that ends a state, usually ἄχρι οὗ with subjunctive.

senses.label: While, as long as
senses.definition: ἄχρι οὗ with present or imperfect, of a continuing period.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke favours phrases like 'until the day' and 'to this day' to mark periods in salvation history and witness.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation calls for faithfulness 'to death' and 'to the end'.

study.translationNote: In REV 2:10 'faithful unto death' can be read as 'until you die' (time) or 'even to the point of death' (degree); versions differ (KJV 'unto death', NIV 'even to the point of death').

background.note: In Homer ἄχρις is an adverb, 'utterly', of a stone crushing bone.
ἄχρι οὗ 'until' is common in wills and contracts.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the limit set by ἄχρι implies a change afterward (law 'until the seed came', GAL 3:19) or simply marks how far something reaches.
study.caution: In ROM 11:25 ('until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in') scholars debate what ἄχρι οὗ implies for Israel after that point.

study.summary: Negative adverb of time 'no longer, no more': a state that has ended, a thing that will never happen again, a logical 'then no longer', and with other negatives 'not any more'.

senses.label: No longer (changed state)
senses.definition: A former condition has ceased because something has changed.

senses.label: Never again
senses.definition: Something will not happen any more in the future.

senses.label: Then no longer (logical)
senses.definition: In argument: if one thing holds, the other cannot.

senses.label: Not any more (with negatives)
senses.definition: Reinforces another negative: 'no one dared any more'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's 'no longer' expresses the new existence in Christ: no longer slaves, strangers or under death.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John marks turning points: belief no longer resting on hearsay, disciples no longer walking with Jesus, no longer slaves but friends.

study.translationNote: In JOH 4:42 some versions keep 'no longer because of your words' (ESV), others soften it to 'not only because' (MSB), as the Samaritans' faith now rests on their own hearing.

background.note: Common from Homer on: 'no more, no longer'.
Used in letters for a ceased action: 'he no longer comes to me'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask what changed to make the 'no longer' true: a new event in time, or a logical consequence of an argument.
study.caution: In ROM 7:17, 20 ('it is no longer I who do it') scholars debate whether οὐκέτι marks a change in time or a logical conclusion, part of the wider debate over the 'I' of Romans 7.

study.summary: Interjection 'woe! alas!', expressing grief or denunciation: prophetic announcement of judgment, pitying lament over coming distress, and as a noun 'a woe', a calamity.

senses.label: Woe to (denunciation)
senses.definition: A prophetic announcement of coming judgment on those addressed, usually with the dative.
senses.note: Often followed by ὅτι giving the reason.

senses.label: Alas (lament, pity)
senses.definition: A cry of grief or sympathy over people facing distress.

senses.label: A woe, calamity
senses.definition: Used as a noun for a disaster, or in 'woe is me' for something laid upon one.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew gathers a series of woes against scribes and Pharisees.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke pairs the beatitudes with matching woes on the rich, the full and the praised.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation announces three numbered woes and laments Babylon's fall.

study.translationNote: Most versions keep 'woe', but where pity rather than judgment is meant some render 'how terrible' or 'how miserable' (MAR 13:17).

background.note: Renders the prophets' hôy and ʾôy in laments and oracles of judgment.
Not in classical Greek, but found in a popular farce: 'woe to you, woe to me'.
Also used by the Stoic Epictetus, showing it was current in spoken Koine.

study.exegesisTip: Read οὐαί as a prophetic cry that grieves and warns at once, not as a personal curse.

study.summary: Preposition with the genitive 'before': of place (in front of, ahead of), of time (earlier than, ago, before an action), of predecessors, of existence before creation, and of preference ('above all').

senses.label: In front of, ahead of
senses.definition: Spatial position; πρὸ προσώπου 'before the face of' (a Hebraism) means 'ahead of'.

senses.label: Before (time)
senses.definition: Earlier than an event or season; with a period, 'ago'.
senses.note: 2CO 12:2 'fourteen years ago'.

senses.label: Before doing (with infinitive)
senses.definition: πρὸ τοῦ with infinitive: before someone does something.

senses.label: Before me (predecessors)
senses.definition: Of persons who came or acted earlier.

senses.label: Before creation, before time
senses.definition: God's purpose, choice or the Son's glory existing before the world or the ages.

senses.label: Above all (preference)
senses.definition: πρὸ πάντων 'above all, most of all'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul locates election and grace 'before the foundation of the world' and 'before the ages'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John speaks of the Son's glory and the Father's love 'before the world was'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the Septuagint idiom πρὸ προσώπου for messengers sent ahead.

study.translationNote: πρὸ πάντων is 'above all' in JAM 5:12 and 1PE 4:8 but 'before all things' in COL 1:17, where versions keep the ambiguity between time and rank.

background.note: From Homer, 'in front of' a city or ships.
πρὸ προσώπου imitates Hebrew lip̄nê, 'before the face of'.
πρὸ πάντων 'above all' was a stock phrase in letters wishing health.
'Two days before the feast' parallels JOH 12:1 without any Latin influence.

study.exegesisTip: Check whether πρό is spatial, temporal or of rank; in COL 1:17 the choice affects the Christology.
study.caution: Whether πρὸ πάντων in COL 1:17 means 'before all things' in time, 'above all' in rank, or both, is debated; and JOH 12:1 'six days before the Passover' has been explained as a Latinism or a native Greek idiom.

study.summary: Interrogative adverb 'where?': direct and indirect questions of place, rhetorical 'where is ...?' implying absence, and in colloquial Koine 'whither, where to'.

senses.label: Where? (direct question)
senses.definition: Asks the location of a person or thing.

senses.label: Where is ...? (rhetorical)
senses.definition: Implies that the thing asked about is nowhere to be found or has no ground.

senses.label: Where (indirect)
senses.definition: In indirect questions or like ὅπου, 'the place where'.

senses.label: Where to, whither
senses.definition: With verbs of motion, the destination.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John repeatedly pairs 'where from' and 'where to' for Jesus' heavenly origin and departure, which others fail to grasp.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses rhetorical 'Where is ...?' to dismiss boasting, worldly wisdom and death.

background.note: Interrogative 'where?' from Homer on, often with a dative of the person.
Everyday letters ask 'where did you put the notice of payment?'.
Koine uses ποῦ for 'where to', as in 'where shall I flee from death?'.

study.exegesisTip: In John, ask whether 'where' concerns a physical place or Jesus' origin and destination with the Father.

study.summary: The abyss: the bottomless depth beneath the earth, which in the NT is the realm of the dead and the prison of demonic powers.

senses.label: Realm of the dead
senses.definition: The deep underworld where the dead are, set over against heaven as the furthest place one could go.
senses.note: Paul's paraphrase of Deuteronomy 30:13, applied to Christ being brought up from the dead.

senses.label: Prison of evil spirits
senses.definition: The place of confinement for demons, the beast and Satan, which can be locked, opened and sealed by God's authority.

background.note: Originally an adjective meaning 'bottomless, unfathomable', used of deep springs, seas and boundless wealth.
As a noun it usually renders Hebrew tehom, the great watery deep of creation.

study.exegesisTip: In Revelation the abyss is always under God's control: it has a key that is given, it is opened and shut by heavenly agents, and what comes out of it goes to destruction.

study.summary: Unleavened; in the plural it names the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and Paul uses it figuratively of a church free from the 'leaven' of sin.

senses.label: Feast of Unleavened Bread
senses.definition: The neuter plural 'the unleavened (loaves)' names the week-long festival joined to Passover, when no leaven was eaten.
senses.note: The NT, like other Jewish writers of the time, can treat Passover and Unleavened Bread as one festival.

senses.label: Free from corrupting leaven
senses.definition: Figuratively, believers as a pure, new batch of dough, and the sincerity and truth that should mark their life.

background.note: Regularly renders Hebrew matstsah, the flat unleavened bread of Passover and of offerings.

study.exegesisTip: In 1 Corinthians 5:7 Paul tells the church to clean out the old leaven 'as you really are unleavened': they are to become in practice what Christ the Passover lamb has already made them.

study.summary: To praise, in the NT always of praising God aloud, often in joyful response to what he has done.

senses.label: Praise God
senses.definition: To give God spoken or sung praise, extolling him for his acts and character.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the verb for the joyful response of angels, shepherds, disciples, the early church and a healed man to God's saving work.

background.note: An older word in inscriptions, it is about four times as frequent as epaineo in the Septuagint, especially for praising God.

study.summary: A party or school marked by its own opinions; in Acts a neutral term for Jewish parties, in the letters a divisive faction or destructive teaching.

senses.label: Party, sect, school
senses.definition: A group holding distinctive views, such as the Sadducees, the Pharisees or the 'Nazarenes', without necessarily implying error.

senses.label: Divisive faction
senses.definition: A breakaway grouping within the church that damages its unity; listed among the works of the flesh.

senses.label: Destructive teaching
senses.definition: Self-chosen teachings opposed to the truth, brought in secretly by false teachers and leading to ruin.

background.note: From the verb 'to choose', the noun can mean a choice or opinion, and later a party holding particular principles.

study.exegesisTip: In Acts 24:14 Paul refuses the label 'sect' for the Way, presenting it instead as faithful worship of the God of Israel's fathers.
study.caution: The later technical sense 'heresy' (false doctrine judged by the church) should not be read back into Acts, where the word simply means a party or school.

study.summary: Carefully, accurately; with exactness in investigation, knowledge, teaching or conduct.

senses.label: Carefully, accurately
senses.definition: With precision and thoroughness, whether in searching, writing an account, teaching, knowing or living.

senses.label: More accurately
senses.definition: The comparative form: more exactly or more thoroughly than before, as in explaining the way of God or examining a case.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word for his own careful research and for precise knowledge of 'the Way'.

background.note: Common in letters for knowing or reporting something exactly, as with 'you know accurately' in 1 Thessalonians 5:2.

study.exegesisTip: Apollos taught 'accurately' about Jesus yet Priscilla and Aquila explained the way of God to him 'more accurately': the comparative marks fuller knowledge, not a correction of falsehood.

study.summary: To anoint by rubbing or pouring oil or perfume on someone, for grooming, honor, burial or healing.

senses.label: Grooming and hospitality
senses.definition: Putting oil on one's head as everyday care or as a courtesy to a guest.

senses.label: Anointing as homage
senses.definition: Pouring costly perfume on Jesus as an act of love and honor, or bringing spices to anoint his body after death.

senses.label: Anointing the sick
senses.definition: Applying oil to sick people in connection with healing and prayer.

background.note: An ordinary everyday word in the papyri, used even of greasing a yoke-band.

study.caution: This is the common word for physical anointing, while chrio is used in the NT for God's anointing; but the line is not rigid, so meaning should not be built on the choice of verb alone.

study.summary: A grapevine; used literally, of Christ as the true vine, and in Revelation of 'the vine of the earth' harvested for judgment.

senses.label: Grapevine
senses.definition: The plant that bears grapes, including the phrase 'fruit of the vine' for wine at the Last Supper.

senses.label: Christ the true vine
senses.definition: Jesus as the genuine vine whose branches, his disciples, bear fruit only by remaining in him.

senses.label: Vine of the earth
senses.definition: An image of the earth's people ripe for judgment, gathered and thrown into the winepress of God's wrath.

background.note: Any climbing plant with tendrils, especially the grapevine; common from Homer on.

study.summary: To compel or constrain someone to do something, whether by force, pressure or urgent persuasion.

senses.label: Force, compel
senses.definition: To bring pressure on someone so that they must act, such as forcing believers to blaspheme or Gentiles to be circumcised.

senses.label: Urge strongly, insist
senses.definition: To press someone urgently, without physical force, as Jesus sending the disciples off or a host insisting guests come in.

background.note: Can be used in a weakened sense of simply having something done.

study.exegesisTip: In Acts 26:11 the imperfect tense probably means Paul 'tried to force' believers to blaspheme, not that he succeeded.

study.summary: To rise or spring up, especially of the sun or light; once causative, 'make the sun rise', and once of the Lord 'arising' from Judah.

senses.label: Make rise
senses.definition: Transitive: God causes his sun to rise on evil and good alike.

senses.label: Rise, dawn
senses.definition: Of the sun, light, a cloud or the morning star coming up over the horizon, sometimes figuratively of saving light.

senses.label: Spring from a lineage
senses.definition: Of the Lord arising or descending from the tribe of Judah.

background.note: Renders both Hebrew zarach ('rise, shine') and tsamach ('sprout'), so it can speak of sunrise and of a shoot springing up.

study.exegesisTip: Because the verb was used both for sunrise and for a sprouting shoot, Hebrews 7:14 may echo messianic hopes of a rising light or 'Branch' from David's line.

study.summary: To reject as unfit after scrutiny, used chiefly of the rejection of Jesus, the stone the builders refused.

senses.label: The rejected stone
senses.definition: From Psalm 118: the builders examined the stone and discarded it, yet God made it the head of the corner.

senses.label: Son of Man rejected
senses.definition: Jesus' prediction that the leaders and 'this generation' would refuse him.

senses.label: Esau rejected
senses.definition: Esau was turned down when he later wanted to inherit the blessing.

background.note: Used for rejecting a candidate for office found unqualified on official scrutiny.
Used of goods that might be rejected on inspection, such as a dagger not up to standard.

study.exegesisTip: The verb implies a verdict after testing: the human judges examined Jesus and declared him unfit, a verdict God reversed.

study.summary: Male, of the male sex, used of humanity as created male and female and of male children.

senses.label: Male, as a sex
senses.definition: The male of humankind, especially in the creation pairing 'male and female' and of men in Romans 1.

senses.label: Male child
senses.definition: A male offspring, such as the firstborn son dedicated to the Lord or the son born to the woman in Revelation 12.

background.note: The form arsen is attested in papyri, for example of the birth of a male child.

study.exegesisTip: In Galatians 3:28 Paul shifts from 'neither ... nor' to 'no male and female', echoing Genesis 1:27: the created pairing does not decide standing in Christ.

study.summary: A synagogue leader, the official responsible for arranging and overseeing the synagogue's meetings and worship.

senses.label: Synagogue leader
senses.definition: An officer who supervised synagogue services, for example inviting visitors to speak; a synagogue could have more than one.
senses.note: Named holders are Jairus, Crispus and Sosthenes.

background.note: Also attested in inscriptions for the head of a guild or association.

study.summary: Ungodly, lacking reverence for God; used of sinners whom God justifies and of the wicked who face his judgment.

senses.label: Ungodly whom God justifies
senses.definition: People without reverence for God, for whom Christ died and whom God declares righteous through faith.

senses.label: Ungodly under judgment
senses.definition: Those who live in defiance of God, for whom the law is laid down and on whom his judgment will fall.

background.note: The opposite of eusebes; used of impious and sacrilegious people.

study.exegesisTip: Romans 4:5 is striking because the Greek OT forbids acquitting the wicked, yet Paul says God 'justifies the ungodly' through faith.

study.summary: Lightning or a flash of light, used of the sudden visible coming of the Son of Man, of heavenly brilliance and of theophany.

senses.label: Lightning in comparisons
senses.definition: Lightning as an image of something sudden, universally visible or dazzling, such as the Son of Man's coming or Satan's fall.

senses.label: Lightnings of God's presence
senses.definition: Plural: flashes of lightning with thunder, marking God's throne and his acts of judgment.

senses.label: Bright gleam
senses.definition: The shining of a lamp that lights someone up.

background.note: Used of the light of a lamp as well as of lightning.

study.exegesisTip: The lightnings, voices and thunders of Revelation echo the theophany at Sinai.

study.summary: Firm, secure, reliable; often with the legal sense of something valid and guaranteed.

senses.label: Firm, steadfast
senses.definition: Holding fast without wavering, as hope and confidence kept firm to the end, or an anchor that holds.

senses.label: Valid, guaranteed, sure
senses.definition: Legally binding or certain to stand, as a promise, a spoken word, a will, a calling or the prophetic word.

background.note: A technical word for legally guaranteed security, such as a lease that is to remain 'secure'.

study.exegesisTip: Hebrews 9:17 uses the legal sense: a will becomes valid only once the one who made it has died.
study.caution: Verse numbering at 2 Corinthians 1:6 differs between editions. In Hebrews 3:6 the words 'firm to the end' are missing from some early manuscripts.

study.summary: A book or scroll, usually of sacred writings, including the 'book of life'.

senses.label: Book of Scripture
senses.definition: A section of the Scriptures cited by name, such as the book of Moses, Isaiah, the Psalms or the Prophets.

senses.label: Book, written record
senses.definition: Other written works: the record of Jesus' origin, or books of magic burned at Ephesus.

senses.label: Book of life
senses.definition: God's register of those who belong to him.

background.note: In its rare occurrences the word tends to carry a sense of sacredness or venerable antiquity.

study.caution: Whether 'book of the genealogy' in Matthew 1:1 heads only the genealogy or the whole Gospel is debated; the phrase echoes Genesis.

study.summary: The belly or womb; chiefly in the idiom 'to have in the womb', meaning to be pregnant.

senses.label: Womb; be pregnant
senses.definition: With 'have in the womb' it means to be pregnant, and with 'conceive in the womb', to become pregnant.

senses.label: Belly; glutton
senses.definition: The belly as the seat of appetite; 'lazy bellies' means idle gluttons.
senses.note: Quoted from a Cretan poet, traditionally Epimenides.

background.note: The idiom 'to have in the womb' is common in medical writers and papyri.

study.summary: To fill or load something full, such as a vessel, a boat, a house or the temple.

senses.label: Fill a container
senses.definition: To fill something with a substance, such as a sponge with sour wine, jars with water, baskets with fragments or a censer with fire.

senses.label: Be filled
senses.definition: Passive: of a boat swamped with water, a house filled with guests, or the temple filled with smoke from God's glory.

study.translationNote: In Luke 15:16 some versions follow manuscripts reading 'longed to fill his stomach' with the pods; others follow manuscripts reading 'longed to be fed'.

background.note: Used of loading a ship with grain, the original use of the word.

study.summary: Offspring or brood, as in 'brood of vipers'; in this text also used for produce or fruit, as in 'fruit of the vine'.

senses.label: Offspring, brood
senses.definition: Children or descendants; 'brood of vipers' brands hearers as sharing the serpent's nature.

senses.label: Produce, fruit
senses.definition: What the earth yields: the fruit of the vine, harvested crops, and figuratively the 'harvest' of righteousness.

background.note: The single-n spelling genema for crops and produce is very common in the papyri.

study.caution: Many manuscripts distinguish gennema (offspring, from gennao) from genema (produce, from ginomai); the text used here spells both with double n, but they are different words in meaning.

study.summary: A mind's conclusion: purpose, opinion, considered advice or consent.

senses.label: Purpose, decision
senses.definition: A resolve or intention, such as Paul's decision to return through Macedonia, or the shared purpose God puts in the kings' hearts.

senses.label: Opinion, considered judgment
senses.definition: A view or counsel given, such as Paul's advice where he has no command of the Lord, or a church united in judgment.

senses.label: Consent
senses.definition: Agreement or approval freely given.

background.note: Used of acting by one's own free will, close to Philemon 14.

study.exegesisTip: In 1 Corinthians 7 Paul separates his own considered judgment from a command of the Lord, yet still presents it as trustworthy counsel.

study.summary: A corner or angle; used of street corners, a secluded spot, the four corners of the earth and the 'head of the corner'.

senses.label: Corner, hidden spot
senses.definition: A literal corner of the streets, or figuratively an out-of-the-way place where things happen unseen.

senses.label: Corners of the earth
senses.definition: The four extremities of the world, meaning the whole earth.

senses.label: Head of the corner
senses.definition: From Psalm 118: the rejected stone given the chief place in the building, applied to Christ.

background.note: The idiom 'whispering in a corner' for doing things obscurely lies behind Paul's 'not done in a corner'.

study.caution: Whether 'head of the corner' means a foundation cornerstone or a capstone at the top of the building is debated.

study.summary: Here, hither; mostly as a call 'Come!', and once of time, 'until now'.

senses.label: Come! (summons)
senses.definition: Used like a command to call someone to come, or to introduce a further command or a revelation.

senses.label: Until now
senses.definition: In 'until hither', of time up to the present.

background.note: The temporal phrase 'until now' is found in papyri.

study.summary: To scatter abroad or disperse, whether people and flocks, grain in winnowing, or property squandered.

senses.label: Scatter people
senses.definition: To disperse sheep, followers, the proud or God's children, opposed to gathering them together.

senses.label: Winnow, scatter seed
senses.definition: In the parable of the talents, the scattering done in sowing or winnowing grain, paired with gathering a harvest.

senses.label: Squander
senses.definition: To waste possessions.

background.note: Used of the bread once scattered on the hills and gathered into one, in the Didache's prayer for the church.

study.summary: An adverb meaning 'as a gift, freely', and by extension 'without cause' or 'to no purpose'.

senses.label: Freely, without payment
senses.definition: Given or received at no cost, as a gift.

senses.label: Without cause
senses.definition: With no reason or justification.
senses.note: Quoting the Psalms.

senses.label: In vain, for nothing
senses.definition: To no purpose: if righteousness came through the law, Christ died for nothing.

study.exegesisTip: In Romans 3:24 'freely' and 'by his grace' reinforce each other: justification is pure gift.

study.summary: Well-pleasing, acceptable, chiefly of what pleases God.

senses.label: Pleasing to God
senses.definition: Acceptable to God or the Lord, of believers' lives, offerings, conduct and God's own will.

senses.label: Satisfactory to a master
senses.definition: Giving satisfaction to an earthly master.

background.note: Found in inscriptions of persons who gave satisfaction in public service.

study.summary: Good pleasure, goodwill or desire; most often God's gracious will, sometimes human goodwill or longing.

senses.label: God's good pleasure
senses.definition: What God has gladly willed and chosen to do, especially in revealing and saving.

senses.label: Human goodwill, desire
senses.definition: A person's goodwill or heartfelt desire, such as Paul's longing for Israel's salvation.

study.translationNote: Luke 2:14 differs by one letter in the manuscripts: 'goodwill toward men' (nominative) or 'among those with whom he is pleased' (genitive), which most modern versions follow.

background.note: Apparently confined to Jewish and Christian writings, used especially of God's favor.

study.summary: To take down or bring down: lowering Jesus' body from the cross, pulling down buildings or rulers, and demolishing arguments.

senses.label: Take down from the cross
senses.definition: The usual term for removing a body after crucifixion.

senses.label: Pull down, overthrow
senses.definition: To tear down a building, depose rulers, destroy nations or diminish a goddess's greatness.

senses.label: Demolish arguments
senses.definition: To overthrow reasonings raised against the knowledge of God.

background.note: Used for pulling down a structure, such as demolishing roofs.

study.summary: 'And from there', a contraction of 'and' with 'thence', marking the next stage of a journey or, once, of a sequence in time.

senses.label: And from there
senses.definition: Marks movement onward from a place just named.

senses.label: And then
senses.definition: Marks the next step in time.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Almost all uses are in Acts, especially in travel narratives.

study.summary: Rest or a place of rest, in Hebrews the rest of God which his people are invited to enter.

senses.label: God's resting place
senses.definition: The dwelling where God rests, which no human-built house can contain.
senses.note: Quoting Isaiah 66:1.

senses.label: God's rest for his people
senses.definition: From Psalm 95: the rest God promised, which the unbelieving wilderness generation failed to enter and which remains open to those who believe.

background.note: Used for a place of rest, as in Psalm 95 ('my rest'), the text Hebrews expounds.

study.exegesisTip: Hebrews links the rest of Psalm 95 with God's own rest after creation, so the promise is more than the land of Canaan.
study.caution: Interpreters differ on whether this rest is entered now by faith, at final salvation, or both.

study.summary: To look down on, despise or treat with contempt; once to disregard something as of no account.

senses.label: Despise, look down on
senses.definition: To hold someone or something in contempt, such as a master, little ones, God's kindness, the church, a young leader or authority.

senses.label: Disregard
senses.definition: To treat as unimportant: Jesus disregarded the shame of the cross.

background.note: Used of someone despising another's age, much like 1 Timothy 4:12.

study.summary: κίνδυνος means danger or peril, used by Paul of the real threats to life he faced as an apostle.

senses.label: Danger, peril
senses.definition: A situation of threat or risk to one's life or safety; in the plural, repeated perils from many quarters.
senses.note: In 2 Corinthians 11:26 Paul repeats the word eight times in one verse, piling up perils from rivers, bandits, his own people, Gentiles, city, wilderness, sea and false brothers.

background.note: Common in private letters for the perils of life; a second-century BC letter congratulates a man on being saved 'out of great dangers'.

study.exegesisTip: In ROM 8:35 'danger' stands in a list of hardships Paul had personally endured (compare 2CO 11:26); none of them can separate believers from Christ's love.

study.summary: κλάσμα is a broken piece or fragment, in the NT always the leftover pieces of bread (and fish) gathered after Jesus fed the crowds.

senses.label: Broken pieces of bread
senses.definition: Fragments broken off the loaves in the miraculous feedings and gathered up afterward in baskets.

background.note: Used of the broken bread of the community meal and Eucharist in an early church manual.

study.exegesisTip: The abundance of leftover pieces is part of the point: Jesus not only meets the need but provides more than enough, and in MAR 8:19-20 he makes the disciples recount the baskets to rebuke their failure to understand.

study.summary: κλαυθμός is loud weeping or wailing, whether in present grief or in the anguish of those excluded at the final judgment.

senses.label: Weeping in grief
senses.definition: Audible crying and lament over loss or parting.

senses.label: Weeping of the condemned
senses.definition: In the fixed phrase 'weeping and gnashing of teeth', the anguish and remorse of those shut out of God's kingdom.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses the formula 'there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth' six times, often closing a parable or warning of judgment.

background.note: Used from Homer onward for lamentation and wailing.

study.summary: κρούω means to knock, especially at a door to seek entry, and becomes a picture of persistent prayer and of Christ seeking fellowship.

senses.label: Knock at a door
senses.definition: To strike a door to be let in, whether in narrative or parable.

senses.label: Knock in persistent prayer
senses.definition: Figuratively, to keep asking God, with the promise that the door will be opened.

senses.label: Christ knocking
senses.definition: The risen Christ standing at the door of a lukewarm church, calling for a response.

background.note: The verb is used of knocking at a door in a second-century BC papyrus, as in Luke and Acts.

study.exegesisTip: The present tense in MAT 7:7-8 suggests continuing action: keep knocking.

study.summary: λαμπάς is a torch or oil-fed lamp, a source of light carried or burning in the dark.

senses.label: Torch or lamp
senses.definition: A light carried in procession or used to light a room, fed with oil.

senses.label: Blazing heavenly light
senses.definition: In visions, flaming torches before God's throne or a star burning like a torch.

study.translationNote: In the parable of the ten virgins most versions say 'lamps', while some prefer 'torches', since the word usually means a torch; both fit a light needing oil.

background.note: Listed among supplies (wood, charcoal, lamps, torches) for an official visit in the second century AD.

study.summary: λαμπρός means bright, shining or splendid, used of radiant or fine clothing, of luxuries, and of the clear river and bright morning star.

senses.label: Splendid, shining clothing
senses.definition: Bright or fine garments, whether of the rich, of angels, of the Bride, or (in mockery) put on Jesus.

senses.label: Splendid things, luxuries
senses.definition: Substantive use for the glittering luxuries of Babylon that are lost.

senses.label: Bright, clear
senses.definition: Shining or clear like crystal, of the river of life and of Christ the morning star.

background.note: Used from Homer for the bright light of sun and stars.

study.exegesisTip: James uses fine clothing to expose favoritism toward the rich in the assembly (JAM 2:2-3), while in REV 19:8 bright linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.

study.summary: λεπρός describes a person with a serious skin disease ('leper'), ritually unclean under the Law and excluded from normal community life.

senses.label: Person with skin disease
senses.definition: One suffering from 'leprosy', healed or cleansed by Jesus and his disciples as a sign of the kingdom.

senses.label: Simon 'the leper'
senses.definition: Epithet of Simon of Bethany, presumably formerly afflicted.

background.note: The adjective originally meant scaly or rough, even of rugged ground.

study.exegesisTip: Because such sufferers were unclean, Jesus touching and cleansing them (MAT 8:2, MAR 1:40) shows his power overturning impurity rather than being defiled by it.
study.caution: Biblical 'leprosy' covered a range of skin conditions and need not be identified with modern Hansen's disease.

study.summary: λέων is a lion, an image of ferocious danger and devouring power, but also of royal strength in Christ the Lion of Judah.

senses.label: Lion as deadly threat
senses.definition: The lion as a devouring beast, literal or as a figure for mortal danger and the devil.

senses.label: Lion in apocalyptic imagery
senses.definition: Visionary creatures and voices with lion-like features, signalling power and terror.

senses.label: Christ, Lion of Judah
senses.definition: Messianic title of Christ as the conquering king from Judah's tribe.

background.note: Used figuratively of a bold person in a first-century acrostic: 'a lion he was who took it'.

study.exegesisTip: In REV 5:5 John hears of a Lion but turns and sees a slain Lamb: Christ's royal victory is won through his sacrificial death.

study.summary: λιθοβολέω means to stone: to pelt someone with stones, usually to kill them, whether as legal execution or mob violence.

senses.label: Execute by stoning
