senses.definition: Underlining a statement: 'indeed, certainly', or with 'behold' to draw attention.

study.translationNote: Because English has no exact equivalent, many versions leave δή untranslated.
study.caution: In some verses (such as 2CO 12:1 and REV 2:10) the particle appears in the Byzantine text but not in modern critical texts.

study.summary: δηλόω means to make clear or known: to inform someone, or to reveal and indicate a meaning.

senses.label: Inform, report
senses.definition: To make known by report or message.

senses.label: Reveal, indicate
senses.definition: To bring to light or signify a meaning, as the Day reveals each one's work or the Spirit indicates truth in Scripture.

background.note: Exceedingly common in letters and legal papers for informing someone or stating terms.

study.summary: διαστρέφω means to twist or distort, and so to pervert people or truth, or (as a participle) to be perverse and morally warped.

senses.label: Perverse, morally twisted
senses.definition: Of a generation or people distorted in character and turned from God's ways.

senses.label: Pervert, mislead
senses.definition: To lead people astray or turn them away, or to twist the Lord's straight ways and the truth.

background.note: Moral writers use it of people thoroughly warped in nature.

study.exegesisTip: The phrase 'crooked and perverse generation' echoes the Song of Moses' description of faithless Israel.

study.summary: διατίθεμαι means to arrange or dispose: to make a covenant, to make a will, or to assign something to someone.

senses.label: Make a covenant
senses.definition: To establish a covenant with someone, as God did with the fathers and promises to do in the new covenant.

senses.label: Make a will
senses.definition: To dispose of property by testament; the testator's death puts the will in force.

senses.label: Assign, confer
senses.definition: To appoint or bestow something on someone, as Jesus confers a kingdom on his disciples.

study.translationNote: Versions differ in HEB 9:16-17 between 'will/testator' and 'covenant/covenant-maker', reflecting a debate over whether the writer shifts to the legal sense of a will.

background.note: The standard formula opening wills reads 'these are the dispositions made by ...'.

study.caution: Some interpreters argue HEB 9:16-17 still speaks of covenant-making ratified by a death (sacrificial), not of a testament.

study.summary: To destroy thoroughly or ruin, whether physically (moth, ships, the aging body) or morally (to corrupt or deprave).

senses.label: Destroy, wear away
senses.definition: To ruin or destroy something completely; passive, to be destroyed or to waste away.
senses.note: In 2 Cor 4:16 the outer self is steadily wasting away while the inner self is renewed.

senses.label: Corrupt, deprave
senses.definition: To corrupt morally; passive, to be corrupted in mind.

background.note: Commonly used of the death or loss of livestock, a completed process of damage.

study.exegesisTip: Rev 11:18 plays on the word: God will 'destroy those who destroy the earth', so the judgment fits the crime.

study.summary: To wake someone fully or rouse; used of waking from sleep, of a sea stirred up by wind, and of stirring up the mind by reminders.

senses.label: Wake from sleep
senses.definition: To wake someone up, or (passive) to wake up and get up.

senses.label: Be stirred up (sea)
senses.definition: Of the sea, to be roused and agitated by a strong wind.

senses.label: Stir up the mind
senses.definition: Figuratively, to arouse readers to alert, wholesome thinking by reminding them.

study.summary: A testing, or the proven character that results from passing a test.

senses.label: Test, ordeal
senses.definition: The process of being tested or put to the proof.

senses.label: Proven character, proof
senses.definition: The result of testing: tested and approved worth, or the evidence that demonstrates it.
senses.note: In Rom 5:4 endurance produces proven character, which in turn produces hope.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: The word appears only in Paul in the NT and is not found in earlier Greek.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'experience', 'character', 'proof' and 'test' because the word can name either the testing or its approved result.

study.summary: Tested and approved, genuine; originally used of metal or coin that passed assay, then of people proven trustworthy.

senses.label: Approved after testing
senses.definition: Of persons, shown to be genuine and acceptable, having stood the test, before God or people.

background.note: Regularly used of money that is genuine and current, 'approved' silver or gold.

study.exegesisTip: The opposite is ἀδόκιμος, 'failing the test, disqualified'; Paul pairs them in 2 Cor 13:5-7.

study.summary: To enslave or make a slave; passive, to be enslaved or bound, literally or figuratively.

senses.label: Enslave
senses.definition: To bring a people into literal bondage.

senses.label: Be enslaved to a power
senses.definition: Figuratively, to be in bondage to something: righteousness, God, wine, or the elemental principles of the world.

senses.label: Make oneself a servant; be bound
senses.definition: To place oneself at others' service voluntarily, or (passive) to be under obligation.
senses.note: In 1 Cor 7:15 the believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse is 'not enslaved', i.e. not bound.

study.translationNote: In 1 Cor 7:15 versions differ between 'not bound' and 'not enslaved'; interpreters debate whether this frees the deserted believer to remarry.

study.summary: The flat roof of a house (housetop), used as living, working and praying space in Palestine.

senses.label: Housetop, flat roof
senses.definition: The flat roof of a house, reached by an outside stair and used for rest, prayer or public announcement.

background.note: In earlier poetry the word meant 'house' or 'hall'; the sense 'housetop' is mainly Septuagintal and later.
Used of a house roof from which a young slave leaned to watch performers in the street.

study.exegesisTip: 'Proclaim from the housetops' means announcing publicly from the most visible place in a town.

study.summary: An idolater, one who worships idols; always in NT lists of those excluded from God's kingdom or from church fellowship.

senses.label: Idol worshipper
senses.definition: A person who worships images or false gods, or, figuratively, gives to something else the devotion due to God.
senses.note: Eph 5:5 counts the greedy person as an idolater.

study.summary: Adverb meaning 'without cause' or 'in vain, to no purpose'.

senses.label: Without cause
senses.definition: Without reason or justification.

senses.label: In vain, for nothing
senses.definition: To no purpose, fruitlessly, without result.

study.translationNote: In Matt 5:22 some versions read 'angry with his brother without a cause' and others omit the phrase, because the word is absent from some early manuscripts.
study.caution: The reading in Matt 5:22 is textually uncertain; many modern editions omit it.

study.summary: To bring or carry in; also to bring someone into a situation, as in 'lead us not into temptation'.

senses.label: Carry in, bring in
senses.definition: To carry a person or thing into a place.

senses.label: Bring into a situation
senses.definition: To lead or bring someone into a condition, such as testing.

senses.label: Bring to one's hearing
senses.definition: To present or introduce ideas to listeners.

study.summary: 'Easier', the comparative of 'easy (with little labor)', used in Jesus' sayings that compare two things.

senses.label: Easier
senses.definition: Requiring less effort; used in comparisons, 'it is easier to ... than to ...'.

study.exegesisTip: In the camel-and-needle saying the comparison is a deliberate hyperbole of impossibility, answered by 'with God all things are possible'.

study.summary: To pray, or to wish; both senses can blend when a wish is expressed before God.

senses.label: Pray
senses.definition: To make a request to God on behalf of oneself or others.

senses.label: Wish
senses.definition: To express a wish or desire, sometimes one that cannot be fulfilled.
senses.note: In Rom 9:3 the imperfect expresses a wish Paul could wish if it were possible.

study.translationNote: Versions differ between 'pray' and 'wish' in Acts 26:29, Rom 9:3 and 3 John 2, because the verb covers both.

background.note: Standard in letter openings wishing the recipient good health, closely parallel to 3 John 2.

study.summary: One who is zealous or eagerly devoted to something; also a title for Simon, 'the Zealot'.

senses.label: Zealous, eagerly devoted
senses.definition: Eagerly devoted to or zealous for something or someone, such as the law, God, ancestral traditions, spiritual gifts or good works.

senses.label: Zealot (title)
senses.definition: A designation of the apostle Simon, either for his zeal or for membership in a nationalist party.

background.note: Describes God as 'jealous' (zealous) for His people's exclusive devotion.

study.caution: Whether Simon belonged to the organized Zealot movement or was simply known for his zeal is debated.

study.summary: An inquiry or debate, often a contentious dispute or speculative controversy.

senses.label: Dispute, debate
senses.definition: A discussion or argument between parties over a question.

senses.label: Investigation
senses.definition: A judicial or formal inquiry into a matter.

senses.label: Speculative controversy
senses.definition: Idle or foolish questions and speculations that breed quarrels rather than godliness.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In the Pastoral Letters the word is consistently negative, for empty controversies to be avoided.

background.note: Used technically of legal inquiries and suits, as in Acts 25:20.

study.summary: Wonderful, marvelous, something to be wondered at.

senses.label: Marvelous, wonderful
senses.definition: Causing wonder and awe, especially of God's works and deeds.

senses.label: Surprising, remarkable
senses.definition: Of something astonishing; with a negative, 'no wonder'.

study.summary: Sulfur (brimstone), linked with fire as an image of divine judgment.

senses.label: Sulfur, brimstone
senses.definition: Burning sulfur, associated with fire in God's judgment, from Sodom to the lake of fire.

background.note: Fire and sulfur rained on Sodom and Gomorrah, the background to Luke 17:29 and Revelation's imagery.

study.summary: Noise and confusion, especially an uproar or riot of an excited crowd.

senses.label: Riot, uproar
senses.definition: Public disorder or tumult of an excited crowd.

senses.label: Commotion of mourners
senses.definition: The noisy confusion of people wailing over a death.

background.note: Used of a village riot.

study.summary: Cleansing or purification, whether ritual cleansing under the Law or the removal of sins.

senses.label: Ritual purification
senses.definition: Ceremonial cleansing required by Jewish law or custom, after childbirth or healed leprosy, or by washing.

senses.label: Cleansing from sins
senses.definition: The removal of the guilt and defilement of sin.

study.exegesisTip: Heb 1:3 presents the Son's sacrifice as the purification that the Law's rites only foreshadowed.

study.summary: To swallow down or devour; figuratively, to swallow up, overwhelm or destroy.

senses.label: Swallow, gulp down
senses.definition: To swallow something literally.

senses.label: Devour
senses.definition: To devour as a predator does its prey.

senses.label: Swallow up, overwhelm
senses.definition: Figuratively, to engulf, overwhelm or do away with entirely.

study.summary: To bend, bow or lay down; intransitively, of a day, to decline toward evening.

senses.label: Bow, lay down (head)
senses.definition: To bow the head or face, or to lay the head down to rest.

senses.label: Turn to flight
senses.definition: To make enemy armies give way and flee.

senses.label: Decline (of day)
senses.definition: Of the day, to wane or draw toward evening.

study.exegesisTip: The Son of Man has nowhere to 'lay' (κλίνῃ) His head, yet on the cross He 'bowed' (κλίνας) His head and gave up His spirit (John 19:30).

study.summary: A grain or seed, of mustard or wheat.

senses.label: Seed, grain
senses.definition: A single seed or kernel, often as an image of smallness or of life through death.

study.summary: To hang or suspend; middle, to hang (from something), including hanging on a tree as execution.

senses.label: Hang (on a tree)
senses.definition: To put someone to death by hanging on wood, or to hang there, used of crucifixion.

senses.label: Hang, suspend
senses.definition: To hang something on or from an object.

senses.label: Depend on
senses.definition: Figuratively, to hang upon, to depend on as on a peg.

background.note: The Septuagint uses the verb for hanging a condemned man on a tree, the idiom behind the apostles' 'hanging him on a tree' and Gal 3:13.

study.summary: To acquire, get or gain for oneself, often by purchase.

senses.label: Acquire, obtain
senses.definition: To get possession of something, by purchase, earning or other means.

senses.label: Gain, win
senses.definition: To gain or secure something non-material, such as one's soul or life.

study.translationNote: In 1 Thess 4:4 'vessel' is taken by some as one's own body ('control his body') and by others as a wife ('take a wife'), and versions differ accordingly.
study.caution: Interpreters remain divided over 1 Thess 4:4: the present tense normally means 'acquire', which suits 'take a wife', while 'possess/control' (fitting 'body') is usually expressed by the perfect.

study.summary: To be lord or master over, to rule or have dominion.

senses.label: Rule, lord it over
senses.definition: Of persons, to exercise lordship or authority over others.

senses.label: Have dominion (powers)
senses.definition: Of death, sin or the law, to hold mastery over someone.

study.summary: To shine, give light.

senses.label: Shine, give light
senses.definition: To give off light, literally (lamp, lightning, Jesus' transfigured face, angelic light) or figuratively (believers' lives, God's light in the heart).

background.note: An inscription over a church built on a pagan temple speaks of saving light shining where darkness had covered, recalling 2 Cor 4:6.

study.summary: To whip or flog; figuratively, to chastise as a father disciplines.

senses.label: Flog, scourge
senses.definition: To beat with a whip as a judicial or synagogue punishment.

senses.label: Chastise
senses.definition: Figuratively, of God's fatherly discipline of His children.

background.note: The regular term for punishment by scourging.

study.summary: To translate from one language into another; in the NT, in the formula 'which is translated'.

senses.label: Translate
senses.definition: To render a Hebrew or Aramaic word or name into Greek; usually in the phrase 'which translated means'.

background.note: Used of a Greek translation of a demotic Egyptian document.

study.summary: An imitator, one who follows another's example; always with 'become' in the NT.

senses.label: Imitator, follower
senses.definition: One who copies the conduct and example of another, whether of Paul, Christ, God, the churches or the faithful.

study.exegesisTip: The constant pairing with 'become' points to a moral effort of growing into the pattern set by the model.

study.summary: Remembrance or mention, especially remembering others in prayer.

senses.label: Remembrance in prayer
senses.definition: Mentioning or remembering someone in prayer.

senses.label: Memory, recollection
senses.definition: A remembrance or recollection of someone.

background.note: The phrase 'making mention' of someone was standard in letters, often linked to prayer to the gods.

study.summary: An adulteress; used as an adjective for a generation unfaithful to God and for spiritual adultery.

senses.label: Adulteress
senses.definition: A married woman who has relations with another man.

senses.label: Spiritually unfaithful
senses.definition: Unfaithful to God, as a wife to her husband; used of 'this generation' and of believers who love the world.

senses.label: Adultery (desire)
senses.definition: Adulterous desire, eyes 'full of an adulteress'.

study.exegesisTip: Behind the figurative use stands the prophetic image of Israel as an unfaithful wife of God.

study.summary: The south wind, and hence the south as a direction or region.

senses.label: South wind
senses.definition: The wind blowing from the south.

senses.label: South (direction)
senses.definition: The southern direction or quarter.

senses.label: Southern region
senses.definition: The lands of the south; the queen of Sheba is 'the queen of the south'.

study.summary: Ξηρός means "dry": it describes a hand or limb withered by disease, the dry land as opposed to the sea, and, in a proverb, dry wood.

senses.label: Withered, shrunken (of the body)
senses.definition: Of a limb or person shrivelled and disabled by disease, such as the man with the withered hand healed on the Sabbath, or the paralysed invalids at Bethesda.

senses.label: Dry land
senses.definition: As a noun (ἡ ξηρά, understood with γῆ), the land as distinct from the sea.
senses.note: "Sea and dry land" in MAT 23:15 is an idiom for going to any length; HEB 11:29 recalls Israel crossing the Red Sea on dry ground.

senses.label: Dry wood (proverbial)
senses.definition: In Jesus' saying about green and dry wood: if such things happen while the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry and ready for burning?

background.note: Everyday papyri use the word for dried produce such as hay, branches and meal.

study.exegesisTip: In LUK 23:31 the contrast is usually understood this way: if the Romans treat the innocent Jesus (green, living wood) like this, the judgment coming on guilty Jerusalem (dry wood, fit for fire) will be far worse.

study.summary: Πανταχοῦ is an adverb meaning "everywhere, in all places", used of the gospel's wide spread and of what is said or done generally.

senses.label: Everywhere, in every place
senses.definition: Without limit of place: the apostles preached everywhere, Paul taught the same in every church, God commands people everywhere to repent, and the Christian sect was spoken against everywhere.

background.note: A common everyday adverb in the papyri, e.g. of searching everywhere for timber.

study.summary: Παράβασις means "transgression": stepping over a line that has been clearly drawn, the breaking of a known command or law.

senses.label: Transgression of a known command
senses.definition: A specific violation of an expressed law or commandment, such as breaking the Mosaic law, Adam's breach of God's explicit command, or Eve's transgression.

senses.label: Transgressions under the law/covenant
senses.definition: The violations that the law made visible and that called for just penalty, and from which Christ's death redeems those under the first covenant.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul ties παράβασις closely to law: where there is no law there is no transgression, and Adam's sin is called a transgression because it broke an explicit command.

study.exegesisTip: Paul uses παράβασις more narrowly than ἁμαρτία (sin). Sin existed before the law (ROM 5:13–14), but it becomes 'transgression' when it violates a stated command. That is why the law can be said to be 'added because of transgressions' (GAL 3:19).
study.caution: GAL 3:19 ('added because of transgressions') is read in different ways: to restrain transgressions, or to expose and even multiply them by defining sin as transgression (compare ROM 4:15). Both readings are held by serious interpreters.

study.summary: Πεντήκοντα is the indeclinable numeral "fifty".

senses.label: Fifty
senses.definition: The number fifty, used of debts, a debt reduced in a bill, Jesus' age as reckoned by his opponents, groups at the feeding of the five thousand, and in compound numbers (153 fish, about 450 years).

study.caution: Many symbolic explanations of the 153 fish in JOH 21:11 have been proposed. None is certain, and the text itself stresses only the large size of the catch and that the net did not break.

study.summary: Περιβλέπω, used in the middle voice, means "to look around", sometimes at a group of people with a searching or meaningful gaze.

senses.label: Look around at people
senses.definition: To survey those present with a deliberate gaze, often before a significant word or act, e.g. with anger at hardened hearts, or at those sitting around him as his true family.

senses.label: Look about, scan a place
senses.definition: To look all around in order to find someone or take in a scene, e.g. searching for the woman who touched him, looking over the temple, or the disciples finding only Jesus after the transfiguration.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Almost all uses are in Mark, who repeatedly notes Jesus' searching glance around him as a vivid narrative detail before he speaks or acts.

study.summary: Περιζώννυμι means "to gird": to fasten a belt around oneself, tucking up long robes for work, travel or battle, or to wear a sash.

senses.label: Gird oneself for action
senses.definition: To belt up one's garment ready for service, travel or readiness, sometimes figuratively of spiritual alertness, as in 'girded with truth'.
senses.note: In LUK 12:37 the master astonishingly girds himself to serve his own servants.

senses.label: Wear a sash around
senses.definition: Passive: to have a belt or sash fastened around the body, of the golden sash at the chest of the Son of Man and the angels.

study.exegesisTip: A golden sash worn high at the chest (REV 1:13) suggests dignity and rest rather than labour, unlike the waist-girding for work in LUK 12 and 17.

study.summary: Πνέω means "to blow", always of the wind in the NT.

senses.label: Blow (of wind)
senses.definition: Of wind moving or blowing: storm winds beating on a house, the south wind bringing heat, a strong wind on the lake, the wind restrained by angels, and the wind that 'blows where it wishes'.

senses.label: The breeze (substantive)
senses.definition: The participle used as a noun ('the blowing [breeze]'), into which sailors hoisted the foresail.

study.exegesisTip: In JOH 3:8 πνέω is paired with πνεῦμα, which can mean both 'wind' and 'Spirit'. Jesus plays on the double sense: the Spirit's work, like the wind, is free and unseen but its effects are real.

study.summary: Πολεμέω means "to make war, fight": in Revelation, cosmic and eschatological warfare, and in James, bitter quarrelling among believers.

senses.label: Wage war (cosmic conflict)
senses.definition: To engage in armed conflict, used in Revelation of Michael against the dragon, the beast's apparent invincibility, enemies against the Lamb, and Christ's righteous warfare with the sword of his mouth.
senses.note: Often built with μετά ('war with/against').

senses.label: Fight, quarrel (hyperbolic)
senses.definition: Used hyperbolically of personal strife and disputes within the community.

background.note: The construction πολεμέω μετά ('make war with/against'), frequent in Revelation, also appears in non-biblical Greek, so it need not be put down to Hebrew influence.

study.summary: Πονηρία means "wickedness": active, malicious evil, either as an inner disposition or as wicked deeds.

senses.label: Wickedness, malice (disposition)
senses.definition: Evil disposition or intent, including malicious purpose hidden behind a question, and the inner corruption of those who are outwardly clean.

senses.label: Wicked deeds (plural)
senses.definition: In the plural, specific acts or ways of wickedness.

senses.label: Spiritual forces of evil
senses.definition: In the phrase 'the spiritual forces of wickedness', the evil powers in the heavenly realms opposed to believers.

study.exegesisTip: Πονηρία tends to denote evil that is active and harmful to others, while κακία (paired with it in 1CO 5:8) is a broader word for badness or vicious disposition.

study.summary: Ποταπός is an interrogative adjective meaning "of what sort?", often used in exclamations of wonder ("what great...!").

senses.label: Of what sort? (question)
senses.definition: Asking about the nature or character of a person or thing: what kind of man this is, what kind of greeting, what sort of woman, what sort of people you ought to be.

senses.label: What great...! (exclamation)
senses.definition: In exclamations expressing amazement at the quality or greatness of something: the temple's stones, the Father's love.

study.exegesisTip: In 1JO 3:1 the word conveys astonished wonder: 'See what (amazing) love the Father has given us', not merely 'what kind of love'.

study.summary: Πρέπω means "to be fitting, proper, suitable": what fits the nature of a person or situation.

senses.label: Be fitting, appropriate
senses.definition: Of conduct or teaching that suits a person's status or profession, such as what befits saints, women who profess godliness, or sound doctrine; πρέπον ἐστίν means 'it is right/proper'.

senses.label: Fitting for God / Christ
senses.definition: Of what suits God's character and purpose: it was fitting for God to perfect the Savior through suffering, and fitting for us to have such a high priest.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the word of the fittingness of God's saving plan, presenting Christ's suffering and priesthood as worthy of God and suited to human need.

study.summary: Προσφωνέω means "to call out to, address" someone, and also "to call to oneself, summon".

senses.label: Call out to, address
senses.definition: To speak out to someone, often publicly or loudly: children calling to one another in the marketplace, Pilate addressing the crowd again, Paul addressing the people in Aramaic.

senses.label: Call to oneself, summon
senses.definition: To call someone over to oneself, as Jesus called his disciples before choosing the Twelve and called the bent woman to him.

study.summary: Πρόφασις means a "pretext" or "pretence": an alleged reason put forward to hide the real one, and also a (valid) excuse.

senses.label: Pretext, false show
senses.definition: An outward reason or appearance masking the true motive: long prayers 'for show', sailors pretending to lay out anchors, preaching Christ from pretence, or a pretext for greed.

senses.label: Excuse
senses.definition: A reason that could be offered in one's defence. Having heard Jesus, the world has no excuse for its sin.

study.translationNote: In the warnings against the scribes (MAR 12:40, LUK 20:47) the dative προφάσει is rendered 'for a pretence' (older versions) or 'for show' (modern ones). Both express prayer offered for appearance rather than devotion.
study.caution: The verse about devouring widows' houses in Matthew (numbered MAT 23:13 or 23:14 in different editions) is absent from many early manuscripts and is omitted or bracketed in most modern critical texts.

study.summary: Ῥήγνυμι (also ῥήσσω) means "to tear, burst, break apart", also "to throw down" in a convulsion, and "to break forth" into a shout.

senses.label: Tear, burst
senses.definition: To break something apart violently: new wine bursting old wineskins, or animals turning to tear someone to pieces.

senses.label: Throw down in convulsion
senses.definition: Of a demon dashing its victim to the ground or throwing him into a convulsion.

senses.label: Break forth (in shouting)
senses.definition: In the quoted Isaiah text, to burst into a cry of joy.

study.summary: Ῥίπτω means "to throw, hurl, cast" something or someone, and in the perfect passive "to lie prostrate, be cast down".

senses.label: Throw, cast, hurl
senses.definition: To throw something away or down with force: Judas flinging the silver into the temple, sailors throwing the ship's tackle overboard or casting anchors, someone thrown into the sea.

senses.label: Throw down, lay down (persons)
senses.definition: Of persons: a demon throwing a man down, or crowds hastily laying the sick at Jesus' feet.

senses.label: Lying prostrate, helpless
senses.definition: Perfect passive participle: the crowds were like sheep without a shepherd, harassed and lying helpless.

study.summary: Ῥομφαία originally meant a large broad sword and is used in the NT for a sword, chiefly the sharp two-edged sword from Christ's mouth in Revelation.

senses.label: Sword of Christ's mouth
senses.definition: The sharp two-edged sword that proceeds from the mouth of the exalted Christ, symbolizing his word of judgment by which he makes war and strikes the nations.

senses.label: Sword (instrument of death)
senses.definition: A literal sword as a means of killing, one of the judgments of the fourth horseman.

senses.label: Piercing grief (metaphor)
senses.definition: Simeon's prophecy that a sword would pierce Mary's soul, referring to the anguish she would suffer over her son.

study.summary: Σκιά means "shadow": literal shade, the gloom of 'the shadow of death', and a foreshadowing outline of a reality still to come.

senses.label: Shade, shadow
senses.definition: The shade cast when light is blocked: birds nesting in the shade of the mustard plant, people hoping Peter's shadow would fall on them.

senses.label: Shadow of death
senses.definition: Figuratively, the deep darkness of a people in spiritual death, on whom the light of the Messiah dawns.

senses.label: Foreshadowing, outline
senses.definition: An outline or prefiguring copy that points to a coming reality: the law and its rituals as a shadow of good things to come, with the substance belonging to Christ.

study.exegesisTip: In COL 2:17 and HEB 10:1 'shadow' is contrasted with 'body' (σῶμα) or 'image' (εἰκών). The shadow is real but provisional, an advance sign that the reality itself is coming.

study.summary: Σπεῖρα is a military term for a Roman "cohort", a unit of troops commanded by a tribune.

senses.label: Cohort, detachment of soldiers
senses.definition: A Roman cohort (nominally about 600 men), or a detachment drawn from it: the troops who mocked Jesus in the praetorium, those who came to arrest him, the Jerusalem garrison, and the named 'Italian' and 'Augustan' cohorts.

background.note: Common in papyri for a numbered auxiliary cohort, e.g. a prefect of 'the first cohort of the Damascenes'.

study.caution: In the arrest scene (JOH 18:3, 12) 'the whole cohort' need not mean its full strength. A detachment under the tribune is probably meant.

study.summary: Στοιχεῖον means a basic component in a series, "element": the ABCs or rudiments of teaching, the physical elements of the universe, and the debated "elements of the world".

senses.label: Rudiments, ABCs
senses.definition: The first principles or basic elements of a subject, like the alphabet of God's revelation that the readers needed to learn again.

senses.label: Elements of the world
senses.definition: The 'elemental things of the world' that held people in bondage before Christ, which believers have died to: elementary religious principles, or the spiritual powers associated with the elements.

senses.label: Physical elements, heavenly bodies
senses.definition: The basic components of the physical universe (possibly the heavenly bodies) that will melt and be dissolved by fire on the day of the Lord.

study.translationNote: Versions render τὰ στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου in Galatians and Colossians as 'elementary principles', 'basic principles', 'elemental spirits' or 'elemental forces'. The renderings reflect the scholarly debate over the phrase.

background.note: Used for the letters of the alphabet, the basic members of a series.

study.exegesisTip: In GAL 4:3–9 Paul puts Jewish law-observance and the Galatians' former pagan religion under the same heading: both are 'weak and beggarly elements' that enslave, compared with sonship in Christ.
study.caution: The meaning of 'the elements of the world' (GAL 4:3, 9; COL 2:8, 20) is disputed. Proposals include elementary teachings or rudimentary religious practices, the physical elements, and the spirits or powers thought to rule them. Each view has strong advocates.

study.summary: Στρατεύομαι means "to serve as a soldier", and is used figuratively of the believer's spiritual warfare and of desires that wage war against the soul.

senses.label: Serve as a soldier
senses.definition: Literal military service: soldiers asking John what to do, no soldier serving at his own expense, a soldier not entangled in civilian affairs.

senses.label: Wage spiritual warfare
senses.definition: Figuratively, the minister's struggle for the gospel, waged not with worldly weapons, and Timothy's 'good warfare'.

senses.label: War against (of passions)
senses.definition: Of sinful desires that campaign within a person, at war in the members and against the soul.

background.note: Very common in the papyri for those serving in the army.

study.summary: Στρώννυμι means "to spread" something out, and so "to furnish" a room with couches or "to make" a bed.

senses.label: Spread out
senses.definition: To spread garments (and branches) on the road before Jesus at his entry into Jerusalem.

senses.label: Furnish (a room)
senses.definition: Perfect passive participle: an upper room furnished with spread couches for a meal.

senses.label: Make one's bed
senses.definition: Peter's command to the healed Aeneas: 'make your bed' (or possibly 'prepare your own meal-couch').

study.summary: Συγχαίρω means "to rejoice with" someone, sharing their joy, and possibly "to congratulate".

senses.label: Rejoice with (persons)
senses.definition: To share someone else's joy: neighbours rejoicing with Elizabeth, friends invited to rejoice over the lost found, Paul and the Philippians rejoicing together.

senses.label: Rejoice together in (things)
senses.definition: To share in rejoicing over something: all members rejoice when one is honoured, and love rejoices with the truth.

study.translationNote: In PHP 2:17–18 some scholars render the word 'congratulate', a well-attested secular sense, rather than 'rejoice with'.

background.note: Used in private letters for sharing in another's joy, e.g. a mother rejoicing with her son over his education.

study.summary: Σύνεσις means "understanding, insight": the capacity to grasp how things fit together, and that capacity as a faculty of the mind.

senses.label: Understanding, insight
senses.definition: Intelligent comprehension or insight, often spiritual, given by God: the boy Jesus' understanding, Paul's insight into the mystery of Christ, spiritual understanding of God's will; it is also human cleverness that God sets aside.

senses.label: The mind (faculty)
senses.definition: The faculty of understanding, listed with heart and soul and strength as that with which God is to be loved.

study.exegesisTip: In COL 1:9 and 2:2 σύνεσις is paired with wisdom and knowledge of God's mystery. It is understanding that grasps how God's purposes connect, given by the Spirit.

study.summary: Συντελέω means "to bring to an end, complete", and also "to accomplish, carry out, bring to fulfilment".

senses.label: Finish, come to an end
senses.definition: To complete a set period or activity: Jesus finishing his sayings, the forty days ending, the devil finishing every temptation, the seven days nearly completed.

senses.label: Accomplish, bring to fulfilment
senses.definition: To carry something out fully: the end-time events being accomplished, the Lord executing his word on the earth, and establishing a new covenant.

study.exegesisTip: In HEB 8:8 (quoting Jeremiah) συντελέσω replaces the more usual 'make' a covenant, which may stress that God will bring the covenant to completion.

study.summary: Ταπεινοφροσύνη means "humility, lowliness of mind": a modest estimate of oneself that puts others first, though in Colossians it describes a false, self-chosen ascetic humility.

senses.label: Humility, lowliness of mind
senses.definition: The Christian virtue of thinking modestly of oneself and serving others, counting others more significant, and clothing oneself with humility toward one another.

senses.label: False humility, self-abasement
senses.definition: A showy, ascetic self-humiliation (perhaps including fasting) promoted by false teachers. It looks wise but has no value against the flesh.

study.translationNote: In COL 2:18, 23 versions vary between 'false humility', 'self-abasement' and 'asceticism', because the word there refers to ascetic practice rather than true humility.

study.summary: Τάφος means a "grave" or "tomb".

senses.label: Tomb, grave
senses.definition: A burial place: the tombs of the prophets, Jesus' tomb watched by the women and sealed and guarded.

senses.label: Tomb (metaphor)
senses.definition: Used figuratively: whitewashed tombs outwardly beautiful but full of corruption, and the throat of the wicked as an open grave.

study.summary: Τάχος means "speed", and in the NT it occurs only in the phrase ἐν τάχει, "quickly, soon, without delay".

senses.label: Quickly, soon (ἐν τάχει)
senses.definition: Without delay, speedily: Peter told to get up quickly, Paul told to leave Jerusalem quickly, God's speedy vindication of his elect, Satan's soon defeat, and things that must soon take place.

study.caution: In REV 1:1, 22:6 and LUK 18:8 ἐν τάχει is variously taken as 'soon' (imminence) or 'quickly, suddenly' (speed once events begin). Interpreters of different schools disagree.

study.summary: Τράχηλος means "neck", used literally and in idioms for embracing, subjection to a yoke and risking one's life.

senses.label: Neck (literal)
senses.definition: The neck, as where a millstone would be hung on one who causes little ones to stumble.

senses.label: Fall on the neck (embrace)
senses.definition: In the idiom 'to fall on someone's neck', to embrace warmly, as the father did the prodigal and the Ephesian elders did Paul.

senses.label: Neck in figurative idioms
senses.definition: Putting a yoke on the disciples' neck, i.e. imposing the law's burden; and Prisca and Aquila who 'laid down their own necks', i.e. risked their lives.

study.summary: Τρέφω means "to feed, nourish", also "to bring up, rear" a child.

senses.label: Feed, nourish, sustain
senses.definition: To provide food or sustenance: God feeding the birds, feeding the hungry, a region supplied with food from the king's land, the woman nourished in the wilderness.

senses.label: Bring up, rear
senses.definition: To raise a child to maturity, of Nazareth where Jesus had been brought up.

senses.label: Fatten (figurative)
senses.definition: The rich have fattened their hearts in a day of slaughter, i.e. indulged themselves like animals fattened for slaughter.

study.summary: Φθάνω originally meant "to come before, precede", but in later Greek usually means "to arrive, reach, attain".

senses.label: Come upon, arrive
senses.definition: To come or arrive, especially suddenly: the kingdom of God has come upon you, and wrath has come upon them.

senses.label: Reach, attain
senses.definition: To reach a goal or point: Israel did not attain the law of righteousness, Paul came as far as Corinth with the gospel, and believers should hold to what they have attained.

senses.label: Precede, go before
senses.definition: The classical sense of getting ahead of someone: the living will by no means precede those who have fallen asleep.

study.translationNote: The KJV's 'shall not prevent' in 1TH 4:15 uses 'prevent' in its old sense of 'go before'. Modern versions render it 'precede'.

background.note: Papyri show both the older sense 'anticipate, do beforehand' and the later sense 'arrive, reach'.

study.exegesisTip: In MAT 12:28 and LUK 11:20 'has come upon you' indicates that God's kingdom is already present in Jesus' exorcisms, not merely near.

study.summary: Unrighteousness: the opposite of δικαιοσύνη — injustice in dealing, wickedness as a moral condition opposed to truth, and occasionally a single wrong act; in genitive phrases it means 'unrighteous' or 'dishonest'.

senses.label: Injustice, unjust dealing
senses.definition: Failure to give what is right or due, especially injustice by a judge or in God's dealings.
senses.note: 'Is there injustice with God?' (Rom 9:14) is the question of God's fairness.

senses.label: Wickedness, unrighteousness
senses.definition: Moral wrongness as a condition or power in human life, opposed to God's truth and righteousness.
senses.note: Repeatedly set against ἀλήθεια: love 'does not rejoice at ἀδικία but rejoices with the truth' (1 Cor 13:6).

senses.label: Falseness, untruth
senses.definition: Where the contrast is with truthfulness, the lack of integrity that makes one a false witness.
senses.note: Contrasted with ἀληθής: one who seeks the Sender's glory is true, 'and there is no ἀδικία in him'.

senses.label: Genitive: 'unrighteous', 'dishonest'
senses.definition: In Semitic-style genitive phrases the noun works as an adjective: 'wages of unrighteousness' = ill-gotten gain, 'workers of unrighteousness' = evildoers.
senses.note: 'Steward of unrighteousness' (Luke 16:8) = dishonest manager; 'mammon of unrighteousness' (16:9) = worldly wealth.

senses.label: A wrong, wrongful act
senses.definition: A specific unrighteous deed; in the plural, misdeeds or iniquities.
senses.note: Ironic in 2 Cor 12:13: 'forgive me this wrong' — not having been a burden to them.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul sets ἀδικία against both God's righteousness and the truth: people 'suppress the truth in unrighteousness', and those who perish 'took pleasure in unrighteousness'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke favours the genitive idiom: the 'judge of unrighteousness', the 'steward of unrighteousness', the 'reward of unrighteousness' Judas gained, and Simon's 'bond of unrighteousness'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: 1 John equates all unrighteousness with sin while noting not all sin is 'to death', and promises cleansing 'from all unrighteousness' on confession.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'unrighteousness' (KJV, ESV), 'wickedness' (NIV), 'injustice' and 'iniquity'. 'Unrighteousness' keeps the visible link with δικαιοσύνη (Rom 3:5), while 'wickedness' reads more naturally. Genitive phrases are often turned into adjectives ('dishonest manager', Luke 16:8). In Matt 23:25 the Byzantine text has ἀδικίας where critical editions read ἀκρασίας ('self-indulgence').

background.note: In classical Greek it is the standard word for wrongdoing and injustice, the opposite of justice in moral philosophy.
It can also denote a single wrongful act or offence.
Contracts use the formula ἐπ᾽ ἀδικίᾳ, 'to the injury of' another party; this legal idiom is essentially absent from the NT.

study.exegesisTip: Read ἀδικία against its opposites in context — δικαιοσύνη (justice), ἀλήθεια (truth) — and treat genitive phrases like 'mammon of unrighteousness' as adjectival.
study.caution: Whether 'unrighteous mammon' (Luke 16:9) means wealth wrongly gained or simply worldly wealth belonging to this unjust age is debated.

study.summary: To look up (raise the eyes, often toward heaven), and especially to gain or regain sight; in the Gospels and Acts mostly of the blind healed by Jesus or restored in his name.

senses.label: Look up
senses.definition: To raise one's eyes, whether to heaven in prayer or to see someone or something.
senses.note: Of Jesus looking up to heaven before blessing the loaves (Mark 6:41) and before healing (Mark 7:34).

senses.label: Gain or regain sight
senses.definition: To be able to see again (or for the first time) after blindness, as a result of healing.
senses.note: 'The blind receive sight' echoes Isaiah's messianic signs (Matt 11:5).

senses.label: Sight given to the born-blind
senses.definition: Used even of a man who had never seen, where the prefix ἀνα- no longer implies 'again'.
senses.note: John 9:18: 'he had been blind and had received sight'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word for Saul's restoration at Damascus and plays on both senses: 'Brother Saul, receive your sight' — 'and at that very hour I looked up at him'.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark's two-stage healing at Bethsaida begins with the man 'looking up' and seeing people 'like trees walking', where the verb may already mean 'beginning to see'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John concentrates the verb in the healing of the man born blind, where physical sight becomes a sign of spiritual sight.

study.translationNote: Because the word can mean either 'look up' or 'see again', versions differ in ambiguous places: Mark 8:24 ('he looked up' vs 'he began to see') and Acts 22:13 ('I looked up at him' vs 'I regained my sight and saw him').

background.note: Classical writers use it for looking up, e.g. toward the light in Plato's cave.
An Asclepius healing inscription uses ἀνέβλεψεν of a blind man recovering sight in the temple, closely parallel to John 9.

study.exegesisTip: Decide from context whether the word means a gesture (looking up) or a healing (receiving sight); with εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν it is the gesture of prayer.

study.summary: To uncover or reveal: to bring hidden things into the open, and especially God's disclosure of truth, of his Son, and of realities — glory, judgment, the man of lawlessness — to be unveiled at the end.

senses.label: Uncover what is hidden
senses.definition: To bring something concealed into the open so that it becomes known.
senses.note: 'Nothing is covered that will not be revealed' (Matt 10:26).

senses.label: Divine revelation of truth
senses.definition: God (or the Son, or the Spirit) making known what human insight cannot reach.
senses.note: Explicitly contrasted with 'flesh and blood' (Matt 16:17; Gal 1:16).

senses.label: Revelation to believers, prophets
senses.definition: Particular disclosures given to individuals, prophets or a congregation for guidance.

senses.label: God's righteousness and wrath disclosed
senses.definition: God's saving righteousness and his wrath made manifest in the present through the gospel and in history.
senses.note: Present tense in Rom 1:17–18: the disclosure is now under way.

senses.label: End-time unveiling
senses.definition: The future manifestation of what is now hidden: the Son of Man, coming glory and salvation, or the man of lawlessness.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb for God's present disclosure of righteousness and wrath in the gospel, for his own call ('to reveal his Son in me'), and for the future revealing of glory and of the lawless one.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter frames salvation and glory as 'ready to be revealed in the last time', and notes that the prophets were shown they served a later generation.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: In Matthew and Luke the Father hides things from the wise and reveals them to 'infants', and the Son reveals the Father to whom he chooses.

study.translationNote: In Gal 1:16 ἀποκαλύψαι τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ ἐν ἐμοί is rendered 'in me' (KJV, ESV) or 'to me' (NIV, NRSV): the first suggests inward revelation, the second a revelation given to Paul. Some versions recast Rom 1:17 actively ('the gospel reveals').

background.note: The literal sense is 'uncover', e.g. uncovering the head.
Plato uses it figuratively for disclosing one's thinking.
In the Septuagint, chiefly for Hebrew gālâ, it carries the special sense of God revealing himself.
Papyri use it of shore land 'uncovered' as the Nile receded and became cultivable.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who reveals, to whom, and whether the unveiling is present (Rom 1:17–18) or still future (Rom 8:18; 1 Pet 1:5).
study.caution: Whether 'in me' (Gal 1:16) stresses an inner experience or simply means 'to me', and what restrains the lawless one until he is 'revealed' (2 Thess 2:6–8), are long-debated.

study.summary: A tree: literally the trees of field and orchard, and in Jesus' teaching the fruit tree whose produce shows its true nature — an image of the person known by deeds.

senses.label: Tree (literal)
senses.definition: An actual tree, as a source of branches or as part of creation.
senses.note: A half-healed man sees people 'like trees, walking' (Mark 8:24).

senses.label: Fruit tree: person known by deeds
senses.definition: The good or rotten tree whose fruit reveals its nature, picturing a person's character shown in conduct.

senses.label: Tree facing judgment
senses.definition: The fruitless tree about to be cut down and burned, or uprooted, as an image of judgment.
senses.note: Jude's false teachers: 'autumn trees without fruit, twice dead, uprooted'.

senses.label: Kingdom growth image
senses.definition: In the mustard-seed parable, the tiny seed that becomes a tree sheltering birds pictures the growth of God's kingdom.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses the tree-and-fruit image repeatedly, from the Baptist's warning to the Sermon on the Mount and the Beelzebul debate.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In Revelation trees are part of the earth protected from, then struck by, the judgments.

background.note: A third-century BC law specifies how far from a neighbour's boundary olive, fig and other trees must be planted.
An Asclepius inscription tells of a blind man whose first sight after healing was of the trees in the sanctuary, recalling Mark 8:24.

study.exegesisTip: In the fruit-tree sayings the point is that what a person does shows what a person is: the tree must be made good for its fruit to be good (Matt 12:33).

study.summary: To lie or be laid: of persons lying (an infant, a corpse), of things placed or standing somewhere, figuratively of something being in place, and of what is appointed, destined or laid down.

senses.label: Lie (of persons)
senses.definition: Of a person lying somewhere: the infant Jesus in the manger, or a dead body in the tomb.
senses.note: 'Come, see the place where he lay' (Matt 28:6).

senses.label: Be placed, stand (things)
senses.definition: Of objects lying or set in a place: jars, grave-clothes, a throne, a city on a hill, goods stored up.
senses.note: Functions as the passive of τίθημι.

senses.label: Be in place (figurative)
senses.definition: Of something already set and ready, or of a condition resting on someone: the axe at the root, the foundation laid, the veil over the heart, the world under the evil one.

senses.label: Be appointed, destined
senses.definition: To be set or appointed for a purpose, or (of law) laid down for someone.
senses.note: 'This child is destined for the fall and rising of many' (Luke 2:34).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the verb for the grave-clothes lying in the empty tomb, quiet evidence that the body had not been taken, and in 1 John for the world 'lying in' the evil one.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke's infancy narrative pairs the sign of the baby 'lying in a manger' with Simeon's word that he 'is set' for the fall and rising of many.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses it of what is appointed: believers are 'destined' for afflictions, he is 'set' for the defence of the gospel, and the law is not 'laid down' for the righteous.

study.translationNote: English must choose different verbs: 'lie', 'stand', 'be set', 'be appointed/destined'. In 1 John 5:19 versions vary between 'lies in the evil one', 'lies in the power of the evil one' and 'is under the control of the evil one'. Phil 1:16 is 1:17 in versions following the Byzantine order.

background.note: A petition speaks of the bed 'where my husband's body was lying', the same use as of Jesus' body.
Epitaphs begin 'Here I lie', with κεῖμαι of the dead.
Of contracts 'laid down' and in force, illustrating 'the law is not laid down for the righteous'.
Of people 'being in' difficult circumstances, a parallel to 'the world lies in the evil one'.

study.exegesisTip: With εἰς + accusative (Luke 2:34; Phil 1:16; 1 Thess 3:3) κεῖμαι means 'be appointed for', not merely 'lie'.
study.caution: Whether ἐν τῷ πονηρῷ in 1 John 5:19 means 'in the evil one' (personal, as most take it from v. 18) or 'in evil' is debated.

study.summary: To order or command, normally by someone with authority — a king, governor, tribune, council or Jesus — usually followed by an infinitive stating what is to be done.

senses.label: Official order
senses.definition: A command issued by a ruler or official, often for an arrest, release, flogging or transfer.
senses.note: Typically with the accusative and a (often passive) infinitive: 'ordered him to be brought'.

senses.label: Jesus' commands and directions
senses.definition: Jesus directing crowds, disciples or others to do something.

senses.label: Bid, request a command
senses.definition: Asking someone to give an order, or bidding in a personal setting.
senses.note: Peter: 'Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you' (Matt 14:28).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Most uses describe Roman officials and Jewish councils giving orders during Paul's arrest and trials, showing the chain of authority around the apostle.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses it of Herod, Pilate and the master in a parable, and of Jesus' authoritative directions to the crowds and disciples.

background.note: Used from Homer onward, originally 'urge on', then 'bid, order'.
Rare in the Septuagint, appearing mainly in later books such as Tobit and Maccabees.
Common in papyri for instructions and decrees, e.g. 'what do you order about these things?'

study.exegesisTip: Note who gives the order: κελεύω stresses the speaker's authority, so its use for Jesus quietly presents him as one who commands.

study.summary: A cloud: ordinary rain clouds, but above all the cloud of God's presence (transfiguration, Exodus, ascension) and the clouds with which the Son of Man comes in glory.

senses.label: Natural cloud
senses.definition: An ordinary cloud, as a sign of coming rain, or as an image of emptiness when it brings none.
senses.note: 'Waterless clouds' picture teachers who promise much but give nothing (Jude 12).

senses.label: Cloud of God's presence
senses.definition: The cloud that marks and veils God's presence, as at the transfiguration and in the wilderness.
senses.note: A voice speaks 'from the cloud' (Luke 9:35).

senses.label: Clouds of the Son's coming
senses.definition: The clouds on or with which the Son of Man ascends and comes in power and glory.

senses.label: Clouds of heavenly ascent
senses.definition: Clouds as the means by which God's people or witnesses are taken up to heaven.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation uses clouds for Christ's coming, the angel 'clothed with a cloud', the witnesses' ascent, and the One 'like a son of man' seated on a white cloud for the harvest.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul reads Israel's passage 'under the cloud' as a baptism into Moses, and pictures believers caught up 'in clouds' to meet the Lord.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke links the cloud of Jesus' ascension with his return 'in a cloud'.

background.note: From Homer onward, also metaphorically, as of the dark cloud of death.
Chiefly for Hebrew ʿānān, the pillar of cloud that led and protected Israel.
An inscription speaks metaphorically of a 'cloud of plague'.

study.exegesisTip: Clouds in theophany scenes recall the Exodus cloud and Daniel's 'one like a son of man' coming with the clouds of heaven: they signal divine presence and glory, not weather.
study.caution: Whether the Son of Man's 'coming on the clouds' (Matt 24:30; Mark 14:62) refers to his return at the end or, as in Daniel, to his vindication and enthronement before God is debated.

study.summary: Over and above: more than is needed, abundant, or extraordinary; neuter τὸ περισσόν 'advantage'; the comparative περισσότερος means 'greater, more', and adverbially 'all the more'.

senses.label: Beyond what is needed
senses.definition: Over and above the requirement, hence superfluous; ἐκ περισσοῦ 'beyond measure'.
senses.note: 'Whatever is more than these comes from evil' (Matt 5:37).

senses.label: Abundant, in fullness
senses.definition: Present in more than sufficient measure.
senses.note: 'That they may have life, and have it abundantly.'

senses.label: Advantage, pre-eminence
senses.definition: What sets someone apart or gives them an edge; something extraordinary.
senses.note: 'What advantage has the Jew?' (Rom 3:1); John is 'more than a prophet' (Matt 11:9).

senses.label: Comparative: greater, more
senses.definition: Greater in degree or amount: greater condemnation, greater honour, excessive sorrow.

senses.label: Adverbial: even more, abundantly
senses.definition: Neuter comparative used as an adverb, 'even more, more abundantly'.
senses.note: 'I worked harder than all of them' (1 Cor 15:10).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses τὸ περισσόν for Israel's 'advantage' and the comparative for his labour 'more than all' and the 'greater honour' given to weaker members.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the adverbial comparative in its arguments: God wished 'even more' to show the unchangeableness of his purpose, and the point is 'even more' evident from Melchizedek.

study.translationNote: John 10:10 is 'more abundantly' (KJV), 'abundantly' (ESV) or 'to the full' (NIV). In Matt 5:47 versions read 'what more are you doing than others?' or 'what are you doing that is extraordinary?'. The comparative is often simply 'more' or 'greater', as popular Greek used it like πλείων.

background.note: Originally 'beyond the regular number or size', hence prodigious.
Also 'out of the common, extraordinary', of notable knowledge.
A letter speaks of the "surplus" donkeys to be sold, the plain sense of over and above.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether the context stresses quantity (abundant, more) or quality (extraordinary, advantage); Matt 5:47 and Rom 3:1 turn on the second.
study.caution: In Matt 5:47 τί περισσὸν ποιεῖτε may mean 'what more than others' or 'what extraordinary thing', and interpreters differ.

study.summary: Sexual immorality: any illicit sexual intercourse (broader than adultery), including incest and prostitution; in Matthew's divorce sayings marital unfaithfulness; figuratively, idolatrous unfaithfulness to God, especially Babylon's in Revelation.

senses.label: Sexual immorality in general
senses.definition: Unlawful sexual relations of any kind, a vice believers must flee and abstain from.
senses.note: Listed alongside but distinct from adultery (μοιχεία) in Matt 15:19 and Mark 7:21.

senses.label: Specific forbidden unions
senses.definition: Particular illicit relationships, such as a man living with his father's wife.
senses.note: The apostolic decree may have Leviticus' forbidden unions in view.

senses.label: Unfaithfulness grounding divorce
senses.definition: In the exception clause, sexual unfaithfulness that breaks the marriage bond.

senses.label: Idolatrous unfaithfulness (figurative)
senses.definition: Following the prophets' image of Israel as an unfaithful wife, spiritual and idolatrous unfaithfulness to God, and the seductive corruption of Babylon.
senses.note: 'Born of πορνεία' (John 8:41) may imply a slur on Jesus' birth or deny idolatrous descent.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul grounds his ban on πορνεία in the body belonging to the Lord and in God's will for holiness.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation uses the word both literally among sins left unrepented and figuratively for Babylon's intoxicating, corrupting influence over the nations.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Only Matthew's divorce sayings contain the exception 'except for πορνεία'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts lists πορνεία among the four requirements of the apostolic decree for Gentile believers.

study.translationNote: The KJV's 'fornication' now suggests only sex between unmarried people, which is too narrow; most modern versions use 'sexual immorality'. In Matt 5:32 and 19:9 renderings include 'unchastity', 'marital unfaithfulness' and 'sexual immorality', reflecting different views of the exception clause.

background.note: Rare in classical Greek, where it means prostitution.
The Septuagint uses it metaphorically for Israel's idolatry, the source of Revelation's imagery.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether πορνεία is literal sexual sin, a specific forbidden union, or the prophetic image of idolatry; Revelation often blends the last two.
study.caution: The exception clause (Matt 5:32; 19:9) is much debated: πορνεία has been taken as adultery, any sexual sin, unions within forbidden degrees, or unfaithfulness during betrothal; the same Levitical reading is proposed for the Acts decree.

study.summary: A soldier: in the NT mostly Roman soldiers — those who mocked and crucified Jesus and those who guarded Peter and Paul — and figuratively a Christian worker as a 'good soldier of Christ Jesus'.

senses.label: Soldier under command
senses.definition: A soldier within a chain of command, carrying out a superior's orders.
senses.note: The centurion's faith rests on this model of authority (Matt 8:9).

senses.label: Soldiers at Jesus' passion
senses.definition: The governor's soldiers who mocked, crucified and guarded Jesus.

senses.label: Guards of prisoners
senses.definition: Soldiers assigned to arrest, guard or escort prisoners, especially Peter and Paul.

senses.label: Christian as soldier (figurative)
senses.definition: A believer devoted to Christ's service, enduring hardship with single-minded loyalty.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts shows soldiers guarding Peter and escorting Paul, and also a 'devout soldier' in Cornelius's household.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John records the soldiers dividing Jesus' garments and piercing his side, both told as fulfilment of Scripture.

background.note: Standard classical term for a soldier, later especially a professional soldier.
Papyri record extortion by soldiers in villages, the kind of abuse John the Baptist warned against.
A fourth-century letter asks pardon for a deserting soldier, recalling the appeal for Onesimus in Philemon.

study.exegesisTip: In 2 Tim 2:3–4 the soldier image stresses endurance and undivided loyalty to the one who enlisted him.

study.summary: To understand: to grasp the meaning of words, events or Scripture, and especially to perceive spiritual truth with the heart; often in the negative, of Isaiah's 'hearing but not understanding'.

senses.label: Grasp the meaning
senses.definition: To comprehend what is said or done, catching the sense of a saying, parable, event or Scripture.
senses.note: Often with ὅτι, 'understood that…' (Matt 16:12; 17:13).

senses.label: Receive the word with insight
senses.definition: To take in God's message so that it is inwardly grasped and bears fruit, the mark of the good soil in the parable of the sower.

senses.label: Failure to understand (spiritual dullness)
senses.definition: Negated, the word describes hearts that hear and see without perceiving, echoing Isaiah 6:9–10, or disciples who miss the meaning of Jesus' signs.
senses.note: 'Do you still not understand?' (Mark 8:17, 21).

senses.label: Moral and religious insight
senses.definition: Understanding that issues in right relation to God and discernment of his will; ὁ συνίων is 'the one who understands', the wise man in a religious sense.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew makes understanding a mark of true disciples: in contrast to the crowds they 'understand' the parables and Jesus' teaching.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark presses the disciples' own failure to understand, even after the feeding miracles.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke stresses that understanding Jesus' suffering comes only when the risen Lord opens minds to the Scriptures; Acts closes with Isaiah's word of non-understanding.

background.note: The literal sense is 'to send or bring together'; in Homer it already means to hear and take heed, to mark what is said.
A third-century BC letter uses 'I understand' where a parallel letter has ἐπίσταμαι, showing the ordinary sense 'know, perceive'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask what is or is not understood (a parable, a sign, Scripture, God's will) and whether the context ties understanding to repentance and fruit.
study.caution: Whether ἵνα … μὴ συνιῶσιν in Mark 4:12 (cf. Luke 8:10) expresses purpose ('in order that they may not understand') or result, or simply marks the fulfilment of Isaiah, is debated.

study.summary: To bring to an end: to finish a task or period, carry out what is required, see God's plan or Scripture fulfilled, and (in commerce) to pay what is owed.

senses.label: Finish, bring to an end
senses.definition: To complete an activity or a set period so that it is over.
senses.note: Matt 10:23, 'you will not finish (going through) the towns of Israel'.

senses.label: Carry out, perform, keep
senses.definition: To do fully what is prescribed or written, such as the requirements of the Law or the royal law of love.
senses.note: Gal 5:16, 'you will not carry out the desire of the flesh'.

senses.label: Be fulfilled, accomplished
senses.definition: Passive: of God's purposes, prophecy, or Christ's appointed suffering reaching their intended completion.
senses.note: Also of God's wrath and words being completed (Rev 15:1; 17:17).

senses.label: Pay (taxes, dues)
senses.definition: To discharge a payment owed, such as the temple tax or civil taxes.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew closes each of Jesus' five great discourses with the formula 'when Jesus had finished…'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's Gospel uses the perfect τετέλεσται at the cross: Jesus' work is accomplished. Revelation uses the passive for the completion of God's mystery, wrath and decreed periods.

study.translationNote: Versions render the same verb as 'finish', 'complete', 'accomplish', 'fulfil' or 'pay' depending on context; John 19:30 is usually 'It is finished', though some prefer 'It is accomplished' or 'completed' to bring out the link with 19:28.

background.note: Common for accomplishing what is requested: 'until you accomplish this for me'.
Widely used for paying taxes and rent; tax receipts are often headed τετέλεσται, 'paid'.

study.exegesisTip: Notice whether the verb is active (someone finishes or performs) or passive (something is fulfilled, often by God's design), and what is being brought to its end.
study.caution: Because receipts were marked τετέλεσται, some read John 19:30 as 'paid in full'; most scholars see the main sense as completion of the work and Scripture (cf. 19:28), with any commercial nuance at most secondary.

study.summary: Sister: a female sibling by birth, and by extension a woman who belongs to the family of Jesus' followers, a fellow believer.

senses.label: Sister by birth
senses.definition: A female sibling in a natural family.
senses.note: Includes the sisters of Jesus (Mark 6:3; Matt 13:56).

senses.label: Family of Jesus' disciples
senses.definition: Those who do God's will form Jesus' true family; family left for his sake is restored in the community of disciples.

senses.label: Fellow believer (Christian woman)
senses.definition: A woman who is a member of the Christian community, addressed and treated as family.
senses.note: 1 Tim 5:2 tells Timothy to treat younger women 'as sisters, with absolute purity'.

senses.label: Sister congregation
senses.definition: Figuratively, a church described as a sister whose 'children' (members) send greetings.
senses.note: Most interpreters take the 'elect sister' as a sister church.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's uses centre on Martha and Mary, the sisters of Lazarus, whose grief and faith frame the raising of Lazarus.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses 'sister' of believing women as members of the household of faith, commending them (Phoebe) and giving them standing in marriage questions.

study.translationNote: In 1 Cor 9:5 ἀδελφὴν γυναῖκα is rendered 'a believing wife' (ESV, NIV) or 'a sister, a wife' (KJV); 'sister' here means a fellow believer, not a sibling.

background.note: In Egypt a wife could be addressed as 'sister', reflecting sibling marriage and later affectionate usage: 'Hilarion to Alis his sister'.
'Sister' was also an honorary royal title: Berenice, a cousin, is called the king's 'sister and wife'.
The Septuagint uses 'sister' as a term of endearment for the beloved in the Song of Songs.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether 'sister' is literal kinship or the new family of faith; in Jesus' sayings the second often redefines the first.
study.caution: The 'sisters' of Jesus (Mark 6:3; Matt 13:56) are understood as later daughters of Mary and Joseph, daughters of Joseph by an earlier marriage, or cousins; the term itself does not settle the question.

study.summary: True: corresponding to fact (a true saying, valid testimony, a real event), and of persons, truthful and honest; God is supremely ἀληθής.

senses.label: True to fact
senses.definition: Of statements, reports and sayings: corresponding to reality, not false.

senses.label: Valid (as testimony)
senses.definition: Of witness in a legal setting: trustworthy and admissible, so that it establishes the matter.
senses.note: John 8:17 recalls the rule that two witnesses establish a matter.

senses.label: Real, genuine
senses.definition: Actually so, not illusory or counterfeit.
senses.note: Acts 12:9: Peter did not know what was happening was real; he thought it a vision.

senses.label: Truthful, honest (of persons)
senses.definition: Of people or God: speaking and acting in truth, without deceit or flattery.
senses.note: 2 Cor 6:8: apostles regarded as deceivers 'yet true'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John (about two-thirds of the uses) develops the word within a trial of testimony: whether witness to Jesus is valid, and that God who sent him is truthful.

study.translationNote: In John 5:31 and 8:13–17 older versions say 'true' and newer ones 'valid' (NIV, MSB); the issue is legal admissibility of self-testimony, which explains why 5:31 ('not true') and 8:14 ('true') do not contradict.

background.note: From Homer on it means 'true' as opposed to false, as in the phrase 'to tell the truth'.
Common in legal formulas such as 'if what I write is true', with the ordinary sense 'true in fact'.
Also used of being genuinely so, e.g. legitimate children or that a boy is truly of priestly family.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether a statement's factual truth, a witness's legal validity, or a person's truthful character is in view.
study.caution: The distinction ἀληθής 'true to fact' versus ἀληθινός 'genuine, real' is useful but not rigid, since John overlaps them; nor should the etymology 'unconcealed' be read into NT usage.

study.summary: Weak: without strength — physically sick or frail, lacking power or status, and in Paul weak in conscience or faith; also the moral frailty of human nature.

senses.label: Sick, ill
senses.definition: Bodily debilitated by illness or disability; substantively 'the sick'.

senses.label: Physically weak, frail
senses.definition: Lacking bodily strength or impressive presence.
senses.note: 1 Pet 3:7, the wife as 'the weaker vessel'.

senses.label: Powerless, insignificant, ineffective
senses.definition: Lacking power, standing or effectiveness, whether people of low status or principles and laws unable to save.
senses.note: 1 Cor 1:25, 'the weakness of God' is stronger than men.

senses.label: Morally and spiritually weak
senses.definition: Unable in oneself to resist sin or stand firm; helpless before God.
senses.note: 'The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.'

senses.label: Weak in conscience
senses.definition: A believer whose conscience is not yet secure in Christian freedom and who is easily caused to stumble.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (about half the uses) turns weakness into a theme: God chooses the weak, apostles appear weak, and the strong must bear with the weak in conscience.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word of the sick whom Jesus' messengers heal.

study.translationNote: The same word is rendered 'sick' (Matt 25; Acts 5) or 'weak'; in Matt 26:41 some versions say 'the body is weak' instead of 'the flesh is weak', and in Rom 5:6 'weak' becomes 'helpless' or 'powerless' (NIV).

background.note: Herodotus uses it of the sick and weak left behind by an army.
A petitioner complains of being despised 'as a weak woman', i.e. without power to defend herself.
Epictetus couples 'the weak' with the uneducated, a moral use like Paul's.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether weakness is bodily illness, low status, moral frailty or an uninformed conscience; Paul often plays these against human ideas of strength.
study.caution: Who the 'weak' in 1 Cor 8 were — Gentile converts still feeling the reality of idols, or scrupulous Jewish believers — and how far they match the weak of Rom 14–15 is debated.

study.summary: To be a slave, serve as a slave: literal bondage, wholehearted service of God or Christ, enslavement to sin, idols or appetites, and loving service of others.

senses.label: Be a slave, be in bondage
senses.definition: To be in the condition of a slave or a subject people, under another's control.
senses.note: Gal 4:25, Jerusalem 'is in slavery with her children'.

senses.label: Serve God or Christ
senses.definition: To give oneself in total, obedient service to God or Christ as one's master.
senses.note: 'You cannot serve both God and money' (Luke 16:13).

senses.label: Enslaved to sin or false masters
senses.definition: To be under the power of sin, false gods, cosmic 'elements', or one's own appetites and passions.
senses.note: Rom 16:18, serving 'their own belly'.

senses.label: Serve others
senses.definition: To render humble, devoted service to people, as a son to a father or believers to one another in love.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul frames life as service under one of two masters: sin, the law of sin and idols, or God, Christ and one another in love; freedom in Christ is freedom to serve.

study.translationNote: Most versions say 'serve', but the word means service as a slave (δοῦλος); 'be a slave to' (Rom 6:6; Gal 4:8) keeps the note of total belonging that 'serve' can soften.

background.note: The Septuagint uses it chiefly for Hebrew ʿābad, both for subjection to a ruler and for serving God.
Greek moralists spoke of being a slave to belly, sleep or lust, close to Paul's 'serving their own appetites'.
A religious use ('I serve your angel') appears in a syncretistic magical text, though such use is rare in pagan sources.

study.exegesisTip: Look at the dative: whom or what one serves (God, Christ, sin, the belly, one another) defines the master and the kind of slavery.
study.caution: In Rom 12:11 most manuscripts read 'serving the Lord' (κυρίῳ), but some read 'serving the time/opportunity' (καιρῷ); the original reading is debated.

study.summary: To leave behind: depart from a place or person, leave someone somewhere, forsake or abandon, leave survivors at death, or leave remaining and reserve.

senses.label: Leave, depart from
senses.definition: To go away from a place or people, leaving them behind.
senses.note: Acts 21:3, sailing past Cyprus 'leaving it on the left'.

senses.label: Leave someone in a place or state
senses.definition: To leave a person behind somewhere, or in a condition, for a purpose.

senses.label: Forsake, abandon
senses.definition: To give up or turn away from someone or something, often for a higher loyalty.
senses.note: Leaving father and mother for marriage (Gen 2:24 cited).

senses.label: Leave behind at death
senses.definition: To leave a widow, children or heirs on one's death.

senses.label: Leave remaining, reserve
senses.definition: To cause or allow to remain; to keep back for oneself.
senses.note: Rom 11:4, 'I have reserved for myself seven thousand'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses it most often, from Levi leaving everything to follow Jesus to the movements and imprisonment of Paul.

background.note: Very common in wills and estate papers for property left or bequeathed.
Also of leaving someone 'in the lurch', close to the sense of forsaking.

study.exegesisTip: The participle καταλιπών ('leaving them, he went') in Matthew is often a vivid narrative idiom rather than a separate act of abandonment.

study.summary: White: the colour white, and especially the brilliant whiteness of heavenly beings and glory; in Revelation the white robes of the redeemed signify purity and victory.

senses.label: White in colour
senses.definition: Of ordinary objects or features that are white, such as hair, a horse, a cloud or a stone.

senses.label: Dazzling, heavenly brightness
senses.definition: The shining white of Jesus' transfigured clothing and of angels, signalling heavenly glory.
senses.note: Also the 'great white throne' of judgment (Rev 20:11).

senses.label: White robes of the redeemed
senses.definition: Garments of the faithful in Revelation, symbolising purity, victory and fitness for God's presence.
senses.note: The elders and the martyrs are likewise clothed in white (Rev 4:4; 6:11).

senses.label: Ripe for harvest
senses.definition: Of fields whose grain has turned pale, ready to be reaped.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Nearly all of John's uses are in Revelation, where white marks the heavenly world, victory and purity: robes, horses, stone, cloud and throne.

study.translationNote: In John 4:35 'white unto harvest' (KJV) is often rendered 'ripe for harvest' (NIV, MSB), which gives the meaning rather than the colour.

background.note: Ecclesiastes urges, 'let your garments be always white', white clothing as a sign of festivity.
An inscription requires entry into a temple 'pure, in white clothing', illustrating ceremonial use.
In a list of soldiers one Apollonius is 'the fair' (λευκός) as distinct from 'the dark'.

study.exegesisTip: In the Gospels and Acts white usually signals a heavenly appearance; in Revelation ask what the white object symbolises in its setting.
study.caution: The 'white stone' of Rev 2:17 is variously explained as a juror's vote of acquittal, a token of admission to a feast, an amulet, or a reference to the manna; no explanation is certain.

study.summary: To grieve: actively, to cause someone pain or sorrow; passively, to be sad, distressed or hurt, including godly sorrow that leads to repentance.

senses.label: Cause grief or pain
senses.definition: To distress or hurt someone, whether by words, discipline or conduct.
senses.note: Eph 4:30: 'do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God'.

senses.label: Be sad, sorrowful
senses.definition: Passive: to feel grief or sorrow, as at loss, bad news or a hard demand.
senses.note: Also of trials (1 Pet 1:6) and Peter's hurt at Jesus' third question (John 21:17).

senses.label: Be distressed, hurt by conduct
senses.definition: To be offended or upset by what others do.

senses.label: Sorrow leading to repentance
senses.definition: Grief 'according to God' that produces repentance and earnestness rather than despair.
senses.note: 2 Cor 6:10, 'sorrowful, yet always rejoicing'.

senses.label: Jesus' anguish
senses.definition: The deep distress of Jesus in Gethsemane.

authorNotes.author: Paul
