authorNotes.note: Paul's uses cluster in 2 Corinthians, around the painful visit and severe letter that grieved the church yet led to repentance.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew notes the disciples' deep grief at Jesus' passion predictions and at the announcement of betrayal.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John promises that the disciples' grief will be turned into joy.

background.note: A letter urges 'do not grieve over the departed', a close parallel to 1 Thess 4:13.
A pagan epitaph shows a stoic face toward death: 'I am not, and I do not grieve'.
In classical Greek it is the opposite of 'to gladden', of pain in body or mind.

study.exegesisTip: Ask what kind of grief is meant — loss, offence, or sorrow 'according to God' — and whether it ends in despair or in joy and repentance.
study.caution: Who caused the grief in 2 Cor 2:5 — the incestuous man of 1 Cor 5 or another opponent of Paul — is debated.

study.summary: To learn: to acquire knowledge by instruction, to grasp a lesson or meaning, to find out a fact, and to learn by experience or habit how to live.

senses.label: Learn by instruction
senses.definition: To receive teaching from someone and come to know it; often of the apostolic tradition or of learning Christ.
senses.note: Eph 4:20, 'you did not so learn Christ'.

senses.label: Grasp a lesson or meaning
senses.definition: To understand the point of a saying, example or Scripture.

senses.label: Find out, ascertain
senses.definition: Especially in the aorist: to discover or be informed of a fact.

senses.label: Learn by experience, practice
senses.definition: To come to know something through experience, or to acquire a habit or way of life.
senses.note: Heb 5:8, 'He learned obedience from what He suffered'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word of received Christian teaching that shapes life, and of lessons learned in practice, such as contentment.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses a play on 'learned' (ἔμαθεν) and 'suffered' (ἔπαθεν) for the Son's learning obedience.

study.translationNote: In 1 Tim 5:13 most versions say 'they learn to be idle', taking ἀργαί as the thing learned, while others read 'being idle, they learn (to go) from house to house'.

background.note: A mother rejoices 'on hearing that you are learning Egyptian letters'.
The aorist imperative μάθε means 'know, find out', as in Acts 23:27.

study.exegesisTip: Note what is learned and from whom (Christ, Scripture, apostles, experience): learning in the NT is meant to issue in a way of life.
study.caution: The construction of 1 Tim 5:13 (ἀργαὶ μανθάνουσιν) is debated, and the force of 'let a woman learn in quietness' (1 Tim 2:11) is much disputed.

study.summary: Negative particle 'lest (perhaps)': introduces a feared or prevented outcome after warnings and verbs of caution, and in later Greek also a tentative 'perhaps' or a hesitant question ('could it be that…?', 'whether perhaps').

senses.label: Lest, so that not (purpose)
senses.definition: Introduces a negative purpose or an outcome to be averted: 'otherwise', 'so that … not'. The idea is chance ('lest haply') more than time.
senses.note: In the quotation of Isa 6:9–10 it marks the dreaded result of hardening: 'otherwise they might turn' (MAR 4:12).

senses.label: Lest, after warnings and fears
senses.definition: After verbs of taking heed, fearing or warning, it states the danger to be guarded against: 'take care lest…'.
senses.note: With the verb understood: 'lest perhaps you be found fighting against God' (ACT 5:39).

senses.label: Perhaps, possibly
senses.definition: In a main clause, a cautious statement of possibility: 'perhaps', 'it may be that'.
senses.note: The wise virgins: 'perhaps there will not be enough for us and you'.

senses.label: Hesitant question
senses.definition: In a direct question it expects a doubtful or negative answer ('surely … not?', 'can it be that…?'); in an indirect question it means 'whether perhaps'.
senses.note: 2 Tim 2:25: 'in the hope that perhaps God will grant them repentance'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word in the widest range: practical warnings in parables, 'whether perhaps' John was the Christ, and Gamaliel's caution against fighting God.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses it in its solemn warnings, urging readers to take care lest they drift away, harbour an unbelieving heart or fall short of God's rest.

study.translationNote: English versions vary between 'lest', 'otherwise', 'so that … not' and 'perhaps', because the particle covers purpose, fear, possibility and questioning. In JOH 7:26 some render it as a statement ('surely the rulers do not know?'), others as an open question ('Can it be that the rulers really know?').

background.note: In Homer it can mean 'never', especially in oaths, and introduces prohibitions and warnings.
Everyday letters use it for 'lest haply': officials withdraw a memorandum lest they come to grief at the audit.
A close parallel to Luke 21:34: 'we are taking precautions lest he should deal despitefully with us'.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether the clause states a danger to avoid ('lest'), a cautious possibility ('perhaps'), or a hesitant question; the tone of the whole sentence depends on it.
study.caution: In MAR 4:12 (and parallels) whether μήποτε expresses purpose or result of Jesus' parables is debated; at HEB 9:17 manuscripts and editors differ between μήποτε ('never'/'is it ever?') and μὴ τότε ('not … then').

study.summary: To fill (aorist and future forms of πίμπλημι): literally to fill a space or vessel; especially in Luke–Acts, of people suddenly filled with the Holy Spirit or an overpowering emotion; also of time or prophecy being fulfilled.

senses.label: Fill a place or object
senses.definition: To make something full, with a thing or with people.
senses.note: The sponge soaked with sour wine (JOH 19:29); the city filled with confusion (ACT 19:29).

senses.label: Filled with the Holy Spirit
senses.definition: Of persons seized and empowered by the Spirit, usually for inspired speech or bold witness.
senses.note: Also ACT 9:17 (Saul) and ACT 13:9 (Paul before Elymas).

senses.label: Overcome by an emotion
senses.definition: Of people taken possession of by a strong feeling such as rage, awe, amazement or jealousy.

senses.label: Time or prophecy fulfilled
senses.definition: Of an appointed period running its course ('the time came') or of written prophecy being accomplished.
senses.note: A Septuagintal idiom reflecting Hebrew mālēʾ ('be full, be completed').

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Nearly all uses are Lukan. Luke's characteristic 'filled with the Holy Spirit' (passive aorist with genitive) marks moments of Spirit-given speech, alongside the same construction for being filled with wrath or fear.

study.translationNote: In the time sense most modern versions paraphrase ('the time came for her to give birth', LUK 1:57), while the KJV keeps the idiom ('her full time came', 'the days were accomplished'). Lexicons list these forms under πίμπλημι, so the word may not appear under πλήθω in some tools.

background.note: The intransitive πλήθω means 'to be full', e.g. of a river full of corpses in Homer.
Ordinary use with accusative and genitive, as in Matt 27:48: 'fill the jar with green mustard'.
The aorist passive with genitive, frequent in Luke, appears in a magical text: 'filled with divine wisdom'.
Mainly renders Hebrew mālēʾ, including the completion of an appointed time.

study.exegesisTip: In Luke–Acts compare 'filled (ἐπλήσθη) with the Spirit' for a particular moment of empowerment with 'full (πλήρης) of the Spirit' for an abiding character.
study.caution: How sharply Luke distinguishes repeated 'fillings' for specific tasks (πίμπλημι) from an ongoing state ('full of the Spirit', or Paul's command to 'be filled' using πληρόω) is debated, as is its relation to Spirit-baptism.

study.summary: Spiritual: belonging to, produced by, or animated by God's Spirit (as opposed to the merely natural or fleshly); used of gifts, persons, blessings, the resurrection body and, once, of spiritual (evil) powers.

senses.label: From or of the Spirit
senses.definition: Of things that come from, belong to or are marked by the divine Spirit: gifts, blessings, wisdom, songs, words.
senses.note: The law itself is 'spiritual', of divine origin and character, in contrast to the 'fleshly' self (ROM 7:14).

senses.label: Spiritual persons
senses.definition: People led and enabled by God's Spirit, mature enough to discern and to restore others.
senses.note: Contrasted with the 'natural' (ψυχικός) person and the 'fleshly' (σαρκικός) believer (1Co 2:14–3:1).

senses.label: Spiritual gifts and things
senses.definition: Neuter plural τὰ πνευματικά: gifts or manifestations of the Spirit, or spiritual benefits contrasted with material ones.
senses.note: In ROM 15:27 and 1CO 9:11 spiritual blessings are set against material (σαρκικά) support.

senses.label: Spiritual body
senses.definition: The resurrection body, animated and governed by God's Spirit, in contrast to the present 'natural' (ψυχικόν) body.
senses.note: Spirit-empowered, not necessarily immaterial.

senses.label: Typological, Spirit-given provision
senses.definition: Of Israel's wilderness food, drink and rock as supernatural provisions pointing to Christ.

senses.label: Spiritual beings or forces
senses.definition: Neuter plural for beings of the spirit realm, here hostile powers of evil.
senses.note: 'Spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Almost exclusively Pauline. Paul sets πνευματικός against ψυχικός ('natural') and σαρκικός ('fleshly'), so that 'spiritual' means shaped by the Holy Spirit, not merely inward or non-physical.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: Peter applies temple language to the church: believers are a 'spiritual house' offering 'spiritual sacrifices'.

study.translationNote: In 1CO 12:1 τῶν πνευματικῶν can be masculine ('spiritual people') or neuter ('spiritual things/gifts'); most versions supply 'gifts', some note 'spiritual persons'. In 1CO 2:13 the closing phrase is rendered variously ('interpreting spiritual truths to spiritual people', 'combining spiritual thoughts with spiritual words').

background.note: In Aristotle and scientific writers it means 'of wind or air', 'pneumatic'.
It could describe something of subtle, air-like substance, e.g. a 'dry vapour'.
Rare in the papyri; one text speaks of a 'spiritual threatening'.

study.exegesisTip: When Paul calls something 'spiritual', ask whether the contrast is with 'fleshly' or 'natural'; the word usually points to the Holy Spirit's work rather than to the immaterial.
study.caution: Scholars debate whether 1CO 12:1 refers to 'spiritual gifts' or 'spiritual people', and what kind of body the 'spiritual body' of 1CO 15:44 is (Spirit-animated physical body or a body of heavenly substance).

study.summary: Hearing: the sense or act of hearing, the ear, and what is heard: a report or rumour, or a message proclaimed, notably the gospel message received with faith.

senses.label: Sense or act of hearing
senses.definition: The faculty of hearing, or the act of listening; in the Hebraic idiom ἀκοῇ ἀκούσετε, 'you will indeed hear'.

senses.label: Ear(s)
senses.definition: The organ of hearing; 'into the ears of the people' = in their hearing.
senses.note: 'Itching ears' (2TI 4:3); 'dull of hearing', literally 'dull in your ears' (HEB 5:11).

senses.label: Message, preaching
senses.definition: What is heard as proclaimed: the prophetic or apostolic message.
senses.note: 'Lord, who has believed our message?' (Isa 53:1). λόγος ἀκοῆς = 'the word heard' (1TH 2:13).

senses.label: Report, news, rumour
senses.definition: Reports spreading about a person or events.
senses.note: 'Wars and rumours of wars' (MAT 24:6).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul makes ἀκοή a key term for how faith arises: faith comes from the message heard, and the Spirit was received 'by hearing with faith' rather than by works of the law.

study.translationNote: In ROM 10:17 versions vary between 'hearing' (KJV, ESV) and 'the message' (NIV); in GAL 3:2, 5 ἐξ ἀκοῆς πίστεως is rendered 'by hearing with faith', 'by believing what you heard' or 'by the message of faith', depending on whether the act of hearing or the thing heard is meant.

background.note: From Homer it means a sound heard and also tidings; historians use ἀκοῇ for knowledge 'by hearsay'.
Herodotus speaks of learning things 'by hearsay' (ἀκοῇ).
Renders Hebrew words from šāmaʿ; the idiom 'if you will diligently hear' uses ἀκοῇ with ἀκούειν.
Used concretely of the ear: 'it came to my ears'; also joined with smell as in 1 Cor 12:17.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether ἀκοή means the act of hearing, the ear, or the message heard; in Rom 10 and Gal 3 the choice shapes how faith and proclamation are related.
study.caution: Whether ἀκοὴ πίστεως in GAL 3:2, 5 means 'hearing accompanied by faith' or 'the message that calls for faith' (or 'the message of the faith') is a long-standing exegetical debate.

study.summary: Weakness: bodily sickness or disability, the frailty and limitation of human existence, and, in Paul, the weakness through which God's power is displayed.

senses.label: Sickness, disease
senses.definition: A bodily illness or disabling condition; plural 'sicknesses, infirmities'.
senses.note: 'This sickness will not end in death' (JOH 11:4); Timothy's 'frequent ailments' (1TI 5:23).

senses.label: Human frailty, mortal weakness
senses.definition: The limitation and vulnerability of human nature and the mortal body, including liability to temptation.
senses.note: Christ 'was crucified in weakness' (2CO 13:4); the Spirit helps 'our weakness' in prayer (ROM 8:26).

senses.label: Limited understanding
senses.definition: Moral or intellectual frailty requiring accommodation in teaching.
senses.note: 'Because of the weakness of your flesh' Paul speaks in human terms.

senses.label: Weakness as setting for God's power
senses.definition: The apostle's lack of impressive strength, hardship and humiliation, in which Christ's power is made perfect.
senses.note: 'My power is perfected in weakness' (2CO 12:9).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul turns weakness into a theme of boasting: his weaknesses display Christ's power, mirroring Christ crucified in weakness.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses it of the human frailty shared by priests and by the high priest who sympathizes with 'our weaknesses', yet without sin.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses it in healing narratives for diseases and disabling conditions.

study.translationNote: The same word is rendered 'sickness', 'infirmity', 'disease' or 'weakness' depending on context (e.g. MAT 8:17 'infirmities'); in 2 Corinthians the KJV's 'infirmities' can obscure the link with Paul's broader theme of 'weakness'.

background.note: Classical writers use it for want of strength, including bodily sickliness, the weakness of old age and even poverty.
Plato uses it morally of 'the weakness of human nature'.
Very common of illness: a man 'unable to sail through weakness', illustrating Gal 4:13 'because of a weakness of the flesh'.
Someone signs on another's behalf 'because of his weakness', a frequent reason in documents.

study.exegesisTip: Look for what the weakness is contrasted with (health, divine power, glory, strength) to decide whether illness, mortal frailty or apostolic lowliness is meant.
study.caution: The nature of the 'weakness of the flesh' that led Paul to preach in Galatia (GAL 4:13; eye disease, malaria, injuries from persecution) and its relation to his 'thorn in the flesh' are much debated.

study.summary: Star: a heavenly body; in the NT the star of the Magi, stars falling as end-time signs, and symbolic stars in Revelation (angels of the churches, the morning star) and Jude.

senses.label: Star in the sky
senses.definition: A literal heavenly body, differing from others in brightness.
senses.note: The star that guided the Magi (Matt 2).

senses.label: Stars in cosmic upheaval
senses.definition: Stars falling or darkened as signs of God's judgment and the end of the age, in prophetic imagery.
senses.note: A 'star fallen from heaven' given a key may be a personal being (REV 9:1).

senses.label: Symbol of angels or messengers
senses.definition: In Revelation, the seven stars in Christ's hand are 'the angels of the seven churches'; stars also crown the woman.

senses.label: The morning star
senses.definition: Messianic title of Christ, and the reward he gives to those who overcome.
senses.note: Cf. Num 24:17, 'a star shall come out of Jacob'.

senses.label: Wandering stars
senses.definition: Figurative for false teachers, erratic and doomed to darkness.
senses.note: Probably planets or meteors that do not keep a fixed course.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation accounts for most uses, all symbolic: stars as angels, judgment signs, fallen beings and Christ as 'the bright morning star'.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew alone narrates the star that announced the King's birth and led the Magi to Bethlehem.

background.note: From Homer onward of stars and also of shooting stars or meteors; used metaphorically of illustrious persons.
An inscription says Amon Ra 'shone like a bright star' on the despairing, a figure like Revelation's.
Outside inscriptions the word appears mainly in astronomical, astrological and magical texts.

study.exegesisTip: In Revelation read stars symbolically, following the book's own key ('the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches', REV 1:20).
study.caution: The nature of the Magi's star (miraculous light, comet, planetary conjunction) and the identity of the 'angels' of the churches (heavenly angels, human messengers or leaders, or the churches' spirit) are debated.

study.summary: To make known, reveal, declare; in the NT mostly of God revealing his mystery and will, or of apostles solemnly declaring the gospel; rarely 'to know, discern' (Phil 1:22).

senses.label: Reveal (divine disclosure)
senses.definition: Of God or Christ making known what was hidden: his name, his will, his mystery, his power.
senses.note: Also ROM 9:22, ROM 9:23 (God making known his power and the riches of his glory).

senses.label: Make known, inform
senses.definition: To tell, report or communicate news or facts to others.
senses.note: Tychicus is sent to 'make known' Paul's circumstances (EPH 6:21; COL 4:7).

senses.label: Declare solemnly
senses.definition: A formula introducing an important statement of the gospel or apostolic teaching: 'I want you to know'.

senses.label: Make requests known
senses.definition: To present one's petitions to God in prayer.

senses.label: Know, discern
senses.definition: To know or be able to say, the common classical sense.
senses.note: 'What I shall choose I do not know' (or 'cannot tell').

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul links the verb with 'mystery': God has now made known his long-hidden plan in Christ, including the Gentiles' share in it.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John, Jesus makes the Father's name and words known to his disciples, treating them as friends.

study.translationNote: In PHP 1:22 versions differ between 'I do not know' (most) and 'I cannot tell / I will not say' (making it 'make known'), since elsewhere in the NT the verb always means 'make known'.

background.note: Classical Greek uses it both for 'make known, point out' and for 'gain knowledge of, discover'.
In the Septuagint it mainly renders the causative of Hebrew yādaʿ, 'cause to know'.
In legal papyri it means to identify or vouch for a person ('whom you are to recognize at your own risk').
Later letters use it plainly for 'make known': 'I make the matter known to your nobility'.

study.exegesisTip: Note who makes known and what is revealed; in Ephesians and Colossians the verb belongs to the language of revealed 'mystery', not human discovery.
study.caution: Whether PHP 1:22 is the only NT instance of the sense 'know' or should be read as 'I do not declare (which I prefer)' is debated.

study.summary: Conjunction 'because, since' (= διὰ τοῦτο ὅτι), giving a cause; often weakened to 'for', introducing an explanation or a Scripture proof; in late Greek sometimes simply 'that'.

senses.label: Because (cause)
senses.definition: States the reason for an action or situation, usually more emphatically than ὅτι.
senses.note: 'There was no room for them in the inn' (LUK 2:7).

senses.label: For (explanatory ground)
senses.definition: Introduces a supporting explanation or ground for what precedes, close to γάρ.

senses.label: For (introducing Scripture)
senses.definition: Introduces a quotation from the Old Testament that grounds the argument: 'for it is written'.

senses.label: Since (reason in exhortation)
senses.definition: Gives the reason motivating a command or appeal, often God's action or judgment.
senses.note: 'Lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near' (LUK 21:28).

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter uses διότι to introduce Scripture proofs (Lev, Isa), where other writers would use γάρ or γέγραπται.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In Romans Paul uses it in key steps of argument, grounding God's wrath and the failure of works of law.

background.note: Classical prose uses it for 'because, for the reason that', and also in indirect questions ('why').
In the papyri, as in the Septuagint and late Greek generally, it often means simply 'that': 'you know that the place is deserted'.
The Rosetta Stone uses it for 'that' after an expression of making known.
Frequent in the Septuagint, mostly for Hebrew kî.

study.exegesisTip: Check whether διότι gives the real cause ('because') or simply supports the previous statement ('for'); the logic of Paul's argument in Rom 1–3 depends on it.
study.caution: In Romans 8, where creation waits 'in hope', manuscripts differ between διότι and ὅτι, and interpreters debate whether it means 'because' or gives the content of hope ('in hope that creation itself will be set free').

study.summary: To look at, behold, see: usually attentive, deliberate looking at something or someone; in John's writings especially the eyewitness 'seeing' of Jesus' glory that grounds testimony.

senses.label: Look at attentively
senses.definition: To gaze at, observe carefully, go out to view something.
senses.note: 'What did you go out into the wilderness to look at?'

senses.label: See, notice
senses.definition: To catch sight of, perceive with the eyes in the course of events.

senses.label: Witness, behold as eyewitness
senses.definition: To see with one's own eyes as a witness, especially Christ's glory and saving acts, leading to testimony or faith.
senses.note: 'No one has ever seen God' (1JO 4:12).

senses.label: Be seen (passive)
senses.definition: Passive: to be seen or noticed by others, especially seeking an audience for one's piety.
senses.note: 'To be seen by them' (πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι).

senses.label: Visit, see someone
senses.definition: To see a person in the sense of visiting them.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses θεάομαι for the apostolic eyewitness of the incarnate Word: 'we beheld his glory', 'what we have looked upon', 'we have seen and testify'.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses the passive for hypocritical religion done 'to be seen' by people.

study.translationNote: Versions use 'see', 'behold', 'look at' or 'gaze upon'; older versions' 'beheld' (JOH 1:14) suggests sustained contemplation, while modern 'have seen' is plainer.

background.note: Classical writers use it of looking with wonder, especially as a spectator at a show (cf. θέα 'sight', θέατρον 'theatre').
A recipient of a vision in the Serapeum writes 'I have beheld this vision'.
It can mean no more than ordinary seeing: a woman longs 'to see' her mother.

study.exegesisTip: In John 1:14 and 1 John 1:1 notice that θεάομαι stands beside other sense verbs (heard, seen, touched) to stress real, physical eyewitness.
study.caution: Whether θεάομαι in John always means physical sight, or also implies spiritual perception of what is seen (JOH 1:14), is debated; some older claims of a sharp difference from ὁράω and θεωρέω are overstated.

study.summary: To accomplish, produce, bring about: an emphatic, result-oriented 'work' — to commit deeds (often evil), to produce effects (suffering produces endurance), to work out to completion, or to prepare.

senses.label: Produce, bring about
senses.definition: To cause a result or effect: something produces or yields something else.
senses.note: 'Suffering produces endurance' (ROM 5:3); 'the law brings wrath' (ROM 4:15).

senses.label: Do, commit, practise
senses.definition: To carry out an action, especially wrongdoing.
senses.note: In ROM 7:15–20 'what I do' is repeatedly this verb, set against what the self wills.

senses.label: Accomplish, work out fully
senses.definition: To bring a task to completion or carry it through to its goal.
senses.note: 'Work out your own salvation' (PHP 2:12), followed at once by 'for it is God who works in you'.

senses.label: Prepare, fashion
senses.definition: To make someone ready for a purpose.
senses.note: God 'has prepared us for this very thing'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Almost all uses are Pauline. Paul uses it for causal chains (law → wrath, sin → death, suffering → endurance, godly grief → repentance) and for the self's divided 'doing' in Romans 7.

study.translationNote: Versions vary widely: 'produce', 'work', 'bring about', 'do', 'commit', 'accomplish'. In EPH 6:13 ἅπαντα κατεργασάμενοι is usually 'having done everything', but some render 'having overcome everything'.

background.note: Classical writers use it for achieving by labour and accomplishing great things; also of overcoming an opponent.
Very common in leases for cultivating land: 'that he shall cultivate at his own expense ten arourae'.
An inscription honours a man who 'accomplishes the best things for his country'.

study.exegesisTip: The prefix stresses the result rather than the process: ask what outcome is produced or what deed is carried through.
study.caution: PHP 2:12 is debated: individual working out of salvation in obedience, or the community's working out its common life ('your salvation' plural); the meaning of EPH 6:13 ('having done all' vs 'having overcome all') is also disputed.

study.summary: Repentance: a change of mind and heart that turns a person from sin to God and shows itself in changed conduct; in the NT a gift of God and a core element of gospel preaching.

senses.label: Turning from sin to God
senses.definition: A decisive inner reorientation away from sin and toward God, expected to bear fruit in a changed life.
senses.note: Paired with faith in God (Acts 20:21; Heb 6:1) and with 'deeds worthy of repentance' (Acts 26:20).

senses.label: Repentance prompted by godly grief
senses.definition: Sorrow over wrongdoing that issues in genuine change and so leads to salvation, as distinct from mere regret.
senses.note: Paul distinguishes 'godly sorrow', which produces repentance, from worldly sorrow.

senses.label: Baptism of repentance
senses.definition: John's baptism as the outward sign of a people turning back to God in readiness for the coming One and forgiveness.

senses.label: Call of sinners to repentance
senses.definition: The goal of Jesus' mission and of apostolic preaching: summoning sinners to turn to God, proclaimed together with forgiveness.

senses.label: Repentance as God's gift
senses.definition: Repentance granted or led by God, not merely achieved by human effort.
senses.note: 'God has granted even the Gentiles repentance unto life' (Acts 11:18).

senses.label: Opportunity for repentance
senses.definition: The possibility of a change of mind being restored or found, which Hebrews warns can be lost.
senses.note: Esau 'found no place for repentance' though he sought the blessing with tears.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the noun most (about half the NT total), joining repentance to forgiveness of sins as the content of the message to all nations and stressing that it shows itself in deeds.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews treats repentance from dead works as a foundation not to be relaid, and warns of the impossibility of renewing apostates to repentance.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the noun rarely, but presents it as led or granted by God and produced by godly grief.

study.translationNote: Nearly all English versions say 'repentance'. The Latin Vulgate's paenitentia and the older Catholic Douay-Rheims rendering 'penance' (e.g. 'fruit worthy of penance') suggested acts of penance, a reading Reformation translators contested; the Greek stresses a change of mind and direction rather than a penitential act.

background.note: In Thucydides the word is used of the Athenians' change of mind over their harsh decree against Mytilene: a reconsidering, not necessarily a moral repentance.
Rare in the Greek OT; it appears in Wisdom of God giving room for repentance and in Sirach of Enoch as an example of repentance.
The Letter of Aristeas describes God by his gentleness turning people from wickedness and leading them to repentance, showing the deeper religious sense before the NT.
Later Christian papyri mention a 'day of repentance' in a church calendar and a 'monastery of repentance' at Alexandria.

study.exegesisTip: Look at what repentance is paired with (faith, forgiveness, fruit, deeds) and who gives it; NT repentance is a turning of the whole person, not only remorse.
study.caution: Scholars debate how much the Greek sense 'change of mind' governs NT usage versus the Hebrew idea of 'turning back' (šûb); and in Heb 12:17 whether the 'repentance' Esau could not find was his own or a change in Isaac's decision.

study.summary: New or young: of things, new or fresh (new wine, a new batch, the new covenant); of persons, young, and in the comparative 'younger', often the younger members of a community.

senses.label: New, freshly made
senses.definition: New in time, recently produced, especially new wine that is still fermenting.
senses.note: New wine needs new wineskins: Jesus' teaching cannot be contained in old forms.

senses.label: New in God's new order
senses.definition: Figuratively, the new life, people and covenant God brings about, contrasted with what is old.
senses.note: The 'new' person is put on and is continually being renewed (Col 3:10).

senses.label: Young, youthful
senses.definition: Of persons, young in age; the comparative 'younger' can simply mean young in contrast to old.
senses.note: In John 21:18 'when you were younger' contrasts with 'when you are old'.

senses.label: The younger as lowest rank
senses.definition: The youngest as the one of least status, who serves others.
senses.note: 'Let the greatest among you become like the youngest.'

senses.label: Younger members of community
senses.definition: Plural 'the younger (men or women)' as a recognized group in church or society, contrasted with elders.
senses.note: In 1 Pet 5:5 the younger are told to submit to the elders (πρεσβύτεροι).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word for the believer's new identity and for the community as a new, unleavened batch, and (in the Pastorals) for younger men and women in the household of faith.

study.translationNote: English 'new' covers both νέος and καινός, so the reader cannot see which Greek word stands behind 'new self' or 'new covenant'. The comparative νεώτεροι is rendered 'young men', 'younger men' or 'the young', and in Acts 5:6 some take it as a group of junior attendants rather than simply youths.

background.note: From Homer onward νέος means young, of children and youths and of men up to about thirty.
In the Septuagint it renders Hebrew words for 'young' and 'little' and also חָדָשׁ 'new', as of new grain offerings.
Papyri speak of the 'new year' and of repaying 'out of the new crop'.
Inscriptions show οἱ νέοι as an organized club of young men of military age, between the ephebes and the council of elders.

study.exegesisTip: Decide first whether νέος describes a thing (new) or a person (young), and with the comparative ask whether a recognized group of 'younger ones' is in view.
study.caution: The older distinction that νέος means new in time and καινός new in quality is often overstated; Hebrews, for example, calls the same covenant both νέα and καινή, so many scholars treat the words as largely overlapping in the NT.

study.summary: Mind: the faculty of perceiving, understanding and judging, especially as the moral and spiritual outlook that can be corrupted or renewed; also a particular way of thinking, purpose or opinion.

senses.label: Understanding, intellect
senses.definition: The capacity to perceive and comprehend, needed to grasp Scripture or a riddle and exceeded by God's peace.
senses.note: In 2 Thess 2:2 'shaken from your mind' means losing one's settled composure.

senses.label: Mind versus spirit in worship
senses.definition: Rational, intelligible thought, distinguished from ecstatic speech in a tongue.
senses.note: Paul wants prayer and singing with the spirit and with the mind.

senses.label: Mind assenting to God's law
senses.definition: The inner self that recognizes and approves God's law, yet is opposed by sin at work in the flesh.

senses.label: Corrupted moral outlook
senses.definition: A mindset darkened or perverted so that it no longer judges rightly about God and conduct.
senses.note: 'A depraved (ἀδόκιμος) mind' (Rom 1:28): one that fails the test.

senses.label: Renewed mind
senses.definition: The believer's way of thinking transformed by God, enabling discernment of God's will.

senses.label: Thought, purpose, opinion
senses.definition: A particular mind or intention: the plans of the Lord, or a shared conviction or personal judgment.
senses.note: 'Who has known the mind of the Lord?' (from Isa 40:13); 'we have the mind of Christ'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Almost all NT uses are Paul's. For him the mind is the moral as well as intellectual center: handed over to depravity apart from God, yet renewed in Christ to discern God's will.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation uses the word in calls for insight to decode its symbols.

study.translationNote: Most versions say 'mind', but in places 'understanding' (Phil 4:7), 'thinking' (Eph 4:17) or 'reason' appear. Col 2:18 ('mind of his flesh') is rendered 'fleshly mind', 'sensuous mind' or 'unspiritual mind', each interpreting the genitive.

background.note: Papyri use νοῦς for the intended sense of a document, as officials failing to grasp the meaning of a royal decree.
In letters κατὰ νοῦν means 'according to one's wish', as in a prayer that the recipient prosper.

study.exegesisTip: In Paul, read νοῦς as the whole inner outlook that directs life, not merely the intellect; the issue is what has shaped it.
study.caution: In 1 Cor 14:14 interpreters differ on whether 'my spirit' is the human spirit or the Holy Spirit's gift working in the person, which affects how mind and spirit are contrasted; the identity of the 'I' in Rom 7:23–25 is also debated.

study.summary: A child (boy or girl) by age or relation, and, like Hebrew ʿebed, a servant or slave; used of God's servant Israel, David, and especially Jesus as the Servant of God.

senses.label: Child, boy, girl
senses.definition: A young person, emphasizing age; also a child in relation to a parent.
senses.note: Feminine of Jairus' daughter (Luke 8:51, 54); 'your boy' of the official's son (John 4:51).

senses.label: Girl (feminine)
senses.definition: A young girl, used with the feminine article, including in direct address.
senses.note: 'Child, arise!' (Luke 8:54).

senses.label: Son of a parent
senses.definition: A child viewed as someone's offspring.

senses.label: Servant, slave, attendant
senses.definition: A household slave or servant; also a king's attendants or courtiers.
senses.note: Herod's 'servants' (Matt 14:2) are his courtiers.

senses.label: Servant of God (Israel, David)
senses.definition: A title, from the OT 'servant of the LORD', for Israel and for David as chosen agents of God.

senses.label: Jesus as God's Servant
senses.definition: Jesus as the Servant of God of Isaiah, chosen, glorified through suffering, and raised.
senses.note: Matt 12:18 quotes Isaiah 42:1.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word most, and Acts preserves early Jerusalem preaching and prayer that call Jesus God's 'holy Servant', echoing Isaiah's Servant.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew applies Isaiah 42 to Jesus' quiet healing ministry.

study.translationNote: Because παῖς can mean child or servant, versions differ. The KJV has 'his Son Jesus' and 'holy child Jesus' in Acts 3–4, where modern versions read 'servant', recognizing Isaiah's Servant. In the centurion story (Matt 8:6) most say 'servant', but some prefer 'boy' or 'son'.

background.note: The Septuagint chiefly uses παῖς to render Hebrew ʿebed, including 'servant of God' for Israel in Isaiah.
Papyri commonly list slaves as παῖδες, male and female.
A legal code deals with a foundling child taken from a dung-heap and adopted as a son.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether age, parentage or service is in view; when God calls someone 'my παῖς', hear the OT Servant of the LORD.
study.caution: Whether the centurion's παῖς (Matt 8:6; Luke 7:7) was a slave or a son is debated, since Luke also calls him a δοῦλος while John's similar story has a son; whether Acts 3–4 deliberately evokes Isaiah's Suffering Servant is also discussed.

study.summary: To be present, be here; also to have come or arrived. Of things and times, to be at hand; the participle means 'the present' or 'what one has'.

senses.label: Be present with others
senses.definition: Of persons, to be there in someone's company or before someone.

senses.label: Present in person, not absent
senses.definition: Paul's participle παρών, 'when present', set against being absent and writing by letter.
senses.note: Paul can be absent in body but present in spirit (1 Cor 5:3).

senses.label: Have come, arrived
senses.definition: To have arrived and now be here.
senses.note: The gospel 'has come to you' (Col 1:6).

senses.label: Times and things at hand
senses.definition: Of time, to have arrived; of things, to be present or available; τὸ παρόν = the present moment, τὰ παρόντα = what one has.
senses.note: 'Be content with what you have' (Heb 13:5).

senses.label: The beast's coming
senses.definition: Of the beast that 'was, and is not, and will be present', a future appearing.
senses.note: The phrase seems to parody God as the one 'who is and who was and who is to come'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul repeatedly contrasts being present (παρών) with being absent (ἀπών), defending the consistency of his letters with his personal visits.

study.translationNote: Matt 26:50 (ἐφ' ὃ πάρει) is elliptical: older versions and some modern ones ask 'why have you come?', while others read a command, 'do what you came for'.

background.note: Homer invokes the Muses who 'are present and know all things'.
Papyri use the verb for being at home or present in person.
Court records use the participle for someone who 'came forward' to speak, supporting the sense 'arrive'.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether the verb stresses being present (a state) or having arrived (the result of coming); context often favors 'have come'.
study.caution: In Luke 13:1 some take παρῆσαν as 'some who were present' and others as 'some arrived' to report the news.

study.summary: Presence or arrival; in the NT especially the coming (Parousia) of Christ at the end of the age, a term that in the Hellenistic world denoted the official visit of a ruler.

senses.label: Personal presence
senses.definition: Being present in person, as opposed to absence.
senses.note: 'His bodily presence is weak' (2 Cor 10:10).

senses.label: Arrival of a person
senses.definition: The coming or arrival of a colleague or apostle.
senses.note: The arrival of Titus comforted Paul (2 Cor 7:6).

senses.label: Christ's coming at the end
senses.definition: The future, public coming of Jesus as Lord to raise the dead, gather his people and judge.
senses.note: Also 'the coming of the day of God' (2 Pet 3:12).

senses.label: Coming as goal of Christian hope
senses.definition: The Lord's coming as the moment when believers' lives are reviewed and their holiness shown.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew alone among the Gospels uses the word, always in the Olivet Discourse of the Son of Man's coming.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's main use is in the Thessalonian letters; he also speaks of the lawless one's counterfeit 'coming', which the Lord's appearing will destroy.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 2 Peter defends the promised coming against scoffers, grounding it in the apostles' eyewitness of Jesus' majesty.

study.translationNote: Most versions say 'coming' in the eschatological texts and 'presence' where Paul contrasts presence with absence. A few literal versions render 'presence' throughout, which can suggest a prolonged, even invisible presence rather than an arrival.

background.note: Classical writers use the word for the presence of persons or things, e.g. of a master.
In later Septuagint books it means arrival or presence.
From Ptolemaic times it is the technical term for the visit of a king or official, with levies to supply provisions.
A papyrus records contributions for a crown to be presented to the king on his arrival.

study.exegesisTip: Hear the royal-visit background: the Parousia is the arrival of the reigning Lord, for which his people prepare.
study.caution: Interpreters disagree whether some 'coming' passages in Matt 24 refer to the events of AD 70 or only to the final return.

study.summary: To throw around: chiefly to clothe someone or wrap oneself in a garment, often of symbolic white robes; once (in some manuscripts) of throwing up a siege rampart around a city.

senses.label: Clothe another person
senses.definition: To put clothing on someone, whether in compassion or in mockery.
senses.note: Soldiers dress Jesus in a purple robe (John 19:2).

senses.label: Clothe oneself, put on
senses.definition: Middle voice: to dress oneself or wrap a garment around oneself.
senses.note: 'Not even Solomon in all his glory was arrayed like one of these.'

senses.label: Be dressed in, wear
senses.definition: Perfect passive: to have a garment wrapped around one, i.e. be wearing it.

senses.label: Symbolic heavenly clothing
senses.definition: Garments in visions that express identity, victory or glory, such as white robes, a cloud, the sun or a blood-dipped robe.

senses.label: Throw up around (siege)
senses.definition: To set a palisade or rampart around a city in a siege.
senses.note: Other manuscripts have a related verb here.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation uses the word far more than any other book, mainly for white garments signifying purity and victory given to the faithful.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses it in the judgment of the nations for clothing the naked as service done to Christ.

background.note: In Homer the verb is used of throwing one's arms around someone.
The Septuagint uses it for wrapping oneself in a garment, as with the tassels on one's cloak.
A petitioner complains that robbers stripped him of the garment he had wrapped around him.
Papyri also use it of building enclosing walls and, figuratively, of covering someone with dishonor.

study.exegesisTip: Note the voice: active (clothing another), middle (dressing oneself) and perfect passive (being dressed), and in Revelation ask what the garment symbolizes.

study.summary: To turn one's mind to: pay attention, heed; with a warning, beware or be on guard; also to attach oneself to, follow or devote oneself to persons, teachings or practices.

senses.label: Pay attention, heed
senses.definition: To give careful attention to a message or word.
senses.note: The Lord opened Lydia's heart to heed Paul's words (Acts 16:14).

senses.label: Beware of, be on guard
senses.definition: To watch out for a danger, often with ἀπό: false prophets, opponents, or the leaven of the Pharisees.
senses.note: Matt 6:1: 'be careful not to' do righteousness to be seen.

senses.label: Watch over oneself or others
senses.definition: With a reflexive, to take heed to oneself; also to keep watch over and care for others.
senses.note: Elders must watch over themselves and the flock (Acts 20:28).

senses.label: Follow, give allegiance to
senses.definition: To attach oneself to a person or teaching and follow it.
senses.note: The Samaritans had followed Simon the magician (Acts 8:10–11).

senses.label: Devote oneself to
senses.definition: To give oneself to an activity or practice, good or bad.
senses.note: Devote yourself to public reading (1 Tim 4:13); not given to much wine (1 Tim 3:8).

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: In Matthew the imperative 'beware' is a recurring warning of Jesus against false prophets, persecutors and the Pharisees' teaching.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke favors 'take heed to yourselves' and describes crowds giving attention either to the gospel or to a rival.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: The Pastoral Letters use the verb for being drawn to myths, deceiving spirits and wine, or for devotion to Scripture reading.

study.translationNote: English versions vary between 'beware', 'take heed', 'be careful', 'pay attention' and 'devote oneself', because the one Greek verb covers attention, caution and devotion.

background.note: The basic classical sense is to hold toward, especially to bring a ship to land.
The Septuagint often uses 'take heed to yourself' as a warning formula.
A writer takes heed lest an opponent find something to say against his correspondent.
A father urges his son to give undivided attention to his books.

study.exegesisTip: Check what follows: a dative of a message (heed), ἀπό or a reflexive (beware, watch yourself), or a dative of a person or practice (follow, devote oneself).

study.summary: To bring to completion: finish a task or period, fulfill; to bring something or someone to its goal or perfection, especially in Hebrews (Christ and believers perfected) and 1 John (love perfected).

senses.label: Finish, accomplish a task
senses.definition: To bring a work or course to completion.
senses.note: In John 19:28 Scripture is 'fulfilled' with this verb.

senses.label: Complete a period
senses.definition: To come to the end of a set time.

senses.label: Bring to the goal (Christ)
senses.definition: To make Jesus fully what he must be as Savior and High Priest through suffering, death and exaltation.
senses.note: 'On the third day I will reach my goal' (Luke 13:32).

senses.label: Perfect the worshipper
senses.definition: To bring people into full, lasting access to God, which the law and sacrifices could not do but Christ's offering does.

senses.label: Bring to full expression
senses.definition: To bring faith, love or power to completion or maturity in action.
senses.note: 'Faith was perfected by works' (Jas 2:22).

senses.label: Maturity of believers
senses.definition: Of persons, reaching spiritual completeness or full unity.
senses.note: Paul denies he is already 'made perfect'.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews makes 'perfecting' a key theme: Christ was perfected through suffering, and by one offering he has perfected those being sanctified, which the law could not do.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In the Gospel Jesus completes the work the Father gave him; in 1 John God's love is 'perfected' in those who keep his word and love one another.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'make perfect', 'complete', 'finish' and 'reach the goal'. 'Perfect' can suggest moral flawlessness; in Hebrews and Luke 13:32 many prefer 'complete' or 'reach the goal' to bring out the idea of fulfilled purpose.

background.note: Classical writers use it of completing acts and works.
In the Pentateuch 'to perfect the hands' renders the Hebrew idiom 'fill the hands', i.e. to consecrate priests, a background for Hebrews.
Legal papyri use it for executing a deed in proper form.
In 4 Maccabees and later Christian epitaphs the verb is used of dying as a martyr, 'being perfected'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask what goal is in view: a finished task, a fulfilled vocation, full access to God, or love brought to mature expression.
study.caution: Scholars debate whether Christ's 'perfection' in Hebrews means moral development through obedience, vocational qualification as High Priest, or consecration in the priestly sense; most see the second and third as central without denying real growth through suffering.

study.summary: To love with warm personal affection, as a friend or family member; to like or be fond of doing something; and to kiss as a sign of affection or greeting.

senses.label: Love with personal affection
senses.definition: To hold a person dear with the affection of friendship or family.
senses.note: 'Lord, the one you love is sick' (John 11:3).

senses.label: Love of God and Christ
senses.definition: The Father's love for the Son and for disciples, Christ's love for his churches, and believers' love for the Lord.

senses.label: Like, be fond of
senses.definition: To have a liking for things, or (with an infinitive) to love to do something, often disapprovingly.
senses.note: Hypocrites 'love to pray standing' to be seen (Matt 6:5).

senses.label: Kiss
senses.definition: To kiss as a sign of greeting or affection, notably Judas' kiss as a signal.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses φιλέω far more than other writers, often interchangeably with ἀγαπάω for the Father's love, Jesus' love for his friends, and the disciples' love for him.

study.translationNote: Most versions render both φιλέω and ἀγαπάω as 'love', so the shift between them in John 21:15–17 is invisible; some versions or notes try to mark it ('you know that I love you' vs 'I am your friend' or 'I have affection for you'). φιλέω is also translated 'kiss' and, in Matt 10:37, 'love more than'.

background.note: In Homer the verb expresses friendship and affection; Achilles says there can be no friendship between him and Hector.
In the Septuagint it often renders Hebrew 'kiss', as when Isaac kisses Jacob.
Private letters use it for affection between family and friends.
Letters close with greetings to 'those who love us (or you) in truth', a close parallel to Titus 3:15.

study.exegesisTip: Do not assume φιλέω is a lesser love than ἀγαπάω; let context decide, noting that John uses both of the Father's love for the Son.
study.caution: Whether the alternation of ἀγαπάω and φιλέω in John 21:15–17 is meaningful or simply stylistic variation is debated; many modern scholars see them as largely synonymous here.

study.summary: A vineyard: a planted plot of vines. In the Gospels it is above all the setting of Jesus' parables, where the vineyard and its owner picture God's people and God's claim on their fruit.

senses.label: Vineyard, plot of vines
senses.definition: Land planted and worked for grapes, owned, leased out and harvested; also used as an everyday example of labour that rightly shares in its own produce.
senses.note: Paul's 'Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit?' (1CO 9:7) argues for a worker's right to support.

senses.label: Parable image of God's people
senses.definition: In the parable of the tenants the vineyard stands for Israel entrusted to its leaders, echoing Isaiah's song of the vineyard; its 'owner' (ὁ κύριος τοῦ ἀμπελῶνος) represents God.
senses.note: Cf. ISA 5:7, where the vineyard of the Lord is the house of Israel.

senses.label: Setting of kingdom service
senses.definition: In the parable of the workers the vineyard is the sphere where the owner hires labourers and pays them by his own generous standard, illustrating the kingdom of heaven.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew has three vineyard parables in sequence (the workers, the two sons, the tenants), all turning on who actually does the owner's will.

background.note: The word is attested in fourth-century BC prose, though it is commoner in Hellenistic Greek.
The Septuagint uses it regularly for Hebrew kerem, from Noah's planting of a vineyard onward; Isaiah's vineyard song supplies the background to Jesus' parable.
Papyri use it constantly of taxable vine-land and of vineyards owned by families, including a document contemporary with the NT.

study.exegesisTip: In the tenants parable, read the vineyard through Isaiah 5: the question is not ownership of land but whether those entrusted with God's people render him its fruit.

study.summary: To lead or bring up (to a higher place, before people, from the dead), to offer up a sacrifice, and in the middle/passive the nautical 'put out to sea'—Luke's characteristic sailing term.

senses.label: Lead or bring up
senses.definition: To conduct someone upward or to a destination, as to Jerusalem, into the wilderness, or up to a house.
senses.note: Going 'up' to Jerusalem and into the hills reflects geography as well as movement.

senses.label: Bring up from the dead
senses.definition: To raise someone from the realm of the dead, used of God's raising of Christ.

senses.label: Bring out before people
senses.definition: To bring a prisoner out and present him publicly, as for trial.

senses.label: Offer up a sacrifice
senses.definition: To bring a victim up to the altar as an offering.
senses.note: Used of Israel's sacrifice to the golden calf.

senses.label: Put out to sea
senses.definition: Middle/passive: to set sail, launch out from harbour onto the open sea.
senses.note: A standard seafaring term since Homer.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Twenty of the NT uses are Luke's, most in the nautical sense, giving the sea voyages of Acts their precise sailing vocabulary.

study.translationNote: Older versions render the sailing sense with 'launch forth', 'loosed' or 'departed' (KJV), while modern ones say 'set sail' or 'put out to sea'; the Greek is one technical verb throughout.

background.note: Homer already uses it of carrying people up to the high sea by ship.
An inscription speaks of a person being 'brought before the people', a close parallel to Herod's plan for Peter.
An inscription uses it of a benefactor offering up two bulls, matching the sacrificial sense.
A papyrus of 1 BC uses it of a cargo shipped to Italy, showing the everyday nautical use.

study.exegesisTip: Note the voice: active forms mean 'bring up/offer', while middle or passive forms in Luke–Acts almost always mean 'set sail'.
study.caution: In HEB 13:20 some hear an echo of God 'bringing up' Moses the shepherd from the sea, others simply the resurrection; the phrase 'the great Shepherd' makes the echo plausible but not certain.

study.summary: To take up (adopt a foundling), and more often to take away or do away with: to kill or execute a person, or to abolish an arrangement.

senses.label: Take up, adopt
senses.definition: Middle: to pick up and take as one's own, used of Pharaoh's daughter adopting the exposed infant Moses.
senses.note: Echoes EXO 2:5; the papyri use the word technically for taking up an exposed foundling.

senses.label: Kill, put to death
senses.definition: To do away with a person, by murder, execution or judicial killing.
senses.note: Used of Herod's massacre, of Jesus' death, and of plots against apostles.

senses.label: Abolish, set aside
senses.definition: Of things: to take away or annul, as one covenant order is removed to establish another.
senses.note: Classical writers use it of repealing laws.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Nearly all NT uses are Lukan; the verb recurs in the repeated plots to kill Jesus and Paul, sharpening the narrative of hostility.

background.note: Homer uses it of lifting a sacrificial victim from the ground and of carrying off prizes.
A papyrus of AD 49 says a man 'picked up from the dung-heap a male foundling', the technical sense behind Acts 7:21.
A fourth-century papyrus uses it of people wishing to kill the writer.

study.exegesisTip: In Acts the verb repeatedly marks deliberate intent to eliminate God's messengers, tying the apostles' experience to the death of Jesus.

study.summary: Not believing or not trustworthy: of things, incredible; of persons, lacking faith, and in Paul especially 'unbeliever', a non-Christian outsider; sometimes 'unfaithful'.

senses.label: Incredible, unbelievable
senses.definition: Of a thing: beyond belief, not to be credited.
senses.note: Paul asks why God's raising the dead should be judged incredible.

senses.label: Without faith, unbelieving
senses.definition: Of persons who fail to trust God or Jesus, refusing or lacking faith.
senses.note: 'Faithless generation' (MAR 9:19) rebukes failure of trust.

senses.label: Unbeliever, non-Christian
senses.definition: Substantively, a person outside the Christian faith, in contrast to 'believers'.
senses.note: Neutral description in marriage and meal questions; in 2CO 4:4 those blinded to the gospel.

senses.label: Unfaithful, untrustworthy
senses.definition: Passive sense: not reliable or faithful in a trust, as of a servant who betrays his charge.
senses.note: Contrast the 'faithful steward' of the same parable.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word mainly in the Corinthian letters as a fixed term for non-Christians in mixed marriages, lawsuits, meals and worship.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's uses frame faith as decisive: Thomas is told not to be faithless, and the faithless are listed among those excluded from the new creation.

study.translationNote: Versions differ between active and passive senses: LUK 12:46 is 'unbelievers' (KJV, MSB) or 'unfaithful' (NIV, ESV); JOH 20:27 'be not faithless' (KJV) or 'stop doubting' (NIV); the KJV's 'infidel' (1TI 5:8) simply means 'unbeliever'.

background.note: In classical Greek the word is chiefly passive: 'not to be trusted, faithless', as of treacherous persons in Homer.
The Septuagint uses it only rarely, e.g. of an unreliable or faithless planting.
An Epidaurus healing inscription moves from 'incredible' to 'incredulous', jokingly naming a doubter 'Apistos'.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether the context stresses lack of faith (active) or lack of faithfulness (passive), since πιστός/ἄπιστος cover both trust and trustworthiness.
study.caution: In LUK 12:46 and REV 21:8 scholars debate whether ἄπιστοι means non-believers or the unfaithful who betray their trust; both readings have support.

study.summary: To make grow or, more often, to grow and increase: of plants, children, peoples, the spreading word of God, and believers' growth in grace and knowledge.

senses.label: Cause to grow
senses.definition: Transitive: to make something grow or increase, used of God giving growth.
senses.note: Paul plants, Apollos waters, but God gives the growth.

senses.label: Grow, of plants
senses.definition: Of natural growth of seed and plants.

senses.label: Grow up, of children
senses.definition: Of physical and personal maturing of a child.

senses.label: Increase, spread
senses.definition: Of a people multiplying or the word of God spreading and gaining ground.
senses.note: Paired with πληθύνω, echoing the creation blessing 'increase and multiply'.

senses.label: Grow spiritually
senses.definition: Of believers and the church maturing in faith, knowledge and grace toward Christ.
senses.note: Also of the church as a building growing into a temple (EPH 2:21).

senses.label: Increase in stature or influence
senses.definition: Of a person becoming greater in prominence.
senses.note: 'He must increase, but I must decrease.'

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the verb in summary statements on the growth of John and Jesus and of the word of God in Acts, marking stages of progress.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul speaks of corporate growth: the church as body or building grows from Christ and into him, with God as the source of growth.

background.note: The Septuagint uses it mainly for Hebrew pārâ in the formula 'increase and multiply'.
Hellenistic inscriptions use the older form αὔξω transitively, of increasing honours paid to the gods.
The intransitive 'grow, increase' appears of the human race multiplying.

study.exegesisTip: Watch for the pairing with 'multiply' or 'be strong' in Acts and Luke: Luke uses the verb to mark how God advances his work despite opposition.

study.summary: To be awake and so to watch: literally staying awake, figuratively being spiritually alert and vigilant, especially in readiness for the Lord's coming; once perhaps 'to be alive'.

senses.label: Stay awake
senses.definition: To keep awake rather than sleep, as on guard or keeping vigil.
senses.note: Gethsemane: the disciples fail to stay awake with Jesus.

senses.label: Be watchful, alert
senses.definition: To be spiritually vigilant and ready, especially for the unexpected return of the Lord or against danger.
senses.note: Often paired with prayer or sobriety.

senses.label: Be on guard
senses.definition: To keep careful watch over oneself or a community against error, temptation or the devil.

senses.label: Be alive
senses.definition: Metaphorically 'to be awake' as opposed to 'asleep' in death.
senses.note: 'Whether we are awake or asleep we will live with him.'

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark's discourse ends with a threefold command to watch, applied to 'all', and then shows the disciples failing to watch in Gethsemane.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul joins watchfulness with sobriety and prayer as marks of those who belong to the day.

study.translationNote: English versions vary between 'watch', 'keep watch', 'stay awake' and 'be alert' for the same verb; 'watch' can mislead if taken as 'look at', since the sense is wakeful vigilance.

background.note: A new present formed from the perfect ἐγρήγορα, it is post-classical and occurs only in some later books of the Septuagint; Atticist grammarians condemned it.

study.exegesisTip: The command is rooted in not knowing the hour: vigilance means steady readiness in daily faithfulness, not date-setting.
study.caution: In 1TH 5:10 interpreters debate whether 'awake or asleep' means alive or dead (as in 4:13–17) or morally watchful or careless (as in 5:6); most take it as alive or dead.

study.summary: To test or assay (as metals), examine; to discern by testing; and, as the result, to approve or see fit. The test is usually expected to prove genuineness.

senses.label: Test, examine
senses.definition: To put something or someone to the test to establish its quality or genuineness, including self-examination.
senses.note: Fire tests gold (1PE 1:7) and each person's work (1CO 3:13).

senses.label: Examine oneself
senses.definition: To scrutinize one's own life and faith before God.

senses.label: Discern, interpret
senses.definition: To assess rightly and so recognize what is true or God's will.

senses.label: Approve as proven
senses.definition: To recognize as tested and fit, approve for a task.
senses.note: 1TH 2:4: approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel.

senses.label: See fit, think worth
senses.definition: To judge something worth doing or holding, to deem acceptable.
senses.note: ROM 1:28 plays on the word: they did not see fit to acknowledge God, so he gave them over to an 'unfit' (ἀδόκιμος) mind.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb for testing God's will, self-examination and testing others' work, and for approval of proven ministers.

study.translationNote: In ROM 2:18 and PHP 1:10, τὰ διαφέροντα with this verb is rendered 'approve the things that are excellent' (KJV, NIV) or 'discern what is best' (ESV), because the verb covers both testing and approving.

background.note: Classical Greek uses it of assaying purple dye and gold, and of examining candidates for office.
The Septuagint uses it of refining silver and gold and of God testing hearts.
A papyrus refers to physicians who have 'passed the examination', showing the sense 'approved after testing'.
The Rosetta Stone says Ptolemy was 'approved' by Hephaestus, i.e. tested and installed as king.

study.exegesisTip: Contrast πειράζω: δοκιμάζω usually tests in order to prove genuine, while πειράζω can tempt toward failure.
study.caution: Whether τὰ διαφέροντα in ROM 2:18 and PHP 1:10 means 'test the things that differ' or 'approve what is excellent' is debated; both senses of the verb were current.

study.summary: An image or likeness derived from an original: the emperor's head on a coin, an idol-statue, humanity as God's image, Christ as the visible image of the invisible God, and believers renewed in his image.

senses.label: Likeness on a coin
senses.definition: The portrait of the ruler stamped on money, marking ownership and authority.
senses.note: 'Whose image is this?'—Caesar's.

senses.label: Idol, cult statue
senses.definition: A carved or made likeness used as an object of worship.

senses.label: Humanity as God's image
senses.definition: Human beings as reflecting and representing God, and believers being renewed and conformed to that image in Christ.
senses.note: Echoes GEN 1:27, made 'in the image of God'.

senses.label: Christ the image of God
senses.definition: Christ as the perfect, visible representation of the invisible God.

senses.label: True form, reality
senses.definition: The real substance of a thing in contrast to a mere shadow or outline.
senses.note: The law had a shadow, not the very image, of the good things to come.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: All of John's uses (in Revelation) concern the image of the beast, the focus of false worship that the faithful refuse.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul builds a theology of image: Christ is God's image, and salvation is being conformed to and transformed into that image.

study.translationNote: Most versions keep 'image'; in HEB 10:1 renderings vary ('the very image' KJV, 'the true form' ESV, 'the realities themselves' NIV) because the contrast is with a shadow.

background.note: The word is used of portraits and statues from Herodotus on.
The Rosetta Stone calls Ptolemy V 'living image of Zeus', a royal title illuminating Christ as 'image of God'.
In official documents the word means a written personal description used to identify a person, as in a slave sale.

study.exegesisTip: An εἰκών implies an original it derives from and represents, unlike a mere resemblance (ὁμοίωμα); ask what archetype the image reveals.
study.caution: In 1CO 15:49 manuscripts divide between 'we shall bear' and 'let us bear' the image of the heavenly man, and editors and commentators differ.

study.summary: A living creature or animal. Mostly used in Revelation of the four heavenly 'living creatures' around God's throne; elsewhere of sacrificial animals and of irrational beasts.

senses.label: Animal, irrational beast
senses.definition: A living creature lacking reason, acting by instinct.
senses.note: False teachers are compared to unreasoning animals.

senses.label: Sacrificial animal
senses.definition: Animals whose blood is offered in sacrifice.

senses.label: Heavenly living creatures
senses.definition: The four beings around the throne in Revelation who worship continually and take part in the unfolding judgments.
senses.note: Modelled on the creatures of Ezekiel 1 and Isaiah 6.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: All of John's uses are in Revelation, of the four creatures with faces of lion, ox, man and eagle who lead heaven's worship.

study.translationNote: The KJV renders the creatures of Revelation 'beasts', the same word it uses for θηρίον, the monstrous beast; modern versions say 'living creatures', preserving the Greek distinction.

background.note: Plato defines it as anything that partakes of life.
Egyptian papyri speak often of 'sacred animals' maintained at royal expense.

study.exegesisTip: Do not confuse the four ζῷα, worshipping beings close to God, with the θηρίον, the hostile beast of Revelation 13.
study.caution: The symbolism of the four creatures is debated: cherubim-like angelic beings, representatives of all creation, or (in later tradition) the four Gospel writers.

study.summary: An altar for sacrifice: the temple's altar of burnt offering or of incense, Israel's altars generally, the heavenly altar in Revelation, and figuratively the Christian 'altar' of Hebrews.

senses.label: Temple altar of burnt offering
senses.definition: The great altar in the Jerusalem temple court where gifts and sacrifices were offered.
senses.note: Jesus says the altar sanctifies the gift (MAT 23:19).

senses.label: Altar of incense
senses.definition: The golden altar inside the sanctuary on which incense was burned.

senses.label: Altars in general
senses.definition: Any altar for sacrifice to God, as in the patriarchal and prophetic narratives.

senses.label: Participation in sacrifice
senses.definition: The altar standing for the sacrificial worship in which eaters of the offerings share.
senses.note: Paul uses it to warn against sharing in idol feasts.

senses.label: Heavenly altar
senses.definition: The altar before God's throne in Revelation, linked with martyrs, prayers and judgment.

senses.label: Christian 'altar'
senses.definition: Figuratively, the sacrifice of Christ from which believers draw benefit.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In Revelation the altar is in heaven: the souls of martyrs lie under it, the saints' prayers rise from it, and fire from it falls in judgment.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses the altar to teach that reconciliation precedes worship and that oaths by the altar are binding.

background.note: The word first appears in the Septuagint, which reserves it for the altar of Israel's God and uses βωμός mostly for pagan altars.

study.exegesisTip: Biblical Greek generally keeps θυσιαστήριον for the altar of the true God, so its choice signals legitimate worship.
study.caution: The 'altar' of HEB 13:10 is identified variously with the cross, with Christ's sacrifice itself, or with the Lord's Supper; most commentators favour Christ's sacrifice.

study.summary: The belly or abdominal cavity: the stomach as organ of digestion and appetite, the womb in conception and birth, and once figuratively the innermost self.

senses.label: Belly, stomach
senses.definition: The abdominal cavity and its organs, especially the stomach into which food passes; also the belly of the great fish that swallowed Jonah.
senses.note: In Mark 7:19 food goes into the stomach, not the heart, so it cannot defile.

senses.label: Appetite as a master
senses.definition: The belly as a figure for bodily appetite and self-indulgence, treated as the thing a person really serves.
senses.note: 'Whose god is their belly' (Phil 3:19) and 'serve their own belly' (Rom 16:18).

senses.label: Womb
senses.definition: The mother's womb as the place of conception, pregnancy and birth.

senses.label: From birth (idiom)
senses.definition: The Semitic phrase 'from the mother's womb' means from birth, from the very beginning of life.
senses.note: Gal 1:15 echoes the prophetic call language of Isa 49:1 and Jer 1:5.

senses.label: Innermost being
senses.definition: Figuratively, the inner self, the depths of a person, as the Hebrew word for belly can mean.
senses.note: 'Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.'

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word most, chiefly for the womb in the birth narratives (John leaping in Elizabeth's womb, Mary's womb blessed) and for those lame 'from their mother's womb'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the belly as a symbol of appetite: 'food for the stomach' is a Corinthian slogan he answers, and false teachers serve their belly.

study.translationNote: English versions choose between 'belly', 'stomach' and 'womb' by context. In John 7:38 the KJV keeps 'belly', while modern versions use 'heart' or 'innermost being' to convey the figurative sense.

background.note: Classical Greek uses the word for the body cavity, the belly or abdomen, and often specifically the stomach.
The Septuagint uses it for the womb, including 'from my mother's womb' as an expression for from birth.
Papyri use it plainly for the belly or abdomen, for instance of a burn or wound.
Comedy coined the term 'belly-god' for a glutton, illustrating Paul's 'whose god is their belly'.

study.exegesisTip: Let the context decide among stomach, appetite, womb and inner self; 'from the mother's womb' is an idiom for 'from birth'.
study.caution: In John 7:38 it is debated whether 'his belly' refers to the believer or to Christ himself as the source of living water; the answer depends partly on how verses 37–38 are punctuated.

study.summary: To grow weary from exertion, and hence to toil or work hard; Paul's favourite word for the strenuous labour of ministry and Christian service.

senses.label: Grow weary, be tired
senses.definition: To be worn out or exhausted from exertion, travel or burdens.
senses.note: Jesus 'weary from the journey' (John 4:6) shows his real humanity.

senses.label: Toil, work hard
senses.definition: To labour with effort, especially manual work or work for one's living.
senses.note: The lilies 'do not toil' (Matt 6:28).

senses.label: Labour in ministry
senses.definition: To expend strenuous effort in the work of the gospel, teaching, leading and serving the church.
senses.note: Several of those praised for such labour are women (Rom 16:6, 12).

senses.label: Labour in vain or to an end
senses.definition: With εἰς, toil directed toward a goal, often with concern that it might prove empty.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb (14 times) for apostolic and congregational labour, insisting that his toil is empowered by God's grace and worrying that it might be in vain.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John has both senses: Jesus weary at the well, and the disciples reaping what others laboured for.

background.note: In classical Greek the verb means to be tired or grow weary.
The Septuagint uses it for Hebrew yāgaʿ, both of weariness and of toil.
The active sense 'work hard' appears in astrological writing of people labouring cheerfully at their tasks.

study.exegesisTip: Notice how Paul pairs his own hard work with God's enabling power (1 Cor 15:10; Col 1:29): toil and grace are not opposites.
study.caution: Lightfoot suggested the word carries an athletic image of strenuous training, but it is often used with no such metaphor, so the athletic sense should not be pressed.

study.summary: To hinder, prevent or forbid someone from doing something, by word or action; also to withhold something from someone.

senses.label: Hinder, prevent
senses.definition: To stand in the way of a person or action so that it does not happen.
senses.note: Hebrews 7:23: death prevented the Levitical priests from continuing in office.

senses.label: Forbid, prohibit
senses.definition: To order someone not to do something or to oppose it by command.

senses.label: Bar from baptism
senses.definition: In the question 'what prevents…?' it asks whether anything stands in the way of admitting someone to baptism or fellowship.

senses.label: Restrain, check
senses.definition: To restrain a person or impulse, or to stop a course of action.
senses.note: The Spirit 'forbade' Paul to preach in Asia (Acts 16:6).

senses.label: Withhold
senses.definition: With ἀπό, to keep something back from someone, refusing to let them have it.
senses.note: 'Do not withhold your tunic.'

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the verb most (12 times), notably in the repeated question whether anything hinders the inclusion of outsiders such as the eunuch and Cornelius's household.

study.translationNote: The KJV sometimes renders the word 'let' in the old sense 'hinder' (Rom 1:13), which modern readers can misread as 'allow'; modern versions use 'prevent', 'hinder' or 'forbid'.

background.note: The Septuagint uses the verb with 'from' for withholding something from someone, the pattern behind Luke 6:29.
Papyri use it of being prevented from building a wall and of something forbidden by law.
A second-century text asks why someone did not stop a wrongdoer, using the verb for restraining.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who or what is doing the hindering (disciples, opponents, death, the Spirit) and what is being stopped.
study.caution: Some scholars (notably Cullmann) have argued that 'what prevents?' in Acts 8:36 and related texts reflects an early baptismal formula; others see only ordinary narrative language.

study.summary: To remember or call to mind; in biblical usage often to remember with concern and act on it, as when God remembers his mercy or 'remembers sins no more'.

senses.label: Recall, call to mind
senses.definition: To remember something said or done in the past, often bringing it to mind at a decisive moment.
senses.note: Peter 'remembered the word of Jesus' (Matt 26:75).

senses.label: Remember with care, act on
senses.definition: To be mindful of someone so as to show favour, help or concern, especially of God remembering his covenant and people.
senses.note: 'Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom' (Luke 23:42).

senses.label: Not remember = forgive
senses.definition: With a negative, of God no longer holding sins in mind against people, that is, forgiving them.
senses.note: Quoting the new covenant promise of Jer 31:34.

senses.label: Keep in mind
senses.definition: In the perfect, to hold someone or something in continuing remembrance.

senses.label: Be remembered before God
senses.definition: Passive: to come into God's notice for reward or for judgment.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John notes that the disciples 'remembered' Scripture and Jesus' words only after the resurrection, when they understood them.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word for God's covenant faithfulness in the birth hymns and for remembering Jesus' words after Easter.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses it of God's caring regard for humanity, of his not remembering sins, and of believers remembering prisoners.

background.note: In Homer the active means 'remind'; the NT uses only middle and passive forms meaning 'remember'.
The Septuagint uses the word chiefly for Hebrew zākar, where remembering implies acting on behalf of someone.
A papyrus letter says 'remember how' you acted, much as the angels say 'remember how he told you' in Luke 24:6.
A Christian grave inscription prays 'Lord, remember your servant in your kingdom'.

study.exegesisTip: When God is the subject, 'remember' usually means to act on behalf of someone, not merely to recall a fact.

study.summary: Negative adverb of time, 'not yet': something has not happened so far but may or will; used for unfulfilled events, slow understanding, and in John for Jesus' appointed hour.
