senses.label: Not yet (events)
senses.definition: States that an event has not happened up to a given point, often implying it will.
senses.note: 'The end is not yet' (Matt 24:6).

senses.label: Appointed hour not yet
senses.definition: Of a divinely set time that has not yet arrived, especially Jesus' 'hour' of death and glorification.

senses.label: Not yet, but coming
senses.definition: Of what belongs to the future fulfilment of God's purposes, contrasted with the present.
senses.note: 'Now we are God's children; what we will be has not yet appeared' (1 John 3:2).

senses.label: Still not (rebuke)
senses.definition: In questions or statements expressing reproach that someone has still not understood or progressed.

senses.label: Not yet reached (measure)
senses.definition: That a limit or measure has not been reached.
senses.note: 'Not yet fifty years old' (John 8:57).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses οὔπω far more than any other writer (14 times), building suspense around Jesus' 'hour' that has 'not yet' come until the passion.

background.note: From Homer onward the word means 'not yet', the opposite of 'no longer'.
A worried letter-writer says he is not even anointing himself until he hears news.
Business papyri use it of payment not yet received.

study.exegesisTip: A 'not yet' usually implies a coming 'then'; ask what event is awaited and who determines its timing.
study.caution: In John 7:8 some important manuscripts read οὐκ ('I am not going up'), while others read οὔπω ('not yet'); many think οὔπω was introduced to ease the tension with Jesus later going up to the feast.

study.summary: A false step, lapse or trespass: a deviation from the right path; in the NT a culpable offence against God or others that needs forgiveness.

senses.label: Trespass needing forgiveness
senses.definition: A wrong act against God or another person, which must be forgiven or confessed.
senses.note: In Jesus' teaching, receiving forgiveness is tied to forgiving others' trespasses.

senses.label: Trespasses as deadly state
senses.definition: Accumulated wrongdoing viewed as the condition of spiritual death from which God raises people.

senses.label: Adam's trespass
senses.definition: The one transgression of Adam through which condemnation and death came to all.
senses.note: Contrasted with Christ's 'one act of righteousness'.

senses.label: Israel's false step
senses.definition: Israel's stumble in rejecting the Messiah, which became the occasion for salvation to reach the Gentiles.
senses.note: Paul plays on the image of stumbling versus falling.

senses.label: Lapse of a believer
senses.definition: A fault into which a member of the community is overtaken, to be met with gentle restoration.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word most (16 times), especially for Adam's trespass in Romans 5 and for the trespasses God forgives and does not count against people.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew applies it to wrongs between people that must be forgiven if one is to be forgiven by the Father.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'trespass' (KJV, ESV), 'transgression' (NASB in places), 'sin', 'offence' and 'fault' (James 5:16 KJV). All are acceptable; 'trespass' best preserves the image of a step outside the proper way.

background.note: The Septuagint uses it for unfaithfulness and transgression against God.
A royal ordinance uses it for permitted errors in measurement, showing the basic idea of a slip or deviation.

study.exegesisTip: The word pictures a step aside from the right path; in Romans 5 and 11 watch how Paul builds an argument on this image of falling.
study.caution: Some suggest the word implies a lesser or unintentional slip, as in some papyri, but NT usage (e.g. Adam's trespass) shows a culpable sin, and it overlaps heavily with ἁμαρτία.

study.summary: To be hungry or hunger; used of physical hunger, of the poor and needy, of apostolic hardship, and figuratively of a deep longing for righteousness or for Christ.

senses.label: Be physically hungry
senses.definition: To feel hunger from lack of food, as after fasting or a journey.
senses.note: Jesus' hunger after forty days shows his true humanity.

senses.label: The hungry poor
senses.definition: The hungry as needy people whom God fills and whom his people must feed.
senses.note: In Matt 25 Jesus identifies himself with the hungry.

senses.label: Want, hardship
senses.definition: Going hungry as part of privation or the hardships of ministry.
senses.note: Paul has learned contentment whether full or hungry (Phil 4:12).

senses.label: Spiritual longing
senses.definition: Figuratively, an intense desire for what only God can satisfy, which Christ fulfils.
senses.note: 'Whoever comes to me will never hunger' (John 6:35).

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew's beatitude speaks of those who 'hunger and thirst for righteousness', and his judgment scene makes feeding the hungry a feeding of Christ.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke stresses reversal: the hungry are filled and blessed now, while the full will go hungry.

background.note: The verb is used of ordinary hunger from Homer onward.
The Septuagint uses it of famine-hunger, as when all Egypt was hungry in Joseph's day.
A court record asks whether a man pressed for grain during a famine though hungry himself.

study.exegesisTip: Compare Matthew's 'hunger and thirst for righteousness' (Matt 5:6) with Luke's 'you who hunger now' (Luke 6:21) to see different emphases on spiritual longing and literal need.

study.summary: A vessel, container or implement; in the plural household goods or gear; and figuratively a person as an instrument God uses or as a frail container.

senses.label: Vessel, container
senses.definition: A jar, dish or other container, of any material.

senses.label: Sacred vessels
senses.definition: The utensils used in worship at the tabernacle.

senses.label: Goods, possessions
senses.definition: In the plural, a person's household belongings or property.

senses.label: Object, gear
senses.definition: Some object or equipment: the sheet-like object in Peter's vision, or a ship's tackle.

senses.label: Person as God's instrument
senses.definition: A person viewed as a vessel chosen, prepared or used by God, or as an object of his wrath or mercy.
senses.note: Paul is a 'chosen instrument' (Acts 9:15).

senses.label: Body; frail human vessel
senses.definition: The human body or person as a fragile container, including the wife as the 'weaker vessel'.
senses.note: 'Treasure in jars of clay' (2 Cor 4:7).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul develops the potter image: God forms vessels for honour and dishonour, of wrath and of mercy, and believers must cleanse themselves to be vessels for honourable use.

study.translationNote: Versions differ sharply at 1 Thess 4:4: 'control his own body' (ESV, NIV) or 'take a wife for himself' (RSV). Elsewhere the word is rendered 'vessel', 'jar', 'goods', 'instrument' or 'sheet' by context.

background.note: Classical Greek uses it for any implement or vessel, and in the plural for household gear and sacred vessels.
Papyri use it for furniture, household goods and a ship's necessary tackle.
An uncanonical gospel fragment calls the temple vessels 'the holy vessels'.

study.exegesisTip: When σκεῦος refers to a person, ask whether the stress falls on usefulness to God (an instrument) or on frailty (a clay jar).
study.caution: In 1 Thess 4:4 scholars divide over whether σκεῦος means one's own body (so 'control his body') or a wife (so 'acquire a wife'); both readings have strong support.

study.summary: Saviour, deliverer, preserver: a title used in the NT of God and of Jesus Christ, set against its use for gods, kings and emperors in the Greco-Roman world.

senses.label: God as Saviour
senses.definition: God the Father as the one who rescues and preserves his people, as in the Old Testament.
senses.note: 'God our Saviour' is frequent in the Pastoral Letters.

senses.label: Jesus as Saviour
senses.definition: Jesus Christ as the one through whom God delivers from sin and death.

senses.label: Saviour of the world
senses.definition: Christ as Saviour not of one nation only but of all humanity.
senses.note: Confessed first by Samaritans (John 4:42).

senses.label: God and Saviour Jesus
senses.definition: In the formula 'our God and Saviour' or 'Lord and Saviour', a joint title applied to Jesus Christ.

senses.label: Saviour of the church
senses.definition: Christ as the preserver and deliverer of his body, the church.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Ten of Paul's twelve uses come in the Pastoral Letters, which alternate 'God our Saviour' and 'Christ Jesus our Saviour', sometimes in neighbouring verses.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 2 Peter always joins the title with 'Lord' or 'God' in the phrase 'our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ'.

study.translationNote: In Titus 2:13 and 2 Pet 1:1 most modern versions render 'our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ' (one person), while the KJV has 'the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ', which can be read as two persons.

background.note: The Septuagint calls God the Saviour of his people.
Classical writers call gods and great men 'saviour' of a city or of Greece.
Ptolemaic kings and Roman emperors bore the title; an Ephesian inscription hails Julius Caesar as 'common saviour of human life'.
The title was also given to officials, as when a petitioner calls a prefect his 'saviour'.

study.exegesisTip: Notice the contrast with imperial titles: calling Jesus 'Saviour of the world' claimed for him what Caesar's propaganda claimed for the emperor.
study.caution: Whether Titus 2:13 and 2 Pet 1:1 call Jesus 'God' depends on whether 'God' and 'Saviour' refer to one person; most grammarians favour one person, but some scholars still read two.

study.summary: To give as a favour: to grant freely, to show kindness, to hand someone over as a favour, and especially to forgive a debt or wrong graciously.

senses.label: Give freely, bestow
senses.definition: To give something as a gracious gift, unearned by the recipient.
senses.note: Even suffering for Christ is 'granted' as a gift (Phil 1:29).

senses.label: Show favour
senses.definition: To act graciously toward someone, granting them something by favour rather than obligation.
senses.note: God 'granted' the inheritance to Abraham by promise (Gal 3:18).

senses.label: Hand over as a favour
senses.definition: To release a prisoner to someone, or hand a person over to others, as a concession.
senses.note: A murderer was 'granted' to the crowd instead of Jesus (Acts 3:14).

senses.label: Cancel a debt
senses.definition: To remit what is owed, freely letting a debtor off.

senses.label: Forgive a wrong
senses.definition: To pardon an offence freely, especially as God in Christ has forgiven.
senses.note: 2 Cor 12:13 is ironic: 'forgive me this wrong!'

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb both for God's free giving and for forgiving one another, grounding human forgiveness in God's forgiveness in Christ.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke has the debt-cancelling parable and uses the verb for granting a prisoner as a favour in the trials of Jesus and Paul.

study.translationNote: Because one Greek verb covers giving and forgiving, English versions shift between 'give', 'grant', 'hand over' and 'forgive', which hides the common idea of gracious favour behind them.

background.note: The verb is rare in the Septuagint, used for granting a favour.
A prefect tells an accused man he deserves scourging but 'I give you to the crowds', a striking parallel to Jesus' trial.
A deed of gift uses the verb for an irrevocable free grant.

study.exegesisTip: Hear χάρις, 'grace', in this verb: forgiving and giving are both acts of unearned favour.

study.summary: To ruin, spoil or corrupt: used of wrecking God's temple, of moral corruption of character and mind, and of the self-ruin of the ungodly.

senses.label: Destroy, ruin
senses.definition: To bring to ruin; in 1 Corinthians of damaging God's temple, the church, with God's matching judgment on the one who does it.

senses.label: Corrupt morally
senses.definition: To deprave or lead astray character, minds or the old self from integrity and devotion to Christ.

background.note: Marriage contracts forbade a wife to 'ruin the common household' with this verb, the same idea of damaging a shared house that 1 Corinthians applies to God's temple.

study.exegesisTip: In 1CO 3:17 the same verb names both the sin and its penalty: whoever ruins God's temple, God will ruin. The punishment fits the crime.

study.summary: A kiss, whether the ordinary kiss of welcome or the 'holy kiss' exchanged among believers as a sign of their family bond.

senses.label: Kiss of greeting
senses.definition: The customary kiss given in welcome or friendship; Judas turned this sign of affection into the signal of betrayal.

senses.label: Holy kiss among believers
senses.definition: The kiss of greeting exchanged in the churches, called 'holy' or 'of love', expressing fellowship as brothers and sisters in Christ.

study.exegesisTip: In LUK 7:45 Jesus contrasts the host's omission of the expected welcome kiss with the woman's continual kissing of his feet: hospitality withheld versus love lavished.

study.summary: A flame, often in the phrase 'flame of fire', describing torment, the presence of God, his servants and judgment, and the blazing eyes of the risen Christ.

senses.label: Tormenting flame
senses.definition: The flame in which the rich man suffers after death.

senses.label: Flame of divine presence
senses.definition: Fire marking God's appearing, his ministering servants, or his judgment at Christ's coming.

senses.label: Eyes like blazing fire
senses.definition: Image of the penetrating, searching gaze of the exalted Christ.

study.summary: A murderer, one guilty of deliberate killing; the word appears in accusations and in lists of those excluded from God's people.

senses.label: Murderer, killer
senses.definition: A person who has committed murder; used of the killers of the king's servants, of Barabbas, in Stephen's charge against his hearers, and in the islanders' suspicion of Paul.

senses.label: Among the condemned
senses.definition: The murderer as a type of wrongdoer that believers must not be and that is shut out of the city of God.

study.exegesisTip: ACT 3:14 sharpens Peter's charge: the crowd asked for 'a man who was a murderer' and rejected the Righteous One.

study.summary: A well or dug shaft; in John the deep well of Jacob, in Revelation the shaft leading down to the abyss.

senses.label: Well, cistern
senses.definition: A man-made well or pit dug for water, deep enough that an animal or child could fall into it.

senses.label: Shaft of the abyss
senses.definition: The opening or shaft leading down into the abyss, unlocked in the fifth trumpet vision.

study.translationNote: In LUK 14:5 some versions say 'pit', others 'well'; the word denotes a dug well or cistern into which an animal could fall.

background.note: Wills and leases mention wells built of brick or stone with reels and ropes, the ordinary farm well.

study.summary: To puff up or inflate; in the passive, to be puffed up with pride, almost entirely in Paul's rebuke of Corinthian arrogance.

senses.label: Make proud
senses.definition: To inflate a person with self-importance; knowledge without love does this.

senses.label: Be arrogant, conceited
senses.definition: To be swollen with pride, whether in favouring one leader over another, in defying the apostle, or in a mind set on the flesh; love is never like this.

study.exegesisTip: Six of the seven uses are in 1 Corinthians. 1CO 8:1 contrasts what 'puffs up' with what 'builds up': inflated knowledge versus love that constructs the church.

study.summary: To let down or lower something or someone, usually by ropes: a paralytic through a roof, fishing nets, a lifeboat, and Paul in a basket.

senses.label: Lower an object
senses.definition: To let down a mat, nets, ship's gear or a boat.

senses.label: Lower a person
senses.definition: To let a person down over a wall in a basket.

study.caution: What the sailors 'lowered' in ACT 27:17 (literally 'the gear') is uncertain: a sea anchor, the mainsail or other rigging have all been proposed.

study.summary: Lip, usually the lips as the organ of speech, and once the 'lip' or edge of the sea, the shore.

senses.label: Lips in speech
senses.definition: The lips as the means of speaking, praising or confessing, often contrasted with the heart or linked with deceit.

senses.label: Shore, edge
senses.definition: The edge of the sea, the seashore where sand lies beyond counting.

background.note: Used of the rim or brim of vessels, the same 'edge' sense found in the seashore image.

study.exegesisTip: Most uses come in Old Testament quotations, where 'lips' stand for what a person says as opposed to what is in the heart.

study.summary: In the plural, wealth or riches; also money, including a specific sum, an attempted payment for spiritual power, and a hoped-for bribe.

senses.label: Wealth, riches
senses.definition: Possessions as a whole; those who have them find it hard to enter God's kingdom.

senses.label: Money
senses.definition: Cash or a sum of money, as in Barnabas's proceeds, Simon's offer and Felix's hoped-for bribe.

study.exegesisTip: In ACT 4:37 the singular refers to the specific sum from the sale of the field, which Barnabas laid at the apostles' feet.
study.caution: The phrase 'those who trust in riches' in MAR 10:24 is absent from some early manuscripts, so some versions omit it.

study.summary: Good in the sense of useful, pleasant or kind: of things that are good to use or taste, and of people, above all God, who are gracious and kind.

senses.label: Good, pleasant, easy
senses.definition: Of things that serve well or are agreeable, such as a well-fitting yoke, mellow old wine, or good moral character.

senses.label: Kind, gracious
senses.definition: Of persons, especially God, who show generous kindness even to the ungrateful; believers are to imitate it.

study.translationNote: In MAT 11:30 most versions render 'easy', while some prefer 'kindly' or 'well-fitting'; the word stresses a yoke that is good to bear, not one without demands.

background.note: Used of excellent character and as an epithet of gods who helped worshippers.

study.exegesisTip: In ROM 2:4 the neuter with the article ('the kindness of God') stands for God's kindness as a quality that is meant to lead to repentance.

study.summary: A psalm: a song sung with musical accompaniment, used both of the biblical Psalms and of songs offered in Christian worship.

senses.label: Biblical Psalms
senses.definition: The Old Testament book of Psalms or a single psalm in it, cited as Scripture.

senses.label: Psalm in worship
senses.definition: A song of praise brought by believers when they gather or used to teach and encourage one another.

background.note: Originally the plucking or twanging of strings, then the sound of a harp, and later a song sung to the harp.

study.caution: Whether 'psalms, hymns and spiritual songs' (EPH 5:19; COL 3:16) are three distinct kinds of song or overlapping terms for Christian song is debated.

study.summary: A song; in the NT always a song of praise to God or the Lamb, whether sung by believers or by the redeemed in heaven.

senses.label: Spiritual songs
senses.definition: Songs prompted by the Spirit through which believers teach, encourage and give thanks.

senses.label: Heavenly song of praise
senses.definition: The 'new song' of the redeemed and the song of Moses and of the Lamb celebrating God's saving acts.

background.note: In general Greek it could be any song, including laments and dirges as well as songs of joy.

study.summary: Originally an athletic contest; in the NT the struggle of faith and ministry, the opposition it meets, and the earnest effort spent for others.

senses.label: Contest of faith
senses.definition: The Christian life pictured as a contest or race to be fought or run to the finish.

senses.label: Struggle against opposition
senses.definition: Conflict and hardship faced in preaching and living the gospel.

senses.label: Earnest striving
senses.definition: Intense concern and effort, possibly in prayer, on behalf of others.

background.note: Common of public games and competitions, the background to the athletic imagery.

study.caution: In COL 2:1 interpreters differ on whether Paul means inner anxiety and prayer or outward conflict endured for the churches.

study.summary: The shore or beach of a sea or lake: where crowds stood, nets were sorted, the risen Jesus waited, and Paul's shipwrecked ship ran aground.

senses.label: Shore, beach
senses.definition: The strip of land at the water's edge, whether of the Sea of Galilee or the Mediterranean.

background.note: Used of the shore of a lake (Lake Moeris), matching its use for the lakeshore of Galilee.

study.exegesisTip: In ACT 27:39 the point is a bay with a beach, a shore suitable for running the ship aground.

study.summary: Shame: the humiliation a person feels or endures, and the shameful things or deeds that bring disgrace.

senses.label: Humiliation, disgrace
senses.definition: The shame felt or suffered, as by a guest sent to the lowest place or by Christ on the cross.

senses.label: Shameful things
senses.definition: What is disgraceful, such as hidden shameful ways, exposed nakedness, or the shameful deeds of false teachers.

study.exegesisTip: In HEB 12:2 Jesus 'despised the shame': he treated the disgrace of crucifixion as of no account compared with the joy set before him.

study.summary: The extreme point of something: the farthest ends of earth and heaven, the tip of a finger, the top of a staff.

senses.label: Farthest end
senses.definition: The utmost limit, in the phrase 'from one end to the other' of heaven or earth.

senses.label: Tip, top
senses.definition: The end point of an object, such as a fingertip or the top of a staff.

study.caution: HEB 11:21 follows the Greek Old Testament wording 'top of his staff'; the Hebrew text of the Genesis passage is usually read as 'head of the bed'.

study.summary: To change or alter; used of changing customs or tone, of the transformation of believers' bodies and of creation, and of exchanging God's glory for idols.

senses.label: Change, alter
senses.definition: To make something different, such as customs or tone of voice.

senses.label: Transform
senses.definition: To be changed in nature: the living at Christ's return, and the heavens rolled up like a garment.

senses.label: Exchange
senses.definition: To swap one thing for another, as humanity did in trading God's glory for images.

study.summary: Something devoted to God for destruction; hence a curse, or a person placed under God's curse.

senses.label: Curse, solemn oath
senses.definition: A binding curse invoked on oneself as an oath.

senses.label: Accursed, under God's curse
senses.definition: A person or thing given over to God's judgment and cut off from blessing.

background.note: Renders the Hebrew idea of something devoted to God and banned, often for destruction.
Appears at the end of a pagan curse tablet from Megara, showing the 'curse' sense outside Jewish usage.

study.exegesisTip: In ROM 9:3 Paul's wish to be 'accursed, cut off from Christ' for Israel shows how far his love for his people goes.
study.caution: In some manuscripts the word also appears in Luke's description of the temple's votive offerings, in its older sense of 'thing dedicated'.

study.summary: To remind someone; in the passive, to remember or call to mind.

senses.label: Remind
senses.definition: To cause someone to recall something or to remind them to do it.

senses.label: Remember, recall
senses.definition: To bring something back to mind, such as Jesus' words or past experiences.

study.summary: To fill up or complete: to fulfill prophecy or Christ's law, to fill a measure or a place, and to supply what is lacking.

senses.label: Fulfill
senses.definition: To bring a prophecy to fulfillment or to carry out a law fully.

senses.label: Fill up, occupy
senses.definition: To fill a measure to the full, or to occupy a place or position.

senses.label: Supply what is lacking
senses.definition: To make up a deficiency for someone else.

background.note: Used of making up rent and completing contracts, the everyday sense of making something good in full.

study.caution: In 1CO 14:16 it is unclear whether the 'outsider' occupies a physical seat in the assembly or simply stands in the position of one who does not understand.

study.summary: More tolerable or bearable, used by Jesus to say that judgment will be lighter for notorious cities than for towns that reject him.

senses.label: More bearable
senses.definition: Easier to endure, comparing the fate of Sodom, Gomorrah, Tyre and Sidon on judgment day with that of towns that refused Jesus and his messengers.

study.exegesisTip: The comparison implies degrees of judgment depending on how much light people received.

study.summary: Foolish or without understanding: people who fail to grasp what they should, and desires that make no sense.

senses.label: Foolish, unthinking
senses.definition: Of people who lack understanding or fail to use it, whether slow to believe the prophets, unlearned, or sliding back into the flesh.

senses.label: Senseless desires
senses.definition: Of cravings that are irrational and harmful.

study.exegesisTip: In GAL 3:1, 3 the rebuke is not about intelligence but about failing to think through what they already know of Christ crucified and the Spirit.

study.summary: Unfeigned or genuine, without any play-acting, describing true love, faith and wisdom.

senses.label: Genuine, without pretence
senses.definition: Real and sincere, not put on for show; used of love, brotherly affection, faith and the wisdom from above.

background.note: Used of God's unfeigned justice in the Wisdom of Solomon.

study.exegesisTip: The word is built on the term for an actor; genuine love or faith is the opposite of a stage role.

study.summary: Worthily, in a manner worthy of someone or something, usually describing conduct that fits God, the Lord, the gospel or one's calling.

senses.label: Live worthily
senses.definition: To conduct one's life in a way that fits one's calling, the gospel, the Lord or God.

senses.label: Treat others worthily
senses.definition: To welcome or send on fellow believers in a way that befits God and his people.

background.note: Inscriptions often praise people who acted 'worthily of the god', a phrase NT writers turned to the Christian life.

study.summary: Disobedient, unwilling to be persuaded or to obey, whether toward parents or toward God.

senses.label: Disobedient to parents
senses.definition: Refusing to obey one's parents, listed among the marks of a corrupt society.

senses.label: Disobedient toward God
senses.definition: Resisting God's will or revelation; Paul was not like this toward his vision.

study.summary: Opposite, in front of, in the presence of, or against, depending on context.

senses.label: Opposite, facing
senses.definition: Located across from something.

senses.label: Before, in the presence
senses.definition: In the sight of others, or before one's eyes.

senses.label: Against, contrary to
senses.definition: In opposition to decrees or authority.

background.note: Used with the genitive for 'opposite', as in 'opposite his door'.

study.summary: To receive or welcome gladly, used of welcoming people and of accepting a message or a benefit with approval.

senses.label: Welcome a person
senses.definition: To receive someone warmly, as Jesus, missionaries or visitors were received.

senses.label: Accept, acknowledge
senses.definition: To accept a message or acknowledge benefits with approval.

background.note: In a Christian letter the writer asks his master to 'receive me kindly'.

study.summary: To go away on a journey abroad, used in parables of an owner or master leaving and of the prodigal son heading to a far country.

senses.label: Go abroad, depart
senses.definition: To leave home for another country or a long journey.

background.note: Marriage contracts pair 'being at home and being abroad', the ordinary sense of absence from home.

study.exegesisTip: In the parables the owner's absence sets up a period of trust in which servants or tenants are left responsible until he returns.

study.summary: A barn or storehouse for grain, used both literally and as an image of the final harvest when God gathers his people.

senses.label: Barn, storehouse
senses.definition: A building for storing harvested grain and goods.

senses.label: Image of final gathering
senses.definition: The barn into which the wheat is gathered, picturing God's gathering of the righteous at the judgment.

study.summary: To cut off; used of limbs, an ear and ropes, and once sarcastically by Paul of self-castration.

senses.label: Cut off
senses.definition: To sever something, such as a hand, foot, ear or ropes.

senses.label: Castrate oneself
senses.definition: In the middle voice, to mutilate oneself; Paul's biting wish for those pressing circumcision.

study.translationNote: GAL 5:12 is rendered variously as 'cut themselves off', 'mutilate themselves' or 'emasculate themselves'; most scholars favour the physical sense.
study.caution: A minority read GAL 5:12 as a wish that the agitators would cut themselves off from the community rather than a reference to castration.

study.summary: To hide away or keep concealed; used literally of hiding money and, above all, of God's wisdom and saving purpose kept hidden until he chose to reveal it.

senses.label: Hide an object
senses.definition: To put something out of sight for safekeeping, as the servant buried his master's money.

senses.label: God's concealing of truth
senses.definition: God's sovereign act of keeping spiritual understanding hidden from the self-reliant 'wise' while revealing it to the childlike.
senses.note: Paired with ἀποκαλύπτω, 'reveal', in both verses.

senses.label: Mystery hidden for ages
senses.definition: Of God's wisdom and plan in Christ, kept hidden through past ages and generations and now made known (perfect passive participle).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses only the perfect passive participle, always tied to μυστήριον or God's wisdom: what was once hidden is now disclosed in the gospel.

background.note: From Homer on it means to hide or keep something back from someone; Herodotus uses it of withholding information about one's wealth.

study.exegesisTip: In Paul the 'hidden' never means permanently secret: the participle always sits beside a statement that the mystery has now been revealed or proclaimed.

study.summary: To leave behind; in the passive, to remain or be left over; and to abandon or desert a place.

senses.label: Leave behind
senses.definition: To leave a thing or person somewhere on departing.

senses.label: Remain, be left (passive)
senses.definition: Passive: to be still in store or still available, of a Sabbath rest that remains for God's people, or of no sacrifice remaining for deliberate sin.

senses.label: Desert, abandon
senses.definition: To forsake one's proper place, of angels who abandoned their own dwelling.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the impersonal passive 'there remains' to argue what is still open (the promised rest) and what is no longer available (another sacrifice for wilful sin).

background.note: A standard term in wills for leaving property or naming an heir.

study.summary: To defraud or rob someone of what is due, to deprive; passive, to be deprived of or bereft of something.

senses.label: Defraud, cheat
senses.definition: To take or withhold what rightfully belongs to another, especially by fraud, as in the commandment 'do not defraud' and in lawsuits among believers.
senses.note: In 1CO 6:7 the middle/passive means to let oneself be defrauded.

senses.label: Withhold wages fraudulently
senses.definition: Of wages kept back by fraud from labourers.

senses.label: Deprive; be bereft
senses.definition: To deny someone what is owed, of spouses refusing marital relations; passive, to be robbed of, of men bereft of the truth.

background.note: Used absolutely of officials 'defrauding' those entitled to provisions, as in Mark's commandment.

study.exegesisTip: In 1CO 7:5 Paul applies the language of withholding what is owed to marriage: sexual relations are a debt each spouse owes the other.

study.summary: To say goodbye to or take leave of someone; figuratively, to part with or renounce something.

senses.label: Bid farewell, take leave
senses.definition: To say goodbye to people on departing.

senses.label: Renounce, give up
senses.definition: To part with or say farewell to all one's possessions as the cost of discipleship.

study.translationNote: In LUK 14:33 versions vary between 'forsake', 'renounce', 'give up' and 'say goodbye to'; the same verb as 'bid farewell' elsewhere, it pictures taking leave of one's possessions.

background.note: Common in letters for saying goodbye; in one papyrus it has the stronger sense 'get rid of'.

study.exegesisTip: LUK 9:61 and LUK 14:33 use the same verb: the would-be disciple wanted to bid farewell to family, but Jesus asks his followers to bid farewell to everything they own.

study.summary: To push away from oneself; hence to reject or repudiate a person, message or conscience.

senses.label: Push aside
senses.definition: To shove someone away physically, as the Israelite pushed Moses aside.

senses.label: Reject, repudiate
senses.definition: To refuse and cast off a person or thing: Israel rejecting Moses, hearers rejecting God's word, some rejecting a good conscience.

senses.label: God casting off his people
senses.definition: Of God repudiating Israel, which Paul firmly denies.

background.note: Used of being illegally ousted from something.

study.exegesisTip: Paul's question in ROM 11:1-2 echoes the Old Testament assurance that the LORD will not cast off his people (1SA 12:22).

study.summary: Ungodliness or impiety: irreverence toward God and the wicked conduct that flows from it.

senses.label: Ungodliness, impiety
senses.definition: A disposition and way of life that refuses God due reverence, often paired with injustice toward people.

senses.label: Ungodly deeds, sins
senses.definition: Plural or descriptive genitive: specific acts or desires of impiety, which God removes from Jacob or will judge.

authorNotes.author: Jude
authorNotes.note: Jude piles up the word-group (ungodly, ungodliness, act ungodly) to characterise the false teachers.

background.note: Classical Greek set impiety toward the gods against injustice toward men; it was also a legal charge.

study.exegesisTip: In ROM 1:18 ἀσέβεια (wrong toward God) and ἀδικία (wrong toward people) together sum up human sin; Paul traces the second back to the first.

study.summary: To dishonour, insult or treat shamefully; passive, to be disgraced.

senses.label: Treat shamefully, insult
senses.definition: To heap indignity on someone, by abuse or by contempt, including dishonouring God by breaking his law.

senses.label: Be disgraced (passive)
senses.definition: To suffer dishonour: the apostles counted worthy of disgrace for Jesus' name, and bodies degraded through impurity.

background.note: Of the shame of being insulted in public.

study.exegesisTip: ACT 5:41 contains a deliberate paradox: the apostles were 'deemed worthy' (κατηξιώθησαν) to be 'dishonoured'.

study.summary: A non-Greek, foreigner; one whose language is unintelligible to the speaker, without necessarily implying cruelty or lack of culture.

senses.label: Non-Greek peoples
senses.definition: People outside Greek language and culture, paired with Greeks or listed among ethnic categories.

senses.label: Local non-Greek inhabitants
senses.definition: The native people of Malta, who did not speak Greek, yet showed unusual kindness.

senses.label: Foreigner in speech
senses.definition: One who cannot be understood, of mutual incomprehension when a language is not known.

study.translationNote: 'Barbarian' (KJV) now suggests savagery; modern versions use 'non-Greeks', 'foreigners' or 'islanders', closer to the word's linguistic sense.

background.note: Originally all non-Greek-speaking peoples, often set against Greeks.

study.summary: Weight or burden, literal or figurative: toil, obligation, a believer's load, or a weight of glory.

senses.label: Burden to be borne
senses.definition: A heavy load of toil, obligation or trouble that someone must carry.

senses.label: Weight of glory
senses.definition: A positive 'weight': abundance and substance of eternal glory outweighing present light affliction.

senses.label: Weight, claim, importance
senses.definition: In the phrase ἐν βάρει εἶναι: either to be burdensome (claim support) or to carry weight/authority as apostles.

study.translationNote: In 1TH 2:6 versions divide between 'we might have been burdensome' (claiming financial support) and 'we could have made demands / asserted authority'.

background.note: Used of burdensome public duties and of tax burdens.

study.exegesisTip: 2CO 4:17 may play on the Hebrew idea of 'glory' (kavod) as heaviness: light affliction versus a heavy weight of glory.
study.caution: The sense in 1TH 2:6 (burden vs. dignity) is disputed; Paul's refusal of support nearby favours financial burden, but 'authority' is also defended.

study.summary: Heavy; figuratively burdensome, weighty or serious, and of persons fierce or savage.

senses.label: Heavy, burdensome
senses.definition: Hard to bear, of loads imposed by the Pharisees and (negated) of God's commandments.

senses.label: Weighty, serious, important
senses.definition: Of great importance or gravity: the weightier matters of the law, serious charges, and Paul's forceful letters.

senses.label: Fierce, savage
senses.definition: Of wolves (false teachers): violent and cruel.

background.note: Used of being seriously ill.

study.summary: Torment or torture, the suffering inflicted in God's end-time judgments in Revelation.

senses.label: Torment, torture
senses.definition: Severe pain inflicted as punishment: the scorpion-like sting of the locusts, the unending torment of beast-worshippers, and the judgment of Babylon.

study.exegesisTip: REV 18:7 states a principle of measured retribution: Babylon receives torment in proportion to her self-glorification and luxury.

study.summary: An abomination: something detestable to God, especially idolatry and what defiles worship.

senses.label: Abomination of desolation
senses.definition: From Daniel: a sacrilegious object or act set up in the holy place that brings desolation.

senses.label: What God detests
senses.definition: Anything loathsome to God: human pride, idolatrous and immoral practices, and those who do them.

background.note: Common in the Greek Old Testament for what God abhors, especially idols; the phrase for an idol set up in the temple comes from Daniel and Maccabees.

study.exegesisTip: In LUK 16:15 Jesus applies cult language to moral values: what people exalt can be as repugnant to God as an idol.
study.caution: The identity of the 'abomination of desolation' (Antiochus, Roman desecration in AD 70, or a future event) is debated.

study.summary: The language of a particular people or region, one's own native tongue.

senses.label: Native language
senses.definition: The particular language of a people or region, especially one's mother tongue, including Aramaic ('the Hebrew language') in Jerusalem.

study.translationNote: 'The Hebrew dialect' in ACT 21:40, 22:2 and 26:14 is usually understood as Aramaic, the everyday language of Judea, though some argue for Hebrew.

background.note: Classically 'discourse' or 'conversation', later 'articulate speech' and then a particular language.

study.exegesisTip: At Pentecost the stress falls on each hearer's own native language, not just an intelligible Greek (ACT 2:8).

study.summary: To cross over from one side to the other, usually by boat across a lake or sea.

senses.label: Cross over by water
senses.definition: To go across the Sea of Galilee or the sea in a boat.

senses.label: Pass across a gulf
senses.definition: To cross the great chasm fixed between the realm of Abraham and that of the rich man.

study.summary: Decay or corruption, specifically the decomposition of the body in the grave.

senses.label: Bodily decay in the grave
senses.definition: The rotting of the body after death; 'to see corruption' means to undergo it, which Christ did not.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Both Peter and Paul argue from Psalm 16: David saw decay, so the promise that the Holy One would not see it was fulfilled in the risen Jesus.

background.note: Classically 'destruction, ruin'; also moral corruption.

study.summary: To interpret or explain the meaning of something; also to translate from one language to another.

senses.label: Explain, expound
senses.definition: To set out the meaning of Scripture, as Jesus did concerning himself.

senses.label: Interpret tongues
senses.definition: To render speech in tongues intelligible to the church so it may be edified.

senses.label: Translate
senses.definition: To give the equivalent of a name in another language.

background.note: Used of Egyptian contracts translated into Greek.

study.summary: Twice; in the idiom 'once and twice' it means more than once, repeatedly.

senses.label: Twice
senses.definition: On two occasions or two times, as the rooster crowing twice or fasting twice a week.

senses.label: Again and again
senses.definition: In καὶ ἅπαξ καὶ δίς: more than once, repeatedly.

senses.label: Doubly
senses.definition: Of trees 'twice dead': utterly, thoroughly dead.

background.note: A condemned man speaks of saluting his 'second death', a phrase sometimes compared with Jude's 'twice dead'.

study.caution: 'Twice dead' in JUD 1:12 may mean completely dead (fruitless and then uprooted), or allude to spiritual death followed by final judgment; interpreters differ.

study.summary: A beam or log of timber, used by Jesus as a hyperbolic image for one's own large fault.

senses.label: Beam (hyperbole)
senses.definition: A heavy timber beam lodged in one's own eye, contrasted with a speck in a brother's eye, picturing gross self-blindness while judging others.

study.translationNote: Older versions say 'beam' or 'mote and beam'; some modern ones say 'log' or 'plank' to convey the comic exaggeration.

background.note: Used of heavy structural beams, e.g. over an oil press.

study.summary: A strengthened 'if': if indeed, if after all, since; it introduces a condition the writer often assumes to be true.

senses.label: If indeed, since
senses.definition: Introduces a condition assumed or expected to hold, often with near-causal force.

senses.label: Even if, if in fact
senses.definition: Introduces a supposition granted for argument's sake or one the writer rejects.

study.translationNote: Versions render it 'if', 'if indeed', 'if so be', 'since' or 'after all' (2TH 1:6), depending on how strongly they think the condition is assumed.
study.caution: Whether εἴπερ expresses certainty ('since') or a real condition ('provided that') depends on context; in ROM 8:17 suffering with Christ is a true condition of sharing his glory.

study.summary: Well; used in phrases for doing good, faring well, and as the master's commendation 'Well done!'.

senses.label: Well done! (commendation)
senses.definition: An exclamation of approval to a faithful servant.

senses.label: Do good, fare well
senses.definition: In set phrases: εὖ ποιεῖν, to do good to someone; εὖ πράσσειν, to do well or fare well; εὖ γίνεσθαι, to go well with someone.

background.note: Rare in the papyri except in letter formulas such as 'you will do well' (please) and closing wishes for prosperity.

study.summary: Passive in the NT: to suffer loss, forfeit, or be harmed.

senses.label: Forfeit one's life/self
senses.definition: To lose one's very soul or self, the ultimate loss set against gaining the world.

senses.label: Suffer loss
senses.definition: To lose what one had or might have had: reward when work is burned, or everything for Christ.

senses.label: Be harmed
senses.definition: To suffer damage at someone's hands.

background.note: Often in the technical sense of being fined.

study.exegesisTip: The word is commercial language of profit and loss, which Jesus (gain the world, forfeit the soul) and Paul (PHP 3:7-8) both use deliberately.

study.summary: A yoke, used figuratively for submission or bondage; once, a pair of scales.

senses.label: Yoke of submission
senses.definition: A figure for subjection to a teacher, law or master: Christ's easy yoke, the burden of the law, or slavery.

senses.label: Balance, pair of scales
senses.definition: The beam of a balance used for weighing, signalling scarcity and rationing.

background.note: Used literally of farm yokes; the related neuter form means a balance.

study.exegesisTip: Jewish teaching spoke of taking 'the yoke of the Torah'; Jesus offers his own yoke as gentle, while Peter and Paul call the law's demands a yoke too heavy to bear.

study.summary: To be confident, courageous or bold.

senses.label: Be confident, courageous
senses.definition: To have settled courage and assurance, especially in the face of death or danger.

senses.label: Have confidence in
senses.definition: To be fully confident about someone.

senses.label: Be bold toward
senses.definition: To act boldly or severely toward people.

background.note: Used of having confidence in one's evidence or one's cause.

study.summary: To lay a foundation; figuratively, to establish firmly.

senses.label: Found, lay foundations
senses.definition: To set something on a foundation, of a house on rock or the earth created by the Lord.

senses.label: Establish firmly
senses.definition: To make believers stable and secure, grounded in love and faith.

background.note: Literally to lay foundations, also figuratively of a kingdom firmly founded.

study.summary: To warm; middle, to warm oneself.

senses.label: Warm oneself
senses.definition: To warm oneself at a fire, of Peter in the high priest's courtyard, or (in a hollow blessing) to keep warm with clothing.

study.exegesisTip: James' 'be warmed and filled' mocks well-wishing that provides nothing that actually warms.

study.summary: Of a mother, to nurse or breastfeed; of an infant, to suck.

senses.label: Nurse, give suck
senses.definition: Of mothers or breasts: to breastfeed a child.

senses.label: Suckling infants
senses.definition: Participle of babies still nursing.

background.note: Frequent in contracts for wet-nurses.

study.summary: Mortal, subject to death; as a noun, what is mortal.

senses.label: Mortal body
senses.definition: Describing the present body or flesh as liable to death, yet the sphere where life in Christ is lived and revealed.

senses.label: The mortal (noun)
senses.definition: Neuter: mortal nature which will put on immortality and be swallowed up by life.

background.note: From Homer, the standard contrast between mortals and immortal gods.

study.summary: Incense: fragrant material burnt in worship, and the offering of it.

senses.label: Temple incense offering
senses.definition: The incense burnt in the temple and the hour when it was offered.

senses.label: Heavenly incense, prayers
senses.definition: Incense in heaven linked with or symbolising the prayers of the saints.

senses.label: Incense as trade goods
senses.definition: Aromatic substances among Babylon's luxury cargo.

background.note: Usually plural for fragrant substances burned in sacrifice.

study.summary: To sit or be seated, usually describing a continuing position.

senses.label: Sit, be seated
senses.definition: To be in a sitting position, of teaching, listening, resting, staying at home, or sitting in council.

study.summary: To mistreat or harm; also to embitter someone's mind against others.

senses.label: Mistreat, harm
senses.definition: To do harm to people, by oppression or persecution.

senses.label: Embitter, poison minds
senses.definition: To make people hostile or ill-disposed toward others.

background.note: From Homer, to maltreat or distress.

study.summary: The camel, the largest animal familiar in Palestine, mentioned for John's rough clothing and in Jesus' proverbial hyperboles.

senses.label: Camel (literal)
senses.definition: The animal itself; John the Baptist wore a garment woven of camel's hair, the coarse dress of a desert prophet.

senses.label: In proverbial hyperbole
senses.definition: The largest common animal set against the smallest opening or creature, to picture something humanly impossible or grotesquely inconsistent: a camel through a needle's eye, or swallowing a camel while straining out a gnat.

background.note: Camels appear constantly in Roman-era papyri as beasts of burden, e.g. loads of wheat or seed taxed at the customs house.

study.exegesisTip: In MAT 23:24 the contrast is sharpened because both the gnat and the camel were unclean animals: the scrupulous strain out the tiny one and gulp the huge one.
study.caution: The saying about the needle's eye is deliberate hyperbole (the disciples respond, 'Who then can be saved?'). The popular idea of a small 'Needle Gate' in Jerusalem has no ancient evidence, and the variant κάμιλος ('rope') is a late, weakly attested reading.

study.summary: A tiny dry particle such as a chip, splinter or bit of straw, used by Jesus for the small fault one is quick to see in another.

senses.label: Speck, splinter (figurative fault)
senses.definition: A minute bit of chaff or wood in the eye, contrasted with a 'beam' (δοκός) in one's own eye; a picture of a brother's minor failing scrutinized by someone blind to his own far greater one.

study.translationNote: Older English versions say 'mote' (a tiny particle); modern versions use 'speck' or 'splinter'. All aim at the contrast between something minute and the huge 'beam' or 'log'.

background.note: Used of dry twigs and straws such as birds gather for their nests.

study.exegesisTip: The point is not that the brother's fault should be ignored: the passage ends with seeing clearly to remove the speck, after first dealing with one's own beam.

study.summary: To reconcile, that is, to change a relationship of hostility into one of peace; used by Paul of God reconciling people to himself through Christ, and once of a wife returning to her husband.

senses.label: Reconcile to God
senses.definition: God's act, through the death of his Son, of bringing estranged and hostile people (and 'the world') into peace with himself; in the passive, people 'are reconciled' to God and are urged to accept it.

senses.label: Be reconciled to a spouse
senses.definition: Of a separated wife being restored to her husband.

background.note: The basic sense was 'exchange', especially of money, and in the middle exchanging one thing for another; the personal sense 'reconcile' grew from changing enmity into friendship.

study.exegesisTip: In Paul, God is always the one who reconciles and humans (or the world) are the ones reconciled; God takes the initiative 'while we were enemies' (ROM 5:10), and the apostolic appeal is 'be reconciled to God' (2CO 5:20).

study.summary: The curtain or veil of the sanctuary, in the NT always the inner veil that screened off the Most Holy Place.

senses.label: Temple veil torn
senses.definition: The inner curtain of the Jerusalem temple, torn in two at Jesus' death, signalling that access to God's presence was opened (and/or judgment on the temple).

senses.label: Tabernacle curtain in Hebrews
senses.definition: The 'second curtain' before the Most Holy Place, behind which Christ, our forerunner, has entered; figuratively identified with his flesh, through which a new and living way to God has been opened.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Uses the veil to explain Christ's priestly entry into God's presence and the believer's resulting access: hope enters 'within the curtain', and the way runs 'through the curtain, that is, his flesh'.

study.translationNote: Some versions say 'veil', others 'curtain'; both render the same woven hanging.

background.note: Chiefly renders the Hebrew term for the veil before the Holy of Holies.
Not exclusively biblical: a 4th-century BC temple inventory from Samos uses it of a table-cover.

study.summary: A curse, either the doom pronounced by God's law on the disobedient or the cursing words that come from human lips.

senses.label: Curse of the law
senses.definition: The condemnation the law pronounces on all who fail to keep it; Christ redeemed his people from it by himself 'becoming a curse', bearing that sentence on the cross.

senses.label: Doom, being accursed
senses.definition: The state of lying under God's curse: land near to being cursed and burned, or false teachers called 'children of a curse' (a Hebrew-style idiom for accursed people).

senses.label: Cursing speech
senses.definition: Spoken imprecation, the opposite of blessing, coming inconsistently from the same mouth.

background.note: Standard word for laying curses on someone.

study.exegesisTip: In GAL 3:13 Paul uses the abstract noun for a person: Christ did not merely bear a curse but 'became a curse' for us, explained by the citation about one hanged on a tree.

study.summary: To curse, to call down evil on someone; the perfect passive participle describes those who stand under God's curse.

senses.label: Curse someone or something
senses.definition: To utter an imprecation against a person or thing; believers are to answer it with blessing rather than return it, and Jesus' curse on the fig tree took effect.

senses.label: Accursed (passive participle)
senses.definition: Those under God's sentence of condemnation, sent away from him at the final judgment.

background.note: From Homer onward, 'call down curses' on someone.

study.exegesisTip: In the Gospels and Paul the verb regularly stands opposite εὐλογέω ('bless'), showing that the Christian response to being cursed is blessing.

study.summary: To kiss, often with the sense of kissing warmly or repeatedly, in greeting, devotion, welcome or farewell.

senses.label: Kiss (greeting, love, farewell)
senses.definition: To kiss someone as a sign of affection or devotion: the sinful woman continually kissing Jesus' feet, the father welcoming the prodigal, the Ephesian elders bidding Paul farewell.

senses.label: Judas's kiss
senses.definition: The kiss of greeting Judas gave Jesus as the agreed signal for his arrest.

background.note: Used of kissing hands and feet in supplication or gratitude.

study.caution: Some lexicons render 'kiss fervently', and in MAT 26:49 and MAR 14:45 the compound follows the simple φιλέω of the agreed signal. But examples outside the NT show the compound often meant simply 'kiss', so how much intensity the prefix adds is debated.

study.summary: An accuser, a prosecutor who brings charges against someone, whether in a Roman court or, of Satan, before God.

senses.label: Legal accuser
senses.definition: Those who bring formal charges against a person before a judge, as Paul's accusers before the Roman governors, or the men who brought the woman to Jesus.

senses.label: Satan, the accuser
senses.definition: The devil as the one who accuses believers before God day and night, now cast down.

background.note: Regular legal term for a prosecutor or plaintiff in court proceedings.

study.exegesisTip: ACT 25:16 reflects Roman legal principle: the accused must meet his accusers face to face and have opportunity to make a defence.

study.summary: A wooden box or chest, used in the NT of Noah's ark and of the ark of the covenant.

senses.label: Noah's ark
senses.definition: The great vessel Noah built for the saving of his household through the flood.

senses.label: Ark of the covenant
senses.definition: The gold-covered chest in the tabernacle's Most Holy Place, and its heavenly counterpart seen in God's temple.

background.note: Used of the official chest in which documents were deposited for safekeeping.

study.summary: A key; in the NT always figurative, for authority to open or shut, admit or exclude.

senses.label: Authority to grant access
senses.definition: The power to open the way into the kingdom or into knowledge of God, given to Peter, or taken away by lawyers who hinder others.

senses.label: Christ's sovereign authority
senses.definition: The risen Christ holds the keys of Death and Hades and the key of David, so that what he opens no one can shut.

senses.label: Key of the Abyss
senses.definition: Authority, given by God, to open or lock the bottomless pit.

background.note: Leases speak of a granary being handed over 'with its doors and keys'.

study.exegesisTip: The key of David in REV 3:7 echoes Isaiah's oracle in which a royal steward is given the key of David's house, with power to open and shut.

study.summary: Scarlet or crimson, the costly red dye; in Revelation the color of the beast and of Babylon's luxurious clothing.

senses.label: Scarlet (color, dyed material)
senses.definition: Dyed scarlet: the soldiers' mocking robe on Jesus and the scarlet wool used in Moses' covenant sprinkling.

senses.label: Scarlet in Revelation
senses.definition: The scarlet beast, and scarlet cloth or garments as part of Babylon's luxury and trade.

background.note: A pawnshop account values a scarlet shirt at almost twice a new white one, showing the cost of the dye.

study.summary: The bosom or chest, the fold of a garment, or a bay; used figuratively of intimate closeness and honored fellowship.

senses.label: Bosom: closest intimacy
senses.definition: The place on or beside the chest, as of one reclining next to another at a meal; hence a place of honor and closeness, Lazarus at Abraham's side and the Son in the Father's bosom.

senses.label: Fold of a garment, lap
senses.definition: The fold of a loose robe above the belt, used as a pocket into which measured grain is poured.

senses.label: Bay
senses.definition: A bay or inlet of the coast.

study.translationNote: Older versions keep 'bosom' (JOH 1:18, LUK 16:22); many modern versions say 'at the Father's side' or 'Abraham's side', and 'lap' in LUK 6:38.

background.note: Jewish and Christian epitaphs pray for rest 'in the bosoms of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob'.
Used of a gulf, as in the Gulf of Issus.

study.summary: A basket, the kind used for the leftover fragments after the feeding of the five thousand.

senses.label: Basket (of leftovers)
senses.definition: A carrying basket; the disciples collected twelve basketfuls of fragments after Jesus fed the five thousand.

background.note: Such baskets came in different sizes, e.g. holding forty or twenty pounds in military accounts.

study.exegesisTip: Matthew and Mark keep this word for the feeding of the five thousand and use σπυρίς for the four thousand, a distinction preserved even in Jesus' recall in MAR 8:19 and MAT 16:9.
study.caution: The common claim that the σπυρίς was much larger is uncertain; evidence suggests the two words differed more in material or type than in size.

study.summary: To cry out or shout loudly, whether in urgent appeal, in command, or in the clamor of a crowd.

senses.label: Shout, clamor
senses.definition: To raise the voice loudly: the Servant who will not shout or clamor in the streets, and the crowd and chief priests shouting for Barabbas and for crucifixion.

senses.label: Cry out urgently
senses.definition: A loud cry of appeal (the Canaanite woman) or of authoritative summons (Jesus calling Lazarus from the tomb).

background.note: Of men, cry aloud or shout (also used of dogs baying).

study.summary: A cry or shout, whether an announcement, an uproar, an angry outcry, or a cry of anguish.

senses.label: Loud cry, shout
senses.definition: A loud call or announcement, as the midnight cry heralding the bridegroom or an angel calling out.

senses.label: Clamor, angry shouting
senses.definition: Uproar in dispute, and the shouting of quarrelsome anger that believers must put away.

senses.label: Cry of anguish
senses.definition: Loud crying in distress: Jesus' prayers with strong crying and tears, and the crying that will be no more in the new creation.

background.note: Used both of joyful acclamation for a king and of a village disturbance.

study.summary: To escape notice, be hidden from someone; with a participle, to do something without realizing it.

senses.label: Escape notice, be hidden
senses.definition: To remain unnoticed or concealed, as Jesus could not stay hidden, nor the healed woman; with a person as object, something escapes his notice.

senses.label: Do unawares (with participle)
senses.definition: In the classical idiom with a participle, to do something without knowing it: some entertained angels unawares.

background.note: Common phrase 'it did not escape my notice'.

study.exegesisTip: In 2PE 3:5 the participle θέλοντας suggests the scoffers' ignorance is willful: the fact escapes them because they want it to.

study.summary: To be lacking or wanting; in the middle/passive, to fall short of or be in need of something.

senses.label: Be lacking (active)
senses.definition: Something is missing or still needed: one thing the rich ruler lacked, things left unfinished in Crete, nothing to be lacking for traveling workers.

senses.label: Lack, fall short (middle/passive)
senses.definition: To be deficient in or lack something, whether completeness of character, wisdom, or daily food.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: Links the word in a chain: perseverance makes believers complete, 'lacking in nothing', and whoever 'lacks' wisdom should ask God.

background.note: A technical term in accounts for a deficit.

study.summary: Service, ministry, especially the sacred service of priests, and by extension Christian giving and self-offering seen as service to God.

senses.label: Priestly ministry
senses.definition: The ritual service of priests in temple or tabernacle: Zechariah's term of duty, the vessels of ministry, and Christ's superior priestly ministry.

senses.label: Service as offering to God
senses.definition: Believers' faith and practical help described in sacrificial language: the Philippians' faith and service, their aid to Paul, and the Corinthian collection for the saints.

background.note: At Athens, a public service such as equipping a chorus or warship, performed by wealthy citizens at their own expense.
Also used of religious service in Egyptian temples.

study.summary: To bathe or wash, usually the whole body rather than a part, used literally and once of cleansing from sins.

senses.label: Bathe, wash the body
senses.definition: To wash a person's whole body or wounds: Dorcas's body prepared for burial, the jailer washing Paul and Silas, a sow that washes itself only to wallow again.

senses.label: Washed clean (religious)
senses.definition: The completed washing that makes a person clean, with spiritual meaning: one who has bathed needs only the feet washed, bodies washed with pure water, and (in some manuscripts) Christ washing us from our sins.

study.translationNote: In REV 1:5 the KJV follows manuscripts reading λούσαντι 'washed us from our sins'; most modern versions follow λύσαντι 'freed (loosed) us from our sins'.

background.note: Common for bathing oneself, e.g. a man writing that he had not bathed since parting from his wife.

study.exegesisTip: In JOH 13:10 Jesus contrasts λούω (a full bath) with νίπτω (washing a part, the feet): the one already bathed needs only partial washing.

study.summary: A wolf, the predator of the flock, used as a picture of hostile persecutors and destructive false teachers.

senses.label: Wolf (danger to the flock)
senses.definition: The wolf that attacks and scatters sheep; disciples are sent out like sheep or lambs among wolves, and the hired hand flees when the wolf comes.

senses.label: False teachers
senses.definition: Deceivers who look harmless but are ravenous inwardly, or 'savage wolves' who come in among God's flock after Paul's departure.

background.note: Homer already calls wolves 'flesh-eating'.

study.summary: A magus: originally a member of the Persian priestly caste skilled in dreams and astrology, and more generally a practitioner of magic, a sorcerer.

senses.label: Eastern wise men (Magi)
senses.definition: Learned men from the East, probably astrologers of Persian or Babylonian tradition, who followed the star to worship the newborn king.

senses.label: Sorcerer, magician
senses.definition: A practitioner of magic, here the Jewish false prophet Bar-Jesus (Elymas) who opposed Paul at Paphos.

study.translationNote: In Matthew 2 versions vary between 'wise men' (KJV), 'Magi' and 'astrologers'; in Acts 13 the same word is rendered 'sorcerer' or 'magician'.

background.note: Originally the name of a Median tribe, then of Persian priests and dream-interpreters.
Also used pejoratively of a charlatan or impostor.

study.caution: Matthew does not say there were three Magi or that they were kings; those details come from later tradition (the number from the three gifts).

study.summary: Long, of time or space: 'long' prayers and a 'far-off' country or people.

senses.label: Long (of prayers)
senses.definition: Lengthy prayers made for show by those who devour widows' houses.

senses.label: Distant, far off
senses.definition: Far away in space: a distant country in Jesus' parables; and 'those who are far off', to whom the promise of the Spirit also extends.

study.exegesisTip: In ACT 2:39 'all who are far off' probably reaches beyond the Jews of Jerusalem to the dispersion and ultimately to Gentiles whom the Lord calls.

study.summary: A whip or scourge; literally a flogging, and figuratively a painful disease or affliction.

senses.label: Whip, flogging
senses.definition: Scourging as punishment or interrogation, as ordered for Paul and endured by the faithful of old.

senses.label: Affliction, disease
senses.definition: A tormenting illness pictured as a scourge, from which Jesus healed many, including the woman with the hemorrhage.

study.translationNote: In the healing passages versions vary between 'plague', 'disease', 'affliction' and 'suffering'.

background.note: The figurative sense of a scourge or plague sent by a god goes back to Homer ('the scourge of Zeus').

study.summary: Vain, empty, futile: lacking any real substance or result; in the plural, idols as 'worthless things'.

senses.label: Futile, without result
senses.definition: Producing nothing and achieving nothing: faith if Christ is not raised, the reasonings of the worldly wise, pointless disputes, religion that does not bridle the tongue, an inherited empty way of life.

senses.label: Idols, worthless things
senses.definition: As a noun, the false gods and idolatrous practices from which people must turn to the living God.

background.note: Used of 'useless expense'.

study.exegesisTip: The LXX often uses this word and its cognates for idols, which explains its use for pagan gods in ACT 14:15.

study.summary: To be drunk with wine; figuratively, to be intoxicated with something such as bloodshed.

senses.label: Be drunk
senses.definition: To be intoxicated with wine, as the careless servant's companions, guests at the end of a feast, the night-time drunkard, or Corinthians at the Lord's Supper; Peter denies the disciples are drunk at Pentecost.

senses.label: Drunk with blood (figurative)
senses.definition: Glutted and exhilarated with violence: the woman drunk with the blood of the saints and martyrs.

study.translationNote: In JOH 2:10 versions range from 'well drunk' and 'had too much to drink' to 'drunk freely'; the steward's point is that guests have drunk plentifully and no longer notice quality.

study.summary: Care, anxiety, worry: a mind divided and preoccupied, whether by the pressures of life or by concern for others.

senses.label: Worldly anxieties
senses.definition: The cares of this age and of daily life that choke the word and weigh down the heart.

senses.label: Anxiety cast on God
senses.definition: Every worry believers carry, which they are to throw on God because he cares for them.

senses.label: Pastoral concern
senses.definition: Paul's daily burden of care for all the churches.

background.note: A wife writes that she lies sleepless with one anxiety, her husband's safety.

study.summary: A mediator or go-between who stands between two parties to make or guarantee an agreement.

senses.label: Mediator of the law
senses.definition: The intermediary (Moses) through whom the law was given; Paul contrasts this with God's direct, one-sided promise.

senses.label: Christ the mediator
senses.definition: Jesus as the one mediator between God and humanity and the mediator and guarantor of the new and better covenant, established by his death.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Always links the word with 'covenant': Christ is mediator of a better, new covenant.

background.note: Common in legal documents for an arbitrator appointed between parties.

study.caution: GAL 3:20 ('a mediator is not of one, but God is one') is notoriously difficult, and interpreters have proposed many explanations.

study.summary: To regret, feel remorse, or change one's mind afterward about something done or decided.

senses.label: Change one's mind, repent
senses.definition: To think better of a decision and turn around, as the son who refused and then went, or the leaders who did not change their minds and believe John.

senses.label: Regret, feel remorse
senses.definition: Sorrow over what one has done: Judas's remorse, or Paul's passing regret over a severe letter.

senses.label: God will not change his mind
senses.definition: God's oath establishing the Son's eternal priesthood is irrevocable.

study.translationNote: KJV renders 'repent' throughout, including Judas in MAT 27:3; modern versions often use 'regret', 'feel remorse' or 'change one's mind', to separate it from μετανοέω.

background.note: Used in a warning: 'if you do not stop your malpractices, you will repent it'.

study.caution: The word does not always mean saving repentance; Judas regretted his act without being restored. Still, the distinction from μετανοέω is not rigid (see MAT 21:29, 32).

study.summary: To transfer or move to another place, to change; in the middle, to desert or go over to another side.

senses.label: Transfer, take away
senses.definition: To move from one place to another: the patriarchs' bones carried to Shechem, and Enoch taken up by God so that he did not see death.

senses.label: Change, pervert
senses.definition: To alter something into something else: a change of priesthood requiring a change of law, or turning God's grace into license for immorality.

senses.label: Desert, turn away (middle)
senses.definition: To defect from one allegiance to another, as the Galatians turning from God who called them to a different gospel.

background.note: Used of a soldier's transfer from one military unit to another.

study.exegesisTip: In GAL 1:6 the present tense ('you are deserting') shows the defection was still under way, so Paul writes to stop it.

study.summary: Sharing in, partaking of; as a noun, a partner or companion.

senses.label: Partner, companion
senses.definition: An associate in work or status: Peter's fishing partners, and the 'companions' above whom the Son is anointed.

senses.label: Sharer in
senses.definition: One who participates in something: the heavenly calling, Christ, the Holy Spirit, or the Father's discipline.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Uses the word for believers' participation in heavenly realities, sometimes tied to a condition of holding firm to the end.

background.note: Common for business partners or associates.

study.summary: Μοιχάω (used in the middle voice, μοιχᾶσθαι) means to commit adultery, and in the Gospels it is always about divorce followed by remarriage.

senses.label: Commit adultery (by remarriage)
senses.definition: To break the marriage bond sexually. Jesus applies it to a man who divorces his wife and marries another, to a man who marries a divorced woman, and to a woman who divorces her husband and marries again.
senses.note: At MAR 10:11 the adultery is committed 'against her', meaning against the first wife.

background.note: The Greek translators of Jeremiah and Ezekiel use this verb for Israel's unfaithfulness to God, pictured as adultery.

study.exegesisTip: Mark 10:12 has the woman as the one who divorces, a case that fits Greco-Roman law better than Jewish law. The saying treats husband and wife as equally bound.

study.summary: Μόλις is an adverb meaning 'with difficulty, only just, scarcely'. It describes something that happens, but barely.

senses.label: With difficulty, barely
senses.definition: Something is achieved only with great effort or narrowly, as when the apostles barely restrain the crowd or the ship struggles along the coast.
senses.note: At 1PE 4:18, quoting Proverbs, it means the righteous are saved only through hardship, not that their salvation is uncertain.

senses.label: Rarely, hardly ever
senses.definition: Something hardly ever happens: a person will scarcely die even for a righteous man.

background.note: Used in everyday letters for doing something with difficulty, e.g. a man who could only just pay by selling all his property.

study.summary: Μόσχος means a calf or young bull, especially one used for a feast or a sacrifice.

senses.label: Calf for a feast
senses.definition: The fattened calf that the father kills to celebrate his returning son.

senses.label: Sacrificial calf
senses.definition: Calves whose blood was used in the old covenant rites, set against Christ's entering with his own blood.

senses.label: Calf-like living creature
senses.definition: The second living creature around God's throne looks like a calf or ox.

background.note: A papyrus certificate shows an official who sealed sacred calves after inspecting them and finding them without blemish.

study.summary: Νήφω literally means to be sober. In the NT it always means being clear-headed, self-controlled and alert, especially in view of the Lord's coming.

senses.label: Be sober-minded, alert
senses.definition: To keep a clear, self-controlled mind, free from anything that dulls judgment. It is often paired with staying awake, hope or prayer.
senses.note: In 1 Thessalonians the picture of drunkenness at night stands in the background.

study.translationNote: Translations vary between 'be sober', 'be sober-minded', 'be self-controlled' and 'keep your head'. These are attempts to give the figurative sense of a clear mind, not a narrow warning about wine.

background.note: Literally, to drink no wine and stay sober, as opposed to being drunk.
A letter-writer wants his reader to read a letter 'in a sober mood', meaning with a clear head.

study.exegesisTip: Peter and Paul pair νήφω with γρηγορέω ('stay awake'): being sober and being awake together describe readiness for the end.

study.summary: Νόημα means a thought, plan or purpose. By extension it can mean the mind that produces thoughts, and all six NT uses are Paul's.

senses.label: Thought, scheme, design
senses.definition: A thought or purpose, including the hostile schemes of Satan and the thoughts that must be made obedient to Christ.

senses.label: Mind, understanding
senses.definition: The thinking faculty, which can be hardened or blinded so that it cannot see the gospel.

study.translationNote: Many versions render the plural as 'minds' at 2CO 3:14, 2CO 4:4, 2CO 11:3 and PHP 4:7, while others prefer 'thoughts'. Some scholars argue that 'thoughts' fits every occurrence.

background.note: Used since Homer for a thought or purpose formed in the mind.

study.summary: Οὐράνιος means 'heavenly', belonging to or coming from heaven. In Matthew it is used above all of God as 'your heavenly Father'.

senses.label: Heavenly (of the Father)
senses.definition: It describes God the Father as the one whose home is in heaven, who forgives, provides and judges.

senses.label: From or in heaven
senses.definition: Belonging to heaven or sent from it: the heavenly army of angels, and the heavenly vision Paul obeyed.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses 'heavenly Father' as an alternative to 'your Father in heaven'.

background.note: Common in the magical papyri of heavenly spirits, as opposed to earthly ones and those under the earth.

study.summary: Παιδεία is the training of a child. It covers both instruction and the correction or discipline a father gives.

senses.label: Training, instruction
senses.definition: The upbringing and moral education of a child or believer, which shapes them toward what is right.

senses.label: Fatherly discipline
senses.definition: Corrective discipline, including hardship, that God gives his children as a sign of sonship and to make them holy.
senses.note: Hebrews builds on the wisdom teaching of Proverbs 3.

study.translationNote: Older versions use 'nurture' or 'chastening' and newer ones 'training' or 'discipline'. The Greek holds teaching and correction together in one word.

background.note: In classical Greek it is the standard word for education and culture.
In the Septuagint it chiefly translates Hebrew musar, which joins instruction with correction.

study.exegesisTip: In Hebrews 12 suffering is reframed as παιδεία. The point is not punishment for its own sake but a father training a son.

study.summary: Πάλαι is an adverb of time meaning 'long ago, formerly', or of a recent past, 'already, for some time'.

senses.label: Long ago, of old
senses.definition: At a time well in the past, e.g. God speaking to the fathers long ago, or people marked out long ago for condemnation.

senses.label: Former (with article)
senses.definition: Used like an adjective with the article: one's former or past sins.

senses.label: Already, some time ago
senses.definition: Of time only just past: Pilate asks whether Jesus had already died.

background.note: Common in letters, e.g. securities that 'ought to have been here long ago'.

study.summary: Παρασκευή literally means 'preparation'. In the NT it is the Jewish name for the day of preparation before the Sabbath, i.e. Friday.

senses.label: Preparation Day (Friday)
senses.definition: The day before the Sabbath, when everything had to be made ready. It is the day of Jesus' crucifixion and burial.
senses.note: Mark explains it as προσάββατον, 'the day before the Sabbath'.

senses.label: Preparation of the Passover
senses.definition: John's phrase for the day of Jesus' trial, in connection with the Passover.

background.note: The Didache tells Christians to fast on Wednesday and on 'the preparation', meaning Friday. In Modern Greek it is still the name for Friday.

study.caution: Scholars disagree on 'the Preparation of the Passover' (JOH 19:14). Some read it as the day before Passover, which would put the crucifixion as the Passover lambs were slain. Others read it as the Friday of Passover week, in line with the Synoptics.

study.summary: Παρατηρέω means to watch closely. In the Gospels and Acts this is usually done with hostile intent, and in Galatians it means to scrupulously observe religious days.

senses.label: Watch closely, spy on
