senses.definition: To keep someone or something under close watch, usually looking for a chance to accuse or harm: Jesus' opponents watch him on the Sabbath, and Saul's enemies watch the gates.
senses.note: At LUK 20:20 it may be absolute: 'watching their opportunity'.

senses.label: Observe (religious days)
senses.definition: To keep special days, months, seasons and years carefully, as religious obligations.

background.note: Used of keeping a strict watch over something, e.g. an order to guard a stone bowl closely.

study.summary: Πενθερά means mother-in-law, the mother of one's husband or wife.

senses.label: Peter's mother-in-law
senses.definition: Simon Peter's wife's mother, whom Jesus healed of a fever.

senses.label: Mother-in-law in conflict
senses.definition: In Jesus' words echoing Micah: the gospel divides even mother-in-law and daughter-in-law.

background.note: Used in ordinary letters, e.g. a message sent to someone's mother-in-law about a farm.

study.exegesisTip: The healing of Peter's mother-in-law assumes that Peter was married.

study.summary: Πεντακισχίλιοι is the number five thousand. It is used in all four Gospels for the men fed by Jesus from five loaves.

senses.label: Five thousand (fed)
senses.definition: The number of men, not counting women and children, whom Jesus fed with five loaves. Jesus later reminds the disciples of this miracle.

study.exegesisTip: Matthew adds 'besides women and children', so the whole crowd was larger than the figure given.

study.summary: Πεποίθησις means confidence or trust, a settled reliance on someone or something. All its NT uses are in Paul.

senses.label: Confidence in God or others
senses.definition: Assured trust, coming from God through Christ or directed toward fellow believers. It underlies Paul's plans and gives access to God.
senses.note: At 2CO 10:2 it is the bold confidence Paul is ready to show against his opponents.

senses.label: Confidence in the flesh
senses.definition: Reliance on one's human credentials and religious status, which Paul could claim but gives up for Christ.

background.note: Its one Septuagint use is the Assyrian officer's taunt to Hezekiah about what his confidence rests on.

study.summary: Περιάγω means to lead someone around, or, used without an object, to go around a region.

senses.label: Go about, travel around
senses.definition: To travel through an area, as Jesus went through Galilee's towns and villages teaching, or the Pharisees crossed sea and land for a convert. In Acts the blinded Elymas gropes about.

senses.label: Take along with one
senses.definition: To bring someone along as a travelling companion, e.g. a believing wife on missionary journeys.

background.note: Used of leading visitors around, e.g. showing guests all the gardens.

study.summary: Πηλός means wet earth: mud, or a potter's clay.

senses.label: Mud (for healing)
senses.definition: The mud Jesus made from his saliva and put on the eyes of the man born blind. Making it on the Sabbath became an issue.

senses.label: Potter's clay
senses.definition: The clay from which a potter shapes vessels, an image of God's right to shape people as he wills.
senses.note: Paul draws on the potter-and-clay image of Isaiah and Jeremiah.

study.translationNote: Older versions use 'clay' in John 9 and most modern ones use 'mud'. The Greek word covers both.

background.note: Used of the clay worked by masons and potters.

study.summary: Πήρα is a traveller's bag or pouch, usually made of leather. Jesus told those he sent out on mission not to take one.

senses.label: Traveller's bag
senses.definition: A bag for provisions on a journey. The disciples were sent without it, trusting God's provision, and later told to take one.

study.translationNote: The KJV's 'scrip' is an old word for a small bag. Modern versions use 'bag' or 'knapsack'.

background.note: From Homer on it is the pouch carried by beggars and wanderers.

study.caution: Deissmann argued that the word can mean a beggar's collecting bag, as used by wandering cult priests. If so, Jesus forbade begging, not just luggage. Most interpreters still take it as a bag for provisions.

study.summary: Πλέω means to sail or travel by sea.

senses.label: Sail, voyage
senses.definition: To travel by ship, as Jesus and the disciples on the lake and Paul on his voyages. The participle can mean 'those on board'.
senses.note: At REV 18:17, 'everyone who sails to a place' likely means sea travellers or traders.

background.note: Common in letters about voyages, e.g. a man unable to make a voyage because of illness.

study.summary: Πλοιάριον is a small boat. In NT use it is hardly different from the ordinary word πλοῖον.

senses.label: Small boat
senses.definition: A boat on the Sea of Galilee, kept ready for Jesus, used by fishermen, or by people crossing the lake.

background.note: Formed as a diminutive of πλοῖον, 'skiff, small boat'.

study.summary: Ποιητής means a maker or doer. In the NT it is either a poet or, mostly, one who actually carries out what the word or law says.

senses.label: Doer, one who obeys
senses.definition: Someone who puts the law or the word into practice rather than only hearing it.
senses.note: At JAM 4:11 the one who judges the law has set himself above it instead of doing it.

senses.label: Poet
senses.definition: A composer of verse, as when Paul quotes Greek poets in Athens.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James sets the 'doer' against the mere 'hearer' (ἀκροατής) of the word.

background.note: Its common classical sense is 'poet'.

study.summary: Πού is an unaccented (enclitic) particle meaning 'somewhere', or with numbers 'about, roughly'.

senses.label: Somewhere (citing Scripture)
senses.definition: Used to introduce a quotation without naming its location: 'someone has testified somewhere'.
senses.note: This is a literary convention for citing a well-known text, not a sign that the writer was unsure.

senses.label: About, approximately
senses.definition: With a number: Abraham was about a hundred years old.

background.note: Used in the same way to introduce a quotation from the Psalms.

study.caution: This should not be confused with the accented interrogative ποῦ, 'where?', which is a separate and much more common word.

study.summary: Πρᾶξις means a deed or action. In the plural it often means practices, usually bad ones, and it can also mean a body part's function.

senses.label: Deed, conduct
senses.definition: What a person has done, for which each will be repaid, or an action taken by a group.

senses.label: Evil practices
senses.definition: Sinful deeds or habitual practices to be confessed, put to death or put off.
senses.note: At ACT 19:18 this probably refers to magical practices, as the next verse suggests.

senses.label: Function
senses.definition: The particular task or role of a body part.

background.note: In the magical papyri πρᾶξις can mean a spell, e.g. one 'for driving out demons'. This throws light on the confessions at Ephesus.

study.summary: Προκόπτω means to advance or make progress, whether in growth, in a way of life, in evil, or in time.

senses.label: Grow, progress
senses.definition: To advance in good qualities or standing, as Jesus grew in wisdom and Paul advanced in Judaism.

senses.label: Advance in evil
senses.definition: To go further, especially into ungodliness or from bad to worse. Of false teachers it can also mean they will not get far.

senses.label: Be far advanced (time)
senses.definition: Of time running its course: the night is far gone.

background.note: A soldier writes that he hopes 'to be quickly promoted', using this verb.
An inscription praises a youth as 'advancing in age' and in piety, a close parallel to Luke's wording.

study.summary: Προορίζω means to decide beforehand, to predestine. In the NT God is always the subject, and his set purpose leads to salvation and glory.

senses.label: Predestine, foreordain
senses.definition: God marks out in advance what will happen or what people will become: Christ's passion, believers' conformity to Christ, their adoption as sons, and hidden wisdom for their glory.

study.exegesisTip: Note the goal named each time: 'to be conformed to the image of his Son', 'for adoption', 'for our glory'. The word stresses God's gracious purpose more than the mechanics of choice.
study.caution: How predestination relates to human response is a long-standing theological debate. The word itself shows God's advance purpose but does not settle that debate.

study.summary: Πρόσκομμα means stumbling, or something that makes others stumble, an obstacle to faith or conscience.

senses.label: Stone of stumbling
senses.definition: Drawn from Isaiah: Christ is the stone over which unbelieving Israel trips.

senses.label: Occasion of stumbling
senses.definition: Conduct or freedom that leads a weaker believer to sin against conscience.
senses.note: At ROM 14:20 'eating with offence' may mean eating that harms others or eating against one's own conscience.

background.note: The 'stone of stumbling' phrase comes from the Greek of Isaiah.

study.exegesisTip: It often appears next to σκάνδαλον ('snare, offence'). Together the two words describe being tripped up spiritually.

study.summary: Προσμένω means to stay on or remain with someone, and figuratively to keep on in devotion to the Lord or to prayer.

senses.label: Stay on, remain
senses.definition: To stay on in a place for a while longer.

senses.label: Remain with someone
senses.definition: To stay in someone's company, as the crowd stayed with Jesus for three days.

senses.label: Continue in, cleave to
senses.definition: To hold on faithfully: to the Lord with a steadfast heart, or to prayer night and day.

background.note: Used in classical Greek for waiting or staying a long time.

study.summary: Πυρετός means a fever, a sickness Jesus and Paul healed.

senses.label: Fever
senses.definition: A feverish illness, such as Peter's mother-in-law's 'high fever', the official's son's fever, and Publius' father's fevers with dysentery.
senses.note: At LUK 4:39 Jesus 'rebuked' the fever, as he rebukes spirits and storms.

background.note: Luke's phrase 'held by fever' (συνέχεσθαι) also appears in a papyrus describing a man bedridden with fever.

study.summary: Πυρόω means to burn or set on fire. In the NT it is always passive: to burn, glow, or be refined by fire, and figuratively to burn with passion or distress.

senses.label: Be on fire, glow
senses.definition: Literally ablaze or burning: flaming arrows, the heavens dissolving in fire, and feet like bronze glowing in a furnace.

senses.label: Refined by fire
senses.definition: Of metal purified in fire, an image of genuine spiritual wealth.

senses.label: Burn inwardly
senses.definition: To be inflamed with sexual desire, or with grief and indignation when another believer is made to stumble.

study.translationNote: At REV 1:15 some versions say 'refined' and others 'glowing'. At 2CO 11:29 versions differ between 'burn with indignation' and 'burn with grief'.

background.note: In the Septuagint it chiefly translates the Hebrew verb for refining metal, used of God testing his people.

study.caution: Some interpreters read 1CO 7:9 as burning in judgment, but most take it as burning with unfulfilled desire.

study.summary: Πώποτε means 'ever yet, at any time'. In the NT it always appears with a negative, meaning 'never'.

senses.label: Ever (with negative: never)
senses.definition: At any time up to now, or with a future verb at any time to come: no one has ever seen God, and whoever believes will never thirst.

background.note: The emphatic 'never at all' construction (οὐ μή … πώποτε) found in John is also attested in the papyri.

study.exegesisTip: John's 'no one has ever seen God' (JOH 1:18 and 1JO 4:12) leads to how God is now known: through the Son, and through love among believers.

study.summary: Σημαίνω means to indicate, make known or signify, often in a veiled or prophetic way.

senses.label: Indicate (veiled meaning)
senses.definition: To hint at something by one's words. John uses it of Jesus indicating by what kind of death he, or Peter, would die.

senses.label: Make known, predict
senses.definition: To communicate or announce, whether a prophetic forecast, a revelation sent by an angel, or charges stated against a prisoner.

study.translationNote: At REV 1:1 the KJV's 'signified' (shown by signs) and modern versions' 'made known' reflect different readings of the verb.

background.note: Used in ordinary letters for informing someone in writing.

study.caution: Some interpreters link ἐσήμανεν at REV 1:1 to σημεῖον ('sign') and take it as a hint at Revelation's symbolic style. Others take it simply as 'made known'.

study.summary: Σινδών is fine linen cloth, or a garment or sheet made of it. In the Gospels it is used for Jesus' burial cloth and the young man's wrap.

senses.label: Linen burial cloth
senses.definition: A clean linen sheet bought by Joseph of Arimathea to wrap Jesus' body for burial.

senses.label: Linen wrap
senses.definition: A linen garment worn over a bare body by the young man who fled naked at Jesus' arrest.

background.note: Herodotus uses it for the fine linen bands that wrapped Egyptian mummies.
A funeral-expense letter lists 'the price of a linen cloth', showing it was ordinary burial practice.

study.summary: To harden or make stubborn, used in the NT only figuratively of a heart or will closed against God.

senses.label: God hardens
senses.definition: God's sovereign act of confirming a person in stubbornness, set in contrast with his showing mercy.

senses.label: Harden one's own heart
senses.definition: To make one's heart unresponsive to God's voice, as Israel did in the wilderness; a warning drawn from Psalm 95.

senses.label: Become hardened, obstinate
senses.definition: Passive: to grow stubborn and unbelieving, whether by refusing the message or through sin's deceitfulness.

background.note: The Greek Old Testament uses the verb for the hardening of Pharaoh's heart in the Exodus account, the background to Paul's argument in Romans 9.

study.exegesisTip: Hebrews places the warning next to 'Today': hardening is presented as a present danger for believers who keep hearing God's voice and fail to respond.

study.summary: To look at attentively, keep an eye on, or fix one's attention on something or someone.

senses.label: Watch out, take care
senses.definition: To keep a careful, watchful eye on a danger, whether false teachers or one's own vulnerability.

senses.label: Observe as an example
senses.definition: To mark and study people whose conduct is worth imitating.

senses.label: Fix attention on, regard
senses.definition: To make something the object of one's concern or gaze, such as unseen eternal realities or the interests of others.

background.note: Used in official letters for seeing to it that something is or is not done.

study.summary: To hurry or make haste; once used transitively, of believers hastening or eagerly awaiting the day of God.

senses.label: Hurry, make haste
senses.definition: To move or act quickly, often joined with another verb of going or coming.

senses.label: Hasten, eagerly desire
senses.definition: With an object: to speed something on, or to strive eagerly for it; said of the coming of the day of God.

study.translationNote: In 2 Peter 3:12 some versions say believers 'hasten' the day of God, others that they 'earnestly desire' it; both meanings of the transitive verb are attested.

background.note: Common in letters for hurrying to do or reach something, and also used with a direct object ('hasten this').

study.caution: Whether 2PE 3:12 means believers actually speed the day's arrival (e.g. by holy living and prayer) or simply long for it is debated.

study.summary: A cave or cavern, used both literally and in Jesus' quotation 'den of robbers'.

senses.label: Cave, cavern
senses.definition: A natural cave used as a tomb, a refuge for the persecuted, or a hiding place from judgment.

senses.label: Den of robbers
senses.definition: A robbers' hideout; Jesus applies Jeremiah's phrase to the temple turned into a place of exploitation.

background.note: The phrase 'den of robbers' comes from Jeremiah's temple sermon.
Plato's famous allegory of the cave uses this word.

study.exegesisTip: A robbers' den is where thieves retreat to feel safe after their crimes; the image implies people treated the temple as a refuge while their lives contradicted it.

study.summary: A stade, a unit of distance of about 185 metres (some 600 feet), and by extension a racecourse of that length.

senses.label: Stade (unit of distance)
senses.definition: A measure of length of 600 Greek feet, roughly an eighth of a Roman mile, used for distances and dimensions.

senses.label: Racecourse, stadium
senses.definition: The running track (originally one stade long) where athletes competed.

study.translationNote: Older versions render the measure 'furlongs'; many modern versions convert to miles or kilometres, while others keep 'stadia' in Revelation where the numbers are symbolic (e.g. 12,000).

background.note: Used as a heading for a list of athletes, showing the racecourse sense.

study.exegesisTip: In Revelation the numbers (1,600; 12,000) carry symbolic weight; converting them to modern units can obscure that.

study.summary: To groan or sigh deeply, expressing inner distress, longing or grievance.

senses.label: Groan in longing
senses.definition: The inward groaning of believers who long for the redemption of the body and the heavenly dwelling.

senses.label: Sigh deeply, grieve
senses.definition: To sigh out of deep feeling, as Jesus did before healing, or as leaders burdened with grief.

senses.label: Grumble against
senses.definition: With 'against', to complain or hold a grievance toward another person.

study.exegesisTip: In Romans 8 the same groaning runs through creation, believers and the Spirit (related words); here believers groan 'within themselves'.

study.summary: To talk with someone, converse or confer together.

senses.label: Talk with, converse
senses.definition: To speak together with someone, as Moses and Elijah with Jesus, or a crowd among themselves.

senses.label: Confer, consult
senses.definition: To hold a discussion in order to reach a decision or plan.

background.note: Used in letters of having a conversation with someone about business.

study.summary: Literally 'throw together': to ponder, confer, meet or engage with, and (middle) contribute; a word used only by Luke.

senses.label: Ponder, weigh in mind
senses.definition: To put things together in thought, reflecting on their meaning.

senses.label: Confer, debate
senses.definition: To exchange words with others, whether in consultation or argument.

senses.label: Meet, engage with
senses.definition: To come together with someone, whether in friendly meeting or in battle.
senses.note: In the middle voice it means to contribute or be a help to, as Apollos was to the believers in ACT 18:27.

background.note: Common for having a meeting with someone about business, and in the middle for contributing one's share.

study.exegesisTip: In LUK 2:19 Mary does more than remember; she turns the events over, trying to put together their meaning.

study.summary: To bring together: to knit together, to put arguments together (conclude, prove), or to instruct.

senses.label: Knit together, unite
senses.definition: To join parts into a coherent whole, used of Christ's body held together by its ligaments and of believers united in love.

senses.label: Conclude, prove
senses.definition: To put evidence together so as to draw a conclusion or demonstrate a point.

senses.label: Instruct
senses.definition: To teach or advise, as in the Greek Old Testament; used in quoting Isaiah's question about instructing the Lord.

background.note: In the Greek Old Testament the verb regularly means 'teach', including Isaiah's question quoted by Paul.

study.caution: In COL 2:2 a minority (following the Latin tradition) read 'instructed in love' rather than 'knit together in love'; the body imagery of COL 2:19 favours the latter.

study.summary: Literally 'sound together': to agree, be in harmony, or come to terms.

senses.label: Agree, be in accord
senses.definition: To be of one mind or to harmonise, whether in prayer, in a conspiracy, or of Scripture agreeing with events.

senses.label: Agree on terms
senses.definition: To make an agreement about a wage or price.

senses.label: Match, fit
senses.definition: Of things, to suit or correspond with one another, as a new patch fails to match an old garment.

background.note: Originally of sounds in musical harmony.
Common in contracts for what was agreed between parties.

study.summary: To meet someone, and figuratively of events that 'meet' a person, i.e. befall him.

senses.label: Meet
senses.definition: To come face to face with someone, whether by chance or intentionally.

senses.label: Befall, happen to
senses.definition: Of events: to come upon a person.

background.note: Used in letters both for meeting people and for things turning out for someone.

study.summary: To join in approving, to consent to or be content with something.

senses.label: Approve, side with
senses.definition: To give one's approval to another's actions, especially wrongdoing, thereby sharing responsibility for it.

senses.label: Be willing, consent
senses.definition: With an infinitive: to agree to or be content to do something.

background.note: Frequent in sales and legal documents for the consent of a party to an agreement.

study.exegesisTip: Paul uses the word of his own approval of Stephen's death (ACT 22:20) and also in ROM 1:32, where approving others' sin is presented as the climax of guilt.

study.summary: Completion or consummation, used in the NT of the end or culmination of the age(s).

senses.label: Consummation of the age
senses.definition: The completion of the present age at the final judgment and Christ's coming.

senses.label: Climax of the ages
senses.definition: The decisive culmination of history in which Christ appeared once for all to put away sin.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Only Matthew uses the phrase 'the end of the age', in parables of judgment, the disciples' question and the closing promise of Christ's presence.

background.note: In classical Greek it meant a joint contribution toward public expenses.
Used of the completion of a period of time ('down to the end of the 21st year').

study.exegesisTip: The word suggests completion and fulfilment rather than mere termination.

study.summary: To be of sound mind; hence to think sensibly and exercise self-control.

senses.label: Be in one's right mind
senses.definition: To be sane and mentally sound, as opposed to being demon-possessed or 'out of one's mind'.

senses.label: Think soberly, be self-controlled
senses.definition: To exercise sound judgment and moderation, avoiding arrogance or excess.

background.note: Used of being sane and, very often, of temperance and self-restraint, a central Greek virtue.

study.exegesisTip: In ROM 12:3 Paul plays on the root 'think' (not to think too highly, but to think so as to think soberly).

study.summary: To eat; originally 'munch, chew', but in NT-era Greek an ordinary word for eating.

senses.label: Eat, share a meal
senses.definition: To eat in the ordinary sense, including sharing bread at table.

senses.label: Feed on Christ
senses.definition: To receive Christ, his flesh and himself, as the source of eternal life.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In the Bread of Life discourse John switches to this verb from the usual word for 'eat', and also uses it in Jesus' quotation about the betrayer.

background.note: Originally of animals nibbling or munching food.

study.caution: Some see the switch in JOH 6:54 as stressing a vivid, physical 'chewing'; others note that by this period the verb was simply a common word for eat.

study.summary: Perishable, subject to decay and death, regularly contrasted with what is imperishable.

senses.label: Perishable, mortal
senses.definition: Subject to decay, describing mortal humanity, earthly prizes, silver and gold, and natural seed.

senses.label: The perishable body
senses.definition: Neuter with 'this': the present mortal body that must put on imperishability at the resurrection.

study.exegesisTip: Almost every occurrence sets the word against its opposite (imperishable or imperishability), contrasting the transient with God and what he gives.

study.summary: Brotherly love, in the NT the affectionate love of believers for one another as members of God's family.

senses.label: Love for fellow believers
senses.definition: The warm family affection Christians are to show one another as brothers and sisters in Christ.

background.note: In 4 Maccabees it describes love between blood brothers.
Outside the NT it refers to love for actual siblings.

study.exegesisTip: The NT transfers a word for love between siblings to the church, treating believers as a real family.

study.summary: To bear or carry habitually; usually to wear clothing.

senses.label: Wear (clothing)
senses.definition: To have on as clothing, such as fine garments or the crown of thorns and purple robe.

senses.label: Bear constantly
senses.definition: To carry regularly as a mark of one's office or nature, such as the ruler's sword or the image of Adam or of Christ.

background.note: Common in letters for wearing clothes.

study.caution: In 1CO 15:49 manuscripts differ between 'let us bear' and 'we shall bear' the image of the heavenly man.

study.summary: A load or burden; literally a ship's cargo, figuratively a burden of obligation or responsibility.

senses.label: Ship's cargo
senses.definition: The freight carried by a ship.

senses.label: Imposed burden
senses.definition: Religious obligations laid on people, either the heavy loads of the scribes or the light burden of Christ.

senses.label: One's own load
senses.definition: The responsibility each person must carry before God.

background.note: Common for freight carried by boats.

study.exegesisTip: In Galatians 6 Paul uses a different word for the 'burdens' believers bear for one another; here it is the load each must carry himself, so the two statements do not contradict.

study.summary: A leaf; in the NT always plural, 'leaves' or foliage.

senses.label: Leaves of the fig tree
senses.definition: Foliage of the fig tree, as a sign of the season or a show without fruit.

senses.label: Leaves of the tree of life
senses.definition: The leaves of the tree in the new Jerusalem, given for the healing of the nations.

background.note: Homer compares generations of men to leaves.

study.summary: Winter, and (properly) wintry weather, hence a storm.

senses.label: Winter
senses.definition: The winter season, a hard time for flight or travel.

senses.label: Storm, stormy weather
senses.definition: Foul weather or a violent storm.

background.note: Used both for the winter season and for being driven by a storm.

study.caution: MAT 16:3 belongs to a passage absent from some early manuscripts.

study.summary: Made with hands, i.e. of human workmanship, contrasted with what God makes.

senses.label: Man-made sanctuary
senses.definition: A temple or sanctuary built by human hands, which cannot contain God and is only a copy of the true sanctuary.

senses.label: Circumcision by hand
senses.definition: Physical circumcision performed by human hands, as opposed to God's inward work.

background.note: In the Greek Old Testament it is used of idols, so the word carried a polemical edge.
A traveller mentions visiting 'works of art made by hands' along the Nile.

study.exegesisTip: Because the word described idols, calling the temple 'made with hands' (ACT 7:48) was a pointed statement.

study.summary: Pertaining to the natural life (the soul) as opposed to the Spirit: natural, unspiritual.

senses.label: Unspiritual person
senses.definition: A person living on a merely natural level, without the Spirit of God and unable to receive his things.

senses.label: Natural body
senses.definition: The present body suited to natural life, contrasted with the resurrection body animated by the Spirit.

senses.label: Unspiritual wisdom
senses.definition: Wisdom that is earthly and merely human, not from above.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'natural', 'unspiritual', 'worldly' and (older) 'sensual'; 'sensual' can mislead, since the word means 'merely natural', not 'sexual' or 'pleasure-seeking'.
study.exegesisTip: The contrast in every passage is with the Spirit (spiritual, from above, having the Spirit).
study.caution: The 'natural body' versus 'spiritual body' in 1 Corinthians 15 is not material versus immaterial, but a body suited to natural life versus one wholly governed by the Spirit.

study.summary: Exultation, exuberant and often expressive joy.

senses.label: Exultant joy
senses.definition: Deep, overflowing gladness at God's saving acts or presence.

senses.label: Oil of gladness
senses.definition: In a quotation of Psalm 45, the festive anointing oil of joy marking the King's exaltation.

background.note: Common in the Greek Psalms, often paired with words for gladness.

study.summary: To sing, in the NT always of songs of praise to God.

senses.label: Sing to the Lord
senses.definition: To sing praise to the Lord as part of the church's worship, from the heart.

senses.label: Sing a heavenly song
senses.definition: With 'song' as object: the redeemed and heavenly beings singing a new song, or the song of Moses and the Lamb.

background.note: Used of hymns being sung.

study.summary: An eagle; where carrion is in view, a vulture.

senses.label: Eagle
senses.definition: The great bird of prey, an image of swift, powerful flight in Revelation's visions.

senses.label: Vulture
senses.definition: A carrion bird gathering around a corpse, in a proverbial saying about the coming of the Son of Man.

study.translationNote: Older versions have 'eagles' in MAT 24:28 and LUK 17:37; modern versions usually have 'vultures', since the birds gather at a carcass.

background.note: In Homer the eagle is a bird of omen.

study.summary: To be ashamed, or to be put to shame and disgraced.

senses.label: Be ashamed to do
senses.definition: To feel too much shame to do something.

senses.label: Be put to shame
senses.definition: To be disgraced or found wanting, especially before God or at Christ's coming; believers are urged not to be ashamed.

background.note: Used in letters of someone too ashamed to come back.

study.exegesisTip: In PHP 1:20 and 1JO 2:28 shame is set against boldness, reflecting the biblical hope of not being put to shame before God.

study.summary: Responsible for; as a noun, the cause or source of something, or the ground for a charge.

senses.label: Source, cause
senses.definition: The one responsible for bringing something about, or a reason that justifies an action.

senses.label: Ground for a charge
senses.definition: Guilt or a crime that would justify a legal charge.

background.note: Used of the person found to be the culprit and held accountable.

study.exegesisTip: Pilate's repeated verdict in LUK 23:4, LUK 23:14 and LUK 23:22 finds no guilt in Jesus; HEB 5:9 uses the word positively of Christ as the cause of eternal salvation.

study.summary: Instability, hence disorder, unrest or upheaval in society or in a community.

senses.label: Uprisings, unrest
senses.definition: Political or public upheavals and riots.

senses.label: Disorder, confusion
senses.definition: Turmoil and disorder within a community, produced by rivalry and opposed to God's peace.

background.note: A literary papyrus calls a faithless lover a 'contriver of instability'.

study.summary: A fisherman, and in Jesus' call, a 'fisher of men'.

senses.label: Fisherman
senses.definition: One who catches fish for a living, the occupation of the first disciples.

senses.label: Fishers of men
senses.definition: Jesus' image for the disciples' new calling to gather people for the kingdom.

background.note: Used of fishermen as early as Homer.

study.summary: To be careless about, pay no attention to, or neglect something that deserves care.

senses.label: Pay no attention
senses.definition: Used absolutely: to shrug something off and take no notice, as the invited guests did with the king's wedding summons.

senses.label: Neglect, disregard
senses.definition: With a genitive object: to leave uncared for or fail to attend to something (a gift, salvation) or someone; of God, to cease caring for a covenant-breaking people.

senses.label: Fail to (do)
senses.definition: With a negative and an infinitive: not to be remiss in doing something, i.e. to take care to do it.
senses.note: Some manuscripts read a different verb ("I will be ready") here.

background.note: Common in everyday letters, both absolutely ("don't neglect it") and with a genitive, e.g. a writer insisting he had not neglected a key.

study.exegesisTip: In Hebrews 2:3 the danger is not open rejection but simple drift: failing to give due attention to the message of salvation (cf. 2:1).

study.summary: Blameless: so living or constituted that no fault can justly be found.

senses.label: Blameless in conduct
senses.definition: Of people whose observance or character gives no ground for complaint, whether measured by the law or by God's standard at Christ's coming.

senses.label: Faultless, without defect
senses.definition: Of a thing (the first covenant) that would have been adequate and needed no replacement.

background.note: Used chiefly for Hebrew tam ("blameless, complete"), notably of Job.
Found in a marriage contract of a wife who conducts herself blamelessly, and often on epitaphs.

study.exegesisTip: Philippians 3:6 describes Paul's former standing measured by outward legal righteousness; he does not claim sinlessness but irreproachable observance, which he then counts as loss.

study.summary: Sand, especially the sand of the seashore, used literally and as an image of countless numbers.

senses.label: Sand as poor foundation
senses.definition: Loose sandy ground, an unstable base for building, in Jesus' parable of the two builders.

senses.label: Countless as seashore sand
senses.definition: The proverbial image (from God's promise to Abraham) for an innumerable multitude.

senses.label: Seashore
senses.definition: The sandy shore of the sea as a location in John's vision.
senses.note: Some editions place this clause at Revelation 12:18 and read "he stood" (the dragon) rather than "I stood".

study.translationNote: At Revelation 13:1/12:18 versions differ on whether John or the dragon stands on the sand, reflecting a textual variant.

background.note: Used in Egyptian documents of clearing drifted sand out of canals and watercourses.

study.summary: To cry out or shout suddenly and loudly, from fear, distress or excitement.

senses.label: Shriek (demon-possessed)
senses.definition: The sudden outcry of a person controlled by an unclean spirit when confronted by Jesus.

senses.label: Cry out in fear
senses.definition: The disciples' terrified shout on seeing Jesus walking on the sea.

senses.label: Shout together (crowd)
senses.definition: The crowd's united clamour demanding Jesus' death and Barabbas' release.

background.note: Used of people shouting for help when a temple caught fire, implying vigorous outcry.

study.summary: Rest or relief: a cessation from toil or torment that brings refreshment.

senses.label: Rest for the soul
senses.definition: The inner refreshment Jesus promises to the weary who take his yoke.

senses.label: Resting place
senses.definition: A place of rest sought in vain by an expelled unclean spirit.

senses.label: Respite, cessation
senses.definition: With a negative: no pause day or night, whether in the living creatures' unceasing worship or in the torment of the beast's worshippers.

background.note: Used of rest from something, e.g. respite from evils.
Used of relief from public duties granted to an old man or to discharged veterans.

study.exegesisTip: Revelation uses the same phrase, 'they have no rest day and night', both for the creatures' ceaseless praise (4:8) and for the worshippers' endless torment (14:11), a deliberate contrast.

study.summary: Irreproachable: one against whom no charge can be brought.

senses.label: Blameless at judgment
senses.definition: Unaccused before God, the state in which Christ will present believers on his day.

senses.label: Above reproach (leaders)
senses.definition: A qualification for elders, overseers and deacons: having a character no one can justly accuse.

background.note: A deserted wife's petition claims she had conducted herself blamelessly in every respect; the word was also common in honorific decrees.

study.exegesisTip: The word is legal in flavour (from 'to bring a charge'): it describes freedom from any accusation, not sinless perfection.

study.summary: Loosening or relaxation: easing of restraint, or relief from affliction.

senses.label: Some freedom (custody)
senses.definition: A relaxation of the conditions of imprisonment granted to Paul under guard.

senses.label: Relief, rest from pressure
senses.definition: Respite from distress, set by Paul in contrast to affliction (thlipsis), whether experienced now or granted at Christ's return.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Always set against affliction (thlipsis), stated or implied.

background.note: Literally the slackening of lyre strings, opposite of tightening.
Used of exemption from public duties and of relief from taxation.

study.summary: An opponent, especially the opposing party in a lawsuit; by extension an adversary.

senses.label: Opponent at law
senses.definition: The other party in a legal dispute, the accuser on the way to court or the one against whom a widow seeks justice.

senses.label: The devil as adversary
senses.definition: The devil as the believer's hostile opponent, perhaps with the overtone of accuser.

background.note: A common legal term for the opposing party, e.g. in a lawsuit over a foundling child.

study.summary: To set oneself against, oppose or resist (a military term used figuratively).

senses.label: Oppose, resist (people)
senses.definition: Human opposition to a person or to authority, from Jewish resistance to Paul to resisting governing authorities; in James 5:6 the righteous person does not resist.

senses.label: God opposes the proud
senses.definition: God ranged in opposition against the arrogant, quoting Proverbs 3:34.

background.note: Used in legal proceedings of the opposing party.

study.exegesisTip: The word pictures drawing up a battle line against someone; 'God opposes the proud' means he actively sets himself against them.

study.summary: Antichrist: one who opposes Christ, and perhaps sets himself up in Christ's place; in John, both an expected figure and present false teachers.

senses.label: Expected end-time Antichrist
senses.definition: The awaited opponent of Christ whose coming the readers had heard of.

senses.label: Present antichrists, false teachers
senses.definition: Anyone who denies the Father and the Son or that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh; John says many such have already appeared.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: The term occurs only in John's letters, where he defines it by denial of who Jesus is.

study.exegesisTip: John deliberately shifts attention from a single future figure to the 'spirit of antichrist' already at work in denial of Jesus' incarnation.
study.caution: Whether 'anti-' means primarily 'against' Christ or 'in place of' Christ (a rival or substitute) is debated; the word may embrace both.

study.summary: Unseen, invisible; used of God and of unseen realities.

senses.label: Invisible God
senses.definition: God himself, who cannot be seen, yet is revealed in the Son and perceived by faith.

senses.label: Invisible things
senses.definition: Unseen realities: God's invisible attributes known through creation, and invisible created powers.

background.note: Used philosophically of the unseen world as distinct from the visible.

study.exegesisTip: Romans 1:20 is a deliberate paradox: God's invisible qualities are 'clearly seen' through what he has made.

study.summary: To carry off, bear away or take somewhere.

senses.label: Lead away (prisoner)
senses.definition: To take someone off by force, as the Sanhedrin did with the bound Jesus.

senses.label: Carry, convey
senses.definition: To bear something or someone to a destination: a gift to Jerusalem, or Lazarus carried by angels.

senses.label: Carry away in vision
senses.definition: Of the angel transporting John 'in the Spirit' to a place of revelation.

background.note: A boy's letter scolds his father for not taking him off to town; elsewhere used of carrying off property by force.

study.summary: Silver as a metal, or articles made of it.

senses.label: Silver (metal, wealth)
senses.definition: Silver as a precious material or form of wealth, listed with gold and other valuables.

senses.label: Silver as idol material
senses.definition: Silver worked by craftsmen into images of the divine.

background.note: Silver as a metal from Homer onward.

study.exegesisTip: In 1 Corinthians 3:12 silver stands among durable materials that survive the testing fire, in contrast to wood, hay and straw.

study.summary: Excellence or virtue: moral goodness in people, and the excellent, praiseworthy acts of God.

senses.label: Moral excellence (human)
senses.definition: Virtuous quality of character that believers are to pursue and think upon.

senses.label: God's excellence
senses.definition: The excellence or power of God by which he calls his people.

senses.label: God's praiseworthy deeds
senses.definition: Plural: the mighty, praiseworthy acts of God that his people proclaim (echoing Isaiah 43:21).

study.translationNote: In 1 Peter 2:9 versions vary between 'praises', 'excellencies' and 'virtues', because the Septuagint used this word for Hebrew tehillah ('praise').

background.note: In Isaiah the plural renders Hebrew tehillah, 'praise', shaping 1 Peter 2:9.
Could mean prowess or excellence broadly, not just moral virtue.

study.summary: Rapacious, grasping; as a noun, a swindler or extortioner who seizes what belongs to others.

senses.label: Ravenous (wolves)
senses.definition: Adjective describing false prophets as wolves eager to tear and devour.

senses.label: Swindler, extortioner
senses.definition: A person who greedily takes others' property by fraud or force; listed among vices excluding from the kingdom.

study.translationNote: Older versions say 'extortioners', modern ones often 'swindlers' or 'robbers'; the word covers grasping gain by any unjust means.

study.summary: Weak, sick or ailing; usually as a noun, 'the sick'.

senses.label: The sick (healed)
senses.definition: Ill people to whom Jesus and his disciples brought healing, often by laying on hands or anointing.

senses.label: Sick under discipline
senses.definition: Members of the Corinthian church suffering illness as a result of unworthy participation in the Lord's Supper.

study.caution: Mark 16:18 belongs to the longer ending of Mark, which many early manuscripts lack.

study.summary: Without understanding: lacking insight, often with a moral dimension of foolish insensitivity to God.

senses.label: Dull, slow to understand
senses.definition: Disciples failing to grasp Jesus' teaching.

senses.label: Senseless, morally foolish
senses.definition: Lacking discernment toward God, a darkened heart and character typical of those who suppress the truth.

background.note: Deuteronomy 32:21, quoted at Romans 10:19, uses it for Hebrew nabal, 'foolish'.

study.summary: Firm, secure or certain; something that can be relied upon.

senses.label: Certain facts
senses.definition: As a neuter noun: the certain truth or definite information about a matter.

senses.label: Safe, safeguard
senses.definition: That which keeps someone safe or is a protection.

senses.label: Secure, steadfast
senses.definition: Firm and immovable, of hope as an anchor.

background.note: Common of putting things in a safe place.

study.summary: To make unseen; hence to destroy, disfigure, or (passive) vanish or perish.

senses.label: Disfigure (face)
senses.definition: To make the face unrecognisable, likely by neglect or dirt, to display fasting.

senses.label: Destroy, ruin
senses.definition: Of moth and rust consuming earthly treasures.

senses.label: Vanish, perish
senses.definition: Passive: to disappear like a mist, or to perish under judgment.

background.note: Used of destroying crops: 'the hippopotamus has destroyed nothing'.

study.exegesisTip: Matthew 6:16 contains a wordplay: the hypocrites make their faces 'disappear' so that they may 'appear' (phanōsin) to others as fasting.

study.summary: Royal, belonging to a king; as a noun, a royal official.

senses.label: Royal official
senses.definition: A person in the king's service, probably an officer of Herod Antipas.

senses.label: Belonging to the king
senses.definition: Of the king's territory and his royal robes.

senses.label: Supreme royal law
senses.definition: The law of love, regal either as supreme over other laws or as given by the King.

background.note: Common, e.g. the 'royal road' and royal revenues.

study.caution: Whether James's 'royal law' means the supreme law or the law of the King (or of the kingdom) is debated.

study.summary: A thorn bush or bramble, most famously the burning bush of Moses.

senses.label: Burning bush
senses.definition: The bush from which God spoke to Moses, also used as a title for that Scripture passage.

senses.label: Bramble
senses.definition: A thorny shrub that cannot produce grapes.

background.note: Used for Hebrew seneh, the bush of Exodus 3.

study.exegesisTip: 'At the bush' (Mark 12:26; Luke 20:37) refers to the section of Exodus about the bush, an ancient way of citing Scripture before chapter numbers.

study.summary: Profane, unhallowed: lacking any relation to what is holy, or treating it with contempt.

senses.label: Profane person
senses.definition: Someone godless and irreverent, who despises sacred things, as Esau did.

senses.label: Irreverent talk, myths
senses.definition: Worthless, unholy speech and fables that do not lead to godliness.

background.note: Originally of ground that may be walked on, not sacred, as opposed to holy precincts.

study.summary: Slanderous, blasphemous; as a noun, a blasphemer.

senses.label: Blasphemous (words)
senses.definition: Speech that slanders God or holy things.

senses.label: Abusive, slanderous
senses.definition: Of people or accusations that revile and insult.

senses.label: Blasphemer
senses.definition: A person who reviles God, Paul's description of his former self.

study.summary: Made of fine linen; as a noun, fine linen cloth or clothing.

senses.label: Luxury linen (Babylon)
senses.definition: Costly fine linen traded and worn by Babylon as a sign of wealth.

senses.label: Pure linen (saints)
senses.definition: Bright clean linen worn by the Lamb's bride and heaven's armies, interpreted as the saints' righteous acts.

background.note: Fine linen production in Egypt was a royal monopoly run in the temples.

study.exegesisTip: Revelation contrasts Babylon's purchased linen (18:16) with the bride's linen given to her (19:8).

study.summary: Treasury; in the temple, the area or the receptacles for offerings.

senses.label: Temple treasury
senses.definition: The chests or place in the temple court where people put offerings, as the widow did.

senses.label: Treasury area
senses.definition: The part of the temple courts near the treasury where Jesus taught.

background.note: Used of temple storerooms and treasury chambers.

study.caution: It is uncertain whether the word refers to a room, a court area, or the trumpet-shaped collection chests.

study.summary: Milk, literally and as a picture of elementary or nourishing spiritual teaching.

senses.label: Literal milk
senses.definition: The milk of a flock as the shepherd's rightful food.

senses.label: Elementary teaching
senses.definition: Basic instruction suited to spiritual infants, contrasted with solid food.

senses.label: Spiritual nourishment
senses.definition: The pure spiritual milk that newborn believers crave in order to grow.

study.translationNote: In 1 Peter 2:2 'pure spiritual milk' is sometimes rendered 'sincere milk of the word', depending on how logikos is understood.

background.note: Appears in a household account entry for milk bought for the children.

study.exegesisTip: Paul and Hebrews use milk negatively (immaturity), but Peter uses it positively: all believers should crave it.

study.summary: To spend or pay out; in a bad sense, to waste or squander.

senses.label: Spend, pay expenses
senses.definition: To pay costs for something or someone, or to spend oneself in service.

senses.label: Squander
senses.definition: To use up wastefully, on self-indulgence.

background.note: Common in accounts; also with 'in' as in James 4:3.

study.summary: Fourteen.

senses.label: Fourteen generations
senses.definition: The three sets of fourteen generations in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus.

senses.label: Fourteen years
senses.definition: Time spans in Paul's autobiography.

study.exegesisTip: Matthew's three groups of fourteen may play on the numerical value of David's name in Hebrew (D-W-D = 4+6+4).

study.summary: Acceptable or welcome; pleasing to God or to people.

senses.label: Time of favour
senses.definition: A season when God shows favour and grants salvation.

senses.label: Accepted by people
senses.definition: Welcome, received; no prophet is accepted in his hometown.

senses.label: Acceptable to God
senses.definition: Approved and welcomed by God, of people and offerings.

background.note: Common in sacrificial language for Hebrew ratson, 'favour'.

study.exegesisTip: Luke 4:19 and 4:24 echo each other: Jesus proclaims the 'acceptable' year, yet he is not 'acceptable' in Nazareth.

study.summary: To remain or continue, often in a state or relationship.

senses.label: Remain in a state
senses.definition: Continue as one was, e.g. Zechariah remaining mute, or everything continuing unchanged.

senses.label: Stand by, persist
senses.definition: Continue faithfully with someone or something.

senses.label: Endure forever
senses.definition: Of God's permanence compared with perishing creation.

background.note: Used of a friendship that remains, 'so that we may remain on good terms'.

study.summary: To pass or journey through a place, used by Luke of Jesus, crowds and missionaries on the move, and by Paul of his planned trip through Rome to Spain.

senses.label: Travel through a region
senses.definition: To make one's way through fields, towns or territory, often on an itinerant teaching or mission journey.

senses.label: Pass by, be on the way
senses.definition: To be passing along or passing through on the way to somewhere else, without staying.
senses.note: In ROM 15:24 Paul pictures Rome as a stop in passing on his journey to Spain.

study.summary: To be thoroughly at a loss or greatly perplexed, used by Luke of people confronted by events they cannot explain.

senses.label: Be utterly perplexed
senses.definition: To be completely at a loss about the meaning of something astonishing, such as reports about Jesus, the empty tomb, Pentecost, the apostles' escape, or a vision.

background.note: Plato uses it of being at a loss what one ought to do; it is a strengthened form of the ordinary verb for being at a loss.

study.exegesisTip: Luke repeatedly uses this perplexity as the moment just before divine explanation arrives (angels at the tomb, Peter's sermon, the messengers from Cornelius).

study.summary: To tear apart or burst, used of rending garments in grief or outrage, of a net tearing under a great catch, and of a demoniac snapping his chains.

senses.label: Tear one's clothes
senses.definition: To rip one's garments as a public sign of horror, grief or protest at blasphemy.
senses.note: The high priest does it at what he judges blasphemy; Paul and Barnabas do it when the crowd tries to worship them.

senses.label: Break, burst apart
senses.definition: To burst or snap something under strain, such as a fishing net or chains.

background.note: A late papyrus uses the verb of assailants tearing a man's clothing off him.

study.summary: Adverb meaning justly or righteously: either in accordance with fair judgment, or in a manner that is morally upright.

senses.label: Justly, deservedly
senses.definition: In accordance with justice, as a fair verdict or deserved penalty.
senses.note: In 1PE 2:23 Christ entrusts himself to God, who judges justly.

senses.label: Uprightly, as is right
senses.definition: In a morally upright way that matches God's standard of conduct.
senses.note: In 1CO 15:34 the sense is 'come to your senses as you ought'.

study.summary: A formal decree or binding ordinance issued by an authority, whether the emperor, the apostolic council, or the commandments of the Mosaic law.

senses.label: Imperial decree
senses.definition: An official edict of the Roman emperor.

senses.label: Apostolic decisions
senses.definition: The binding decisions reached by the apostles and elders at Jerusalem and delivered to the churches.

senses.label: Legal ordinances of the law
senses.definition: The commandments of the Mosaic law viewed as written regulations that stood against people and divided Jew from Gentile.

background.note: The word was used especially of decrees of the Roman Senate, conveying a positive ordinance from a distant, unquestionable authority.
An imperial edict on the crown-tax calls itself 'this my decree', paralleling Luke's use for the emperor's orders.

study.caution: The construction in COL 2:14 is disputed: the 'decrees' may describe what the record of debt consisted of, or the regulations by which it condemned us. Either way it refers to legal demands, not to 'dogma' in the later sense of Christian doctrine.

study.summary: Slavery or bondage, used figuratively of the enslaved condition of life under fear, the law, death and corruption, in contrast to the freedom of God's children.

senses.label: Spiritual bondage
senses.definition: A state of enslavement that dominates a person, set against the freedom and sonship given in Christ.
senses.note: It is linked with fear (ROM 8:15; HEB 2:15) and with the Sinai covenant (GAL 4:24).

senses.label: Creation's bondage to decay
senses.definition: The subjection of the created order to corruption and decay, from which it will be freed.

study.exegesisTip: Each occurrence sets slavery against freedom or adoption, echoing Israel's deliverance from slavery in Egypt.

study.summary: The setting of the sun, hence the west, usually paired with 'east' to describe all directions or the whole world.

senses.label: The west
senses.definition: The region of sunset, used to give direction or, with 'east', to express the whole extent of the earth.
senses.note: In LUK 12:54 a cloud rising from the west (the Mediterranean) signals rain.

background.note: Property boundaries in documents contrast 'on the east' and 'on the west' with the same plural forms.

study.exegesisTip: In MAT 8:11 and LUK 13:29, people coming 'from east and west' signals the inclusion of the nations at the messianic banquet.

study.summary: A conditional particle, 'if indeed' or 'if after all', which Paul uses to state a condition he generally assumes to be true while still pressing it on his readers.

senses.label: If indeed, since
senses.definition: Introduces a condition presented as true or expected to be true, sometimes with a note of reminder or warning.
senses.note: In COL 1:23 the condition is a real one: continuing in the faith is the evidence of genuine reconciliation.

senses.label: If it really was
senses.definition: Introduces a condition the writer hopes is not true.

study.translationNote: Versions differ between 'if indeed' and 'surely' or 'assuming that' (especially in EPH 3:2 and EPH 4:21), because the particle states a condition the writer generally assumes to be true.

study.summary: That which is seen: the visible form or appearance of something, and by extension a sort or kind.

senses.label: Visible form, appearance
senses.definition: The outward, visible form or appearance of a person or thing.

senses.label: Sight, what is seen
senses.definition: Visible appearance as the basis for living, set against faith.

senses.label: Kind, sort
senses.definition: A class or variety of something.

study.translationNote: In 1TH 5:22 older versions read 'every appearance of evil', modern ones 'every form (kind) of evil'; common commercial usage of the phrase 'of every kind' supports the latter.

background.note: Business documents constantly use the phrase 'of every kind' (literally 'of every form') for categories of goods or payments.

study.caution: In 2CO 5:7 some take the word as 'what is seen' (the visible form of things) rather than the faculty of sight; the contrast with faith is clear either way.

study.summary: To listen to, either in the sense of heeding and obeying, or, in the passive, of a prayer or person being heard and answered by God.

senses.label: Heard by God (prayer)
senses.definition: Passive: of a person praying or of a prayer, to be heard favourably and answered.

senses.label: Heed, obey
senses.definition: To listen to someone in the sense of paying attention and obeying.

background.note: A letter-writer complains that the recipient is unwilling to listen to him, the same sense of heeding found in 1 Corinthians.

study.caution: In HEB 5:7 the phrase after 'heard' is usually read 'because of his reverence', but some read it as 'heard (and delivered) from his fear'.

study.summary: An entering or entrance: the act of coming in or arriving, a welcome received, or access into a holy place or the kingdom.

senses.label: Arrival, coming
senses.definition: The act of coming on the scene, as Jesus' public appearance.

senses.label: Visit, reception
senses.definition: A coming to people and the reception given there.

senses.label: Entry, access
senses.definition: Entrance or access into God's presence or his eternal kingdom; possibly the way or place of entry.

background.note: In everyday documents it most often means the entrance of a house or temple.

study.caution: In HEB 10:19 and 2PE 1:11 it is debated whether the word means the act of entering or the way of entrance.

study.summary: Well received or acceptable, especially to God, used of offerings, service and gifts, and of the God-appointed 'acceptable time' of salvation.

senses.label: Acceptable offering or service
senses.definition: Gladly received and approved, whether by God or by fellow believers.
senses.note: ROM 15:16 and 1PE 2:5 use sacrificial language: the Gentiles and believers' spiritual sacrifices are acceptable to God.

senses.label: Favourable time
senses.definition: A time of divine favour, when God welcomes and helps.

study.summary: Well-formed or becoming; used of what is seemly and presentable, and, in later Greek, of people of high standing or good social position.

senses.label: Prominent, of high standing
senses.definition: Socially respected, influential and usually wealthy.

senses.label: Seemly, presentable
senses.definition: Fitting and proper in conduct, or (of body parts) presentable and not needing special covering.

background.note: In Roman Egypt the word could designate local notables or officials responsible for public order.

study.summary: A question or matter of dispute, used in Acts of controversies over Jewish law and belief that Roman officials regarded as internal religious matters.

senses.label: Disputed question, controversy
senses.definition: A point of debate, especially concerning the Jewish law, customs or religious beliefs.

background.note: Used in official documents of an inquiry, as when an official is warned he will be held accountable in any inquiry about facts left unknown.

study.exegesisTip: Gallio, Claudius Lysias and Festus all use or are described with this word to dismiss the charges against Paul as matters of Jewish religion, not crimes under Roman law.

study.summary: Female; used as a noun for 'female' or 'woman', especially in the creation phrase 'male and female'.

senses.label: Female (creation)
senses.definition: The female sex as created by God, in the pairing 'male and female'.
senses.note: In GAL 3:28 the phrase echoes the creation account while declaring that this distinction gives no different standing in Christ.

senses.label: Women
senses.definition: Women or the female sex, with emphasis on sexual identity.

background.note: A husband writes to his wife: if the child is a boy, keep it; if a girl, expose it.

study.exegesisTip: Paul's choice of 'females' and 'males' rather than 'women' and 'men' in ROM 1:26-27 deliberately recalls the creation language of Genesis.

study.summary: A breastplate or corslet protecting the chest, used figuratively of righteousness, faith and love, and literally of armour in John's visions.

senses.label: Spiritual breastplate
senses.definition: A figure for the protection that righteousness, faith and love give the believer.

senses.label: Armour in visions
senses.definition: Chest armour worn by the locust-like creatures and the horsemen in Revelation.

background.note: The image of putting on righteousness as a breastplate comes from Isaiah's picture of God armed for salvation.
Homer describes bronze corslets of warriors.

study.summary: In order or in succession; with the article it can mean 'the time afterward' or 'those who followed'.

senses.label: In orderly sequence
senses.definition: Point by point or step by step, in a connected order.
senses.note: In ACT 18:23 it describes travelling from place to place in succession.

senses.label: Those following, afterward
senses.definition: With the article: those who came after in succession, or the period that followed.

study.caution: In LUK 1:3 'orderly' need not mean strictly chronological; it may describe a well-arranged, coherent account.

study.summary: A conjunction meaning either 'according as, in proportion as' or, more commonly in late Greek, 'because'.

senses.label: Because, since
senses.definition: Gives the reason for what has just been said.

senses.label: According as
senses.definition: In proportion to, to the degree that; here of distribution according to each person's need.

background.note: Common in official documents in the formula 'as has been written' or 'just as'.

study.summary: A concessive particle with a participle meaning 'although' or 'even though'.

senses.label: Although, even though
senses.definition: Introduces a fact that might be expected to prevent what the main clause affirms.
senses.note: In HEB 5:8 it stresses that even though he was the Son, Jesus learned obedience through suffering.

study.summary: An evildoer or criminal, someone who does harm and deserves punishment by the authorities.

senses.label: Evildoer, criminal
senses.definition: A person who does wrong, especially the kind of wrongdoing that civil authorities punish.
senses.note: Peter urges believers to give no ground for the accusation, so that slander as 'evildoers' is shown to be false.

background.note: A marriage-related promise not to use harmful drugs (literally 'evil-doing' drugs), suggesting a possible association with poisoning or magic.

study.caution: Some suggest that in 1PE 4:15 the word may specifically mean a sorcerer or poisoner, but most take it in the general sense of criminal or wrongdoer.

study.summary: Originally a straight rod or measuring rule; in the NT a standard to live by, and an assigned sphere or limit of work.

senses.label: Assigned field, limit
senses.definition: The measured area of ministry God has allotted, beyond which one should not boast.

senses.label: Rule, standard
senses.definition: A rule or norm by which believers walk.

study.translationNote: In 2 Corinthians 10, older versions say 'rule' or 'measure', modern ones 'sphere', 'field' or 'area of influence', reflecting the sense of a measured, assigned territory.

background.note: Homer uses it of the straight rods that hold a shield in shape.
An official is told to apply doubtful cases to the rule laid down for him, a metaphorical use like GAL 6:16.

study.caution: The later sense 'canon of Scripture' is post-NT and should not be read into these passages.

study.summary: To pronounce a sentence against someone; to condemn, especially to condemn the innocent.

senses.label: Condemn, pass sentence
senses.definition: To declare someone guilty and deserving punishment, whether by human judges or at God's judgment.
senses.note: MAT 12:7 and JAM 5:6 stress the condemnation of the innocent or righteous.

background.note: A standard legal term for obtaining or passing a judgment against someone in a lawsuit.

study.summary: To speak against someone, slander or run down, whether a believer speaking against a brother or outsiders maligning Christians.

senses.label: Speak against, slander
senses.definition: To speak evil of another person, defaming or disparaging them.
senses.note: In JAM 4:11 speaking against a brother amounts to speaking against God's law itself.

background.note: An inscription expresses the wish that ill-disposed people have no ground to speak against the writers.

study.summary: To trample underfoot, used literally of things or people being trodden down, and figuratively of contemptuously spurning the Son of God.

senses.label: Trample underfoot
senses.definition: To tread something or someone down with the feet.

senses.label: Treat with contempt
senses.definition: To spurn and disregard with scorn, as one treads on something worthless.

background.note: Already in Homer and Plato the verb is used figuratively of trampling on oaths and laws.

study.summary: Opposite or over against; also, figuratively, before or in the sight of someone.

senses.label: Opposite, facing
senses.definition: In a position directly across from something.
senses.note: The village 'opposite' in MAR 11:2 is the one ahead of the disciples.

senses.label: In the sight of God
senses.definition: In the presence of God, before him.

background.note: A papyrus describes a woman sitting on the sand with a child opposite her.

study.summary: Right in front of, in the very presence of; used of standing or speaking before God.

senses.label: In God's presence
senses.definition: Before God, as in his sight and under his scrutiny, whether in speaking or in being presented holy and blameless.

background.note: A Christian amulet says 'I bow my head before you'.

study.summary: To empty; in the NT figuratively, to make empty, void or of no effect, and in Philippians of Christ emptying himself.

senses.label: Make void, nullify
senses.definition: To deprive something of its force or content so that it becomes empty or meaningless.

senses.label: Christ emptied himself
senses.definition: Christ's voluntary self-humbling in taking the form of a servant and becoming human.

study.translationNote: In PHP 2:7 some versions translate literally 'emptied himself', others 'made himself nothing' or 'made himself of no reputation'.

background.note: A papyrus text of the poet Cercidas speaks of a god emptying a usurer of his wealth, supporting the literal 'emptied' in PHP 2:7.

study.exegesisTip: In PHP 2:7 the emptying is explained by the participles that follow: taking the form of a servant and being made in human likeness.
study.caution: PHP 2:7 does not say what Christ emptied himself of; reading it as giving up his divine nature goes beyond the text.

study.summary: A garden or cultivated plot, used of a man's garden in a parable and of the gardens of Jesus' arrest and burial in John.

senses.label: Garden
senses.definition: A cultivated, enclosed plot planted with plants or trees.

background.note: Homer uses the word of the orchard-garden of Alcinous.

study.summary: To strike with the fist or buffet, used of the beating of Jesus and of harsh treatment suffered by believers.

senses.label: Strike with fists
senses.definition: To beat or punch someone, as an act of abuse.

senses.label: Mistreat, torment
senses.definition: To treat roughly or torment repeatedly, figuratively of ongoing affliction.
senses.note: In 2CO 12:7 the messenger of Satan 'buffets' Paul.

study.caution: The identity of Paul's thorn in the flesh in 2CO 12:7 is unknown; the verb shows it was a repeated, humiliating affliction but not what it was.

study.summary: A pool, used in John of the pools of Bethesda and Siloam in Jerusalem.

senses.label: Pool
senses.definition: A pool of water for bathing or water storage.

background.note: Plato uses it of a swimming-bath.

study.summary: χιλιάς is the noun for 'a thousand' as a unit (a 'chiliad'), usually in the plural with a number in front: 'five thousands', 'twelve thousands'. Luke and Paul use it for real headcounts. Most uses are in Revelation, where large round numbers built on the thousand describe God's people, the angelic host and the holy city.

senses.label: A thousand (literal count)
senses.definition: The number one thousand used for an actual count of people or soldiers, usually in the plural with a multiplier (e.g. 'five thousands' = 5,000).
senses.note: In LUK 14:31 the word appears twice: ten thousand against twenty thousand.

senses.label: Thousands in Revelation's visionary numbers
senses.definition: Counts of a thousand or multiples of a thousand in apocalyptic vision, often combined with twelve or with 'myriads', to express completeness or vast size.
senses.note: The 144,000 (12 × 12 × 1,000) sealed out of Israel's twelve tribes and the city measuring 12,000 stadia show the pattern.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Nineteen of the NT uses are in Revelation. They fall into a few groups: the angelic host ('thousands of thousands'), the 12,000 sealed from each tribe and the 144,000 standing with the Lamb, the 7,000 killed in the earthquake, and the city's 12,000 stadia. In apocalyptic writing such numbers are usually read as structured symbols, not as census figures.

study.translationNote: Greek counts 'thousands' as units, so 'twenty-three thousands' is simply rendered 'twenty-three thousand'. In REV 21:16 some versions convert 12,000 stadia into miles or kilometres (about 1,400 miles / 2,200 km). That gives a sense of scale but hides the symbolic twelve.

background.note: From Herodotus and the tragedians on, the word is the ordinary noun for a group of a thousand, as in Aeschylus' count of the Persian fleet.
Plato speaks of the soul wandering 'nine thousand years'. The thousand-unit is used for long spans of time as well as for crowds.

study.exegesisTip: Watch which multipliers go with the word. In Revelation, twelve (tribes, apostles) multiplied by a thousand recurs deliberately (REV 7:4, REV 14:1, REV 21:16). Recognising that pattern matters more than the arithmetic.
study.caution: Interpreters disagree on whether Revelation's 144,000 is literal or symbolic, and on whether this group is the same as the countless multitude described right after it. The thousand-year reign of Revelation 20 uses the adjective χίλιοι, not this noun. Paul's 23,000 in 1CO 10:8 differs from the 24,000 of the Numbers account, and commentators explain the gap in different ways.

study.summary: ἀγνοέω means 'not to know': to be unaware or ignorant of something, or to fail to understand it. Paul uses it most, especially in his formula 'I do not want you to be unaware, brothers', which introduces something important. In the passive it means to be unknown or unrecognised. Hebrews uses it for sins committed in ignorance.

senses.label: Be unaware, not know (a fact)
senses.definition: To lack knowledge of a fact or situation. Paul uses it in the formula 'I do not want you to be ignorant', which draws attention to new or weighty information.
senses.note: The negative question 'Do you not know…?' (ROM 6:3, ROM 7:1) appeals to something readers ought to know already.

senses.label: Be ignorant of (with culpability)
senses.definition: Failing to know or acknowledge what one should, often with a sense of blameworthy or wilful ignorance.
senses.note: In ACT 13:27 and 1TI 1:13 ignorance explains the wrong but does not excuse it. In ACT 17:23 Paul announces the God whom the Athenians worship 'without knowing'.

senses.label: Not understand
senses.definition: To fail to grasp the meaning of something said, even though it was heard.
senses.note: Both verses describe the disciples failing to grasp Jesus' prediction of his death.

senses.label: Sin in ignorance
senses.definition: Absolute use, 'those who are ignorant', meaning those who go astray through ignorance or inadvertence, as in the Law's sins of ignorance.
senses.note: Paired with 'those who are misled', echoing the Levitical offerings for unwitting sins.

senses.label: Be unknown, unrecognised (passive)
senses.definition: In the passive, to be unknown or unrecognised by others, or not acknowledged.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: 'I (we) do not want you to be unaware, brothers' is a recurring Pauline phrase for introducing important teaching or news, about his travel plans, his sufferings, Israel's future or believers who have died.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke presents the rulers' ignorance of Jesus as the means by which they fulfilled the prophets. Ignorance is a theme that leaves room for repentance.

study.translationNote: English versions render the word as 'be unaware', 'be ignorant', 'not know' or 'not understand' depending on context. At 1CO 14:38 the manuscripts divide between an active imperative ('let him be ignorant') and a passive ('he is not recognised'), and versions follow different readings.

background.note: In Homer the verb can mean failing to recognise a person, as when Odysseus wonders whether his father will know him.
Letters use a close parallel to Paul's formula, 'I trust you are not unaware', showing it was an ordinary epistolary idiom.
An official instruction aims that 'nothing be concealed' (literally 'not be unknown'), which shows the verb can carry a sense of deliberate ignoring.

study.exegesisTip: When Paul says 'I do not want you to be unaware', treat it as a signpost: what follows is the point he wants to stress (e.g. ROM 11:25, 1TH 4:13).
study.caution: The reading at 1CO 14:38 is textually uncertain (active 'let him be ignorant' or passive 'he is not acknowledged', possibly by God). Do not build doctrine on either form alone.

study.summary: ἀντί is a preposition with the genitive. Its basic idea is one thing standing over against another, which yields 'instead of, in place of, in exchange for'. In the NT it marks substitution, succession, price paid, and repayment of good or evil. The set phrase ἀνθ᾽ ὧν means 'because'. It is the preposition in Jesus' saying that he came to give his life as a ransom 'for many'.

senses.label: Instead of, in place of
senses.definition: One thing takes the place of another or is given in its stead.
senses.note: In JAM 4:15 it is used with the articular infinitive: 'instead of your saying'.

senses.label: Succession
senses.definition: One person replaces another in an office or position.
senses.note: Archelaus reigned 'in place of' his father Herod.

senses.label: Substitution / ransom
senses.definition: Something given in exchange for others or on their behalf as their replacement, especially Jesus' life given as a ransom 'for many'.
senses.note: Joined with λύτρον ('ransom price'), ἀντί points to exchange and substitution.

senses.label: In exchange for, for the price of
senses.definition: The price or thing received in a trade, or the prize for which something is endured.
senses.note: Esau sold his birthright 'for a single meal'. 'Grace in place of grace' (JOH 1:16) describes grace continually succeeding grace.

senses.label: Requital: evil for evil
senses.definition: Repayment of one thing for another, in the commands not to return evil for evil, or in the law of like-for-like retribution.

senses.label: ἀνθ᾽ ὧν / ἀντὶ τούτου: because, therefore
senses.definition: In the fixed phrase ἀνθ᾽ ὧν ('in return for which things') it means 'because' or 'therefore'. ἀντὶ τούτου means 'for this reason'.
senses.note: EPH 5:31 renders the Hebrew 'therefore' of the Genesis marriage text.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke alone in the Gospels uses the causal ἀνθ᾽ ὧν ('because'), a Septuagint-flavoured phrase, for Zechariah's unbelief, Jerusalem's failure to recognise its visitation, and Herod's death.

study.translationNote: Most versions translate ἀντί with English 'for', which can hide the exchange idea. 'A ransom for many' (MAR 10:45) means 'in place of many'. 'For the joy set before him' (HEB 12:2) is usually taken as 'for the sake of' (to obtain) the joy, but a minority render it 'instead of the joy'.

background.note: The original local sense, 'opposite, facing', survives rarely, e.g. in Xenophon. That spatial picture of one thing set over against another underlies the later meaning 'instead of'.
In everyday documents the commonest meaning is simply 'instead of', e.g. appointing 'others in their place'.
The Rosetta Stone uses ἀνθ᾽ ὧν for 'because, in return for which', the same idiom found in Luke.

study.exegesisTip: Ask what is being exchanged for what. In MAR 10:45 a single life is given for many lives. In ROM 12:17 the disciple refuses to return evil for evil. In HEB 12:16 a birthright is traded for one meal. The 'in exchange for' idea links all of these uses.
study.caution: Interpreters debate HEB 12:2. Most take it as 'for the sake of the joy' (to obtain it), but some read 'instead of the joy' (giving up a joy already available). Both are grammatically possible. Do not press ἀντί in MAR 10:45 beyond what the ransom image itself carries.

study.summary: βάπτισμα, from βαπτίζω ('immerse, dip'), means 'baptism', the immersion and the rite it marks. In the Gospels and Acts it usually refers to John's 'baptism of repentance'. Paul and Peter use it for Christian baptism into Christ's death and resurrection. Jesus uses it as a metaphor for the overwhelming suffering he must undergo. The noun appears only in Christian writings.

senses.label: John's baptism
senses.definition: The rite John the Baptist administered in the Jordan, a 'baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins' that prepared people for the coming one.
senses.note: The question of where John's baptism came from, 'from heaven or from men?', became a test of authority (MAR 11:30, LUK 20:4).

senses.label: Christian baptism
senses.definition: The rite of initiation into Christ, understood as union with him in his death, burial and resurrection, and as a pledge toward God.

senses.label: Baptism of suffering (metaphor)
senses.definition: Jesus' coming passion pictured as being plunged under or overwhelmed, alongside the image of the 'cup'.
senses.note: The disciples will share it too (MAR 10:39), which points to their own suffering.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses John's baptism as a historical marker. The apostolic witness runs 'from the baptism of John' (ACT 1:22, ACT 10:37). Acts also shows disciples who knew only John's baptism being brought further (ACT 18:25, ACT 19:3).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul treats baptism as burial with Christ and the start of a new life, and as a sign of the church's unity ('one Lord, one faith, one baptism').

authorNotes.author: Peter
