authorNotes.note: Peter links baptism to Noah's flood as its antitype. It saves not by washing the body but as the appeal or pledge of a good conscience toward God, through Christ's resurrection.

study.translationNote: 'Baptism' is a transliteration, not a translation. The underlying idea is immersion or being plunged in. Some versions bring this out in Jesus' metaphorical sayings ('a baptism to undergo', LUK 12:50).

background.note: The noun is essentially a Christian coinage, formed when the verb became a technical term. A fragment of an uncanonical gospel asks what 'new baptism' Jesus preached.

study.exegesisTip: Distinguish βάπτισμα (the baptism as an event or rite) from βαπτισμός (washings in general, e.g. Jewish ablutions). Ask whose baptism a text means: John's, Christian, or Jesus' 'baptism' of suffering.
study.caution: The word does not settle debates about the mode, subjects or effect of baptism. Those rest on wider theology. In COL 2:12 some manuscripts read βαπτισμός. The two sayings in MAT 20:22–23 appear only in the Byzantine text.

study.summary: δέομαι means 'to ask urgently, beg, implore'. It is a request born of need, related to the idea of lacking something. People use it toward Jesus or toward other people, and Luke and Paul also use it for earnest prayer to God. Luke uses it most.

senses.label: Beg, implore (a person)
senses.definition: An urgent, often humble appeal from one person to another, frequently someone in distress before Jesus.
senses.note: Often with the genitive of the person asked: 'he begged him'.

senses.label: Request, ask (polite or formal)
senses.definition: A courteous request or plea in speech or a letter, sometimes amounting to 'please'.
senses.note: In 2CO 8:4 the Macedonians beg Paul for the privilege of sharing in the collection.

senses.label: Plead on God's behalf
senses.definition: The apostolic appeal to people, made as Christ's ambassadors, to be reconciled to God.

senses.label: Pray, petition God
senses.definition: Earnest prayer to God for a specific need, often with the content stated ('that…', 'whether perhaps…').
senses.note: Related to the noun δέησις, 'petition'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the verb far more than any other writer. People in need beg Jesus, Jesus prays for Peter ('I have prayed for you'), and the church prays until the place is shaken.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses it for persistent intercession ('night and day praying most earnestly') and for gentle but urgent appeals to his churches.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'beg', 'beseech', 'implore', 'ask' and 'pray'. The Greek is the same. Context decides whether the appeal is to a person or to God. Older 'I pray you' (2CO 10:2) is a polite 'please', not prayer.

background.note: δέομαι was the standard verb in petitions to sovereigns ('we beg you…'). Petitions to ordinary officials more often used ἀξιόω ('I claim'), so δέομαι marked humble entreaty.
The verb also keeps its root sense 'to need', as in 'we need more time'.

study.exegesisTip: δέομαι stresses the need behind the request. Compare the more general αἰτέω ('ask') and προσεύχομαι ('pray'). In passages like LUK 22:32 and ROM 1:10 it shows prayer as a specific, felt petition.

study.summary: καθεύδω means 'to sleep'. Most often it is literal sleep, as when the disciples sleep in Gethsemane or Jesus sleeps in the storm-tossed boat. It is also used figuratively for death, in Jesus' 'she is not dead but asleep', and for spiritual dullness, in calls to wake up and keep watch.

senses.label: Sleep (literal)
senses.definition: Ordinary physical sleep.

senses.label: Sleep instead of watching (Gethsemane)
senses.definition: The disciples' sleep in Gethsemane, set against Jesus' call to watch and pray.

senses.label: Sleep as a picture of death
senses.definition: Death described as sleep, implying that it is temporary and that waking will follow.
senses.note: The girl really had died. Jesus calls it sleep because he is about to raise her.

senses.label: Spiritual insensibility
senses.definition: Moral or spiritual dullness, being unprepared and unaware of the hour, the opposite of being awake and watchful.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In 1 Thessalonians 5 Paul uses sleeping and waking for both moral alertness (1TH 5:6, 1TH 5:7) and, most likely, death and life (1TH 5:10): whether we are 'awake or asleep', we live with Christ.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark repeats the verb in Gethsemane and in the warning that the master should not find his servants sleeping, which ties discipleship to watchfulness.

study.translationNote: Most versions translate the verb literally. In 1TH 5:10 some versions add 'whether alive or dead' to make the death metaphor clear, while others keep 'awake or asleep'.

background.note: From Homer on, it is the ordinary verb for lying down to sleep.
Philosophers set sleeping against being awake, the same contrast the NT draws in its calls to watchfulness.
Rules for visitors who slept at a healing shrine required men and women to sleep in separate places.

study.exegesisTip: Note the pairing with γρηγορέω ('be awake, watch'). Where the two appear together (1TH 5:6, 1TH 5:10), work out whether the contrast is moral alertness or life and death.
study.caution: Interpreters disagree on 1TH 5:10. Most take καθεύδω there as death, echoing chapter 4. Others read it as moral sleep, as in 5:6. Paul used a different verb (κοιμάομαι) for the dead in chapter 4, so the meaning is not obvious.

study.summary: κατηγορέω means 'to accuse, bring charges against', literally 'to speak against' someone, usually before a judge. The Gospels use it for opponents watching Jesus to find grounds for a charge, and Acts for the formal prosecution of Paul. It also describes the accusing conscience and Satan accusing believers before God.

senses.label: Seek grounds to accuse
senses.definition: Watching or questioning someone in order to bring a charge against him.

senses.label: Bring formal charges in court
senses.definition: Acting as accuser or prosecutor before a governor or tribunal.
senses.note: Passive 'to be accused' (MAT 27:12, ACT 22:30). 'The accused' is ὁ κατηγορούμενος (ACT 25:16).

senses.label: Accuse before God
senses.definition: Accusing someone before God's judgment, by Moses' writings or by the devil.
senses.note: In REV 12:10 the devil accuses 'day and night', but he is thrown down.

senses.label: Inner accusation of conscience
senses.definition: One's own thoughts accusing (or defending) one, like witnesses in an inner court.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the verb in a legal setting throughout Jesus' trial and Paul's hearings before Felix and Festus. The repeated theme is that the accusers cannot prove their charges.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John reverses the roles. Jesus will not be Israel's accuser, because Moses already accuses them. In Revelation the accuser of the brothers is thrown down.

background.note: In Attic Greek it is the regular legal term for prosecuting someone, the opposite of ἀπολογέομαι ('make a defence'), the same pair found in ROM 2:15.
Plato uses it for denouncing someone publicly to the city, as Socrates' accuser did.
Papyri use it for laying charges before an official, e.g. a herdsman accusing others.

study.exegesisTip: Look for the courtroom pairing with ἀπολογέομαι ('defend'), as in ROM 2:15, where conscience serves as both prosecution and defence.

study.summary: πέραν is an adverb meaning 'on the other side, across, beyond', usually with water in between. As a preposition with the genitive it means 'beyond' (beyond the Jordan, across the sea). With the article, τὸ πέραν, it means 'the other side', the far shore of the Sea of Galilee. The Transjordan region later called Perea takes its name from it.

senses.label: Beyond (the Jordan)
senses.definition: As a preposition with the genitive: the region east of the Jordan, the Transjordan.
senses.note: 'Beyond the Jordan' functions almost as a place name.

senses.label: Across (a sea or stream)
senses.definition: On the far side of a body of water such as the Sea of Galilee or the Kidron brook.

senses.label: The other side (τὸ πέραν)
senses.definition: With the article as a noun: the opposite shore, the region on the other side, especially in the lake crossings.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John dates John the Baptist's ministry to 'Bethany beyond the Jordan', and Jesus later withdraws there. He also follows the crowds' movements across the sea in chapter 6.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark repeatedly marks boat crossings 'to the other side', a structuring feature of Jesus' Galilean ministry that moves between Jewish and Gentile shores.

background.note: In early poetry it is always used with the genitive and especially of water: islands 'across the sea'.
Thucydides uses it of lands beyond the Hellespont.
Papyri use it for 'opposite the city of Oxyrhynchus' and τὸ πέραν for 'the region beyond', as in the Gospels.

study.exegesisTip: In the Synoptic lake narratives, 'to the other side' often signals a move into Gentile territory (e.g. the Gerasene/Gergesene region, MAT 8:28, MAR 5:1). Track the direction of each crossing.
study.caution: The site of 'Bethany beyond the Jordan' (JOH 1:28) is uncertain. It is different from Bethany near Jerusalem, and some manuscripts read 'Bethabara'.

study.summary: πληγή, from πλήσσω ('strike'), means a blow or stroke, and by extension the wound or stripe it leaves. Luke and Paul use it of beatings. Revelation uses it of the beast's 'death-blow' and, most of all, of the plagues God sends on the earth, echoing the plagues of Egypt.

senses.label: Blow, stripe, beating
senses.definition: Physical blows, especially flogging with rods or whips, usually in the plural.

senses.label: Wound
senses.definition: The wound or welt left by blows.
senses.note: The jailer 'washed them from their stripes'.

senses.label: Death-blow (Revelation 13)
senses.definition: The fatal wound of the beast, which was healed: 'the stroke of death'.

senses.label: Plague, calamity from God
senses.definition: A divinely sent disaster or judgment, as in the bowl and trumpet judgments.
senses.note: The 'seven last plagues' (REV 15:1, REV 21:9).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Most NT uses are in Revelation. The plagues recall the Exodus plagues: they are judgments that call for repentance, yet people 'did not repent' (REV 9:20, REV 16:9). God's people are urged to come out of Babylon so as not to share her plagues.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul lists 'beatings' among his apostolic sufferings as proof of genuine ministry.

study.translationNote: One Greek word becomes 'stripes', 'blows', 'wounds' or 'plagues' in English. In Revelation the link between the beast's 'wound' (REV 13:3) and the 'plagues' is lost in translation, though both are πληγή.

background.note: From Homer on, it means a blow or stroke.
Complaints describe assaults with blows from a rod, the everyday sense behind Paul's 'beatings'.
A municipal law prescribes a flogging of fifty strokes in the pillory.

study.exegesisTip: Read the plagues of Revelation against the Exodus story, where the Septuagint uses the same word for the plagues on Egypt. The judgments are both punishment and a call to repent.
study.caution: Interpreters disagree about who or what the beast's healed 'death-blow' (REV 13:3) refers to, e.g. a parody of Christ's resurrection or allusions to Roman emperors. The word itself only means a mortal wound.

study.summary: πλοῦτος means 'wealth, riches'. The Gospels and James use it for material possessions, which can deceive and decay. Paul, who uses it most, mainly applies it figuratively to the inexhaustible abundance of God's kindness, glory and grace in Christ, and to the spiritual enrichment given to the nations.

senses.label: Material wealth
senses.definition: Money and possessions, often shown as deceptive, fleeting or a threat to faith.

senses.label: The abundance of God's attributes
senses.definition: The overflowing fullness of God's kindness, glory, grace and wisdom.
senses.note: Usually with a genitive: 'riches of his grace/glory'.

senses.label: Spiritual enrichment, treasure
senses.definition: Blessing and spiritual benefit given to people, or the treasure found in Christ.
senses.note: In ROM 11:12, Israel's stumbling meant 'riches for the world'.

senses.label: A wealth of a human quality
senses.definition: A rich abundance of a quality in people, such as generosity or understanding.

senses.label: Riches as an attribute ascribed to the Lamb
senses.definition: Wealth as one of the honours the Lamb is worthy to receive in worship.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Fifteen of the twenty-two uses are Paul's, nearly all figurative. He constantly speaks of 'the riches of' God's kindness, glory, grace or Christ, piling up intensifiers such as 'surpassing' and 'unsearchable'.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James announces that the hoarded wealth of oppressive rich people has already rotted, a prophetic warning of judgment.

background.note: From Homer on, the ordinary word for wealth. Plato contrasts it with poverty.
A papyrus speaks of someone 'puffed up by wealth', the same danger warned of in 1TI 6:17.

study.exegesisTip: In Paul, look at the genitive after πλοῦτος. It names what God is rich in (grace, glory, kindness), and the context shows what that richness does for the reader. In Hellenistic Greek the noun sometimes takes neuter forms (τὸ πλοῦτος), especially in Paul, without any change of meaning.

study.summary: πωλέω is the ordinary verb 'to sell'. In the NT it moves from the everyday market (sparrows, meat, oil) to the temple traders Jesus drove out, and above all to the call to sell one's possessions for the kingdom, which the early Jerusalem church put into practice.

senses.label: Sell in the marketplace
senses.definition: To hand over goods for money in ordinary trade; the passive describes what is 'sold' or on sale, sometimes with the price in the genitive.
senses.note: The cheapness of sparrows 'sold' for a tiny coin sets up Jesus' point about the Father's care for each one.

senses.label: The temple traders
senses.definition: Participle 'those selling' for the dealers in sacrificial animals and doves in the temple courts, whom Jesus expelled.

senses.label: Selling possessions for the kingdom
senses.definition: Selling one's property in order to give to the poor or to gain the kingdom; a mark of radical discipleship in Jesus' teaching and in the Jerusalem church.
senses.note: In Acts the selling was voluntary: Peter tells Ananias the property and its proceeds remained his own.

senses.label: Selling to meet a pressing need
senses.definition: Parting with something of value to obtain what an emergency requires.
senses.note: Jesus' saying about selling a cloak to buy a sword is widely read as vivid language for the hostility the disciples are about to face, not a call to arms.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the verb most, and ties Jesus' command to sell and give alms to its realization in the early community, where believers sold lands and houses and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet, and to its counterfeit in Ananias and Sapphira.

background.note: In classical Greek the verb meant to sell or offer for sale, set against ὠνεῖσθαι, 'to buy'.
The papyri use it constantly for plain selling, including a man who managed to pay a debt only by selling all his property, a close parallel to the rich man told to sell all he had.
An egg-seller undertakes to sell only in the public market and not secretly or from his own house, showing the regulated market setting assumed in passages about goods 'sold in the meat market'.

study.exegesisTip: Watch the pairing with 'buy' (ἀγοράζω): in the temple scenes and in Revelation's mark of the beast, 'buying and selling' together means the whole sphere of economic life.

study.summary: σοφός means 'wise' or 'skilled'. Paul, who has most of the uses, sets the self-confident 'wise' of this age, whom God shames through the cross, against true wisdom that shows itself in godly living; the word is also used of God himself, the 'only wise God'.

senses.label: Skilled, expert
senses.definition: Having technical skill in a craft; the old sense of the word, used by Paul of himself as an expert builder laying a foundation.

senses.label: The learned, the cultured class
senses.definition: Those reckoned educated or intellectually accomplished in human society, often in a pair such as 'wise and foolish' or 'wise and understanding'.
senses.note: In Jesus' prayer the 'wise and learned' are those whose own insight keeps them from receiving what God reveals to 'little children'.

senses.label: Worldly wisdom judged by God
senses.definition: Those who are wise by the standards of this age, whose wisdom God overturns and exposes as futile through the message of the cross.
senses.note: Paul's Old Testament quotations here come from Isaiah, Job and the Psalms.

senses.label: Practically and morally wise
senses.definition: Having the discernment to live and judge well before God, shown in conduct rather than claims.
senses.note: James asks the 'wise' to prove it by good conduct done in gentleness.

senses.label: Wise teachers sent by God
senses.definition: Messengers whom Jesus sends to Israel alongside prophets and scribes, echoing the Jewish category of the sage.

senses.label: Of God
senses.definition: God as the one truly and solely wise, in doxologies; Paul can even say God's 'foolishness' is wiser than human wisdom.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's use is concentrated in 1 Corinthians 1–3, where he answers a church impressed by eloquence and philosophy: the 'wise' of this age are brought to nothing, and whoever thinks himself wise must become a fool in order to become truly wise.

background.note: In early Greek σοφός meant skilled in a craft or art, used of a charioteer, a pilot, a seer, and especially of poets and musicians, before it came to mean wise in a theoretical sense.
A calendar papyrus speaks of 'a wise man' who expounds the whole truth; the word was also a favourite term of praise in epitaphs.

study.exegesisTip: In 1 Corinthians, ask whose standard of wisdom is in view: 'wise according to the flesh' and 'wise in this age' are qualified phrases, and Paul does not reject wisdom as such but the world's wisdom that cannot know God.
study.caution: The phrase 'the only wise God' in 1 Timothy 1:17 and Jude 25 rests on the later majority of manuscripts; most early manuscripts read 'the only God' there, so modern translations based on them omit 'wise'.

study.summary: συνέδριον is a 'council', a body that sits together. In the NT it nearly always means the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem led by the high priest, before which Jesus, the apostles, Stephen and Paul were tried; occasionally it denotes local Jewish courts, a meeting of the council, or its chamber.

senses.label: The Sanhedrin
senses.definition: The supreme Jewish council and court in Jerusalem, composed of chief priests, elders and scribes under the high priest.

senses.label: Local councils
senses.definition: Local Jewish courts, such as those attached to synagogues, before which Jesus' followers would be brought.
senses.note: The plural 'councils' shows that more than the Jerusalem body is in view.

senses.label: A session of the council
senses.definition: A meeting convened for deliberation.
senses.note: The chief priests and Pharisees 'gathered a council' to decide what to do about Jesus.

senses.label: The council chamber
senses.definition: The place where the council met, from which accused persons could be sent out or into which they were brought.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Most uses are in Acts, which narrates a series of hearings before the Sanhedrin: Peter and John, the apostles, Stephen, and Paul, who exploits the Pharisee–Sadducee division within it. Gamaliel's counsel is given 'in the council'.

study.translationNote: Some versions transliterate as 'Sanhedrin' (the Hebrew loanword is itself borrowed from συνέδριον), while others keep the generic 'council'. 'Sanhedrin' makes clear the supreme Jerusalem body is meant, but can mislead where the word means local courts.

background.note: In classical Greek it was any council or meeting of delegates, used for example of a council of war and of the Areopagus at Athens.
Papyri use it for an assembly called together, such as a general meeting of village police officers.
In the Greek Old Testament it can mean a circle or company of people gathered together, as when Jeremiah says he did not sit in the company of revellers.

study.caution: In Matthew 5:22 it is debated whether 'the council' means the Jerusalem Sanhedrin or a local court; either way Jesus climbs from local judgment to the council to the fire of Gehenna to show how seriously God takes contemptuous anger.

study.summary: τελώνης is a 'tax collector' or toll collector. In the Gospels tax collectors are a byword for despised outsiders, regularly paired with 'sinners', yet Jesus calls one as an apostle, eats with them, and holds up their repentance against the self-righteous.

senses.label: Collector of tolls and taxes
senses.definition: A man who collected customs, tolls or taxes, usually on contract from those who bought the right to collect them, with ample room for overcharging.
senses.note: John the Baptist tells tax collectors to collect no more than is fixed for them.

senses.label: Byword for the despised and morally suspect
senses.definition: Grouped with 'sinners', Gentiles and prostitutes as people respectable Jews avoided; used proverbially for the lowest moral standard.
senses.note: The charge that Jesus is 'a friend of tax collectors and sinners' turns their ill repute into a picture of his mission.

senses.label: Outsiders who respond to God
senses.definition: Tax collectors as those who accept John's message and repent, entering the kingdom ahead of the religious leaders.
senses.note: In the parable it is the tax collector, not the Pharisee, who goes home justified.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke especially stresses tax collectors' openness: they come to be baptized, acknowledge God's justice, draw near to hear Jesus, and supply the model of humble prayer in the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Only Matthew's list of the Twelve labels Matthew 'the tax collector', and Matthew uses the word in sayings about church discipline and the kingdom, where tax collectors and prostitutes go in first.

study.translationNote: The traditional 'publican' comes from the Latin publicanus. The Gospel tax collectors were not Roman publicani, wealthy companies who contracted for provincial revenue, but local collectors of tolls and dues, often Jews, which is why modern versions say 'tax collector'.

background.note: Classical writers used the word for farmers or collectors of tolls and taxes, often with contempt; Aristophanes and Aeschines both refer to them.
A comic line said of a whole town 'all tax collectors, all robbers', showing the stock reputation of the trade.
A government order of the second century BC instructs that nobody be wronged by tax collectors who try to extort by false accusation, the very wrong Zacchaeus later confesses.
Papyri name tax collectors who held the contract for a particular tax, such as the tax on ferry-boats at a city.

study.exegesisTip: Note the company the word keeps: 'tax collectors and sinners', 'the Gentile and the tax collector', 'tax collectors and prostitutes'. These pairings show it functions as a social label for those outside respectable piety.

study.summary: τεσσαράκοντα is the number 'forty'. Besides ordinary counts, it marks periods of testing and preparation that echo Israel's forty years in the wilderness: Jesus' forty days in the desert and the forty days of his resurrection appearances. In Revelation it appears in compound numbers such as forty-two months and 144,000.

senses.label: Jesus' forty days of testing
senses.definition: The forty days Jesus spent fasting and being tempted in the wilderness.
senses.note: The number recalls Israel's forty years of testing and Moses' and Elijah's forty days.

senses.label: Israel's forty years in the wilderness
senses.definition: The wilderness generation's forty years of wandering, rebellion and God's patience, recalled in sermons and warnings.

senses.label: Other periods in sacred history
senses.definition: Forty-year spans in Israel's story and the forty days between Jesus' resurrection and ascension.

senses.label: Ordinary counts
senses.definition: Forty as a plain number of years, people or lashes, including compounds such as forty-six.
senses.note: Paul's 'forty lashes less one' reflects the limit of forty strokes in the Law, kept one short to avoid exceeding it.

senses.label: In compound numbers in Revelation
senses.definition: Part of the symbolic numbers forty-two months and 144,000, and the wall measurement of 144 cubits.
senses.note: Forty-two months equals the 1,260 days and 'time, times and half a time' of the same visions.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews takes up Psalm 95's 'forty years' and applies it both to the time Israel saw God's works and to the time of his anger with them, warning readers not to repeat their unbelief.

background.note: The numeral is used from Homer onward.
Documents of the period show both spellings, τεσσαράκοντα and τεσσεράκοντα, sometimes in the same text.

study.exegesisTip: When forty marks a time of trial or preparation, read it against Israel's forty years in the wilderness; the Gospel temptation accounts present Jesus as succeeding where Israel failed.
study.caution: Critical editions of the Greek NT spell the word τεσσεράκοντα, so it may be listed under that form. Not every occurrence is symbolic; ages, head-counts and building times are simply numbers.

study.summary: ἀληθῶς is the adverb 'truly, really, surely'. It underlines that something is genuinely so: in confessions that Jesus is truly the Son of God, in solemn sayings of Jesus, in sudden realizations, and, in John especially, in marking what is real and authentic.

senses.label: Truly, in confession
senses.definition: Affirming that what is confessed about Jesus really is the case, often after a striking event.
senses.note: The centurion's 'Truly this was the Son of God' at the cross is a climax of Mark's Gospel.

senses.label: Truly, in solemn assertion
senses.definition: Introducing or strengthening a weighty statement, 'I tell you truly'.

senses.label: Surely, certainly
senses.definition: Expressing that something is evidently so, often in a realization or accusation.
senses.note: Peter, freed from prison, realizes 'now I know for certain' that the Lord sent his angel.

senses.label: Genuinely, really (as opposed to in appearance)
senses.definition: Marking someone or something as authentic, true to its name.
senses.note: Paul thanks God that the Thessalonians received his message not as human words but as what it truly is, the word of God.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John has over half the uses, fitting his concern with what is true and genuine: a true Israelite without deceit, people who are truly disciples by abiding in Jesus' word, and the love of God truly perfected in those who keep his word.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses 'I tell you truly' in sayings where the parallel Gospels have Jesus' Hebrew-derived 'Amen, I tell you', giving the same solemn force in plain Greek.

background.note: In the Greek Old Testament it often renders Hebrew words built on the root of 'amen', meaning 'surely, indeed'.

study.exegesisTip: Where ἀληθῶς qualifies a noun, as in 'truly an Israelite' or 'truly disciples', it contrasts genuine reality with mere appearance or claim.
study.caution: In John 6:55 manuscripts differ between the adverb ('my flesh truly is food') and the adjective ('my flesh is true food'); the sense is much the same.

study.summary: βασιλεύω means 'to be king, to reign'. It is used of earthly rulers, of the eternal reign of God and Christ, of believers who will reign with Christ, and, in Paul's vivid language, of sin and death reigning as tyrants over humanity until grace reigns in their place.

senses.label: Earthly kings reign
senses.definition: To rule as king over a territory or people.
senses.note: In the parable the citizens refuse to have the nobleman 'reign over' them, a picture of rejecting Jesus' kingship.

senses.label: God and Christ reign
senses.definition: The royal rule of God and of the Messiah, now and forever.
senses.note: Paul says Christ must reign until all enemies, death last of all, are put under his feet.

senses.label: Believers reign with Christ
senses.definition: God's people sharing in Christ's royal rule, in life now through grace and fully in the age to come.

senses.label: Sin and death reign
senses.definition: Personified powers exercising tyrannical rule over humanity since Adam, a rule broken by the reign of grace.
senses.note: Paul calls believers not to let sin reign in their mortal bodies.

senses.label: Ironic 'reigning'
senses.definition: Paul's sarcasm toward Corinthians who acted as if they had already begun to reign as kings.
senses.note: He wishes they really did reign, so that the suffering apostles might reign with them.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In Romans 5–6 Paul turns the verb into a picture of two rival regimes: death and sin reigned through Adam, but those who receive grace will reign in life through Christ, and grace now reigns through righteousness.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation uses it for God taking up his reign in triumph and for the saints who reign with Christ, a destiny promised to a persecuted church.

background.note: From Homer onward the verb means to be king or rule.
An early saying of Jesus preserved on papyrus uses the aorist for coming to reign: 'he shall reign, and having reigned he shall rest'.

study.exegesisTip: The aorist can mean 'began to reign' (ingressive): in the heavenly hymns God has 'taken his great power and begun to reign', marking the moment his rule is openly established.
study.caution: The 'thousand years' during which the saints reign with Christ is interpreted very differently (premillennial, amillennial, postmillennial); the verb itself does not settle the debate.

study.summary: γένος comes from the root 'to become, be born' and covers groups united by birth or common nature: a family, descendants or offspring, a people or nation, and more generally a kind or sort, whether of fish, demons or spiritual gifts such as tongues.

senses.label: Family, lineage
senses.definition: A family or clan, those descended from a common ancestor.
senses.note: Paul addresses his hearers as 'sons of Abraham's family'.

senses.label: Offspring
senses.definition: Descendant or offspring of someone.
senses.note: At Athens Paul quotes a Greek poet (Aratus) that humans are God's offspring, and argues that God cannot be like a man-made image.

senses.label: Race, nation, people
senses.definition: A people or nationality; with the dative it means 'by birth' or 'by origin'.
senses.note: Paul is 'of the people of Israel', and he advanced beyond many his age 'among my people'.

senses.label: The church as a chosen race
senses.definition: Applied to believers as God's new people, a 'chosen race' in Old Testament language for Israel.

senses.label: Kind, sort, class
senses.definition: A category or variety of things sharing a nature.
senses.note: Paul speaks of 'kinds of tongues' and of the many 'kinds of sounds' in the world.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word mostly for national or family origin when introducing people, Barnabas a Cypriot, Aquila of Pontus, Apollos of Alexandria, and for Israel as a people in Stephen's speech.

background.note: From Homer the word means race, stock or kin, often in statements of where a person comes from by birth.
A papyrus has a man prove himself 'to be of priestly family', closely matching those 'of high-priestly family' in Acts.
In business papyri it often means a kind or category of goods, and payments 'in kind' rather than in money.

study.exegesisTip: Notice the dative τῷ γένει, 'by birth/origin', used in introducing people; it identifies ethnic background rather than describing character.
study.caution: 'This kind' in Matthew 17:21 is part of a verse absent from many early manuscripts, and 'and fasting' in Mark 9:29 is also textually uncertain.

study.summary: διδασκαλία means 'teaching', either the activity of instructing or the content taught. In the Pastoral Letters it becomes a key term for the apostolic body of teaching, the 'sound' or healthy doctrine that shapes godly life, set against human and demonic teachings.

senses.label: The activity of teaching
senses.definition: The act or ministry of instructing others.
senses.note: Scripture is useful 'for teaching', and elders who labour in teaching deserve double honour.

senses.label: Instruction for God's people
senses.definition: What serves to instruct, as Scripture written for the instruction of believers.

senses.label: Sound apostolic teaching
senses.definition: The body of Christian teaching handed on by the apostles, described as healthy and as something believers' lives should adorn.
senses.note: Paul tells slaves to 'adorn the teaching of God our Savior' by their conduct.

senses.label: Human and demonic teachings
senses.definition: Teachings that come from humans or from evil spirits rather than God, often in the plural.
senses.note: Jesus quotes Isaiah against those who teach human commandments as doctrine.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Most uses are in 1–2 Timothy and Titus, where 'sound (healthy) teaching' is a standard against which false teaching is measured, and where teaching is inseparable from conduct.

study.translationNote: Older versions often render 'doctrine', modern ones 'teaching'. 'Doctrine' can suggest an abstract system, while the word can also mean the act of teaching; context decides.

background.note: Classical writers use it for teaching or instruction, and also for training a chorus.
Isaiah's complaint about people who teach human commandments and teachings is the text Jesus quotes against the tradition of the elders.
A prefect explains that his orders rest on 'instruction' drawn from what happens in every city, showing its sense of information or direction.

study.exegesisTip: Compare διδαχή, the near synonym: both mean teaching, but διδασκαλία dominates the Pastorals, where the emphasis falls on an established, transmitted body of teaching.

study.summary: εὐδοκέω means 'to be well pleased'. With an infinitive it expresses a willing decision, 'to think it good, choose gladly', used both of God's gracious purposes and of believers' freely chosen acts; with an object it means 'to take delight in', most memorably in the Father's voice over his beloved Son.

senses.label: God's gracious decision
senses.definition: God choosing freely and gladly to act, an expression of his good pleasure.
senses.note: Your Father 'has been pleased to give you the kingdom'.

senses.label: People's willing resolve
senses.definition: Humans deciding gladly or being determined to do something.
senses.note: The Macedonian and Achaian churches 'were pleased' to share with the poor in Jerusalem, freely and willingly.

senses.label: The Father's delight in the Son
senses.definition: God's approval and delight in Jesus as his beloved Son and chosen Servant.
senses.note: The words echo Isaiah's servant 'in whom my soul delights'.

senses.label: God's pleasure or displeasure in people and offerings
senses.definition: God accepting or not accepting persons and sacrifices.
senses.note: God was not pleased with most of the wilderness generation, nor with sacrifices as such.

senses.label: Taking pleasure in things
senses.definition: Delighting in or approving of something, for good or ill.
senses.note: Paul delights in weaknesses for Christ's sake; others delight in unrighteousness.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb for God's sovereign good pleasure in salvation, in his call, and in the fullness dwelling in Christ, and also for the free resolve of believers, as in the collection for Jerusalem.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses it in quoting Psalm 40, God 'took no pleasure' in sacrifices, and Habakkuk, God takes no pleasure in one who shrinks back.

study.translationNote: English struggles to cover the verb's range: 'be well pleased', 'delight in', 'think it good', 'be willing', 'resolve'. The underlying idea is a free choice made with pleasure.

background.note: In the Greek Old Testament it chiefly renders Hebrew רָצָה, God accepting and delighting in his people.
In legal papyri it is the standard word for giving consent; a marriage contract forbids the husband to dispose of property without the bride's consent.

study.exegesisTip: Check the construction: with an infinitive it means a decision gladly taken ('was pleased to...'); with 'in' or an object it means delight or approval in a person or thing.
study.caution: In Colossians 1:19 the subject is debated: either 'God was pleased for all the fullness to dwell in him' or 'all the fullness was pleased to dwell in him'. The aorist in 'in whom I am well pleased' is likewise read either as a timeless statement or as pointing to a past choice.

study.summary: θερίζω is the ordinary farming verb 'to reap, harvest' (from θέρος, summer). In the NT it describes literal harvest work, but it is used far more often as a picture: reaping the results of what one has sown, gathering people into God's kingdom, and the final judgment as God's harvest of the earth.

senses.label: Reap a crop (literal)
senses.definition: To cut and gather ripe grain at harvest time, the farmer's summer work.
senses.note: In Jesus' saying about the birds, sowing, reaping and storing in barns together sum up the whole anxious labor of providing food, which God's care makes unnecessary.

senses.label: Reap the consequences (sowing and reaping)
senses.definition: To receive the outcome that corresponds to what one has done, as surely as a harvest follows the seed that was sown.
senses.note: Paul uses the proverb both as a warning (sowing to the flesh reaps corruption) and as encouragement to generous giving (sowing bountifully reaps bountifully).

senses.label: Benefit from another's labor
senses.definition: To gather in a harvest one did not plant, or to receive a fitting return for work done for others.
senses.note: In the parables of the talents and the minas the servant calls his master a hard man who reaps where he did not sow; in 1 Corinthians 9 Paul argues that those who sowed spiritual things may rightly reap material support.

senses.label: Gather people into the kingdom (mission harvest)
senses.definition: To bring in those whom God has made ready to believe, so that the reaper shares in the fruit of others' earlier sowing.
senses.note: Jesus applies the proverb 'one sows and another reaps' to the disciples entering into the work of those who went before them in Samaria.

senses.label: Harvest of the earth (eschatological judgment)
senses.definition: God's final gathering of humanity at the end of the age, pictured as reaping a ripe crop with a sickle.
senses.note: The imagery draws on Joel 3:13 (put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb only figuratively, in the moral law of sowing and reaping: what a person sows determines what he reaps, whether corruption or eternal life, sparing or generous returns, or rightful material support for gospel workers.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In the Gospel the harvest is present and missionary: the fields are already white and the reaper is already gathering fruit for eternal life. In Revelation the harvest is future and judicial, the reaping of the whole earth.

background.note: Classical Greek used the verb for reaping grain and already paired it metaphorically with sowing: Gorgias rebukes someone who 'sowed shamefully and reaped wretchedly.'
Papyri use it in agricultural contracts and disputes, e.g. a farmer petitioning that others not be allowed to reap the crop until his case is decided.
In the Greek Old Testament it chiefly renders Hebrew qatsar, 'to harvest', for the reaping of grain fields.

study.exegesisTip: Watch for θερίζω paired with σπείρω (sow): wherever the two appear together the writer is drawing on a proverbial principle, and the point lies in how the sowing and the reaping correspond, whether in kind (flesh/corruption, Spirit/life) or in measure (sparingly/bountifully).

study.summary: καθίστημι is a causative verb meaning 'to set down, put in place'. In the NT it means chiefly 'to appoint' someone to an office or put someone in charge, 'to make or constitute' someone something, and in the passive 'to be made, become, be rendered'. Once it means simply 'to conduct, bring' a person to a place.

senses.label: Put in charge of
senses.definition: To place someone over a household, possessions or a task with responsibility for it, typically with ἐπί.
senses.note: In the parables the faithful servant who has been set over the household is rewarded by being set over all his master's possessions.

senses.label: Appoint to an office
senses.definition: To install someone formally in a position of service or leadership, such as elders, deacons-to-be, or priests.
senses.note: Hebrews uses the verb for the appointment of high priests, whether under the Law or, by the oath, the Son.

senses.label: Make someone something (constitute as)
senses.definition: With a double accusative, to make someone ruler, judge or governor, that is, to give him that status.
senses.note: 'Who made you a ruler and a judge over us?' (Exodus 2:14) questions Moses' authority, and Jesus' 'Who made me a judge?' uses the same idiom.

senses.label: Be made, become, be rendered (passive)
senses.definition: To be brought into a certain condition or standing, or to put oneself into it.
senses.note: Paul says the many were made sinners through Adam and will be made righteous through Christ; 2 Peter says the virtues keep believers from being rendered useless or unfruitful. James uses the same passive of the tongue and of the world's friend who makes himself God's enemy.

senses.label: Conduct, bring
senses.definition: To escort someone to a destination.
senses.note: Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens; this plain sense is common in the papyri.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the verb as a technical term for the appointment of high priests: every high priest is appointed for people in matters pertaining to God, and the Law appoints weak men while the oath appoints the Son, perfected forever.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In Romans 5:19 the passive describes the status into which Adam's disobedience and Christ's obedience bring 'the many': made sinners, made righteous.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'appoint', 'put in charge', 'make' and 'ordain' (KJV) because the verb covers both formal installation in office and simply causing someone to have a role or status. In Romans 5:19 'made sinners/made righteous' and 'constituted sinners/righteous' both try to render a passive that describes a standing brought about by another.

background.note: Its basic classical meaning is literal, 'set down, place', as of setting down a mixing bowl in Homer.
In the papyri it is the normal word for appointing officials and guardians (e.g. 'I have appointed Isocrates as scribe'), and is also used technically of bringing someone before a judge.
The LXX uses it for many Hebrew verbs of appointing and setting, most often paqad, 'to appoint, set over', as when Pharaoh's officer set Joseph over his household.

study.exegesisTip: Notice who does the appointing. In the parables it is the master, in Acts the apostles, in Titus Paul's delegate, and in Hebrews the Law or God's oath. The verb puts the stress on the authority that confers the position, not on the person's own claim to it.
study.caution: Romans 5:19 is debated: some read 'were made sinners' forensically (counted or treated as sinners on account of Adam), others as describing the actual condition of sinfulness that resulted. The verb itself can carry either nuance, so the decision rests on the argument of Romans 5:12–21 as a whole.

study.summary: κἀκεῖνος is a contraction of καί + ἐκεῖνος, 'and that one' or 'that one too'. It links a new statement to a person or thing already mentioned, either simply continuing the account ('and he') or adding someone to what was said of another ('he also, they too').

senses.label: And he/she/they (narrative connective)
senses.definition: Continues the account with a new action by someone already named, much like 'and he' or 'and that one'.
senses.note: In the parable of the tenants each new servant is introduced and then 'him too' they beat or killed, building the pattern of rejection.

senses.label: He too, they also (additive)
senses.definition: Extends what was said of one person or group to another: 'that one as well'.
senses.note: Jesus' 'other sheep' must also be brought; the one who feeds on him will also live because of him; the one who believes will also do the works he does.

senses.label: Just as they did (comparison)
senses.definition: In comparisons with καθώς or a similar word, points back to another group as the pattern: 'as they also did'.
senses.note: Israel in the wilderness serves as the comparison: they craved evil things; they too had good news proclaimed to them; we are saved in the same way as they.

senses.label: That one (emphatic resumption)
senses.definition: Picks up a subject already named and lays stress on it: 'and it is that which', 'and he is the one who'.
senses.note: 'What comes out of the mouth comes from the heart, and those things defile a person'; 'if we deny him, he also will deny us.'

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John favors the word for parallels between Jesus and his disciples or between Father and Son: as Jesus lives because of the Father, the one who feeds on him will also live; believers will also do his works; he wants them also to be with him.

study.exegesisTip: Because the word combines 'and' with a demonstrative, the main interpretive question is usually its antecedent. Ask who 'that one' points back to, and whether καί means simply 'and' or 'also, too'. The second makes the sentence a deliberate parallel.
study.caution: In John 19:35 ('and that one knows he is telling the truth') the referent is disputed: it may be the eyewitness himself, the evangelist vouching for him, or Christ (or God) as guarantor of the testimony. The grammar alone does not settle it.

study.summary: λατρεύω originally meant to work for hire or to serve, but in biblical Greek it is always religious: to serve or worship God (or, in a bad sense, false gods). It covers both cultic service in the sanctuary and the whole of a life devoted to God, and the NT uses it for Christian worship as the true service of God.

senses.label: Serve/worship the true God
senses.definition: To render religious service and devotion to God, as his servant and worshipper.
senses.note: Jesus answers Satan with Deuteronomy 6:13: worship the Lord your God and serve him only, joining προσκυνέω and λατρεύω.

senses.label: Worship idols or created things
senses.definition: To give religious service to false gods or created things in place of the Creator.
senses.note: Stephen recalls that God gave Israel over to serve the host of heaven; Paul says humans worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator.

senses.label: Perform sanctuary service (priestly worship)
senses.definition: To carry out the cultic worship of the tabernacle or temple; the participle means 'the worshipper'.
senses.note: Hebrews contrasts those who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things with the access Christ has opened.

senses.label: Devoted life of worship
senses.definition: A whole life given over to God in prayer, fasting and earnest devotion.
senses.note: Anna served God with fasting and prayer night and day; the twelve tribes earnestly serve God night and day in hope of the promise.

senses.label: Spiritual, new-covenant worship
senses.definition: Worship rendered in the Spirit and with a purified conscience, through Christ, rather than through external rites.
senses.note: Paul's gospel ministry is itself the service he renders God in his spirit.

senses.label: Heavenly, eschatological worship
senses.definition: The unending service of God's people before his throne in the new creation.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the verb for the old-covenant cult (worshippers who serve a shadow and whose conscience is never cleansed) and then claims it for Christians, whose consciences Christ's blood cleanses to serve the living God acceptably with reverence and awe.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul turns the cultic verb inward and toward mission: he serves God in his spirit in the gospel, with a clean conscience, and believers are the true circumcision who worship by the Spirit of God, while idolaters serve the creature.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke presents devout Jewish service of God (Zechariah's hope, Anna, the twelve tribes) as continuous with the faith Paul professes, who serves the God of the fathers.

study.translationNote: Versions alternate between 'serve' and 'worship' for the same verb (e.g. Revelation 22:3, Hebrews 12:28). The Greek does not distinguish the two: in biblical usage λατρεύω is service that is itself worship, so either English word captures only half of it.

background.note: In classical Greek the word meant to work for hire or pay, or to be in servitude, and only secondarily to serve the gods.
Sophocles uses it of being subject or enslaved to someone.

The LXX reserves it for the worship of God or of other gods, chiefly translating Hebrew 'avad, as in God's purpose that Israel would serve him on this mountain; ordinary servitude is rendered by δουλεύω instead.

study.exegesisTip: Compare λατρεύω with λειτουργέω and δουλεύω. λειτουργέω tends toward official or priestly ministry and δουλεύω toward a slave's subjection; λατρεύω is religious service offered to a deity. When the NT applies it to prayer, ministry or the whole life of believers, it is deliberately transferring temple language to the people of God.
study.caution: In Philippians 3:3 the manuscripts differ: most read 'who worship by the Spirit of God', some 'who worship God in the Spirit'. The difference affects whether the Spirit is the means or the object of worship is stated.

study.summary: μηκέτι means 'no longer, no more, not again'. It is the form of 'no longer' used with the negative μή, in commands, prohibitions, wishes, purpose clauses, infinitives and participles. Its typical NT use marks a decisive break: something that was true or habitual must now stop.

senses.label: Stop doing (commands and prohibitions)
senses.definition: With an imperative or subjunctive, forbids continuing an action already going on: 'no longer do this'.
senses.note: 'Sin no more' (John 5:14); 'let the thief no longer steal' (Ephesians 4:28).

senses.label: No longer (the break of the new life)
senses.definition: In purpose clauses or infinitives, describes the former way of life that the work of Christ ends.
senses.note: Christ died so that those who live might no longer live for themselves (2 Corinthians 5:15).

senses.label: No longer able (changed circumstances)
senses.definition: With an infinitive or participle, states that a situation has changed so that something is no longer possible or bearable.
senses.note: 'When we could bear it no longer' (1 Thessalonians 3:1); 'having no more room in these regions' (Romans 15:23).

senses.label: Never again (wish or curse)
senses.definition: Expresses that something should not happen ever again.
senses.note: Jesus' word to the fig tree; Christ raised from the dead 'no more to return to corruption'.

senses.label: Not any longer (reported commands and demands)
senses.definition: In indirect speech, reports an order or demand that someone stop or no longer do something.
senses.note: The council threatened the apostles to speak no more in Jesus' name; the crowd cried that Paul ought not to live any longer.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word to mark the boundary between the old life and the new: no longer enslaved to sin, no longer living for oneself, no longer infants tossed by every wind, no longer walking as the Gentiles do, no longer stealing.

background.note: The word goes back to Homer and Hesiod with the same meaning, 'no more, no longer'.
A second-century letter uses the same purpose construction as Paul (ἵνα μηκέτι): 'you say this so that I may no longer be believed'.

study.exegesisTip: μηκέτι and οὐκέτι both mean 'no longer'. The choice is mostly grammatical (μή-negatives go with commands, subjunctives, infinitives and participles), so the word does not by itself make a statement softer or stronger. Its force comes from the contrast it implies with what used to be.
study.caution: It is often said that μή with a present imperative always means 'stop doing what you are doing'. That is not reliable; in 1 Timothy 5:23 the 'stop' sense comes from the ἔτι ('any longer') built into μηκέτι, which is why Paul needed it.

study.summary: μνημονεύω means 'to remember, call to mind'. In the NT, remembering is rarely just mental recall: it usually means remembering so as to act, whether to take warning, to persevere, to imitate, or to care for someone. Occasionally it means 'to mention'.

senses.label: Recall, call to mind
senses.definition: To bring past events or words back to memory.
senses.note: Jesus rebukes the disciples' failure to remember the feeding miracles; the woman in labor no longer remembers her anguish for joy.

senses.label: Remember and take warning (heed)
senses.definition: To keep something in mind so that it shapes present conduct, often as a warning or call to repentance.
senses.note: 'Remember Lot's wife'; 'Remember from where you have fallen, and repent'.

senses.label: Remember with care or loyalty
senses.definition: To be mindful of people in a way that leads to support, prayer, imitation or faithfulness.
senses.note: Remembering the poor means caring for them in practice; remembering one's leaders leads to imitating their faith.

senses.label: God remembers sins (for judgment)
senses.definition: God keeps wrongdoing in view in order to judge it.
senses.note: Babylon's sins have piled up to heaven and God has remembered her iniquities.

senses.label: Mention, make mention of
senses.definition: To speak of something or call it to attention.
senses.note: Joseph, at his death, made mention of the exodus of Israel.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's 'remember' is relational and practical: remember the poor, remember my chains, remember Jesus Christ raised from the dead, remember what you once were as Gentiles. He also remembers the Thessalonians' work of faith before God.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In the Gospel Jesus speaks so that the disciples will remember his words when persecution comes; in Revelation the risen Christ calls lapsing churches to remember what they received and repent.

background.note: From Herodotus and the tragedians onward it means to call to mind or remember.
An honorary inscription praises a people for always remembering its benefactors, both living and dead, a close parallel to the call to remember one's leaders.
In a court record one party says 'I do not remember what took place in the negotiation' and is answered 'Do you not then remember?'

study.exegesisTip: In biblical thought remembering is active, not merely mental. When a command says 'remember', ask what action the remembering is meant to produce: repentance, endurance, generosity, imitation or worship.
study.caution: In Hebrews 11:15 the verb is usually rendered 'if they had been thinking of (remembering) the land they left', but some take it as 'if they had been making mention of'. The genitive construction allows either.

study.summary: νηστεύω means 'to fast', to go without food (often also drink) for a period, usually for religious reasons such as humility, mourning, repentance or seeking God. All NT uses come from the Gospels and Acts, where Jesus fasts, teaches how to fast, explains why his disciples did not fast while he was with them, and the early church fasts when seeking God's direction.

senses.label: Go without food (literal fast)
senses.definition: To abstain from eating for a set time.
senses.note: Jesus' forty-day fast in the wilderness recalls Moses and Elijah and Israel's forty years of testing.

senses.label: Fasting as regular Jewish piety
senses.definition: Fasting as an established discipline of devout groups, practiced at set times.
senses.note: The Pharisee in the parable boasts of fasting twice a week, more than the Law required.

senses.label: Fasting before God, not for show
senses.definition: Fasting done in secret as an act toward the Father, not to gain a reputation for piety.
senses.note: Jesus assumes his followers will fast ('when you fast') but forbids performing it for an audience.

senses.label: Fasting and the bridegroom's presence
senses.definition: Fasting as mourning, inappropriate while Jesus the bridegroom is present but fitting after he is taken away.
senses.note: The saying treats Jesus' presence as a wedding celebration; fasting returns in the church's life after his departure.

senses.label: Fasting with prayer in the church
senses.definition: Fasting together with prayer while worshipping and seeking God's guidance, especially before sending out workers.
senses.note: The Antioch church was worshipping and fasting when the Spirit set apart Barnabas and Saul, and they fasted and prayed before laying hands on them.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke shows fasting continuing among Jesus' followers after his departure, as the bridegroom saying anticipated: the church at Antioch fasts while worshipping and again before commissioning missionaries.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew places fasting alongside almsgiving and prayer as the three acts of piety to be done before the Father who sees in secret.

background.note: Classical writers use the word for ordinary fasting, as in Aristophanes.
Empedocles uses it figuratively with a genitive: to 'fast from wickedness'.
A papyrus fragment of sayings attributed to Jesus has 'unless you fast to the world, you will not find the kingdom of God', using the same figurative construction.

study.exegesisTip: In the Gospels the question is not whether fasting is good but when and how: not for show (Matthew 6), and not while the bridegroom is present (Mark 2). Read each passage for what it says about the timing and motive of fasting in relation to Jesus.
study.caution: Manuscripts differ on several references to fasting. In Acts 10:30 Cornelius' 'fasting' is found in the Byzantine text but not in many early manuscripts, and similar additions of fasting appear in some manuscripts elsewhere. Build no doctrine on a reading the manuscripts do not share.

study.summary: χιλίαρχος literally means 'commander of a thousand'. In the NT it usually refers to a Roman military tribune, the officer commanding a cohort, most often the commander of the Jerusalem garrison who arrested and protected Paul. More generally it denotes high-ranking military officers.

senses.label: Roman tribune, cohort commander
senses.definition: The Roman military tribune in command of a cohort, nominally a thousand men, such as the garrison commander in Jerusalem.
senses.note: Acts names this officer as Lysias. He rescues Paul from the mob, prepares to examine him by flogging, discovers Paul is a Roman citizen by birth (having bought his own citizenship), and sends him under guard to Caesarea.

senses.label: Commander at Jesus' arrest
senses.definition: The officer in charge of the cohort that came with the temple police to arrest Jesus.

senses.label: High military officers generally
senses.definition: Senior military commanders as a class of powerful people, alongside nobles, kings and the rich.
senses.note: Herod's birthday guests included his military commanders; in Revelation commanders appear among the mighty of the earth who flee and fall in God's judgment.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Almost all occurrences are in Acts 21–25, where the tribune is a key figure: his intervention repeatedly saves Paul's life and, as Luke tells it, he finds no charge against Paul deserving death or chains.

study.translationNote: Versions render it 'chief captain' (KJV), 'commander', 'tribune' or 'commanding officer'. 'Tribune' is the precise Roman title; 'commander of a thousand' is the literal Greek sense, used in the Septuagint for Israel's officers over thousands.

background.note: Classical Greek used it for a captain over a thousand men, already in Aeschylus.
Xenophon uses it especially of the commandant of a garrison.
Inscriptions use it as the Greek equivalent of the Roman tribunus militum, as in 'tribune of a legion'.

study.exegesisTip: Follow the tribune through Acts 21–23 as a single character: Luke uses this Roman official's actions and letter to show that Roman authority found Paul innocent and protected him from his accusers.
study.caution: John 18:12 mentions a cohort (σπεῖρα) and its tribune at Jesus' arrest. Interpreters disagree whether John means Roman soldiers took part or uses the military terms loosely for Jewish temple forces; the vocabulary itself is Roman.

study.summary: αἰτία means 'cause, reason', and in legal settings 'charge, accusation' or 'ground for a charge', the crime for which someone is held responsible. In the passion narratives and Acts it repeatedly marks the innocence of Jesus and Paul: officials find no αἰτία in them.

senses.label: Reason, cause
senses.definition: The reason or motive for something; often in the phrases 'for this reason' (δι᾽ ἣν αἰτίαν) and 'for what reason'.
senses.note: Paul's 'for which reason' (2 Timothy 1:6, 12) and 'for this reason' (Titus 1:13) are standard connective formulas.

senses.label: Ground (for divorce)
senses.definition: A legally valid ground or justification for an action.
senses.note: 'Is it lawful to divorce one's wife for any cause?' reflects contemporary Jewish debate over what counted as grounds for divorce.

senses.label: Case, situation
senses.definition: The state of affairs or relationship in question.
senses.note: 'If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry.'

senses.label: Charge, accusation
senses.definition: The formal accusation brought against someone in court, true or false.
senses.note: The inscription on the cross stated Jesus' 'charge': the King of the Jews.

senses.label: Ground for guilt, crime
senses.definition: A cause for punishment; a crime that would justify a sentence.
senses.note: Pilate's thrice-repeated 'I find no αἰτία in him' declares that there is no basis for a sentence.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John has Pilate say three times that he finds no ground for a charge against Jesus, making the Roman judge a witness to Jesus' innocence.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the legal sense to show that Jesus and Paul alike were innocent: though they found no cause for death in Jesus they asked for his execution, and the Romans found no cause of death in Paul.

study.translationNote: The same word is rendered 'cause', 'reason', 'charge', 'accusation', 'crime', 'fault' or 'basis for a charge' depending on context. In the trial scenes, 'I find no fault/no crime/no basis for a charge' are different ways of rendering one legal phrase: there is nothing to justify a sentence.

background.note: Classical Greek used it mainly for responsibility in a bad sense, blame or guilt, and so for an accusation, from Pindar and Herodotus onward.
The papyri show the forensic use: an official 'was sent to Alexandria to meet a charge'.
It also appears in the everyday sense of blame ('lest you be blamed') and in the common phrase 'for this reason'.

study.exegesisTip: In trial scenes, distinguish αἰτία as the accusation brought (what the accusers allege) from αἰτία as the ground for guilt (what the judge must find). Pilate's and Festus' statements turn on the second: the accusations exist, but the basis for a sentence does not.

study.summary: ἀκροβυστία means 'foreskin', and so 'uncircumcision', the state of being uncircumcised, and collectively 'the uncircumcised', the Gentiles. Almost all uses are in Paul, who uses the word to argue that physical circumcision or its lack counts for nothing before God; what matters is faith, a new creation and keeping God's commands.

senses.label: Foreskin; physical uncircumcision
senses.definition: The foreskin, or the bodily state of not being circumcised.
senses.note: 'Men having foreskin' (Acts 11:3) is a blunt Jewish way of saying Gentiles. Abraham was counted righteous while still in uncircumcision.

senses.label: The uncircumcised (Gentiles)
senses.definition: Collectively, Gentiles as distinct from Jews, 'the circumcision'.
senses.note: Paul was entrusted with the gospel 'of the uncircumcision' as Peter with that 'of the circumcision'. Ephesians notes Gentiles were 'called uncircumcision' by others, a label used by Jews.

senses.label: Covenant status reversed
senses.definition: Uncircumcision considered in relation to keeping the Law: a lawbreaking Jew's circumcision becomes uncircumcision, and a law-keeping Gentile's uncircumcision is reckoned as circumcision.

senses.label: Of no account in Christ
senses.definition: In formulas that set circumcision and uncircumcision aside as irrelevant to standing before God.
senses.note: What counts instead is keeping God's commands, faith working through love, and a new creation.

senses.label: Spiritual uncircumcision
senses.definition: Figuratively, the state of being outside God's covenant and alienated from him, the condition before new life in Christ.
senses.note: 'Dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh', answered by the circumcision made without hands in Christ.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word nineteen times, always in tension with περιτομή (circumcision). His argument moves from the body to the covenant: Abraham was justified while uncircumcised, so he is the father of uncircumcised believers, and in Christ neither state counts.

study.translationNote: English versions alternate between 'uncircumcision' (the state), 'the uncircumcised' (the people) and sometimes 'Gentiles', because the Greek word does all three. Older versions keep the physical term; some modern versions paraphrase Colossians 2:13 as 'sinful nature' rather than 'uncircumcision of the flesh'.

background.note: The LXX uses it for the foreskin in the covenant of circumcision given to Abraham, translating Hebrew 'orlah.
The ordinary Greek medical term was ἀκροποσθία, found in Hippocrates; ἀκροβυστία appears to be a Jewish-Greek alteration of it, perhaps to avoid a vulgar word.

study.exegesisTip: Read ἀκροβυστία together with its partner περιτομή in each passage and ask whether Paul means the physical rite, the ethnic group, or covenant standing. His arguments often shift between these within a few verses, as in Romans 2 and 4.
study.caution: The word's formation is uncertain. Some derive it from ἄκρος plus a Semitic word associated with shame; others see an alteration of ἀκροποσθία modeled on a rare Greek word. No interpretive weight should rest on either etymology.

study.summary: Dust, especially the dust of a town clinging to travellers' feet, which Jesus' messengers shook off as a solemn testimony against those who rejected them.

senses.label: Dust shaken off in testimony
senses.definition: The dust of a town on the feet, shaken or wiped off as a symbolic act disowning a place that refuses the message, leaving it answerable to God.

senses.label: Dust thrown in protest
senses.definition: Dust flung into the air by an enraged crowd as a sign of violent protest.

background.note: Classical writers use the word for a cloud of dust stirred up, as by a moving army.

study.exegesisTip: Shaking off the dust (MAT 10:14; ACT 13:51) was a public gesture separating the messengers from the town's guilt; LUK 9:5 calls it 'a testimony against them'.

study.summary: The edge or tassel of a garment, in the Gospels the tassel that the Law required Israelites to wear on the corners of the outer cloak.

senses.label: Tassel of Jesus' cloak
senses.definition: The fringe or tassel of Jesus' outer garment, which the sick touched in faith to be healed.
senses.note: The required tassels (Num 15:38-39) marked Jesus as a Law-observant Jew.

senses.label: Tassels enlarged for display
senses.definition: The tassels on the garments of scribes and Pharisees, lengthened to make their piety conspicuous.

study.translationNote: Older versions say 'hem' or 'border'; many modern versions say 'fringe' or 'tassel', reflecting the Jewish tassels of Num 15:38 rather than a simple edge of cloth.

background.note: In the Greek OT it renders the Hebrew word for the commanded tassels on the corners of garments.

study.summary: To encircle or surround, whether people gathering round someone, an army besieging a city, or Israel marching round Jericho.

senses.label: Gather round a person
senses.definition: To form a ring around someone, whether in hostile pressure or in protective concern.

senses.label: Surround, besiege a place
senses.definition: To encircle a city or camp militarily, or to march around it.

background.note: In the Greek OT it chiefly renders Hebrew sabab, 'go around, surround', including the circling of Jericho (Josh 6).

study.summary: A wave of the sea, used of storm waves battering boats and ships, and figuratively of godless people as wild, foaming waves.

senses.label: Waves of the sea
senses.definition: Literal waves, especially storm-driven waves that swamp a boat or break up a ship.

senses.label: Wild waves, figurative
senses.definition: An image of ungodly teachers: restless and uncontrolled, throwing up their shameful deeds like foam on the shore.

background.note: From Homer on it is the ordinary word for a wave or billow of the sea or a river.

study.exegesisTip: Jude's image echoes Isa 57:20, where the wicked are like the tossing sea casting up mire and mud.

study.summary: A dog, a despised scavenging animal in the biblical world, and so a term of contempt for people who are unclean or hostile to what is holy.

senses.label: Literal dog
senses.definition: A dog, here the scavenging street dog, as in the dogs licking Lazarus's sores and the proverb of the dog returning to its vomit.

senses.label: Term of contempt
senses.definition: A metaphor of reproach for those who are impure, hostile, or unfit for holy things: those who would profane what is sacred, Paul's opponents, and those excluded from the holy city.
senses.note: In PHP 3:2 Paul turns on his opponents a label Jews sometimes used for unclean Gentiles.

background.note: A soldier's letter complains that his mother has abandoned him like a dog, showing the word's use as an image of contemptuous treatment.

study.summary: Service rendered to God, worship, whether the priestly rites of Israel's sanctuary or the whole-life worship of believers.

senses.label: Israel's sanctuary worship
senses.definition: The divinely ordained worship and priestly rites of the tabernacle and temple, one of Israel's privileges.

senses.label: Service offered to God
senses.definition: Any act regarded as worship or service to God: tragically, the killing of disciples thought to please God, or believers' offering of their whole selves.

study.translationNote: In ROM 12:1 versions vary between 'spiritual worship', 'reasonable service' and 'true and proper worship', because the adjective logikos can mean rational, spiritual, or fitting.

background.note: In the Greek OT it is always used of divine service, rendering Hebrew 'abodah, e.g. the Passover rite.
Plato already uses it for service to the gods.

study.summary: A public servant or minister, used of those who serve God in an official, often priestly, capacity, and of one who serves another's needs.

senses.label: Servant in God's service
senses.definition: One appointed to serve God: civil authorities as his servants, angels as his ministers, and Paul as a priestly minister of Christ to the Gentiles.

senses.label: Priestly minister of sanctuary
senses.definition: Christ as the officiating minister in the true, heavenly sanctuary.

senses.label: One who ministers to needs
senses.definition: A representative who serves someone's practical needs on behalf of others, as Epaphroditus did for Paul.

background.note: In Ptolemaic papyri the word often means simply a workman, alongside builders.

study.exegesisTip: In ROM 15:16 the surrounding priestly language (offering, sanctified) shows Paul presents his mission as a priestly service.

study.summary: A winepress, the trough in which grapes were trodden, used literally in a parable and figuratively of God's wrath in Revelation.

senses.label: Winepress in a vineyard
senses.definition: The vat or trough cut into the rock for treading grapes, part of a vineyard's equipment.

senses.label: Winepress of God's wrath
senses.definition: A picture of final judgment, where the wicked are crushed like grapes underfoot.

background.note: Leases speak of wine to be delivered 'at the vat', new and unadulterated.

study.exegesisTip: Revelation draws on Isa 63:1-6 and Joel 3:13, where treading the winepress pictures the Lord's judgment on the nations.

study.summary: To be mad or out of one's mind, used as an accusation against Jesus, Rhoda, Paul, and Christians speaking in tongues.

senses.label: Be insane, out of mind
senses.definition: To rave or be mad, said dismissively of someone whose words or behaviour seem irrational to the hearers.

background.note: An account of a trial before an emperor offers a close parallel to Paul before Festus: the accused replies that he is neither mad nor beside himself.

study.summary: Manna, the food God gave Israel in the wilderness, recalled by Jesus as a type of himself and promised as hidden manna to the victorious.

senses.label: Wilderness food of Israel
senses.definition: The bread from heaven that fed Israel in the desert, which Jesus contrasts with himself as the bread that gives eternal life; a jar of it was kept in the ark.

senses.label: Hidden manna, symbolic
senses.definition: A symbol of the heavenly sustenance and life that Christ gives to the one who overcomes.

background.note: The Greek OT transliterates the Hebrew man for the wilderness food.

study.summary: To affirm solemnly as before witnesses, or to charge and urge someone earnestly.

senses.label: Solemnly declare, testify
senses.definition: To assert something with the weight of a sworn declaration.

senses.label: Solemnly charge, urge
senses.definition: To insist or exhort earnestly, as though calling God to witness.

senses.label: Bear witness to people
senses.definition: To testify publicly to small and great alike about God's purposes.

background.note: Papyri show the original sense 'call to witness' passing into 'swear, asseverate' and also 'testify to'.

study.caution: Lightfoot held the verb never simply means 'bear witness' in the NT, but Koine papyri show that sense; readings of ACT 26:22 differ accordingly.

study.summary: To move from one place or state to another: to remove, transfer, depose, or lead people away from their allegiance.

senses.label: Remove, depose
senses.definition: To remove someone from an office or position, as a steward from management or God removing Saul from kingship.

senses.label: Move, transfer
senses.definition: To relocate physically, as moving mountains, or to transfer believers from the dominion of darkness into Christ's kingdom.

senses.label: Turn away, mislead
senses.definition: To lead people away from their former beliefs, as Paul was accused of drawing crowds away from the gods.

background.note: Used in leases for removing from a tenancy, and in inscriptions as a formula for death.

study.exegesisTip: COL 1:13 may evoke the ancient practice of transferring whole populations from one realm to another.

study.summary: A part or share, especially one's portion in something valuable, and once a district or administrative division of a region.

senses.label: Share, portion
senses.definition: One's allotted portion or part in something, such as the good portion Mary chose, the saints' inheritance, or a share in the gospel ministry.

senses.label: Common part, fellowship
senses.definition: What one has in common with another; in a rhetorical question it denies any shared part between believer and unbeliever.

senses.label: District of a region
senses.definition: A geographical or administrative division of a province.

study.translationNote: In ACT 16:12 versions differ ('leading city of the district', 'chief city of that part'), partly because of a textual variant about Philippi's rank.

background.note: Papyri use it for administrative divisions of a nome, supporting its geographical sense in ACT 16:12.
In the Greek OT it chiefly renders Hebrew heleq, 'portion', as in the Lord being the Levites' portion.

study.summary: To give a share of something, impart, whether material goods to the needy or spiritual gifts and one's own life.

senses.label: Share material goods
senses.definition: To give part of one's possessions to those in need, generously and without ulterior motive.

senses.label: Impart spiritual blessing
senses.definition: To bestow something spiritual, such as a gift of the Spirit, or the gospel together with oneself.

background.note: Classical Greek uses it for giving someone a share in something, such as land or political rights.

study.summary: To receive a share of, partake of, especially food or blessing; with an accusative, to obtain or find (an opportunity).

senses.label: Partake of food
senses.definition: To take one's share of food, to eat.

senses.label: Share in a benefit
senses.definition: To receive a portion of something good: the farmer's share of the crop, the land's blessing, God's holiness.

senses.label: Obtain an opportunity
senses.definition: To get or find, as Felix said he would call Paul when he found a convenient time.

background.note: The genitive construction with food, as in ACT 2:46, occurs in the papyri.

study.summary: To change the outward form or appearance of something, whether disguise, true transformation, or applying a lesson by a figure of speech.

senses.label: Disguise oneself as
senses.definition: To assume a false appearance, as Satan and his servants masquerade as an angel of light and servants of righteousness.

senses.label: Transform the body
senses.definition: To change the form of believers' lowly bodies to conform to Christ's glorious body.
