'Trial' stresses outward hardship; 'temptation' stresses inner enticement to sin.

background.note: The Greek Old Testament uses the word of the great 'trials' God displayed in bringing Israel out of Egypt.
Sirach says Abraham was found faithful when tested, a classic example of trial as the proving of loyalty.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who is behind the test and what it aims at. When God permits a test it aims to prove and strengthen faith; when the devil or desire is the source it aims at a fall. The same Greek word covers both, so the context decides.
study.caution: The petition in the Lord's Prayer is debated: some take it as an everyday plea to be kept from temptation, others as a prayer to be spared the final eschatological trial. Both readings have defenders.

study.summary: σκηνή is a tent or booth, a temporary dwelling. In the New Testament it most often refers to the wilderness tabernacle (its compartments and its heavenly original), especially in Hebrews; it can also mean temporary shelters, God's dwelling with his people, and figuratively the 'house' of David.

senses.label: Tent, booth, shelter
senses.definition: A temporary dwelling made of cloth, skins or branches.
senses.note: Abraham and the patriarchs lived in tents as strangers in the promised land.

senses.label: The Mosaic tabernacle
senses.definition: The portable sanctuary Israel built in the wilderness, 'the tent of witness'.

senses.label: A compartment of the tabernacle
senses.definition: In Hebrews, the 'first' (outer) tent and the 'second' (inner) tent, the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place.

senses.label: The heavenly tabernacle
senses.definition: The true sanctuary set up by the Lord, of which the earthly tent was a copy, where Christ ministers.

senses.label: God's dwelling with people
senses.definition: God's presence living among his people, and the eternal dwellings of the faithful.
senses.note: 'The dwelling of God is with men' fulfils the tabernacle's promise of God living among his people.

senses.label: Figurative house or shrine
senses.definition: The fallen 'tent' of David, his royal house or dynasty, and the portable shrine of a pagan god.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Half the New Testament uses are in Hebrews, which argues from the layout and rituals of the wilderness tabernacle that the earthly tent was a copy and shadow of the true heavenly sanctuary, where Christ has entered once for all.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation speaks of God's tabernacle in heaven and climaxes with the announcement that God's tabernacle is with humankind, using the same image as the related verb for the Word who 'tabernacled' among us in John's Gospel.

study.translationNote: Versions use 'tabernacle', 'tent', 'sanctuary', 'shelter', 'booth' or 'dwelling'. All render the same word; 'tabernacle' is used when the sacred tent is in view, but it hides the simple, temporary character of a tent.

background.note: In classical Greek it is a tent or booth, as of soldiers or of an encampment.
A Zenon letter mentions a leather tent, typical of everyday use for temporary shelters.

study.exegesisTip: In Hebrews 9 track which 'tent' is meant: the whole tabernacle, the outer 'first' tent, the inner 'second' tent, or the 'greater and more perfect tent'. The argument turns on these distinctions.
study.caution: In Hebrews 9:8 scholars debate whether 'the first tent' means the outer compartment or the earthly tabernacle (and the old covenant order) as a whole. Whether Peter's proposed booths at the Transfiguration allude to the Feast of Tabernacles is also uncertain.

study.summary: τοσοῦτος is a demonstrative of quantity, 'so great, so much', plural 'so many', and of time 'so long'. It often stresses how remarkable an amount or degree is, and it pairs with ὅσος in comparisons of degree ('as much as..., so much...').

senses.label: So great
senses.definition: Of size or degree, emphasising how remarkable something is.
senses.note: Jesus had not found 'such great faith' in Israel as in the centurion.

senses.label: So many
senses.definition: In the plural, of number.
senses.note: John notes that despite 'so many signs' they did not believe, and that the net was not torn although there were so many fish.

senses.label: So long
senses.definition: Of time, a long duration.
senses.note: 'Have I been with you so long, and you do not know me, Philip?'

senses.label: For so much
senses.definition: In the genitive, a price: 'for such an amount'.

senses.label: By so much (comparison)
senses.definition: Correlated with ὅσος or καθ' ὅσον to express proportion: 'by as much as..., by so much'.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the word in proportional comparisons to measure Christ's superiority: he became 'so much better than the angels' and the guarantor of 'so much better a covenant'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John's Gospel the word highlights culpable unbelief and divine abundance: so many signs, so long with Jesus, so many fish.

background.note: In classical prose it is often answered by the relative ὅσος, 'as great as...', the same correlation found in Hebrews.
A papyrus letter uses it of time: 'so long a time having elapsed'.

study.summary: τρέχω means to run. In the Gospels it describes the hurried movements of people around Jesus, especially on Easter morning. Paul and Hebrews take it from the athletic stadium as a picture of the Christian life and of apostolic labour, and in 2 Thessalonians the word of the Lord itself 'runs'.

senses.label: Run (literally)
senses.definition: To move quickly on foot, often expressing urgency, eagerness or joy.
senses.note: The father who runs to meet the prodigal son abandons dignity for compassion.

senses.label: Run a race
senses.definition: Athletic running as a picture of disciplined, purposeful Christian living aimed at the prize.

senses.label: Strive, labour
senses.definition: Exert oneself toward a goal, especially in Paul's apostolic work, which he hopes will not prove to have been 'in vain'.

senses.label: Human striving
senses.definition: Human effort set in contrast to God's sovereign mercy.
senses.note: 'It does not depend on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy.'

senses.label: Spread swiftly
senses.definition: Of the word of the Lord, to advance rapidly and freely.

senses.label: Rush (in battle)
senses.definition: Of horses and chariots charging into battle.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Half the uses are Paul's, who draws repeatedly on the stadium: the Christian runs with purpose to win the prize; the Galatians 'were running well' until hindered; Paul fears his own running could prove empty.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's resurrection account depicts Mary Magdalene, Peter and the beloved disciple running to and from the empty tomb, conveying urgency and excitement.

background.note: The verb is used from Homer onward for running.
A report of a trial before the emperor uses it literally ('ran and told his lord') and in the derived sense of pressing on: 'Onward, my son, to death.'

study.exegesisTip: When Paul uses τρέχω, check for other athletic terms nearby (prize, crown, stadium, goal); the metaphor usually controls the whole paragraph.

study.summary: φανερός means visible, plain, evident or known. It describes what is open to view or easily recognised, especially what is brought out of concealment. The New Testament uses it for hidden things being disclosed, for the plainness of God's self-revelation, and in the phrase 'in the open' as the opposite of 'in secret'.

senses.label: Evident, plain
senses.definition: Clearly seen or recognisable, so that it cannot be denied.
senses.note: 'The works of the flesh are evident': they show themselves plainly in conduct.

senses.label: Become known, be disclosed
senses.definition: With γίνομαι or ἔρχομαι, of what was hidden or unrecognised coming into the open.
senses.note: On the last day each person's work will become evident, tested by fire.

senses.label: Recognised, made clear
senses.definition: Shown to be what it is, approved or recognised publicly.
senses.note: Paul's imprisonment became recognised throughout the praetorian guard as being 'in Christ'.

senses.label: Make known
senses.definition: With ποιέω, to make someone publicly known or reveal his identity.
senses.note: Jesus orders the demons and the healed not to make him known.

senses.label: Outward, open (ἐν τῷ φανερῷ)
senses.definition: The phrase 'in the open' as the opposite of 'in secret': what is outward or public.
senses.note: Paul says a true Jew is not one outwardly; circumcision is not what is outward in the flesh.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: For Paul the word belongs to the language of revelation and judgment: what can be known of God is plain, the works of the flesh are evident, the Day will reveal each person's work, and prophecy lays bare the secrets of the heart.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark sets the word within the messianic secret: Jesus forbids being made known, yet insists that nothing hidden will stay hidden, and his name becomes known even to Herod.

study.translationNote: In Matthew 6 many older versions say the Father 'will reward you openly', following manuscripts that read 'in the open'; most modern versions omit 'openly', following earlier manuscripts. In Romans 1:19 'plain in them' may mean 'within them' or 'among them', and versions vary.

background.note: Herodotus uses it of something that can be plainly seen, as the contents of a transparent coffin.
In letters and petitions 'I make it known to you' is a standard formula for informing someone.

study.exegesisTip: Notice the hidden/open pairing that runs through Jesus' sayings and Paul's teaching on judgment: what is now concealed will become φανερός, which is both a warning and a comfort.

study.summary: ἀπώλεια (from ἀπόλλυμι, 'destroy, lose') means destruction, ruin or loss. It can describe something simply wasted, as when the disciples called the anointing at Bethany a 'waste' of perfume, or wealth that perishes. Most NT uses, though, carry the weight of final ruin: the end of the broad road, the fate of God's enemies, set against σωτηρία ('salvation'). The traditional English word is 'perdition'.

senses.label: Waste, loss
senses.definition: Something used up to no purpose or thrown away. This is the everyday, non-theological sense.
senses.note: The onlookers at Bethany judged the costly ointment 'lost' because it had not been sold for the poor.

senses.label: Ruin, perishing (in this life)
senses.definition: The destruction of a person or thing: ruin brought about by greed, by a curse, or by being handed over to enemies.
senses.note: Peter's 'may your silver perish with you' (literally 'be unto destruction') is a solemn curse formula. In 1 Tim 6:9 'ruin and destruction' may already look toward final loss.

senses.label: Final perdition
senses.definition: Eschatological ruin, the loss of eternal life under God's judgment. It is the direct opposite of salvation.
senses.note: PHP 1:28 and HEB 10:39 set ἀπώλεια explicitly against σωτηρία / 'preserving of the soul'.

senses.label: 'Son of perdition'
senses.definition: A Semitic idiom ('son of X' = one belonging to or destined for X) for a person marked out for ruin. It is used of Judas and of the eschatological 'man of lawlessness'.

senses.label: Destructive teaching and its outcome
senses.definition: In 2 Peter, false teachers bring in 'heresies of destruction' (teachings that ruin people) and themselves head for destruction that 'does not slumber'.

senses.label: The beast's destiny
senses.definition: In Revelation the beast 'goes into destruction'. Its apparent power is already moving toward its appointed end.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 2 Peter uses the word more than any other NT book. It ties the false teachers' doctrine, their character and their end together: what they teach destroys, and they will be destroyed on the day of judgment.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses ἀπώλεια as the opposite of salvation. It is the 'end' of the enemies of the cross and the fate of 'vessels of wrath', with God's patience delaying it.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In the Gospel, Judas is the one 'son of perdition' lost from those the Father gave the Son. In Revelation the beast's whole career ends in ἀπώλεια.

study.translationNote: Older versions (KJV) often have 'perdition', 'damnation' or 'pernicious'; modern versions mostly have 'destruction'. In the Bethany story the same word is rightly rendered 'waste'. So the English varies with context, not with any difference in the Greek.

background.note: In classical prose the word means destruction; Aristotle uses it in his ethics.
The Greek Old Testament can use it for a 'thing lost', property that has gone missing.
An astrological papyrus uses the weaker sense: someone will spend and lose possessions he has acquired.
A magical spell orders a demon out and hands it over 'to black chaos in utter destruction'. This is close to the strong sense familiar from the NT.

study.exegesisTip: Look for the opposite term. Where ἀπώλεια stands against σωτηρία or 'life' (the narrow road, PHP 1:28, HEB 10:39), it means final ruin, not merely physical death or loss.
study.caution: The word itself means ruin or loss, not necessarily ceasing to exist. Interpreters who argue for annihilation and those who argue for conscious punishment both appeal to it, so the lexeme alone cannot settle that debate.

study.summary: ἆρα is an interrogative particle that introduces a question, often with a note of anxiety, doubt or impatience. In the NT, strictly speaking, it is rare and literary, found only in Luke and Paul ('when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith?'). In unaccented manuscripts it looks identical to the inferential particle ἄρα ('then, so'), and some text editions group under this word the many questions of the form 'Who then…?' and the phrase 'if perhaps…'.

senses.label: Anxious question expecting 'no'
senses.definition: It marks a question that implies doubt or a negative answer: 'Will he really…?', 'Do you actually…?'
senses.note: In ACT 8:30 it is strengthened as ἆρά γε: 'Do you really understand what you are reading?'

senses.label: Rhetorical question rejected
senses.definition: It poses an inference only to deny it at once: 'Is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!'
senses.note: Editors differ on whether to accent ἆρα (question) or ἄρα (inference) here; the sense is much the same.

senses.label: 'Then' in a direct question
senses.definition: Inferential 'then' that draws a question out of what precedes it: 'Who then is the greatest?', 'What then will this child be?'
senses.note: Strictly this is the inferential particle ἄρα ('then, so') in a question; without accents the two particles are spelled the same, so they are often treated together.

senses.label: 'If perhaps' (εἰ ἄρα)
senses.definition: After εἰ it expresses a tentative hope or an open question: 'to see if perhaps…', 'whether indeed…'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke, the most literary NT writer, is the one who uses the true interrogative ἆρα. Jesus' haunting question about whether faith will be found at his coming is an example.

study.translationNote: Because the particle often has no direct English equivalent, translations either leave it out or render it 'then', 'really' or 'perhaps'. The difference between ἆρα and ἄρα comes from editors' accents, not from the original manuscripts.

background.note: In classical Greek the particle simply marks a question, and context decides the expected answer. In a speech of Demosthenes it implies a negative answer.
In Xenophon's Cyropaedia the same particle introduces a question expecting 'yes'.
In a record of an interview with a Roman emperor, a condemned man asks: 'Was it the senate, or you, the archpirate?'

study.exegesisTip: In LUK 18:8 the particle gives the question its tone. Jesus does not deny that faith will exist; he presses on the hearers whether they will persevere in prayer and faith until he comes.
study.caution: The earliest manuscripts were written without accents, so the distinction between interrogative ἆρα and inferential ἄρα is an editorial judgment. Word counts for this word differ widely between editions for that reason.

study.summary: ἀργύριον, from ἄργυρος ('silver'), originally meant a piece of silver. In the NT it means silver as a precious metal, money in general (like French argent), or specific silver coins: most famously the thirty pieces paid to Judas.

senses.label: Silver (the metal)
senses.definition: Silver as a valuable material, often paired with gold as the standard of earthly wealth.

senses.label: Money
senses.definition: Cash or funds in general, whatever the coinage.

senses.label: Silver coins, 'pieces of silver'
senses.definition: Individual silver coins, counted. In the Judas narrative the coins were probably shekels or tetradrachms.
senses.note: In ACT 19:19 the 'fifty thousand of silver' are probably drachmas.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew tells the price of Jesus in detail. He gives the thirty pieces of silver, Judas' return of them, the priests' scruple about putting 'blood money' into the treasury, and the fulfillment of prophecy. Later, money also buys the soldiers' silence about the resurrection.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke contrasts silver with the gifts of God. Peter has no silver but gives healing, Simon's attempt to buy the Spirit with money is cursed, and Paul coveted no one's silver.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: Silver and gold are called 'perishable', unable to ransom; redemption came through Christ's precious blood.

study.translationNote: Versions switch between 'silver', 'money' and 'pieces of silver' for the same Greek word, depending on whether the stress falls on the metal, on funds in general, or on counted coins.

background.note: Thucydides uses the word of a fixed sum of money.
Aristophanes uses it collectively for money in general.
In the Greek Old Testament it regularly renders the Hebrew word for silver/money, beginning with Abram's wealth.
A marriage contract of 311–310 BC requires repayment of 1000 drachmae of Alexander's silver coinage.

study.exegesisTip: In Matthew's passion narrative, follow the coins: they go from the priests to Judas, back to the temple, and into a potter's field. Matthew presents them as the measure of how cheaply Jesus was valued.

study.summary: ἀριθμός means number: the count or total of something. Luke uses it to measure the growth of the church; John's Gospel uses it of the five thousand fed. Revelation uses it for vast heavenly hosts and for the symbolic 'number of the beast', where letters stand for numbers.

senses.label: Number, total
senses.definition: The count of people or things, often given with a figure or described as countless.

senses.label: Growing number of believers
senses.definition: Luke's way of reporting the church's expansion: the number of disciples multiplied.

senses.label: Membership: 'of the number of'
senses.definition: Being counted within a group, as Judas was 'of the number of the Twelve'.

senses.label: Symbolic or name-number
senses.definition: A number that stands for a name or identity, especially the beast's number, which those who have wisdom are told to calculate.

senses.label: Countless multitudes
senses.definition: Huge round figures that express the immensity of God's people or of hostile forces.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Most NT occurrences are in Revelation. Its numbers carry symbolic weight: myriads of angels, the sealed 144,000, armies beyond counting, and the beast's 'number of a man'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke tracks the church's growth with this word, as the number of believers rises and multiplies.

background.note: Plato pairs the word with bulk: a thing is 'less neither in bulk nor in number'.
The Greek Old Testament can use the dative ἀριθμῷ ('in number') to mean simply 'few'.
A papyrus of AD 207 speaks of brothers 'five in number'.
Graffiti from Pompeii show Greek-speakers turning names into numbers, for example 'I love her whose number is 545'. This illustrates how readers would understand the beast's number.

study.exegesisTip: In Revelation 13 the instruction to 'calculate' the number presupposes gematria, the ancient practice of adding up the numerical values of a name's letters.
study.caution: The identity behind the number of the beast is disputed. Proposals range from a Hebrew spelling of 'Nero Caesar' to purely symbolic readings of 666 as falling short of perfection, and some manuscripts read 616. None is certain.

study.summary: βλασφημία is abusive, injurious speech. When people are its target it means slander or railing. When God, his Spirit or his name is the target it is blasphemy in the strict sense: speech that insults or dishonors God. The English loanword covers only the second use, so the same Greek word appears as 'slander' in vice lists and 'blasphemy' in Jesus' trial.

senses.label: Slander, abusive speech against people
senses.definition: Defamatory or insulting language against others, listed among the sins of the tongue that believers must put away.

senses.label: Blasphemy against God
senses.definition: Speech that insults God or claims his prerogatives. This was the charge laid against Jesus for forgiving sins and calling himself the Son of God.

senses.label: Blasphemy against the Spirit
senses.definition: Deliberately slandering the Spirit's work, such as calling Jesus' Spirit-empowered deeds demonic. Jesus says this alone will not be forgiven.

senses.label: Blasphemous names and words of the beast
senses.definition: In Revelation, the anti-God power bears 'names of blasphemy' and speaks blasphemies against God, his dwelling and his people.

senses.label: Railing judgment
senses.definition: A verdict delivered in insulting terms. Michael would not pronounce one even against the devil.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark frames Jesus' ministry with the charge: it first appears when he forgives a paralytic and returns at his condemnation by the Sanhedrin. In Mark's irony the accusers are the real blasphemers.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In Paul's letters the word always means slander between people. It appears in lists of speech-sins to be put off as part of the old self.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In Revelation, blasphemy marks the beast and its system. In the Gospel it is the charge raised against Jesus' claim to be one with the Father.

study.translationNote: Translations render the same word 'slander', 'evil speaking', 'abusive language', 'railing' or 'blasphemy'. The choice depends on whether the insult is aimed at people or at God; the Greek does not make that distinction.

background.note: In Euripides the word is used for an ill-omened, profane utterance made during a sacrifice.
In the orators it is ordinary slander or abuse directed against a person.
In Ezekiel the Greek Old Testament uses the plural for Edom's revilings against the mountains of Israel, which the LORD hears.

study.exegesisTip: In Mark, the unforgivable blasphemy against the Spirit is explained by the setting: the scribes said Jesus 'has an unclean spirit'. It is a settled attribution of God's saving work to Satan, not a careless word.
study.caution: What exactly constitutes blasphemy against the Spirit, and whether a believer can commit it, has been debated throughout church history. Interpreters agree that the context ties it to hardened rejection of Jesus' Spirit-empowered work.

study.summary: γεωργός (γῆ 'earth' + ἔργον 'work') is one who works the land: a farmer, or in viticulture a vine-grower. Most NT uses come from Jesus' parable of the wicked tenants, where the γεωργοί lease a vineyard from an absent owner. Elsewhere the farmer models patient, hard work, and in John the Father himself is the vinedresser.

senses.label: Farmer, cultivator
senses.definition: A person who tills the soil and waits for its produce. Used as an example of toil and patience.

senses.label: Tenant vine-growers
senses.definition: Those who rent and work someone else's vineyard and owe the owner a share of the fruit. In the parable they stand for Israel's leaders.
senses.note: The parable echoes Isaiah's song of the vineyard. Leasing land to tenants for a share of the crop was common practice in first-century Palestine and Egypt.

senses.label: Vinedresser (God the Father)
senses.definition: The one who tends the vine, pruning and removing branches. Jesus applies the title to his Father.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John reverses the parable's picture. The vinedresser is not a hireling but the Father, who cares for the true vine and its branches.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James makes the farmer a model of patience as he waits for the early and late rains before harvest, just as believers wait for the Lord's coming.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: The hard-working farmer, who has the first right to the crop, is one of three pictures (with soldier and athlete) of committed ministry.

study.translationNote: KJV's 'husbandmen' is the older English for farm workers. Modern versions say 'tenants', 'tenant farmers' or 'vine-growers' in the parable and 'farmer' elsewhere. In the parable it matters that the men are tenants, not owners.

background.note: In classical Greek the noun is the normal word for a husbandman or farmer.
Aristotle distinguishes farmers from hired laborers.
Papers from 223–222 BC deal with the insolvency of tenant farmers who found their task too heavy, showing the burdens of such tenants.

study.exegesisTip: In the parable, notice who the γεωργοί are. Mark and Luke record that the chief priests and scribes knew the story was told against them: they are the tenants who withhold the fruit and kill the heir.

study.summary: γονεύς ('begetter', related to γίνομαι and γεννάω) is used in the NT, as in Koine generally, almost only in the plural: οἱ γονεῖς, 'parents'. It appears in the infancy narratives, in the story of the man born blind, in teaching about duty to parents, and in warnings that loyalty to Christ may divide families.

senses.label: Parents (as a couple)
senses.definition: A child's father and mother together. These are narrative references to particular parents.

senses.label: Parents as owed honor and obedience
senses.definition: Parents as those children must obey; disobedience to them marks a corrupt society.

senses.label: Parents as providers
senses.definition: Parents' natural duty to provide for their children, which Paul uses to explain why he will not burden the church.

senses.label: Family ties strained by discipleship
senses.definition: Parents in sayings about following Jesus: some leave parents for the kingdom, and persecution can set children against parents.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: All of John's uses are in chapter 9. The parents of the man born blind confirm the miracle but, fearing expulsion from the synagogue, refuse to say who healed him, unlike their son.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul puts obedience to parents in the household codes ('in the Lord') and lists disobedience to parents among the signs of a society given up to sin and of the last days.

background.note: In early Greek poetry the word already appears mostly in the plural, meaning parents.
Herodotus extends it to an ancestor: 'ancestor in the fifth generation'.
A papyrus of 223–222 BC calls the 'Sibling Gods' and the 'Saviour Gods' 'their parents', using the plural γονεῖς. In Koine usage the word occurs in the plural.

study.exegesisTip: In Ephesians 'obey your parents in the Lord' is grounded in the fifth commandment with its promise. Children's obedience is presented as part of their discipleship, not merely social convention.

study.summary: δέησις (from δέομαι, 'to lack, to ask') is a request or entreaty that grows out of need. In the NT it is always prayer addressed to God: supplication. It often appears with προσευχή ('prayer'), where δέησις highlights the specific petition and the sense of need behind it.

senses.label: Supplication to God
senses.definition: A specific request poured out to God from a sense of need, which God hears.
senses.note: In HEB 5:7 it is paired with ἱκετηρίαι ('pleas') for Jesus' anguished prayers 'with loud cries and tears'.

senses.label: Petition alongside general prayer
senses.definition: Combined with προσευχή, it stresses specific requests within the whole life of prayer.

senses.label: Intercession for others
senses.definition: Prayer made on behalf of others, often with ὑπέρ or περί ('for').

senses.label: 'Making supplications' as a devotional practice
senses.definition: The phrase δεήσεις ποιεῖσθαι for regular devotional prayer, often linked with fasting.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word most often, for his own constant prayers for churches and for theirs for him. He frequently pairs it with προσευχή and thanksgiving.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke shows prayer as persistent practice: Zechariah's supplication heard, Anna's fasting and supplications night and day, and the disciples devoting themselves to prayer.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'prayer', 'supplication', 'petition' and 'request'. Where δέησις stands next to προσευχή, careful versions use 'petition' or 'supplication' so that the two words are not both rendered 'prayer'.

background.note: Classical orators use the word for entreaty.
The Greek Psalter can use the word for a lack or need, its root sense.
In a Ptolemaic document a prisoner pleads 'with supplication and entreaty, in the name of God and of fair play'.
In the Serapeum documents a man petitions an official on behalf of the Twins 'with supplication'. This shows the word as a strong, earnest request.

study.exegesisTip: Notice the link to need. The verb δέομαι means 'to lack', so δέησις reminds readers that prayer comes from dependence. JAM 5:16 promises that such prayer of a righteous person is powerful in its working.
study.caution: Older word studies drew sharp distinctions between δέησις, προσευχή and ἔντευξις in 1 Tim 2:1. The list is better read as a cumulative call to every kind of prayer than as a technical classification.

study.summary: διακρίνω (διά 'between' + κρίνω 'judge') literally means to separate. In the active voice it means to distinguish, discern or judge between. In the middle and passive it means to dispute with someone or, in a distinctive NT use, to be divided within oneself: to doubt or waver. Readers need to see both the 'discerning' and the 'doubting' senses, because English versions hide that they come from one verb.

senses.label: Make a distinction, differentiate
senses.definition: To treat one person differently from another, or to set someone apart as superior.
senses.note: In JAM 2:4 the passive may mean either 'you made distinctions among yourselves' (favouritism) or 'you became divided in yourselves'.

senses.label: Discern, evaluate, judge
senses.definition: To assess correctly, interpret, or decide a dispute: reading the sky, settling a case between believers, weighing prophecy, judging oneself.

senses.label: Dispute, contend (middle)
senses.definition: To take issue with someone, or to argue a case against an opponent.
senses.note: In JUD 1:9 Michael 'contended with the devil' as if in a legal case over Moses' body.

senses.label: Doubt, waver (middle/passive)
senses.definition: To be divided in one's mind and hesitate between trust and distrust. This is the opposite of faith.
senses.note: In ACT 10:20 and ACT 11:12 'without hesitating' tells Peter to go to Gentiles without misgivings.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses both senses. He warns against eating the Lord's Supper 'not discerning the body' and urges believers to judge themselves; elsewhere Abraham 'did not waver' at the promise and the one who doubts while eating is condemned.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James pictures the doubter as a wave tossed by the wind and asking God with a divided mind. He also uses the verb for partiality in the assembly.

authorNotes.author: Jude
authorNotes.note: Jude uses the verb in a legal sense of Michael disputing with the devil, and again in a textually difficult instruction about how to treat others.

study.translationNote: English versions render this one verb as 'discern', 'judge', 'make a difference', 'contend', 'doubt', 'waver' or 'hesitate'. In JUD 1:22 the Byzantine text is read as 'making a distinction', while modern critical texts are read as 'have mercy on those who doubt'.

background.note: Homer uses the verb literally of goatherds separating their mixed flocks.
An inscription of the 3rd century BC uses it of appointed judges deciding disputed contracts.
A papyrus of 218 BC uses the passive with a person in the dative for having one's case decided against someone. This illustrates Michael's dispute with the devil in Jude.

study.exegesisTip: 1 Corinthians 11:29–34 plays on κρίνω and its compounds: not discerning the body brings judgment (κρίμα), and those who judge themselves rightly (διεκρίνομεν) would not be judged. The wordplay connects careful discernment with escaping the Lord's discipline.
study.caution: The sense 'to doubt' is not found in the Septuagint and is rare in earlier Greek. It may have developed in or near early Christian usage. In JAM 2:4 and JUD 1:22 scholars disagree on whether 'distinguish' or 'doubt' is meant.

study.summary: δῶρον (from δίδωμι, 'give') is a gift or present. In the NT it most often means a gift brought to God: an offering at the altar, a contribution to the temple treasury, something declared 'Corban', or the 'gifts and sacrifices' offered by priests. Paul uses it once, for salvation as 'the gift of God'.

senses.label: Gift, present (between people)
senses.definition: Something given as a token of honor or celebration.
senses.note: The magi's gifts are tribute fit for a king. In Revelation the earth-dwellers exchange gifts in celebration over the slain witnesses.

senses.label: Offering at the altar
senses.definition: A sacrifice or gift presented to God in worship.

senses.label: Dedicated gift, Corban
senses.definition: Property formally declared devoted to God. Jesus condemns using this to evade support of parents.

senses.label: Contribution to the temple treasury
senses.definition: Money given to God through the temple chests.

senses.label: Priestly 'gifts and sacrifices'
senses.definition: The fixed pair in Hebrews for everything the Levitical priests offered. Hebrews says these could not perfect the worshiper's conscience.

senses.label: God's gift of salvation
senses.definition: Salvation by grace through faith, given by God and not achieved by human effort.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses the word most. He moves from the magi's gifts to teaching that reconciliation must come before offering, and to the polemic about swearing by the altar or the gift on it.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses 'gifts and sacrifices' to sum up the old priesthood. Christ, too, must have something to offer, and he offers himself.

study.translationNote: Where δῶρον refers to temple worship, many versions say 'offering' or 'gift' depending on whether the setting is an altar or the treasury. In Mark 7 the Aramaic 'Corban' is glossed by the Gospel writer himself with δῶρον.

background.note: Homer uses the word for gifts of honor.
In Aeschylus altars blaze with gifts, meaning offerings to the gods.
The Greek Old Testament uses it for Abel's offering. More generally it is the usual rendering of the Hebrew qorban.
In a boy's letter from the 2nd–3rd century AD the word has its ordinary sense, 'you sent me a present'.

study.exegesisTip: In MAT 5:23–24 the gift is already at the altar, yet Jesus says to leave it and be reconciled first. Worship offered to God does not excuse broken relationships with others.
study.caution: In EPH 2:8 'this' (neuter τοῦτο) most likely refers to the whole process of being saved by grace through faith, not to 'faith' alone (feminine). Interpreters still debate exactly what 'the gift of God' covers.

study.summary: κατέχω is a strengthened form of ἔχω ('have, hold'): to hold firmly. Depending on context it means to hold fast or possess something, to take possession of it, to hold someone back or restrain them, and, as a sailing term, to steer for a shore. In Paul and Hebrews it is a key word for holding firmly to the gospel and to the hope believers confess.

senses.label: hold fast, keep firmly
senses.definition: To keep a firm grip on something received, especially the gospel, apostolic traditions, what is good, or the believer's confidence and hope, so as not to let it go.
senses.note: In these passages the holding is the evidence of real faith: 'if you hold firmly' (1 Cor 15:2; Heb 3:6, 14) makes perseverance the mark of genuine belonging.

senses.label: possess, have as one's own
senses.definition: To have something in one's possession or control; the intensive counterpart of simple 'having'.
senses.note: 2 Cor 6:10 plays on the two verbs: 'as having nothing (ἔχοντες), yet possessing (κατέχοντες) everything.'

senses.label: take possession of, seize
senses.definition: To lay hold of something and make it one's own, or to occupy a place.
senses.note: In Luke 14:9 the humiliated guest must 'take' (occupy) the lowest place.

senses.label: hold back, restrain, detain
senses.definition: To keep someone from leaving or acting, to suppress, or to hold in bondage.
senses.note: Rom 1:18 speaks of people who 'suppress' the truth by their unrighteousness; Rom 7:6 of the law 'by which we were held captive'. In 2 Thess 2:6–7 'the restrainer' (neuter and masculine) holds back the lawless one.

senses.label: be held by (a disease)
senses.definition: Passive: to be gripped or afflicted by an illness.
senses.note: This verse belongs to a passage absent from the earliest manuscripts.

senses.label: steer for, make for (nautical)
senses.definition: Intransitive sailing term: to hold a ship on course toward a place.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word for the full range from tenacious faith (holding fast the gospel and the traditions) to the sinful suppression of truth and the mysterious 'restrainer' of the end times.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: All three uses call readers to hold their confidence and confession of hope firm to the end, the letter's central exhortation against drifting away.

study.translationNote: English versions vary widely ('hold fast', 'keep', 'possess', 'suppress', 'restrain', 'make for the shore') because the one Greek verb covers both holding on to something and holding something or someone back. In 2 Thess 2:6–7 some versions say 'restrains', older ones 'withholdeth' or 'letteth' (old English 'let' = hinder).

background.note: Homer already uses the verb for holding someone back against his will.
A royal ordinance grants legal ownership of lands to those who have held possession of them, the 'possess' sense found in 2 Cor 6:10.
An official report argues that a man had taken possession of (become owner of) a house, the 'take possession' sense of Luke 14:9.
The verb is used of arresting or detaining a person.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the object is something held on to (the gospel, the good, hope) or someone held back (Jesus by the crowds, Onesimus by Paul, the lawless one by the restrainer). The same verb carries opposite moral weight: believers 'hold fast' the truth (1 Thess 5:21) while the ungodly 'hold down' the truth (Rom 1:18).
study.caution: The identity of 'what restrains' and 'the one who restrains' in 2 Thess 2:6–7 is much debated (proposals include the Roman state, Paul's preaching mission, the Holy Spirit, or an angelic power); the verb itself only says that something is presently holding back the lawless one.

study.summary: κοινωνία means a sharing or partnership: having something in common with others, participating in it together. In the NT it describes believers' shared life in Christ and the Spirit, their participation in Christ's body, blood and sufferings, partnership in spreading the gospel, and the concrete sharing of money with needy believers.

senses.label: fellowship, communion with God and Christ
senses.definition: Participation in a shared relationship with God the Father, his Son and the Spirit, into which believers are called.
senses.note: The genitive often names what or whom one shares in: 'fellowship of his Son' (1 Cor 1:9), 'fellowship of the Spirit' (Phil 2:1).

senses.label: fellowship among believers
senses.definition: The shared common life and mutual belonging of Christians with one another.
senses.note: The 'right hand of fellowship' (Gal 2:9) was a pledge of partnership; 2 Cor 6:14 denies any such common ground between light and darkness.

senses.label: participation, sharing in
senses.definition: Having a real share in something, such as Christ's blood and body at the Lord's Supper or his sufferings.
senses.note: In 1 Cor 10:16 the cup and bread are a 'participation' in Christ's blood and body, which is why sharing in idol feasts is incompatible.

senses.label: partnership in the gospel and faith
senses.definition: Active cooperation and common cause in advancing the gospel, including support of those who preach it.
senses.note: Philippians' 'partnership' included their financial gifts to Paul.

senses.label: contribution, generous sharing
senses.definition: The concrete expression of fellowship in a gift of money or goods for those in need.
senses.note: Paul calls the collection for the Jerusalem poor a κοινωνία: giving is a form of fellowship, not mere charity.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's usage ranges from mystical-sounding participation in Christ (his Son, his body and blood, his sufferings) to very practical partnership and money-sharing; for him these belong together.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In 1 John fellowship with the Father and Son and fellowship with one another are inseparable, and both depend on walking in the light rather than in darkness.

study.translationNote: Versions render the word 'fellowship', 'communion', 'participation', 'sharing', 'partnership' or 'contribution'. The choice is interpretive: 'communion' in 1 Cor 10:16 (KJV) suggests the sacrament, 'participation' or 'sharing' stresses the believer's real share in Christ; 'contribution' in Rom 15:26 names the gift itself while hiding the idea of fellowship behind it.

background.note: Plato argues that where there is no communion (partnership) there can be no friendship.
Aristotle uses the word for the political community, the partnership that makes up a city-state.
A marriage contract speaks of a couple coming together for a 'partnership of life', showing the word could describe the closest human relationship.
Used of a business partnership: a man states that he has no partnership with his half-brother.

study.exegesisTip: Look at the genitive or prepositional phrase that follows: it tells you what is shared ('of his Son', 'of the Spirit', 'of his sufferings') or toward whom it is directed ('for the poor', 'in the gospel'). Fellowship in the NT is participation in a common reality, not just friendly company.
study.caution: Whether 'the fellowship of the Holy Spirit' means fellowship created by the Spirit or participation in the Spirit himself is debated (Phil 2:1).

study.summary: κόπος, from κόπτω ('strike'), means toil that wears a person out: hard, wearying labor, and also the trouble or annoyance one causes another. Paul uses it for the exhausting work of gospel ministry, while the Gospels use the idiom 'to cause trouble' for someone.

senses.label: wearying toil, hard labor
senses.definition: Exhausting effort, especially in ministry and Christian service, often paired with μόχθος ('hardship') for emphasis.
senses.note: Paul worked 'night and day' at a trade so as not to burden his churches; κόπος includes such manual labor alongside preaching.

senses.label: labor springing from love or faith
senses.definition: Costly effort as an expression of Christian love, which God notices and rewards.
senses.note: The 'labor of love' (1 Thess 1:3) stresses that love is costly and tiring.

senses.label: labors, hardships (plural)
senses.definition: In the plural, the many toils and sufferings of apostolic work, or the labors from which the faithful dead rest.

senses.label: trouble, bother (to cause)
senses.definition: In the idiom κόπους (or κόπον) παρέχειν τινί, to give someone trouble, to bother them.
senses.note: Here the focus is the annoyance inflicted on another, not one's own work: 'Why do you trouble the woman?'

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: For Paul κόπος is the hallmark of genuine apostolic ministry; he lists his labors as credentials and fears his labor among converts might prove empty, yet assures believers that labor in the Lord is not in vain.

study.translationNote: Most versions say 'labor' or 'toil', but in the Gospel idiom κόπους παρέχειν they rightly say 'trouble' or 'bother', so readers may not realize it is the same word. Some versions translate 'work' in 1 Thess 1:3, which loses the idea of weariness.

background.note: Sophocles uses the word of the pain of a disease.
The idiom 'to give trouble' appears in a letter: 'if he gives you trouble, go up with him', exactly the Gospel phrase.
A farmer complains that they never had so much trouble winnowing barley, the word for wearisome work.

study.exegesisTip: Classical synonyms help: πόνος stresses the effort required, κόπος the fatigue that results, μόχθος the hardship. When Paul pairs κόπος and μόχθος he is stressing how draining his work was, not adding a separate item.

study.summary: κρυπτός means hidden or secret. Jesus uses it for the private sphere of piety seen only by God and for hidden things that will one day be revealed; Paul uses it for the hidden inner life of the heart that God judges, in contrast to outward appearance.

senses.label: in secret, privately (ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ)
senses.definition: Out of public view; the hidden sphere of giving and prayer where only God the Father sees.
senses.note: The phrase contrasts genuine piety with performance for human applause.

senses.label: secretly, not openly (ἐν κρυπτῷ)
senses.definition: Acting in a concealed or low-profile way rather than publicly.
senses.note: In John 18:20 Jesus insists he said 'nothing in secret'; his teaching was public.

senses.label: hidden things to be revealed
senses.definition: What is now concealed but will be brought into the open, by the spread of Jesus' message or at the judgment.

senses.label: the hidden inner person, secrets of the heart
senses.definition: The inward, unseen reality of a person: thoughts, motives and character, as distinct from outward show.
senses.note: Rom 2:29: the true Jew is one 'inwardly' (ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ), with a circumcision of the heart; 1 Pet 3:4: 'the hidden person of the heart'.

senses.label: secret, shameful things
senses.definition: Underhanded or disgraceful practices done out of sight.
senses.note: Paul renounces 'the hidden things of shame', contrasting them with open proclamation of the truth.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew concentrates the word in the Sermon on the Mount: the Father 'who sees in secret' rewards giving, prayer and fasting done without display.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the hidden/visible contrast theologically: God judges the hidden things of people, and true covenant identity is inward rather than outward.

study.translationNote: In Rom 2:29 versions vary between 'inwardly', 'one inwardly', and 'in secret'; the Greek contrasts what is hidden (inner) with what is visible (outward). In Matt 6:18 the Byzantine text has κρυπτός while many modern editions read the related κρυφαῖος, with no difference in meaning.

background.note: Homer describes a door fitted with a secret bolt, the basic physical sense 'concealed'.
Herodotus speaks of a hidden passage that had been dug.
In a slave sale the seller accepts liability for any hidden defect, a legal use of 'hidden'.

study.exegesisTip: Watch for the paired opposite: κρυπτός is usually set against φανερός ('visible, open') or a verb of revealing. The contrast, not the word alone, carries the point, whether about reward, judgment or true identity.

study.summary: κτίσις, from κτίζω ('found, create'), originally meant the founding of a city. In biblical Greek it means God's act of creating, and what he has created: an individual creature, the whole created order, or, in Paul, the 'new creation' in Christ. Once (1 Pet 2:13) it refers to a human institution or authority.

senses.label: the act of creation
senses.definition: God's creating of the world, especially in the phrase 'from the beginning of creation'.

senses.label: created thing, creature
senses.definition: Any single created being or thing, as opposed to the Creator.
senses.note: Rom 1:25 contrasts worship of 'the creature' with worship of 'the Creator'.

senses.label: the whole creation, created order
senses.definition: The sum of everything God has made, over which Christ stands as firstborn and to which the gospel goes.
senses.note: In Heb 9:11 the heavenly tent is 'not of this creation'.

senses.label: creation awaiting redemption
senses.definition: The (non-human) created world, subjected to frustration and decay, groaning as it waits for the revelation of God's children.

senses.label: new creation
senses.definition: The new reality brought about by God in Christ, applied both to the person in Christ and to the new order that makes circumcision irrelevant.

senses.label: human institution, authority
senses.definition: Something established by people, such as a governing authority.
senses.note: 'Submit to every human institution (or creature) for the Lord's sake'; the following verses name the king and governors.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul gives the word its richest theology: creation reveals God's power (Rom 1:20), groans for liberation (Rom 8), and is answered by the 'new creation' in Christ.

study.translationNote: The same word is rendered 'creation', 'creature' and 'ordinance/institution'. In 2 Cor 5:17 versions differ between 'he is a new creation', 'he is a new creature' and 'there is a new creation', because the Greek has no verb: it can describe the transformed person or announce the new world that has dawned. In 1 Pet 2:13 'ordinance' or 'institution' is preferred because the context is human rulers.

background.note: Thucydides uses the word for the founding or settling of a colony, its ordinary classical sense.
An inscription dates priests 'from the founding' of a cult, showing κτίσις as the regular term for a foundation.
The Wisdom of Solomon uses the word collectively for the whole created order, as in the NT.

study.exegesisTip: Decide in each verse whether κτίσις is the act (creating), the product (a creature), or the whole (creation). In Rom 8:19–22 most interpreters take it as the non-human creation, since believers are mentioned separately in 8:23.
study.caution: In Rom 8:19–22 the scope of 'creation' is debated: most take it as the sub-human world, but some include unbelieving humanity or angels. In 2 Cor 5:17 scholars debate whether Paul primarily means individual renewal or the cosmic new age breaking in.

study.summary: μεριμνάω means to have one's mind occupied and divided by concern. It can be negative, anxious worry that distracts from trust in God (the Sermon on the Mount, Martha), or positive, earnest care and concern for the Lord's affairs or for other people (Paul). The context decides which.

senses.label: be anxious, worry
senses.definition: To be weighed down or distracted by anxious concern over life's needs or the future, which Jesus forbids his followers.
senses.note: Phil 4:6 'Do not be anxious about anything' echoes Jesus' teaching, replacing worry with thankful prayer.

senses.label: be anxious about what to say
senses.definition: To worry in advance about one's defense when put on trial.
senses.note: Jesus promises that the Spirit will give the words.

senses.label: be troubled, distracted
senses.definition: To be preoccupied and agitated by many concerns, losing sight of what matters most.
senses.note: Martha is 'anxious and troubled about many things' while one thing is needed.

senses.label: care for, be concerned about
senses.definition: With an object, to give one's attention and concern to someone or something, positively for the Lord or for others, or with divided interests for worldly affairs.
senses.note: In 1 Cor 7 the issue is not sinful worry but divided attention; Timothy 'genuinely cares' for the Philippians (Phil 2:20).

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew's six uses in Matt 6 form a sustained argument against anxiety: life is more than food, worry adds nothing, the Father knows your needs, so seek the kingdom first.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb both negatively and positively: believers should not be anxious, yet should care for the Lord's affairs and for one another.

study.translationNote: Older English ('take no thought', KJV) once meant 'do not be anxious', but today sounds like 'do not plan ahead', which is not Jesus' point. Modern versions say 'do not worry' or 'do not be anxious'. Where the sense is positive (1 Cor 7; Phil 2:20) they switch to 'be concerned', 'care for', which can hide that it is the same verb.

background.note: Sophocles' Oedipus asks a herdsman what work he was occupied with, showing the neutral sense 'be occupied with', compared to 1 Cor 7:33.
Xenophon uses the verb of philosophers pondering the heavens, 'concern oneself with, think about'.
The psalmist is 'anxious' over his sin.
A letter-writer writes in haste so that the recipient need not worry, the over-anxious sense found in Matt 6:25.

study.exegesisTip: Check what the verb's object is and what is contrasted with it. When the object is food, clothing, tomorrow, or 'many things', the verb is the anxiety Jesus forbids; when it is 'the things of the Lord' or other believers, it is commendable care. The word itself suggests a mind pulled in different directions.

study.summary: παλαιός means old: something that has existed a long time, often with the added idea of being worn out or superseded by something new. Jesus uses it of old garments and wine set against the new; Paul uses it theologically for the 'old self' crucified with Christ, the 'old leaven' and the 'old covenant'.

senses.label: old, worn out (things)
senses.definition: Of objects such as garments and wineskins: aged and worn by use, unable to hold what is new.
senses.note: Jesus' parables contrast the old forms with the newness of his ministry.

senses.label: old, aged (preferred)
senses.definition: Long-standing and therefore valued, like matured wine or treasures of old.
senses.note: 'The old is good' (Luke 5:39) describes the reluctance of people to try the new; the scribe trained for the kingdom brings out things new and old (Matt 13:52).

senses.label: the old self
senses.definition: The person one was before union with Christ, under the dominion of sin, which has been crucified and is to be put off.

senses.label: old leaven
senses.definition: The former corrupt way of life (malice and wickedness) to be purged out, by analogy with removing leaven at Passover.

senses.label: old covenant
senses.definition: The Mosaic covenant, now read with a veil over it until one turns to Christ.
senses.note: The only NT use of 'old covenant' as a phrase.

senses.label: old (long-familiar) commandment
senses.definition: A command known from the beginning, not an innovation.
senses.note: John's 'old commandment' is the love command they had heard from the start; it is also 'new' in Christ (2:8).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul always sets παλαιός against newness in Christ: the old self versus the new, the old leaven versus the new batch, the old covenant versus the new.

study.translationNote: In Rom 6:6, Eph 4:22 and Col 3:9 the literal 'old man' (KJV) is rendered 'old self', 'old nature' or 'former self'. 'Old nature' can suggest a part of the believer still present, while 'old self' or 'old man' better reflects Paul's picture of the former person who died with Christ.

background.note: A letter contrasts old dates with freshly gathered new ones, the ordinary old/new contrast of the Gospel parables.
A Christian letter speaks of acting 'according to the old custom', a long-established practice, comparable to John's 'old commandment'.
In Joshua the Gibeonites' worn-out sacks, wineskins and sandals are 'old', the sense of 'worn by use'.

study.exegesisTip: παλαιός is usually paired with καινός or νέος ('new'). Ask what the new thing is in each contrast, because the 'old' is defined by it: the garment by the new patch, the old self by the new self, the old covenant by the new covenant ministry.
study.caution: Whether 'old self' in Rom 6:6 means the believer's former identity (now dead) or a sinful nature still at work is debated; Rom 6:6 and Col 3:9 present it as something already crucified or put off, while Eph 4:22 frames putting it off as an ongoing call (scholars differ over whether the infinitives there are commands or describe what was taught).

study.summary: παρατίθημι means 'to place beside' or 'set before'. In the active it is used for serving food and for setting a parable before hearers; in the middle it means to entrust something to someone's care, as Jesus commits his spirit to the Father and Paul commits believers and teaching to God or to faithful people. Once it means to set out evidence.

senses.label: set before, serve (food)
senses.definition: To put food in front of people to eat.
senses.note: In Acts 16:34 the jailer 'set a table' (a meal) before Paul and Silas.

senses.label: set before (teaching)
senses.definition: To present a parable or teaching for hearers to consider.

senses.label: entrust, commit (to someone's care)
senses.definition: Middle voice: to hand something or someone over to another for safekeeping, as a deposit.
senses.note: Jesus' last words, 'into your hands I commit my spirit' (Luke 23:46), quote Ps 31:5.

senses.label: commit (a charge or teaching) to others
senses.definition: To pass on instruction or a responsibility to a trusted person who must guard it.
senses.note: 2 Tim 2:2 describes a chain of faithful transmission: entrust to reliable people who will teach others.

senses.label: set forth, demonstrate
senses.definition: To bring forward evidence or a line of proof.
senses.note: Paul 'explaining and demonstrating' from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word for both meals and entrusting; in Acts entrusting to God becomes the farewell act of missionaries leaving young churches.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In the Pastoral Letters the middle voice expresses the transmission of the apostolic deposit: Timothy is entrusted with a charge and must entrust it in turn.

study.translationNote: The same verb is rendered 'set before', 'serve', 'put forth' (a parable), 'commit', 'commend' and 'entrust'. 'Commend' (KJV in Luke 23:46 and Acts) today sounds like praise, but the Greek means to hand over for safekeeping.

background.note: In the Odyssey the verb is used for placing a seat beside someone, the literal 'place beside'.
A man records that he deposited a pair of buckles as a pledge with someone, the 'entrust, deposit' sense of the middle.
In a letter of recommendation the writer 'commits' a man to the recipient's care, as in Acts 14:23 and 20:32.
Petitioners approach the strategus adding a statement of their case, the sense 'bring forward, set out' comparable to 'demonstrating' in Acts 17:3.

study.exegesisTip: Note the voice. The active 'set before' looks at what is offered; the middle 'entrust' looks at a deposit placed in another's keeping, with the expectation that it will be guarded and accounted for (compare the related noun παραθήκη, 'deposit').

study.summary: πόλεμος means war, either a whole conflict between nations or a single battle. In the Gospels it belongs to the signs before the end; in Revelation it names the final battles between the beast and God's people and Christ; James uses it figuratively for quarrels among believers.

senses.label: war (armed conflict)
senses.definition: Organized armed conflict between nations or kings, including the wars that mark the period before the end.
senses.note: Jesus warns that wars 'must happen' but are not yet the end.

senses.label: battle, fight
senses.definition: A particular engagement or the fighting itself, for which one prepares.
senses.note: Rev 12:7 describes war in heaven between Michael and the dragon.

senses.label: make war (eschatological conflict)
senses.definition: In the phrase 'make war with' (πόλεμον ποιεῖν μετά), hostile powers wage war against the saints or against Christ.

senses.label: the great final battle
senses.definition: The gathering of the nations for the battle of the great day of God.

senses.label: quarrels, conflicts (figurative)
senses.definition: Hostile disputes among people, rooted in their selfish desires.
senses.note: James pairs πόλεμοι with μάχαι ('fights'), probably as hyperbole for bitter quarrels within the community.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: All of John's uses are in Revelation, where πόλεμος describes the cosmic conflict between the dragon, the beast and the saints, ending in Christ's victory.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James alone uses the word figuratively, tracing community 'wars' to the desires that war within believers.

study.translationNote: Versions alternate between 'war' and 'battle'. The Greek covers both a whole war and a single battle, so in Luke 14:31 ('to meet another king in war/battle') and Rev 16:14 either is possible.

background.note: Already in Homer the word means war, which became its usual meaning in later Greek, though Homer can also use it of a battle or even a single combat.
A petition reminds the emperors of the city's loyalty in the war against the Jews.
An inscription honors Augustus as the savior who ended war, a contrast with the peace Christ brings.
David asks how the battle progressed, using πόλεμος of a specific battle.

study.exegesisTip: In Revelation look for the formula 'make war with' (πόλεμον ποιεῖν μετά): it ties together the beast's war on the saints and the final war against the Lamb, a war already decided.

study.summary: πότε is the interrogative adverb 'when?' It asks about the time of an event, in direct questions ('When did we see you hungry?') and indirect ones ('you do not know when the time will come'). With ἕως it forms the exclamation 'how long?', expressing impatience or longing.

senses.label: when? (direct question)
senses.definition: Asks at what time something happened or will happen.
senses.note: In Matt 25 both the righteous and the wicked ask 'when?', unaware that they had met the Son of Man in the needy.

senses.label: when (indirect question)
senses.definition: Introduces a question about time inside a statement, especially about the coming of the end or the master's return.
senses.note: The emphasis is that the time is unknown, so disciples must keep watch.

senses.label: how long? (ἕως πότε)
senses.definition: With ἕως, 'until when?': an exclamation of impatience, distress or longing.
senses.note: Jesus' 'How long must I bear with you?' and the martyrs' 'How long, O Lord?' (Rev 6:10) echo the laments of the Psalms.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark's apocalyptic discourse frames the question 'when?' and then answers that no one knows, turning curiosity about timing into a call to stay awake.

background.note: Sophocles' chorus cries 'until when will it end?', an expression like the NT's 'how long?'.
A letter asks the recipient to make clear 'when it will be convenient' to send something, an indirect question as in Matt 24:3.

study.exegesisTip: Distinguish πότε ('when?', a question) from the unaccented enclitic ποτέ ('once, ever, at some time'), which is a different use of the same form. Questions about 'when' in the Gospels are regularly redirected by Jesus to readiness rather than dates.

study.summary: A meeting, used in the phrase εἰς ἀπάντησιν, 'to meet', especially of going out to welcome and escort an arriving person.

senses.label: Going out to meet
senses.definition: The act of meeting someone; in the NT always εἰς ἀπάντησιν, of people going out to receive an arriving bridegroom, apostle or the Lord.
senses.note: MAT 25:1 has this word in the Byzantine text; the critical text reads ὑπάντησιν there.

background.note: Used for going out to receive a newly arriving magistrate, a near-technical term for the official welcome of a dignitary.
Common in the LXX for going out 'to meet' someone, rendering Hebrew liqra't.

study.exegesisTip: In 1TH 4:17 and ACT 28:15 the phrase pictures a welcoming party going out to greet an arriving dignitary; at 1TH 4:17 believers meet the Lord as he comes.
study.caution: Some infer from the welcome custom that the escort then returns with the Lord to earth in 1TH 4:17; the word itself shows the meeting, not the direction afterward.

study.summary: To deceive, lead someone into error by false words or self-delusion.

senses.label: Deceive, mislead
senses.definition: To lead someone astray by falsehood, whether others by empty words, Eve by the serpent, or oneself by self-deception.

background.note: Used from Homer on for cheating or deceiving.
Rare in the papyri; the verb was falling out of everyday use, though common in the LXX.

study.exegesisTip: In JAM 1:26 the one deceived is the person's own heart: religion without a bridled tongue is self-deception.

study.summary: A threat or threatening, especially intimidation used against believers or by masters against slaves.

senses.label: Threat, threatening
senses.definition: A threatening word or attitude intended to intimidate, as the Sanhedrin's threats, Saul's murderous menace, or a master's threats toward slaves.
senses.note: ACT 4:17 (ἀπειλῇ ἀπειλησόμεθα, 'let us strictly threaten') is in the Byzantine text only.

background.note: Common from Homer on, mostly plural, for threats.
In a complaint someone 'drove me away with a threat'.

study.summary: Literally to step off or disembark; figuratively, of events, to turn out or result.

senses.label: Disembark, get out
senses.definition: To step off a boat onto land.

senses.label: Turn out, result
senses.definition: Of events or circumstances, to issue in a certain outcome.

background.note: Regular for disembarking from a ship.
Used of how affairs will 'turn out' for the writer and recipient, as in PHP 1:19.

study.exegesisTip: In PHP 1:19 Paul's wording echoes Job 13:16 LXX: his circumstances will turn out for his deliverance.

study.summary: To enter in a list or register; middle, to have oneself registered, as in a census.

senses.label: Register in a census
senses.definition: Of a government enrolment: to register people, or (middle) to get oneself registered.

senses.label: Enrolled in heaven
senses.definition: Passive, of the firstborn whose names are recorded as citizens in heaven.

background.note: Used for scribes entering each nation in a list.
A standard term for declaring persons or property to officials.

study.summary: To show forth, exhibit, demonstrate, or proclaim someone to be something.

senses.label: Exhibit, attest
senses.definition: To display or publicly accredit someone, as God attested Jesus by miracles or exhibited the apostles last, like condemned men.

senses.label: Prove
senses.definition: To establish charges by evidence.

senses.label: Proclaim oneself as
senses.definition: To declare or proclaim someone in a role; of the man of lawlessness presenting himself as God.

background.note: Common for proclaiming an appointment to office, e.g. Nero 'has been declared Emperor'.

study.exegesisTip: In 2TH 2:4 the official sense of proclaiming an accession fits: the lawless one proclaims himself God.

study.summary: To tithe: to pay a tenth of one's goods, or to collect a tenth from others.

senses.label: Pay tithes of
senses.definition: To give a tenth of produce or income, as the Pharisees did scrupulously.

senses.label: Collect tithes from
senses.definition: With a personal object, to take a tenth from people, as the Levitical priests did.

background.note: Used of Jacob's vow to give God a tenth.

study.summary: To be laid away or stored up; figuratively, to be reserved or appointed for someone.

senses.label: Laid away
senses.definition: Literally put away and kept, like a mina wrapped in a cloth.

senses.label: Reserved, appointed for
senses.definition: Kept in store for someone: hope and a crown laid up in heaven, or death appointed for all.

background.note: A non-Christian epitaph says that 'for all mortals to die is laid up', closely parallel to HEB 9:27.
Used of grain or money laid up in store.

study.summary: To behead, used in the NT only of Herod's execution of John the Baptist.

senses.label: Behead
senses.definition: To execute by cutting off the head.

study.summary: An answer or reply.

senses.label: Answer, reply
senses.definition: A spoken response to a question, such as Jesus' answers that amazed hearers, or the answer he refused Pilate.

background.note: Used in inscriptions for official replies, but rare in the papyri until late, as in a sixth-century letter.

study.summary: To roll away, used of the stone at the entrance of Jesus' tomb.

senses.label: Roll away
senses.definition: To roll a heavy stone away from an opening.

background.note: Used of rolling the stone from the mouth of a well.

study.summary: To sail away, set sail from a place.

senses.label: Sail away
senses.definition: To depart by ship for a destination.

background.note: Used from Homer on of sailing off, often homeward.

study.summary: To be at a loss, perplexed, not knowing what to do or think.

senses.label: Be perplexed, at a loss
senses.definition: To be uncertain or baffled about something, without a way forward.
senses.note: MAR 6:20 and LUK 24:4 have this verb in the critical text.

study.translationNote: At MAR 6:20 older translations follow the reading 'did many things', while newer ones follow 'was greatly perplexed' (ἠπόρει).

background.note: A man ruined by creditors 'was at his wit's end'.

study.exegesisTip: 2CO 4:8 plays on ἀπορούμενοι and the compound ἐξαπορούμενοι: perplexed, but not utterly at a loss.

study.summary: To draw or pull away; passive, to withdraw or tear oneself away.

senses.label: Draw out a sword
senses.definition: To pull a sword from its sheath.

senses.label: Draw people away
senses.definition: To lure disciples away to follow oneself.

senses.label: Withdraw, part from
senses.definition: Passive, to withdraw or be parted from others, sometimes with a sense of reluctance.

background.note: Used of withdrawing a gang of workmen, or removing an apprentice from his master.

study.summary: Apostleship: the office and commission of an apostle of Christ.

senses.label: Apostleship
senses.definition: The commission and office of being sent as Christ's apostle, to Jews or to Gentiles.

background.note: Originally a sending off or dispatching, as of ships.

study.summary: Active, to kindle or light a fire or lamp; middle, to take hold of or touch.

senses.label: Kindle, light
senses.definition: Active: to set alight a lamp or fire.

senses.label: Touch, take hold of
senses.definition: Middle (ἅπτομαι): to touch or lay hold of, as in Jesus' healing touch, sexual contact, ritual contact, or hostile grasp.
senses.note: Often listed separately as ἅπτομαι.

background.note: The root sense is to fasten or bind to, as a lyre-string.

study.summary: Pleasing, acceptable, approved by someone.

senses.label: Pleasing to God
senses.definition: What pleases God, done by Jesus and by obedient believers.

senses.label: Acceptable, agreeable
senses.definition: Pleasing or fitting to people; what seemed right to the apostles or pleased the Jews.

background.note: Very common in commerce for goods that are 'satisfactory' or acceptable.

study.summary: A meal, originally breakfast, in the NT a midday meal or a festive dinner.

senses.label: Meal, dinner
senses.definition: A noon or main meal, including a host's dinner or a wedding feast, and the feast of God's kingdom.
senses.note: LUK 14:15 has this word in the Byzantine text; the critical text reads ἄρτον.

background.note: In Homer the morning meal; later the midday meal.
Used in accounts for children's meals.

study.exegesisTip: In LUK 14:12 ἄριστον (midday meal) is paired with δεῖπνον (evening meal): whatever meal you give.

study.summary: A chariot, whether a traveling carriage or a war-chariot.

senses.label: Traveling chariot
senses.definition: The carriage in which the Ethiopian official rode.

senses.label: War-chariot
senses.definition: Horse-drawn chariots rushing into battle, used in a simile.

background.note: Especially the war-chariot in Homer.

study.summary: A leader who goes first: founder, author or originator, and also prince or leader; used of Jesus.

senses.label: Author, originator
senses.definition: One who begins and founds something, as the source of life, salvation or faith.

senses.label: Leader, prince
senses.definition: A ruler or leader, exalted alongside the title Savior.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'author', 'prince', 'pioneer', 'founder', 'champion' and 'captain', because the word combines the ideas of origin and of leadership; in HEB 2:10 and HEB 12:2 either nuance is possible.

background.note: A crowd hails an official as 'source of our blessings', reflecting the Latin auctor.
Used of the founding god or hero of a city or family.

study.caution: Scholars debate whether 'founder' or 'leader' dominates in each verse; the contexts often allow both.

study.summary: Spices or aromatic substances, used in the NT for anointing Jesus' body for burial.

senses.label: Burial spices
senses.definition: Aromatic substances prepared for anointing or wrapping a body.

background.note: Spices appear among articles listed for a sacrifice.

study.summary: Unquenchable, describing the fire of final judgment.

senses.label: Unquenchable fire
senses.definition: Fire that cannot be put out, used of the fire of judgment and Gehenna.
senses.note: MAR 9:45 has this word in the Byzantine text only.

background.note: Used from Homer for an unquenchable flame and ceaseless laughter or fame.

study.summary: Spotless, without stain; of a sacrificial lamb, and figuratively of moral purity.

senses.label: Without blemish
senses.definition: Physically spotless, like an unblemished sacrificial lamb, applied to Christ.

senses.label: Morally unstained
senses.definition: Kept free of moral defilement, whether a commandment, oneself, or believers awaiting Christ.

background.note: An inscription from about 300 BC applies it to sound, white, 'spotless' stones.

study.summary: A star, mostly the stars of the sky; once a star image of a pagan god.

senses.label: Stars of heaven
senses.definition: The heavenly bodies, as signs, navigation markers, or a picture of countless descendants.

senses.label: Star of a god
senses.definition: The star symbol of the god Rephan, carried in idolatry.

background.note: A calendar mentions astronomers noting the risings and settings of the stars.

study.summary: To make secure or fast, guard securely.

senses.label: Secure, make fast
senses.definition: To guard or fasten something securely against escape or theft, as the tomb, or prisoners' feet in stocks.

background.note: Common for securing or arresting a person or seizing goods.

study.summary: Without honor, dishonored or despised; comparative, less honorable.

senses.label: Without honor
senses.definition: Not given due respect, as a prophet in his hometown or apostles despised by the world.

senses.label: Less honorable
senses.definition: Comparative, of body parts regarded as less honorable.

background.note: Used from Homer for one unhonored; in Attic law it meant deprived of civic rights.

study.summary: An adverb meaning 'here' or 'there', in that very place.

senses.label: Here, there
senses.definition: In this or that place, of staying or being left somewhere.
senses.note: LUK 9:27 has this adverb in the critical text.

background.note: Used from Homer for 'just there' or 'in this very place'.

study.caution: Formally identical with the genitive pronoun αὐτοῦ ('his'), which is far more common; only context shows the adverb.

study.summary: Without fear; fearlessly, or in a bad sense shamelessly.

senses.label: Without fear
senses.definition: Free from fear or intimidation, in worship, in speaking the word, or in a visitor's safety.

senses.label: Without reverence
senses.definition: Without proper fear of God, shamelessly or irreverently.

background.note: Paired with speaking freely, 'fearlessly and boldly'.

study.summary: Foolishness, lack of sense; a vice in Mark and Paul's ironic 'folly' of boasting.

senses.label: Moral folly
senses.definition: Senselessness listed among the evils coming from the heart.

senses.label: Foolish boasting
senses.definition: Paul's ironic description of his own boasting, adopted to answer rivals.

background.note: Opposed to σωφροσύνη (sound-mindedness) and wisdom.
Used from Homer on for thoughtless folly.

study.summary: Voiceless, mute; of a silent lamb, dumb idols, a beast, or a sound without meaning.

senses.label: Silent, mute
senses.definition: Without voice or speech: the silent lamb of Isaiah, mute idols, a donkey that cannot speak.

senses.label: Without meaning
senses.definition: Of a language or sound: lacking signification.

background.note: A dumb child is among the cures recorded at Epidaurus.

study.summary: βαθύς means "deep," used literally of a well and figuratively of very early dawn, heavy sleep and the so-called "deep things" of Satan.

senses.label: Deep (physical depth)
senses.definition: Extending far down, as of a well.

senses.label: Deep, intense (time, sleep)
senses.definition: Figuratively of something at its fullest degree: the very earliest dawn, or a heavy, sound sleep.
senses.note: ὄρθρου βαθέως = "at early dawn," while it was still very early.

senses.label: Profound, hidden things
senses.definition: As a neuter plural noun, "deep things": secret teachings claimed by false teachers, ironically called the deep things of Satan.

background.note: Used of time in the same way as Luke's "deep dawn": "very late in the deep evening."

study.exegesisTip: In REV 2:24 "as they say" signals that "the deep things" was the false teachers' own boast; Christ relabels their esoteric knowledge as satanic.

study.summary: βαλάντιον is a purse or money-bag, mentioned in Jesus' instructions about what disciples should carry.

senses.label: Purse, money-bag
senses.definition: A small bag for carrying money; in Luke a symbol of provision for a journey and of where one's treasure is kept.
