study.exegesisTip: LUK 22:35-36 deliberately reverses the earlier mission instruction of LUK 10:4: the disciples now face a hostile world and must take a purse.

study.summary: βαπτισμός is an act of dipping or washing, used of Jewish ceremonial washings and, in HEB 6:2, of teaching about washings that may include Christian baptism.

senses.label: Ceremonial washing of objects
senses.definition: Ritual washing or rinsing of cups, pitchers and other vessels according to Jewish tradition.

senses.label: Ritual washings (lustrations)
senses.definition: Purification rites in general, including the various washings of the old covenant and, in Hebrews' list of basic teachings, instruction about washings.

study.translationNote: In HEB 6:2 some versions render "baptisms," others "washings" or "cleansing rites," reflecting uncertainty over whether Christian baptism is in view.
study.exegesisTip: βαπτισμός (the act) differs from βάπτισμα, the usual NT word for Christian baptism; the plural in HEB 6:2 likely means teaching that distinguished Christian baptism from other washings (Jewish rites, John's baptism).
study.caution: Whether HEB 6:2 refers to Christian baptism, Jewish purifications, or both is debated.

study.summary: βασίλισσα means "queen," a ruling queen or a woman who boasts of reigning as one.

senses.label: Queen
senses.definition: A female sovereign: the Queen of the South (Sheba) who sought Solomon's wisdom, and Candace, queen of the Ethiopians.

senses.label: Queen (figurative boast)
senses.definition: Babylon's proud self-description as an enthroned queen secure from loss.

background.note: The regular title for the wife of the reigning Ptolemaic king.

study.summary: βλαστάνω means to sprout or bud, and transitively to cause to grow or produce.

senses.label: Sprout, bud
senses.definition: Intransitive: of seed or plants springing up, and of Aaron's staff that miraculously budded.

senses.label: Produce, bring forth
senses.definition: Transitive: of the earth yielding its crop after rain.

study.summary: γείτων means a neighbor, someone who lives nearby.

senses.label: Neighbor
senses.definition: A person living close by, often grouped with friends and relatives as part of one's local circle.

background.note: Common in everyday documents, e.g. a complainant's suspicion against his neighbors.

study.exegesisTip: Unlike πλησίον (the "neighbor" to be loved), γείτων is simply the person next door.

study.summary: γλυκύς means sweet, used of fresh (not salt) water and of the scroll sweet as honey in the prophet's mouth.

senses.label: Fresh (of water)
senses.definition: Sweet, drinkable water as opposed to salty or bitter water.

senses.label: Sweet to the taste
senses.definition: Sweet like honey, contrasted with the bitterness that follows.

background.note: The superlative is common as a term of affection, e.g. "your sweetest native city."

study.exegesisTip: REV 10:9-10 echoes Ezekiel's scroll: God's word is sweet to receive, but its message of judgment is bitter to digest.

study.summary: γνήσιος, originally "legitimately born," means genuine or true, and as a noun the genuineness of something.

senses.label: True, genuine (relationship)
senses.definition: Genuine, legitimate in a relationship: a true child in the faith, a true yokefellow.

senses.label: Genuineness, sincerity
senses.definition: As a neuter noun, the genuine quality of something, here the sincerity of love.

background.note: Basic sense "lawfully begotten," contrasted with a bastard (νόθος).
In marriage contracts a γυνὴ γνησία is a lawful wedded wife.

study.exegesisTip: Calling Timothy and Titus his γνήσιον τέκνον, Paul uses the language of legitimate sonship: they are his authentic spiritual offspring and representatives.

study.summary: γογγυσμός is murmuring or grumbling, either low-voiced talk in a crowd or discontented complaint.

senses.label: Muttering, whispered talk
senses.definition: Low, private talk among a crowd, here debate about Jesus.

senses.label: Grumbling, complaint
senses.definition: Discontented complaining, whether a grievance against others or a grudging spirit in service.

background.note: Used of Israel's murmuring against God and Moses in the wilderness, the backdrop to PHP 2:14.

study.summary: γονυπετέω means to fall on one's knees, usually before someone in supplication.

senses.label: Kneel before in supplication
senses.definition: To fall on the knees before someone in earnest request or reverence.

senses.label: Kneel in mock homage
senses.definition: Of the soldiers kneeling before Jesus in pretended honor while mocking him.

study.summary: γυμνάζω, from athletic training, means to train or exercise, always figuratively in the NT.

senses.label: Train for godliness
senses.definition: To discipline oneself, or be trained by practice or by God's discipline, toward spiritual maturity.

senses.label: Trained in vice
senses.definition: Negatively, a heart thoroughly practiced in greed.

background.note: Used generally of training both body and soul.

study.exegesisTip: The word evokes the gymnasium: 1TI 4:7-8 contrasts bodily training with training in godliness.

study.summary: δαίμων, in Greek generally a divine power, means in the NT an evil spirit or demon.

senses.label: Demon, evil spirit
senses.definition: A hostile spiritual being that possesses people and haunts desolate places; equivalent to δαιμόνιον.

background.note: In Homer the word can denote a god or goddess, or divine power generally.
Still used positively of a guardian spirit: Nero is called the "good genius" of the world.

study.summary: δαμάζω means to tame or subdue, used of a violent demoniac, wild animals, and the untameable tongue.

senses.label: Subdue, bring under control
senses.definition: To overpower and restrain a person no one could hold.

senses.label: Tame
senses.definition: To domesticate animals, and figuratively to bring the tongue under control, which no human can do.

study.summary: δανείζω means to lend (money), and in the middle voice to borrow.

senses.label: Lend
senses.definition: To lend money or goods, ordinarily with expectation of repayment; Jesus calls for lending without such expectation.

senses.label: Borrow (middle voice)
senses.definition: To obtain a loan from someone.

background.note: A very common commercial term, e.g. "I lent to Theotimus 7½ artabae of wheat."

study.summary: δειπνέω means to eat the main meal of the day, to dine or have supper.

senses.label: Dine, eat supper
senses.definition: To take the principal (evening) meal, including the Last Supper ("after supper").

senses.label: Share a meal (fellowship)
senses.definition: Figuratively of Christ's intimate fellowship with the one who opens the door.

background.note: Invitations ask guests "to dine at the table of the lord Sarapis," illuminating the cultic meals Paul addresses in Corinth.

study.summary: δεκάτη is a tenth part, a tithe, used in Hebrews of Abraham's tithe to Melchizedek and the Levitical tithes.

senses.label: Tenth, tithe
senses.definition: A tenth portion given as an offering; Abraham's gift shows Melchizedek's superiority to Levi.

background.note: Abraham gives Melchizedek a tenth of everything, the text Hebrews expounds.

study.summary: δεσμωτήριον is a prison, a place where people are kept in bonds.

senses.label: Prison, jail
senses.definition: A place of confinement for prisoners, as for John the Baptist and the apostles.

background.note: Standard Attic word for a prison.

study.summary: δῆλος means clear or evident, chiefly in the phrase δῆλον ὅτι, "it is evident that."

senses.label: Evident, revealing
senses.definition: Making someone recognizable: Peter's accent gives him away.

senses.label: "It is clear that"
senses.definition: Impersonal δῆλον (ἐστιν) ὅτι introducing an obvious conclusion.

background.note: Same idiom: "that this is forbidden by the law is clear."

study.caution: In GAL 3:11 the structure is debated: δῆλον may state that no one is justified by the law, or (reading the ὅτι clauses differently) that the righteous will live by faith.

study.summary: δῆμος means the people, the populace of a Greek city, especially as gathered in assembly.

senses.label: The people, citizen assembly
senses.definition: The populace of a city, gathered publicly or as a civic assembly, before which accusations or defenses are made.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between "people," "crowd" and "assembly," depending on whether the word is taken as a formal civic body or a gathered mob.
study.exegesisTip: In ACT 19 the δῆμος meets in the theater, an irregular gathering that the town clerk contrasts with the lawful assembly (ἐκκλησία).
study.caution: Scholars differ on whether δῆμος in Acts is a technical term for the civic assembly or simply the crowd.

study.summary: δημόσιος means public, belonging to the people; its dative feminine δημοσίᾳ is used adverbially for "publicly."

senses.label: Public (property)
senses.definition: Belonging to the city or state, as the public jail.

senses.label: Publicly, in public
senses.definition: Adverbial δημοσίᾳ: openly, before the people.

study.exegesisTip: In ACT 20:20 "publicly and from house to house" describes Paul's teaching both in open settings and in homes.

study.summary: διαδίδωμι means to distribute, to give out portions to several recipients.

senses.label: Distribute, give out
senses.definition: To hand out among many: plunder divided up, possessions given to the poor, bread distributed, goods shared according to need.

background.note: Used of official distributions made through superintendents.

study.summary: διαρπάζω means to plunder thoroughly, used in Jesus' parable of binding the strong man.

senses.label: Plunder, carry off
senses.definition: To seize and carry off goods as plunder, picturing Jesus' victory over Satan in freeing those he held.

background.note: Used of plundering a city.

study.summary: διάφορος means different or various, and in the comparative "more excellent," surpassing others.

senses.label: Different, various
senses.definition: Differing from one another: varied gifts, various washings.

senses.label: More excellent (comparative)
senses.definition: Comparative διαφορώτερος: superior, surpassing, of Christ's name and ministry.

background.note: Plain sense "various": "the production of various persons."

study.summary: διηνεκής means continuous or unbroken; in the phrase εἰς τὸ διηνεκές it means "perpetually, for all time."

senses.label: Perpetually, for all time
senses.definition: Εἰς τὸ διηνεκές: without interruption, permanently; of Melchizedek's priesthood, of endlessly repeated sacrifices, and of Christ's once-for-all offering and its lasting effect.

background.note: The phrase εἰς τὸ διηνεκές appears in ordinary documents meaning "in perpetuity."

study.exegesisTip: Hebrews contrasts the endless repetition of the old sacrifices (HEB 10:1) with the permanent result of Christ's single sacrifice (HEB 10:14).
study.caution: In HEB 10:12 it is debated whether "for all time" goes with the single sacrifice offered or with his sitting down at God's right hand.

study.summary: δίκη means justice, especially a judicial sentence or penalty, and personified as the goddess Justice.

senses.label: Sentence, judgment
senses.definition: A judicial ruling requested against someone.

senses.label: Penalty, punishment
senses.definition: The penalty imposed in judgment, in the idioms "pay the penalty" and "undergo punishment."

senses.label: Justice personified
senses.definition: Dikē, the avenging goddess of justice in Greek belief, invoked by the Maltese islanders.

background.note: "That they may pay the fitting penalty (δίκην ὑπόσχωσι) for their disobedience," the same idiom as JUD 1:7.

study.summary: διορύσσω means to dig through, the burglar's method of breaking into a house through its wall.

senses.label: Break in, dig through
senses.definition: To break into a house by digging through its (often mud-brick) wall; used of thieves and of a house being broken into.

background.note: The exact phrase of the Gospels: a man charged "because he broke into a house."
Used of digging through a house wall.

study.summary: διπλοῦς means double or twofold.

senses.label: Double, twofold
senses.definition: Twice as much: double honor for elders, double repayment for Babylon.

senses.label: Twice as much (comparative)
senses.definition: Comparative διπλότερον: in twofold measure, twice as much a son of hell.

background.note: Common in contracts for double payments, e.g. "double the rent."

study.caution: Whether the "double honor" of 1TI 5:17 includes financial support is debated, though the following verse (wages) makes it likely.

study.summary: δίστομος, literally "double-mouthed," means two-edged, describing a sharp sword.

senses.label: Two-edged (sword)
senses.definition: Sharpened on both edges; an image of the penetrating word of God and of the sword proceeding from Christ's mouth.

background.note: Used of a two-edged sword.

study.summary: δόμα means a gift, something given.

senses.label: Gift
senses.definition: Something given, whether good gifts from parents, gifts given by the ascended Christ, or a material gift to Paul.

study.exegesisTip: In EPH 4:8 Paul applies Psalm 68 (LXX "received gifts") as "gave gifts," referring to the ministers Christ gives to the church.

study.summary: εἰδωλολατρεία means idolatry, the worship of idols, and by extension anything that takes God's place.

senses.label: Idol worship
senses.definition: Worship of images and false gods, including participation in pagan cultic rites.

senses.label: Greed as idolatry
senses.definition: Figuratively, covetousness, which gives possessions the devotion owed to God.

study.summary: εἰρηνεύω means to live at peace or keep the peace, used in the NT always of harmonious relations among people, especially within the believing community.

senses.label: Be at peace with others
senses.definition: To keep peace and live harmoniously with one another, as a fruit of shared life and mutual regard.
senses.note: In Rom 12:18 the scope widens to 'all people', qualified by 'if possible, as far as it depends on you'.

background.note: An Augustan inscription says land and sea 'are at peace', a picture of the Pax Romana.

study.exegesisTip: In every NT use the verb is a present imperative or participle: a continuing practice rather than a one-time reconciliation.

study.summary: εἴσειμι is a literary verb meaning to go in or enter, used of entering the temple, the sanctuary, or a person's presence.

senses.label: Go in, enter
senses.definition: To go into a place, especially the temple precincts or the first tent of the tabernacle, or to go in to see someone.
senses.note: In Acts 21:18 Paul 'went in' to James (πρὸς Ἰάκωβον); in Heb 9:6 the present tense pictures the priests' regular entry for their duties.

background.note: Very common in notices of time, e.g. 'the coming month' (τοῦ εἰσιόντος μηνός).

study.summary: εὐοδόω, literally 'to have a good journey', is used in the NT in the passive of being prospered or succeeding, whether in travel plans, income, or general well-being.

senses.label: Succeed in a journey
senses.definition: To be granted success in getting somewhere; Paul prays that by God's will he may at last succeed in coming to Rome.

senses.label: Prosper, do well
senses.definition: To fare well or be prospered, of material gain set aside for the collection or of a person's overall welfare matching the health of the soul.
senses.note: In 1 Cor 16:2 'as he may prosper' means in proportion to what one has gained.

background.note: In the LXX it chiefly renders Hebrew tsalach, 'to prosper, succeed', often of God granting success to a person's way.

study.exegesisTip: The passive voice in all NT uses frames success as something granted (by God), not achieved.
study.caution: 3 John 2 is often cited for a promise of material prosperity; John is expressing a customary letter-opening wish for the recipient's welfare, not stating a doctrine.

study.summary: εὐσεβής describes a person who is devout or godly, showing genuine reverence for God in conduct.

senses.label: Devout, godly
senses.definition: Reverent toward God and faithful in religious duty; used of the God-fearer Cornelius and his soldier, of Ananias, and of the godly whom the Lord rescues.
senses.note: In 2 Pet 2:9 the godly are contrasted with the unrighteous (ἀδίκους).

background.note: Opposed to δυσσεβής, 'impious', and used of piety and discharging sacred duties.

study.caution: In Acts 22:12 many manuscripts read εὐλαβής ('devout') instead, so some translations rest on a different word there.

study.summary: ζημία means loss or damage, used of material loss in the shipwreck narrative and of Paul's counting his former advantages as loss for Christ.

senses.label: Material loss, damage
senses.definition: Damage or loss to ship, cargo, and life incurred through a dangerous voyage.

senses.label: Loss in spiritual reckoning
senses.definition: Something reckoned as a debit rather than a gain; Paul counts his former privileges and all things as loss compared with knowing Christ.
senses.note: Set directly against κέρδος, 'gain', in accounting language.

background.note: Commonly opposed to κέρδος, 'gain', as Paul does in Phil 3:7.

study.exegesisTip: Phil 3:7-8 uses bookkeeping terms (gain, loss, reckon): Paul moves his assets into the loss column.

study.summary: ζόφος denotes deep, gloomy darkness, especially the darkness of the underworld reserved for fallen angels and false teachers.

senses.label: Darkness of judgment
senses.definition: The gloom of the place of punishment, where rebellious angels are kept and the 'blackest darkness' is reserved for the ungodly.
senses.note: The phrase ὁ ζόφος τοῦ σκότους intensifies the idea: 'the gloom of darkness'.

senses.label: Gloom at Sinai
senses.definition: The physical darkness surrounding the Sinai theophany.
senses.note: Found in the critical text; other manuscripts read σκότος here.

background.note: In Homer the word denotes the gloom of the nether world, the realm allotted to Hades.

study.summary: ζυμόω means to leaven, to cause dough to ferment and rise, used in parables and proverbs about pervasive influence.

senses.label: Leaven the whole
senses.definition: Of leaven working through flour or dough until all of it is affected; an image of the kingdom's hidden, spreading growth or of corruption spreading through a community.
senses.note: In the parable the image is positive; in Paul's proverb it is a warning about tolerated sin or false teaching.

background.note: Used of dough that had or had not been leavened in the Exodus Passover account.

study.caution: The same image carries opposite values in the Gospels and Paul; context, not the word, determines whether leaven is good or bad.

study.summary: θεραπεία means service or care, and in the NT either healing (medical care) or, collectively, a household of servants.

senses.label: Healing, cure
senses.definition: Care that restores health; those in need of healing, and the healing of the nations by the leaves of the tree of life.

senses.label: Household servants
senses.definition: The body of domestic attendants placed under a steward who must give them food at the proper time.
senses.note: In Matt 24:45 the critical text reads οἰκετεία instead.

background.note: Used of someone staying at a temple of Isis for medical treatment of an illness.

study.summary: θορυβέω means to make an uproar or be in a commotion, used of noisy mourners and of stirring a city into a riot.

senses.label: Make a noisy commotion
senses.definition: Middle/passive: to be in an uproar, especially of loud, demonstrative mourning; hence 'do not be alarmed' or 'stop the commotion'.

senses.label: Throw into uproar
senses.definition: Active, transitive: to throw a city into confusion and disorder.

background.note: Used in a letter: 'do not be disturbed, for when you come you will know what it means'.

study.summary: θρηνέω means to lament or wail, especially to sing a dirge or mourn aloud for the dead.

senses.label: Sing a dirge, wail
senses.definition: To lament aloud, as in funeral songs or the grief of the disciples while the world rejoices.

senses.label: Bewail someone
senses.definition: With a person as object: to mourn for someone, as the women did for Jesus on the way to the cross.

background.note: Used of the Muses singing a dirge in turn for Achilles.

study.summary: θρησκεία denotes religion as expressed in worship and practice, whether Jewish observance, misguided angel-worship, or the true religion James defines.

senses.label: Religion, religious practice
senses.definition: A system of worship and religious observance; Paul's Jewish faith, and religion that James tests by conduct toward the needy and personal purity.

senses.label: Worship of angels
senses.definition: Cultic veneration directed toward angels, or possibly worship such as angels perform, which the false teachers at Colossae promoted.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James redefines 'pure religion' not by ritual but by caring for orphans and widows and keeping unstained by the world.

background.note: Herodotus uses it of religious observance concerning sacred rites.

study.caution: In Col 2:18 'worship of angels' may mean worship offered to angels or worship performed by angels (visionary participation); interpreters differ.

study.summary: θυρωρός is a doorkeeper or porter, a servant charged with watching and opening the door or gate.

senses.label: Doorkeeper, gatekeeper
senses.definition: A man or woman stationed at a door or gate to guard it and admit people: the servant told to keep watch, the gatekeeper of the sheepfold, and the servant girl at the high priest's courtyard.
senses.note: In John 18:16-17 the doorkeeper is a woman (ἡ θυρωρός).

background.note: Women doorkeepers are attested in papyri, illustrating the servant girl of John 18.

study.summary: καθίημι means to let down or lower something, used by Luke of lowering a paralytic through a roof, Paul over a wall, and the sheet in Peter's vision.

senses.label: Let down, lower
senses.definition: To lower someone or something from above, through a roof or wall, or (in a vision) down from heaven.

background.note: Homer uses it of lowering sails into ships.

study.summary: καθό means 'as' or 'according as', expressing manner or proportion.

senses.label: As, in the way that
senses.definition: Expresses the manner required: we do not know how to pray as we ought.

senses.label: In proportion as
senses.definition: According to the measure of something: a gift is acceptable according to what one has, and believers rejoice to the degree that they share Christ's sufferings.

study.exegesisTip: In 1 Pet 4:13 καθό can mean 'insofar as' (proportion) rather than simply 'because', tying the measure of joy to the measure of shared suffering.

study.summary: κακολογέω means to speak evil of, revile, or curse someone or something.

senses.label: Curse, revile
senses.definition: To speak abusively of a person; in the quoted Mosaic law, cursing father or mother, and in Mark, speaking evil of Jesus.

senses.label: Malign a teaching
senses.definition: To speak evil publicly of the Christian movement, 'the Way'.

background.note: Used in a complaint of someone who 'insulted me immoderately with much shameful abuse'.

study.summary: κακοπαθέω means to suffer hardship or misfortune, and to endure it patiently.

senses.label: Endure hardship
senses.definition: To bear trouble and affliction willingly for the gospel, like a soldier or an evangelist.
senses.note: In 2 Tim 2:3 the critical text reads the compound συγκακοπάθησον, 'share in suffering'.

senses.label: Be in trouble
senses.definition: To be in distress or suffering misfortune of any kind, the situation that calls for prayer.

background.note: Thucydides and Xenophon use it of being in distress or hardship.

study.summary: κακοποιέω means to do evil or harm, the opposite of doing good.

senses.label: Do harm
senses.definition: To inflict harm, contrasted with doing good and saving life on the Sabbath.

senses.label: Do wrong morally
senses.definition: To practise evil conduct, as opposed to doing good; suffering for wrongdoing, and the evildoer who has not seen God.

background.note: A warning: 'if you do not stop your malpractices in the village you will repent it'.

study.exegesisTip: Each NT use pairs it with ἀγαθοποιέω ('do good'), so the meaning is defined by the contrast.

study.summary: κακοῦργος is a criminal or evildoer, used of the men crucified with Jesus and of Paul imprisoned as if a criminal.

senses.label: Criminal, malefactor
senses.definition: One who commits serious crime and is treated accordingly by the authorities.
senses.note: Paul says he is chained 'as a criminal', though the word of God is not bound.

background.note: Someone was put in prison on the claim that he was a criminal.

study.summary: κάλυμμα means a covering or veil, used by Paul of Moses' veil and of the veil that lies over Israel's understanding of Scripture.

senses.label: Moses' face veil
senses.definition: The literal veil Moses put over his face after speaking with God.

senses.label: Veil over understanding
senses.definition: A figurative covering on the heart and mind that prevents grasping the old covenant's meaning, removed when one turns to the Lord.

background.note: Used of the veil Moses put on his face in Exodus 34, the passage Paul expounds.

study.exegesisTip: 2 Cor 3:16 echoes Exod 34:34, where Moses removed the veil whenever he went in before the Lord.

study.summary: κάμινος is a furnace or kiln, used as an image of fiery judgment and of intense heat and smoke.

senses.label: Furnace of judgment
senses.definition: The 'furnace of fire' into which the wicked are cast at the end of the age.
senses.note: Recalls the fiery furnace of Daniel 3.

senses.label: Furnace as comparison
senses.definition: A burning furnace as an image for glowing refined metal or billowing smoke.

background.note: A kiln or furnace for smelting, baking, or firing bricks.

study.summary: κάμπτω means to bend, used in the NT only of bending the knee in worship or submission.

senses.label: Bow the knee
senses.definition: To kneel as an act of worship, prayer, or homage, whether to Baal, to God in prayer, or universally to God and to Jesus.
senses.note: Rom 14:11 and Phil 2:10 echo Isa 45:23, applied in Philippians to the name of Jesus.

study.exegesisTip: Phil 2:10 applies to Jesus a text (Isa 45:23) in which every knee bows to the LORD alone.

study.summary: κατάγνυμι means to break, used of not breaking a bruised reed and of breaking the legs of the crucified.

senses.label: Break
senses.definition: To break or snap something, literally the legs of crucified men to hasten death, and figuratively the Servant's gentleness that will not break a bruised reed.

background.note: The augmented form κατέαξαν appears of breaking the doors of houses.

study.exegesisTip: The soldiers' not breaking Jesus' legs (John 19:33) sets up John's following note that Scripture was fulfilled about his bones.

study.summary: κατακαυχάομαι means to boast against or triumph over someone or something.

senses.label: Boast against
senses.definition: To exult arrogantly over others; Gentile believers boasting over the broken-off branches, or boasting that lies against the truth.

senses.label: Triumph over
senses.definition: To prevail over and have the last word; mercy triumphs over judgment.

study.summary: κατακλυσμός means a flood or deluge, used in the NT exclusively of Noah's flood.

senses.label: Noah's flood
senses.definition: The great deluge that swept away the ungodly world of Noah's day, used as a pattern of sudden judgment.

background.note: Plato uses it of great floods that destroyed earlier civilizations.
In Genesis it renders mabbul, the technical term for Noah's flood.

study.summary: κατακυριεύω means to exercise dominion over or subdue, often with the connotation of domineering power.

senses.label: Lord it over
senses.definition: To rule over others in a domineering way, as Gentile rulers do and as church elders must not.

senses.label: Overpower
senses.definition: To gain mastery over by force, as the demonized man did to the sons of Sceva.

background.note: Used in the creation mandate to 'subdue' the earth.

study.summary: καταλλαγή means reconciliation, the change from enmity to friendship, used by Paul of God's reconciling the world to himself through Christ.

senses.label: Reconciliation with God
senses.definition: The restored relationship between God and sinners that God accomplishes through Christ, received as a gift and proclaimed in a ministry and message.

study.translationNote: The KJV renders Rom 5:11 'atonement', in the older sense 'at-one-ment'; modern versions read 'reconciliation'.

background.note: Demosthenes uses it of reconciliation between hostile parties.

study.exegesisTip: In Paul, God is always the reconciler and humans (or the world) the reconciled; the initiative lies with God.

study.summary: καταμαρτυρέω means to testify against someone, used in the Gospels of the accusations at Jesus' trials.

senses.label: Testify against
senses.definition: To bring evidence or charges against an accused person, as witnesses and accusers did before the high priest and Pilate.
senses.note: In Mark 15:4 the critical text reads κατηγοροῦσιν ('accuse').

background.note: A standard legal term in Attic orators for bearing witness against someone.

study.summary: καταξιόω means to count or deem worthy, always in the NT of being judged worthy by God.

senses.label: Be counted worthy
senses.definition: To be judged fit by God for a privilege: sharing in the coming age and resurrection, escaping coming judgments, suffering for Jesus' name, or the kingdom of God.
senses.note: In Luke 21:36 the critical text reads κατισχύσητε ('have strength').

background.note: Like the simple verb, it means 'count worthy', not 'make worthy'; the passive is attested in papyri.

study.caution: The verb means 'deem worthy', not 'make worthy'; it describes God's verdict rather than a process of earning merit.

study.summary: καταπαύω means to bring to rest or restrain, and intransitively to rest, used in Hebrews of God's rest and the rest of his people.

senses.label: Restrain, stop
senses.definition: To hold others back from doing something.

senses.label: Give rest
senses.definition: To bring a people into rest, as Joshua did only provisionally.

senses.label: Rest from works
senses.definition: To cease from work and rest, as God did on the seventh day and as believers do on entering his rest.

background.note: Homer uses the active sense 'put an end to', of stopping the anger of the gods.

study.summary: κατασείω means to wave or motion with the hand, a speaker's gesture to call a crowd to silence.

senses.label: Motion with the hand
senses.definition: To shake or wave the hand as a signal, especially to quiet a crowd before speaking.

study.summary: To settle or take up lodging somewhere: used of birds nesting in the branches of the grown mustard plant, and of the body resting in hope.

senses.label: Nest, settle (of birds)
senses.definition: Of birds coming to roost or nest in the branches or shade of the mustard plant grown into a tree, picturing the kingdom's surprising growth.

senses.label: Dwell, rest securely
senses.definition: To abide or rest settled; in Peter's quotation of Psalm 16, the body 'will rest in hope', applied to Christ's resurrection.

background.note: In classical prose the verb is used of troops taking up their quarters or encamping.

study.summary: An accusation or formal charge brought against someone.

senses.label: Charge, accusation
senses.definition: A charge laid against a person, whether in court (Pilate's question), as grounds sought against Jesus, or as a complaint against a church elder.
senses.note: In LUK 6:7 the critical text reads the related verb instead of this noun.

senses.label: Open to the charge of
senses.definition: With a genitive of the fault: being liable to an accusation of a certain vice, here of dissipation among an elder's children.

background.note: Standard classical word for an accusation, often set against a defence speech.
Used in a legal setting of the proofs supporting an accusation before a lawsuit.

study.summary: To scorch or burn with heat, used of sun-withered seedlings and of people seared in the fourth bowl judgment.

senses.label: Be scorched (plants)
senses.definition: Passive: of shallow-rooted seedlings burnt by the rising sun and withering, an image of shallow reception of the word.

senses.label: Scorch (people in judgment)
senses.definition: Of the sun given power to sear people with fire, and of people scorched with fierce heat in the plague of the fourth bowl.

study.summary: To shear (a sheep) or, in the middle voice, to have one's hair cut off.

senses.label: Shear a sheep
senses.definition: To shear; in the quotation of Isaiah 53 the silent lamb before its shearer pictures the Servant's silent submission.

senses.label: Have one's hair cut
senses.definition: Middle: to have one's hair cut short or cut off, whether in connection with a vow or as a shameful act for a woman in Paul's argument about head-covering.

background.note: Used in a papyrus of shearing sheep.

study.caution: In ACT 18:18 the grammar allows either Paul or Aquila to be the one who had his hair cut under a vow; most interpreters take it of Paul.

study.summary: A sharp point: the sting of a scorpion-like creature, the sting of death, or a goad for driving animals.

senses.label: Sting
senses.definition: The stinging tail of the scorpion-like locusts of Revelation, and metaphorically the sting of death, which Paul identifies as sin.

senses.label: Goad
senses.definition: A pointed stick for driving oxen; 'to kick against the goads' is a proverb for futile resistance to a superior power.

background.note: Used from Homer onward of the goad for driving horses, and the proverb about kicking against the goads is classical.

study.summary: A Latin loanword (census) for the Roman poll-tax, the tax at issue in the question about paying tribute to Caesar.

senses.label: Poll-tax, tribute
senses.definition: The capitation tax levied by Rome or by kings on subjects; the coin 'of the tax' was the denarius.

background.note: Also used of a census conducted by a Roman census officer.

study.exegesisTip: In MAT 17:25 it is paired with customs duties, contrasting direct tax on persons with tolls on goods.

study.summary: A lyre or harp, a stringed instrument used in Paul's illustration and in the heavenly worship of Revelation.

senses.label: Lyre, harp
senses.definition: A stringed instrument; Paul uses it to illustrate that sound must be distinct to be understood, and in Revelation the elders and the victorious saints hold harps in worship.

background.note: The ordinary classical word for the lyre.

study.summary: To be in danger or at risk, whether of physical peril or of an undesirable outcome.

senses.label: Be in physical danger
senses.definition: To be in peril of one's life, as the disciples in the swamping boat or Paul facing danger every hour.

senses.label: Run the risk of
senses.definition: With an infinitive: to be in danger that something will happen, such as a trade falling into disrepute or a town being charged with riot.

background.note: A soldier writes that Serapis saved him when he was in danger at sea.

study.summary: A branch or shoot of a vine, used by Jesus for disciples who live from union with him, the true vine.

senses.label: Vine branch
senses.definition: A branch of the grapevine; disciples are branches that bear fruit only by remaining in Christ, while fruitless branches are removed and burned.

background.note: Used of vine-cuttings gathered in vineyard work.

study.summary: A bed, especially the marriage bed, and by extension sexual intercourse or conception.

senses.label: Bed
senses.definition: An ordinary bed in which a household sleeps.

senses.label: Marriage bed
senses.definition: The marriage bed as the sphere of marital union, to be kept undefiled.

senses.label: Sexual relations, conception
senses.definition: Sexual intercourse: 'having a bed' of a woman conceiving by one man; in the plural, illicit sexual indulgence.

background.note: Used of a sickbed in a letter by a woman too ill to get up.
Classical writers already use it especially of the marriage bed.

study.summary: To cut short or shorten, used of God curtailing the days of the great distress for the sake of the elect.

senses.label: Cut short (time)
senses.definition: To curtail a period; God shortens the days of tribulation so that some may be saved.

background.note: Its basic sense is to mutilate or cut off, as of cutting off hands and feet.

study.summary: A skull, used in the Gospels to translate the Aramaic name Golgotha, the place of the crucifixion.

senses.label: Skull (place name)
senses.definition: The Greek rendering of Golgotha, 'Place of the Skull', where Jesus was crucified.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke gives only the Greek name, 'the place called Skull', omitting the Aramaic Golgotha.

study.translationNote: The KJV's 'Calvary' in LUK 23:33 comes from the Latin calvaria, 'skull'; modern versions translate it 'The Skull'.
study.caution: The reason for the name (the shape of the hill, or skulls of the executed) is not stated in the text.

study.summary: To strengthen; in the passive, to grow or become strong, physically or spiritually.

senses.label: Grow strong
senses.definition: Passive: to grow strong, of John and Jesus maturing 'in spirit' as children, and of believers urged to be strong.
senses.note: In LUK 2:40 the critical text lacks 'in spirit'.

senses.label: Be strengthened by the Spirit
senses.definition: To be made strong with power through God's Spirit in the inner person.

background.note: Common in the Septuagint, e.g. of strengthening someone's hands.

study.summary: 'Most excellent', a respectful title of address used for people of high rank.

senses.label: Most excellent (honorific)
senses.definition: A title of honour like 'Your Excellency', used of the Roman governors Felix and Festus and of Theophilus.

background.note: Common as an honorific title in addressing high officials such as a prefect.

study.caution: Whether the title implies that Theophilus held an official rank, or is simply courteous address, is debated.

study.summary: 'Better', the neuter of the comparative of 'good', used of what is more advantageous or more excellent.

senses.label: Better, preferable
senses.definition: More advantageous or desirable: better to marry than to burn, better not to give a virgin in marriage, and departing to be with Christ as far better.

senses.label: Better things
senses.definition: Plural: better things that belong with salvation, confidently expected of the readers.

study.summary: A possession or piece of property, especially land.

senses.label: Possessions, wealth
senses.definition: Plural: one's property or possessions, such as the rich young man's great holdings or what believers sold to share with the needy.

senses.label: Piece of land
senses.definition: A single piece of property or field, such as that sold by Ananias.

background.note: Frequently used of an allotment of land or a vineyard.

study.summary: A domestic animal, especially a beast of burden for riding or carrying, or livestock in general.

senses.label: Mount, pack animal
senses.definition: An animal for riding, such as the Samaritan's mount or the animals provided for Paul.

senses.label: Livestock, animals
senses.definition: Animals generally, as cattle among the cargoes of Babylon, or land animals distinguished from fish and birds.

background.note: Used specifically of donkeys as beasts of burden.

study.summary: A created thing or creature, anything made by God.

senses.label: Creature, created thing
senses.definition: Something God has made: every creature is good, believers are firstfruits of his creatures, and all creatures praise God and the Lamb.

study.summary: Crippled or maimed, especially through a deformed or missing limb.

senses.label: Crippled
senses.definition: Deformed or disabled in a limb, among the sick brought to Jesus and healed.

senses.label: Maimed
senses.definition: Missing a limb; Jesus says it is better to enter life maimed than to keep a hand or foot that causes sin.

background.note: In medical writers it describes a club-footed or deformed limb.

study.summary: A little dog or house dog, used in Jesus' exchange with the Gentile woman.

senses.label: Little dog, house dog
senses.definition: A small dog under the household table; Jesus contrasts the children's bread with the little dogs, and the woman answers that even they eat the crumbs.

background.note: A diminutive of the word for dog, 'little dog, puppy', in classical prose.

study.exegesisTip: The household setting (children, table, crumbs) suggests pet dogs rather than street scavengers.
study.caution: How much the diminutive softens the term is debated, since diminutives had often lost their force in Koine.

study.summary: Lordship or dominion, used of ranks of spiritual powers and of authority that false teachers despise.

senses.label: Dominion (spiritual power)
senses.definition: A class of supernatural powers, listed with rulers and authorities, created through Christ and subject to him.

senses.label: Authority, lordship
senses.definition: Authority that is rejected or despised by the ungodly.

study.caution: In 2PE 2:10 and JUD 1:8 interpreters differ over whether the authority despised is the Lord's, angelic powers, or human authority.

study.summary: To obtain by lot or receive as one's portion, and once to cast lots.

senses.label: Be chosen by lot
senses.definition: To be selected by lot for a duty, as Zechariah for offering incense.

senses.label: Receive, obtain
senses.definition: To receive as one's allotted portion, as Judas his share in the ministry or believers a faith of equal standing.

senses.label: Cast lots
senses.definition: To draw lots to decide something, as the soldiers did for Jesus' tunic.

background.note: An inscription speaks of a priest chosen by lot.

study.exegesisTip: In 2PE 1:1 the verb stresses that faith is received as a gift allotted by God, not achieved.

study.summary: Secretly or privately, without others knowing.

senses.label: Secretly, privately
senses.definition: Done out of public view: Joseph planned to divorce Mary quietly, Herod summoned the Magi in secret, Martha called Mary aside, and the magistrates wanted to release Paul quietly.

background.note: Used of flax secretly carried off.

study.summary: Speech or talk, including a person's way of speaking or accent.

senses.label: Accent, way of speaking
senses.definition: The distinctive Galilean manner of speech that gave Peter away.

senses.label: Words, what is said
senses.definition: What someone says: the woman's report, or Jesus' speech that his opponents could not understand.

background.note: Classically it often meant chatter or idle talk.

study.exegesisTip: In JOH 8:43 Jesus distinguishes his speech, which they fail to grasp, from his word, which they cannot bear to hear.

study.summary: A garden herb or vegetable.

senses.label: Garden plant, vegetable
senses.definition: Cultivated plants or herbs: the mustard grows larger than all garden plants, Pharisees tithe every herb, and the weak in faith eat only vegetables.

background.note: Used of vegetables sold at market.

study.summary: A Roman legion (Latin legio), used for an enormous number, of angels or of demons.

senses.label: Legion (vast number)
senses.definition: A legion of about six thousand soldiers, used of more than twelve legions of angels at Jesus' disposal.

senses.label: Legion (demon name)
senses.definition: The name given by the demons possessing the Gerasene man, because they were many.

background.note: Common in papyri of soldiers serving in a legion.

study.summary: Leprosy, a disfiguring skin disease that made a person ritually unclean.

senses.label: Leprosy
senses.definition: A serious skin disease that excluded people from community and worship; Jesus touched and cleansed a man full of it.

background.note: Classical writers use it of a disease that makes the skin scaly.

study.caution: The biblical term covers a range of skin conditions and is not limited to modern leprosy (Hansen's disease).

study.summary: To revile or abuse someone with insulting words.

senses.label: Revile, insult
senses.definition: To heap verbal abuse on someone, as the Pharisees on the healed blind man or Paul toward the high priest; Paul and Christ, when reviled, did not retaliate.

background.note: Rules of a religious association fine a member found reviling another.

study.summary: To be a disciple, or transitively to make disciples of others.

senses.label: Be or become a disciple
senses.definition: To be a disciple of Jesus, or to be trained as a disciple for the kingdom of heaven.
senses.note: In MAT 27:57 the Byzantine text has the active (was a disciple), the critical text the passive (had become a disciple).

senses.label: Make disciples
senses.definition: To make disciples of people, the commission to the nations and the work of Paul and Barnabas in Derbe.

study.exegesisTip: In MAT 28:19 'make disciples' is the main command; going, baptizing and teaching describe how it is done.

study.summary: Soft, of luxurious clothing; of men, soft or effeminate in a sexual sense.

senses.label: Soft, fine (clothing)
senses.definition: Soft, luxurious garments such as courtiers wear, contrasted with John the Baptist.

senses.label: Effeminate (sexual sense)
senses.definition: In a vice list, men who are 'soft', most likely those taking the passive role in male homosexual acts.

study.translationNote: Versions differ for 1CO 6:9: older ones say 'effeminate', while many modern ones combine it with the following word as 'men who practice homosexuality'.

background.note: A musician is described as 'the soft one', probably in the same sense as in 1 Corinthians.

study.caution: The precise reference in 1CO 6:9 is debated; most lexicons take it of the passive partner in male sexual relations.

study.summary: An Aramaic loanword for wealth or possessions, used by Jesus of money viewed as a rival master to God.

senses.label: Wealth as rival master
senses.definition: Riches or property, personified as a master that claims a person's service in competition with God.

senses.label: Wealth, worldly riches
senses.definition: Material possessions as something to be used faithfully and generously; called 'unrighteous' because it belongs to this present, corrupt order.

study.translationNote: Older versions keep the loanword 'mammon'; modern versions translate it as 'money', 'wealth' or 'worldly wealth'.
study.exegesisTip: In LUK 16:9 and 16:11 the phrase 'mammon of unrighteousness' describes wealth as belonging to this unjust age, not necessarily money gained dishonestly.

study.summary: A fight or battle, used in the NT of quarrels, disputes and conflicts rather than military combat.

senses.label: Quarrel, dispute
senses.definition: Strife and contention, especially arguments arising from speculative questions or debates about the law.

senses.label: Conflicts, fightings
senses.definition: Hostile clashes and opposition, whether outward troubles Paul faced or bitter conflicts within a community.
senses.note: In JAM 4:1, paired with πόλεμοι, it may carry something of its stronger sense 'fights'.

background.note: In Homer and classical Greek the word chiefly means a battle or combat between armies.
A fortune-telling papyrus uses the plural for domestic quarrels, the weaker sense found in the NT.

study.summary: To fight, and by extension to quarrel or dispute with words.

senses.label: Fight physically
senses.definition: To come to blows, as the two Israelites whom Moses tried to reconcile.

senses.label: Quarrel, dispute
senses.definition: To contend in words or with hostile attitude; to be quarrelsome.

background.note: A fourth-century letter uses the verb figuratively of stubbornly fighting against one's fate.

study.summary: To make drunk; in the passive, to get drunk or become intoxicated.

senses.label: Get drunk
senses.definition: To become intoxicated with wine, condemned as part of a careless, dissolute life.

senses.label: Intoxicated, figuratively
senses.definition: Made drunk by the 'wine' of Babylon's immorality, i.e. seduced and stupefied by her influence.

study.exegesisTip: EPH 5:18 contrasts being made drunk with wine with being filled by the Spirit: two opposing sources of control.

study.summary: Honey, mentioned as part of John the Baptist's wilderness diet and as an image of sweetness.

senses.label: Honey as food
senses.definition: Wild honey found in the desert, eaten by John the Baptist with locusts.

senses.label: Sweet as honey
senses.definition: A comparison for the sweetness of the scroll in the prophet's mouth, echoing Ezekiel's experience.

background.note: Honey appears in everyday use, for example in a medical prescription mixing honey and rose-extract.

study.summary: Midnight, the middle of the night.

senses.label: Midnight
senses.definition: The middle of the night, sometimes as one of the night watches, used to mark the time of an event.

background.note: A third-century letter uses the same phrase as ACT 16:25, 'about midnight'.

study.summary: In the middle voice, to send for someone or summon them to oneself.

senses.label: Send for, summon
senses.definition: To call someone to come from another place, usually by sending a messenger.

background.note: Used in the same middle sense of an emperor summoning someone to his presence.

study.summary: To transform or change into another form, used of Jesus' transfiguration and of believers' inner transformation.

senses.label: Transfigured
senses.definition: Of Jesus visibly changed in appearance before the three disciples, his glory shining out.

senses.label: Transformed inwardly
senses.definition: Of believers progressively changed in character into Christ's likeness by the renewal of the mind and the work of the Spirit.

background.note: A magical papyrus speaks of a god who is transformed into all forms.

study.exegesisTip: In ROM 12:2 the verb stands in contrast to being 'conformed' to this age: a change from within rather than outward pressure.

study.summary: A change of dwelling, deportation; in the NT the Babylonian exile.

senses.label: Babylonian exile
senses.definition: The deportation of Judah to Babylon, used as a turning point in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus.

background.note: Used in the Greek Old Testament of the captivity of the Jews.

study.summary: To disclose or make known, including the legal sense of reporting information to authorities.

senses.label: Report, inform
senses.definition: To give information to authorities about a person's whereabouts or a plot.

senses.label: Make known, indicate
senses.definition: To point out or reveal something, whether in Scripture or by a remark.

background.note: Used in the forensic sense, inviting anyone to report a runaway slave to officials.

study.summary: To mix or mingle one thing with another.

senses.label: Mix, mingle
senses.definition: To combine substances, whether literally (wine with gall) or in grim or visionary images (blood with sacrifices, hail and fire with blood, a sea of glass with fire).

study.summary: To imitate or follow the example of someone or something.

senses.label: Imitate a person
senses.definition: To follow the example set by apostles or leaders in conduct and faith.

senses.label: Imitate a quality
senses.definition: To copy what is good rather than what is evil.

background.note: A second-century document urges 'imitate your father', showing the everyday sense.

study.summary: A hired worker paid wages, as opposed to an owner or family member.

senses.label: Hired worker
senses.definition: A wage-earning labourer, such as the men working in Zebedee's fishing boat.

senses.label: Hireling shepherd
senses.definition: A hired hand who tends sheep for pay and flees in danger because he has no real care for them, contrasted with the good shepherd.

background.note: Frequently used of mercenary soldiers.

study.summary: Adultery: sexual unfaithfulness involving a married person.

senses.label: Adultery
senses.definition: Breaking the marriage covenant by sexual relations with someone other than one's spouse; listed among sins that come from the heart and works of the flesh.

background.note: The standard Attic word for adultery.

study.summary: An adulterer, one who violates marriage; once figuratively of spiritual unfaithfulness to God.

senses.label: Adulterer
senses.definition: A man who has sexual relations with another's wife or is unfaithful to his own marriage; named among those under God's judgment.

senses.label: Spiritually unfaithful
senses.definition: Those who betray their covenant loyalty to God by friendship with the world.

background.note: Aristophanes alludes to the shaving of the head as a punishment for an adulterer.

study.summary: A mill or millstone, especially the large stone turned by a donkey.

senses.label: Millstone
senses.definition: The heavy grinding stone; a 'donkey millstone' hung around the neck pictures certain, drowning judgment, and a great stone thrown into the sea pictures Babylon's fall.

senses.label: Mill, grinding
senses.definition: A hand mill and its sound, a sign of ordinary daily life.

background.note: A lease requires a mill to be returned safe and uninjured.

study.summary: To make foolish; in the passive, to become foolish, or of salt to become tasteless.

senses.label: Make foolish
senses.definition: To show something to be folly; God exposes the wisdom of the world as foolish.

senses.label: Become foolish
senses.definition: To become fools, of those who rejected God while claiming wisdom.

senses.label: Lose taste
senses.definition: Of salt that has become insipid and useless.

background.note: In classical Greek the verb is intransitive, 'to be foolish, play the fool'.

study.summary: Victory, a later form of νίκη.

senses.label: Victory
senses.definition: Triumph or conquest, of justice brought to victory and of God's victory over death through Christ.

background.note: Used apparently of victory in a lawsuit.
The phrase εἰς νῖκος often means 'for ever' in the Greek Old Testament.

study.exegesisTip: The phrase 'into victory' in MAT 12:20 and 1CO 15:54 echoes Old Testament wording where it can also carry the sense 'finally, for ever'.

study.summary: A household servant or domestic slave.

senses.label: Household servant
senses.definition: A servant belonging to a household and answerable to its master.

background.note: Used in a legal text of a slave belonging to another master.

study.summary: To make old; in the passive, to grow old or wear out; of a covenant, to declare or make obsolete.

senses.label: Wear out
senses.definition: Of things worn out by time and use, like purses or clothes.

senses.label: Make obsolete
senses.definition: To treat or declare something as old and passing away, of the first covenant superseded by the new.

background.note: Used of a temple building that had grown old.

study.summary: To overstep or transgress, and also to turn aside or depart.

senses.label: Transgress, break
senses.definition: To violate a tradition or a command.

senses.label: Turn aside, abandon
senses.definition: To fall away from or desert a position, as Judas did from his apostleship.

background.note: Used of breaking oaths.

study.summary: To provoke to jealousy or rivalry.

senses.label: Provoke to jealousy
senses.definition: To arouse jealousy in someone, whether God stirring Israel through the Gentiles or believers provoking the Lord by idolatry.

background.note: Used in the Greek Old Testament of provoking God to jealousy by sin.

study.exegesisTip: Paul's use in Romans draws on Deuteronomy 32:21: God's mercy to Gentiles is meant to stir Israel to return.

study.summary: To follow closely or accompany, and figuratively to investigate carefully or follow a teaching.

senses.label: Accompany as result
senses.definition: Of signs that will attend those who believe.

senses.label: Investigate carefully
senses.definition: To trace or follow events closely, as Luke did before writing his account.

senses.label: Follow as standard
senses.definition: To adhere to a teaching and way of life as one's pattern.

background.note: Used of loss that resulted from a broken dyke, the 'resulting' sense.

study.caution: In LUK 1:3 some take the verb to mean that Luke had been closely familiar with events rather than having researched them; most versions render 'investigated'.

study.summary: To comfort, console or encourage.

senses.label: Console the grieving
senses.definition: To comfort those mourning a death.

senses.label: Encourage, cheer
senses.definition: To speak encouragingly to those who are fainthearted or need strengthening.

background.note: A Christian letter speaks of comforting a sick mistress while awaiting her husband's arrival.

study.summary: To prepare or make ready; middle, to prepare oneself.

senses.label: Prepare a meal
senses.definition: To get food ready.

senses.label: Prepare oneself, be ready
senses.definition: To make preparations, for battle or for giving.

background.note: Used of preparing a meal, as in ACT 10:10.

study.summary: To carry aside or away; to remove or to be carried off course.

senses.label: Take away, remove
senses.definition: To remove or let pass, as Jesus asks the Father to take the cup from him.

senses.label: Be carried away
senses.definition: To be driven along or led astray, of clouds by winds or believers by strange teachings.

study.summary: To spend the winter at a place.

senses.label: Spend the winter
senses.definition: To stay somewhere through the winter, when sea travel was dangerous.

background.note: An inscription speaks of troops that wintered in a city.

study.summary: A resident foreigner or sojourner living where they lack citizenship.

senses.label: Alien, sojourner
senses.definition: A person living in a land not their own, as Abraham's descendants in Egypt and Moses in Midian.

senses.label: Outsider, spiritual exile
senses.definition: Figuratively, those once outside God's people, or believers as strangers in this world.

background.note: In classical Greek the word meant 'dwelling near, neighbouring'.

study.summary: A patriarch: a father or founder of a family or nation.

senses.label: Founding father
senses.definition: A head or founder of Israel, used of Abraham, Jacob's twelve sons and David.

study.summary: To obey one in authority or follow advice.

senses.label: Obey God
senses.definition: To submit to God's authority, above human authority.

senses.label: Obey, follow advice
senses.definition: To heed authorities or advice.

background.note: Used in marriage contracts of a wife obeying her husband.

study.summary: προφητεία is the speaking forth of God's mind and purpose. In the NT it covers the prophetic word of Scripture, the Spirit-given gift of prophecy in the church, particular prophetic utterances, the prophetic ministry of God's witnesses, and the book of Revelation, which calls itself 'the prophecy'.

senses.label: Prophecy of Scripture
senses.definition: The prophetic word recorded in the Old Testament, regarded as God's message spoken through the prophets and coming true in its fulfilment.
senses.note: In 2 Peter the point is that Scripture's prophecy did not come from human will but from men carried along by the Holy Spirit.

senses.label: The gift of prophecy
senses.definition: The Spirit-given ability, distributed among believers, to receive and pass on a message from God for the church's upbuilding, encouragement and comfort.
senses.note: Paul ranks it highly because it is intelligible and builds up the congregation, but places it beneath love.

senses.label: Prophetic utterances
senses.definition: Individual prophetic messages, usually in the plural, which the church is to weigh rather than despise; including words spoken over a person at his commissioning.
senses.note: The prophecies concerning Timothy accompanied his setting apart and serve him as encouragement in his 'good fight'.

senses.label: Prophetic ministry
senses.definition: The activity or period of prophesying carried out by God's appointed witnesses, and the prophetic Spirit that bears witness to Jesus.

senses.label: The book as prophecy
senses.definition: The message of the book of Revelation itself, described as 'the words of this prophecy' to be read, kept, not sealed, and neither added to nor taken from.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul treats prophecy as a charisma for the edification of the gathered church: it is to be exercised in proportion to faith, preferred to uninterpreted tongues, tested rather than despised, and it is partial and temporary compared with love.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation presents itself as prophecy in the full OT sense, binding on its hearers, and links the prophetic Spirit to the testimony of Jesus.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 2 Peter uses the word for the prophecy of Scripture and insists on its divine origin.

study.translationNote: Romans 12:6 'according to the proportion (ἀναλογία) of faith' is rendered either 'in proportion to his faith' (the prophet's own measure of trust) or 'in agreement with the faith' (conformity to the body of Christian belief); both readings are defended.

background.note: In the Greek OT the word can denote a concrete prophecy or prophetic message, as of the word of Oded the prophet heard by King Asa.
In Egyptian papyri the word names the paid temple office of 'prophet', which could be bought and sold, as in documents about the temple of Soknebtunis.

study.exegesisTip: Notice the range: in Revelation and 2 Peter prophecy is authoritative revelation, while in 1 Corinthians and 1 Thessalonians congregational prophecies are to be evaluated. Ask in each passage what authority the speaker claims and how the hearers are told to respond.
study.caution: 2 Peter 1:20 ('no prophecy of Scripture is of one's own ἐπίλυσις') is disputed: it may refer to the prophet's own interpretation of what he saw (origin) or to private interpretation by the reader. When prophecies 'will be done away' (1 Cor 13:8) is also debated, whether at Christ's return or at some earlier point; the context of seeing 'face to face' favours the former for most interpreters.

study.summary: στρέφω means 'to turn'. Most often it describes a person turning round to face someone (especially Jesus turning to speak). It can also mean to turn something toward someone, to turn in a new direction or allegiance, to change one thing into another, and, inwardly, to turn or be changed.

senses.label: Turn round (to face someone)
senses.definition: Passive/middle, usually the participle στραφείς: to turn oneself about, often before speaking or looking at someone.
senses.note: Frequent in Luke for Jesus turning to address a person or crowd.

senses.label: Turn something toward someone
senses.definition: Active with an object: to turn or present something, as offering the other cheek, or of swine turning on someone.

senses.label: Turn toward or away (change direction or allegiance)
senses.definition: To turn one's course or heart in a new direction: to go over to the Gentiles, to turn back in heart to Egypt, or of God turning away and handing people over.

senses.label: Change into
senses.definition: With εἰς: to turn or transform one thing into another.
senses.note: As water is turned into blood, echoing the Exodus plagues.

senses.label: Turn inwardly, be changed
senses.definition: Figuratively, a change of heart and attitude, the turning that leads to becoming like a child before God.
senses.note: Close to ἐπιστρέφω, 'turn, be converted'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke repeatedly uses 'turning' to mark a moment when Jesus addresses someone pointedly; in Acts the verb describes Israel's turning back to Egypt and the apostles' turning to the Gentiles.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John's Gospel turning is tied to recognition: the first disciples are addressed as Jesus turns, and Mary Magdalene turns twice before recognizing the risen Lord.

background.note: Homer uses the verb of ploughmen turning their teams at the end of the furrow in the scene on Achilles' shield.
The passive participle 'having turned and seen' appears in a second-century account, matching the Gospels' narrative idiom.

study.exegesisTip: In Matthew 18:3 the aorist passive ('unless you turn and become like children') pictures a decisive reversal of direction, not gradual improvement; compare the compounds ἐπιστρέφω and ὑποστρέφω, which carry the turning/returning idea elsewhere.
study.caution: Several verses read στρέφω in some manuscripts and a compound (such as ἐπιστρέφω or ἀποστρέφω) in others, so counts and wording differ between editions.

study.summary: τέλειος describes what has reached its goal (τέλος): full-grown and mature, or complete and lacking nothing. In the NT it describes mature believers in contrast to infants, whole-hearted devotion to God, and things that are complete and flawless, such as God's will, God's law, perfect love, and the heavenly tent.

senses.label: Mature, full-grown
senses.definition: Of persons, grown up as opposed to infants; spiritually adult in understanding and discernment.
senses.note: Often explicitly contrasted with νήπιος, 'infant'.

senses.label: Complete, whole (of character)
senses.definition: Undivided and complete in goodness and devotion to God, lacking nothing; also of God himself as the standard.
senses.note: Not a claim of sinlessness but of wholeness, like the OT 'blameless' (tamim).

senses.label: Perfect, flawless (of things)
senses.definition: Of things that are complete and without defect: God's will, a gift from above, the law of liberty, love that drives out fear, and the greater tent not made with hands.

senses.label: The complete (τὸ τέλειον)
senses.definition: As a neuter noun: the final, complete state that replaces what is partial.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: For Paul τέλειος is mainly maturity: the goal of ministry is to present everyone mature in Christ, grown up to the measure of Christ's fullness, no longer childish in thinking.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James uses the word five times for wholeness that lacks nothing: endurance doing its complete work, the perfect gift from God, the perfect law, and the one who does not stumble in speech.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: In Matthew the word sums up the undivided obedience Jesus calls for, modelled on the Father's own character and tested by willingness to give up possessions.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses it for the mature who can digest solid food, and of the 'more perfect' heavenly tent; it belongs to the letter's wider theme of bringing to completion.

study.translationNote: English versions alternate between 'perfect' and 'mature' (and sometimes 'complete'). 'Perfect' can suggest flawlessness, while the Greek usually stresses having reached the intended end: grown up, whole, lacking nothing. Context decides which emphasis fits.

background.note: Used of persons who are of age: a woman's heirs 'being of age'.
Of animals, 'full-grown' cocks in an account.
Of objects in good working order: 'one perfect Theban mill'.

study.exegesisTip: Watch for the contrast with infancy (1 Cor 2:6; 1 Cor 14:20; Eph 4:13): the image is growth to adulthood. In James 1:4 note the play on words: let endurance have its τέλειον work so that you may be τέλειοι.
study.caution: What 'the perfect' (τὸ τέλειον) in 1 Corinthians 13:10 refers to is debated: most see the state brought by Christ's return, when we see 'face to face'; others propose the completed NT or the church's maturity. Whether Paul's usage borrows from the vocabulary of the mystery religions has been argued, but most lexicographers think it unlikely.

study.summary: τίκτω means to give birth to, bring forth. In the NT it is always used of the mother giving birth (or, in the passive, of a child being born), above all of the birth of Jesus; figuratively, it describes the earth producing vegetation and desire giving birth to sin.

senses.label: Give birth (literal)
senses.definition: Of a woman bringing forth a child, whether with an object ('bear a son') or absolutely ('her time to give birth').

senses.label: Be born (passive)
senses.definition: In the passive: to be born, used of the birth of the Messiah-King and Saviour.
senses.note: The aorist passive ἐτέχθη is a later form; classical Greek would say ἐγένετο.

senses.label: Bear children (ongoing)
senses.definition: The present participle 'the one who bears' describes a woman as a mother, in contrast to the barren.

senses.label: Produce, bring forth (figurative)
senses.definition: Of the land producing vegetation, and of desire that has conceived giving birth to sin.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the verb in his birth narratives, for Elizabeth and Mary, stressing that the time came for them to give birth.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Jesus uses childbirth as a picture of sorrow turning to joy; in Revelation 12 the woman's labour and the dragon waiting to devour her child are a cosmic retelling of the Messiah's birth.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James traces a chain of birth: desire conceives and gives birth to sin, and sin when full-grown brings forth death.

background.note: Homer uses the verb of animals: in Libya the ewes bear lambs three times a year.
A husband's letter to his pregnant wife (1 B.C.) gives instructions about what she is to do when she gives birth, showing the everyday sense.
A third-century letter gives instructions that if Tamun bears a child she is to be made to take diligent care of the baby.

study.exegesisTip: Compare τίκτω (bearing, the mother's act) with γεννάω (begetting or being born, often used of the father and of spiritual birth). In Galatians 4:27 the present participle describes a lasting state, 'the woman who is a mother'.

study.summary: τιμάω means to honour, to treat someone as having worth and to show it in respect, obedience or tangible support. It occurs most in the commandment to honour father and mother and in the claim that honouring the Son is honouring the Father. Once it keeps its older commercial sense, 'set a price on'.

senses.label: Honour parents
senses.definition: To show due respect to father and mother, including obedience and practical care, as the fifth commandment requires.
senses.note: In Matthew 15 and Mark 7 Jesus treats evading support of parents through a vow as failing to honour them.

senses.label: Honour God and his Son
senses.definition: To give God and Christ the reverence that is their due; true honour is of the heart, not merely of the lips.

senses.label: Honour from God
senses.definition: God's honouring of those who serve Christ.

senses.label: Show respect and give support
senses.definition: To treat people with due regard and honour, sometimes expressed in material provision or gifts.
senses.note: In Acts 28:10 the islanders 'honoured with many honours', that is, gifts and provisions.

senses.label: Set a price on
senses.definition: To value or fix the price of something; used of the price set on Jesus, quoting the prophet.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the verb to tie the Son's honour to the Father's: whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father, and Jesus honours his Father while being dishonoured.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In the Pastoral Letters honouring genuine widows involves the church's practical support, alongside the fifth commandment in Ephesians.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: Peter frames 'honour everyone' and 'honour the king' around 'love the brotherhood, fear God'.

study.translationNote: Some versions render 1 Timothy 5:3 'honour' and others 'support' or 'care for', because the context (verses about provision for widows) shows the honour is expressed financially.

background.note: Homer has Antilochus remark that the immortals still honour older men.
A civic decree resolves 'to honour' a gymnasiarch, the standard public use of the verb.
The sense 'set a value on' appears in a document valuing a cow at three and a half talents.

study.exegesisTip: Honour in the Bible is not only an attitude but an action with content. In Mark 7:10 and the verses that follow, failing to honour parents means withholding support from them, so ask what honour concretely requires in each passage.
study.caution: How far 'honour' in 1 Timothy 5:3 (and the related 'double honour' for elders) implies payment is debated; the context makes material support at least part of it.

study.summary: χρύσεος (contracted χρυσοῦς) means golden: made of gold or overlaid with gold. Apart from one use in 2 Timothy and two in Hebrews, it belongs to Revelation, where golden lampstands, crowns, bowls, censers and the altar picture the splendour of God's heavenly temple, and the harlot's golden cup shows counterfeit splendour.

senses.label: Golden objects of worship
senses.definition: Made of or overlaid with gold, describing temple and tabernacle furnishings, both the earthly tabernacle and the heavenly sanctuary of Revelation.

senses.label: Golden adornments and regalia
senses.definition: Gold crowns, sashes and other ornaments marking royal or priestly dignity, and the harlot's gold cup.

senses.label: Gold as costly material
senses.definition: Gold as the most valuable material, contrasted with silver, wood and clay, whether in household vessels or in idols.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation's imagery of gold draws on the tabernacle and temple: the churches are golden lampstands, the elders wear golden crowns, and the prayers of the saints rise from golden bowls and a golden altar; the same splendour is imitated by Babylon's golden cup.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews lists the gold furnishings of the first covenant's sanctuary as part of a system that pointed beyond itself.

background.note: Sappho, in the Aeolic form, calls on Aphrodite who left her father's golden house.
Used for gold jewellery such as a golden earring.
A soldier's letter reports receiving travelling money from Caesar: three gold pieces.

study.exegesisTip: In Revelation, compare the golden things of the heavenly temple with Babylon's golden cup: the same material is used both for true worship and for its seductive imitation.
study.caution: In Hebrews 9:4 the golden θυμιατήριον may be the altar of incense or a golden censer, and why it is said to belong to the Most Holy Place is debated.

study.summary: ἀναγγέλλω means to bring back word, report, and in Koine Greek more broadly to announce or declare. In the NT it is used of messengers reporting what has happened, of missionaries reporting what God has done, of the proclamation of God's message, and in John of the Messiah and the Spirit disclosing truth.

senses.label: Report, bring back word
senses.definition: To tell others what one has seen or experienced, often on returning.

senses.label: Tell what God has done
senses.definition: To recount God's mighty acts to others as testimony.

senses.label: Announce, proclaim
senses.definition: To declare God's message publicly and fully, as in apostolic teaching and preaching.

senses.label: Disclose, make known
senses.definition: To reveal and explain what was previously hidden, of the Messiah's teaching and the Spirit's work.

senses.label: Confess, disclose openly
senses.definition: To declare openly one's own deeds.
senses.note: New believers at Ephesus openly disclosed their magical practices.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the verb for revelation: the Samaritan woman expects the Messiah to declare all things, the Spirit will declare what belongs to Jesus and what is to come, and the letter's message is announced as received from him.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: In Acts the verb describes missionary reports to the churches and Paul's insistence that he did not hold back from declaring the whole counsel of God.

background.note: Aeschylus uses it of messengers coming back with reports of riddling oracles.
Thucydides uses it of bringing word of the truce to Brasidas.
A third-century B.C. letter speaks of reporting what had happened, showing the everyday Koine sense 'report'.

study.exegesisTip: In John 16:13-15 the verb is repeated three times: the Spirit does not originate a new message but takes what is Christ's and declares it. That frames how the Spirit's teaching relates to Jesus' own.
study.caution: Do not press the prefix ἀνα- ('back, again') in every verse; in Hellenistic Greek ἀναγγέλλω had largely become equivalent to ἀπαγγέλλω, 'announce, report'.

study.summary: ἀνάγκη means necessity or compulsion, and from that, the pressure of hardship or distress. The NT uses it for what must be so ('it is necessary'), for being under constraint or obligation (as Paul to preach), and for times of crisis and distress.

senses.label: Necessity, it is necessary
senses.definition: What must be, logically or in God's ordering; often ἀνάγκη with an infinitive, 'it is necessary'.

senses.label: Compulsion, being obliged
senses.definition: Constraint on a person: 'to have necessity' meaning to be obliged, and 'of necessity' meaning under compulsion rather than freely.
senses.note: Several of these contrast compulsion with willing, free action.

senses.label: A laid-on obligation
senses.definition: An inward or divinely imposed constraint that a person cannot escape.
senses.note: 'Necessity is laid upon me' explains why Paul cannot boast in preaching.

senses.label: Distress, crisis, hardship
senses.definition: Pressure of circumstances: calamity, affliction, often paired with tribulation.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses ἀνάγκη both for compulsion that he refuses to impose on others (giving, Philemon's kindness) and for the hardships he endured in ministry, as well as the constraint laid on him to preach.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the word for theological necessity: a change of priesthood necessarily involves a change of law, and a covenant requires a death.

study.translationNote: In 1 Corinthians 7:26 'the present ἀνάγκη' is translated 'distress', 'crisis' or 'necessity'; the choice reflects how one understands the situation Paul has in mind.

background.note: Hector foresees for Andromache that 'hard necessity will lie upon you' in slavery, the same idiom of necessity being laid on someone found in 1 Corinthians 9:16.
The phrase 'I was obliged to' (literally 'I had necessity') with an infinitive, as in Luke 14:18 and Jude 3.
An inscription uses the plural for calamities and hardships, as Paul does in 2 Corinthians 6:4.

study.exegesisTip: In Matthew 18:7 'it is necessary that stumbling blocks come' does not remove guilt: 'woe to the one through whom they come'. Divine necessity and human responsibility stand together.
