study.caution: The 'present distress' of 1 Corinthians 7:26 may be a local crisis (such as famine or persecution) or the pressure of the last days generally; interpreters differ. In Luke 23:17 the verse containing the word is absent from many manuscripts.

study.summary: ἀποκάλυψις means an uncovering, a revelation. In the NT it is always God's act of making known what was hidden: revelations given to apostles and prophets, revelatory words in worship, and above all the future unveiling of Jesus Christ in glory at his coming. It is also the opening word and title of the book of Revelation.

senses.label: Revelation given to a person
senses.definition: A disclosure of divine truth or guidance by God to an individual, such as the gospel Paul received or the visions he was shown.

senses.label: Revelation in the congregation
senses.definition: A revelatory word brought to the gathered church alongside teaching, prophecy and tongues, and the Spirit's gift of insight into God.

senses.label: The unveiling of Christ at his coming
senses.definition: The future public manifestation of Jesus Christ in glory, eagerly awaited by believers and bringing grace, glory and judgment.

senses.label: Disclosure of final realities
senses.definition: The coming manifestation of God's righteous judgment and of the glorified children of God.

senses.label: Revelation to the nations; the book
senses.definition: Light that discloses God's salvation to the Gentiles; and the content God gave to Jesus Christ to show his servants, the book's title.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word both for present revelations (the source of his gospel, guidance to go up to Jerusalem, visions) and for the future revelation of Christ and of God's children, toward which creation itself strains.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: In 1 Peter the word always points to the future 'revelation of Jesus Christ', the goal that makes present suffering bearable and on which hope is set.

study.translationNote: The English 'apocalypse' transliterates this word. In ordinary speech that suggests catastrophe, but the Greek means 'unveiling, disclosure'.

background.note: In the Greek OT the noun appears for the literal uncovering of nakedness, in Saul's insult to Jonathan about his mother.
Sirach uses it for the disclosure of a man's deeds at the end of his life.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who reveals, what is revealed and when. Many uses are about a person (Christ) being unveiled rather than information being given, and many look to the future.
study.caution: In phrases like 'revelation of Jesus Christ' (Galatians 1:12; Revelation 1:1) it is debated whether Christ is the one revealing, the one revealed, or both.

study.summary: θησαυρός (from τίθημι, 'to put') is first a place where valuables are stored (a chest, treasury or storehouse) and then the treasure itself. Jesus uses it for what a person stores up, on earth or in heaven, and for the storehouse of the heart; Paul applies it to the gospel and to Christ, in whom all wisdom is stored.

senses.label: Treasure chest, casket
senses.definition: A container in which valuables are kept.
senses.note: The magi opened their treasure chests to present gifts.

senses.label: Storehouse (often the heart)
senses.definition: A storeroom from which things are brought out; metaphorically the heart as the store from which words and deeds come.

senses.label: Treasure, stored wealth
senses.definition: Accumulated valuables or wealth, on which a person's heart becomes set.

senses.label: Treasure in heaven
senses.definition: Reward with God, laid up by generosity and following Jesus, which cannot decay or be stolen.

senses.label: Spiritual treasure
senses.definition: The supreme worth of the gospel's light carried by frail messengers, and the riches of wisdom and knowledge hidden in Christ.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew gathers most uses: treasures on earth versus in heaven, the heart following its treasure, the good and evil storehouse of the heart, the hidden treasure of the kingdom, and the scribe bringing out new and old from his storeroom.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul turns the word to the gospel itself, held in clay jars so that the power is plainly God's, and to Christ as the one in whom every treasure of wisdom is stored.

background.note: Hesiod calls a sparing tongue the best treasure among men.
Aeschylus calls the silver mines of Laureion a 'treasure of the earth'.
Very common in Egypt for a granary or storehouse for grain and other produce, including the public granary.

study.exegesisTip: Keep the 'storehouse' sense in view: in Matthew 12:35 and Luke 6:45 the heart is a storeroom, so speech is only bringing out what has already been stored up.

study.summary: θυμός is passionate, boiling anger: the hot surge of rage that flares up. In Paul's vice lists it is a human sin to be put away; in Luke–Acts it describes crowds seized with fury; in Revelation it becomes the language of God's righteous wrath poured out in judgment, and also of the intoxicating 'passion' of Babylon's immorality.

senses.label: Outbursts of human rage (a sin)
senses.definition: Fits or flare-ups of anger, listed among the works of the flesh and the behaviours believers must put off; the plural points to repeated eruptions of temper.
senses.note: Usually paired with ὀργή (anger), bitterness, slander and malice — it is a relational, community-destroying sin.

senses.label: Being filled with fury
senses.definition: A sudden, overpowering rage that takes hold of a group or person, especially in hostile reaction to a message.
senses.note: The synagogue at Nazareth and the Ephesian silversmiths' crowd are 'filled with θυμός'; the devil comes down 'having great fury' because his time is short.

senses.label: God's wrath in judgment
senses.definition: The holy, active indignation of God against sin, revealed in the final judgment and pictured in Revelation as a winepress, a cup of wine, and bowls poured out.
senses.note: Revelation draws on the prophets' image of the cup of the LORD's wrath; here θυμός carries no hint of loss of control.

senses.label: The 'fury of his wrath' (intensive pairing)
senses.definition: Combined with ὀργή in a genitive phrase to express the full intensity of God's anger.
senses.note: Literally 'the wine of the fury of the wrath of God' — piled-up terms for emphasis.

senses.label: The 'passion' of Babylon's immorality
senses.definition: In the phrase 'the wine of the θυμός of her sexual immorality', the word describes the maddening, intoxicating passion with which Babylon seduces the nations — while echoing the wrath that this sin brings.
senses.note: Translations vary between 'passion', 'wrath' and 'maddening wine'; the phrase may deliberately fuse both ideas.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses θυμός of sinful human anger in catalogues of vices (to be renounced), but also of God's eschatological wrath alongside ὀργή against those who disobey the truth.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Ten of the eighteen uses are in Revelation, where θυμός dominates the judgment visions: the winepress, the seven last plagues and the bowls are all 'of the θυμός of God'.

study.translationNote: English versions alternate between 'wrath', 'rage', 'fury', 'anger' and 'passion' for this word. The variety is partly to distinguish it from ὀργή when the two stand side by side (e.g. 'anger and wrath' vs 'wrath and fury'), and partly because of the difficult phrase in Revelation 14:8 and 18:3, where some render 'the wine of the passion of her immorality' and others 'the maddening wine of her adulteries'.

background.note: In an alphabetic acrostic of the early first century AD, a thief who stole a garment is told he 'will meet with anger' (θυμοῦ περιπεσεῖται).
An erotic fragment of the 2nd century BC has the speaker say, 'know that I have an unconquerable θυμός when strife takes hold of me' — anger as a rising passion.
Revelation's 'wine of the passion of her immorality' echoes the prophetic picture of Babylon as a golden cup that made the nations drunk.

study.exegesisTip: When θυμός and ὀργή occur together, older lexicographers distinguished θυμός as the sudden boiling-up of anger and ὀργή as a more settled, lasting indignation. This helps explain why θυμοί appears in the plural in vice lists (repeated outbursts), but do not press the distinction in every text — the two are often near-synonyms used together for emphasis.
study.caution: God's θυμός in Revelation and Romans should not be read as an uncontrolled temper; it is just judgment against sin. Conversely, the word's application to God does not legitimize human θυμός, which Paul consistently lists as a sin to be put away.

study.summary: καταγγέλλω means to proclaim or announce publicly, often with a note of authoritative, official proclamation. In the NT it is used almost entirely of making known the message about Christ — his death, resurrection, the forgiveness of sins and the way of salvation — by Luke (mostly in Acts) and Paul.

senses.label: Proclaim the gospel message
senses.definition: To announce publicly the content of the Christian message: the word of God, the resurrection, forgiveness of sins, the way of salvation, the gospel.

senses.label: Proclaim Christ himself
senses.definition: With a personal object: to make Christ known as the content of preaching — who he is and what he has done.
senses.note: In Philippians Paul rejoices that Christ is proclaimed even when some do so from rivalry, because the message itself goes out.

senses.label: Proclaim the Lord's death in the Supper
senses.definition: The church's eating and drinking at the Lord's Supper is itself a public announcement of Christ's death until he returns.
senses.note: The verb can be read as indicative ('you proclaim') or imperative ('proclaim!'); most take it as a statement of what the meal does.

senses.label: Announce or make known (general)
senses.definition: To declare or report something publicly, whether by prophets foretelling 'these days', by opponents accusing Paul of advocating illegal customs, or by news that spreads widely.
senses.note: In Romans 1:8 the Romans' faith 'is being proclaimed' — reported — throughout the world.

senses.label: Proclaim the unknown God / light
senses.definition: To reveal and declare something previously unknown or hidden, such as the God the Athenians worshipped in ignorance, or light to Jews and Gentiles.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Eleven uses, all in Acts, make καταγγέλλω one of Luke's characteristic verbs for apostolic mission preaching, standing beside εὐαγγελίζομαι and κηρύσσω.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb for his own apostolic proclamation and that of others, stressing its content (Christ, the gospel) rather than the preacher's eloquence or motives.

study.translationNote: In 1 Corinthians 2:1 some manuscripts read 'the testimony (μαρτύριον) of God' and others 'the mystery (μυστήριον) of God', so English versions differ on what Paul says he proclaimed. The verb itself is consistently rendered 'proclaim', 'declare' or 'preach'.

background.note: Lysias uses the verb for formally declaring war (πόλεμον κατηγγέλκασι) — a public, official announcement.
Xenophon uses it in the sense 'denounce', of informing on someone's plot.
A widow appoints a representative after 'the lamentable news announced to me' of her husband's death.
A civic decree of AD 37 says the accession of Gaius Caesar 'has been proclaimed' — the official, authoritative sense also heard in the NT.

study.exegesisTip: Compare καταγγέλλω with εὐαγγελίζομαι (announce good news) and κηρύσσω (herald). καταγγέλλω emphasizes the public, authoritative declaration of a fixed content; note what the object is in each verse — a Person, an event, or a message.

study.summary: κενός means 'empty'. In the NT it is used literally of people sent away empty-handed, and far more often metaphorically: words and deceptions that are hollow (lacking truth), efforts that are fruitless or in vain, and — once — a person who is hollow or foolish. Paul especially uses it, frequently in the phrase εἰς κενόν, 'in vain'.

senses.label: Empty-handed
senses.definition: Of persons: sent away with nothing, without receiving or bringing anything.
senses.note: In the parable of the tenants the servants are sent back without fruit; in Mary's song God sends the rich away empty.

senses.label: Hollow, without truth or substance
senses.definition: Of words, arguments or deceptions that have no real content, being devoid of truth.
senses.note: Paul warns against 'empty words' and 'empty deceit' that lead believers astray.

senses.label: Vain, fruitless, to no effect
senses.definition: Of labor, faith, preaching or grace that would come to nothing, achieving no result.
senses.note: If Christ is not raised, preaching and faith are κενός — empty of content and effect.

senses.label: εἰς κενόν: 'in vain'
senses.definition: The phrase 'into emptiness' means 'to no purpose, for nothing', used of running, labouring or receiving grace without result.
senses.note: In the NT this phrase is used only by Paul, often with athletic or labor imagery.

senses.label: Hollow person, fool
senses.definition: Addressed to a person: empty-headed, pretentious, lacking real substance.
senses.note: 'O empty man' — one whose faith is a mere claim without deeds.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Twelve of eighteen uses are Pauline. Paul is concerned that his apostolic labor and his converts' reception of grace not prove 'empty', and he grounds the meaningfulness of Christian work in the resurrection.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James uniquely applies κενός to a person: the one who claims faith without works is a 'hollow' man.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'empty', 'vain', 'hollow', 'empty-handed' and 'foolish' depending on whether the context concerns content (empty words), result (labor in vain), or a person (JAM 2:20, 'foolish' or 'senseless' person).

background.note: A 3rd-century BC complaint mentions a boat that should not be brought back 'empty' to the city — the plain literal sense.
An inscription of AD 137 distinguishes unladen (κεναί) from laden camels.
εἰς κενόν is used of water from a pipe running to waste — the same idiom Paul uses for wasted labor.

study.exegesisTip: κενός is often paired with μάταιος. A traditional distinction is that κενός describes the hollowness of a thing's content or quality, while μάταιος describes the futility of its aim or outcome; the overlap is large, but asking 'empty of what?' in each text sharpens interpretation.

study.summary: κληρονομέω means 'to inherit', and from there 'to receive as one's own possession, obtain'. In the NT it rarely concerns family estates; it is used of receiving the promised blessings of God — the land/earth, the kingdom, eternal life, salvation, the promises — as an inheritance given by God rather than earned.

senses.label: Inherit as heir (literal)
senses.definition: To receive property or status as an heir; used in Paul's allegory from Genesis about the son of the slave not inheriting with the son of the free woman.
senses.note: The only absolute use (without object) in the NT.

senses.label: Inherit the kingdom of God
senses.definition: To come into possession of God's kingdom at the consummation — a gift prepared by God, from which the unrighteous are excluded.
senses.note: Paul's warnings are about moral character; 'flesh and blood' (1CO 15:50) refers to mortal, perishable human nature.

senses.label: Inherit eternal life
senses.definition: To obtain the life of the age to come; the phrase found in the question 'what must I do to inherit eternal life?'

senses.label: Inherit the earth / promises / blessing
senses.definition: To come into secure possession of what God has promised — the earth, the promises, salvation, a blessing, all things.
senses.note: MAT 5:5 echoes Psalm 37:11, where the meek 'inherit the land'.

senses.label: Obtain a name or blessing as one's due
senses.definition: To acquire or come into possession of something, with the idea of inheritance in the background.
senses.note: Christ 'has inherited' a name superior to the angels; Esau later wished to 'inherit the blessing' but was rejected.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb mostly in solemn negative warnings: certain kinds of people 'will not inherit the kingdom of God'.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses inheritance language for Christ's exalted name and for believers who, through faith and patience, inherit the promises — with Esau as the warning example.

background.note: Isocrates speaks of inheriting a father's friendship as one inherits his property — classical usage takes the genitive of the thing inherited.
The sense 'obtain, come into possession of' appears in 1 Maccabees, where David 'inherited the throne of a kingdom' — reflecting the LXX use for Hebrew yarash, 'take possession'.
A petition of AD 135 speaks of inheriting a grandmother's belongings, with the accusative of the thing, as in the NT.
A 3rd-century letter reports that another man's wife has been made his heir — the verb with a personal object.

study.exegesisTip: Behind the NT usage lies the Septuagint, where κληρονομέω mostly translates Hebrew yarash, 'take possession (of the land)'. Inheriting in the NT therefore means receiving secure, God-given possession of what he has promised, not necessarily someone's death and a will.
study.caution: Paul's warnings that the unrighteous 'will not inherit the kingdom' (1CO 6:9–10; GAL 5:21) are interpreted differently — as describing unbelievers, as warnings to professing believers, or as concerning reward. The verb itself does not settle the debate.

study.summary: κοιμάω (in the NT always middle/passive, κοιμάομαι) means 'to sleep, fall asleep'. Besides ordinary sleep, it is the NT's characteristic gentle way of speaking of the death of believers: they have 'fallen asleep', a figure that carries the hope of being awakened in resurrection.

senses.label: Sleep, fall asleep (literal)
senses.definition: Ordinary physical sleep.
senses.note: In JOH 11:12 the disciples misunderstand Jesus, taking his words of Lazarus as literal sleep.

senses.label: Fall asleep in death (believers)
senses.definition: To die, used as a euphemism, especially of God's people, implying that death is temporary and will end in resurrection.
senses.note: Christ is 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep' (1CO 15:20).

senses.label: Die (general, of past generations)
senses.definition: Of death in general, including generations gone before.
senses.note: In 1CO 7:39 the phrase 'if her husband falls asleep' simply means 'dies'.

senses.label: Asleep vs. alive at the Lord's coming
senses.definition: Paul contrasts those who 'have fallen asleep' with those alive at Christ's return; 'we shall not all sleep' (1CO 15:51).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Half the NT uses are Pauline, concentrated in his resurrection teaching (1 Corinthians 15; 1 Thessalonians 4), where the sleep image comforts grieving believers.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's Lazarus story turns on the double meaning: Jesus says Lazarus 'has fallen asleep' and he will wake him, while the disciples hear literal sleep.

study.translationNote: Some versions keep the metaphor ('fallen asleep'), others explain it ('died', 'sleep in death'), especially in 1 Thessalonians 4 and Acts 7:60. Keeping the metaphor preserves the note of hope; explaining it prevents readers from missing that death is meant.

background.note: In Homer Hera asks Sleep to 'lull to sleep' Zeus's eyes — the active sense 'put to sleep'.
A 2nd-century letter: 'I made the night-strategus sleep on guard at the house' — ordinary sleep.
A pagan epitaph says the dead 'sleeps the eternal sleep', voicing the hopelessness against which Paul writes.
Christian inscriptions record that a servant of God 'fell asleep' (ἐκοιμήθη), adopting the NT euphemism for a believer's death.

study.exegesisTip: Sleep as a figure for death was used by pagans too, but in the NT it is set in the context of resurrection: one sleeps in order to be awakened. Note the parallel with ἐγείρω ('raise, wake') in the same passages.
study.caution: The metaphor describes how death appears and its temporary character; it does not by itself teach 'soul sleep' (unconscious existence between death and resurrection). That question must be decided from other texts.

study.summary: μήν means 'month' — a (lunar) month as a unit of time. In the NT it is mostly used in time spans (three months, six months, forty-two months), in Luke's birth narratives and Paul's travels in Acts, in Revelation's symbolic periods, and once by Paul of the observance of calendar months.

senses.label: Month as a span of time
senses.definition: A period of about thirty days, used in stating how long something lasted.

senses.label: A month in a pregnancy or calendar
senses.definition: A specific month counted in a sequence, such as the sixth month of Elizabeth's pregnancy.

senses.label: Symbolic periods in Revelation
senses.definition: Fixed periods of judgment or trial: five months of the locusts' torment, forty-two months of the nations trampling the city and the beast's authority, and a tree bearing fruit every month.
senses.note: Forty-two months equals three and a half years (cf. 1,260 days), a limited period drawn from Daniel.

senses.label: Months as religious observances
senses.definition: In the plural, calendar observances such as new-moon festivals or sacred months, which the Galatians were adopting.
senses.note: Paul treats keeping 'days and months and seasons and years' as a return to bondage under elemental things.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses months to mark the careful chronology of the birth narratives and of Paul's ministry (eighteen months in Corinth, three months in Ephesus' synagogue).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In Revelation months are part of numerically symbolic time: limited, measured periods under God's control.

background.note: A loan of 106 BC charges interest 'two drachmae on the mina each month'.
A dating formula: 'the twenty-fifth day of the month Mechir' — μήν with Egyptian month names.

study.exegesisTip: Months in Israel's calendar were lunar, beginning with the new moon, so 'months' in Galatians 4:10 naturally suggests new-moon and festival observances. In Revelation, read numbers of months against Daniel's 'time, times and half a time'.
study.caution: Do not confuse this noun with the particle μήν ('surely, indeed'), a different word with the same spelling. Interpreters debate whether the Galatians' 'months' were Jewish festivals, pagan calendar observances, or both.

study.summary: οἰκοδομή means 'building' — both the act of building and the structure built. In the Gospels it refers to the temple buildings; Paul uses it almost always figuratively, either of the church as God's building or, most often, of 'building up' (edification): the strengthening of believers and the community in faith and love.

senses.label: Building, structure (literal)
senses.definition: A physical building, here the buildings of the Jerusalem temple complex.
senses.note: The disciples admire the buildings Jesus says will be thrown down.

senses.label: God's building (the church)
senses.definition: Believers corporately pictured as a structure God is constructing, growing into a holy temple.

senses.label: The resurrection body as a building
senses.definition: The future, eternal body from God contrasted with the earthly 'tent'.
senses.note: 'A building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.'

senses.label: Building up, edification
senses.definition: The process of strengthening and maturing others in faith, the goal by which speech, gifts, ministry and apostolic authority are measured.
senses.note: In 1 Corinthians 14 every gift in worship is tested by whether it builds up the church.

senses.label: Building up the body of Christ
senses.definition: The corporate growth of the church toward maturity, achieved through gifted ministers and every member's contribution in love.

senses.label: Apostolic authority for building up
senses.definition: Paul describes the authority the Lord gave him as being for building up, not for tearing down.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Fifteen of eighteen uses are Pauline. For Paul 'edification' is a central criterion of Christian conduct: love builds up, and everything in the gathered church should be done 'for building up'.

study.translationNote: Older versions often use 'edification' or 'edifying', a Latin-derived word that literally means 'building'. Modern versions prefer 'building up' or 'strengthening', which preserves the image but can hide that the same word is used for the temple buildings and for 'God's building'.

background.note: A 2nd-century BC document uses the word of the building of a dovecote — its everyday literal sense.
An inscription of 25 BC records 'the building of the enclosure' dedicated to the god Soknopaios.

study.exegesisTip: Notice how Paul blends the image of the church as a temple-building with the idea of growth (EPH 2:21; 4:16): the building 'grows'. Edification in Paul is corporate and relational, not primarily private self-improvement.
study.caution: The word was regarded as non-classical by later purists, but it was standard in everyday Koine. 'Edification' in the NT is not mere emotional uplift; it means building up faith, understanding and love.

study.summary: παραχρῆμα is an adverb meaning 'on the spot, immediately, instantly'. Almost all uses are in Luke–Acts, where it highlights the instantaneous effect of Jesus' and the apostles' healings and of God's judgments — events that happen at once, leaving no doubt about their source.

senses.label: Instant healing
senses.definition: Describing the immediate completeness of a cure at Jesus' word or touch, or through the apostles.
senses.note: The healed person often gets up and acts at once, demonstrating the cure.

senses.label: Instant restoration of life or speech
senses.definition: Of the sudden reversal of death, muteness or blindness.

senses.label: Immediate divine judgment
senses.definition: Of God's punishment falling at once, so that it is unmistakably his act.
senses.note: The fig tree withers, Sapphira falls, Herod is struck, Elymas is blinded — all 'immediately'.

senses.label: Immediately (in narrative sequence)
senses.definition: Of events following at once, without delay, in the flow of a story.
senses.note: The cock crows while Peter is still speaking; the jailer is baptized at once.

senses.label: Expected imminently
senses.definition: Of something thought about to happen at any moment.
senses.note: People supposed the kingdom of God 'was going to appear immediately'; Jesus corrects this with a parable of delay.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Sixteen of eighteen uses are Lukan. Where Mark often uses εὐθύς, Luke prefers παραχρῆμα, especially to mark miracles and judgments as instantaneous.

study.translationNote: Rendered 'immediately', 'at once', 'instantly', 'forthwith' or 'straightway'. In MAT 21:20 versions often render it 'so quickly' because it stands in a question of astonishment.

background.note: Herodotus uses the adverb for 'on the spot, forthwith'.
Thucydides uses τὰ παραχρῆμα for 'the present' in contrast to things to come.
A letter of 152 BC: 'I will come to you immediately.'
In money transactions παραχρῆμα διὰ χειρός means 'directly from hand to hand' — a common business phrase.

study.exegesisTip: Watch how Luke uses the word to underscore that a healing was complete and visible, not gradual; it functions as narrative evidence of divine power. Contrast LUK 19:11, where 'immediately' expresses a mistaken expectation.

study.summary: περιτέμνω means 'to cut around', and in the NT always 'to circumcise' — the covenant rite given to Abraham. It appears in narratives of the circumcision of John, Jesus and Timothy, in the early church's controversy over whether Gentiles must be circumcised, in Paul's insistence that circumcision adds nothing to Christ, and once metaphorically of a spiritual circumcision performed by Christ.

senses.label: Circumcise (covenant rite)
senses.definition: To perform the rite of circumcision, normally on a male child on the eighth day, as the sign of the covenant with Abraham.
senses.note: In JOH 7:22 Jesus notes that circumcision is performed even on the Sabbath.

senses.label: Be circumcised (as a requirement for Gentiles)
senses.definition: Passive/middle: to receive circumcision, in the debate over whether Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law to be saved.
senses.note: Titus, a Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised (GAL 2:3).

senses.label: Circumcision as a matter of legal obligation
senses.definition: Accepting circumcision as a means of standing before God, which Paul says obligates one to the whole law and makes Christ of no benefit.

senses.label: Circumcised state (indifferent in Christ)
senses.definition: Being circumcised or uncircumcised as one's condition when called; Paul tells believers to remain as they are.
senses.note: Paul circumcised Timothy for missionary reasons (ACT 16:3), yet was accused of teaching Jews not to circumcise (ACT 21:21).

senses.label: Spiritual circumcision
senses.definition: Metaphorically, the inward 'circumcision not made with hands' that believers receive in Christ, the putting off of the body of the flesh.
senses.note: Builds on the OT call to circumcise the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16; Jeremiah 4:4).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul consistently denies that circumcision has saving value for Gentiles; in Christ what matters is new creation and faith working through love, while circumcision in Christ is spiritual.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke shows the rite faithfully observed in Jesus' family, then narrates the church's controversy and the Jerusalem council's decision not to require it of Gentiles.

study.translationNote: In Galatians 5:2 and 6:12–13 the present middle/passive is best rendered 'let yourselves be circumcised' or 'receive circumcision', showing that the Galatians were considering accepting it voluntarily.

background.note: Herodotus uses the verb of circumcision as a custom of certain peoples, noting those who do not circumcise.
Hesiod uses the basic sense 'cut around' of pruning vines.
A document of AD 171 speaks of a boy being circumcised 'according to the custom' — the verb was in use for an Egyptian practice, where circumcision was ritual preparation for priests.
A 2nd-century BC document refers to circumcision as an Egyptian custom, here applied to a girl in preparation for marriage.

study.exegesisTip: Pay attention to voice: active (someone circumcises another), passive/middle (to be circumcised or have oneself circumcised). In Galatians the middle stresses the Gentiles' own choice to adopt the rite.
study.caution: Paul's opposition is not to circumcision as an ethnic or cultural practice for Jews (see ACT 16:3; 1CO 7:18), but to requiring it of Gentiles as a condition of belonging to God's people.

study.summary: ποιμήν means 'shepherd'. It is used literally of the shepherds at Jesus' birth, in images of sheep without a shepherd and of judgment, and supremely of Jesus as the good shepherd, the great shepherd and the shepherd of souls. Once (EPH 4:11) it denotes church leaders — 'pastors' — who care for God's people.

senses.label: Shepherd (literal)
senses.definition: One who tends and guards sheep.
senses.note: The shepherd separating sheep from goats (MAT 25:32) is a picture of the final judgment.

senses.label: Leader of God's people (the missing shepherd)
senses.definition: In the image of 'sheep without a shepherd', the leader who should feed, guide and protect the people.
senses.note: Echoes Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34.

senses.label: Christ the shepherd
senses.definition: Jesus as the true, good, great shepherd who knows, leads and lays down his life for the sheep, and as overseer of souls.

senses.label: The stricken shepherd
senses.definition: Jesus as the shepherd struck down (Zechariah 13:7), whose death scatters the disciples.

senses.label: The true shepherd vs. the hired hand
senses.definition: The one who enters by the door and owns the sheep, contrasted with the hireling who abandons them.

senses.label: Pastor (church leader)
senses.definition: One of Christ's gifts to the church: those who shepherd the congregation, closely linked with teaching.
senses.note: The only NT use of the noun for a church office; related verbs and nouns elsewhere apply shepherding to elders.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's Gospel develops the most extended shepherd discourse: Jesus is the good shepherd who lays down his life, knows his own, and gathers 'other sheep' into one flock.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: Peter calls Christ 'the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls', to whom straying sheep have returned.

study.translationNote: In Ephesians 4:11 most versions render ποιμένας as 'pastors', while some prefer 'shepherds' to keep the link with the rest of the NT's shepherd imagery. 'Pastor' is simply the Latin word for shepherd.

background.note: Homer regularly calls Agamemnon 'shepherd of the people', using the word metaphorically for a ruler.
Abel is described as a 'shepherd of sheep'.
A complainant in 221 BC asks not to be allowed to be lawlessly insulted by shepherds — shepherds did not always appear in a favourable light.
Shepherds let their flocks into the pasture of another man's olive-yard.

study.exegesisTip: Read NT shepherd language against the OT: God as Israel's shepherd (Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34) and the failure of Israel's leaders. When Jesus claims to be the good shepherd, he takes up a role the OT reserves for God and his promised Davidic ruler.
study.caution: Ephesians 4:11 ('pastors and teachers') is debated: whether it names one combined role (pastor-teachers) or two related ones. The grammar allows either.

study.summary: πολλάκις is the ordinary Greek adverb 'often, many times'. In the NT it marks repeated events in narrative, an apostle's repeated efforts and hardships, and, in Hebrews, the endlessly repeated sacrifices of the old order set against Christ's once-for-all offering.

senses.label: Repeated occurrence in narrative
senses.definition: Of something that happened again and again: a boy's frequent seizures, a demoniac's repeated chaining, Jesus' habit of meeting with his disciples in one place, Saul's repeated punishing of believers.
senses.note: In JOH 18:2 the frequency explains how Judas knew where to find Jesus.

senses.label: Repeated intention, effort or kindness
senses.definition: Of a person's habitual purpose or conduct: Paul often planned to visit Rome, Titus' companion often proved earnest, Paul often warned the Philippians, Onesiphorus often refreshed him; also of rain that falls often on the land.

senses.label: Repeated hardship in ministry
senses.definition: In Paul's catalogue of sufferings the adverb stresses that dangers, sleeplessness and hunger were not isolated incidents but recurring features of his apostolic life.

senses.label: Repetition of sacrifice (contrasted with 'once')
senses.definition: In Hebrews 'often' characterizes the high priest's yearly entry and the priests' daily offerings, which had to be repeated because they could never take away sins, in contrast to Christ's single offering.
senses.note: The contrast is with ἅπαξ / ἐφάπαξ, 'once, once for all'.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews turns a colourless adverb into a theological argument: repetition is the mark of inadequacy. Had Christ's sacrifice been like the old ones, he would have had to suffer often since the foundation of the world.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word mostly autobiographically, for his repeated plans, warnings and sufferings, underlining the persistence of his labour for the churches.

background.note: Used from Homer onward as the normal adverb of time, 'many times, often'.
Herodotus pairs it with its opposite, 'many times and not once', the same contrast between often and once that Hebrews exploits.
Common in everyday letters, e.g. 'the man about whom you write to me so often'.

study.exegesisTip: In Hebrews 9–10 read πολλάκις alongside ἅπαξ ('once'): the author's point turns on the difference between repeated and single action.

study.summary: προάγω means 'lead forward' (transitive) or, more often in the NT, 'go before, precede' (intransitive), whether in space (walking ahead, leading a procession) or in time (what came previously). It is used notably of the risen Jesus going ahead of his disciples into Galilee.

senses.label: Lead out, bring forward
senses.definition: Transitive: to bring a person out or before someone, including bringing a prisoner forward for trial or examination.
senses.note: In ACT 12:6 and ACT 25:26 the sense is judicial: to bring out before a tribunal.

senses.label: Go ahead, lead the way
senses.definition: Intransitive or with an object: to go in front of others, physically leading or preceding them, as the star before the magi, the disciples crossing the lake ahead of Jesus, or crowds walking in front in a procession.
senses.note: In MAR 11:9 and MAT 21:9 'those going before' are contrasted with 'those following'.

senses.label: The risen Lord going before to Galilee
senses.definition: Jesus' promise that after his resurrection he would go ahead of his disciples into Galilee, where they would see him; the image is of the shepherd leading the scattered flock.

senses.label: Precede in order or time
senses.definition: To come before something else: tax collectors entering the kingdom ahead of the religious leaders, sins going ahead of some people to judgment, prophecies made earlier about Timothy, and the 'preceding' commandment set aside in Hebrews.
senses.note: In HEB 7:18 the participle simply means 'former, previous'.

senses.label: Go too far, run ahead
senses.definition: Negatively, to advance beyond proper bounds: whoever 'goes ahead' and does not remain in the teaching of Christ does not have God.
senses.note: Many manuscripts here read a different verb meaning 'transgress'.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark's picture of Jesus walking ahead of his frightened disciples on the road to Jerusalem anticipates his promise to go ahead of them into Galilee after rising: he leads the way both to the cross and beyond it.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke alone uses the transitive sense, of bringing people out, often in legal settings.

study.translationNote: English versions vary between 'go before', 'go ahead of', 'precede' and, in Matthew 21:31, 'enter ahead of you' or 'go into the kingdom before you'. Some take that verse to imply that the leaders may follow later; others hear it as a sharp statement of displacement.

background.note: In classical Greek the verb commonly means to lead someone forward or onward.
An inscription uses it exactly as in Mark 6:45: 'I bade Timothy go before me to Rome.'
The participle means 'previous', as in Hebrews 7:18: 'the preceding month'.

study.exegesisTip: Note whether the verb has an object: with a person as object it is often 'go before someone' (MAT 2:9), but in Acts it can mean 'bring someone out'.
study.caution: In 2 John 9 and Acts 12:6 the manuscripts differ, so the presence of this verb (rather than a near-synonym) in those verses depends on the Greek text followed.

study.summary: προστίθημι means 'add, put to, give in addition'. Beyond adding to a quantity, NT writers use it of God giving more to his people, of converts being added to the church, of the law being 'added' to the promise, and, following a Septuagint idiom, of doing something again or further.

senses.label: Add to, increase
senses.definition: To put one thing to another so that the total grows: adding a cubit to one's span of life, Herod adding imprisoning John to his evils, the apostles asking the Lord to 'add' to their faith.

senses.label: Be given in addition by God
senses.definition: In the divine passive, of what God supplies over and above: those who seek the kingdom first will have food and clothing added; those who listen will be given more.

senses.label: Be added to the community
senses.definition: Of people joined to the believing community, the Lord himself adding those being saved.
senses.note: In ACT 2:47 the Lord is the subject who adds; growth is presented as God's work.

senses.label: Added (the law)
senses.definition: Paul says the law 'was added' because of transgressions, coming in later than the promise to Abraham and for a limited time, 'until the seed should come'.
senses.note: The word stresses that the law is supplementary to, not the basis of, the promise.

senses.label: Do again, proceed further (Septuagint idiom)
senses.definition: With an infinitive or participle, to do an action again or further: he 'proceeded to send' another servant, Herod 'went on' to arrest Peter too, Jesus 'went on to tell' a parable; Israel begged that no further word be spoken to them.

senses.label: Be gathered to one's fathers
senses.definition: A euphemism for death taken from Old Testament idiom: David 'was laid with his fathers'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the verb far more than any other writer, both for the growth of the church and in the biblical-sounding idiom 'he proceeded to do', a style that echoes the Greek Old Testament.

study.translationNote: In Luke 20:11–12 the Greek literally says 'he added to send'; modern versions render the idiom 'he sent another' or 'again he sent', which conveys the meaning rather than the form.

background.note: The construction with an infinitive mirrors Hebrew yasaph, 'to do again': in Genesis 4:2 Eve 'added to bear', that is, she bore again.
Demosthenes uses the verb of towns that voluntarily attached themselves to a side, a usage compared with converts 'being added' in Acts 2:41.
Used of adding a further statement: 'I will add a fact, my lord, which will excite your wonder', comparable to Hebrews 12:19.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who does the adding. In ACT 2:47 and MAT 6:33 the passive or the subject points to God as the giver, which shapes the meaning of church growth and provision.
study.caution: Scholars differ on whether the 'add to do' construction is a Hebraism or acceptable Greek; Luke's frequent use is at least strongly influenced by Septuagint style.

study.summary: πυλών is a gateway: the entrance structure of a large house or palace, opening onto the street, or the great gate (often a gate-tower) of a walled city. In Revelation it names the twelve pearl gates of the new Jerusalem.

senses.label: Gateway of a house
senses.definition: The entrance passage or porch of a substantial house or palace, leading from the street into the courtyard; a place where beggars lay, visitors stood, and servants answered.
senses.note: ACT 12:13 speaks of 'the door of the gateway': the gateway was a structure with a smaller door in it.

senses.label: Gate of a city or temple precinct
senses.definition: A monumental gate of a city or sacred precinct; at Lystra the priest of Zeus brought garlanded oxen to the gates.

senses.label: Gates of the new Jerusalem
senses.definition: The twelve gates of the heavenly city, named for the twelve tribes, each made of a single pearl, never shut, through which the redeemed enter.
senses.note: The open gates (REV 21:25) express perfect security and free access.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Most uses are in Revelation's description of the new Jerusalem, where the gates, guarded by angels and inscribed with Israel's tribes, symbolize the city's completeness and open welcome to those washed clean.

study.translationNote: Older English sometimes renders the word 'porch' (Matthew 26:71) because in a house it denoted the entrance hall or gateway rather than a simple door; 'gateway' or 'entrance' is usually closest.

background.note: In documents it is the gateway of a house: a complainant reports an attack on his house in the village 'at the gateway'.
Used of the gateway of a house already in third-century BC papyri.

study.exegesisTip: Distinguish πυλών (the whole gateway structure) from θύρα (a door) and πύλη (a gate): ACT 12:13 uses two of them together.
study.caution: At ACT 14:13 it is debated whether the gates are those of the city, of the temple of Zeus, or of the house where the apostles stayed.

study.summary: ῥύομαι means 'rescue, deliver', drawing someone out of danger to safety. God or Christ is almost always the deliverer, whether from enemies and deadly peril, from 'the evil one', or from the power of sin, death and coming wrath.

senses.label: Rescue from danger and enemies
senses.definition: To save someone from physical threat, persecution or hostile people.
senses.note: In 2CO 1:10 Paul uses past, present and future forms together: God has rescued, does rescue and will rescue.

senses.label: Deliver from evil / the evil one
senses.definition: In the Lord's Prayer and related confessions, to keep or snatch the believer from evil or the evil one and bring him safely into God's kingdom.

senses.label: Rescue from sin, death and wrath
senses.definition: Of God's saving act in Christ: delivering from 'this body of death', from the dominion of darkness, and from the coming wrath.

senses.label: The Deliverer
senses.definition: The participle used as a title, 'the Deliverer' who will come from Zion and turn ungodliness away from Jacob.
senses.note: Paul quotes ISA 59:20, where the participle renders the Hebrew go'el, 'redeemer'.

senses.label: Rescue of the righteous in judgment
senses.definition: God's rescue of the godly when he judges the wicked, as he rescued Lot from Sodom; mockers at the cross taunt that God should rescue Jesus if he wants him.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb both for his own escapes from persecution and for God's decisive rescue from sin and wrath, so that personal deliverances become signs of the final one.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 2 Peter makes Lot's rescue a pattern: the Lord knows how to rescue the godly while keeping the unrighteous for judgment.

study.translationNote: In Matthew 6:13 the Greek τοῦ πονηροῦ can be neuter ('from evil') or masculine ('from the evil one'). Older English versions read 'from evil'; many modern versions prefer 'the evil one' because Matthew often uses the masculine for Satan.

background.note: A sixth-century Christian amulet quotes the Lord's Prayer as 'deliver us from wickedness', showing an early reading of Matthew 6:13 as impersonal evil.
A statue inscription honours Hadrian as saviour, 'who rescued and nourished his own Greece', the verb being used of a ruler's deliverance.

study.exegesisTip: Look at the preposition: ἀπό ('from') and ἐκ ('out of') both occur; ἐκ often pictures being drawn out of the grip of a danger already present (ROM 7:24, COL 1:13).
study.caution: Whether 'evil' or 'the evil one' is meant in the Lord's Prayer cannot be settled on grammar alone; both readings have ancient support.

study.summary: στέφανος is a crown in the sense of a wreath or garland: the victor's prize at games, a festive or honorary chaplet, and also a royal crown. In the NT it names Jesus' mock crown of thorns, the believer's eschatological reward, Paul's converts as his pride, and the crowns of Revelation's visions.

senses.label: Crown of thorns
senses.definition: The wreath of thorns the soldiers plaited and pressed on Jesus' head in mockery of his claim to be king.
senses.note: The mockery parodies royal honours, yet the Gospels present him as truly king.

senses.label: Victor's wreath
senses.definition: The perishable garland won by athletes in the games, contrasted with the imperishable crown for which Christians strive.

senses.label: Eschatological reward
senses.definition: The crown God or Christ gives to the faithful at the end: the crown of righteousness, of life, of glory; something to be held fast lest another take it.
senses.note: In 'crown of life' and similar phrases the genitive probably defines the crown: the crown that consists of life, righteousness, glory.

senses.label: Pride and joy (of converts)
senses.definition: Figuratively, the people in whom one glories: Paul calls his converts his joy and crown, his crown of boasting at Christ's coming.

senses.label: Crowns of authority and victory in visions
senses.definition: In Revelation, crowns mark sovereignty, honour or conquest: the elders' golden crowns cast before the throne, the conqueror on the white horse, the locusts, the woman crowned with stars, the Son of Man with a golden crown.
senses.note: Revelation also uses διάδημα ('diadem') for royal crowns on the dragon and beast and on Christ.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In Revelation the crown is promised to the faithful and worn by heavenly figures, and the elders cast theirs before God's throne, acknowledging that all honour belongs to him.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul draws on the athletic games for the image of an imperishable prize and applies the honour of the crown to his own converts.

study.translationNote: 'Crown' is the standard rendering, but English readers often picture a jewelled royal crown; in many passages the image is a victor's or honorary wreath of leaves.

background.note: The root meaning is 'that which encircles': Homer speaks of the 'circle' of battle surrounding a warrior.
Emperor Claudius acknowledges a golden crown sent to him by an athletic club on his victory over the Britons.
The word also denoted the 'crown-tax', a levy collected as a present to the king.
A metaphorical use close to Philippians 4:1: 'great is your crown' of being praised by all.

study.exegesisTip: Ask what kind of crown the context evokes: the athletic games (1CO 9:25), a royal parody (MAT 27:29), or heavenly honour (REV 4:10).
study.caution: The sharp distinction sometimes drawn between στέφανος as a victor's wreath and διάδημα as a royal crown should not be pressed; στέφανος could also denote royal crowns.

study.summary: ἀπέχω has three main uses: transitively, 'have received in full' (a commercial term for giving a receipt); intransitively, 'be distant, far away'; and in the middle voice, 'keep oneself away from, abstain'. Jesus' words that hypocrites 'have their reward' use the receipt sense.

senses.label: Have received in full
senses.definition: To have been paid completely, so that nothing more is owed: those who perform religious acts for human praise have already received their full payment; the rich have had their comfort.
senses.note: Paul uses it in thanking the Philippians: 'I have received full payment'.

senses.label: Have back for good
senses.definition: To get someone back permanently: Onesimus was separated for a while so that Philemon might have him back forever.

senses.label: Be distant
senses.definition: Intransitive: to be some distance away, literally of places and people.
senses.note: In LUK 15:20 the father sees the son while he is still far off.

senses.label: Be far (of the heart)
senses.definition: Figuratively, of hearts far from God despite outward worship.
senses.note: Quoting ISA 29:13.

senses.label: Abstain from (middle)
senses.definition: To keep oneself away from something: from food offered to idols, blood and sexual immorality, from fleshly desires, from every form of evil, or (in false teaching) from certain foods.

senses.label: It is enough? (Mark 14:41)
senses.definition: Jesus' single word in Gethsemane, ἀπέχει, is usually taken impersonally as 'It is enough' or 'Enough!', though other explanations are offered.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: In the Sermon on the Mount the refrain 'they have received their reward' uses the receipt formula: the account is closed, so no reward remains to be paid by the Father.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the middle 'abstain' in ethical commands, linking holiness with keeping away from sexual immorality and every kind of evil.

study.translationNote: Versions render Matthew 6:2 as 'they have their reward' or 'they have received their reward in full'; the fuller rendering better captures the commercial sense of a paid-up receipt.

background.note: In Homer the active means to keep someone or something away from a place.
Constantly used in receipts: 'I have received the agreed price in full', the sense behind 'they have their reward'.
Also used of distance between places: villages or points 'not a mile distant from each other'.

study.exegesisTip: Check voice and construction: active with an object means 'have received in full'; active without an object means 'be distant'; middle with a genitive or ἀπό means 'abstain'.
study.caution: The meaning of ἀπέχει in Mark 14:41 is uncertain. 'It is enough' is the common view, but some take it commercially ('he has received [the money]', of Judas) or as 'the matter is settled'.

study.summary: ἀρέσκω means 'please, be agreeable to, win the favour of'. Besides ordinary pleasing, Paul uses it of the aim of pleasing God, of the danger of people-pleasing, and of accommodating oneself to others for their good, a sense close to 'serve'.

senses.label: Give pleasure, be acceptable
senses.definition: To please someone or meet with approval: a dance pleased Herod; a proposal pleased the whole assembly.
senses.note: ACT 6:5 reflects a Hebrew idiom: the word was pleasing 'before' the multitude.

senses.label: Please God
senses.definition: To live in a way that wins God's approval, the goal of Christian conduct; those in the flesh cannot please God.
senses.note: In 2TI 2:4 the image is a soldier seeking to please his commander.

senses.label: Seek human approval (people-pleasing)
senses.definition: Negatively, to court the favour of people, incompatible with being Christ's servant; also of opponents who do not please God.

senses.label: Accommodate oneself to others for their good
senses.definition: To give up one's own preferences and act for the benefit of others, following Christ, who did not please himself.
senses.note: Here 'pleasing' means serving the neighbour's good and upbuilding, not flattery.

senses.label: Please one's spouse
senses.definition: Of the married person's legitimate concern to please husband or wife, contrasted with the undivided concern of the unmarried for the Lord.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul holds two uses in tension: he refuses to please people to gain approval (GAL 1:10), yet he pleases everyone in all things so that they may be saved (1CO 10:33). The difference lies in the motive: self-interest versus others' good.

background.note: In Homer the middle means to appease or make amends, as Agamemnon proposes to appease Achilles with gifts.
Honorific inscriptions use the verb of benefactors who 'pleased', that is, rendered service to, the council and people, illuminating Paul's sense of pleasing others for their good.
In everyday letters it means simply to like or suit: a colour of wool, 'if it pleases him'.

study.exegesisTip: In each Pauline passage ask whose good the pleasing serves: one's own reputation (GAL 1:10), God's will (1TH 4:1), or the neighbour's edification (ROM 15:2).

study.summary: ἄφεσις means 'release, letting go'. In the NT it almost always denotes the forgiveness or remission of sins, God's release of sinners from guilt and its penalty; in Jesus' Nazareth sermon it keeps its jubilee sense of liberty for captives.

senses.label: Release, liberty
senses.definition: Freedom granted to captives and the oppressed, drawn from Isaiah's jubilee language in Jesus' programmatic sermon at Nazareth.
senses.note: The Greek Old Testament uses the word for the year of release (LEV 25:10).

senses.label: Forgiveness of sins
senses.definition: God's pardon, cancelling the guilt and penalty of sins, offered through repentance and faith and grounded in Christ's blood.
senses.note: Usually in the phrase 'forgiveness of sins'; never used of sins in the Greek Old Testament.

senses.label: Forgiveness as a present possession in Christ
senses.definition: Paul presents forgiveness as part of the redemption believers already have 'in him', through his blood and according to the riches of grace.
senses.note: In EPH 1:7 the object is 'trespasses'.

senses.label: Forgiveness without further sacrifice
senses.definition: In Hebrews, used absolutely: without shedding of blood there is no forgiveness, and where forgiveness has been granted no further offering for sin is needed.

senses.label: No forgiveness
senses.definition: Negatively, of the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit and never has forgiveness.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke makes 'forgiveness of sins' the content of the gospel to be preached to all nations in Jesus' name, and it recurs in nearly every apostolic sermon in Acts.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews links forgiveness to sacrifice and argues that once it has been fully secured the repeated sacrifices cease.

study.translationNote: Older versions often say 'remission of sins', newer ones 'forgiveness of sins'. 'Remission' preserves the idea of cancelling a debt or penalty; 'forgiveness' is the more natural modern English for the same idea.

background.note: Plato uses the word for legal quittance or release from the guilt of homicide.
Inscriptions use it for the remission of debts: a benefactor granted debtors release from their obligations.
With a genitive of persons it denotes the release of prisoners of war, as in Luke 4:18.
The Greek Old Testament can use the plural for water channels, matching an Egyptian technical term for releasing water from sluices.

study.exegesisTip: Note the debt-and-release imagery: the word's everyday background in cancelled debts and freed captives helps explain why Luke 4:18 and the 'forgiveness of sins' belong together.
study.caution: The phrase 'baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins' (MAR 1:4, ACT 2:38) is understood differently across traditions, especially regarding the force of 'for' (εἰς); the word ἄφεσις itself is not in dispute.

study.summary: βρῶμα means 'food', what is eaten. It appears in ordinary settings, in disputes about clean and unclean or idol-related food, in warnings against ascetic food rules, and figuratively of spiritual nourishment.

senses.label: Ordinary food
senses.definition: Food for daily needs, which can be bought, shared or supplied.

senses.label: Food in questions of purity and conscience
senses.definition: Food considered as clean or unclean, or as a matter on which believers' consciences differ; Jesus' teaching that what enters the mouth does not defile, and Paul's call not to destroy a brother for the sake of food.
senses.note: In 1CO 6:13 'food is for the stomach' appears to quote a slogan Paul then qualifies.

senses.label: Food regulations
senses.definition: Rules about what may be eaten, whether the old covenant's regulations or false teachers' bans on foods God created to be received with thanksgiving.

senses.label: Spiritual food
senses.definition: Figuratively, what nourishes the inner life: Jesus' food is doing his Father's will; immature believers can take milk, not solid food; Israel ate spiritual food in the wilderness.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Most of Paul's uses concern how believers handle disputed food: food does not commend us to God, but love governs whether one eats.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the word only once, to say that Jesus' food is to do the will of the one who sent him.

study.translationNote: In Mark 7:19 the participle 'cleansing all foods' is read by most modern versions as Mark's comment, 'Thus he declared all foods clean'; the King James Version, following a different reading, attaches it to the digestive process ('purging all meats').

background.note: Used in classical prose simply for food, what is eaten.
Medical writers use it, often in the plural, for foods in diet.

study.exegesisTip: Paul's arguments in Romans 14 and 1 Corinthians 8 do not turn on food itself but on love for the brother; trace how 'food' is set against the kingdom of God and the conscience of others.
study.caution: The grammar of Mark 7:19 is debated; whether the cleansing of foods is the evangelist's comment or part of Jesus' description affects how directly the verse addresses food laws.

study.summary: The ordinal number 'fifth', used only in Revelation to number the fifth seal, trumpet-angel, bowl-angel and foundation stone in John's numbered series.

senses.label: Fifth in a series
senses.definition: Fifth in order; in Revelation it marks the fifth item of the visionary sequences of seals, trumpets and bowls, and the fifth foundation stone of the new Jerusalem.

study.summary: An end, limit or boundary: spatially 'the ends of the earth', and once the 'end' that an oath puts to all dispute.

senses.label: Farthest limits of the earth
senses.definition: Plural, the extremities or remotest regions of the land or inhabited world, expressing the farthest possible distance.
senses.note: Romans 10:18 quotes Psalm 19 to stress the worldwide reach of the message.

senses.label: End, conclusion of something
senses.definition: The point at which something stops; an oath serves as the end of every dispute, settling it.

background.note: Used in petitions for putting an end to a matter or legal dispute, much as in Hebrews 6:16.

study.summary: To take away something that surrounds, remove; used of removing a veil, casting off anchors, and metaphorically of hope being abandoned and sins being taken away.

senses.label: Remove, take off
senses.definition: To take away something that covers or surrounds, as the veil removed when one turns to the Lord.

senses.label: Cast off (nautical)
senses.definition: As a sailing term, to cast off or slip the anchors; absolutely, to cast loose and put to sea.
senses.note: Acts 28:13 reads this verb in the critical text, where other manuscripts have περιέρχομαι ('sail around').

senses.label: Take away entirely
senses.definition: Metaphorically, to remove completely: all hope of rescue was being taken away, and animal sacrifices could never take away sins.

background.note: Used literally of stripping something off a person, in a report of robbery.

study.summary: To go around or about, of itinerant exorcists, wandering persecuted believers, idle visitors going house to house, and (in some manuscripts) a ship sailing around a coast.

senses.label: Go about, wander
senses.definition: To move from place to place, as itinerant Jewish exorcists or the faithful who wandered about in skins, homeless and persecuted.

senses.label: Go from house to house
senses.definition: With an accusative of place, to make the rounds of houses, describing idle visiting that breeds gossip.

senses.label: Sail around
senses.definition: Of a ship, to make a circuit or tack around a coast before arriving at port.
senses.note: This is the reading of the Byzantine text; the critical text has περιαιρέω here.

study.translationNote: At Acts 28:13 some versions read 'we sailed around' and others 'we weighed anchor' or 'cast off', reflecting a manuscript difference between two similar verbs.

background.note: Used of men going about a city keeping watch, a close parallel to the 'going about' of 1 Timothy 5:13.

study.summary: In the active, to stand around someone; in the middle, to turn oneself away from something, that is, to avoid or shun it.

senses.label: Stand around
senses.definition: Intransitive active forms: to stand around or near, as bystanders or as accusers surrounding a prisoner.

senses.label: Avoid, shun
senses.definition: Middle voice: to turn aside from and keep clear of something, here empty chatter and pointless controversies.

background.note: A second-century papyrus may show the middle in the sense 'avoid', of a woman evading an audit, illustrating the Pastoral Epistles' usage.

study.exegesisTip: In 2 Timothy 2:16 and Titus 3:9 the imperative is a call to steer clear of profitless talk, not merely to refute it.

study.summary: Abundance, overflow or surplus, whether of grace, of joy, of growth in ministry, or of evil that must be put away.

senses.label: Abundance, overflow
senses.definition: A superabundant amount of something good: the abundance of grace, overflowing joy amid affliction, and increase 'to abundance' in ministry.

senses.label: Excess, remaining surplus
senses.definition: An excess or remaining surplus of evil which believers must strip off as they receive the implanted word.
senses.note: Translators differ between 'overflow of wickedness' and 'the evil that remains' (what is left over).

study.translationNote: At James 1:21 renderings vary ('superfluity of naughtiness', 'rampant wickedness', 'evil that is so prevalent'), since the word can mean either excess or remaining surplus.

background.note: An inscription uses it of the surplus of the games-presidents' funds handed over to the city.

study.summary: Rocky or stony; in the parable of the sower it denotes ground where a thin layer of soil covers underlying rock.

senses.label: Rocky ground
senses.definition: Substantive use for shallow soil over bedrock, where seed springs up quickly but withers for lack of root; it pictures hearers who receive the word with joy but fall away under pressure.

background.note: Used of rocky ground in medical-geographical writing.

study.exegesisTip: The problem is not stones scattered in the soil but rock beneath a thin layer of earth, so the plant cannot root deeply.

study.summary: Originally the forearm, then a cubit, a measure of length of about a foot and a half.

senses.label: Cubit (measure of length)
senses.definition: A unit of length (elbow to fingertip), used for the distance of the boat from shore and the measurement of the new Jerusalem's wall.

senses.label: Small added measure
senses.definition: In Jesus' saying about anxiety, a single cubit added to one's ἡλικία, which may mean height or, more likely in context, length of life.

study.translationNote: Versions differ at Matthew 6:27 and Luke 12:25 between 'add one cubit to his stature' and 'add a single hour to his life', depending on whether ἡλικία is taken as height or lifespan.

background.note: Still used for the forearm itself, as in a description of a scar on the right forearm.

study.caution: Whether the cubit in Matthew 6:27 measures stature or is used figuratively for lifespan is debated.

study.summary: To make bitter; literally of waters and of John's stomach, and in the passive figuratively of husbands becoming embittered or harsh toward their wives.

senses.label: Make bitter (literal)
senses.definition: To make bitter to the taste or in effect: waters turned bitter by Wormwood, and the scroll that made John's stomach bitter.

senses.label: Be embittered, harsh
senses.definition: Passive, to become embittered or irritated toward someone, showing harshness instead of love.

background.note: The passive is used of people being exasperated or embittered.

study.summary: Bitterness, used in the NT figuratively of a resentful, hostile spirit and speech.

senses.label: Resentful, embittered spirit
senses.definition: An inner disposition of bitterness and resentment, expressed in hostile speech and spreading to corrupt others.
senses.note: Acts 8:23 'gall of bitterness' describes a malignant state of heart; Hebrews 12:15 echoes Deuteronomy 29 with its 'root of bitterness'.

background.note: Used in a weakened sense of the 'bitterness' or hardness of the times.

study.summary: Breadth or width, as a dimension of measurement and of the broad expanse of the earth.

senses.label: Breadth, width
senses.definition: The dimension of width, listed with length, depth and height for the vastness of Christ's love, and in the measurements of the new Jerusalem.

senses.label: Broad expanse
senses.definition: The wide extent of the earth over which the hostile nations march.

background.note: Used for breadth as a mathematical dimension alongside length and depth.

study.summary: A greedy or covetous person, one who grasps for more than his due, listed by Paul among those excluded from God's kingdom.

senses.label: Greedy, grasping person
senses.definition: One who desires to have more and takes advantage of others to get it; in Ephesians 5:5 such a person is identified as an idolater.

background.note: Used of one who has or claims more than his due, greedy and grasping.

study.summary: Full assurance or settled conviction, and possibly in one place fullness or full realization of hope.

senses.label: Full assurance, conviction
senses.definition: Settled, confident certainty, whether in the preaching of the gospel or in faith and understanding.

senses.label: Full realization
senses.definition: Possibly the full development or complete realization of hope, which believers pursue to the end.
senses.note: Many take this as 'full assurance of hope'.

background.note: Clement of Rome says the apostles went out preaching 'with full assurance of the Holy Spirit'.

study.caution: In Hebrews 6:11 interpreters differ between subjective 'assurance' and the more objective 'fullness' of hope.

study.summary: Richly or abundantly, describing the generous measure in which God gives and in which Christ's word should dwell in believers.

senses.label: Richly, abundantly
senses.definition: In generous, lavish measure: God's provision, the outpouring of the Spirit, the indwelling word of Christ, and the entrance into the eternal kingdom.

background.note: An inscription praises a man for discharging his duties toward people generously and lavishly beyond his means.

study.summary: A citizen, an inhabitant of a city or country, and with a personal genitive a fellow-citizen.

senses.label: Citizen, inhabitant
senses.definition: A member or resident of a city or region, as Paul of Tarsus or a local man in the far country.

senses.label: Fellow-citizen, subject
senses.definition: With a personal genitive, one's fellow-citizen or neighbor, or the subjects of a ruler.
senses.note: Hebrews 8:11 quotes Jeremiah 31, where the word renders 'neighbor'.

study.translationNote: At Hebrews 8:11 some versions read 'neighbor' (following another manuscript reading πλησίον) and others 'fellow citizen'.

background.note: Used from Homer onward for a citizen or freeman.

study.summary: Far, far off; in the comparative, farther.

senses.label: Far away
senses.definition: At a great distance, literally of an approaching king, or figuratively of hearts far from God despite outward honor.

senses.label: Farther (comparative)
senses.definition: Comparative, farther on, as Jesus acted as though he would go farther.

study.summary: Gentle or meek: not weak, but mild, unassertive and free from harshness, used of Jesus himself and of the disposition God blesses.

senses.label: Gentle, meek
senses.definition: Mild and considerate in spirit, not self-assertive or harsh; the quality of Christ as king and teacher and of those who inherit the earth.
senses.note: In the LXX it often renders Hebrew words for the humble or afflicted, as in Psalm 37:11 behind Matthew 5:5.

study.translationNote: Older versions prefer 'meek', newer ones often 'gentle' or 'humble'; the word combines gentleness with humble submission rather than weakness.

background.note: A sepulchral inscription describes a man as 'gentle in private life'.

study.summary: To bring or lead to someone; intransitively, to draw near; once of Christ bringing believers to God.

senses.label: Bring, lead to
senses.definition: To bring a person to someone, as a boy to Jesus or prisoners to magistrates.

senses.label: Bring to God
senses.definition: Christ's death brings believers into God's presence, a phrase with cultic and court overtones of access.

senses.label: Draw near, approach
senses.definition: Intransitive, to come near; the sailors sensed land was approaching them.

background.note: Commonly used for bringing sacrifices to a deity.

study.exegesisTip: In the LXX the verb chiefly renders Hebrew qarab, 'bring near', often of offerings; that background colors 1 Peter 3:18.

study.summary: A proselyte, a Gentile who has converted to Judaism.

senses.label: Convert to Judaism
senses.definition: A Gentile who has fully adopted the Jewish faith; such converts appear at Pentecost, among the Seven, and among synagogue worshippers, and are the object of Pharisaic missionary zeal.

background.note: In the LXX it chiefly renders Hebrew ger, the resident stranger or sojourner in Israel.

study.summary: Temporary, lasting only for a season, as opposed to what is lasting or eternal.

senses.label: Short-lived, not enduring
senses.definition: Of people in the sower parable, lasting only a little while because they have no root.

senses.label: Temporary, transient
senses.definition: Of things, passing and transitory: the visible world contrasted with the eternal, and the fleeting pleasure of sin.

study.summary: Partiality or favoritism, literally 'receiving the face', judging by outward status rather than by what is right.

senses.label: Partiality, favoritism
senses.definition: Showing preferential treatment based on a person's outward standing; God shows none, so believers must not.

study.exegesisTip: The term reflects the Hebrew idiom 'to lift the face', meaning to show favor to someone.

study.summary: The chief or front seat in the synagogue, a place of honor coveted by the scribes and Pharisees.

senses.label: Chief synagogue seat
senses.definition: The most prominent seating in the synagogue, sought as a mark of status; Jesus criticizes the love of such honors.

study.summary: A tower, either a watchtower in a vineyard or a building such as the tower that fell at Siloam.

senses.label: Tower, watchtower
senses.definition: A tall structure; in the vineyard parables a watchtower for guarding the crop, elsewhere a building whose cost must be counted or which collapsed on people.
senses.note: The vineyard parables echo Isaiah 5:2.

background.note: Used of a watchtower in a vineyard or olive grove, as in the Gospel parables.

study.summary: To sprinkle, especially in the ritual sense of purifying by sprinkling blood or water, and figuratively of hearts cleansed from a guilty conscience.

senses.label: Sprinkle for purification
senses.definition: To sprinkle people or objects with blood, ashes or water in Old Testament ritual for cleansing and covenant consecration.

senses.label: Cleanse inwardly
senses.definition: Figuratively, hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience by Christ's blood.

background.note: Used of the effect of purification in the penitential psalm ('purge me with hyssop').

study.exegesisTip: Hebrews uses the ritual imagery of sprinkling to show that Christ's sacrifice accomplishes the inward cleansing that the old rites only pictured.

study.summary: A narrow street, lane or alley in a town.

senses.label: Street, lane
senses.definition: A city street or narrow lane, as places of public display, of the poor, the named Straight Street in Damascus, and a block walked after leaving the prison.

background.note: In classical Greek the word meant the force or rush of a body in motion, not a street.
Papyri use it in the later sense of a street or lane, as in the NT.

study.summary: Sackcloth, a coarse cloth usually of goats' hair, worn as a garment of mourning or repentance.

senses.label: Coarse hair cloth
senses.definition: Dark, coarse cloth of goat hair, used as an image for the darkened sun.

senses.label: Garment of mourning
senses.definition: A rough garment worn as an outward sign of repentance or mourning.

background.note: Worn as mourning, as when Jacob mourned for Joseph.
Commonly means ordinary sacks or sacking, including sacks of hair.

study.summary: Worthy of respect, dignified or honorable; of persons, serious and esteemed; of things, honorable and worthy of reverence.

senses.label: Dignified, worthy of respect
senses.definition: Of persons, serious and dignified in conduct so as to command respect, required of deacons, women and older men.

senses.label: Honorable, noble
senses.definition: Of things, honorable and worthy of reverence, among the qualities believers should dwell on.

background.note: In early Greek it was used chiefly of gods as 'revered, august'.

study.summary: Crooked or bent; literally of winding paths, and figuratively of a perverse generation or harsh, unjust masters.

senses.label: Crooked, winding
senses.definition: Bent or winding, of ways that must be made straight.
senses.note: Quoting Isaiah 40:4.

senses.label: Perverse, morally twisted
senses.definition: Morally crooked and turned from the truth, describing a corrupt generation.
senses.note: Echoing Deuteronomy 32:5.

senses.label: Harsh, unjust
senses.definition: Of masters, harsh, unreasonable or unfair, as opposed to good and gentle.

background.note: Used of winding rivers.

study.summary: Originally to flay or tear; in NT Greek to trouble, bother or harass, and in the passive to be distressed.

senses.label: Harassed, distressed
senses.definition: Passive, worn down and distressed, of crowds like sheep without a shepherd.

senses.label: Trouble, bother
senses.definition: To trouble or inconvenience someone; in the middle, 'do not trouble yourself'.

background.note: Classical usage is physical, of dead bodies torn by fish.
Papyrus letters use 'don't trouble yourself' in the everyday sense found in Luke 7:6.

study.summary: A cloth, handkerchief or napkin (from Latin sudarium, 'sweat-cloth'), also used to cover the face of the dead.

senses.label: Handkerchief, cloth
senses.definition: A small cloth such as a handkerchief, used to wrap money or carried from Paul to the sick.

senses.label: Face cloth for dead
senses.definition: A cloth wrapped around the head or face of a corpse, as with Lazarus and in Jesus' empty tomb.

background.note: Listed among items in a bride's dowry in a marriage contract.

study.summary: To convulse or throw into violent spasms, used in the Gospels of an unclean spirit tearing at the person it possesses as it is cast out.

senses.label: Convulse, throw into spasms
senses.definition: Of a demon violently shaking or throwing down its victim, causing convulsions; describes the spirit's last savage assault before it leaves at Jesus' command.

background.note: In classical Greek the basic sense is to tear or rend, especially of animals mauling flesh; the Gospel use pictures a similarly violent mauling of the body.

study.summary: Eager, earnest, diligent; Paul uses it (mostly in the comparative) of co-workers who act with keen zeal.

senses.label: Earnest, zealous, diligent
senses.definition: Showing eager energy and diligence in a task; the comparative form means 'very eager' or 'all the more earnest', and as an adverb 'very diligently'.
senses.note: In 2CO 8:22 the brother is said to be earnest, and now 'much more earnest' because of his confidence in the Corinthians.

background.note: A second-century letter speaks of a person's zeal and attentiveness to the work of a landholding, using the same word.
