study.summary: Originally 'to cover' (as a roof keeps out rain), in the NT it means to bear up under, endure or put up with something without giving way.

senses.label: Bear up under, endure
senses.definition: To hold out under pressure or hardship, putting up with what is difficult rather than giving way; used of Paul enduring anything rather than hinder the gospel, of his inability to bear any longer the anxiety of not knowing about the Thessalonians, and of love that bears all things.

study.translationNote: In 1CO 13:7 some understand 'covers all things' (love conceals others' faults) rather than 'bears all things'; most versions keep 'bears'.

background.note: A fourth-century letter writer says his father did him much harm 'and I bore it until you come', the same sense of patient endurance found in Paul.

study.caution: The word can mean either 'cover/conceal' or 'bear/endure'; in 1CO 13:7 both are possible, though Paul's other uses favor 'endure'.

study.summary: Barren, unable to bear children; used of Elizabeth, of women in coming days of judgment, and of the 'barren one' of Isaiah's prophecy.

senses.label: Barren woman
senses.definition: A woman who has not borne children, a condition felt as a deep sorrow in Israel; God's reversal of barrenness marks his gracious intervention.
senses.note: In LUK 23:29 Jesus says coming disaster will be so terrible that the childless will be called blessed; in GAL 4:27 Paul quotes Isaiah's promise to the barren one as fulfilled in the children of promise.

study.exegesisTip: Elizabeth's barrenness echoes Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Hannah, whose children were gifts of God's power.

study.summary: Literally narrowness of space; in Paul it means distress or anguish, the feeling of being hemmed in by hardship.

senses.label: Distress, anguish
senses.definition: Severe trouble that leaves no room to escape; paired with θλίψις ('affliction') for the anguish facing evildoers and the hardships that cannot separate believers from Christ's love.

senses.label: Hardships, tight straits
senses.definition: In the plural, concrete situations of distress that Paul endured in his ministry for Christ's sake.

background.note: Classical writers use it literally for want of room, as of ships crowded together at sea.
A sixth-century papyrus speaks of 'the afflictions and distresses which I endured', the same pairing found in Romans.

study.summary: Solid, firm, hard; used of solid food, of God's firm foundation, and of believers standing firm in faith.

senses.label: Solid (food)
senses.definition: Solid food as opposed to milk, a picture of the more advanced teaching suited to mature believers.

senses.label: Firm, unshakable
senses.definition: Stable and immovable, of God's foundation that stands despite false teaching.

senses.label: Steadfast
senses.definition: Of people who stand firm and resist the devil, solid in their faith.

background.note: Often used of grain in the sense of hard, sound wheat.

study.summary: A colonnade or portico, a roofed walkway lined with columns, such as those at the pool of Bethesda and Solomon's Colonnade in the temple.

senses.label: Covered colonnade, portico
senses.definition: A roofed walkway supported by columns; the pool of Bethesda had five, and Solomon's Colonnade on the east side of the temple courts was where Jesus walked and where the early believers gathered.

study.translationNote: Older versions say 'porch' or 'porches'; modern ones prefer 'colonnade' or 'portico', which better describes a long covered walkway.

background.note: A common feature of Greek public architecture, a roofed colonnade or cloister.

study.summary: A sparrow or small bird, used by Jesus as an example of something nearly worthless that God nevertheless cares for.

senses.label: Sparrow
senses.definition: A small bird sold very cheaply in the market; Jesus argues from God's care for even one sparrow to his far greater care for his disciples.
senses.note: Matthew has two for a penny, Luke five for two pennies: an extra one thrown in, yet not forgotten by God.

background.note: A later imperial price list shows that among birds sold for food sparrows were the cheapest, which sharpens the point of Jesus' saying.

study.summary: A pillar or column, especially as a support; used literally of fiery pillars and figuratively of leaders, the church, and faithful believers.

senses.label: Pillar (support, figurative)
senses.definition: A person or body that supports and upholds: the leading apostles regarded as pillars, the church as pillar of the truth, and the overcomer made a permanent pillar in God's temple.

senses.label: Column (in description)
senses.definition: A column-like shape, used to describe an angel's legs as pillars of fire.

background.note: Euripides already uses the image metaphorically: male children are the pillars of a household.
The phrase 'pillar of fire' is used of the guiding pillar in the exodus.

study.summary: To shut in on all sides, enclose; literally of a net enclosing fish, and figuratively of Scripture, the law or God confining all people under sin or disobedience.

senses.label: Enclose (a catch)
senses.definition: To surround and shut in, as a net closing around a great catch of fish.

senses.label: Confine, imprison
senses.definition: To hold people shut up as in a prison with no way out; God has shut up all in disobedience, Scripture has confined all under sin, and the law held Israel in custody, so that mercy and the promise might come through faith.

background.note: Used of being locked up in prison: 'you will be shut up until you pay'.

study.exegesisTip: In Paul the confinement has a gracious purpose: being shut up under sin leads to mercy and faith.

study.summary: A fellow heir or co-heir, one who shares an inheritance with others.

senses.label: Fellow heir, co-heir
senses.definition: One who inherits together with another: believers as co-heirs with Christ, Gentiles as fellow heirs with Jewish believers, Isaac and Jacob as heirs with Abraham, and wives as joint heirs with husbands of the grace of life.

background.note: Found in later legal documents for making someone a co-heir.

study.exegesisTip: Each use stresses shared standing: no believer inherits alone, and Christ himself shares his inheritance.

study.summary: A fig, the fruit of the fig tree.

senses.label: Fig (fruit)
senses.definition: The fruit of the fig tree; used in sayings that a plant yields only fruit of its own kind, and in the account of the fig tree Jesus found without fruit.

background.note: Figs appear often in everyday documents, such as a basket of dessert containing a hundred figs.

study.summary: To take someone along as a companion or assistant on a journey or mission.

senses.label: Take along as companion
senses.definition: To bring someone along as a helper or travel companion, used of John Mark with Barnabas and Saul, of the dispute over taking Mark again, and of Paul taking Titus to Jerusalem.

background.note: In receipts the verb means 'received also by me', a co-signer receiving along with another.

study.summary: To go or travel together with someone; also of crowds coming together to a person.

senses.label: Travel with
senses.definition: To journey along with someone, as disciples and crowds going with Jesus and the risen Jesus walking with the two on the Emmaus road.

senses.label: Gather, come together
senses.definition: Of crowds coming together again to Jesus.

background.note: A standard verb for going or proceeding together in classical prose.

study.summary: To seize forcibly, grab and drag off, or of a ship, to be caught and carried away by a storm.

senses.label: Seize by force
senses.definition: To lay violent hold of someone and drag them off or keep them in one's grip, used of a demon seizing a man, and of mobs seizing Stephen and Paul's companions.

senses.label: Be caught and swept along
senses.definition: Of a ship caught by a violent wind and carried off course.

background.note: In classical Greek, to snatch and carry away by force.

study.summary: That which binds together: a bond, a fastening, or a ligament of the body; used figuratively of what unites or holds captive.

senses.label: Ligament
senses.definition: The connective bands of the body by which the whole body, joined to Christ the head, is held together and grows.

senses.label: Uniting bond
senses.definition: What holds believers together: peace as the bond of the Spirit's unity, and love as the bond of perfection.

senses.label: Bond of captivity
senses.definition: A fetter that holds a person bound, as Simon was bound by wickedness.

background.note: Used of the sinews or ligaments binding the limbs.

study.summary: Two related verb forms: in the aorist, to perceive or realize; in the perfect, to be privy to, share knowledge of, or be conscious of something in oneself.

senses.label: Realize, become aware
senses.definition: To grasp a situation, as Peter realizing what had happened, or the apostles learning of a plot and fleeing.

senses.label: Be privy to, know
senses.definition: To share knowledge of something with another, as Sapphira knowing about the money kept back.

senses.label: Be conscious of (oneself)
senses.definition: To know something against oneself; Paul is not aware of anything against himself, yet that does not acquit him.

study.exegesisTip: The use in 1CO 4:4 is related to the noun for 'conscience': Paul knows nothing against himself, yet leaves the verdict to the Lord.

study.summary: To work together, cooperate, help in a work; used of God working with his servants and of faith working with deeds.

senses.label: Work together with
senses.definition: To cooperate in a task: the Lord working with the apostles, believers who share in the work, Paul as God's co-worker, and Abraham's faith working with his deeds.

senses.label: Work together for good
senses.definition: In ROM 8:28, all things 'work together' for good for those who love God, or God works all things together for good.

study.translationNote: In ROM 8:28 some manuscripts add 'God' as subject ('God works all things together for good'); others read 'all things work together for good'. Versions differ accordingly.

background.note: A late papyrus uses the phrase 'with God's help' (God working together).

study.summary: Intelligent, understanding, discerning; a person able to put things together mentally.

senses.label: Intelligent, discerning
senses.definition: Having insight and understanding. Used of the proconsul Sergius Paulus, and of the worldly 'wise and understanding' from whom God hides what he reveals to the humble, and whose understanding he sets aside.

background.note: Used of gods and people as wise and understanding.

study.summary: To keep safe, preserve or protect; also to treasure something closely in the mind.

senses.label: Preserve, keep intact
senses.definition: Of new wine and new wineskins both kept from ruin.

senses.label: Protect (a person)
senses.definition: Herod kept John safe because he feared him as a righteous man.

senses.label: Treasure in the heart
senses.definition: Mary kept all these words close, pondering them in her heart.

background.note: A letter asks the recipient to do everything possible to protect the writer's wife until he arrives.

study.summary: To agree, make an arrangement or decide together, often in plotting.

senses.label: Agree, arrange together
senses.definition: To make a deal or come to a joint decision: the chief priests agreeing to pay Judas, the Jewish leaders agreeing to put out of the synagogue anyone confessing Jesus, plotters agreeing to request Paul's transfer, and accusers agreeing with the charges against him.

background.note: Common in contracts for making an agreement.

study.summary: Sensible, self-controlled, sound-minded; a basic virtue required of church leaders, older men and younger women.

senses.label: Self-controlled, sensible
senses.definition: Having a sound mind that governs desires and impulses; moderate, prudent and decent in conduct.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'sober-minded', 'self-controlled', 'sensible', 'temperate' and 'discreet' for this single word.

background.note: From Homer on, it describes a sound, prudent mind as opposed to folly.
Epitaphs praise a woman as 'sensible and loving her husband', the same ideal of womanhood found in TIT 2:5.

study.summary: An inner, private room in a house; also a storeroom.

senses.label: Inner room
senses.definition: A private room in the interior of a house, a place of secrecy, for private prayer or whispered words.

senses.label: Storeroom
senses.definition: A storehouse, which ravens do not have, yet God feeds them.

study.translationNote: Older versions say 'closet' (meaning a private room), which modern readers may misunderstand.

background.note: Common in papyri for a storehouse.

study.summary: Lowliness, a humbled or low condition, humiliation.

senses.label: Low estate, humble state
senses.definition: A lowly position or condition: Mary's humble state, the rich brother's low position before God, and the weak earthly body Christ will transform.

senses.label: Humiliation
senses.definition: Being humiliated and brought low, as the Suffering Servant in Isaiah's prophecy.

study.translationNote: In PHP 3:21 older versions have 'vile body', which suggests moral corruption; the sense is 'lowly body' as opposed to Christ's glorious body.

background.note: Used for the affliction or low estate God sees and answers, as with Leah.

study.summary: A bull or ox, mentioned in feasting and sacrifice.

senses.label: Bull, ox
senses.definition: A full-grown bull, used for feasting and for sacrifice, whether in pagan worship or in the Old Covenant sacrifices whose blood could not take away sins.

background.note: Used in everyday letters of working oxen.

study.summary: The comparative of 'quickly': more quickly, faster, or soon.

senses.label: Faster
senses.definition: More quickly than another, as the other disciple outran Peter.

senses.label: Quickly, soon
senses.definition: Without delay, or sooner than expected: Jesus telling Judas to act quickly, Paul hoping to come soon, and the writer of Hebrews hoping to be restored soon.

study.summary: The number four hundred.

senses.label: Four hundred
senses.definition: The number 400, used of the followers of Theudas and in chronological statements about Israel's history.

study.caution: The 400 years of ACT 7:6 and the 430 years of GAL 3:17 come from different Old Testament statements (Genesis 15:13 and Exodus 12:40) and are counted from different starting points; they are traditional round figures rather than a contradiction.

study.summary: A tetrarch, a ruler of part of a kingdom ranking below a king; in the NT always Herod Antipas.

senses.label: Tetrarch (ruler)
senses.definition: A subordinate ruler under Roman authority, used of Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea, who imprisoned and beheaded John the Baptist.

background.note: Originally the ruler of one of four divisions, as of the Thessalians in the fourth century BC.

study.exegesisTip: Mark calls Antipas 'king' as a popular title, but Matthew and Luke use his official rank, tetrarch.

study.summary: A craftsman or artisan; once used of God as the designer of the heavenly city.

senses.label: Craftsman, artisan
senses.definition: A skilled worker in a trade, such as the silversmiths of Ephesus or craftsmen of Babylon.

senses.label: Designer (of God)
senses.definition: God as the architect and builder of the city with foundations that Abraham awaited.

background.note: The Wisdom of Solomon already calls God the craftsman of creation.

study.summary: So great, so large; emphasizes the greatness of something.

senses.label: So great, so large
senses.definition: Of something remarkable in size or significance: so deadly a danger, so great a salvation, ships so large, an earthquake so mighty.

background.note: Used in a fourth-century letter of 'such great distress'.

study.summary: A he-goat, named in Hebrews among the sacrificial animals whose blood could not finally take away sin.

senses.label: He-goat for sacrifice
senses.definition: A male goat, mentioned with bulls and calves as an animal whose blood was offered under the old covenant, contrasted with Christ's own blood.

background.note: Used of the he-goat in contrast to the she-goat.

study.exegesisTip: In every NT use the goat stands for the repeated animal sacrifices of the Day of Atonement and covenant rites, which Hebrews sets against the once-for-all offering of Christ (HEB 10:4).

study.summary: A manger or feeding trough for animals, most famously where the newborn Jesus was laid.

senses.label: Manger, feeding trough
senses.definition: The trough (or the feeding place in a stable) from which livestock eat; the infant Jesus was laid in one because there was no room elsewhere.

senses.label: Stall
senses.definition: By extension the feeding place or stall where an ox or donkey is tied up.

study.translationNote: Most versions say "manger" in LUK 2 and "stall" in LUK 13:15; the Greek word is the same, referring to the animals' feeding place.

background.note: Used in Homer of the manger at which horses are fed.

study.exegesisTip: The manger is itself the "sign" given to the shepherds (LUK 2:12): the Messiah is found in the humblest of places.

study.summary: Worthless or bad; in the NT always morally bad, the opposite of good.

senses.label: Evil deeds, practices
senses.definition: Morally bad, worthless actions, often in the plural as "bad things" done, set against what is good and facing judgment.
senses.note: In ROM 9:11 and 2CO 5:10 this word stands in the critical text where other manuscripts read a more common word for "evil."

senses.label: Bad thing to say
senses.definition: Something bad or discreditable that could be said against someone.

background.note: In a weakened, everyday sense: there is "nothing the matter" with the writers.

study.exegesisTip: The word's root idea is worthlessness rather than violent wickedness; John uses it for the whole pattern of deeds that shrinks from the light (JOH 3:20).

study.summary: A fence, hedge or enclosing wall, and figuratively the partition that divided Jew and Gentile.

senses.label: Fence around a vineyard
senses.definition: A hedge or wall built to protect a vineyard, part of the owner's careful preparation in Jesus' parable.

senses.label: Hedges along roads
senses.definition: Hedgerows or fences lining country roads, where outsiders and wanderers might be found.

senses.label: Dividing partition
senses.definition: Figuratively, the barrier of separation and hostility between Jews and Gentiles, torn down by Christ.

study.translationNote: In EPH 2:14 versions vary between "middle wall of partition" and "dividing wall of hostility"; the phrase is literally "the middle wall of the fence."

background.note: The "dividing wall" has been compared with the inscribed barrier in the Jerusalem Temple that barred Gentiles from the inner courts.

study.caution: Whether EPH 2:14 alludes directly to the Temple barrier or more broadly to the Law as a separating fence is debated.

study.summary: The mindset or way of thinking that governs a person, used by Paul of the outlook of the flesh and of the Spirit.

senses.label: Mindset, outlook
senses.definition: The settled bent of thought and purpose; the "mindset of the flesh" leads to death and hostility to God, the "mindset of the Spirit" to life and peace.

senses.label: The Spirit's intent
senses.definition: What the Holy Spirit has in mind, known by God as the Spirit intercedes for believers.

study.translationNote: Older versions render ROM 8:6 "to be carnally minded is death"; modern ones say "the mind (or mindset) of the flesh"; both convey the same noun.
study.exegesisTip: The word describes not a single thought but the whole orientation of mind and will, which is why Paul can say it is either death or life (ROM 8:6).

study.summary: To guard or keep watch, used literally of a guarded city and figuratively of being held in custody or protected.

senses.label: Guard a city
senses.definition: To keep a city under guard, here to prevent someone from escaping.

senses.label: Hold in custody
senses.definition: To keep confined under guard; under the law people were held as if in protective custody until faith came.

senses.label: Protect, keep safe
senses.definition: To guard and protect, as God's peace guards hearts and minds and God's power keeps believers for final salvation.

background.note: Used of a body of soldiers keeping guard at a village.

study.exegesisTip: The word is military; in PHP 4:7 and 1PE 1:5 the picture may be of a garrison standing watch over a town.

study.summary: Hail, appearing in Revelation as a sign of God's judgment.

senses.label: Hail of judgment
senses.definition: Hail falling from the sky, in Revelation as part of God's judgments, echoing the hail plague of Egypt.
senses.note: REV 16:21 has the word twice, the second for the "plague of hail."

background.note: Homer lists hail with rain and snow as weather sent by Zeus.

study.summary: Green, of fresh vegetation, and also a sickly yellow-green pallor, as of the fourth horse in Revelation.

senses.label: Green, fresh vegetation
senses.definition: Green or freshly growing, of grass and plants; neuter as "anything green."

senses.label: Pale, deathly
senses.definition: A pale greenish-grey colour, the hue of a corpse, describing the horse whose rider is Death.

study.translationNote: In REV 6:8 versions say "pale," "ashen" or "pale green"; the word is the same as "green" grass elsewhere, but here suggests a sickly colour.

background.note: Of draught animals eating green fodder.

study.summary: Made of earth or dust, describing Adam and those who share his earthly nature.

senses.label: Made of dust, earthly
senses.definition: Formed from the dust of the ground like Adam; used of the first man and of all who bear his likeness, in contrast with the heavenly man, Christ.

study.translationNote: Older versions say "earthy," newer ones "of the dust" or "earthly"; the word alludes to Adam formed from dust.
study.exegesisTip: Paul echoes Genesis 2:7: the contrast is not between bad and good but between the body formed from dust and the resurrection body patterned on Christ (1CO 15:49).

study.summary: To touch or handle, and to feel or grope after something, as a blind person does.

senses.label: Touch, handle
senses.definition: To touch with the hands so as to verify something is real, as the disciples handled the risen Jesus.

senses.label: Tangible, able to be touched
senses.definition: Passive: something physical and palpable, like Mount Sinai, in contrast to the heavenly Zion.

senses.label: Grope after
senses.definition: To feel one's way toward something unseen; humanity searching for God.

background.note: Used of the blinded Cyclops groping with his hands.

study.exegesisTip: In ACT 17:27 the image is of someone groping in the dark, yet Paul adds that God is not far from anyone.

study.summary: Cold, used of cold water and figuratively of spiritual coldness.

senses.label: Cold water
senses.definition: Cold (water understood), a simple drink given to a disciple.

senses.label: Spiritually cold
senses.definition: Figuratively cold, set alongside "hot" and "lukewarm" in Christ's rebuke of the church at Laodicea.

background.note: Used on its own, without the word for water, to mean cold water.

study.caution: Interpreters differ on REV 3:15-16: some take "cold" as openly hostile, others as refreshing like cold water, contrasting both useful extremes with tepid Laodicea.

study.summary: A small piece or morsel of food, the one Jesus dipped and gave to Judas.

senses.label: Morsel of bread
senses.definition: A small bite of food, here dipped in the dish and handed to Judas at the Last Supper.

study.translationNote: The KJV says "sop"; modern versions say "morsel" or "piece of bread."

background.note: Used of the customary titbits given to sacred crocodiles.

study.exegesisTip: Offering a dipped morsel could be a gesture of honour, which deepens the tragedy of Judas taking it and going out into the night (JOH 13:30).

study.summary: To press someone into compulsory service, as soldiers could force civilians to carry loads.

senses.label: Compel into service
senses.definition: To requisition a person for forced labour, such as carrying a soldier's pack a mile or carrying Jesus' cross.

background.note: Used of a boat pressed into service by an official.

study.exegesisTip: The word, of Persian origin, describes a practice Jesus' hearers knew from occupying troops; going a second mile turns compulsion into freely given service (MAT 5:41).

study.summary: Holiness, the quality of being holy, in God's Spirit and as the goal of believers' lives.

senses.label: Holiness of the Spirit
senses.definition: The holiness that characterizes the Spirit by whom Christ was declared Son of God in power.

senses.label: Holiness of life
senses.definition: The holy state believers pursue and in which God establishes them, completed in the fear of God and blameless at Christ's coming.

study.caution: In ROM 1:4 "the Spirit of holiness" is usually taken as the Holy Spirit, though some see a reference to Christ's own holy spirit or divine nature.

study.summary: Wild, of things in their natural state, and figuratively fierce or untamed.

senses.label: Wild honey
senses.definition: Growing or found in the wild, not cultivated; John the Baptist's wild honey.

senses.label: Fierce, raging
senses.definition: Savage and untamed, of the raging sea waves to which false teachers are compared.

background.note: Used of a malignant, spreading sore.

study.summary: To be deeply troubled or distressed, used of Jesus in Gethsemane and of Epaphroditus.

senses.label: Be deeply distressed
senses.definition: To be in anguish or severe distress of mind; Jesus in Gethsemane, and Epaphroditus troubled that the Philippians had heard of his illness.

background.note: Used of being excessively concerned about a foster-child.
Paired by Plato with being at a loss.

study.exegesisTip: The same strong word describes both Jesus' anguish before the cross and Epaphroditus' care for others, showing the depth of feeling it conveys.

study.summary: A wrong done, a misdeed or crime, whether against law or against God.

senses.label: Legal wrong, crime
senses.definition: A wrongful act that could be charged in court.

senses.label: Sins before God
senses.definition: The iniquities of Babylon, remembered by God for judgment.

background.note: Aristotle defines it as a deliberate wrong, distinguished from a mistake or misfortune.

study.summary: Immortality, freedom from death, belonging to God alone and given to believers at the resurrection.

senses.label: Immortality
senses.definition: Deathlessness: God alone possesses it inherently, and the mortal body will put it on at the resurrection.

background.note: Used by Plato in discussing the immortality of the soul.

study.exegesisTip: Paul does not speak of an innately immortal soul here: immortality is something the mortal body "puts on" as a gift (1CO 15:53), while God alone has it by nature (1TI 6:16).

study.summary: To choose or prefer one thing over another.

senses.label: Choose, prefer
senses.definition: To pick one course over another, as Paul weighing life and death or Moses preferring hardship with God's people.

senses.label: God's choosing
senses.definition: God's choice of believers for salvation from the beginning.

background.note: Common in wills and contracts for "whatever way I choose."

study.summary: Greedy for dishonest or shameful gain, a trait that disqualifies church leaders.

senses.label: Greedy for shameful gain
senses.definition: Eager for money gained in base or dishonest ways; elders and deacons must not be so.
senses.note: In 1TI 3:3 the word appears only in the Byzantine text.

study.translationNote: The KJV's "greedy of filthy lucre" and modern "greedy for money" or "pursuing dishonest gain" render the same compound of "shameful" and "gain."

background.note: Used of someone sordidly greedy for gain.

study.summary: A request or petition, something asked for, whether from a ruler or from God.

senses.label: Demand to a ruler
senses.definition: What a crowd demanded of Pilate, which he granted.

senses.label: Prayer requests
senses.definition: The specific things believers ask of God in prayer.

background.note: Used for a request or demand.

study.summary: To take captive, literally in war and figuratively of sin's power, of thoughts, and of deceived people.

senses.label: Take captive in war
senses.definition: To carry people off as prisoners of war.

senses.label: Hold captive (figurative)
senses.definition: To bring into subjection: sin enslaving a person, every thought brought into obedience to Christ, or false teachers capturing the gullible.
senses.note: In 2TI 3:6 the critical text has this verb where other manuscripts have a related form.

study.exegesisTip: In 2CO 10:5 Paul continues the military imagery of the preceding verse: like a conquering army, he takes rebellious thoughts prisoner for Christ.

study.summary: Pure, unmixed, hence innocent and guileless in character.

senses.label: Innocent, guileless
senses.definition: Free from any admixture of evil; simple and sincere, without deceit or harmful intent.

study.translationNote: The KJV says "harmless" or "simple"; modern versions say "innocent" or "pure."

background.note: Used of a city recovered unharmed and unravaged.

study.exegesisTip: The root idea is "unmixed": believers are to be shrewd but have no evil mixed into their motives (MAT 10:16).

study.summary: To invalidate, cancel or nullify something that has authority, such as God's word or a covenant.

senses.label: Nullify, invalidate
senses.definition: To set aside or deprive of authority: human tradition nullifying God's command, or the later law being unable to annul God's earlier covenant promise.

background.note: Used in legal documents for revoking a will.

study.exegesisTip: The legal sense fits GAL 3:17: as a ratified will cannot be revoked by later additions, so the Law could not cancel the promise to Abraham.

study.summary: Unable to speak, mute, used of people and of a spirit causing muteness.

senses.label: Mute people
senses.definition: People who cannot speak, whom Jesus enabled to speak.

senses.label: Spirit causing muteness
senses.definition: An evil spirit that made its victim unable to speak.

study.translationNote: The KJV says "dumb"; modern versions say "mute" or "unable to speak."

study.summary: To salt, season or preserve with salt.

senses.label: Make salty again
senses.definition: To restore saltiness; Jesus asks how salt that has lost its taste can be salted.

senses.label: Salted with fire
senses.definition: Figuratively, purified or preserved through fiery testing, likened to sacrifices salted with salt.
senses.note: The second clause of this verse, about sacrifices salted with salt, appears only in the Byzantine text.

study.caution: "Salted with fire" in MAR 9:49 is a notoriously difficult saying; it is variously taken as purifying trial for disciples or as the judgment of the wicked.

study.summary: To leap or jump, and of water to spring or well up.

senses.label: Leap, jump up
senses.definition: To jump, as healed lame men leaped for joy.

senses.label: Water springing up
senses.definition: Of water, to well up or gush, picturing the life Christ gives.

background.note: Used of a thief springing into a farmstead by night.

study.exegesisTip: The leaping of the lame in ACT 3:8 recalls the prophecy that the lame will leap like a deer.

study.summary: To thresh grain, especially of an ox treading it out.

senses.label: Thresh grain
senses.definition: To separate grain from husks by trampling, done by oxen or by a worker; Paul applies the Law about the unmuzzled ox to those who labour in the gospel.

study.exegesisTip: Paul argues from the lesser to the greater: if God provides for the threshing ox, how much more for gospel workers (1CO 9:9-10).

study.summary: Without reason: of animals lacking reason, or of something unreasonable.

senses.label: Irrational, unreasoning
senses.definition: Lacking reason, of brute animals driven by instinct, to which false teachers are compared.

senses.label: Unreasonable, absurd
senses.definition: Contrary to good sense, as sending a prisoner without stating the charges.

background.note: Used substantively for the brute animals.

study.summary: A fox, and figuratively a cunning or crafty person.

senses.label: Fox
senses.definition: The animal, which has a den while the Son of Man has no home.

senses.label: Crafty person
senses.definition: Figuratively Herod Antipas, portrayed as cunning, sly or insignificant.

background.note: Used of someone who is a very fox for craft.

study.caution: Some think calling Herod a "fox" stresses slyness, others his insignificance or destructiveness; craftiness is the most common Greek connotation.

study.summary: To cry out or shout aloud, used of a sudden loud cry from Jesus on the cross, a crowd, and a desperate father.

senses.label: Cry out loudly
senses.definition: To raise one's voice in a loud shout or cry, whether of anguish, appeal or demand.
senses.note: Some manuscripts use the simple verb 'cry' in these verses instead of this compound.

background.note: A condemned man is said to have cried out in the middle of Rome, summoning the Romans to see him led off to death.

study.summary: Reading, especially the public reading of Scripture aloud in the gathered congregation.

senses.label: Public reading of Scripture
senses.definition: The reading aloud of the Law, the Prophets or the old covenant writings in synagogue or church worship.

background.note: Nehemiah 8:8 describes Ezra's public reading of the Law, explained so that the people understood.

study.exegesisTip: In 1 Timothy 4:13 the reading stands alongside exhortation and teaching, showing that the public reading of Scripture was a core part of early Christian worship.

study.summary: To come back to life, used figuratively of the prodigal's restoration and of sin springing back to life.

senses.label: Restored to life (figurative)
senses.definition: Of a person who was as good as dead to his family and has now returned, restored to life and fellowship.

senses.label: Sin springing to life
senses.definition: Of sin, dormant until the commandment came, then becoming active and powerful.

study.summary: To consume or destroy completely, used of fire, of mutual destruction, and of the Lord's overthrow of the lawless one.

senses.label: Consume, destroy
senses.definition: To use up or destroy entirely, as fire consumes or as people tear one another apart.
senses.note: In 2 Thessalonians 2:8 many manuscripts read a different verb meaning 'slay'.

background.note: Commonly used in everyday documents of spending money, e.g. sums expended.

study.exegesisTip: Galatians 5:15 builds a picture of wild animals: biting, devouring, and finally being consumed by one another.

study.summary: To kindle or set on fire.

senses.label: Kindle a fire
senses.definition: To light or set something ablaze, literally of a fire or figuratively of a fire Jesus came to bring or the destructive blaze of the tongue.

study.summary: To stir up, unsettle or throw into turmoil, whether by political agitation or by troubling teaching.

senses.label: Incite revolt, upset society
senses.definition: To stir up public unrest or rebellion; turn a society upside down.

senses.label: Unsettle believers
senses.definition: To disturb and unsettle a church by false teaching.

background.note: A boy writes of his troublesome behaviour that he upsets his mother, showing the word in everyday speech.

study.summary: To bring up, nurture and educate a child.

senses.label: Nurture, bring up
senses.definition: To rear and care for a child, including upbringing and education.

study.exegesisTip: In Acts 22:3 Paul's threefold sequence (born, brought up, educated) was a standard way of describing a person's formation.

study.summary: Above reproach; giving no grounds for any accusation.

senses.label: Irreproachable
senses.definition: So living that no one can rightly lay hold of a charge against you.

background.note: Used by Thucydides of a position not open to attack by enemies.

study.exegesisTip: The word literally means 'not able to be taken hold of'—there is nothing an accuser can grab onto.

study.summary: To go up, whether up a mountain or up to Jerusalem.

senses.label: Go up
senses.definition: To ascend to a higher place, including the customary 'going up' to the capital city of Jerusalem.

background.note: Used of going up to the capital or the main city.

study.summary: A preposition meaning 'without' or 'apart from'.

senses.label: Apart from (one's knowledge)
senses.definition: Apart from the knowledge or consent of someone, as nothing happens apart from the Father's will.

senses.label: Without
senses.definition: In the absence of something, such as words or grumbling.

study.translationNote: In Matthew 10:29 many versions add 'the will of' or 'the knowledge of' to express what the bare preposition implies.

background.note: A papyrus states that nothing happens without the gods.

study.summary: To be fitting or proper; what is due or appropriate.

senses.label: Be fitting, proper
senses.definition: To be appropriate or suitable in moral conduct; with the article, 'what is proper' or one's duty.

background.note: Used of duties or rights belonging to someone, as in an oath of allegiance to Augustus.

study.summary: A murderer or killer of people.

senses.label: Murderer
senses.definition: One who kills a human being; applied to the devil from the beginning and to anyone who hates his brother.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the word only of the devil and of those who hate a brother, making hatred the inner equivalent of murder.

background.note: Euripides uses the word in his Iphigenia in Tauris.

study.summary: Unwashed, referring to hands not ritually washed before eating.

senses.label: Unwashed (ceremonially)
senses.definition: Of hands not washed according to the tradition of the elders, and so regarded as ritually defiled.

background.note: Homer speaks of not pouring a libation to Zeus with unwashed hands.

study.exegesisTip: The issue is ritual purity under tradition, not hygiene; Jesus says true defilement comes from the heart.

study.summary: To set upright or straight again; to restore or rebuild.

senses.label: Straighten up
senses.definition: To make a bent body straight again, or to strengthen weak limbs.

senses.label: Rebuild, restore
senses.definition: To set up again something that has fallen, such as David's tent.

background.note: Herodotus uses it of rebuilding a temple.

study.summary: To take hold of, either to help someone or to share in a benefit.

senses.label: Help, come to aid
senses.definition: To take hold of someone in order to support and help them.

senses.label: Benefit from, partake of
senses.definition: To receive or enjoy the benefit of something, such as a slave's good service.

study.translationNote: In 1 Timothy 6:2 versions differ on whether the phrase means the masters who 'benefit from' the service or those who 'devote themselves to' good works.

study.summary: To take away; in the passive, to be taken away, used of the bridegroom removed from his guests.

senses.label: Be taken away
senses.definition: To be removed or carried away from someone's company.

study.exegesisTip: Jesus' words about the bridegroom being taken away are an early hint of his coming death.

study.summary: To set free or release; in the passive, to be rid of or to depart.

senses.label: Free, deliver
senses.definition: To release people from bondage, such as slavery to the fear of death.

senses.label: Depart, leave
senses.definition: Of diseases leaving the sick.

senses.label: Settle with, be released
senses.definition: In a legal context, to be quit of an opponent by reaching settlement.

background.note: Used in marriage contracts of a wife desiring to be released from her husband.

study.summary: To alienate or estrange; in the passive, to be cut off from God, his people and his life.

senses.label: Alienated, estranged
senses.definition: To be shut out from and a stranger to something, especially Israel's commonwealth and God's life.

study.exegesisTip: In each use the perfect participle describes an ongoing state of estrangement, which is then overcome by reconciliation in Christ.

study.summary: To throw off or cast away, also to lose.

senses.label: Throw off
senses.definition: To cast aside something, like a cloak.

senses.label: Throw away, lose
senses.definition: To give up or lose something valuable, such as confidence, or what is in danger of being lost.
senses.note: In Revelation 3:2 many manuscripts read 'about to die' instead.

background.note: Used in Homer of throwing off a cloak.

study.summary: To reconcile completely, bringing those at enmity into peace with God.

senses.label: Reconcile fully
senses.definition: To restore a broken relationship completely, through Christ's death on the cross.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses this intensified form for the cosmic and communal reach of reconciliation: Jew and Gentile in one body, and all things in heaven and earth.

study.caution: Whether the prefix stresses completeness or a return to an original harmony is debated.

study.summary: Hidden, concealed, or stored away out of sight.

senses.label: Hidden, concealed
senses.definition: Kept secret or out of view, though destined to come to light.

senses.label: Treasured, stored up
senses.definition: Of treasures of wisdom and knowledge stored up in Christ.

background.note: Herodotus uses the phrase 'in secret'.

study.summary: To choke or suffocate; in the passive, to be drowned.

senses.label: Choke (plants)
senses.definition: Of thorns crowding out and stifling young growth.

senses.label: Be drowned
senses.definition: Of the herd of pigs drowning in the lake.

study.summary: A divorce, or the written certificate of divorce.

senses.label: Certificate of divorce
senses.definition: The written document by which a man dismissed his wife.

background.note: Translates the Hebrew 'certificate of divorce' in the law of divorce.

study.summary: Put out of the synagogue; excommunicated from the Jewish community.

senses.label: Expelled from the synagogue
senses.definition: Excluded from synagogue fellowship, a punishment for confessing Jesus as Christ.

study.caution: How formal and widespread such exclusion was in Jesus' lifetime is debated.

study.summary: To escape from something, especially the world's corruption.

senses.label: Escape
senses.definition: To flee from and get free of the corruption and defilements of the world, or those living in error.

study.summary: To speak out, utter, or declare, often of inspired or weighty speech.

senses.label: Speak forth, declare
senses.definition: To utter words clearly and solemnly, as the Spirit gave utterance or in a public address or defence.

background.note: Used of the temple musicians chanting hymns.

study.summary: To go away, depart, or withdraw.

senses.label: Depart, withdraw
senses.definition: To go away from someone or something.

study.summary: Without offence: either not causing others to stumble or blameless oneself.

senses.label: Giving no offence
senses.definition: Not causing others to stumble into sin.

senses.label: Blameless, clear
senses.definition: Without stumbling or fault, as of a clear conscience or blameless life.

background.note: A slave thanks the gods that they keep her master free from harm.

study.summary: Made of silver.

senses.label: Of silver
senses.definition: Made of silver, such as shrines, vessels or idols.

study.summary: To count or number.

senses.label: Count, number
senses.definition: To count up, as God numbers every hair or as no one could count the great multitude.

background.note: Ordinarily used of paying or counting out a price.

study.summary: εἰσπορεύομαι means 'to go in, enter'. It is used of people entering towns, houses and the temple, of food going into the body, of desires entering the heart, of entering God's kingdom, and in the idiom 'going in and out' for living and moving freely among a group.

senses.label: Enter a place
senses.definition: To go into a town, house, room or the temple courts; the present tense often describes people as they are going in, or habitual going in.
senses.note: In Luke 8:16 and 11:33 'those who come in' are the people entering the house, who need the lamp's light.

senses.label: Go in to a person; house after house
senses.definition: To go in to someone in order to visit or meet them, or to enter one house after another, as in Saul's search for believers.
senses.note: In Acts 28:30 Paul, under house arrest in Rome, welcomed all who came in to him.

senses.label: Of food entering the body
senses.definition: Of what goes into a person through the mouth, in Jesus' teaching that nothing entering from outside can defile a person.
senses.note: The contrast is with what 'comes out' (ἐκπορεύομαι) of the heart, which is what truly defiles.

senses.label: Entering in a figurative sense
senses.definition: Of desires and cares that come into the heart and choke the word, and of people entering the kingdom of God.

senses.label: Go in and out among
senses.definition: Paired with 'going out' (ἐκπορεύομαι), an idiom for living and moving freely in fellowship with a group.
senses.note: The phrase reflects an Old Testament idiom for the whole of one's daily life and activity.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark uses the word most often, typically in the vivid present tense of Jesus and his followers going into places, and in the purity teaching of chapter 7.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses it for people coming into a house or the temple, for entering the kingdom, and for Paul's free movement among the believers in Jerusalem and his receiving visitors in Rome.

background.note: Papyri use the verb for going in to a public official, a close parallel to Acts 28:30, where people come in to Paul.

study.exegesisTip: Watch for the pairing with ἐκπορεύομαι ('go out'): in Mark 7 it contrasts what enters a person with what comes out of the heart, while in Acts 9:28 'going in and going out' describes Saul's full acceptance among the disciples.

study.summary: ζῆλος is intense, burning ardour. In a good sense it is zeal or earnest devotion for God, his house or other people; in a bad sense it is jealousy, the resentful rivalry that divides communities. Context alone decides which, and some passages (Romans 10:2, Philippians 3:6) describe sincere but misdirected zeal.

senses.label: Zeal, earnest devotion
senses.definition: Eager, warm commitment to a person or cause, such as Jesus' consuming zeal for God's house or the Corinthians' eager concern for Paul.

senses.label: Misdirected religious zeal
senses.definition: Fervent devotion to God or the law that lacks true knowledge and can even drive persecution.
senses.note: Paul credits Israel with genuine zeal for God and recalls his own zeal as a persecutor; the fault is not the fervour but its lack of understanding.

senses.label: Divine jealousy
senses.definition: God's protective, exclusive ardour for his people, which Paul shares for the church as a bride pledged to Christ.
senses.note: This reflects the Old Testament picture of God as a jealous husband who will not share his people with rivals.

senses.label: Fiery zeal of judgment
senses.definition: The burning fury of God's fire that will consume his adversaries.

senses.label: Jealousy, envious rivalry
senses.definition: Resentful envy of others' success or standing, listed among the works of the flesh and the sources of quarrels and disorder.
senses.note: It is frequently paired with strife (ἔρις) and selfish ambition (ἐριθεία).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses both senses: zeal for God (even misdirected), godly jealousy for the church and eager concern among believers, but also jealousy as a mark of fleshly, divided Christians.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: In Acts the Jewish leaders are 'filled with jealousy' at the apostles' success, a jealousy that leads to persecution.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James contrasts bitter jealousy and selfish ambition with the wisdom from above, tracing disorder and every evil practice to them.

study.translationNote: English versions alternate between 'zeal' and 'jealousy' (older versions also 'envy', 'emulation', 'fervent mind', 'indignation') because the same Greek word covers both. The choice is interpretive: in 2 Corinthians 11:2 'godly jealousy' keeps the marital imagery, while Hebrews 10:27 may be rendered 'fury of fire' or 'raging fire'.

background.note: Hesiod uses the word in the bad sense of jealousy or envy, close to φθόνος.
The Septuagint uses ζῆλος for the Hebrew qin'ah, as of Phinehas, whose zeal turned God's wrath from Israel.
An erotic fragment uses the word of passionate fervour that burns like fire, suggesting heat rather than emulation is the core idea.

study.exegesisTip: Ask what the ardour is directed toward and whose interests it serves: zeal for God's honour or another's good is praised, but the same intensity turned against a rival becomes jealousy. Notice how often the vice appears in lists alongside strife and factions.
study.caution: Do not assume zeal is automatically commendable; Paul's own zeal made him a persecutor (Philippians 3:6), and Israel's zeal was 'not according to knowledge' (Romans 10:2).

study.summary: κατακρίνω means 'to give judgment against, condemn', going beyond κρίνω ('judge') to the adverse verdict and sentence. It is used of the Sanhedrin condemning Jesus, of God's final condemnation, of self-condemnation, of God condemning sin in Christ's flesh, and of people whose example condemns others.

senses.label: Pass sentence, condemn judicially
senses.definition: To pronounce a guilty verdict and sentence, especially the sentence of death passed on Jesus.
senses.note: In John 8:10 Jesus asks whether anyone has condemned the woman, and then refuses to pass sentence on her himself.

senses.label: God's condemnation
senses.definition: God's adverse verdict on the unbelieving and ungodly, at the final judgment or in historical judgment as on Sodom.
senses.note: In Romans 8:34 Paul asks who can condemn those for whom Christ died, rose and intercedes.

senses.label: Condemn oneself
senses.definition: To bring condemnation upon oneself by one's own judgments or actions done against conscience.
senses.note: The one who judges another while doing the same things passes sentence on himself.

senses.label: Condemn sin in the flesh
senses.definition: God's decisive judgment on sin carried out by sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh as a sin offering.
senses.note: Sin itself is condemned, so that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ.

senses.label: Condemn by example
senses.definition: To show others to be guilty by contrast with one's own response, as the Ninevites, the Queen of the South and Noah did.
senses.note: Their faithful response becomes the standard that exposes the unbelief of others.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul distinguishes 'judging' from 'condemning' and centres the word on salvation: God condemned sin in Christ's flesh, so none can condemn his people, and the Lord's discipline keeps believers from being condemned with the world.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses the word both for the Son of Man being condemned to death and for the Ninevites and the Queen of the South condemning 'this generation' at the judgment.

background.note: Herodotus uses the passive of a sentence of death having been passed upon people.
In the papyri the verb is a legal term for a case being decided against someone.
Susanna contrasts condemning with examining judicially: the elders condemned without examining or learning the facts.

study.exegesisTip: Notice where κρίνω and κατακρίνω stand side by side (Romans 2:1; 1 Corinthians 11:32): 'judging' can mean assessing or disciplining, while κατακρίνω is the final adverse verdict. In 1 Corinthians 11:32 the Lord's present judgment is disciplinary so that believers will not face condemnation.

study.summary: καταλύω literally means 'to loosen down'. It is used for tearing down buildings, especially the temple; for overthrowing or annulling something such as the Law or God's work; and, from unharnessing pack animals at day's end, for stopping to lodge for the night.

senses.label: Tear down, demolish
senses.definition: To throw down a building stone by stone, especially the temple in Jesus' prophecy and in the charge brought against him.
senses.note: The accusation that Jesus would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days twisted his saying about the temple of his body.

senses.label: Dissolve the bodily dwelling
senses.definition: Of the earthly 'tent' of the body being taken down at death.

senses.label: Abolish, annul
senses.definition: To do away with a law or system, setting it aside as no longer valid; opposed to 'fulfilling' or 'building up'.
senses.note: In Matthew 5:17 Jesus denies he came to annul the Law and the Prophets; he came to fulfil them.

senses.label: Overthrow, bring to nothing
senses.definition: To ruin or frustrate a work or movement.
senses.note: Gamaliel argues that a human movement will collapse but one from God cannot be overthrown.

senses.label: Lodge, find lodging
senses.definition: Used intransitively of travellers halting for the night and taking up lodging.
senses.note: Related to κατάλυμα, the 'lodging' or 'guest room'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke alone uses the 'lodging' sense, notably of Jesus going to lodge with Zacchaeus, and records Gamaliel's warning that God's work cannot be overthrown.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word for rebuilding what one has torn down (the law as a way of righteousness), for destroying God's work over food, and for the dissolving of the earthly body.

study.translationNote: Matthew 5:17 is rendered 'destroy' in older versions and 'abolish' in most modern ones; the second fits better because the opposite term is 'fulfil', and the issue is whether the Law is annulled, not physically ruined.

background.note: Homer uses the verb for Zeus destroying the citadels of many cities.
In the Septuagint the verb often translates Hebrew lun, 'spend the night', as when Lot urges the visitors to lodge in his house.
Papyri use it for lodging at someone's house, the same sense as in Luke.
An inscription forbids anyone to annul a decree, using the word in the sense of setting aside a law, as in Matthew 5:17.

study.exegesisTip: Look at the word's opposite in each context: 'build' (Galatians 2:18; Mark 15:29), 'fulfil' (Matthew 5:17), or a lasting 'building from God' (2 Corinthians 5:1). The contrast clarifies what kind of 'destroying' is meant.

study.summary: κριτής is 'a judge', one who decides cases and gives verdicts. The NT uses it of ordinary court judges and Roman governors, of Israel's judges before the monarchy, of God and Christ as the final Judge, of people whose conduct becomes the standard for judging others, and of believers who wrongly set themselves up as judges.

senses.label: Human judge, magistrate
senses.definition: An official who hears cases and passes sentence, including a Roman governor.
senses.note: Gallio refuses to be a judge of disputes about Jewish words and names (Acts 18:15).

senses.label: Israel's judges
senses.definition: The leaders God raised up to rule and deliver Israel between the conquest and Samuel.

senses.label: God or Christ as Judge
senses.definition: God, the Judge of all, and Christ, appointed by God to judge the living and the dead.
senses.note: James warns that the Judge is standing at the door.

senses.label: Those whose conduct judges others
senses.definition: People whose own actions become a standard that exposes others' inconsistency.
senses.note: The Pharisees' own exorcists will show up their charge against Jesus as inconsistent.

senses.label: Setting oneself up as judge
senses.definition: Of believers who presume to judge others, whether by favouritism or by judging the law and their neighbours.
senses.note: In James 2:4 they become 'judges with evil thoughts' by favouring the rich.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke has most occurrences, including the parable of the unjust judge and the apostolic preaching of Christ as appointed judge of the living and the dead.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James contrasts the one Lawgiver and Judge with believers who usurp his role by partiality or slander.

background.note: In Aeschylus the word means a judge or umpire who decides between parties.
In the Old Testament sense the 'judges' were rulers in Israel.
A papyrus uses the word of a judge appointed by the Prefect of Egypt.

study.exegesisTip: Note the genitive that often follows: 'judge of unrighteousness' (Luke 18:6) means an unjust judge, and 'judges with evil thoughts' (James 2:4) describes the quality of their judging.

study.summary: κρύπτω means 'to hide, conceal'. It is used of hiding objects such as treasure, money or leaven, of people hiding themselves, of truths hidden from human understanding, and of realities kept hidden by God, such as the believer's life with Christ and the hidden manna.

senses.label: Hide an object
senses.definition: To put something out of sight, as in burying treasure or money or mixing in leaven.

senses.label: Hide oneself
senses.definition: To conceal oneself or be kept hidden from danger or from the presence of the Judge.
senses.note: The passive ἐκρύβη in John 8:59 can be taken as 'hid himself' or 'was hidden'.

senses.label: Cannot remain hidden
senses.definition: Of what is by nature visible and cannot be concealed, whether a city on a hill or good works.

senses.label: Hidden from understanding
senses.definition: Of truths or meanings concealed from people, whether by God's revelation to the humble or as judgment on unbelief.
senses.note: In Luke 19:42 the things that make for peace are hidden from Jerusalem's eyes.

senses.label: Kept secret
senses.definition: Of something kept secret out of fear, like Joseph of Arimathea's discipleship.

senses.label: Hidden with God
senses.definition: Of realities kept safe and unseen with God until they are revealed.
senses.note: The believer's life is hidden with Christ and will appear with him in glory (Colossians 3:4).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the word of Jesus hiding himself from hostility and of Joseph's secret discipleship, while Revelation speaks of the hidden manna and of people trying to hide from the Lamb.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses it in parables of hidden treasure and of the servant who hid his master's money, and for revelation hidden from the wise but given to little children.

background.note: Homer already uses the verb for concealing.
A fourth-century complaint tells of a husband who swore he would no longer hide his keys from his wife, yet hid them again.
An early collection of sayings expands Matthew 5:14 into a saying about a city built on a high hill that can neither fall nor be hidden.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who is doing the hiding and why: people hide valuables, sinners hide from God, and God himself hides truth from the proud or keeps his people's life secure in Christ until it is revealed.

study.summary: μέχρι (also μέχρις) means 'as far as, until'. As a preposition with the genitive it marks the limit of place, time, or degree; as a conjunction it means 'until' something takes place. It sets the end point, such as 'from Adam until Moses' or 'obedient to the point of death'.

senses.label: Until (time)
senses.definition: As a preposition marking the end point of a period: 'until, up to'.
senses.note: The phrase 'to this day' (μέχρι τῆς σήμερον) recurs in Matthew.

senses.label: As far as (place)
senses.definition: Marking the limit of a geographical extent.
senses.note: Paul has preached the gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum.

senses.label: To the point of (degree)
senses.definition: Marking the extreme measure to which something goes, such as death, chains, or blood.
senses.note: Christ became obedient 'to the point of death', meaning his obedience went as far as dying, not that he obeyed death.

senses.label: Until (conjunction)
senses.definition: Introducing a clause, alone or with οὗ: 'until such time as'.
senses.note: Paul labours in birth pains 'until Christ is formed in you' (Galatians 4:19).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word for every kind of limit: the historical span from Adam to Moses, the reach of his mission, Christ's obedience to death, and the goal of the church's growth into maturity.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses it for holding firm to the end, the temporary regulations valid until the time of reformation, and resisting sin to the point of bloodshed.

study.translationNote: Philippians 2:8 'obedient unto death' (KJV) can sound like obedience to death itself; modern versions clarify with 'to the point of death'.

background.note: Thucydides uses μέχρι with a time adverb, 'until then'.
Papyri use the phrase 'up to the present time' in the temporal sense.
A papyrus phrase 'to the end of life' shows the degree sense found in Philippians 2:8.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether μέχρι marks the end point of a period (time), a boundary (place), or an extreme (degree). In Hebrews 9:10 the 'until' marks the old regulations as provisional, valid only until the new order arrived.
study.caution: Like 'until' in English, μέχρι states the limit up to which something holds without necessarily saying what happens afterwards; the context must decide.

study.summary: νίπτω means 'to wash' a part of the body, especially hands, face, or feet (middle: 'wash oneself'). It describes everyday grooming, Jewish ritual handwashing before meals, the blind man washing at Siloam, and the humble service of washing feet, which Jesus makes a model of loving service.

senses.label: Wash one's face or body part
senses.definition: Ordinary washing of a part of the body, as Jesus tells those who fast to wash their faces.

senses.label: Ritual handwashing
senses.definition: Washing the hands before eating in keeping with the tradition of the elders.
senses.note: The issue was ritual purity according to tradition, not hygiene.

senses.label: Washing that brings healing
senses.definition: The washing the man born blind did at the pool of Siloam in obedience to Jesus, through which he received sight.

senses.label: Washing feet
senses.definition: Washing another's feet as an act of hospitality and humble service, done by Jesus for his disciples and required of godly widows.
senses.note: In John 13:8 being washed by Jesus means having a share with him, pointing beyond the literal act to cleansing by him.

senses.label: Partial versus full washing
senses.definition: Washing only the feet, contrasted with the full bath (λούω) of one already clean.
senses.note: The one who has bathed needs only to wash his feet; the picture distinguishes a once-for-all cleansing from ongoing cleansing.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses most occurrences in two scenes: the healing of the blind man, where washing in Siloam ('Sent') brings sight, and the footwashing, where washing is both a symbol of cleansing by Jesus and an example of humble love.

background.note: The Gospel of Peter notes that none of the Jews washed their hands, contrasting the leaders' callousness with Pilate's scruples.

study.exegesisTip: Distinguish νίπτω (washing a part of the body) from λούω (bathing the whole body) and πλύνω (washing clothes). John 13:10 depends on the difference between λούω and νίπτω.

study.summary: πλήρης means 'full, filled', then 'complete'. It describes baskets full of leftovers and a man covered with leprosy, and is used most distinctively of people wholly characterized by something: full of the Holy Spirit, faith, grace, wisdom or good works, or the opposite, full of deceit or rage. John 1:14 calls the incarnate Word 'full of grace and truth'.

senses.label: Physically full
senses.definition: Of containers filled to capacity, such as the baskets of leftovers after the feedings.

senses.label: Covered with
senses.definition: Thoroughly affected by something, like the man 'full of leprosy'.
senses.note: This suggests an advanced, widespread case.

senses.label: Filled with the Spirit and virtues
senses.definition: Of a person wholly characterized and controlled by the Holy Spirit, faith, wisdom, grace, power, or good works.
senses.note: This is a lasting quality of character, not just a momentary experience.

senses.label: Full of evil
senses.definition: Of a person or crowd dominated by deceit or rage.

senses.label: Full of grace and truth
senses.definition: Of the incarnate Word, who embodies God's covenant grace and faithfulness in full measure.
senses.note: This echoes God's self-description in Exodus 34:6 as abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.

senses.label: Complete, full
senses.definition: Of something brought to completion or received in full, such as ripe grain or a full reward.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses 'full of' to describe the Spirit-filled character of Jesus and of the leaders of the early church, such as Stephen and Barnabas, and in contrast the deceit of Elymas.

background.note: Herodotus uses it with the genitive for a city full of houses.
Papyri use πλήρης as an indeclinable word meaning 'in full', and this usage became common from the first century onward.
A receipt says the taxes have been 'paid in full', showing the sense of completeness.

study.exegesisTip: In Luke–Acts, 'full of the Spirit' (πλήρης) describes a settled character qualifying someone for service, while the verb 'be filled' (πίμπλημι) often marks a particular moment of empowered speech.
study.caution: In John 1:14 πλήρης may be the indeclinable form common in everyday Greek, so grammar alone does not decide whether 'full of grace and truth' describes the Word, his glory, or 'him'. Most take it to refer to the Word.

study.summary: πλήρωμα means 'fullness', either what fills something (contents, a patch) or the full measure or complete number of something. Paul develops it into a major theological term: the fullness of time, the full number of Israel and the Gentiles, love as the fulfilling of the law, and above all the fullness of God dwelling in Christ and filling the church.

senses.label: Patch, filler
senses.definition: That which fills up a gap, the piece of new cloth sewn onto an old garment.

senses.label: Contents, full measure
senses.definition: What fills something, like basketfuls of leftover pieces or everything that fills the earth.
senses.note: 1 Corinthians quotes Psalm 24:1, 'the earth and its fullness'.

senses.label: Full number
senses.definition: The complete number or full inclusion of a group.
senses.note: Paul looks ahead to Israel's full inclusion and the full number of the Gentiles coming in.

senses.label: Fulfilment
senses.definition: The act of fully carrying out what is required.
senses.note: Love is the fulfilment of the law.

senses.label: Fullness of time
senses.definition: The completion of the appointed period, the moment God fixed for acting in Christ.

senses.label: Divine fullness
senses.definition: The complete presence, life, and blessing of God, dwelling fully in Christ and communicated to his people, who are being filled and brought to maturity.
senses.note: In Colossians 2:9 all the fullness of deity dwells in Christ bodily.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul turns the word into a key theological term: salvation history reaches its 'fullness' in Christ; all God's fullness dwells in Christ; the church is his fullness; and believers are to be filled to all the fullness of God and grow to the measure of the fullness of Christ.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John says that all believers have received from the incarnate Word's fullness 'grace upon grace'.

study.translationNote: Matthew 9:16 and Mark 2:21 use the word for a 'patch', so versions vary between 'the patch', 'that which is put in to fill it up', and 'the new piece', all meaning the filler.

background.note: Euripides uses it for the contents that fill mixing bowls, meaning the wine.
Herodotus uses it of ships for their full complement or crew.
A papyrus uses it for a full work-gang, which must not be withdrawn until the work is finished.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether πλήρωμα means 'what fills' or 'what is filled' and whose fullness is in view. In Ephesians 1:23 the church is called Christ's fullness, 'the fullness of him who fills all in all', and the sense chosen affects the reading.
study.caution: Scholars disagree on Ephesians 1:23: some take the church as what is filled by Christ, and others as what completes him. Also avoid reading second-century Gnostic speculation about a heavenly 'pleroma' into Paul. Colossians uses the word to insist that God's fullness is found entirely in Christ.

study.summary: ῥαββί is a Semitic loanword (from Hebrew/Aramaic rab, 'great one', with the suffix -i, 'my') meaning literally 'my great one, my master'. In the Gospels it is the respectful form of address for a Jewish teacher, and John explicitly glosses it as 'Teacher'. It is used of John the Baptist and above all of Jesus, by disciples, enquirers and crowds alike, while Jesus forbids his followers to covet it as an honorific title.

senses.label: Honorific title for a Jewish teacher
senses.definition: A title of respect given to recognized teachers of the Law, prized as a mark of public status.
senses.note: Jesus criticizes the scribes and Pharisees for loving to be greeted with it and tells his disciples not to be called 'Rabbi', because they have one Teacher and are all brothers.

senses.label: Address to John the Baptist
senses.definition: Used by John's disciples when speaking to their own teacher.

senses.label: Address to Jesus by disciples
senses.definition: The ordinary way Jesus' followers address him as their teacher and master, often at moments of question, surprise or confusion.
senses.note: In John 1:38 the evangelist translates it for Greek readers as 'Teacher' (διδάσκαλε).

senses.label: Address to Jesus by others
senses.definition: Used by outsiders and enquirers who recognize Jesus as a teacher, without necessarily confessing more about him.
senses.note: Nicodemus, himself a teacher of Israel, gives Jesus the title as a peer recognizing a teacher 'come from God'.

senses.label: Judas' greeting
senses.definition: The title on the lips of Judas at the moment of betrayal, where a mark of respect becomes the signal for arrest.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: In Matthew the disciples address Jesus as 'Lord' (κύριε), while 'Rabbi' is used of Jesus only by Judas, at the Last Supper and at the betrayal. Combined with the prohibition in 23:7–8, this gives the title a pointed, almost ironic tone in his Gospel.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the title more than any other evangelist and explains it for non-Jewish readers. In chapter 1 'Rabbi' begins a chain of rising titles for Jesus: Rabbi, Messiah, Son of God, King of Israel.

study.translationNote: Most modern versions keep 'Rabbi', while the KJV often renders it 'Master'. Keeping the transliteration preserves the Jewish setting and the fact that the evangelists themselves left the word untranslated, explaining it only for Greek readers.

background.note: Greek lexicons treat the word as a Hebrew term known from the Gospels, glossed 'O my Master', not a native Greek word.

study.exegesisTip: Notice who uses the title and when. A disciple calling Jesus 'Rabbi' (Mark 9:5) is showing respect, but in the same Gospels the word can stop short of full confession, as with Nicodemus, or be emptied of meaning, as on Judas' lips (Mark 14:45). Compare it with the higher titles the same speakers or narrators use nearby.
study.caution: Scholars debate how formal 'Rabbi' was in the early first century. It later became the title of an ordained scholar in rabbinic Judaism, but in the Gospels it is best read as a respectful form of address for a teacher, not as evidence of formal ordination.

study.summary: ῥίζα means 'root'. In the Gospels it is the literal root of a tree or plant, and in parables a picture of how deeply the word has taken hold in a hearer. Paul and Hebrews use it for the source or origin of something: the love of money as a root of evils, a bitter root that poisons a community, and the patriarchal root of Israel's olive tree. From Isaiah 11 comes a further sense, the 'root' as the shoot that grows from it, applied to Jesus as the Root of Jesse and of David.

senses.label: Literal root
senses.definition: The root of a tree or plant, the part that anchors and feeds it.
senses.note: The axe laid 'at the root' (Matt 3:10) pictures judgment that removes the whole tree, not just its branches.

senses.label: Inner rootedness of faith
senses.definition: Figuratively, the depth and stability of a hearer's response to the word. To 'have no root in oneself' is to receive the message superficially and fall away under pressure.

senses.label: Source or cause
senses.definition: That from which something grows. Used of a vice that gives rise to many evils, or of a person or attitude from which trouble spreads.
senses.note: Hebrews 12:15 echoes Deuteronomy 29, where a 'root bearing bitterness' is someone in Israel who turns from the LORD and corrupts others.

senses.label: Ancestral root of God's people
senses.definition: The patriarchal origin of Israel, pictured as the root of an olive tree that bears and nourishes both natural and grafted branches.
senses.note: Most interpreters take the root as the patriarchs and the promises given to them; some see Christ, or God's covenant faithfulness.

senses.label: Shoot or descendant
senses.definition: That which springs from a root: a descendant. Used of the Messiah as the promised offspring of Jesse and David.
senses.note: Revelation 22:16 joins 'the Root and the Offspring of David', presenting Jesus as both David's source and his descendant.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's olive-tree image (Rom 11) warns Gentile believers against arrogance: they are supported by a root they did not produce. In Romans 15:12 he quotes Isaiah's 'Root of Jesse' to show that the Gentiles' hope was promised in Israel's own Scriptures.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation uses 'Root of David' as a messianic title for the Lamb who alone can open the scroll and for the risen Jesus speaking at the close of the book.

study.translationNote: In 1 Timothy 6:10 the Greek has no article: 'a root of all kinds of evils' or 'a root of all evils'. The KJV's 'the root of all evil' can suggest that money-love is the only source of every sin, which goes beyond the wording.

background.note: In Homer the word is used of the literal root of a plant, including the magic root Hermes gives Odysseus.
A third-century letter instructs someone to 'burn its roots', referring to an acacia tree, showing the plain everyday sense.
A first-century BC royal inscription of Antiochus I calls the Persians and Greeks 'the most fortunate root of my race', the same sense of ancestry that underlies 'the Root of David'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask which way the image points in each passage. 'Root' can mean what lies beneath and supports (Rom 11:18), what produces something (1 Tim 6:10), or what grows up from the stump (Rom 15:12). Revelation 22:16 deliberately uses both directions at once.
study.caution: In Romans 11 the identity of the root is debated (the patriarchs, Abraham, the covenant, or Christ). The text emphasizes continuity with Israel's heritage, so avoid building doctrine on a single identification.

study.summary: συμφέρω literally means 'bring together', and is used once in that sense of people bringing their magic books to be burned. Usually it is impersonal: συμφέρει, 'it is advantageous, it is better, it profits'. The participle τὸ συμφέρον means 'what is beneficial, the advantage or good' of someone. Jesus uses it to weigh eternal consequences, Caiaphas uses it for political calculation, and Paul uses it as the test for Christian freedom: not 'Is it allowed?' but 'Does it build others up?'

senses.label: Bring together, collect
senses.definition: Transitive and literal: to gather items into one place.

senses.label: It is better, it is to one's advantage
senses.definition: Impersonal συμφέρει, usually with a dative of the person and a clause, saying that one outcome is preferable or more profitable than another.
senses.note: Often best rendered 'it is better for you'. In Matthew 19:10 the disciples conclude that 'it is better not to marry'.

senses.label: Expedient (political calculation)
senses.definition: What is advantageous in a pragmatic sense, used by Caiaphas of sacrificing one man to save the nation.
senses.note: John presents this cynical advice as an unwitting prophecy of Jesus' substitutionary death.

senses.label: Beneficial, profitable (of conduct)
senses.definition: Of actions or choices: helpful, constructive, worth doing.
senses.note: Paul answers the slogan 'all things are lawful' with 'but not all things are beneficial'.

senses.label: The good or advantage of others
senses.definition: The participle τὸ συμφέρον, used as a noun: someone's benefit or welfare, often contrasted with self-interest.
senses.note: Spiritual gifts are given 'for the common good' (1 Cor 12:7), and God disciplines his children 'for our good' (Heb 12:10).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: For Paul the word measures Christian freedom. Lawful things are not automatically beneficial, and what is beneficial is judged by the good of others, not by personal advantage (1 Cor 10:33).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the word for two opposite 'advantages': Caiaphas' calculation that one man should die for the people, and Jesus' assurance that his departure is for the disciples' good because it brings the Spirit.

study.translationNote: English versions vary between 'better', 'expedient', 'profitable', 'beneficial' and 'good' because the Greek idiom ('it brings together for you') has no single English equivalent. 'Expedient' (KJV) sounds calculating today, which suits Caiaphas but not Jesus' words in John 16:7.

background.note: Herodotus uses the active sense 'bring together', of gathering everyone's troubles into the middle.
A letter of AD 99 says 'it is an advantage that it should be dug', showing the everyday impersonal use found in the Gospels.
A third-century papyrus says 'it is inexpedient to buy', using the negated impersonal form as Paul does in 2 Corinthians 12:1.

study.exegesisTip: When the word appears, ask 'advantageous to whom, and judged by what standard?' The contrast between Caiaphas' 'advantage' (John 11:50) and Paul's 'not seeking my own advantage, but that of many' (1 Cor 10:33) shows the same word serving opposite values.

study.summary: ταράσσω means 'stir up, disturb, agitate'.
