It can be used physically of water being stirred, but in the NT it is mostly used of the mind and emotions: being shaken by fear, alarm or grief. It also describes stirring up a crowd or unsettling a church with false teaching. John uses it of Jesus himself being deeply troubled before death, and of Jesus' command to his disciples not to let their hearts be troubled.

senses.label: Stir up (water)
senses.definition: Physically to agitate or disturb water.
senses.note: The stirring of the pool at Bethesda.

senses.label: Alarmed, frightened
senses.definition: Passive: to be thrown into inner turmoil by something sudden or threatening: fear, shock or anxiety.
senses.note: Peter's 'do not be troubled' echoes Isaiah 8:12, applied to believers facing hostility.

senses.label: Jesus' troubled spirit
senses.definition: Deep emotional distress felt by Jesus before death and in the face of betrayal.
senses.note: In 11:33 the active with a reflexive pronoun ('he troubled himself') suggests an emotion Jesus fully takes on, not one forced on him.

senses.label: Hearts not to be troubled
senses.definition: Jesus' command and gift to his disciples: freedom from anxious turmoil because of trust in him.

senses.label: Unsettle, agitate a community
senses.definition: Active: to throw people into confusion, whether by stirring up a crowd against the gospel or by unsettling believers with false teaching.
senses.note: In Galatians those who 'trouble' the churches are teachers pressing circumcision, and Paul says they will bear their judgment.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the word in a deliberate pattern. Jesus is troubled at Lazarus' tomb, at the prospect of his hour, and at Judas' betrayal, and then tells his disciples, 'Let not your heart be troubled.' He bears the turmoil so that he can give them his peace.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the active participle almost as a label, 'those who trouble you', for the agitators in Galatia, the same language the Jerusalem council used about the circumcision party.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'troubled', 'disturbed', 'terrified', 'startled' and 'frightened' depending on context. The Greek word covers the whole range of inner agitation; context shows whether fear, grief or confusion is in view.

background.note: Homer uses the word physically of Poseidon stirring up the sea.
A second-century letter says 'do not be disturbed on this account', the same mental sense as Matthew 2:3.
A first-century letter complains that 'he is upsetting everything again', close to the sense of stirring up trouble in Acts 17.

study.exegesisTip: In John 12:27 Jesus' 'Now my soul is troubled' echoes the language of the lament psalms and prepares for Gethsemane. Reading John 14:1 and 14:27 against 11:33–13:21 shows that the disciples' peace rests on Jesus having first entered into turmoil himself.

study.summary: χάρισμα, from χαρίζομαι ('give freely, graciously') and closely related to χάρις ('grace'), means 'a gift of grace', something freely and undeservedly given. It is almost entirely Pauline. It names God's gift of salvation and eternal life in Christ, the irrevocable gifts given to Israel, and the varied endowments the Spirit distributes to believers for the good of the church. Peter uses it the same way, of gifts to be used in service as stewards of God's grace.

senses.label: The free gift of salvation
senses.definition: God's gracious gift in Christ, especially righteousness and eternal life, contrasted with what is earned.
senses.note: In Romans 6:23 the free gift of eternal life is set against sin's 'wages'.

senses.label: God's gracious gifts to Israel
senses.definition: The privileges and promises God has graciously given to his people, which he does not revoke.

senses.label: Spiritual endowments for service
senses.definition: Abilities and functions given by the Spirit to each believer for building up the body of Christ, such as prophecy, teaching, healing, serving and leading.
senses.note: The lists are varied and illustrative; Paul stresses that one Spirit gives them as he wills and for the common good.

senses.label: Gifts in the church generally
senses.definition: The whole range of spiritual gifts a church possesses or should seek.
senses.note: In Romans 1:11 Paul hopes to share 'some spiritual gift' that will strengthen the Roman believers.

senses.label: A personal gift or calling
senses.definition: A particular gracious endowment given to an individual, such as the capacity for celibacy or the ministry gift given to Timothy.
senses.note: Timothy's gift came through prophecy and the laying on of hands, and he must 'fan it into flame'.

senses.label: A gracious favour (deliverance)
senses.definition: A specific act of God's kindness, here Paul's rescue from deadly danger, granted in answer to prayer.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul ties gifts to grace: every χάρισμα comes from χάρις and so excludes boasting. He uses the same word for salvation itself (Rom 5–6) and for ministry gifts (Rom 12; 1 Cor 12), so service in the church flows from the same grace that saves.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: Peter makes every believer a recipient of some gift and a steward of 'God's varied grace', with speaking and serving as the two broad categories.

study.translationNote: Most versions translate 'gift' or 'spiritual gift', but in Romans 5 'free gift' is common, to bring out the contrast with what is earned. In 2 Corinthians 1:11 versions vary ('gift', 'favour', 'blessing') because the word there refers to a specific act of deliverance, not a lasting ability.

background.note: The word is almost absent from the Greek Old Testament, appearing only as a manuscript variant in Sirach, so the NT's frequent use is essentially Paul's own.
A fourth-century AD papyrus uses the plural for gifts or favours generally ('you know the favours I have done you'), outside any religious context.
A late sixth-century will describes property as acquired 'by purchase and by gift', using the word for an ordinary gift.

study.exegesisTip: Notice how Paul frames each list of gifts with body, love and the common good (the common good in 1 Corinthians 12, love in chapter 13, the one body in Romans 12). The point of the word is not ability but grace: the gift reflects the Giver's generosity and is meant for others.
study.caution: The modern words 'charisma' and 'charismatic' do not match NT usage. χάρισμα is not limited to spectacular or miraculous gifts; it includes eternal life, celibacy, serving and leading. Whether 1 Corinthians 12:31 ('earnestly desire the greater gifts') is a command or a description of the Corinthians' behaviour is debated.

study.summary: ἀθετέω means literally to treat as ἄθετος, 'not set in place', and so to set aside, disregard, invalidate or reject something that has been established. It is used of setting aside a command, covenant or pledge, of nullifying or thwarting a purpose, and of rejecting a person, especially God's messengers, which amounts to rejecting God himself. In the Greek Old Testament it often translates Hebrew words for dealing treacherously and rebelling, so it can carry a sense of breaking faith.

senses.label: Set aside a law, command or pledge
senses.definition: To disregard or violate something that is binding, treating it as void.
senses.note: In 1 Timothy 5:12 younger widows who remarry are said to 'set aside their first pledge'.

senses.label: Nullify, frustrate
senses.definition: To make something ineffective, frustrating a purpose or rendering it void.
senses.note: Paul refuses to 'nullify the grace of God' by seeking righteousness through the law.

senses.label: Reject a person
senses.definition: To refuse and despise someone, especially God's messenger, or authority.
senses.note: Rejecting the messenger is rejecting the One who sent him: 'whoever rejects me rejects him who sent me' (Luke 10:16).

senses.label: Break faith with, refuse
senses.definition: To go back on one's word to someone, refusing a request one has sworn to grant.
senses.note: Herod would not 'break faith with' or 'refuse' the girl because of his oaths.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word for rejecting God's saving purpose (Luke 7:30) and for rejecting Jesus' messengers, which he treats as the same as rejecting Jesus and the Father.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word mostly of things: grace, covenant, a pledge, human wisdom. In 1 Thessalonians 4:8 it is used of a person, to warn that whoever disregards his moral teaching rejects not a man but God, who gives the Holy Spirit.

study.translationNote: English versions vary widely ('reject', 'set aside', 'nullify', 'frustrate', 'despise', 'break faith') because the word covers both treating a thing as invalid and rebuffing a person. In Mark 6:26 'refuse her' and 'break his word to her' are both defensible.

background.note: In the Greek Old Testament the word describes Eli's sons treating the LORD's offering with contempt.
An inscription from Ilium uses the word of cities that might break their mutual agreement, which is close to the sense of breaking faith.
A papyrus from the time of Augustus speaks of 'setting aside what has been agreed', the legal sense of annulling a contract.

study.exegesisTip: Notice what is being set aside in each passage: a command (Mark 7:9), a covenant (Gal 3:15), grace (Gal 2:21), a person (Luke 10:16). The word implies that what is rejected had real standing and authority, so rejecting it is culpable, not neutral.

study.summary: ἀνακρίνω means 'examine closely, investigate, question'. In Luke–Acts it is mainly legal: the interrogation of an accused person before a verdict. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians for scrutinizing, appraising and calling to account: the spiritual person 'discerns' or 'examines' all things, Paul refuses to be finally assessed by any human court, and an unbeliever is 'examined' by prophecy. The Bereans' daily examination of the Scriptures gives the word a positive, careful sense.

senses.label: Judicial examination
senses.definition: To interrogate an accused person or witnesses in a legal hearing in order to establish the facts.
senses.note: Pilate's 'having examined him' (Luke 23:14) is the language of a formal hearing.

senses.label: Careful investigation
senses.definition: To examine or scrutinize something closely to test it.
senses.note: The Bereans examined the Scriptures daily; Paul tells the Corinthians to eat what is sold in the market 'without raising questions' for conscience' sake.

senses.label: Spiritual discernment
senses.definition: To evaluate rightly by the Spirit's illumination; things of God are 'spiritually discerned', and the spiritual person appraises all things.

senses.label: Appraise, pass judgment on a person
senses.definition: To scrutinize and assess someone's conduct or worth, as a court would.
senses.note: In 1 Corinthians 9:3 Paul offers his 'defence to those who examine me'.

senses.label: Called to account by prophecy
senses.definition: To be searched and exposed in conscience, as an unbeliever is when prophecy lays bare the heart.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word for legal hearings, often to stress that examination found Jesus or his apostles innocent (Luke 23:14; Acts 28:18).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: All of Paul's uses are in 1 Corinthians, where the church was evaluating its teachers. He turns the word against them: the spiritual person examines all things, but Paul's own evaluation belongs to the Lord, not to human courts or even to himself.

study.translationNote: Versions use 'examine', 'judge', 'discern', 'appraise' and 'question'. In 1 Corinthians 2 and 4 the KJV's 'judge' can blur the difference between ἀνακρίνω (scrutinize, investigate) and κρίνω (pass a verdict), which Paul keeps distinct in 4:3–5.

background.note: Thucydides uses the word of the Spartans interrogating Pausanias, the formal questioning of a suspect.
In the Greek Old Testament Jonathan promises to 'sound out' his father Saul about David.
A second-century BC inscription directs officials to 'examine the witnesses', the judicial sense found in Luke–Acts.

study.exegesisTip: In 1 Corinthians 4:3–5 Paul distinguishes being examined (ἀνακρίνω) by people from the Lord's final verdict, telling the Corinthians not to 'judge' (κρίνω) before the time. In Athenian law the ἀνάκρισις was a preliminary hearing, not the trial itself, which suits Paul's point that all human appraisal is provisional.

study.summary: ἀπειθέω means 'disobey, refuse to comply, be disobedient', the opposite of πείθομαι ('obey, be persuaded'). In the NT the refusal is usually directed at God, his word or the gospel. So it describes Israel's rebellion in the wilderness and the unbelieving response to Christ, where unbelief and disobedience are two sides of one refusal. Peter and Hebrews use it of those who reject the message; John sets 'disobeying the Son' against 'believing in the Son'.

senses.label: Disobey God, rebel
senses.definition: To refuse to comply with God's will or command; persistent rebellion.
senses.note: Hebrews 3:18 refers to the wilderness generation that could not enter God's rest.

senses.label: Refuse the Son and the gospel
senses.definition: To reject the message about Christ, a refusal that is both unbelief and disobedience.
senses.note: John 3:36 sets 'whoever believes in the Son' against 'whoever does not obey the Son'.

senses.label: Unbelieving opponents
senses.definition: Participle used for those who have rejected the message and actively oppose its messengers.

senses.label: Disobedient people in God's plan
senses.definition: Used of Gentiles and Israel in turn as disobedient, so that all may receive mercy.

senses.label: Not obeying the word (of a spouse)
senses.definition: Of husbands who 'do not obey the word', that is, have not accepted the gospel, who may be won by their wives' conduct.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: Peter uses the word as his standard label for unbelievers: those who stumble over the cornerstone, husbands who do not obey the word, the people of Noah's day, and those who do not obey the gospel of God.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In Romans 11:30–31 Paul presents disobedience as something Gentiles and Israel share in turn, so that God may show mercy to all.

study.translationNote: The KJV often has 'believe not' (e.g. John 3:36, 'he that believeth not the Son'), while most modern versions have 'disobey' or 'does not obey'. The Greek word means disobedience. Where the NT applies it to the gospel, refusing to believe is the disobedience, so 'reject' is a common middle course.

background.note: Euripides uses it with the dative for disobeying a god: Orestes, 'not disobeying the god', killed his mother at Apollo's command.
In Joshua those who disobeyed the LORD's commandments are the generation that died in the wilderness, the same tradition Hebrews 3:18 draws on.
A papyrus of 243–242 BC complains of a man who 'has continued to disobey your orders', showing the word's plain sense of non-compliance.
A royal decree of 139 BC orders officials to 'compel those who disobey' to pay their dues, again of refusing a lawful command.

study.exegesisTip: Read the word against its opposite in context: 'believe' in John 3:36 and 1 Peter 2:7–8, 'obey' elsewhere. The NT does not separate faith from obedience; rejecting the gospel is treated as a refusal of God's rightful claim, not merely an intellectual doubt.
study.caution: Older lexicons sometimes gave 'disbelieve' as a primary meaning. The ordinary Greek evidence shows the core meaning is 'disobey'. The 'unbelief' sense comes from contexts where the thing disobeyed is the message of faith, not from the word itself.

study.summary: γάμος means 'wedding' and especially 'wedding feast', and also 'marriage' as an institution. In the Gospels it is the joyful celebration, often in the plural, that Jesus uses as a picture of the kingdom: the king's feast for his son, the bridegroom's arrival, guests seeking the best seats. John sets Jesus' first sign at a wedding in Cana, and Revelation climaxes with 'the marriage of the Lamb'. Hebrews uses it of marriage itself, to be honoured by all.

senses.label: Wedding celebration, wedding feast
senses.definition: The festivities surrounding a marriage, especially the banquet to which guests were invited. The plural often refers to a single celebration.

senses.label: The wedding gathering or occasion
senses.definition: The event itself, or the place filled with guests, and the proper garment needed to attend it.
senses.note: The man without a 'wedding garment' (Matt 22:11–12) is unprepared for the occasion he has been invited to.

senses.label: Marriage (the institution)
senses.definition: The marriage relationship of husband and wife, to be held in honour.

senses.label: The marriage of the Lamb
senses.definition: The final union of Christ and his people, pictured as a wedding and its feast.
senses.note: Revelation blesses those invited to 'the marriage supper of the Lamb', linking back to the Gospel wedding parables.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew concentrates the word in two parables of the end (22:1–14; 25:1–13). The wedding feast pictures God's kingdom: the invitation is generous, but refusal and unpreparedness bring exclusion.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's Gospel opens Jesus' signs at a wedding (2:1–2), and Revelation ends with the marriage of the Lamb, framing the story with the biblical image of God as bridegroom of his people.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'wedding', 'wedding feast', 'wedding banquet', 'marriage' and 'marriage feast'. The Greek covers both the ceremony and the celebration; the plural (γάμοι) usually means one wedding feast, not several.

background.note: Homer speaks of suitors who 'furnish forth a wedding', the preparations for the festive celebration.
Laban gathers the people and makes a wedding feast for Jacob, using the singular for the celebration.
A third-century papyrus invitation asks a guest 'to dine at the wedding of her children', the same setting as the Gospel parables.
A marriage contract of 92 BC is labelled 'agreement of marriage', showing the word's use for marriage as a legal union.

study.exegesisTip: Jewish weddings could last several days and were the most joyful social events a village knew; refusing an invitation was a serious insult (Matt 22:3–7). Reading the parables with this in mind sharpens their point about the honour and urgency of God's invitation.

study.summary: δεῖπνον is the main meal of the day, normally eaten in the late afternoon or evening: 'dinner, supper', and by extension a formal dinner or banquet. In the Gospels it is the setting for social honour and status (seats of honour, invitations), for Jesus' parable of the great banquet, and for the Last Supper. Paul calls the church's meal 'the Lord's Supper', and Revelation contrasts 'the marriage supper of the Lamb' with 'the great supper of God'.

senses.label: Dinner, banquet
senses.definition: The principal meal of the day, often a formal occasion with guests and seating by rank.
senses.note: The scribes love 'the places of honour at banquets', where reclining position showed social rank.

senses.label: The great banquet (parable)
senses.definition: The feast in Jesus' parable to which the invited guests refuse to come and the poor and outcast are brought in.

senses.label: The Last Supper
senses.definition: The evening meal Jesus shared with his disciples before his death.
senses.note: John uses the word for the meal at which Jesus washed the disciples' feet.

senses.label: The Lord's Supper
senses.definition: The church's shared meal in remembrance of Jesus, which belongs to the Lord.
senses.note: Paul says the Corinthians' divided meal, where some go hungry and others get drunk, is not truly the Lord's Supper.

senses.label: End-time feast
senses.definition: Metaphorically, the final feasts of Revelation: the joyful marriage supper of the Lamb, and the grim 'great supper of God' where the birds feed on the defeated.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses dinner settings to teach about status reversal: do not invite those who can repay you, and the outcasts fill the feast that the invited refuse.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's phrase κυριακὸν δεῖπνον ('the Lord's Supper') makes the meal the Lord's own, so behaviour that shames poorer members contradicts its very nature.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'supper', 'dinner', 'feast' and 'banquet'. 'Supper' is traditional for the Last Supper and the Lord's Supper, but in ancient usage δεῖπνον was the main meal, not a light evening snack. In John 13:2 the manuscripts differ ('supper being ended' in the KJV, 'during supper' in most modern versions); the context of 13:4 and 13:26 shows the meal was still going on.

background.note: In Homer the word can mean the noonday meal; its time of day shifted over the centuries.
By the time of Aristophanes it is the afternoon or evening dinner, the main meal of the day.
A private expense account of about AD 1 records asparagus bought 'for the dinner of Antas', an everyday use of the word.

study.exegesisTip: Meals in the ancient world mapped social rank: who was invited, where they reclined, what they were served. Read Jesus' banquet teaching (Luke 14) and Paul's rebuke (1 Cor 11:20–22) with this in mind; both overturn the normal social ranking of the dinner table.

study.summary: To eat a meal, properly the morning or midday meal (breakfast), and more loosely to dine.

senses.label: eat breakfast
senses.definition: To take the early meal of the day, as when the risen Jesus invites the disciples to eat the fish he has cooked by the lake.

senses.label: take a meal, dine
senses.definition: More generally, to eat a meal as a guest; the Pharisee invites Jesus to dine at his house.

background.note: Classical writers distinguish this earlier meal from the main evening dinner.

study.summary: Left, on the left side; used of the left hand and, in a phrase, of position on someone's left.

senses.label: left hand
senses.definition: The left hand, contrasted with the right; Jesus says giving should be so private that the left hand does not know what the right is doing.

senses.label: on the left
senses.definition: In the phrase 'on the left', of position beside someone, as of the criminal crucified on Jesus' left or the place James and John asked for in the kingdom.

senses.label: left-hand weapons
senses.definition: Of weapons held in the left hand; Paul's 'weapons of righteousness for the right hand and the left' pictures full equipment for attack and defence.

background.note: The phrase 'on the left' is common in everyday documents describing position.

study.summary: Sufficient, enough; what is adequate for a given need.

senses.label: sufficient, enough
senses.definition: Adequate or enough: each day has enough trouble of its own; it is enough for a disciple to be like his teacher; the time already spent living as the pagans do is more than enough.

background.note: Used of a person proving satisfactory in his work.

study.summary: To plough, used of a farm servant at work and of the ploughman who should work in hope of a share in the harvest.

senses.label: plough
senses.definition: To break up soil with a plough; Jesus pictures a servant coming in from ploughing, and Paul argues that the ploughman ploughs in hope of sharing the crop, as a gospel worker may expect support.

background.note: Used plainly of a yoke of oxen going out to plough.

study.summary: Seizure of property: robbery, plundering, or the greedy grasping that produces it.

senses.label: greedy plunder, extortion
senses.definition: The grasping spirit or gain obtained by robbery; Jesus says the Pharisees keep the outside of cup and dish clean while inside they are full of plunder.

senses.label: confiscation of goods
senses.definition: The violent seizure of someone's belongings; the Hebrew believers joyfully accepted the plundering of their property.

study.translationNote: Versions render the Gospel uses as 'extortion', 'greed' or 'robbery', depending on whether they stress the act of seizing or the grasping desire behind it.

background.note: Paired with violence in complaints about robbery.

study.summary: A down payment or first instalment that guarantees the rest will follow; Paul uses it of the Holy Spirit as God's pledge of the full inheritance to come.

senses.label: pledge, down payment
senses.definition: A part payment given in advance as a guarantee of full payment. God has given the Spirit in believers' hearts as the first instalment and guarantee of their future inheritance and resurrection life.

background.note: Used of the pledge Judah left with Tamar as guarantee of a promised payment.
A business term for earnest money, as when a woman selling a cow received a sum as advance payment.

study.exegesisTip: The Spirit is not only a sign of what is coming but an actual first portion of it: what believers have now is the same kind of thing as the full inheritance, given in part.

study.summary: To season food, especially with salt; used figuratively of speech made gracious and wholesome.

senses.label: season with salt
senses.definition: To give flavour to food; Jesus asks with what salt could be seasoned if it lost its saltiness, a warning about disciples losing their distinctive quality.

senses.label: season speech
senses.definition: Figuratively, of words made attractive and fitting; Paul wants believers' speech gracious, seasoned with salt, so they know how to answer everyone.

background.note: Used of leaven that has been prepared or seasoned.

study.summary: The master of a banquet, the person in charge of arranging a feast and its food and drink.

senses.label: master of the banquet
senses.definition: The steward or head of the feast at the wedding in Cana, who tasted the water made wine without knowing its source and praised the bridegroom for keeping the good wine until last.

study.caution: It is unclear whether he was a hired head servant or a guest chosen to preside; either way he oversaw the serving at the feast.

study.summary: To miss the mark, and so to go astray or deviate, used of people who have departed from sound teaching.

senses.label: miss the mark, swerve
senses.definition: To fail to hit the aim and so to wander off; some have swerved from love, a pure heart and sincere faith into empty talk, and others have gone astray concerning the faith and the truth, saying the resurrection has already happened.

background.note: Used of failing to attain what is right, a close parallel to Paul's wording.

study.summary: Firmness or safety: the certainty of something known, or the security of something guarded.

senses.label: certainty
senses.definition: Sureness or reliability of information; Luke writes so that Theophilus may know the certainty of what he was taught.

senses.label: security, safety
senses.definition: Secure condition, freedom from danger; the prison was found locked with all security, and people will say 'peace and security' just before sudden destruction.

background.note: Common in documents for a written guarantee or legal security.

study.summary: Securely or safely; and of knowledge, assuredly, beyond doubt.

senses.label: securely, under guard
senses.definition: So as to keep someone safe from escape; Judas tells the arrest party to lead Jesus away under guard, and the jailer is ordered to keep Paul and Silas securely.

senses.label: assuredly, for certain
senses.definition: With full certainty; Peter calls all Israel to know for certain that God has made Jesus both Lord and Christ.

study.summary: Reckless, wasteful living: dissipation that squanders resources and self-control.

senses.label: dissipation, debauchery
senses.definition: A wild, wasteful, unrestrained way of life; drunkenness leads to it, an elder's children must not be open to the charge of it, and pagan neighbours are surprised believers no longer run with them into its flood.

background.note: Philosophers used it for prodigality, the vice of wasteful spending.

study.exegesisTip: The word pictures a life poured away without restraint, like the prodigal son who squandered his property in reckless living.

study.summary: Childless, without children; used in the Sadducees' question about a woman married in turn to seven brothers.

senses.label: childless
senses.definition: Having no children; in the levirate law cited by the Sadducees, if a man died childless his brother was to marry the widow and raise up offspring for him.

background.note: Common in property documents, as of someone dying childless and without a will.

study.summary: Literally 'out of place': hence unusual or harmful, and especially improper or wrong.

senses.label: wrong, improper
senses.definition: Morally out of place, wicked; the thief says Jesus has done nothing wrong, Festus invites charges if Paul has done anything improper, and Paul asks prayer for rescue from wicked men.

senses.label: unusual, harmful
senses.definition: Out of the ordinary in a damaging way; the islanders saw nothing unusual or harmful happen to Paul after the viper bite.

background.note: Medical writers used it of unusual symptoms.

study.summary: To play the flute or pipe, as at festivals and dances.

senses.label: play the flute
senses.definition: To make music on the reed pipe; children complain 'we played the flute for you and you did not dance', and Paul notes that a tune played on flute or harp must have distinct notes to be recognised.

background.note: The ordinary verb for playing music on the pipe.

study.summary: Suddenly, without warning.

senses.label: suddenly
senses.definition: All at once and unexpectedly: the sound from heaven at Pentecost, the earthquake at Philippi, and the expectation that Paul would suddenly fall dead from the snake bite.

background.note: A standard adverb for something happening unawares.

study.summary: Not made by human hands; used of a dwelling or act that comes from God rather than human work.

senses.label: not made by hands
senses.definition: Not produced by human craftsmanship but by God: the temple Jesus was accused of saying he would build in three days, and the eternal heavenly dwelling believers will receive.

senses.label: spiritual (circumcision)
senses.definition: Of circumcision performed not physically but by Christ, in the putting off of the sinful nature.

study.exegesisTip: It stands in deliberate contrast to things 'made with hands', a term the Old Testament often applies to idols and human shrines.

study.summary: To dip into a liquid, and by extension to dip in dye or stain.

senses.label: dip
senses.definition: To immerse partly in liquid; the rich man asks that Lazarus dip his fingertip in water, and Jesus dips the morsel at the Last Supper.

senses.label: dip, stained
senses.definition: Of a garment dipped in or stained with blood; the rider on the white horse wears a robe dipped in blood.

background.note: Used in connection with the dyers' trade and wool to be dyed.

study.exegesisTip: This verb is distinct from the related 'baptize'; here it simply means a brief dipping, not a religious washing.
study.caution: Some manuscripts in Revelation 19:13 read 'sprinkled with blood' instead of 'dipped'.

study.summary: Torment, severe pain; originally a touchstone for testing metal, then torture used to extract evidence.

senses.label: torment, severe pain
senses.definition: Intense suffering: people brought to Jesus with various diseases and severe pains, and the rich man in Hades in torment, fearing his brothers would come to that place of torment.

background.note: Its first meaning was the touchstone on which gold was tested.

study.summary: Royal, belonging to a king; in the plural, a royal palace.

senses.label: royal
senses.definition: Kingly, belonging to the king; believers are a royal priesthood, echoing God's words to Israel at Sinai.

senses.label: palace
senses.definition: As a plural noun, the king's residence; those who wear fine clothes live in palaces.

background.note: God calls Israel 'a royal priesthood' at Sinai, the phrase Peter applies to the church.

study.caution: In 1 Peter 2:9 some take the word as a noun ('a royal house') standing beside 'priesthood'; most read it as an adjective, 'royal priesthood'.

study.summary: Force or violence, whether of people or of nature.

senses.label: force, violence
senses.definition: Physical force or violent pressure: the apostles were brought in without force, Paul was carried because of the violence of the mob, and the ship's stern was broken by the force of the waves.

background.note: The phrase 'with violence' occurs in complaints just as in Acts.

study.summary: Belonging to everyday life: ordinary, practical matters of livelihood.

senses.label: of daily life
senses.definition: Pertaining to this present life and its business; Jesus warns against hearts weighed down by life's worries, and Paul says believers who will judge angels can surely settle everyday disputes.

background.note: Used of travel on business concerning one's livelihood.

study.summary: A pit or ditch dug in the ground.

senses.label: pit, ditch
senses.definition: A hole or ditch into which one may fall: a sheep fallen into a pit on the Sabbath, and the blind leading the blind into a pit.

background.note: Used of a trench or pit for planting.

study.summary: Slow; of speech and temper restrained, of the heart dull to believe.

senses.label: slow to act
senses.definition: Unhurried, restrained; James urges everyone to be quick to hear, slow to speak and slow to anger.

senses.label: slow of heart
senses.definition: Dull in understanding or response; the risen Jesus calls the Emmaus disciples slow of heart to believe the prophets.

background.note: The adverb is used of people slow at writing who had others sign for them.

study.summary: The arm; in the NT always figuratively, 'the arm of the Lord' as a picture of God's mighty power.

senses.label: arm of God's power
senses.definition: The arm as a symbol of strength in action: God has done mighty deeds with his arm, led Israel out of Egypt with an uplifted arm, and 'to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?'.

background.note: Used literally in descriptions of people, such as a scar on the right arm.

study.summary: A tanner, one who prepares animal hides; used of Simon of Joppa, with whom Peter stayed.

senses.label: tanner
senses.definition: A worker in leather; Peter lodged in Joppa with Simon the tanner, whose house was by the sea.

background.note: Tanners formed a recognised guild in Thyatira.

study.exegesisTip: Tanning involved handling dead animals, which made it an unclean and despised trade among Jews; Peter's lodging there may hint at his growing openness before the Cornelius vision.
study.caution: How strongly Peter's stay with a tanner should be read as significant is debated; Luke does not comment on it.

study.summary: A calm, the stillness of the sea after wind and waves cease.

senses.label: calm of the sea
senses.definition: Stillness on the water; when Jesus rebuked the wind and the sea there was a great calm.

background.note: Plato pairs it with windlessness for a still, calm sea.

study.summary: Origin or birth: one's descent, one's coming into being, and so natural existence.

senses.label: origin, genealogy
senses.definition: Lineage or origin; 'the book of the genesis of Jesus Christ' introduces his genealogy and recalls the 'generations' formula of Genesis.

senses.label: birth
senses.definition: The coming into the world of a child; the account of Jesus' birth, and the joy at John's birth.

senses.label: natural existence
senses.definition: One's natural being or course of life: a man looks at 'the face of his birth' (his natural face) in a mirror, and the tongue sets on fire 'the wheel of existence', the whole course of life.

background.note: The phrase 'book of the generation' follows Genesis.

study.caution: The phrase 'the wheel of genesis' in James 3:6 is much discussed; it may echo a common expression for the cycle of life, but James uses it simply for the whole course of human existence.

study.summary: A load or cargo, especially a ship's freight or a merchant's wares.

senses.label: cargo, merchandise
senses.definition: Goods carried for trade; the ship at Tyre unloaded its cargo, and the merchants mourn Babylon because no one buys their cargo of gold, silver and other luxuries.

background.note: Common for a ship's freight to be loaded with all speed.

study.summary: Nakedness: lack of adequate clothing, or the shame of being exposed.

senses.label: lack of clothing
senses.definition: Destitution and exposure from want of clothing; neither nakedness nor any hardship separates believers from Christ's love, and Paul endured cold and nakedness.

senses.label: shameful nakedness
senses.definition: Exposure as a picture of spiritual poverty; Laodicea is told to buy white garments so the shame of its nakedness is not seen.

background.note: Listed among covenant curses alongside hunger and thirst.

study.summary: Δειλός describes the cowardly, fearful person, used by Jesus of the disciples' panic in the storm and in Revelation of those whose fear leads them to abandon faithfulness.

senses.label: Fearful, lacking courage
senses.definition: Gripped by fear in a way that shows a lack of trust; Jesus pairs the disciples' fear in the storm with their little faith.

senses.label: The cowardly (as a class)
senses.definition: Those who, out of fear, shrink back from loyalty to God; listed first among those excluded from the new creation.

background.note: In Homer the word describes the coward in battle, the opposite of the valiant fighter.

study.exegesisTip: In both storm accounts the rebuke links fear directly to faith: the question is not why they felt danger but why they did not trust the one with them in the boat.

study.summary: Δεκαπέντε is the number fifteen, used of distance, depth and days.

senses.label: Fifteen
senses.definition: The cardinal number fifteen: fifteen stadia from Jerusalem to Bethany, fifteen fathoms of water, and the fifteen days Paul spent with Peter.

study.translationNote: Some versions convert John's fifteen stadia into a modern distance (about two miles or three kilometres) rather than giving the number itself.

background.note: This compound form replaced the older classical form for fifteen and is common in everyday documents of the period.

study.exegesisTip: Paul's mention of only fifteen days with Peter in GAL 1:18 underlines his point that his gospel was not received from the Jerusalem apostles.

study.summary: Δέκατος means 'tenth', used of an hour of the day, a tenth part of a city, and the tenth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem.

senses.label: Tenth in a series
senses.definition: The ordinal 'tenth': the tenth hour of the day (about 4 p.m. by Jewish reckoning) or the tenth of the city's foundation stones.

senses.label: A tenth part
senses.definition: Used as a noun for a tenth portion: a tenth of the city falls in the earthquake.

study.translationNote: Some versions translate John's 'tenth hour' as 'about four in the afternoon'; a few interpreters prefer a Roman reckoning (10 a.m.).

study.summary: Δελεάζω, from the word for bait, means to lure or entice, as a fisherman or hunter baits a trap; in the NT it pictures desire and false teachers drawing people into sin.

senses.label: Lure, entice with bait
senses.definition: To draw someone into sin by an attractive bait: one's own desire entices a person, and false teachers bait unstable souls with sensual appeals.

background.note: Herodotus uses the word of putting meat on a hook as bait, the literal image behind the NT metaphor.

study.exegesisTip: In JAM 1:14 'dragged away' and 'enticed' are fishing and hunting images: temptation works by hiding the hook behind the bait, and James locates the bait in a person's own desire, not in God.

study.summary: Δεσμοφύλαξ is the jailer, the keeper of a prison, used of the Philippian jailer in Acts 16.

senses.label: Jailer, prison keeper
senses.definition: The official responsible for guarding prisoners; the Philippian jailer is charged to keep Paul and Silas securely, nearly takes his life when the doors open, and later relays the order for their release.

background.note: The title appears in Egyptian documents of the third century BC for the official to whom prisoners were handed over.

study.exegesisTip: The jailer's readiness to kill himself (ACT 16:27) reflects that a keeper answered personally for escaped prisoners.

study.summary: Διαβαίνω means to cross over or pass through, whether a chasm, a stretch of sea, or the water to another region.

senses.label: Cross over to a place
senses.definition: To go across from one side to another: crossing the chasm between Abraham's side and the place of torment, or crossing over to Macedonia.

senses.label: Pass through
senses.definition: To go right through an obstacle: Israel passed through the Red Sea as on dry land.

background.note: Everyday letters use the word with 'into' for going over to a nearby town, the same construction as the Macedonian's appeal.
It is the usual Greek rendering of the Hebrew verb for crossing over, especially Israel's crossing of the Jordan.

study.summary: Διαγγέλλω means to announce widely or give formal notice, used of proclaiming God's kingdom and name and of Paul announcing the end of a purification period.

senses.label: Proclaim far and wide
senses.definition: To spread a message abroad: the kingdom of God, or God's name made known in all the earth.

senses.label: Give notice
senses.definition: To announce officially: Paul notifies the temple authorities when the days of purification will be completed.

background.note: Classical writers use it for sending word by a messenger.

study.summary: Διαγίνομαι is used in the NT only of time passing or elapsing.

senses.label: Pass, elapse (of time)
senses.definition: Of a period of time that has gone by: the Sabbath being over, several days having passed, much time having been spent.

background.note: A third-century document uses the same verb to say that much time has elapsed.

study.summary: Διάδημα is the royal diadem, the band worn as the badge of kingship, which in Revelation marks the claims of the dragon and the beast and the true sovereignty of Christ.

senses.label: Royal diadem, crown of rule
senses.definition: The emblem of royal authority: worn by the dragon and the beast as rival claimants to power, and in many by the rider called Faithful and True.

study.translationNote: Many English versions render both διάδημα and στέφανος as 'crown', hiding the difference between a royal diadem and a victor's or honour wreath.

background.note: Originally the band round the tiara of the Persian king, later the standard sign of royalty among Hellenistic kings.

study.exegesisTip: Revelation contrasts the dragon's seven and the beast's ten diadems with the 'many diadems' on Christ's head (REV 19:12): the usurpers' royal claims are outmatched by the true King.

study.summary: Διαζώννυμι means to tie something around oneself, as Jesus wrapped a towel around his waist and Peter put on his outer garment.

senses.label: Wrap around, gird oneself
senses.definition: To tie a cloth or garment around the body: Jesus girds himself with a towel to wash the disciples' feet; Peter wraps his outer garment around him before jumping into the sea.

study.exegesisTip: Girding with a towel was the posture of a household servant; John describes the Lord deliberately taking that role.

study.summary: Διαίρεσις refers to the varieties or distributions of gifts, ministries and workings that the one God apportions in the church.

senses.label: Varieties, distributions
senses.definition: Different kinds of gifts, services and activities, each allotted by the same Spirit, Lord and God.

study.translationNote: Versions differ between 'varieties/diversities' (stressing difference) and 'distributions/allotments' (stressing the act of apportioning); the word can carry both.

background.note: In land documents the word is used of the division or allotment of produce and land among several holders.

study.exegesisTip: Paul goes on to say the one Spirit distributes to each as he wills, so the word likely carries the sense of God's deliberate apportioning, not just variety.

study.summary: Διάκρισις is the act of distinguishing or judging, whether discerning spirits, telling good from evil, or passing judgment on others' opinions.

senses.label: Discernment, distinguishing
senses.definition: The ability to tell things apart: discerning between spirits, or the trained capacity to distinguish good from evil.

senses.label: Judging, disputing
senses.definition: Passing judgment on or quarrelling over another believer's scruples, which Paul forbids.

study.translationNote: In ROM 14:1 versions vary between 'not to pass judgment on opinions' and 'not for disputes over opinions', because the word can mean either deciding about something or quarrelling over it.

study.summary: Διασπείρω means to scatter abroad, used in Acts of the believers dispersed from Jerusalem by persecution, who spread the gospel as they went.

senses.label: Scatter, disperse
senses.definition: To be scattered over a wide area: the Jerusalem believers were driven out through Judea, Samaria and beyond after Stephen's death.

study.exegesisTip: The word's root is 'sow' (σπείρω): Luke shows the scattering intended to crush the church becoming a sowing of the word (ACT 8:4).

study.summary: Διασπορά, 'dispersion', refers to Jews living scattered outside the land of Israel, and by extension to Christians as God's people scattered in the world.

senses.label: Jewish Dispersion
senses.definition: The Jews living among the Greeks outside Palestine, or the place of their scattering.

senses.label: God's scattered people
senses.definition: Believers addressed as the scattered people of God, living as exiles away from their true homeland.

background.note: Used of Israel scattered among the nations as covenant judgment, and of the scattered exiles themselves.

study.caution: Whether James and 1 Peter address Jewish Christians literally living outside Palestine or use 'Dispersion' figuratively of the whole church as exiles is debated; 1 Peter's readers appear to include Gentiles, favouring a figurative sense there.

study.summary: Διαστολή means a distinction or difference, used by Paul to deny any difference between Jew and Gentile before God and of distinct musical notes.

senses.label: Distinction between people
senses.definition: A difference in standing: there is none between Jew and Greek, for all have sinned and all who believe are justified the same way.

senses.label: Distinctness of sound
senses.definition: Clear difference between musical notes, without which no tune can be recognized.

background.note: Used of the distinction God made between his people and Pharaoh's in the plagues.

study.summary: Διαφημίζω means to spread a report widely, whether the news about Jesus or a false story about his body.

senses.label: Spread news abroad
senses.definition: To make something widely known by word of mouth: the healed men spread Jesus' fame; the story that the disciples stole the body circulated among the Jews.

study.exegesisTip: In MAT 9:31 and MAR 1:45 the spreading happens against Jesus' explicit command to tell no one, and it hinders his ministry.

study.summary: Διδακτός means 'taught', used of people taught by God and of words taught by the Spirit rather than by human wisdom.

senses.label: Taught (by someone)
senses.definition: Instructed, with the teacher named in the genitive: all will be taught by God; words taught by human wisdom or by the Spirit.

background.note: Jesus quotes Isaiah's promise that all Zion's children will be taught by the LORD.

study.summary: Διΐστημι means to set apart or stand apart, used of an interval of time or distance and of Jesus parting from his disciples at the ascension.

senses.label: Intervene, go a short distance
senses.definition: Of time or space opening up between events: about an hour passing, or a ship moving on a little before taking another sounding.

senses.label: Part from, withdraw
senses.definition: To separate oneself from others: while blessing them, Jesus parted from the disciples.

study.summary: Δικαστής is a judge, used in the challenge to Moses' authority and in Jesus' refusal to arbitrate an inheritance dispute.

senses.label: Judge, arbiter
senses.definition: One with authority to decide disputes: the Israelite asks who made Moses a ruler and judge; in some manuscripts Jesus asks who made him a judge over two brothers.

background.note: At Athens and elsewhere the term was used of jurors in the law courts.

study.summary: Διόπερ is an emphatic 'therefore', 'for this very reason', introducing a strong conclusion.

senses.label: For this very reason
senses.definition: Introduces a conclusion drawn emphatically from what precedes: Paul's resolve not to cause his brother to stumble, the call to flee idolatry, and the charge to pray for interpretation.

background.note: The conjunction appears in official documents introducing what follows from a stated cause.

study.summary: Διχοστασία means dissension or division, a standing apart into opposing parties, listed by Paul among the works of the flesh.

senses.label: Dissension, division
senses.definition: Splitting into rival groups within a community, a mark of fleshly living and something caused by those who oppose sound teaching.

background.note: Solon uses it of civic sedition tearing a city apart.

study.summary: Δούλη is a female slave or bondservant, used by Mary of herself as the Lord's servant and in Joel's prophecy of the Spirit poured out on servants.

senses.label: Female servant of God
senses.definition: A woman wholly at the disposal of God as her master: Mary's self-description, and the 'maidservants' on whom God pours out his Spirit.

study.translationNote: Traditional versions say 'handmaid'; modern ones 'servant'. The Greek is the ordinary word for a female slave, expressing total submission to the Lord.

study.summary: Δραχμή is the drachma, a Greek silver coin roughly equal to a denarius, a day's wage; it is the lost coin in Jesus' parable.

senses.label: Drachma (silver coin)
senses.definition: A silver coin of about a day's wage; the woman's ten coins and the one she lost and found.

background.note: A silver coin worth six obols in classical Greek currency.

study.summary: Δρόμος, a running or race, is used figuratively of the course of a person's life and ministry that must be completed.

senses.label: Course of life or ministry
senses.definition: The race or career God has set before someone: John the Baptist finishing his course, Paul's resolve to finish his, and his final claim to have completed it.

study.exegesisTip: In 2TI 4:7 the word sits between athletic images (the good contest, kept faith), picturing ministry as a race run to the finish.

study.summary: Δυνάστης is a ruler or person of power, used of earthly rulers God brings down, of a high court official, and of God as the only Sovereign.

senses.label: Ruler, powerful one
senses.definition: One who holds power: the mighty God topples from their thrones, and God himself as the blessed and only Sovereign.

senses.label: Court official
senses.definition: A high-ranking officer in a royal court, such as the Ethiopian treasurer of Queen Candace.

background.note: Sophocles applies the title to Zeus as lord and ruler.

study.summary: Δυσκόλως means 'with difficulty', used in Jesus' saying about how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom.

senses.label: With difficulty, hardly
senses.definition: Only with great difficulty: the rich enter God's kingdom with difficulty.

study.exegesisTip: The following camel saying intensifies 'with difficulty' to humanly impossible, and Jesus then points to what is possible with God.

study.summary: Δωρέομαι means to give freely or grant as a gift, used of Pilate granting Jesus' body and of God's generous gifts in 2 Peter.

senses.label: Grant, give as a gift
senses.definition: To bestow something freely: Pilate grants the body to Joseph; God's power has given all that is needed for life and godliness and has given precious promises.

background.note: Ordinary letters use it of gifts given freely, such as wrist-bands sent by a brother.

study.summary: Εἰλικρίνεια means sincerity or purity of motive, an unmixed transparency of character before God and others.

senses.label: Sincerity, purity of motive
senses.definition: Unmixed, transparent integrity: the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, and Paul's conduct and preaching done in sincerity before God.

background.note: A petition appeals to an official's probity using this word.

study.exegesisTip: In 2CO 2:17 sincerity is set against 'peddling' God's word, the image of a merchant who adulterates his goods for profit.

study.summary: Εὐαγγελιστής is an evangelist, one who proclaims the good news, named as a recognized ministry in the church.

senses.label: Evangelist, gospel preacher
senses.definition: One who proclaims the gospel, especially to those who have not heard it: Philip the evangelist, the evangelists given to the church, and Timothy's charge to do an evangelist's work.

background.note: Later Christian texts use the word of the Gospel writers, as of John the evangelist; this sense is not found in the NT.

study.summary: Εὐαρεστέω means to be well-pleasing, used in Hebrews of pleasing God by faith and of God being pleased with sacrifices of good deeds.

senses.label: Please (God)
senses.definition: To be pleasing and acceptable to God, as Enoch was; impossible without faith.

senses.label: Be well pleased (passive)
senses.definition: Of God being pleased with sacrifices of doing good and sharing.

background.note: The Greek OT says Enoch 'pleased God' where the Hebrew says he 'walked with God', the wording Hebrews follows.

study.summary: Literally 'well-born', of noble birth or high rank; by extension 'noble-minded', of a generous and open disposition.

senses.label: Of noble birth
senses.definition: Belonging to a high-ranking or aristocratic family; socially distinguished.

senses.label: Noble-minded
senses.definition: Showing a noble, generous and fair-minded character; in Acts the comparative describes the Bereans' openness in receiving the message and testing it by Scripture.

background.note: Herodotus reports that among the Thracians being tattooed was esteemed a mark of noble birth, showing the word's basic sense of high birth.
An adoption contract forbids reducing the adopted son to slavery because he is well born and the son of well-born, free parents.

study.exegesisTip: In Acts 17:11 nobility is redefined: the Bereans are 'more noble' not by ancestry but by eager reception of the word combined with daily examination of the Scriptures.

study.summary: Well placed, hence suitable, fit or useful for a purpose.

senses.label: Fit, suitable
senses.definition: Properly suited or useful for some purpose or end; of a person fit for the kingdom, of salt fit for soil or manure pile, and of land producing vegetation useful to those who farm it.

background.note: An official letter asks that suitable persons be appointed to the offices just mentioned, the same sense of fitness for a task as in Luke 9:62.

study.summary: To be in good spirits: to be cheerful, take heart, keep up one's courage.

senses.label: Take courage
senses.definition: To keep up one's spirits in danger, as Paul urges the ship's company in the storm.

senses.label: Be cheerful
senses.definition: To be in a happy, joyful frame of mind, the counterpart of suffering hardship.

background.note: A letter writer tells the recipient not to be anxious about the young barley, since it has been sold, showing the everyday 'cheer up, don't worry' sense.

study.exegesisTip: Paul's encouragement in Acts 27:25 rests not on circumstances but on trust: 'for I believe God that it will be just as he told me.'

study.summary: To have a good opportunity or free time; with 'for/to' something, to spend one's leisure on it.

senses.label: Have time or opportunity
senses.definition: To have the leisure or a suitable occasion to do something.

senses.label: Spend one's time on
senses.definition: To devote one's leisure to an activity; the Athenians spent their time on nothing but telling and hearing the latest novelty.

background.note: A writer promises to come immediately as soon as he has the opportunity, closely parallel to Paul's note on Apollos.

study.summary: Devout, God-fearing: reverent and careful in religious duty.

senses.label: Devout, reverent
senses.definition: Showing careful reverence toward God and faithful observance of his law; used of Simeon, of Jews gathered in Jerusalem, of those who buried Stephen and of Ananias.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: The word is found only in Luke's writings, always describing pious Jews (or a Jewish disciple, Ananias) who are open to God's work.

background.note: In earlier Greek the word mostly meant prudent, discreet or cautious, the root idea from which the religious sense of reverent carefulness developed.

study.summary: Decently, becomingly: in a seemly, orderly manner that commands respect.

senses.label: Decently, becomingly
senses.definition: In a fitting and honorable way; of conduct that is upright in the sight of outsiders and of worship carried out in good order.

background.note: An inscription records that the bulls for the sacrifices were lifted in a seemly manner, showing the word for conduct fitting a public, ceremonial occasion.

study.summary: A prayer addressed to God, or a vow made to him.

senses.label: Prayer
senses.definition: A petition to God; 'the prayer of faith' that will save the sick.

senses.label: Vow
senses.definition: A solemn promise to God, here apparently a Nazirite-type vow involving cutting the hair.

background.note: Herodotus uses the phrase for fulfilling a vow, showing the long-standing votive sense.
A Christian letter says God inclined his ear to 'our prayers' by preserving the writer's mistress.

study.summary: Useful, serviceable, of real benefit to someone.

senses.label: Useful, serviceable
senses.definition: Of good use to a master or to a work; said of the cleansed 'vessel', of Mark in ministry, and of Onesimus, now 'useful' instead of 'useless'.

background.note: A letter speaks of a man well known to be of great value to those in the district.

study.exegesisTip: In Philemon 11 Paul plays on the slave's name Onesimus ('useful') and on the pair achrēstos/euchrēstos ('useless'/'useful').

study.summary: A sweet smell or fragrance, chiefly in the sacrificial phrase 'a fragrant aroma' pleasing to God.

senses.label: Fragrance of Christ
senses.definition: Figuratively, the apostles as the pleasing aroma of Christ offered to God among all who hear the message.

senses.label: Fragrant offering
senses.definition: In the Old Testament sacrificial phrase 'odor of fragrance', used of Christ's self-offering and of the Philippians' gift to Paul as a sacrifice acceptable to God.

background.note: The phrase 'odor of fragrance' is used of sacrifices from Noah's offering onward, the background to Paul's metaphor.

study.summary: Boiling hot; used figuratively in the rebuke to Laodicea, 'neither cold nor hot'.

senses.label: Hot (figurative)
senses.definition: Hot as opposed to cold and lukewarm, a picture of a church whose condition is useful and acceptable rather than tepid and nauseating.

study.caution: Interpreters differ on the image: some read 'hot' as spiritual fervour and 'cold' as open rejection; others relate it to Laodicea's tepid water supply compared with useful hot and cold water, so that both hot and cold are good and only lukewarm is condemned.

study.summary: To be astounded or amazed, often with a note of awe or alarm.

senses.label: Be amazed, astounded
senses.definition: To be struck with astonishment, sometimes mixed with fear, at Jesus' authority, his words, or his determined march to Jerusalem.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Only Mark uses the verb; it is part of his emphasis on the overwhelming, unsettling effect Jesus had on crowds and disciples.

background.note: In Homer the verb describes onlookers astounded at what they see.

study.summary: Amazement or astonishment, often mingled with awe.

senses.label: Amazement, awe
senses.definition: Overwhelming astonishment at a display of divine power, such as an exorcism, the miraculous catch of fish or the healing of the lame man.

background.note: A poetic word from Homer onward for the amazement that seizes onlookers.

study.summary: A theatre, used also as a public meeting place; figuratively, a spectacle.

senses.label: Theatre
senses.definition: The great open-air theatre at Ephesus, where the crowd assembled during the riot.

senses.label: Spectacle
senses.definition: Figuratively, a public show; the apostles exhibited before the world, angels and men like condemned men in an arena.

background.note: An inscription from Ephesus itself orders items to be carried into the theatre at every assembly, confirming its use as the city's meeting place.

study.summary: Divine, belonging to God; as a neuter noun, 'the divine being'.

senses.label: The Deity
senses.definition: With the article as a noun, the divine nature or God himself, which Paul tells the Athenians is not like images of gold, silver or stone.

senses.label: Divine
senses.definition: Belonging to or coming from God; his divine power, and the divine nature believers come to share through his promises.

background.note: The word was very common with an imperial connotation; an inscription describes the birthday of Augustus in such divine terms.

study.exegesisTip: Both Paul at Athens and 2 Peter use vocabulary familiar to Greek religious and philosophical audiences, while filling it with biblical content.
study.caution: 'Partakers of the divine nature' (2 Pet 1:4) does not mean becoming God; in context it is sharing in God's moral life and escaping corruption through his promises.

study.summary: Summer, the warm season of growth and harvest.

senses.label: Summer
senses.definition: The summer season, whose nearness is signalled by the fig tree putting out leaves, in Jesus' parable about recognizing the signs of the end.

background.note: An ancient calendar speaks of the sun's course dividing winter and summer.

study.summary: To touch or handle; by extension, to lay hands on so as to harm.

senses.label: Touch, handle
senses.definition: To come into physical contact with something, as in ascetic prohibitions or the ban on touching Mount Sinai.

senses.label: Harm, injure
senses.definition: To touch with hostile effect; the destroyer was not to touch Israel's firstborn.

background.note: A household instruction says 'do not touch the sauce', showing the plain everyday sense.

study.exegesisTip: Colossians 2:21 quotes the slogans of false teachers ('do not handle, do not taste, do not touch'), which Paul rejects.

study.summary: In the passive, to be alarmed, disturbed or thrown into a panic.

senses.label: Be alarmed
senses.definition: To be agitated or frightened, as by reports of war or by claims that the Day of the Lord has already come.

background.note: In classical poetry the active verb means to cry aloud, from a noun for noise or outcry; the NT passive sense of being alarmed derives from this.

study.summary: A pulling down or demolition, used figuratively of overthrowing strongholds and of tearing down a church.

senses.label: Demolition of strongholds
senses.definition: The destruction of fortifications, a picture of overthrowing arguments and pretensions opposed to God.

senses.label: Tearing down (opposite of building)
senses.definition: Damaging or destroying a community, contrasted with building it up, the purpose of apostolic authority.

background.note: Thucydides uses the word for the literal demolition of fortifications.

study.summary: A seat or chair, including the seat of a teacher.

senses.label: Seat, stool
senses.definition: The seats of the dove-sellers in the temple, which Jesus overturned.

senses.label: Seat of teaching authority
senses.definition: 'Moses' seat', the position of authority from which the scribes and Pharisees taught the law.

background.note: The opening psalm speaks of the 'seat' of scoffers, an example of the word for a place of sitting together in judgment or counsel.

study.summary: A guide or teacher, a master who instructs.

senses.label: Teacher, instructor
senses.definition: One who leads and instructs others; Jesus forbids his disciples to take the title, since Christ alone is their teacher.

background.note: A parent writes asking that a message be sent to the daughter's teacher so he will take more pains with her.

study.summary: To laugh scornfully at someone, to ridicule.

senses.label: Laugh at, ridicule
senses.definition: To mock with derisive laughter; the mourners scorned Jesus for saying the dead girl was only asleep.

background.note: A soldier complains to his mother that everyone laughs at him because his father visited without bringing gifts.

study.summary: To find fault with, blame or condemn; in the passive, to stand condemned.

senses.label: Condemn (of the heart)
senses.definition: To pass an accusing judgment on oneself; the believer's heart may condemn him, but God is greater than the heart.

senses.label: Stand condemned
senses.definition: To be self-evidently in the wrong, as Peter was at Antioch by his inconsistent conduct.

study.translationNote: In Galatians 2:11 some versions say Peter 'stood condemned' (by his own inconsistent actions), while others say he 'was to be blamed'; the Greek participle allows both.

background.note: A letter writer says he will send the letter so that the recipient may read it soberly and be self-condemned.

study.summary: To cover up; in the middle, to cover or veil one's own head.

senses.label: Cover the head, veil oneself
senses.definition: To have one's head covered in public worship; Paul says a woman should and a man should not.

background.note: Homer uses the middle of a man covering his head while weeping.

study.caution: Whether Paul has in view a veil or shawl, or the way the hair is worn, is debated; the verb itself means to be covered.

study.summary: To cause to recline, especially for a meal; in the passive, to recline at table.

senses.label: Make to recline
senses.definition: To have people sit or recline in groups for a meal, as at the feeding of the five thousand.

senses.label: Recline at table
senses.definition: To take one's place at a meal or banquet.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Only Luke uses this verb, fitting his many meal scenes.

background.note: Herodotus uses it of making the Persians recline for dinner in a meadow.

study.summary: Condemnation, the adverse sentence and the penalty or punishment that follows it.

senses.label: Condemnation, penalty
senses.definition: The judicial sentence against sinners and its resulting penalty, brought on all by Adam's trespass and removed for those in Christ Jesus.

background.note: In legal documents the word denotes a judgment for a sum to be paid as a fine or damages, or a burden resulting from a court ruling.

study.exegesisTip: In Romans 8:1 'no condemnation' covers both the verdict and the punishment it carries.

study.summary: A lodging place; a guest room or a place to stay for travellers.

senses.label: Lodging, guest room
senses.definition: A place where travellers stay; the guest room where Jesus ate the Passover, and the lodging in Bethlehem where there was no room for Mary and Joseph.

study.translationNote: In Luke 2:7 many versions say 'inn', but Luke uses the same word for the Passover 'guest room' (LUK 22:11) and a different word for the inn in the parable of the Good Samaritan, so some translations render it 'guest room' or 'lodging'.

background.note: A papyrus refers to the lodging-place provided for the people of Arsinoe in the Serapeum.

study.summary: To be a burden to someone, especially financially, by depending on them for support.

senses.label: Be a burden
senses.definition: To weigh on others by demanding support; Paul insists he never burdened the Corinthians and will not do so.

study.summary: To lay down or deposit; in the middle with 'favor', to lay up goodwill by doing someone a favor.

senses.label: Lay down, place
senses.definition: To lay something in place, as Joseph laid Jesus' body in the tomb.

senses.label: Grant a favor
senses.definition: To do someone a favor so as to win their goodwill; Felix and Festus sought to please the Jewish leaders at Paul's expense.

background.note: A letter writer tells the recipient that by doing this he will have laid up for himself a great store of gratitude, the same idiom as in Acts.

study.summary: To bring or bear down: to bring charges, cast a vote, or be overcome by sleep.

senses.label: Bring charges, cast a vote
senses.definition: To bring accusations against someone, or to cast one's vote (pebble) against the accused.

senses.label: Be overcome by sleep
senses.definition: Passive: to be borne down by deep sleep, as Eutychus was before falling from the window.

study.summary: To make straight, hence to direct or guide along a right path.

senses.label: Guide, direct
senses.definition: To lead or steer in the right direction; used of God guiding our feet into the way of peace, directing the apostles' journey, and directing hearts into his love.

study.summary: Burning heat, the scorching heat of the day or of the sun; possibly in James the hot desert wind (sirocco).

senses.label: Scorching heat
senses.definition: The burning heat of the day or season, especially the midday sun that wearies workers and withers plants.
senses.note: In James 1:11 some understand the scorching east wind (sirocco), the usual sense in the Septuagint; others simply burning heat.

study.translationNote: At James 1:11 versions differ between "scorching heat" and "scorching (or burning) wind", because the word can mean either the heat itself or the hot desert wind that withers vegetation.

background.note: In the Greek Old Testament the word often names the hot east wind, the sirocco, that dries up the land.

study.summary: A centurion, a Roman officer commanding about a hundred soldiers; a Latin loanword used only by Mark at the crucifixion.

senses.label: Roman centurion
senses.definition: An officer in the Roman army in charge of a century (about a hundred men); here the officer supervising Jesus' execution, who confessed him as Son of God and confirmed his death to Pilate.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark uses the Latin loanword where Matthew and Luke use the Greek equivalent ἑκατοντάρχης, one of several Latinisms in his Gospel.

background.note: An inscription from Egypt records a Roman official visiting a temple of Isis together with named centurions, showing the term in ordinary use.

study.exegesisTip: The same officer whose confession climaxes Mark's crucifixion scene (15:39) is the witness Pilate relies on for the fact of Jesus' death (15:44-45).

study.summary: A potter, one who shapes vessels from clay.

senses.label: Potter
senses.definition: A craftsman who makes pottery from clay; used of the 'potter's field' bought with Judas' money and, in Paul, as an image of God's sovereign right over what he makes.

background.note: Homer already pictures a potter testing his wheel to see if it runs.

study.exegesisTip: Romans 9:21 echoes the prophets' potter imagery (Isa 29:16; Jer 18:1-6): the point is the Creator's right, not caprice.

study.summary: To mix, especially wine with water or spices, and so to prepare a drink; in Revelation, of preparing the cup of judgment.

senses.label: Mix a drink
senses.definition: To mix or prepare a cup of wine; used figuratively of God's wrath and of Babylon receiving back a double portion in the cup she mixed for others.
senses.note: In Revelation 14:10 'mixed undiluted' is a striking oxymoron: the wine is prepared at full strength, unweakened by water.

study.translationNote: Because κεράννυμι normally means mixing wine with water, Revelation 14:10 is rendered variously as "poured undiluted" or "mixed full strength"; the sense is that nothing tempers the wrath.

background.note: An inscription speaks of a cup of mixed wine, the everyday use of the verb.

study.summary: Gain, profit or advantage, whether financial or in a wider sense.

senses.label: Gain, advantage
senses.definition: Something counted as profit or advantage; Paul calls death 'gain' and reckons his former privileges, once gains, as loss for Christ.

senses.label: Monetary profit
senses.definition: Financial profit, here 'shameful gain' sought by false teachers.

background.note: From Homer on the ordinary word for gain or profit.

study.exegesisTip: In Philippians 3:7-8 Paul uses accounting language: gains (κέρδη) are re-entered as loss (ζημία) so that he may 'gain' Christ (κερδαίνω).

study.summary: A herald, one who publicly announces a message on behalf of another; used of Paul and of Noah as proclaimers of God's message.

senses.label: Herald, preacher
senses.definition: A public proclaimer commissioned to announce a message with authority; Paul's appointed role for the gospel, and Noah as a herald of righteousness.

study.translationNote: Traditionally rendered "preacher", but the word stresses an official herald who announces what he has been given, not a speaker of his own ideas.

background.note: In Homer heralds are public messengers serving kings and assemblies.
A herald was paid at the public games at Oxyrhynchus, showing the word for an official announcer.

study.summary: A region or district of a country.

senses.label: Region, district
senses.definition: A tract of territory; always plural in Paul for the regions where he worked (Syria and Cilicia, Achaia, and the eastern Mediterranean).

background.note: An inscription speaks of men sent into a named district, the same sense of region.

study.summary: A money-changer, one who exchanged coins for a fee, as in the temple courts.

senses.label: Money-changer
senses.definition: A dealer who changed foreign or common coins into acceptable currency (for the temple tax) for a small commission; Jesus overturned their tables.

background.note: A census document from Ptolemaic Egypt lists money-changers; the word, condemned by Atticist purists, was in everyday use.

study.summary: To grow tired, abate or cease; in the NT always of the wind dying down at Jesus' presence or word.

senses.label: Abate, die down
senses.definition: Of the wind: to cease raging and become still.

background.note: Herodotus uses it of a storm wind abating.

study.summary: A guard of soldiers (from Latin custodia), set to watch Jesus' tomb.

senses.label: Guard, watch
senses.definition: A detachment of soldiers on guard duty; the guard placed at the tomb at the request of the chief priests.

study.translationNote: At Matthew 27:65 Pilate's words may be read "You have a guard" (use your own temple guard) or "Take a guard" (Roman soldiers); the Greek allows either.

background.note: A letter of A.D. 22 using this Latin borrowing for custody is the earliest known example.

study.caution: Whether the guard was Roman or the temple police is debated; the Latin loanword and the need to placate the governor (28:14) suggest Roman soldiers.

study.summary: A steep bank or cliff.

senses.label: Steep bank
senses.definition: A steep slope or overhanging bank down which the herd of pigs rushed into the lake.

background.note: Used of the steep banks of irrigation trenches.

study.summary: A court or tribunal, and so a lawsuit or case brought before one.

senses.label: Lawcourt, tribunal
senses.definition: A place or body of judgment; the rich dragging the poor into court.

senses.label: Legal case
senses.definition: A matter for judgment, a lawsuit; Paul rebukes believers who take trivial everyday cases outside the church.
senses.note: Some render 1 Corinthians 6:2, 4 as 'courts' rather than 'cases'; the sense is close.

study.translationNote: In 1 Corinthians 6 versions vary between "cases" and "courts" ("incompetent to try the smallest cases" vs. "to constitute the smallest law-courts").

background.note: Common in the papyri for an appointed tribunal before which disputes were tried.

study.summary: All around, encircling; used in Revelation of what surrounds God's throne.

senses.label: Round about
senses.definition: On every side, encircling; the rainbow and the elders' thrones around the throne, and the eyes covering the living creatures all around.

study.summary: To bend or stoop down.

senses.label: Stoop down
senses.definition: To bend the body forward or downward; John the Baptist unworthy even to stoop to untie Jesus' sandals, and Jesus bending to write on the ground.
senses.note: The two occurrences in John belong to the account of the woman caught in adultery, which is absent from the earliest manuscripts.

background.note: Homer uses it of Tantalus stooping to drink.

study.summary: A revel or carousal, a drunken party or riotous procession.

senses.label: Carousing, revelry
senses.definition: Riotous feasting and drinking parties, often ending in street processions; always listed among vices of the old life.

background.note: Herodotus pairs it with drinking as festive merrymaking.

study.exegesisTip: Always plural and paired with drunkenness: the word pictures habitual party-going, not a single celebration.

study.summary: A violent storm or squall of wind.

senses.label: Squall, storm
senses.definition: A sudden, furious windstorm, as swept down on the Sea of Galilee; figuratively, the storm that drives empty clouds, an image of false teachers.

background.note: Homer uses it of a furious hurricane.

study.summary: To render service, especially religious service; of priestly ministry, worship, and material help for fellow believers.

senses.label: Priestly service
senses.definition: The official ministry of priests offering sacrifices.

senses.label: Worship the Lord
senses.definition: Serving God in worship and prayer, as the church leaders at Antioch did.

senses.label: Serve materially
senses.definition: To render service to others with material gifts, as the Gentile churches to the Jerusalem saints.

background.note: At Athens the verb meant performing public duties at one's own expense for the state.
Used of twin women performing religious service in the Serapeum at Memphis.

study.exegesisTip: In Romans 15:27 the choice of this cultic word gives the collection for Jerusalem the dignity of an offering.

study.summary: A lepton, the smallest copper coin in circulation.

senses.label: Small copper coin
senses.definition: The smallest coin in use, a tiny fraction of a day's wage; the widow's two coins and the 'last penny' of a debt.

study.translationNote: Traditionally "mite"; modern versions say "small copper coin" or "penny".

background.note: An inscription speaks of 'thin bronze' coinage, the small local copper money.

study.exegesisTip: Mark explains for his readers that two lepta made a quadrans (Latin), a quarter of a Roman as.

study.summary: Made of stone.

senses.label: Made of stone
