senses.definition: Consisting of stone; of the stone water jars at Cana, the stone tablets of the law contrasted with hearts, and idols of stone.

background.note: Common in everyday documents for stone objects such as wine presses.

study.exegesisTip: 2 Corinthians 3:3 echoes Ezekiel's promise to replace the heart of stone with a heart of flesh (Ezek 11:19; 36:26).

study.summary: A harbour or haven for ships.

senses.label: Harbour
senses.definition: A port or haven; Fair Havens on Crete and the harbours considered for wintering on Paul's voyage.

background.note: A receipt records payment of the harbour tax at Memphis.

study.summary: An oracle, a divine utterance; in the NT the words God has spoken, especially in Scripture.

senses.label: Oracles of God
senses.definition: God's utterances as revealed and entrusted to Israel in Scripture, received by Moses, and the basic teaching of God's word; also speech that conveys God's words.

study.translationNote: Older versions say "oracles"; modern ones often "very words of God".

background.note: In Herodotus an oracle, especially one preserved from antiquity.

study.summary: Abuse, reviling, insulting speech.

senses.label: Reviling, abuse
senses.definition: Insulting or slanderous speech; believers are not to return insult for insult, nor give opponents occasion to revile.

background.note: Thucydides uses it of abusive reproach.

study.summary: A plague or pestilence; figuratively, a pest, a dangerous troublemaker.

senses.label: Pestilence, plague
senses.definition: A deadly epidemic disease, listed with famines among the signs before the end.
senses.note: At Matthew 24:7 the word is found in many manuscripts but not in the earliest.

senses.label: Pest (of a person)
senses.definition: A person who spreads trouble like a plague, Tertullus' accusation against Paul.

background.note: Used of a plague in Homer; Demosthenes applies it to a person as a 'pest'.
A letter mentions plague having broken out in the writer's neighbourhood.

study.summary: To set free by paying a ransom; to redeem or deliver.

senses.label: Redeem by ransom
senses.definition: To free someone by payment of a price; Christ gave himself to redeem us from lawlessness, and believers were ransomed not with silver or gold but with his blood.

senses.label: Deliver, set free
senses.definition: To rescue or liberate, as the hoped-for redemption of Israel.

background.note: Used of redeeming clothes from pawn by paying the money owed.

study.exegesisTip: In 1 Peter 1:18-19 the ransom image is explicit: the price was not silver or gold but Christ's precious blood.

study.summary: Redemption, a ransoming or deliverance.

senses.label: Deliverance of Israel
senses.definition: God's saving liberation of his people, eagerly expected in Israel.

senses.label: Redemption through Christ
senses.definition: The eternal release secured by Christ's own blood as high priest.

background.note: In accounts it is used of redeeming pledged cups by payment.

study.summary: A pronouncing of blessing, a declaration that someone is blessed or happy.

senses.label: Blessedness, blessing
senses.definition: The declaration of someone as blessed; David's pronouncement on the person forgiven, and the Galatians' former joy and gratitude toward Paul.
senses.note: In Galatians 4:15 it may mean their sense of blessedness or their congratulation of themselves for having Paul.

background.note: Plato uses it for pronouncing someone happy.

study.exegesisTip: In Romans 4:6-9 the word refers to the beatitude of Psalm 32:1-2 ('Blessed is the one whose transgressions are forgiven').

study.summary: Weakness, illness, sickness.

senses.label: Sickness
senses.definition: Bodily weakness or illness, paired with 'disease' in summaries of Jesus' and the disciples' healing ministry.

background.note: Christian amulets borrow Matthew's phrase 'every disease and every sickness' in prayers for healing.

study.summary: The breast or chest.

senses.label: Breast(s)
senses.definition: A woman's breasts that nurse a child; also the chest, where the risen Christ wears a golden sash.

study.summary: Futility, emptiness, purposelessness.

senses.label: Futility, frustration
senses.definition: Subjection to frustration and failure to reach its goal, as creation now awaits liberation.

senses.label: Empty, worthless thinking
senses.definition: Moral and intellectual emptiness: Gentile thinking without God, and the hollow boasts of false teachers.

study.translationNote: Older versions render "vanity"; modern ones "futility" or "emptiness".

background.note: The keyword of Ecclesiastes: 'vanity of vanities'.

study.exegesisTip: Romans 8:20 likely echoes Ecclesiastes' 'vanity' (hebel): creation is subjected to a frustrating, transient existence.

study.summary: Majesty, magnificence, greatness.

senses.label: Majesty, greatness
senses.definition: Splendid greatness; God's mighty greatness shown in Jesus' healing, Christ's majesty seen at the transfiguration, and the claimed majesty of Artemis.

background.note: Used of the majesty of the Roman people, like Latin maiestas.

study.summary: "Greatness, majesty" — in the NT used only of God, either as a reverent title for God himself or as an attribute ascribed to him in praise.

senses.label: The Majesty (title for God)
senses.definition: A reverent way of naming God himself, at whose right hand the exalted Son is seated.

senses.label: Majesty ascribed to God
senses.definition: The divine greatness attributed to God in a doxology.

background.note: Used in the Greek Old Testament for God's greatness, as in David's prayer of thanks.

study.exegesisTip: In Hebrews "the right hand of the Majesty" avoids naming God directly, in the Jewish manner, while placing the Son in the seat of supreme honor.

study.summary: "Great ones, nobles" — the high-ranking men of a court or society, always plural in the NT.

senses.label: Nobles, magnates
senses.definition: Men of high rank and influence: Herod's courtiers, the grandees of the earth who hide from judgment, and the merchant princes of Babylon.

background.note: Appears in a magical formula for restraining anger against kings or great men.

study.summary: "Drunkenness" — intoxication, named in vice lists and warnings as incompatible with watchful Christian living.

senses.label: Drunkenness, intoxication
senses.definition: The state or habit of being drunk; in the plural, bouts of drunkenness, often paired with carousing.

background.note: Plato uses the word of drunkenness and of drinking to the point of intoxication.
The plural appears in an invitation to festivities celebrating Hadrian's accession, of revelry with laughter and drinking.

study.exegesisTip: The plural in Romans and Galatians points to repeated drinking bouts, not a single lapse; it is regularly linked with κῶμοι (carousing).

study.summary: "Ink" — literally "the black (stuff)", the writing ink of letters on papyrus.

senses.label: Ink
senses.definition: Writing ink, contrasted with the Spirit's writing on hearts or with speaking face to face.

background.note: Demosthenes speaks of grinding ink, part of a schoolroom task.
Plato uses it for writing ink.

study.exegesisTip: In 2 Corinthians 3:3 Paul contrasts a letter written in ink with the living Spirit's work in the Corinthians' hearts, echoing the new-covenant promise of a law written on the heart.

study.summary: "Black" — the color, used of hair and of apocalyptic signs.

senses.label: Black in color
senses.definition: Black, as opposed to white; of a hair, of the third horseman's horse, and of the darkened sun.

background.note: Translates Hebrew for black, as of the horses in Zechariah's vision which lie behind Revelation's horsemen.

study.exegesisTip: The black horse of Revelation 6:5 is linked with scarcity (the scales and rationed grain), while the sun turning black evokes prophetic signs of the Day of the Lord.

study.summary: "Ponder, devise, practice" — to occupy the mind or energy with something, whether plotting, preparing beforehand, or devoting oneself to a task.

senses.label: Devise, plot
senses.definition: To scheme or plan, of the nations plotting in vain against the Lord and his Anointed (from Psalm 2).

senses.label: Prepare one's words beforehand
senses.definition: To rehearse or premeditate what to say when arrested, which Jesus forbids.
senses.note: Found in the Byzantine text of Mark; critical texts read only προμεριμνᾶτε.

senses.label: Practice, be devoted to
senses.definition: To give careful attention to and diligently exercise oneself in something.

study.translationNote: In 1 Timothy 4:15 older versions say "meditate upon these things", while modern versions say "practice" or "be diligent in"; the verb covers both mental attention and active exercise.

background.note: Used of the righteous man's constant attention to God's law.

study.summary: "Find fault, blame" — to censure someone for wrongdoing.

senses.label: Find fault, blame
senses.definition: To hold someone blameworthy: an objector asks why God still finds fault, and God censures Israel when promising a new covenant.
senses.note: MAR 7:2 (the Pharisees finding fault with unwashed hands) is in the Byzantine text only.

study.translationNote: In Hebrews 8:8 manuscripts differ between "finding fault with them" and "finding fault, he says to them", so versions differ on whether the people or the first covenant is blamed.

background.note: Common in letters for blaming someone, e.g. a man blaming another for losing two pigs.

study.summary: "Rather, on the contrary, indeed" — an emphatic particle that corrects or intensifies what has just been said.

senses.label: Corrective: nay rather
senses.definition: Introduces a correction of a previous statement or objection.

senses.label: Affirmative: yes indeed
senses.definition: Strongly affirms in answer to a question.

study.translationNote: At Luke 11:28 versions differ between "Yes, but rather" and "Blessed rather", since the particle can both grant and correct the woman's blessing.
study.exegesisTip: In Luke 11:28 Jesus does not deny that his mother is blessed but redirects the blessing to all who hear and keep God's word.

study.summary: "Mid-heaven" — the highest point of the sky, where something flying is seen and heard by all on earth.

senses.label: Mid-heaven, zenith
senses.definition: The middle of the sky overhead, where an eagle, an angel and the birds fly in John's visions.

background.note: Used as an astronomical term in a horoscope.

study.exegesisTip: Flying "in mid-heaven" makes the message or summons visible and audible to the whole earth.

study.summary: "Change, removal, transfer" — the shifting of something from one place or state to another.

senses.label: Taking away (of Enoch)
senses.definition: Enoch's removal from earth by God without dying.

senses.label: Change of an established order
senses.definition: The change of the law that follows a change of priesthood, and the removal of shakable created things.

background.note: Used of the removal of a stair during house repairs.

study.exegesisTip: Hebrews uses the noun with its related verb (μετατίθημι) to argue that the old priestly order was meant to give way.

study.summary: "Turn, change, pervert" — to change something into a different (often opposite) state.

senses.label: Be turned into
senses.definition: To be changed into something else, as the sun into darkness or laughter into mourning.
senses.note: In JAM 4:9 critical texts read the related verb μετατρέπω.

senses.label: Pervert, distort
senses.definition: To twist something into its opposite, of those seeking to pervert the gospel of Christ.

background.note: Homer uses it for turning about or changing one's mind.

study.summary: "Length" — one of the measurements of an object or space.

senses.label: Length
senses.definition: The long dimension of something: of the foursquare New Jerusalem, and figuratively of the vastness of Christ's love.

background.note: Plato lists length, breadth and depth together as the dimensions of space.

study.summary: "Recompense, payment of what is due" — repayment that can be either reward or punishment.

senses.label: Just punishment
senses.definition: The penalty paid out for transgression under the old covenant.

senses.label: Reward
senses.definition: The reward awaiting those who persevere in faith.

study.exegesisTip: Hebrews uses one word for both sides of divine recompense, presenting God as a just paymaster who repays both disobedience and faithfulness.

study.summary: "Memorial, remembrance" — something that keeps a person or deed in memory, including before God.

senses.label: Memory of a person
senses.definition: A lasting remembrance, as the anointing woman's deed will be told in memory of her.

senses.label: Memorial before God
senses.definition: Something that comes up before God and is remembered by him, like the memorial portion of an offering.

background.note: Herodotus speaks of leaving a memorial of oneself.

study.exegesisTip: Acts 10:4 echoes the sacrificial language of the Greek Old Testament, where a "memorial" portion of the offering was burned before the Lord; Cornelius' prayers and alms rose to God like an offering.

study.summary: "Betroth" — in the passive, to be pledged in marriage, a binding legal stage before the couple lived together.

senses.label: Be betrothed
senses.definition: Of Mary, legally pledged to Joseph in marriage but not yet living with him.

background.note: In early Greek the active means to court or seek a woman in marriage.

study.exegesisTip: Jewish betrothal was a binding commitment that could be ended only by divorce, which explains why Joseph planned to divorce Mary quietly.

study.summary: "Peck measure, basket" — a Roman dry measure (about 8–9 liters) and the vessel holding it.

senses.label: Measuring vessel
senses.definition: A household grain container under which no one would hide a lamp.

study.translationNote: The traditional "bushel" overstates the size; modern versions use "basket" or "bowl" for this smaller measure.

background.note: A standard measure for grain and other dry goods.

study.summary: "Soil, defile" — in the NT always figurative, of moral or spiritual pollution.

senses.label: Defile (figurative)
senses.definition: To stain morally: a weak conscience defiled, garments soiled by compromise, and those not defiled with women.

background.note: Used in a non-canonical gospel fragment of a defiled man entering the temple.

study.caution: Revelation 14:4 is widely read symbolically, of spiritual faithfulness rather than literal celibacy; interpreters differ.

study.summary: "Form" — the outward shape or appearance in which something exists and shows itself.

senses.label: Outward form, appearance
senses.definition: The form in which the risen Jesus appeared to two disciples.

senses.label: Form of God / of a servant
senses.definition: The form in which Christ existed as God and the form of a slave he took on, a form that truly expresses what he is.

study.translationNote: Some versions render Philippians 2:6 as "in very nature God", interpreting form as essential nature; others keep "form".
study.exegesisTip: The parallel "form of God" and "form of a servant" in Philippians 2 contrasts Christ's divine existence with the humble status he truly took on.
study.caution: Scholars debate how much the philosophical sense of "essential form" applies in Philippians 2; some see a general sense of visible form or appearance.

study.summary: "Toil, hardship" — exhausting, strenuous labor.

senses.label: Toil, hard labor
senses.definition: Wearisome work, always paired by Paul with κόπος to describe his manual labor and hardships in ministry.

background.note: Frequent in tragedy for toils and hardships, including the labors of Heracles.

study.summary: "Ten thousand" — the largest Greek number word, used both precisely and for countless multitudes.

senses.label: Ten thousand, countless
senses.definition: A huge, almost unimaginable number: a debt of ten thousand talents, countless guardians, innumerable words.

study.exegesisTip: Ten thousand talents in Matthew 18:24 is a deliberately impossible sum, stressing that the debt can never be repaid.

study.summary: "Sailor" — a seaman, one of a ship's crew.

senses.label: Sailor, seaman
senses.definition: A crewman of a ship, as in Paul's shipwreck and among those mourning Babylon's fall.

background.note: Common in official documents concerning ship crews.
Used by Homer for seamen.

study.summary: "Put to death, make as dead" — of a body past fathering children, or of putting sinful practices to death.

senses.label: Be as good as dead
senses.definition: Of Abraham's aged body, incapable of producing children.

senses.label: Put to death
senses.definition: To kill off sinful habits of earthly life.

study.exegesisTip: In Colossians 3:5 the command follows the believer's union with Christ in death and resurrection (3:1-3): become in practice what you already are in Christ.

study.summary: "Sober, temperate" — clear-headed and self-controlled, especially regarding wine.

senses.label: Temperate, sober
senses.definition: Moderate in the use of wine and so clear-minded; a qualification for overseers, women, and older men.

study.summary: "Teacher of the law" — an expert who taught and interpreted the Law of Moses.

senses.label: Teacher of the Law
senses.definition: A recognized Jewish teacher of the Mosaic law, like Gamaliel, or one who claims that role.

study.exegesisTip: In 1 Timothy 1:7 the term is ironic: people want the status of law teachers without understanding the law they teach.

study.summary: "Keep back for oneself, embezzle" — to secretly appropriate part of what belongs to others.

senses.label: Embezzle, pilfer
senses.definition: To keep back for oneself what belongs to others, as Ananias did with the sale money, or as slaves might steal from masters.

background.note: Used for Achan's taking of devoted things, the model for Ananias' sin.
An official swears not to embezzle and to report anyone who does.

study.exegesisTip: The same verb describes Achan's theft in Joshua 7:1, suggesting Luke presents Ananias' deceit as a similar sin at the start of the new community.

study.summary: "Admonition, warning" — instruction that corrects by appealing to the mind and conscience.

senses.label: Admonition, warning
senses.definition: Corrective counsel or warning: Scripture's warnings, a father's training, and repeated warnings to a divisive person.

study.summary: "Bridal chamber, wedding hall" — used in the phrase "sons of the bridal chamber", the bridegroom's attendants and guests.

senses.label: Wedding hall ("sons of")
senses.definition: "Sons of the bridal chamber" are the bridegroom's friends and guests who celebrate with him, and cannot fast while he is present.

study.translationNote: Older versions keep the literal "children of the bridechamber"; modern ones translate the idiom as "wedding guests" or "friends of the bridegroom".

background.note: A letter about wedding-feast preparations mentions the bridal chamber.

study.summary: "Shave" — to cut off hair close with a razor, in the NT always of the head.

senses.label: Shave the head
senses.definition: To shave the head, for completing a Nazirite-type vow or as a mark of shame for a woman.

study.exegesisTip: In 1 Corinthians 11 a shaved head was a sign of disgrace for a woman, which Paul uses to argue for head covering.

study.summary: "Belonging to the household" — as a noun, members of one's family; figuratively, God's family of believers.

senses.label: Members of one's household
senses.definition: Close relatives, those of one's own family for whom one must provide.

senses.label: Members of God's family
senses.definition: Believers as members of God's household or of the family of faith.

background.note: Used for relatives or members of a household.

study.summary: "Merciful, compassionate" — feeling and showing pity, as God does.

senses.label: Merciful
senses.definition: Compassionate and pitying; describing God, and believers who imitate him.

background.note: Used in God's self-revelation to Moses as merciful and gracious.

study.exegesisTip: Luke 6:36 grounds human mercy in the Father's mercy, echoing God's self-description in Exodus 34:6.

study.summary: To think, suppose or expect; used of a personal opinion or of a mistaken expectation.

senses.label: Suppose, think
senses.definition: To hold an opinion or estimate, often with modest hedging ("I suppose").

senses.label: Expect, imagine (wrongly)
senses.definition: To count on or imagine an outcome, especially one that is mistaken or should not be presumed.
senses.note: James warns the double-minded man not to imagine he will receive anything from the Lord; Paul's rivals imagine they can add to his distress.

background.note: Common in everyday letters for what someone thinks or intends, e.g. a woman 'thinking by this means to escape' the consequences of her misdeeds.

study.summary: Passion; in the NT always an uncontrolled, degrading desire, especially sexual.

senses.label: Degrading passion, lust
senses.definition: An overpowering emotion that a person is driven by rather than governs; in Paul always a sinful, chiefly sexual craving.
senses.note: In Romans God 'hands over' people to such passions as judgment; in 1 Thessalonians it is 'the passion of lust' typical of those who do not know God.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'passion', 'lust' and 'inordinate affection' (KJV, Col 3:5); all point to desire that has taken control.
study.exegesisTip: The word comes from the verb 'to suffer, undergo': the passion is something one is ruled by. Paired with 'desire' (Col 3:5; 1 Th 4:5), it stresses the passive, mastering side of evil craving.

study.summary: A household slave who escorted and supervised a boy until he came of age; used by Paul of temporary guardians and of the Mosaic law.

senses.label: Child's guardian, attendant
senses.definition: A trusted slave charged with a boy's conduct and safety, taking him to school and disciplining him—distinct from both teacher and father.
senses.note: Paul contrasts countless guardians with the one father who begot them through the gospel.

senses.label: The law as guardian
senses.definition: Figuratively, the law's temporary, supervisory role over God's people until the coming of Christ and faith.

study.translationNote: KJV 'schoolmaster' and 'instructor' suggest a teacher; modern versions prefer 'guardian' or 'disciplinarian', since the role was supervision and discipline, not teaching.

background.note: A mother writes that her son and his attendant should see that he goes to a suitable teacher, showing the attendant's general charge over the boy.
Used of the slave who went with a boy from home to school and back.

study.exegesisTip: In Galatians the point is temporariness: once faith has come, 'we are no longer under a guardian' (GAL 3:25), because the heir has come of age.

study.summary: A complete suit of armor; used literally of a strong man's weapons and figuratively of the armor God provides.

senses.label: Full armor (literal)
senses.definition: The complete equipment of a heavily armed soldier, in which a warrior trusts.

senses.label: God's full armor
senses.definition: Figuratively, the whole protective and offensive equipment God gives believers to stand against the devil.

background.note: The full equipment of a hoplite: shield, helmet, breastplate, greaves, sword and lance.

study.exegesisTip: Luke 11:22 shows Christ as the stronger one who strips Satan of his armor; Ephesians 6 clothes believers with God's own armor.

study.summary: Originally a walled park or garden; in the NT, Paradise, the dwelling of God where the righteous are with him.

senses.label: Paradise, abode of the blessed
senses.definition: The place of God's presence where the faithful dead are with him; associated with the tree of life and the restored Eden.
senses.note: Paul equates being caught up to Paradise with the 'third heaven' (2 Cor 12:2–4).

background.note: A Persian loanword first used by Xenophon of the enclosed hunting parks of Persian kings and nobles.
The Greek Old Testament uses it for the 'garden' of Eden (Gen 2:8), the source of its later sense.

study.caution: The exact relation of Paradise to the final new creation is debated; the NT uses the word without detailed description.

study.summary: A deposit entrusted to someone's safekeeping, to be guarded and returned intact.

senses.label: Entrusted deposit
senses.definition: Something placed in another's care for safekeeping, especially the gospel truth committed to Timothy, or what Paul has committed to God.

study.translationNote: In 2 Tim 1:12 'my deposit' may be what Paul has entrusted to God (his life, his salvation) or what God has entrusted to Paul (the gospel); versions differ accordingly.

background.note: A standard legal and banking term for a sum of money held on deposit, e.g. a receipt for 1500 drachmae received as a deposit.

study.exegesisTip: The banking image implies the deposit must be kept unchanged and returned intact; Timothy is not to add to or subtract from the gospel.

study.summary: Disobedience, a refusal to heed what has been heard.

senses.label: Disobedience
senses.definition: Failure or refusal to obey a known command, set against obedience.
senses.note: In Romans 5:19 Adam's disobedience is contrasted with Christ's obedience.

study.exegesisTip: The word literally means 'hearing amiss'; it is the opposite of the word for obedience, which literally means 'hearing under'.

study.summary: To remain or stay with; to continue in a place, office or practice.

senses.label: Stay with someone
senses.definition: To remain in a place or with people for a time.
senses.note: In Philippians Paul expects to remain alive and stay with his readers.

senses.label: Continue in office
senses.definition: To go on serving; the Levitical priests were prevented by death from continuing.

senses.label: Persevere in
senses.definition: To keep on looking into and doing God's word rather than forgetting it.

background.note: Common for 'remain, stand by', and also used euphemistically for continuing in someone's service.

study.summary: Except, apart from; as an adverb, besides or outside.

senses.label: Except (preposition)
senses.definition: With the genitive, naming an exception: 'except for'.
senses.note: Matthew's 'except on the ground of sexual immorality' is the divorce exception clause.

senses.label: Besides, external things
senses.definition: Adverbially, 'the things besides' — either the outward trials just listed or other matters left unmentioned.

study.translationNote: In 2 Cor 11:28 some versions render 'apart from these external things', others 'besides the things I have not mentioned'.
study.caution: The precise scope of the exception in Matthew 5:32 is much debated; the word itself simply marks an exception.

study.summary: A sojourner, someone living temporarily in a foreign place; used of believers whose true home is not this world.

senses.label: Sojourner, temporary resident
senses.definition: A person staying for a time among people not his own; applied to the patriarchs and to Christians as exiles on earth.

study.translationNote: Rendered 'pilgrims', 'strangers', 'exiles' or 'sojourners'; the core idea is temporary residence away from home.

background.note: Abraham calls himself a stranger and sojourner among the Hittites.
Used of foreigners residing temporarily in a district, distinguished from settled inhabitants.

study.summary: A family line or clan descended from a common father; more broadly, a family or people-group.

senses.label: Lineage, family line
senses.definition: Descent traced from an ancestor; Joseph belonged to the house and line of David.

senses.label: Family, people-group
senses.definition: A group united by common descent; all the families of the earth, or every family in heaven and on earth.

study.translationNote: In Eph 3:15 the KJV 'the whole family' differs from modern 'every family'; there is a wordplay with 'Father' (patēr–patria): every family is named from the Father.

background.note: Used of lineage or descent, especially on the father's side.

study.summary: Ancestral, belonging to or received from one's forefathers.

senses.label: Ancestral, of the fathers
senses.definition: Inherited from previous generations: the ancestral law, the God of the fathers, the customs of the fathers.
senses.note: All three occur in Paul's defense speeches, stressing his loyalty to Israel's heritage.

background.note: Common in religious language for 'ancestral gods'.

study.summary: A fetter or shackle for the feet.

senses.label: Fetter, shackle
senses.definition: A chain or band binding the feet, used to restrain the demon-possessed man of the Gerasenes.

background.note: Used of a prisoner kept in custody in fetters.

study.summary: To try or attempt; in the passive, to be put to the test.

senses.label: Try, attempt
senses.definition: To make an effort to do something.

senses.label: Be tested, tempted
senses.definition: In the passive, to undergo testing or temptation.

background.note: Common for 'attempt', e.g. 'so now again I attempt to write to you'.

study.summary: Pentecost, the Jewish Feast of Weeks held on the fiftieth day after Passover.

senses.label: Feast of Pentecost
senses.definition: The harvest festival fifty days after Passover, when the Spirit was poured out and which Paul planned his travels around.

background.note: Literally 'fiftieth'; in Egyptian documents it also named a two-percent tax.

study.summary: To surround or seize; of documents, to contain or stand written.

senses.label: Seize, overwhelm
senses.definition: Of an emotion gripping someone: amazement took hold of Peter and his companions.

senses.label: Contain, stand written
senses.definition: Of a letter or Scripture, to have as its content; 'it stands in Scripture'.

background.note: A standard formula in legal documents for what a will or contract states: 'as it stands in the will'.

study.summary: To cover all around; to blindfold or to overlay.

senses.label: Blindfold
senses.definition: To cover someone's face, as Jesus' captors did while mocking him to 'prophesy'.

senses.label: Overlay
senses.definition: To cover a surface completely; the ark covered all over with gold.

study.summary: To fall in with, run into or encounter, usually something harmful.

senses.label: Fall among, encounter
senses.definition: To come upon unexpectedly and become caught up in: robbers, trials of many kinds.

senses.label: Strike, run aground
senses.definition: Of a ship, to strike a place such as a reef or sandbar.

background.note: Used of meeting with misfortune, e.g. 'he will meet with anger'.

study.exegesisTip: In James 1:2 the verb suggests trials one stumbles into rather than seeks out.

study.summary: To carry around; in the passive, to be swept about.

senses.label: Carry about
senses.definition: To bring from place to place; the sick carried to Jesus, or Paul bearing in his body the dying of Jesus.

senses.label: Be swept about
senses.definition: Figuratively, to be blown around by every wind of teaching, lacking stability.

background.note: Used of carrying someone in one's heart, a figurative 'carry about'.

study.summary: A flat tablet, especially the stone tablets of the covenant.

senses.label: Tablet
senses.definition: A flat slab for inscribing; the stone tablets of the law, contrasted with the human heart on which the Spirit writes.

background.note: The Greek Old Testament uses it consistently for the tablets of the Ten Commandments (e.g. Exod 31:18).
Used of inscribed tablets set up on walls.

study.exegesisTip: 2 Corinthians 3:3 echoes the new-covenant promise of a law written on hearts rather than on stone (Jer 31:33; Ezek 36:26).

study.summary: To widen or make broad; figuratively, to open the heart in affection.

senses.label: Widen, broaden
senses.definition: To make something wider, as the Pharisees enlarged their phylacteries for show.

senses.label: Open the heart wide
senses.definition: Figuratively, to enlarge one's heart in openness and affection toward others.

study.summary: To plait, twist or weave together.

senses.label: Plait, twist
senses.definition: To weave strands together; the soldiers twisted thorns into a crown for Jesus.

background.note: Related forms describe plaited fish-baskets and rope.

study.summary: A voyage or sea journey.

senses.label: Voyage
senses.definition: A journey by sea, completed or still under way.
senses.note: In Acts 27:9 the voyage had become dangerous because the sailing season was ending.

background.note: The late genitive form found in Acts 27:9 also appears in an inscription.

study.summary: To make rich, enrich; in the NT chiefly of spiritual riches.

senses.label: Make rich, enrich
senses.definition: To give abundance; believers enriched in Christ in speech and knowledge, Paul making many rich, and givers enriched for generosity.

background.note: Used of enriching someone with wealth.

study.summary: Strangled; of meat from an animal killed without draining its blood.

senses.label: Strangled (meat)
senses.definition: Meat from animals killed by strangling, so that the blood remained in it; one of the abstentions in the Jerusalem decree.

study.exegesisTip: The prohibition reflects the law's demand that blood be poured out (Lev 17:13–14).
study.caution: Some manuscripts of Acts 15 omit 'strangled', and interpreters differ on whether the decree's terms are mainly food laws or moral prohibitions.

study.summary: Very costly, precious, of great value.

senses.label: Very expensive
senses.definition: Costly in money terms: perfume of pure nard, luxurious clothing.

senses.label: Precious (to God)
senses.definition: Of great worth in God's sight: a gentle and quiet spirit.

background.note: Used of costly coverings and precious stones.

study.exegesisTip: Peter turns the word used for costly clothing in 1 Timothy 2:9 into a description of inner character God values.

study.summary: Toil or labor; then the pain and distress it brings.

senses.label: Hard labor, toil
senses.definition: Strenuous effort on others' behalf.
senses.note: Epaphras' labor for the churches.

senses.label: Pain, anguish
senses.definition: Physical and mental suffering, inflicted in judgment and absent from the new creation.

study.translationNote: In Colossians 4:13 many manuscripts read 'zeal' instead of 'toil', so some versions say 'great zeal'.

background.note: Used in medical prescriptions for ear pain.

study.summary: To ravage or destroy, used of Saul's attack on the church.

senses.label: Ravage, try to destroy
senses.definition: To lay waste violently; Saul's persecution aimed at destroying the church and the faith.
senses.note: The imperfect in Galatians suggests repeated or attempted destruction ('tried to destroy').

background.note: Used of sacking cities and ravaging land in war.

study.summary: Purple, the costly dye or a garment or cloth dyed with it.

senses.label: Purple robe
senses.definition: A purple garment, put on Jesus in mock royal honor, or worn by the rich man as a sign of luxury.

senses.label: Purple cloth
senses.definition: Purple fabric traded as luxury merchandise.

background.note: Purple dye was a costly commodity bought by weight.

study.caution: The soldiers' robe may have been a reddish military cloak (Matthew calls it scarlet), used to suggest royal purple.

study.summary: How often? how many times?

senses.label: How often
senses.definition: An interrogative or exclamatory adverb asking or lamenting how many times.

background.note: Used in a letter: 'see how many times I have sent to you!'

study.summary: πόσις means drinking or drink, paired with βρῶσις (eating, food) in all its NT uses.

senses.label: Drinking, what one drinks
senses.definition: The act of drinking or the drink taken, named together with eating as a matter of religious scruple or judgment.
senses.note: Paul insists that God's kingdom and Christian freedom do not turn on rules about food and drink.

senses.label: Drink (concrete)
senses.definition: That which is drunk; Jesus calls his blood true drink, the real sustenance of eternal life.

background.note: A second-century ostracon speaks of the drinking of beer in connection with a temple festival.

study.exegesisTip: In John 6:55 the pair 'true food … true drink' answers the earlier manna discussion: Jesus himself is the genuine nourishment that the wilderness provisions only pictured.

study.summary: πρεσβυτέριον is a council or body of elders, used of the Jewish Sanhedrin and of a Christian body of elders.

senses.label: Jewish council of elders
senses.definition: The Sanhedrin in Jerusalem, the ruling body of chief priests, scribes and elders.

senses.label: Church body of elders
senses.definition: The group of Christian elders who laid hands on Timothy when his gift was given.

study.translationNote: KJV and many versions keep 'presbytery' in 1 Timothy 4:14, while others render 'the elders' or 'the council of elders'.

study.summary: πρεσβύτης means an old or older man.

senses.label: Old man, older man
senses.definition: A man of advanced age; used of the aged Zechariah, of the older men in the church, and of Paul describing himself.

study.translationNote: In Philemon 9 some versions (e.g. RSV) render 'ambassador', reading the word as a spelling variant of πρεσβευτής; most keep 'old man' or 'aged'.

background.note: Used in third-century documents of an old man giving testimony, 'as an old man and worthy of belief'.

study.caution: Whether Paul calls himself 'an old man' or 'an ambassador' in Philemon 9 is debated, since πρεσβύτης was sometimes written for πρεσβευτής; the context of appeal fits either.

study.summary: πρόδηλος means plainly evident, obvious to all.

senses.label: Clearly evident, obvious
senses.definition: Plain for all to see; the prefix here intensifies ('perfectly clear') rather than meaning 'beforehand'.
senses.note: Hebrews 7:14 uses the neuter impersonally: 'it is evident that our Lord sprang from Judah'.

background.note: Used in a second-century document of a matter that had become clear.

study.summary: προδότης is a betrayer or traitor.

senses.label: Betrayer, traitor
senses.definition: One who betrays a person or trust; said of Judas, of those who handed over the Righteous One, and of the treacherous in the last days.

background.note: Standard classical word for a traitor or betrayer.

study.exegesisTip: Stephen (Acts 7:52) turns the label of Judas on the Council itself: they are now the betrayers and murderers of the Righteous One.

study.summary: πρόθυμος means ready, willing or eager.

senses.label: Willing, ready
senses.definition: Inwardly eager and prepared, as the spirit is willing though the flesh is weak.

senses.label: Eagerness (neuter as noun)
senses.definition: τὸ πρόθυμον, readiness or eagerness: Paul's eagerness to preach the gospel in Rome.

study.summary: προκαταγγέλλω means to announce or declare beforehand.

senses.label: Foretell, announce beforehand
senses.definition: To proclaim in advance what will happen, as God foretold Christ's sufferings through the prophets.

senses.label: Previously promised
senses.definition: Passive participle of a gift announced or pledged in advance.
senses.note: Many modern texts read προεπηγγελμένην ('previously promised') here.

study.summary: προκοπή means progress or advancement.

senses.label: Advance of the gospel
senses.definition: The forward movement and spread of the gospel, furthered even by Paul's imprisonment.

senses.label: Personal spiritual progress
senses.definition: Growth in faith and maturity, of believers or of Timothy in his ministry.

background.note: Used in a second-century letter wishing the recipient 'further advancement' and prosperity.

study.summary: προλαμβάνω means to take beforehand, to do something in advance, or (passive) to be overtaken or caught.

senses.label: Take beforehand
senses.definition: To take one's own meal ahead of others rather than sharing it at the Lord's Supper.

senses.label: Do in advance
senses.definition: With an infinitive, to do something ahead of time: the woman anointed Jesus' body beforehand for burial.

senses.label: Be overtaken, caught
senses.definition: Passive, to be caught or surprised in a wrongdoing.

study.caution: In Galatians 6:1 it is debated whether the sense is 'caught in the act' (discovered) or 'overtaken' by a sin before one is aware.

study.summary: προνοέω means to give careful thought to, take care for, or provide for.

senses.label: Take thought for what is right
senses.definition: To aim at and carefully attend to what is honorable in others' eyes.

senses.label: Provide for
senses.definition: To care for and supply the needs of one's relatives and household.

study.summary: προοράω means to see beforehand or ahead of oneself, and to foresee.

senses.label: Keep before one's eyes
senses.definition: Middle voice, to keep someone continually in view: 'I saw the Lord always before me' (from Psalm 16).

senses.label: See previously
senses.definition: To have seen someone earlier, as Trophimus had been seen with Paul in the city.

senses.label: Foresee
senses.definition: To see in advance what will happen, as David and Scripture foresaw God's saving acts.

study.exegesisTip: In Galatians 3:8 Scripture itself is personified as foreseeing God's justification of the Gentiles and preaching the gospel ahead of time to Abraham.

study.summary: προσαγωγή means access or approach, the believer's entrance into God's presence and grace.

senses.label: Access to God
senses.definition: The right and means of approach into God's favor and presence, given through Christ.

study.exegesisTip: Ephesians 2:18 is Trinitarian: through Christ, in one Spirit, to the Father, with Jew and Gentile approaching together.
study.caution: Some scholars prefer the active sense 'introduction' (being brought in by Christ) rather than 'access' as a standing right; both stress that approach comes through him.

study.summary: προσαιτέω means to beg, to ask for alms.

senses.label: Beg
senses.definition: To ask persistently for alms, as blind beggars did by the roadside.
senses.note: In Mark 10:46 and Luke 18:35 many modern texts have ἐπαιτέω.

background.note: Classical writers use it for asking alms of someone.

study.summary: προσκολλάω (passive) means to be joined closely to, to cleave to, used of a husband united to his wife.

senses.label: Be joined, cleave to
senses.definition: To be closely and permanently united, quoting Genesis 2:24 of the marriage bond.

background.note: A sixth-century will refers to the wife 'joined' to the testator.

study.summary: προστρέχω means to run up to someone.

senses.label: Run to, run up
senses.definition: To hurry toward a person to greet or address him.

study.summary: προτίθεμαι means to set forth publicly, or to set before oneself as a purpose.

senses.label: Set forth publicly
senses.definition: To display or present openly: God put Christ forward as a propitiation.

senses.label: Purpose, plan
senses.definition: To set before oneself, intend: Paul's repeated plans to visit Rome, God's purpose in Christ.

background.note: Common for publicly posting an edict or notice.

study.caution: In Romans 3:25 interpreters divide between 'publicly displayed' and 'purposed' (as in Rom 1:13; Eph 1:9).

study.summary: προχειρίζομαι means to appoint, choose or designate someone for a task.

senses.label: Appoint, designate
senses.definition: To choose and set apart for a purpose: Christ appointed for Israel, Paul appointed to know God's will and to serve as witness.

background.note: Used of officially appointed tax collectors.

study.summary: πρύμνα is the stern, the rear part of a ship.

senses.label: Stern of a ship
senses.definition: The back end of a boat or ship, as opposed to the bow.

background.note: A papyrus uses the phrase 'from prow to stern'.

study.summary: πρωΐα means early morning.

senses.label: Early morning
senses.definition: The early part of the day, used in time phrases such as 'when morning came'.

background.note: Used in a phrase meaning 'from morning until evening'.

study.summary: πτύω means to spit.

senses.label: Spit
senses.definition: To spit, used of Jesus applying saliva in healings of the deaf-mute and blind.

study.summary: πτωχεία means poverty, even destitution.

senses.label: Poverty
senses.definition: The state of being poor; used of the Macedonians' and Smyrna's real poverty and of Christ's voluntary poverty through which believers become rich.

background.note: In classical Greek it denotes beggary.

study.exegesisTip: 2 Corinthians 8:9 and Revelation 2:9 both pair material poverty with true riches.

study.summary: πυκνός means frequent; its neuter forms are used adverbially for 'often'.

senses.label: Frequent
senses.definition: Occurring often, of Timothy's repeated illnesses.

senses.label: Often (adverbial)
senses.definition: Neuter plural or comparative used as an adverb: often, quite often.

background.note: The comparative adverb appears in a request to 'reply to me more often'.

study.summary: πύρωσις means burning, and figuratively a fiery trial.

senses.label: Burning
senses.definition: The burning of Babylon, whose smoke the kings and sailors watch.

senses.label: Fiery trial
senses.definition: A painful ordeal that tests and refines believers like metal in fire.

study.summary: πώρωσις means hardening, a callous dullness of heart and understanding.

senses.label: Hardening, obtuseness
senses.definition: Insensibility or blindness of mind and heart that resists God's truth.

study.translationNote: KJV renders 'blindness' in Rom 11:25 and Eph 4:18, most modern versions 'hardening' or 'hardness'.

background.note: In medical writing it is the formation of a callus that reunites a broken bone.

study.exegesisTip: In Romans 11:25 the hardening is partial ('in part') and temporary ('until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in').

study.summary: ῥάπισμα means a slap or blow, especially with the open hand on the face.

senses.label: Slap, blow
senses.definition: A blow with the hand (or perhaps a rod) inflicted on Jesus during his trial and mockery.

study.translationNote: In Mark 14:65 versions differ between 'blows' or 'slaps' and 'strokes of rods'.

study.summary: ῥαφίς is a needle.

senses.label: Needle
senses.definition: A sewing needle, in Jesus' saying about a camel passing through its eye.
senses.note: In Luke 18:25 many modern texts have βελόνη.

background.note: Listed in a household account as 'thread and needle'.

study.summary: ῥύσις means a flow or issue, used of a flow of blood.

senses.label: Flow of blood
senses.definition: A continuous hemorrhage, of the woman who had suffered it for twelve years.

study.summary: σαρόω means to sweep.

senses.label: Sweep
senses.definition: To sweep a house clean, of the woman searching for her coin and of the house swept and left empty.

background.note: Used metaphorically of a district being 'swept clean'.

study.summary: σεβαστός, 'revered', is the Greek equivalent of Augustus, the Roman emperor's title, and as an adjective 'imperial'.

senses.label: The Emperor (Augustus)
senses.definition: Title of the Roman emperor, here Nero, to whom Paul appealed.

senses.label: Imperial, Augustan
senses.definition: Adjective naming a military cohort connected with the emperor.

background.note: Used in dates by the reign of 'Tiberius Caesar Augustus'.

study.summary: σεμνότης means dignity, gravity or seriousness of conduct worthy of respect.

senses.label: Dignity, gravity
senses.definition: A serious, respectable bearing that commands respect, expected of believers, church leaders and Titus' teaching.

study.summary: δέσμιος means 'bound' and, as a noun, 'a prisoner' — someone held in chains or custody. The Gospels use it of the prisoner released at the Passover feast; Acts uses it of Paul and his fellow captives; Paul himself turns it into a title of identity: 'the prisoner of Christ Jesus', meaning his imprisonment belongs to Christ and serves the gospel.

senses.label: A prisoner in custody
senses.definition: A person held in chains or under guard by civil or military authority; the ordinary, literal sense.
senses.note: In the Gospels the word frames the Passover-release custom, under which Barabbas, 'a notorious prisoner' (MAT 27:16), was freed in place of Jesus.

senses.label: Paul as a prisoner in Roman custody
senses.definition: In the closing chapters of Acts, Paul is repeatedly 'the prisoner' as his case moves from Jerusalem to Caesarea and Rome.
senses.note: Luke's narrative shows Paul's chains becoming the means by which the gospel reaches governors, kings and finally Rome.

senses.label: 'Prisoner of Christ' — captivity owned by the Lord
senses.definition: Paul's self-description: he is in literal chains, but he regards himself as held by and for Christ, so that his imprisonment is part of his apostolic service rather than a defeat.
senses.note: The genitive 'of Christ Jesus' (EPH 3:1) and the phrase 'in the Lord' (EPH 4:1) show whose prisoner Paul considers himself to be — not Caesar's in the final sense, but Christ's.

senses.label: Imprisoned believers to be remembered
senses.definition: Fellow Christians suffering imprisonment, whom the church is called to remember and stand with as if sharing their chains.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul never complains of being 'Rome's prisoner'; he calls himself 'the prisoner of Christ Jesus' or 'the prisoner in the Lord', turning a mark of shame into a credential that adds weight to his appeals (EPH 4:1, PHM 1:9) and that he urges Timothy not to be ashamed of (2TI 1:8).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word most often, tracing Paul's progress as a prisoner and showing that chains do not stop the word: in Philippi other prisoners listen to Paul and Silas singing hymns at midnight.

study.translationNote: Most versions render 'prisoner'. The KJV sometimes says 'in bonds', which keeps the image of chains. In Paul's phrase 'prisoner of Christ Jesus', translations differ on whether to preserve the bare genitive ('of Christ') or interpret it ('for Christ', 'for the sake of Christ'); the Greek allows both 'belonging to Christ' and 'because of Christ'.

background.note: In tragedy the adjective can mean 'bound, captive' of a person held in bonds.
Used in an official order to send a man 'as a prisoner', showing the noun's everyday administrative sense.
A second-century document refers to the guarding of 'the prisoners in custody', the same plain sense as in Acts.

study.exegesisTip: When Paul calls himself 'the prisoner of Christ Jesus', read it as a claim of ownership and purpose: Christ, not Caesar, holds the keys, and the imprisonment serves the Gentiles (EPH 3:1). This frames his appeals as coming from someone who has paid a price for the gospel.
study.caution: Whether Paul's 'prisoner of Christ' means 'imprisoned because of Christ' or 'captive belonging to Christ' is debated; many interpreters think both ideas are present and the reader need not choose sharply.

study.summary: δηνάριον is the Latin denarius, a Roman silver coin. In the Gospels it was the standard day's wage for a labourer, so sums in denarii work as a measure of real value: two hundred denarii is about eight months' pay, a hundred denarii a modest but real debt, and a denarius for a measure of wheat in Revelation signals famine prices.

senses.label: A day's wage
senses.definition: The coin as the usual daily pay of a hired worker, the benchmark by which other sums are understood.
senses.note: In the parable of the vineyard workers every labourer receives a denarius whatever hour he began, so the coin carries the point about the owner's generosity.

senses.label: The coin bearing Caesar's image
senses.definition: The silver coin as the currency of imperial tax, stamped with the emperor's portrait and inscription.
senses.note: Jesus asks to be shown a denarius; the image on it frames his answer, 'Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's.'

senses.label: A unit for reckoning sums and debts
senses.definition: Denarii counted in quantity to express a price, a cost or a debt.
senses.note: Two hundred denarii (MAR 6:37, JOH 6:7) and three hundred (MAR 14:5, JOH 12:5) are large sums for ordinary people; the two denarii the Samaritan leaves (LUK 10:35) would cover roughly two days' lodging.

senses.label: A famine price
senses.definition: A whole day's wage spent for a single measure of grain, a picture of scarcity and inflated prices.
senses.note: A choinix of wheat was roughly one person's daily ration, so the voice describes a time when labour buys only bare survival.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses the coin in two contrasting parables: the servant forgiven an enormous debt who will not forgive a hundred denarii (MAT 18:28), and the vineyard owner who pays a full denarius to everyone (MAT 20:2). The denarius becomes a measure of mercy and grace.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John (with Mark) records exact sums in denarii — two hundred for bread, three hundred for the ointment — which underline the scale of the need and of Mary's gift. Revelation uses the coin to sketch famine conditions.

study.translationNote: The KJV renders 'penny' or 'pence', which badly understates the value for modern readers. Modern versions keep 'denarius/denarii' and often add a footnote that it was about a day's wage; some paraphrases convert sums into 'a year's wages' and similar.

background.note: A receipt records payment of 'two denarii and eight obols' as the price of Colophonian wine, showing the coin in everyday transactions.
An imperial-period inscription uses the same distributive phrase as Matthew, a set amount of denarii 'apiece' to each recipient (compare MAT 20:10).

study.exegesisTip: Convert sums into days of work to feel their weight: a hundred denarii is about three months' wages; the first servant's ten thousand talents (MAT 18:24) is many thousands of times greater. The contrast is the point of the parable.
study.caution: The 'day's wage' equation rests on MAT 20:2 and general evidence; real purchasing power varied by place and period, so precise modern dollar equivalents should not be pressed.

study.summary: διαλογίζομαι means to reason something through, to turn it over in the mind, or to debate it among a group. In the NT it is always inward or private deliberation, and in the Gospels it often describes questioning or suspicious reasoning that Jesus perceives and exposes.

senses.label: To reason inwardly, ponder
senses.definition: To turn a matter over in one's own mind, weighing what it means or what to do.
senses.note: Neutral in itself: Mary ponders the angel's greeting (LUK 1:29), the crowds wonder whether John might be the Messiah (LUK 3:15), and the rich fool reasons about bigger barns (LUK 12:17).

senses.label: To question or object silently in the heart
senses.definition: Unspoken critical reasoning, especially doubt or objection against Jesus' words, which he discerns.
senses.note: When the scribes reason 'in their hearts' that Jesus blasphemes by forgiving sins, Jesus knows their thoughts — itself a sign of his authority.

senses.label: To debate or discuss among themselves
senses.definition: Deliberation carried out in a group, often anxious, calculating or at cross-purposes with Jesus.
senses.note: The disciples argue about bread while missing Jesus' warning; the leaders calculate how to answer about John's baptism; the tenants plot to kill the heir.

senses.label: To take into account, consider
senses.definition: To reckon with a consideration and draw a conclusion from it.
senses.note: Caiaphas tells the council they have not reckoned that one man's death is to their advantage — words John sees as unwitting prophecy.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark repeatedly shows people reasoning among themselves while Jesus perceives what is going on — scribes, disciples and leaders alike — so that the word often marks a failure to grasp who Jesus is.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word for both open-hearted wondering (Mary, the expectant crowds) and self-centred calculation (the rich fool, the wicked tenants), letting the content of the reasoning reveal the heart.

study.translationNote: English versions vary between 'reason', 'think', 'consider', 'question', 'discuss' and 'argue', depending on whether the reasoning is inside one person ('in their hearts') or between several ('among themselves', 'with one another'). The Greek word itself covers both; the accompanying phrase shows which.

background.note: Xenophon uses the verb of debating or arguing about a subject.
Demosthenes uses it in the commercial sense of balancing accounts with someone.
In Egyptian documents the verb is used of the Prefect holding his judicial assize for a district — a technical legal sense not found in the NT.

study.exegesisTip: Notice the prepositional phrase: 'in their hearts' marks silent reasoning, 'among themselves' or 'with one another' marks group discussion. In both cases the Gospels often follow it with Jesus knowing or answering what was not said to him.

study.summary: διψάω means to be thirsty, to suffer thirst. Beyond literal thirst — part of the hardship of the poor, the stranger and the apostle — it becomes in Jesus' teaching an image of deep spiritual longing that he alone satisfies, especially in John's Gospel and Revelation with the promise of living water.

senses.label: Physical thirst as hardship
senses.definition: Literal lack of water, a basic human need and a mark of deprivation.
senses.note: In MAT 25:35 Jesus identifies himself with the thirsty; Paul lists thirst among apostolic hardships (1CO 4:11) and cites Proverbs on giving drink to an enemy (ROM 12:20).

senses.label: Jesus' thirst on the cross
senses.definition: Jesus' cry 'I thirst' at the crucifixion, real bodily thirst that John links to the fulfilment of Scripture.

senses.label: Spiritual longing satisfied by Christ
senses.definition: Figurative thirst: the deep need of the human soul for life, which Jesus promises to quench permanently.
senses.note: The offer is free and open: 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink' (JOH 7:37); 'Let the one who is thirsty come' (REV 22:17).

senses.label: Thirst for righteousness
senses.definition: Intense desire for righteousness, spoken of as hunger and thirst — wanting it as a starving person wants food and water.
senses.note: Here the verb takes a direct object (the righteousness), where classical Greek would use a genitive; the effect is a longing directed at the thing itself.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's writings use thirst as a major theme: Jesus offers water after which one 'will never thirst' (JOH 4:14), invites the thirsty to drink (JOH 7:37), himself thirsts on the cross (JOH 19:28), and Revelation closes with the free gift of the water of life (REV 21:6, REV 22:17).

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew frames thirst ethically: blessing for those who thirst for righteousness (MAT 5:6) and judgment according to how the thirsty 'least of these' were treated (MAT 25:35-44).

background.note: Homer describes Tantalus standing in water 'thirsting' but unable to drink — the classic picture of unsatisfied thirst.
An early collection of sayings attributed to Jesus has him say he found all people drunk and 'none thirsting' among them — the same figurative use.

study.exegesisTip: Read John's thirst passages together: the promise at the well (JOH 4:14), the invitation at the feast (JOH 7:37), the cry from the cross (JOH 19:28) and the final invitation (REV 22:17). The one who satisfies thirst is the one who himself thirsted.

study.summary: εἶτα is an adverb of sequence: 'then, next, after that'. It marks the next step in a series of events or items, often a fresh and distinct stage, and occasionally the next point in an argument ('furthermore').

senses.label: Then, next (in a narrative)
senses.definition: Introduces the next action or event, frequently a new and distinct stage in what happens.
senses.note: In JAM 1:15 it marks the stages of a grim process: desire conceives, then gives birth to sin, and sin when full-grown brings death.

senses.label: Then (in a series or list)
senses.definition: Marks the next item in an ordered enumeration, often after 'first' or alongside 'then' (ἔπειτα).
senses.note: In 1CO 15:5-7 it sets out the order of resurrection appearances; in 1CO 15:24 the final stage, 'then comes the end'.

senses.label: Then, after that (with a following circumstance)
senses.definition: Introduces a subsequent turn of events that changes the situation.
senses.note: In the parable of the sower: the hearers are short-lived, then when trouble comes they fall away.

senses.label: Furthermore (in an argument)
senses.definition: Moves an argument on to a further point.
senses.note: Introduces a further comparison between human fathers and the Father of spirits.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses εἶτα to order lists: the sequence of witnesses to the risen Christ, the order of events at the end, and the order of creation (Adam first, then Eve).

study.translationNote: The word is usually 'then' or 'next', but English versions often smooth it away or vary it ('after that', 'later', 'furthermore'), so it may not be visible in translation. In lists it can be important for sequence, as in 1CO 15:5-7.

background.note: Sophocles uses the pattern 'first … then (εἶτα) …' for successive actions.
A complaint describes being robbed and stripped and 'afterwards' given clothing by friends — εἶτα marking a fresh incident, as Hort noted for JAM 1:15.

study.exegesisTip: Where εἶτα appears in a list, ask whether the order matters to the argument. In 1CO 15:23-24 ('Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to him, then the end') the sequence is the substance of Paul's teaching on the resurrection.
study.caution: Whether the sequence in 1TI 2:13 ('Adam was formed first, then Eve') is simply chronological or carries theological weight about roles is disputed among interpreters; the word itself only marks order.

study.summary: εὐλογία is literally 'good speaking'. In the NT it covers praise offered to God, the act of blessing (a spoken benediction, including the cup 'of blessing' at the Lord's Supper), and above all the blessing God gives — the benefits of salvation promised to Abraham and given in Christ. Paul also uses it of a generous gift, and once of smooth, flattering speech.

senses.label: Blessing given by God
senses.definition: The good God bestows, especially the saving benefits promised to Abraham and now given in Christ.
senses.note: EPH 1:3 sums up all God's gifts in Christ as 'every spiritual blessing'; GAL 3:14 links the blessing of Abraham with the gift of the Spirit.

senses.label: The act of blessing, a benediction
senses.definition: A spoken word of blessing, whether a patriarch's blessing, a thanksgiving over the cup, or speech that blesses rather than curses.
senses.note: 'The cup of blessing' (1CO 10:16) reflects the Jewish cup over which thanks to God was spoken; Esau sought his father's blessing too late (HEB 12:17).

senses.label: Praise ascribed to God and the Lamb
senses.definition: Adoration offered to God, part of the heavenly doxologies.

senses.label: A generous gift, bounty
senses.definition: A gift given freely and generously, so that it blesses the receiver — the opposite of a grudging exaction.
senses.note: In 2CO 9:6 the phrase 'sow bountifully' is literally 'sow with blessings'.

senses.label: Smooth, flattering speech
senses.definition: Fine-sounding talk used to deceive.
senses.note: Here the word keeps its old sense of 'fine speaking', paired with 'smooth talk' used by divisive teachers.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul spans the widest range: the blessing of Abraham reaching the Gentiles (GAL 3:14), every spiritual blessing in Christ (EPH 1:3), the cup of blessing (1CO 10:16), the collection as a generous 'blessing' rather than an extortion (2CO 9:5), and flattering 'fine words' (ROM 16:18).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In Revelation the word appears only in heavenly worship, as praise rendered to God and to the Lamb.

study.translationNote: Most occurrences are 'blessing', but 2CO 9:5-6 is often rendered 'generous gift', 'bounty' or 'bountifully', and ROM 16:18 'flattery' or 'fair speech' — so English hides that one Greek word is used throughout.

background.note: Thucydides uses the word for praise or eulogy of the dead in Pericles' funeral oration.
Plato uses it for 'good or fine language', the root idea behind Paul's 'fine speech' in ROM 16:18.
An inscription reads 'Blessing of the Lord' (Εὐλογία Κυρίου), using the noun for a benefit received from God.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who is blessing whom: God blessing people (benefits), people blessing God (praise), or people blessing others (benediction or gift). In EPH 1:3 both directions meet: 'Blessed be God … who has blessed us with every blessing'.

study.summary: θεμέλιος is a foundation — the base stones on which a building or wall rests. Jesus uses it literally in his parables of building; Paul and others use it figuratively for the fundamental basis of the church and of faith: Christ himself, the apostolic witness, and the first truths of the gospel.

senses.label: Literal foundation of a building
senses.definition: The base of a house, tower, prison or wall, laid first and supporting everything above.
senses.note: In ACT 16:26 an earthquake shakes 'the foundations of the prison'.

senses.label: Foundations of the heavenly city
senses.definition: The foundation stones of the city God builds, an image of the permanent, divinely built home of God's people.
senses.note: Abraham looked for 'the city with foundations'; the New Jerusalem's twelve foundations bear the names of the twelve apostles.

senses.label: Christ and the apostolic gospel as the church's foundation
senses.definition: The basis on which the church is built: Christ, as preached by the apostles and prophets.
senses.note: 'No one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ' (1CO 3:11).

senses.label: Fundamental teaching
senses.definition: The elementary truths of the faith laid at the start, on which maturity builds.
senses.note: Repentance from dead works and faith in God are 'the foundation' not to be relaid endlessly.

senses.label: A secure basis for the future
senses.definition: Something firm laid up or standing that guarantees what is to come.
senses.note: In 2TI 2:19 'God's firm foundation stands' despite false teaching, sealed with assurances that the Lord knows his own.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul pictures himself as an 'expert builder' who laid the foundation, Christ, at Corinth, warning others to take care how they build on it, and he aimed not to build on another's foundation. In Ephesians the church rests on the foundation of the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: In Luke the literal foundation is the point of Jesus' parables: the wise builder digs deep and lays the foundation on rock, and the tower-builder must count the cost before laying it.

background.note: Thucydides describes the foundations of the Athenian walls laid of all kinds of stones in haste.
A third-century BC papyrus speaks of work 'for drying the foundation', using the neuter form as in ACT 16:26.
A builder records that he rebuilt 'on the old foundation', the kind of language Paul uses about not building on another's foundation.

study.exegesisTip: In 1CO 3 and EPH 2:20 the foundation is described differently — Christ himself, and the apostles and prophets. These are compatible: the apostles' witness to Christ is the foundation, with Christ as its centre and cornerstone.
study.caution: Whether 'the apostles and prophets' in EPH 2:20 means the foundation they laid (their teaching) or the foundation they are (themselves) is debated, as is whether the prophets are NT or OT prophets; most interpreters take them as NT prophets alongside the apostles.

study.summary: κακῶς is the adverb 'badly, ill'. In the Gospels it most often appears in the idiom κακῶς ἔχειν, 'to be in a bad way', i.e. to be sick; it also describes severe suffering. In a moral sense it means 'wrongly' — speaking wrongly, speaking evil of someone, or asking with wrong motives.

senses.label: To be ill (κακῶς ἔχειν)
senses.definition: The idiom 'to have it badly', meaning to be sick, describing those brought to Jesus for healing.
senses.note: Jesus' saying that 'those who are sick' need a doctor (MAT 9:12) turns the idiom into a picture of his mission to sinners.

senses.label: Severely, grievously
senses.definition: Of suffering or affliction in an acute degree.
senses.note: The Canaanite woman's daughter is 'cruelly' (badly) demon-possessed.

senses.label: Miserably (as fitting punishment)
senses.definition: In the phrase 'he will destroy those evil men miserably', the adverb echoes the adjective κακός for emphasis.
senses.note: A wordplay — 'bad men badly' — a stock expression in Greek for a deserved ruin.

senses.label: Wrongly (in speech or prayer)
senses.definition: In a moral sense: speaking wrongly or evilly, or asking for the wrong reasons.
senses.note: In ACT 23:5 Paul cites the law against speaking evil of a ruler; in JAM 4:3 people ask 'wrongly', to spend on their pleasures.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses the 'be ill' idiom in his healing summaries and adds the strong 'bad men badly' at the end of the parable of the tenants.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James uses the moral sense: unanswered prayer is explained by asking 'wrongly', with selfish motives.

study.translationNote: Because the Greek idiom 'have badly' means 'be sick', translations render it 'the sick', 'ill', 'diseased'; the KJV's 'sick', 'grievously vexed', 'miserably destroy' and 'ask amiss' all render the same adverb. Readers of English will not see that one word underlies these different expressions.

background.note: In the Greek Old Testament 'to speak badly' of someone translates the Hebrew for cursing, as in the command not to curse a ruler, cited in ACT 23:5.
A third-century letter says the writer meant to come up because friends reported that a man 'was ill' — the same idiom as in the Gospels.
Another letter describes oxen as 'in a bad way', showing the idiom's everyday range.

study.exegesisTip: When you see 'the sick' in the Gospel healing summaries, it is often the idiom 'those having it badly' — a general term that can sit beside specific categories like the demon-possessed (MAR 1:32), which the Gospels usually distinguish from ordinary illness.

study.summary: κερδαίνω means to gain or make a profit. In the NT it moves from commercial profit (trading with entrusted money) to the paradox of gaining the whole world but losing one's life, and then to 'winning' people — a brother restored, or unbelievers won for Christ. Once it means to 'gain' by avoiding a loss.

senses.label: To gain, make a profit (commercial)
senses.definition: To earn by trading or business, to make a profit.
senses.note: In JAM 4:13 the merchants plan to 'do business and make a profit' without reckoning with God.

senses.label: To gain the world at the cost of one's life
senses.definition: To acquire everything this world offers, set against the loss of one's true self.
senses.note: The commercial language is deliberate: the profit-and-loss calculation of discipleship.

senses.label: To win a person
senses.definition: To gain someone — to bring an erring brother back, or to win unbelievers to faith in Christ.
senses.note: In 1PE 3:1 believing wives may win unbelieving husbands 'without a word' by their conduct.

senses.label: To gain Christ
senses.definition: To obtain Christ himself as the supreme gain, for whom every other advantage is counted loss.

senses.label: To spare oneself, avoid (a loss)
senses.definition: To 'gain' in the sense of avoiding damage one would otherwise incur.
senses.note: Paul says they would have 'been spared' this damage and loss if they had stayed at Crete.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses commercial vocabulary for mission and for his own conversion: he becomes a slave to all 'to win' as many as possible (1CO 9:19-22), and counts all his former advantages as loss 'to gain Christ' (PHP 3:8).

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew has the widest range: profit from trading talents, the danger of gaining the world, and gaining a brother through private correction.

study.translationNote: English shifts between 'gain', 'make a profit' and 'win' according to context, so readers may not see that Jesus' saying about 'gaining the world' and Paul's 'winning' people are the same verb. ACT 27:21 is hard to render: the KJV's 'to have gained this harm and loss' is literal, while most modern versions read 'avoided' or 'spared'.

background.note: A question put to an oracle asks 'Am I to profit by the transaction?', using the verb absolutely as in JAM 4:13.

study.exegesisTip: Read MAT 16:26 and PHP 3:8 side by side: Jesus warns against the worst bargain, gaining the world but losing one's life; Paul describes the best bargain, losing everything to gain Christ.

study.summary: κλέπτης is a thief, one who steals secretly — distinct from the λῃστής, the violent robber. The NT uses it literally, morally (theft as a sin that excludes from God's kingdom), and in two vivid figures: the Lord's return or the Day of the Lord coming 'like a thief in the night', and false shepherds who are 'thieves and robbers'.

senses.label: A thief who steals secretly
senses.definition: One who takes others' property by stealth, breaking in or pilfering.
senses.note: JOH 12:6 notes that Judas 'was a thief' who helped himself from the money bag.

senses.label: Theft as a sin
senses.definition: Thieves as a class of wrongdoers, named in vice lists or as a shameful reason for suffering.
senses.note: 1CO 6:11 adds 'and that is what some of you were' — the label belongs to the past of the washed and justified.

senses.label: The unexpected coming 'like a thief'
senses.definition: An image of suddenness and unpreparedness: the Lord or the Day of the Lord arrives without warning, like a burglar at night.
senses.note: The point is surprise, not stealth or harm: believers are told the day should not overtake them like a thief because they are watchful (1TH 5:4).

senses.label: False shepherds as thieves
senses.definition: Those who come to the flock not by the door but to steal, kill and destroy — illegitimate leaders who exploit God's people.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses 'thief' for illegitimate shepherds who climb into the sheepfold (JOH 10:1, JOH 10:10) and for Judas (JOH 12:6); in Revelation the risen Christ warns that he will come like a thief to the unwatchful (REV 3:3, REV 16:15).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul takes up Jesus' image of the thief in the night for the Day of the Lord, but tells believers they are 'sons of light' whom that day need not surprise.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: Peter repeats the thief image to stress the suddenness of the Day of the Lord and its cosmic consequences, and warns believers not to suffer as thieves.

study.translationNote: English versions consistently say 'thief'. In JOH 10:1 and JOH 10:8 it is paired with λῃστής ('robber', 'bandit'): the thief works by stealth, the robber by violence, and the pairing covers both kinds of illegitimate taker.

background.note: Homer already uses the word for a thief, comparing mist to something better than night for a thief.
Plato pairs 'robbers or thieves', the same combination as JOH 10:8.
A third-century BC document mentions 'thieves arriving by night', recalling the 'thief in the night' of 1TH 5:2.

study.exegesisTip: In the 'thief in the night' sayings, the comparison is to the timing, not the character, of the one coming: Christ is not likened to a thief morally. Each passage draws the same lesson — stay awake and ready.
study.caution: In 1TH 5:4 some manuscripts read 'like thieves' (plural, applying to the people surprised) rather than 'like a thief'; most translations follow the singular.

study.summary: κρείττων (also spelled κρείσσων) is the comparative 'better', used grammatically as the comparative of ἀγαθός ('good'). It can mean better in the sense of more advantageous or preferable, or better in rank and quality, superior. Hebrews makes it a keyword: Christ and the new covenant are 'better' than angels, the Levitical priesthood, the old covenant and its sacrifices.

senses.label: Superior in rank or quality
senses.definition: Of higher standing, worth or excellence than something else; in Hebrews, the superiority of the Son, his priesthood, covenant, sacrifice, hope and the heavenly realities over what came before.
senses.note: Hebrews 7:7 states the principle that the lesser is blessed by the 'better' (greater), which proves Melchizedek's superiority to Abraham and Levi.

senses.label: Better possessions and hopes of believers
senses.definition: Of the superior and lasting things God holds out to his people: a better possession, a better homeland, a better resurrection, something better planned for us.
senses.note: In Hebrews 6:9 the 'better things' are the marks that accompany salvation, in contrast to the fruitless land of 6:8.

senses.label: More advantageous, preferable
senses.definition: Better in result or usefulness; with 'it is' and an infinitive, 'it is better to ...', weighing one course against another.
senses.note: In 1 Corinthians 11:17 Paul says the Corinthians meet not 'for the better but for the worse': their gatherings do more harm than good.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Twelve of the NT uses are in Hebrews, where 'better' structures the whole argument: a better hope, covenant, promises, sacrifices, possession, country and resurrection, and blood that speaks better than Abel's.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: Both Petrine uses are 'it is better' comparisons with a moral edge: better to suffer for doing good than evil, and better never to have known the way of righteousness than to turn from it.

study.translationNote: English versions render it 'better', 'superior' or 'greater' depending on context. In Hebrews 1:4 many translations say the Son became 'superior to' or 'much better than' the angels; the Greek word is the same one used for the 'better' covenant and hope, and keeping 'better' lets the reader see the thread through the letter.

background.note: A second-century letter about buying fleeces uses the word with superlative force: the summer ones were 'the best'.
A third-century letter uses the plural for 'better things': 'you doubtless had better things to do; that was why you neglected us'.

study.exegesisTip: Trace every 'better' in Hebrews (1:4; 6:9; 7:7, 19, 22; 8:6; 9:23; 10:34; 11:16, 35, 40; 12:24). Together they show the author's method: not that the old was bad, but that what God has now given in Christ surpasses it.

study.summary: λύπη is grief, sorrow or pain, chiefly of the mind and heart, the opposite of joy (χαρά).
