The NT speaks of the disciples' sorrow at Jesus' departure, Paul's anguish for Israel, the pain caused by discipline and rebuke, and Paul's key distinction between godly grief that leads to repentance and worldly grief that leads to death.

senses.label: Grief, sorrow of heart
senses.definition: Inner distress or sadness caused by loss, bad news or the suffering of others.
senses.note: In Luke 22:45 the disciples are asleep 'from sorrow', grief so heavy that it exhausts them.

senses.label: Sorrow turned to joy
senses.definition: In Jesus' farewell words, the present grief of the disciples at his going, which will be turned into a joy no one can take away, like the pain of childbirth forgotten after the child is born.

senses.label: Pain caused in relationships
senses.definition: The pain or distress given or received between people, as in Paul's painful visit, his painful letter, and the danger that a disciplined believer be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
senses.note: To come 'in sorrow' (2 Cor 2:1) means both to come sad and to bring sadness.

senses.label: Godly grief and worldly grief
senses.definition: Sorrow viewed by its direction and outcome: grief 'according to God' produces repentance leading to salvation, while the world's grief produces death.
senses.note: Paul does not praise sorrow as such; what matters is whether it turns a person to God.

senses.label: Reluctance; painful hardship
senses.definition: Grudging unwillingness ('out of grief') in giving, and the pains or hardships a believer endures, including the painfulness of discipline.
senses.note: In 1 Peter 2:19 the plural means 'sorrows, griefs': suffering unjustly while bearing it for conscience toward God.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Most uses are in 2 Corinthians, where the painful visit and letter, the restoration of the offender and the godly grief that leads to repentance are central to Paul's relationship with the church.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: All of John's uses fall in the Upper Room discourse, where λύπη is set against χαρά: the disciples' grief is real but temporary and will be transformed at Jesus' return to them.

study.translationNote: Some uses are rendered not with a noun but with phrases: 'a painful visit' (2 Cor 2:1), 'reluctantly' or 'grudgingly' (2 Cor 9:7, literally 'out of grief'), and 'sorrows' or 'unjust suffering' (1 Pet 2:19). The underlying idea in each case is pain or grief.

background.note: Aeschylus speaks of the 'sting of grief' that does not truly reach the heart of those who only feign sympathy; λύπη is pain of mind.
Xenophon sets λύπη in opposition to χαρά, joy, the same pairing Jesus uses in John 16.
A first-century letter-writer tells the recipient that if he forgets him, he will cause him endless grief.

study.exegesisTip: In 2 Corinthians 7:8-11 notice how the related verb λυπέω and the noun λύπη interweave: Paul's letter caused grief, but the grief was 'according to God' and produced repentance, earnestness and zeal. The passage is a key text for distinguishing remorse from repentance.

study.summary: νυμφίος is a bridegroom. Besides its literal use at the wedding in Cana and in the fall of Babylon, Jesus applies it to himself: his presence is a wedding feast at which fasting is out of place, and his return is the coming of the bridegroom for whom the wise virgins wait. John the Baptist calls Jesus the bridegroom and himself the bridegroom's friend.

senses.label: Bridegroom (literal)
senses.definition: A man about to be or newly married, the central figure of a wedding celebration.
senses.note: In Revelation 18:23 the silencing of the voice of bridegroom and bride echoes the prophetic judgment formula of Jeremiah (Jer 7:34; 16:9; 25:10): normal joyful life will end in the fallen city.

senses.label: Jesus as the present bridegroom
senses.definition: Jesus' self-description when asked why his disciples do not fast: while the bridegroom is with the wedding guests, it is a time of joy, but he will be 'taken away', and then they will fast.
senses.note: The saying about the bridegroom being 'taken away' is an early hint of Jesus' death.

senses.label: The coming bridegroom
senses.definition: In the parable of the ten virgins, the bridegroom whose arrival is delayed and comes at midnight, representing the Son of Man's return.

senses.label: The bridegroom and his friend
senses.definition: John the Baptist's image: the bride belongs to the bridegroom (Jesus), while the bridegroom's friend (John) rejoices to hear his voice and gladly gives way.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses the image both for Jesus' earthly ministry (no fasting while he is present) and for his future coming in the parable of the ten virgins, linking present joy with watchful readiness.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John the literal bridegroom at Cana (where Jesus supplies the wine the groom should have provided) is followed shortly by the Baptist's identification of Jesus as the true bridegroom.

background.note: Homer describes a father weeping as he burns the bones of his son, a bridegroom (newly married), at his funeral pyre.
In the Greek of Judges 15:6 the word means 'son-in-law', as the Hebrew חָתָן can denote both bridegroom and son-in-law.
An inscription of about 200 BC regulates the lambs that bridegrooms sacrifice and the portion owed to the priest, showing the bridegroom's ritual role in weddings.

study.exegesisTip: The Old Testament pictures God as Israel's husband and bridegroom (e.g. Isa 62:5; Hos 2:19-20). When Jesus calls himself 'the bridegroom', he takes up an image used of God himself, and the NT develops it into Christ and the church as bride (cf. Eph 5; Rev 19, 21).

study.summary: ξηραίνω means 'to dry up'. Actively it is to parch or wither something (the sun withering grass); in the passive it is to become dry, withered or shrivelled. The NT uses it of plants and trees, of a flow of blood or a river that dries up, of a paralysed 'withered' hand or a body becoming rigid, and of a harvest that is fully ripe.

senses.label: Wither (of plants)
senses.definition: Of seedlings, grass, flowers and branches drying up and dying for lack of root or moisture, or under scorching sun; often a picture of human frailty or fruitlessness.
senses.note: James and Peter both draw on Isaiah 40:6-8: human glory and wealth wither like grass, but the word of the Lord endures.

senses.label: Wither (of the fig tree)
senses.definition: Of the fig tree Jesus cursed, which dried up from the roots, an acted parable of judgment on fruitlessness.

senses.label: Dry up (of liquids)
senses.definition: Of a flow being stopped or water drying up: the woman's haemorrhage, and the Euphrates dried up to prepare the way for the kings of the east.

senses.label: Shrivelled, rigid (of the body)
senses.definition: Of a limb wasted or paralysed ('a withered hand'), or of the body becoming stiff in a seizure.
senses.note: Compare 1 Kings 13:4 (LXX), where Jeroboam's outstretched hand 'dried up'.

senses.label: Be ripe (of harvest)
senses.definition: Of grain fully dried and ready for harvest, in the vision of the earth's harvest.
senses.note: Here the drying is not decay but readiness: the harvest of the earth is 'ripe'.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark has the most uses and the widest range: the withered hand, scorched seed, the dried-up haemorrhage, the convulsed boy who 'becomes rigid', and the fig tree withered from the roots.

study.translationNote: Translations vary with the subject: 'withered' for plants and the hand, 'dried up' for the bleeding and the river, 'becomes rigid' or 'stiffens' for the boy in Mark 9:18, and 'ripe' for the harvest in Revelation 14:15. All are the same verb of drying.

background.note: A report of AD 316 about a persea tree describes it as barren for many years and quite dried up, unable to bear fruit, a close parallel to the withered fig tree.
A third-century instruction orders that cut plants be put into water at once so that they do not dry out.

study.exegesisTip: In John 15:6 the branch that does not remain in the vine 'is thrown out and withers': withering follows separation from the source of life, which is the point of the image.

study.summary: οἰκουμένη (literally 'the inhabited [earth]') means the inhabited world. In NT times it commonly denoted the Roman Empire as the civilized world, but it is also used of the whole inhabited earth and, by extension, of its inhabitants. Hebrews uses it once for 'the world to come'.

senses.label: The Roman world
senses.definition: The inhabited world as organized under Roman rule, the empire.
senses.note: Augustus' decree in Luke 2:1 concerns 'all the world' in the sense of the Roman Empire.

senses.label: The whole inhabited earth
senses.definition: The entire world where people live, as the scope of the gospel's proclamation, of end-time distress, or of Satan's kingdoms.

senses.label: The world's inhabitants
senses.definition: By metonymy, the people of the world: those whom the apostles 'turned upside down', who worship Artemis, whom God will judge, or whom Satan deceives.

senses.label: The world to come
senses.definition: The coming inhabited world of the messianic age, which God has subjected not to angels but to the Son and to redeemed humanity.
senses.note: Hebrews 2:5 refers back to 1:6, where God brings the firstborn 'into the inhabited world'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke, writing with an eye on the Roman setting, uses the word most, from Augustus' census and the famine under Claudius to accusations that Christians were stirring up the whole empire, and Paul's proclamation that God will judge the world.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the word for the world into which God brings his firstborn and for 'the world to come', a distinctive eschatological use.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'world', 'earth', 'Roman world' and 'empire'. In Luke 2:1 and Acts 11:28 some translations make the Roman reference explicit ('the entire Roman world'), while others keep 'the whole world'. The Greek word is not κόσμος and carries no moral overtone; it simply means the inhabited earth.

background.note: In Demosthenes the word means the Greek world as opposed to barbarian lands.
Aristotle uses it of the whole inhabited world, including non-Greek lands such as Ethiopia, India and Scythia.
The notice of Nero's accession (AD 54) calls him the expectation and hope of the world and 'the good genius of the world', showing the term's use for the empire in imperial propaganda.
Marcus Aurelius is honoured as benefactor and saviour of the whole inhabited world.

study.exegesisTip: Against a background in which emperors were hailed as saviours of the οἰκουμένη, NT claims that the gospel is preached to the whole inhabited world and that God has fixed a day to judge it by Jesus (Acts 17:31) carry a quiet challenge to imperial pretensions.
study.caution: Expressions such as 'the whole world' in Luke 2:1 and Acts 11:28 reflect ordinary usage for the Roman world and should not be pressed into claims of a literally global census or famine.

study.summary: οὐδέποτε is the adverb 'never, not ever'. It states emphatically that something has not happened, does not or will not happen at any time. In questions ('Have you never read ...?') it presses hearers with what they ought to know from Scripture.

senses.label: Never (past experience)
senses.definition: Denies that something has ever happened, often in expressions of astonishment ('we have never seen anything like this') or of personal history.
senses.note: In Acts 10:14 and 11:8 Peter insists he has never eaten anything common or unclean.

senses.label: Never (absolute denial or vow)
senses.definition: Strong denial covering all time: Jesus' 'I never knew you', Peter's vow never to fall away, love that never fails, sacrifices that can never perfect or take away sins.
senses.note: Hebrews 10:1 and 10:11 stress the permanent inability of repeated sacrifices to deal finally with sin.

senses.label: In rebuking questions
senses.definition: Introduces a question expecting the answer 'yes, we have': 'Have you never read ...?', pointing opponents to Scripture they should already know.

background.note: A letter of the third century BC complains, 'you have never listened to me'; the word appears to be rare in the papyri.

study.exegesisTip: In Matthew 7:23 'I never knew you' denies any genuine relationship at any time, even though the speakers claimed impressive deeds; the issue is not lapsed knowledge but its absence from the start.

study.summary: πάθημα (from πάσχω, 'to suffer, experience') means what one undergoes. In the NT it chiefly means suffering, especially the sufferings of Christ and those believers share with him, but Paul also uses it for 'passions', the impulses of sinful human nature. Once it describes the experience of suffering death.

senses.label: Sufferings of believers
senses.definition: Afflictions and hardships endured by Christians, especially for the gospel, which Scripture sets against the glory to come.

senses.label: The sufferings of Christ
senses.definition: The sufferings Christ endured, foretold by the prophets and followed by glory, and through which he was made perfect as the pioneer of salvation.
senses.note: 1 Peter 1:11 speaks of 'the sufferings destined for Christ and the glories after them'.

senses.label: Sharing Christ's sufferings
senses.definition: Believers' participation in Christ's sufferings, which overflow to them and are a fellowship with him that leads to sharing his glory.
senses.note: This is union with Christ, not an addition to his atoning work.

senses.label: Passions
senses.definition: Inner impulses or passions, specifically the sinful passions at work in fallen human nature, aroused by the law.
senses.note: In Galatians 5:24 'passions' stand alongside 'desires' as what belongs to the flesh that has been crucified.

senses.label: The suffering of death
senses.definition: The experience of undergoing death, as in Jesus being crowned with glory and honour because of 'the suffering of death'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word for both suffering and sinful passions. His suffering texts emphasize that Christ's sufferings 'overflow' into the believer's life and that sharing them is fellowship with Christ (2 Cor 1:5; Phil 3:10).

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter repeatedly pairs the sufferings of Christ with the glory that follows, encouraging suffering believers that the same pattern holds for them.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the word for Jesus' suffering of death, the sufferings by which he was perfected, and the believers' earlier 'great contest of sufferings'.

study.translationNote: Most versions render it 'suffering(s)', but in Romans 7:5 and Galatians 5:24 it is translated 'passions' or 'sinful passions'. The same Greek word covers what one suffers from outside and what one undergoes within, so English needs two different words.

background.note: Sophocles uses it of suffering or misfortune that befalls a person.
Antiphon contrasts involuntary misfortunes (παθήματα) with deliberate and premeditated wrongs, showing the word's sense of what one undergoes rather than does.

study.exegesisTip: In 2 Corinthians 1:5-7 and 1 Peter 4:13 sufferings and comfort, or sufferings and glory, are tied together: notice how the writer moves from sharing Christ's sufferings to sharing his comfort or joy.
study.caution: Colossians 1:24 ('I fill up what is lacking in Christ's afflictions') uses a different word (θλῖψις) for Christ's afflictions; the 'sufferings' Paul rejoices in there are his own. Interpreters differ on the phrase, but it should not be read as implying that Christ's atoning sufferings were insufficient.

study.summary: παρέχω means to hold out, offer, provide or cause. In the active it is to give or furnish something to someone, often with abstract objects ('cause trouble', 'give quiet', 'show kindness'), or to offer the other cheek. In the middle it means to provide from one's own means, or to present oneself as something.

senses.label: Cause trouble
senses.definition: In the idiom κόπους (κόπον) παρέχειν, 'to cause trouble, bother', of harassing someone.
senses.note: In Galatians 6:17 Paul asks that no one trouble him further, since he bears the marks of Jesus on his body.

senses.label: Provide, grant, give
senses.definition: To furnish or bestow something on someone, whether material provision, profit, kindness, quiet, or proof.
senses.note: In Acts 17:31 God 'has given assurance (proof) to all' by raising Jesus from the dead.

senses.label: Offer, present
senses.definition: To hold out or present something to someone, as in turning the other cheek to one who strikes.

senses.label: Provide of one's own part (middle)
senses.definition: In the middle voice, to grant or supply from oneself: a favour, business for craftsmen, or what is just and fair to slaves.

senses.label: Show oneself (middle)
senses.definition: With a reflexive pronoun and a predicate, to present or show oneself as something.
senses.note: Titus is to show himself 'a pattern of good works'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the verb most, for trouble given by persistent askers in Jesus' parables, and in Acts for what people furnish: profit from fortune-telling, business for silversmiths, quiet for Paul's speech, and the islanders' unusual kindness.

study.translationNote: Because the verb's meaning depends on its object, English renderings vary widely: 'bother', 'trouble', 'brought (profit)', 'gave (proof)', 'showed (kindness)', 'grant', 'turn (the other cheek)', 'set an example'. The common idea is presenting or providing something to someone.

background.note: A marriage contract of 311/310 BC stipulates that the husband shall provide his wife with all that is fitting for a freeborn woman.
A second-century letter uses the same idiom as the Gospels: someone 'causes troubles' (κόπους παρέχῃ) about a matter.
A woman declares in a petition that she 'showed herself completely blameless in every respect', the middle with reflexive sense found in Titus 2:7.
In Homer the verb means to furnish or supply, as in providing light for all.

study.exegesisTip: 1 Timothy 6:17 describes God as the one 'who richly provides us with everything to enjoy', which grounds Paul's warning to the rich: they are to trust the Giver rather than the gifts.

study.summary: περισσῶς is an adverb meaning 'exceedingly, beyond measure, all the more'. Its comparative form περισσοτέρως ('more abundantly, all the more, especially') is especially common in Paul. It intensifies emotions, effort or actions: crowds shouting all the louder, disciples utterly astonished, Paul's raging zeal as a persecutor and his abundant labours and love as an apostle.

senses.label: Exceedingly, beyond measure
senses.definition: Intensifies a verb: to an extreme degree, vehemently.
senses.note: In Acts 26:11 Paul describes himself as 'raging beyond measure' against believers before his conversion.

senses.label: All the more, even more (comparative)
senses.definition: The comparative περισσοτέρως: to a greater degree than before or than expected, 'all the more'.
senses.note: In Philippians 1:14 Paul's imprisonment makes the brothers dare all the more to speak the word without fear.

senses.label: Especially, more abundantly
senses.definition: Marks something as true in a special or greater measure: Paul's conduct especially toward the Corinthians, his abundant love and labours, his surpassing zeal for ancestral traditions.
senses.note: 2 Corinthians 12:15 contrasts loving 'more abundantly' with being loved 'less'.

senses.label: Pay closer attention
senses.definition: With verbs of attending, 'all the more carefully', as in the call to give greater heed to what has been heard.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the comparative form repeatedly, especially in 2 Corinthians, to express the overflowing measure of his love, labours, sufferings and joy, as well as his former excessive zeal for Judaism.

study.translationNote: English renderings depend heavily on context: 'exceedingly', 'all the louder', 'even more', 'especially', 'more abundantly', 'more earnestly'. The comparative περισσοτέρως sometimes carries a true comparison ('more than before') and sometimes is simply intensive ('very much'), which is why translations differ.

background.note: In an early second-century letter the adverb means 'superfluously': 'it was unnecessary for you to write to me about the labourers' wages'.
In another second-century text it has the sense 'exceedingly', as in Acts 26:11.

study.exegesisTip: In the Passion narratives the crowd 'cried out all the more' (Matt 27:23; Mark 15:14) in response to Pilate's question 'What evil has he done?': the adverb heightens the irrationality of the demand for crucifixion.

study.summary: πέτρα is rock: bedrock, a rocky mass or cliff, as distinct from a loose stone. It is the solid foundation for the wise builder's house, the rock from which tombs were cut, the rocky ground of the parable, and the rocks that split at Jesus' death. Figuratively it is the rock on which Christ builds his church, the spiritual rock that was Christ, and the 'rock of offence' over which unbelievers stumble.

senses.label: Bedrock as foundation
senses.definition: Solid rock on which a house is founded, so that storms and floods cannot shake it.

senses.label: Rock mass, cliff, rocky ground
senses.definition: Natural rock: the rock from which tombs were hewn, rocks split in the earthquake, rocky ground with shallow soil, and the rocks of the mountains among which people hide.
senses.note: In Revelation 6:15-16 the rocks and caves recall Isaiah 2:10, 19 and Hosea 10:8.

senses.label: The rock on which the church is built
senses.definition: Jesus' wordplay on Peter's name (Πέτρος): 'on this rock I will build my church'.

senses.label: Christ the spiritual rock
senses.definition: The rock from which Israel drank in the wilderness, identified by Paul as Christ, the source of their spiritual drink.
senses.note: Paul draws on the water-from-the-rock accounts (Exod 17:6; Num 20:8-11).

senses.label: Rock of offence
senses.definition: From Isaiah 8:14: Christ as a rock over which those who do not believe stumble and fall.
senses.note: Both Paul and Peter combine Isaiah 8:14 with Isaiah 28:16.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew frames Jesus' ministry with rock imagery: the wise builder on the rock, the church built on 'this rock', and the rocks that split and the rock-cut tomb at his death and burial.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul reads OT rock texts christologically: Christ was the rock in the wilderness, and Christ is the stumbling rock laid in Zion.

background.note: In the Greek Old Testament πέτρα often renders Hebrew צוּר and סֶלַע, words used both for literal rock and, in the Psalms and Deuteronomy, for God as Israel's Rock.
Homer uses πέτρη of a smooth, steep cliff running into the sea.
A third-century BC report speaks of quarrying royal stones 'from the rock', the same idea as tombs hewn out of rock.
A magical text says that at the hearing of the divine name the rocks burst, a vivid parallel to the rocks split at Jesus' death.

study.exegesisTip: In Matthew 16:18 note the shift from Πέτρος (Peter) to πέτρα (rock). The wordplay is clear, but the identity of 'this rock' must be decided from the context of Peter's confession in 16:16.
study.caution: Interpreters disagree on Matthew 16:18: 'this rock' has been taken as Peter himself (as confessing apostle), as Peter's confession of Jesus as the Christ, or as Christ himself. The distinction sometimes drawn between πέτρος ('stone') and πέτρα ('rock') should not be pressed, since Jesus likely spoke Aramaic, where one word (kepha) would serve for both.

study.summary: πλησίον is an adverb meaning 'near'; with the article (ὁ πλησίον) it becomes a noun, 'the one near', i.e. one's neighbour or fellow human being. Almost every NT use goes back to Leviticus 19:18, 'You shall love your neighbour as yourself', which Jesus, Paul and James all treat as the summary of the law's demands toward others.

senses.label: Near, close by (adverb)
senses.definition: Used as a simple adverb of place with a genitive: 'near' something.
senses.note: The only NT instance of the purely local sense: Sychar lay near the field Jacob gave Joseph.

senses.label: Neighbour in the love command
senses.definition: ὁ πλησίον as the object of the command 'love your neighbour as yourself' (Lev 19:18), the other person toward whom covenant love is owed.
senses.note: Jesus pairs it with the command to love God (Deut 6:5) as the second great commandment; Paul and James cite it alone as the sum or 'royal law' of the law.

senses.label: Neighbour redefined: whoever is in need
senses.definition: In the parable of the Good Samaritan the question 'who is my neighbour?' is turned around: the neighbour is not a category of people one must love but the one who acts as neighbour to the person in need.
senses.note: The lawyer asks whom he must count as neighbour; Jesus asks who 'became a neighbour' (πλησίον γεγονέναι) to the wounded man.

senses.label: Fellow person, the other
senses.definition: More generally, the fellow human being or fellow member of the community with whom one lives and whom one may wrong or build up.
senses.note: In Ephesians the neighbour is a fellow believer: 'we are members of one another'.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew alone quotes the popular addition 'and hate your enemy' as a foil, and Jesus answers by extending love to enemies; he also adds the love command to the list of commandments given to the rich young man.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke attaches the love command to the parable of the Good Samaritan, so that 'neighbour' is defined by merciful action across ethnic lines rather than by kinship or nation.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: For Paul the love command is the fulfilment (πλήρωμα) of the whole law; love of neighbour shows itself in building up others rather than pleasing oneself.

study.translationNote: Greek has no separate noun here: 'neighbour' is literally 'the one near'. English 'neighbour' suggests someone living next door, but in Leviticus the Hebrew rea' means a fellow Israelite or fellow person, and Jesus widens it further. In John 4:5 the same word is simply 'near'.

background.note: In the Greek Old Testament ὁ πλησίον chiefly renders Hebrew rea', 'fellow, companion', and the command to love one's neighbour as oneself is quoted from Leviticus 19:18.
In the papyri the adverb is used of physical nearness, as in a second-century will speaking of something 'near my tomb'.

study.exegesisTip: Watch the turn in LUK 10:29 and 10:36: the lawyer treats 'neighbour' as the object he must love (whom?), while Jesus makes it the role the Samaritan takes up (who became a neighbour?). The definition shifts from boundary to behaviour.
study.caution: Do not read 'neighbour' as limited to people physically nearby or to fellow believers only; context decides, and in the Gospels Jesus pointedly removes such limits.

study.summary: ποταμός is a river or stream, and also a torrent of flood water. In the NT it names the Jordan and the river at Philippi, the flood that strikes a house in Jesus' parable, the perils of travel, and in Revelation both the rivers of the earth under judgment and the river of the water of life; Jesus uses it figuratively of the Spirit flowing from the believer.

senses.label: A river
senses.definition: A natural flowing body of water, such as the Jordan, the river outside Philippi, or the Euphrates.
senses.note: Paul's 'dangers from rivers' recalls unbridged rivers in flood on his journeys.

senses.label: Flood torrent
senses.definition: A rushing torrent of water produced by storm or flood, which tests a building's foundation.
senses.note: Matthew has the 'rivers' come after the rain; Luke speaks of a flood (πλημμύρα) in which the river bursts against the house.

senses.label: Rivers in visionary judgment
senses.definition: In Revelation, the earth's rivers struck by trumpet and bowl judgments, and the river of water the dragon pours out to sweep away the woman.

senses.label: River of life (figurative)
senses.definition: Figurative streams of living water: the life-giving Spirit flowing from the believer, and the river of the water of life flowing from God's throne in the new Jerusalem.
senses.note: John 7:39 explains that Jesus spoke of the Spirit; the imagery draws on Ezekiel 47 and Zechariah 14:8.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Most NT uses are Johannine. The Gospel and Revelation share the image of life-giving water: rivers of living water in John 7:38 and the river of the water of life in Revelation 22, framing salvation as a new Eden whose river waters the tree of life.

study.translationNote: Translations vary between 'river', 'stream', 'flood' and 'torrent'. In MAT 7:25 and LUK 6:48 the point is a sudden flash flood, so 'torrent' or 'flood' conveys it better than a placid 'river'.

background.note: From Homer on the word means river or stream, with many descriptive epithets; LSJ cites the line calling Ocean the source from which all rivers flow.
In the Greek Old Testament it renders Hebrew nahar (river, often the Euphrates) and ye'or (the Nile).
In Egyptian documents 'the river' regularly means the Nile, as in a third-century BC text dated 'at the falling of the river'; inscriptions also apply the word to man-made canals.

study.exegesisTip: In JOH 7:38 the phrase 'out of his belly' is ambiguous: it may refer to the believer or (with different punctuation of 7:37-38) to Christ as the source. Either way, 7:39 identifies the rivers as the Spirit.
study.caution: The punctuation of JOH 7:37-38, and so whose 'belly' the rivers flow from, is debated among interpreters; and no single OT verse matches the 'Scripture' Jesus cites.

study.summary: προσδοκάω means to expect, look for, or wait for something or someone, whether in hope, uncertainty or fear. It is a favourite of Luke, who uses it for people waiting on Zechariah, on Jesus, or on the Messiah; Peter uses it for the Christian's eager expectation of the day of God and the new heavens and earth.

senses.label: Wait for a person
senses.definition: To wait for someone's arrival or appearance, sometimes with growing puzzlement or eagerness.
senses.note: In ACT 27:33 the sailors have spent fourteen days 'waiting' in suspense without eating.

senses.label: Look for the coming one (messianic)
senses.definition: To expect the promised deliverer: whether Jesus is 'the one who is to come' or whether they should look for another.
senses.note: LUK 3:15 shows the people 'in expectation', wondering whether John might be the Christ.

senses.label: Expect an outcome
senses.definition: To anticipate that something will happen, with an infinitive or accusative-and-infinitive: expecting to receive alms, or expecting a man to swell up and die.
senses.note: In ACT 28:6 the Maltese expected Paul to fall dead from the snakebite; when he did not, they changed their minds.

senses.label: Unexpected day of reckoning
senses.definition: In the parable of the servant, the master returns 'on a day he does not expect', catching the unfaithful servant off guard.

senses.label: Eager hope for the day of God
senses.definition: The believer's forward-looking expectation of the coming of the day of God and of new heavens and a new earth, which shapes holy living now.
senses.note: Paired with 'hastening' (σπεύδοντας) in 2PE 3:12, it is active, not passive, waiting.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the verb far more than any other writer, for the atmosphere of expectancy that surrounds the coming of salvation: the people waiting for Zechariah, wondering about John, waiting for Jesus to return across the lake.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: In 2 Peter the threefold use frames the ethical appeal: because believers look for the day of God and a new world where righteousness dwells, they should be found spotless and at peace.

study.translationNote: English versions use 'look for', 'wait for', 'expect' and 'anticipate' for the same verb. The Greek covers both the mental expectation and the act of waiting; context decides whether hope, suspense or dread is uppermost.

background.note: Classical writers use it for expectation whether in hope or fear, mostly with a future infinitive, e.g. in Herodotus.
A papyrus announcing Nero's accession describes the emperor as the one 'expected and hoped for' by the world, showing the word's use for longed-for deliverers.

study.exegesisTip: Compare MAT 11:3 with 2PE 3:12: the same verb describes John's uncertain question whether Jesus is the expected one, and the church's confident expectation of his final coming.

study.summary: σκοτία is a later Greek equivalent of σκότος, 'darkness'. It can mean literal darkness, the obscurity of private speech, and above all, in John's writings, the realm of ignorance, sin and alienation from God that stands opposed to the light revealed in Christ.

senses.label: Physical darkness
senses.definition: Literal darkness, the absence of daylight.
senses.note: Even these literal notes in John may carry symbolic overtones: the disciples on the lake before Jesus comes; Mary at the tomb 'while it was still dark'.

senses.label: Secrecy, private speech
senses.definition: 'In the dark' as the setting of private or hidden speech, contrasted with public proclamation 'in the light'.
senses.note: In Matthew, private teaching is to be proclaimed openly; in Luke, hidden words will be exposed.

senses.label: Spiritual and moral darkness
senses.definition: The sphere of ignorance, sin and death in which humanity lives apart from God's revelation, opposed to the light of Christ.
senses.note: Following Jesus means not walking in darkness; the darkness did not overcome (or grasp) the light.

senses.label: Darkness as a way of life opposed to love
senses.definition: In 1 John, darkness is incompatible with the God who is light and characterises the person who hates his brother.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Nearly all NT uses are Johannine, where light and darkness form a sharp moral and spiritual dualism. The darkness is passing away as the true light already shines (1JO 2:8); walking in it shows itself in hatred of one's brother.

study.translationNote: In JOH 1:5 the verb κατέλαβεν can mean 'overcome/seize' or 'comprehend/grasp', so versions differ: 'the darkness has not overcome it' versus 'the darkness comprehended it not'. The noun itself is consistently 'darkness' or 'dark'.

background.note: The word is rare in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Micah's announcement that darkness will come on the false prophets.

study.exegesisTip: John's literal references to darkness (JOH 6:17; 20:1) sit inside a Gospel that uses darkness symbolically; ask whether the narrative detail also signals the disciples' spiritual state.
study.caution: The meaning of κατέλαβεν in JOH 1:5 ('overcome' or 'understand') is genuinely debated; some think John intends both.

study.summary: συκῆ is the fig tree, a common tree of Palestine and a familiar OT symbol of Israel and of peaceful prosperity. In the NT it features in Jesus' cursing of the barren fig tree, the parable of the unfruitful fig tree, the lesson of the budding fig tree as a sign of the end, Nathanael 'under the fig tree', and as an image of fruit consistent with its nature.

senses.label: Fig tree (literal and illustrative)
senses.definition: The fig tree as a plant, used in illustrations from nature: a tree produces fruit according to its kind.
senses.note: Under one's fig tree was a proverbial picture of rest and security (Mic 4:4); some see it as a place of study or prayer for Nathanael.

senses.label: The barren fig tree: judgment
senses.definition: A fig tree with leaves but no fruit, cursed by Jesus and withering, acted out as a sign of judgment on fruitless religion, especially in its link with the temple incident.
senses.note: Mark sandwiches the temple cleansing between the cursing and the discovery of the withered tree.

senses.label: Parable of the unfruitful fig tree
senses.definition: A fig tree that has borne no fruit for three years, given one more year of care before being cut down: a picture of God's patience and of the urgency of repentance.

senses.label: The budding fig tree: sign of nearness
senses.definition: The fig tree putting out leaves signals that summer is near; so the signs Jesus describes show that the end is near.
senses.note: Luke adds 'and all the trees'.

senses.label: Image of cosmic collapse
senses.definition: Stars falling from heaven like unripe figs shaken from a tree by a gale.
senses.note: Echoes Isaiah 34:4.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark notes that 'it was not the season for figs' and frames the temple action with the cursing and withering, inviting readers to see the tree as an acted parable about the temple.

background.note: In the Greek Old Testament it renders Hebrew te'enah, the fig tree, a staple of the promised land.
A third-century BC letter asks for branches of fig trees to be sent, showing the fig as an everyday cultivated tree.

study.exegesisTip: Read the cursing of the fig tree in light of OT passages where Israel is a fig tree or vine expected to bear fruit (e.g. Jer 8:13; Hos 9:10; Mic 7:1); Mark's sandwich structure with the temple makes this connection explicit.
study.caution: Whether the fig tree in the Gospels symbolises Israel as a whole, its leadership, or the temple specifically is debated; avoid pressing every fig-tree text into one allegory.

study.summary: συλλαμβάνω, literally 'take together', has three distinct NT meanings: to seize or arrest someone, to catch (fish); to conceive a child (and figuratively, desire conceiving sin); and, in the middle voice with a dative, to take hold together with someone, i.e. to help.

senses.label: Seize, arrest
senses.definition: To lay hold of a person as a prisoner.
senses.note: Used across all four Gospels of the arrest of Jesus.

senses.label: Seized (by officials or a mob)
senses.definition: Passive or middle uses of a person being taken into custody.
senses.note: Lysias reports Paul was 'seized by the Jews'; Paul himself says the Jews seized him in the temple.

senses.label: Catch (fish)
senses.definition: To take a catch of fish.

senses.label: Conceive
senses.definition: Of a woman becoming pregnant.
senses.note: Luke uses it of both Elizabeth and Mary.

senses.label: Conceive (figurative)
senses.definition: Desire is personified as a woman who conceives and gives birth to sin, which in turn brings forth death.

senses.label: Help, assist
senses.definition: Middle with dative: to take hold together with someone, to come to their aid.
senses.note: Paul asks his 'true companion' to help Euodia and Syntyche.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses every sense of the verb: conception in the infancy narrative, catching fish and helping partners in the miraculous catch, and arrest in the passion and in Acts.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James turns the language of conception into a moral genealogy: desire conceives, gives birth to sin, and sin when full-grown brings forth death.

study.translationNote: Because one verb covers 'arrest', 'conceive' and 'help', English versions necessarily translate it very differently; the sense is fixed by construction (accusative of a person = seize; of a woman, absolute or with 'in the womb' = conceive; middle with dative = help).

background.note: In classical Greek it means to collect or gather together, especially to rally scattered troops.
In the Greek Old Testament it renders both Hebrew harah, 'conceive', and taphas, 'seize', as already at Genesis 4:1.
In the papyri it is a common word for arrest: an official is commended for arresting a steward of a beer-house.
It also means help: a letter asks a friend to assist someone named Apis.

study.exegesisTip: In JAM 1:14-15 follow the birth imagery step by step (enticed, conceived, gives birth, full-grown, brings forth death); it contrasts with 1:18, where God 'brought us forth' by the word of truth.

study.summary: συνιστάω (a later form of συνίστημι), literally 'set together', has two groups of meanings. Transitively it means to introduce or commend someone, and to demonstrate or prove something; intransitively it means to stand with someone, or to hold together, cohere. Paul uses it especially in 2 Corinthians for the debate over 'commending oneself'.

senses.label: Commend, recommend
senses.definition: To introduce a person favourably, vouching for them, as in letters of recommendation.
senses.note: ROM 16:1 is a typical letter of introduction for Phoebe.

senses.label: Show oneself to be, prove
senses.definition: To demonstrate by conduct what one is; 'commend ourselves as servants of God' by endurance, or prove oneself a transgressor.
senses.note: In 2CO 6:4 Paul commends himself not by claims but by hardships endured.

senses.label: Demonstrate, make evident
senses.definition: To bring out clearly or prove a truth or quality.
senses.note: God 'demonstrates' his love in that Christ died for sinners.

senses.label: Stand with (intransitive)
senses.definition: To stand beside someone.
senses.note: Moses and Elijah standing with Jesus at the transfiguration.

senses.label: Hold together, consist (intransitive)
senses.definition: To hold together, cohere, or be formed out of something.
senses.note: In COL 1:17 all things hold together in Christ; in 2PE 3:5 the earth was formed out of water and through water.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In 2 Corinthians 'commending oneself' is a running theme: rivals commend themselves and bring letters of recommendation, while Paul refuses self-praise and points to his converts, his open proclamation of truth, his sufferings, and the Lord's commendation.

study.translationNote: The same verb is rendered 'commend', 'prove', 'show', 'demonstrate', 'stand with' and 'hold together'. In 2 Corinthians English versions vary between 'commend ourselves' and 'recommend ourselves'; in ROM 5:8 between 'commends' (older) and 'demonstrates/proves' (modern), the latter capturing the sense better.

background.note: A common papyrus use is 'introduce, recommend': a writer asks the recipient to hold a man 'as recommended', paralleling Romans 16:1.
A writer is confident he will easily be introduced to the king, showing the sense 'introduce'.
The intransitive 'stand with' appears in a legal formula for someone acting with another, as when a husband assisted his wife.

study.exegesisTip: In 2 Corinthians trace who is commending whom: self-commendation (3:1; 5:12; 10:12, 18) is contrasted with legitimate commendation through conduct (4:2; 6:4) and the Lord's commendation (10:18).
study.caution: Some editions treat these forms under the lemma συνίστημι rather than συνιστάω; they are the same verb.

study.summary: σφραγίς is a seal: the signet that makes an impression, or the impression itself. Seals closed documents, marked ownership and authenticated. In the NT it is used literally of the seven seals on the scroll in Revelation and God's seal on his servants, and figuratively of something that confirms or authenticates, such as circumcision for Abraham's faith or the Corinthians for Paul's apostleship.

senses.label: Signet, seal instrument
senses.definition: The instrument used to make a seal impression, here 'the seal of the living God' with which his servants are marked.

senses.label: Seal on a scroll
senses.definition: The impression closing a document, which must be broken to open it; the seven seals that only the Lamb is worthy to open.
senses.note: Each opening of a seal releases a stage of the visionary judgments.

senses.label: Mark of ownership and protection
senses.definition: God's seal placed on the foreheads of his servants, marking them as his and protecting them from judgment.

senses.label: Confirmation, authentication (figurative)
senses.definition: That which confirms or certifies the genuineness of something.
senses.note: Circumcision sealed the righteousness Abraham already had by faith; the Corinthians' existence as believers validates Paul's apostleship; God's foundation bears an inscription as its seal.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In Revelation the seven seals structure the unfolding judgments of chapters 6-8, and God's seal on his servants (7:2-3; 9:4) marks those he protects, in contrast to the mark of the beast.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word only figuratively, for something that attests or validates: circumcision for Abraham, the Corinthian church for his apostleship, an inscription on God's foundation.

background.note: In classical Greek it is a seal or signet, already in Herodotus, who notes that Babylonians each carried a seal.
A will deposited 'under seals' is returned 'with the seals intact', illustrating seals that close and protect documents.
The Gospel of Peter says they smeared seven seals on Jesus' tomb, an image echoing the seven-sealed scroll of Revelation.

study.exegesisTip: In ROM 4:11 note the order: Abraham was counted righteous before circumcision, so the 'seal' confirms an existing righteousness rather than creating it.
study.caution: Later Christian writers used 'seal' for baptism; that usage should not be read back automatically into NT texts where the word itself does not refer to baptism.

study.summary: τέρας is a wonder, portent or prodigy: an extraordinary event that astonishes and signals something beyond itself. In the NT it is always plural and almost always paired with σημεῖα, 'signs', in the phrase 'signs and wonders', which recalls God's deeds at the Exodus and describes the works of Jesus, the apostles, and also the deceptive works of false messiahs and the lawless one.

senses.label: God's wonders in redemption history
senses.definition: Extraordinary acts of God, especially the wonders done through Moses in Egypt, and cosmic portents of the last days.
senses.note: ACT 2:19 quotes Joel's 'wonders in the heavens above'.

senses.label: Wonders attesting Jesus and the apostles
senses.definition: Miraculous acts by which God accredited Jesus and confirmed the apostolic message.
senses.note: Paul counts signs and wonders among the marks of an apostle (2CO 12:12).

senses.label: Wonders demanded as proof
senses.definition: Spectacular signs sought as a condition of faith, which Jesus rebukes.
senses.note: The only Johannine use; elsewhere John prefers 'signs' alone.

senses.label: Deceptive wonders
senses.definition: Counterfeit wonders done by false christs, false prophets and the lawless one to lead people astray.
senses.note: In 2TH 2:9 they are 'wonders of falsehood'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Over half the NT uses are in Acts, where 'signs and wonders' link Jesus and the apostles with Moses and the Exodus and show God confirming the word of his grace.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul acknowledges signs and wonders in his own ministry but warns that the lawless one will also work them; wonders alone do not prove truth.

study.translationNote: 'Wonders' is the standard rendering. The word stresses the astonishing, portentous character of an event, while σημεῖον stresses its meaning as a pointer and δύναμις the power behind it; together they describe one reality from different angles.

background.note: In the Greek Old Testament it chiefly renders Hebrew mophet, and 'signs and wonders' is a fixed phrase for God's acts in bringing Israel out of Egypt (e.g. Deut 26:8).
Homer uses the word for portents and omens sent by the gods, as in the Odyssey when the gods showed prodigies to Odysseus' men.

study.exegesisTip: Whenever the word appears, look for its partner σημεῖα and ask what the wonder points to: in Acts, to God's attestation of Jesus; in Mark 13 and 2 Thessalonians 2, to deception that must be discerned.

study.summary: τολμάω means to dare, venture, or have the courage to do something; it can be positive (courageous boldness) or negative (presumption, audacity), and once means to bring oneself to endure something. In the Gospels it often appears negatively: after Jesus' answers, no one dared to question him further.

senses.label: Dare (not dare), venture
senses.definition: With an infinitive, to have the nerve to do something, frequently negated: no one dared.
senses.note: In JOH 21:12 the disciples did not dare ask who he was because they knew it was the Lord.

senses.label: Take courage, act boldly
senses.definition: To summon courage and act, a positive boldness.
senses.note: Joseph of Arimathea 'took courage' and went to Pilate for Jesus' body.

senses.label: Presume, have the audacity
senses.definition: To venture to do what one has no right to, presumption or impudence.
senses.note: In JUD 1:9 even Michael did not presume to pronounce a slanderous judgment on the devil.

senses.label: Be bold against opponents
senses.definition: With ἐπί, to show boldness toward someone in confrontation.

senses.label: Bring oneself to, endure
senses.definition: To bring oneself to face something hard, here even to die for a good person.
senses.note: Someone might perhaps 'dare' to die for a good man.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb in his boasting debates: he will not 'dare' to class himself with self-commenders or speak of anything but what Christ has done, yet ironically 'dares' to boast as his opponents do.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'dare', 'presume', 'be bold' and 'take courage' because the verb can carry either admiration or disapproval; the context, not the word, decides which.

background.note: In Homer it means to bring oneself to do or bear something difficult, as when the heart 'dared' in the face of danger.
In papyrus petitions it often describes audacious wrongdoing: an intruder 'dared to carry off my slave'.

study.exegesisTip: In ROM 5:7-8 the verb highlights how rare human self-sacrifice is: someone may scarcely 'dare' to die for a good person, but God demonstrates his love in Christ dying for sinners.

study.summary: τροφή is the ordinary word for food or nourishment, from τρέφω, 'to feed, nourish'. In the NT it covers everyday food and daily sustenance, the meal that restores bodily strength, the keep a worker or servant is owed, and, in Hebrews, the 'solid food' of mature teaching.

senses.label: Food, daily sustenance
senses.definition: What people eat to live; the basic necessity of life alongside clothing, often with emphasis on its ordinariness or its lack.
senses.note: In Matthew 6:25 and Luke 12:23 Jesus sets 'food' beside clothing as the things anxiety fixes on, insisting that life is more than either. James 2:15 speaks of lacking 'daily food', the bare minimum.

senses.label: Taking food, a meal that restores strength
senses.definition: Food actually eaten, especially after fasting or hardship, so that strength returns; also a shared meal.
senses.note: Saul regains strength after his three-day fast (Acts 9:19); in the storm Paul urges the despairing crew to take food 'for your survival' (Acts 27:34). In Acts 2:46 the believers 'shared food' with gladness in their homes.

senses.label: Keep, maintenance owed to a worker
senses.definition: The provision of food that a labourer earns or that a household steward distributes to those in his charge.
senses.note: 'The worker is worthy of his food' (Matthew 10:10) treats food as the missionary's rightful wage; the faithful servant gives the household 'their food at the proper time' (Matthew 24:45).

senses.label: Solid food (metaphor for mature teaching)
senses.definition: Figuratively, the substantial instruction suited to spiritually mature believers, contrasted with the 'milk' of elementary teaching.
senses.note: Hebrews defines who can take solid food: those whose faculties have been trained by practice to distinguish good from evil (5:14).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Half the NT uses are Luke's, and Acts in particular links food with recovery and community: Saul strengthened after his conversion, the church eating together with joy, God's kindness in giving food and gladness to the nations, and the shipwreck meal that revives the crew.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews alone uses the word figuratively, rebuking hearers who should be teachers but still need milk instead of 'solid food'.

study.translationNote: Older English versions often render τροφή as 'meat', which in 1611 meant food in general, not flesh. Modern versions rightly say 'food'; 'meat' in Hebrews 5:12 (KJV 'strong meat') means 'solid food'.

background.note: Thucydides speaks of 'the necessary daily food' (ἡ καθ' ἡμέραν ἀναγκαία τροφή), the same idea as James's 'daily food'.
In the papyri τροφή is everyday fodder and provisions, e.g. a complaint that 'we have not so much as food for our cattle'.
A later papyrus uses the plural for means of support: on her daughter's death a woman says she was deprived of her maintenance, showing the sense of livelihood seen in Matthew 10:10.

study.exegesisTip: Watch the contrast pairs: food and clothing (Matthew 6:25; James 2:15), milk and solid food (Hebrews 5:12). The word itself is plain; the point lies in what it is set against.

study.summary: τύπος (from τύπτω, 'to strike') began as the mark left by a blow, then the impression made by a seal or die, and so came to mean an image, a pattern or model, and an example. In the NT it ranges from the literal nail marks in Jesus' hands to idols, the heavenly pattern of the tabernacle, moral examples for believers to imitate, and persons or events that prefigure what was to come (whence English 'type').

senses.label: Mark, imprint
senses.definition: The visible mark left by a blow or pressure.
senses.note: Thomas demands to see 'the mark of the nails' in Jesus' hands, the word's root meaning.

senses.label: Image, figure (idol)
senses.definition: A shaped figure or statue; in context, idols made for worship.
senses.note: Stephen, quoting Amos, calls the images Israel carried in the wilderness 'the figures you made to worship'.

senses.label: Pattern, model, design
senses.definition: The original or plan according to which something is made; by extension, the form or content of a document or of teaching.
senses.note: Moses built the tabernacle 'according to the pattern' shown him (Acts 7:44; Hebrews 8:5). Paul's 'form of teaching' (Romans 6:17) is a mould into which believers were handed over. Acts 23:25 refers to a letter 'of this form', i.e. with this content.

senses.label: Example to imitate
senses.definition: A person whose conduct serves as a model for others to follow.
senses.note: Leaders are to be patterns for the flock, and whole congregations (the Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians 1:7) can become examples to others.

senses.label: Warning example; prefiguring type
senses.definition: Past persons or events that serve as an instructive pattern for later readers, either as a warning or as an advance sketch of something to come.
senses.note: Israel's wilderness failures happened 'as examples for us' (1 Corinthians 10:6, 11). Adam is 'a type of the one who was to come' (Romans 5:14): one man whose act determines the destiny of many, anticipating Christ by both likeness and contrast.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word most, in two main ways: ethically, presenting himself and his churches as patterns to imitate; and in reading Scripture, treating Adam and the wilderness generation as patterns that bear on the present age.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews quotes the tabernacle instruction to argue that the earthly sanctuary was only a copy of the heavenly reality, so that the 'pattern' points beyond itself.

study.translationNote: Versions render τύπος variously as 'example', 'pattern', 'figure', 'type', 'form' or 'model'. The choice depends on context: a moral model (1 Timothy 4:12) is an 'example', the tabernacle blueprint is a 'pattern', and Adam in Romans 5:14 is variously 'figure', 'type' or 'pattern'.

background.note: Euripides uses τύποι of the impressions of a golden signet ring, the seal-impression sense from which 'pattern' develops.
In Exodus God tells Moses to make the tabernacle furnishings according to the τύπος shown him on the mountain; Acts 7:44 and Hebrews 8:5 echo this.
Business papyri use τύπος for a manufacturing pattern: pots 'of the aforesaid pattern'.
A royal inscription speaks of setting out a 'pattern of piety' for one's descendants, close to the ethical use in 1 Timothy 4:12.

study.exegesisTip: Ask what the τύπος is a pattern of and for whom: a mould that shapes (Romans 6:17), a model to copy (Philippians 3:17), or an earlier figure that anticipates a later fulfilment (Romans 5:14). These are related but not interchangeable.
study.caution: The later theological category 'typology' builds on Romans 5:14 and 1 Corinthians 10, but the NT word itself is broader and usually means simply 'example' or 'pattern'. Not every occurrence implies a divinely intended foreshadowing.

study.summary: ἀνά is the rarest preposition in the NT. Its old sense 'up' survives mainly in compound verbs; on its own it appears in a few fixed uses: distributively ('apiece, each, by'), in the phrase ἀνὰ μέσον ('in the midst of, between'), and in ἀνὰ μέρος ('in turn').

senses.label: Distributive: apiece, each, by
senses.definition: With numbers, it marks an amount assigned to each member of a group or the size of each group.
senses.note: The labourers each receive a denarius; the crowds sit in groups of fifty; the disciples are sent 'two by two'; each stone jar holds two or three measures; each living creature has six wings.

senses.label: ἀνὰ μέσον: among, between, in the midst of
senses.definition: A compound preposition with the genitive, marking position within or between things or people.
senses.note: The enemy sows weeds 'among' the wheat; Paul asks whether there is no one wise enough to judge 'between' brothers; the Lamb 'in the midst of' the throne will shepherd his people.

senses.label: ἀνὰ μέρος: in turn
senses.definition: One after another, by turns.
senses.note: Those speaking in tongues are to do so two or at most three, and 'in turn', not all at once.

senses.label: Adverbial 'each' (ἀνὰ εἷς ἕκαστος)
senses.definition: Used loosely as an adverb reinforcing 'each one'.
senses.note: 'Each one of the gates was of a single pearl.' Grammarians regard this as a colloquial idiom.

study.translationNote: Because ἀνά is distributive, English often renders it with 'each', 'apiece' or 'by' (e.g. 'two by two'), or leaves it untranslated. Where manuscripts include ἀνά in Luke 9:3 ('not two tunics apiece'), it makes clear that each disciple is not to take a spare.

background.note: Property documents use ἀνὰ μέσον for a boundary 'between' one wall and another, showing the phrase was everyday Koine.
Sales record prices with distributive ἀνά, e.g. goods sold 'at five drachmae apiece'.

study.exegesisTip: When you meet ἀνά with a number, read it as a rate or group size ('each', 'by'), not as direction. Its old meaning 'up' lives on in compounds such as ἀναβαίνω ('go up') and ἀναγεννάω ('beget again').
study.caution: The phrase in 1 Corinthians 6:5, literally 'to judge between his brother', is grammatically awkward and has been discussed as a compressed or even corrupt expression; the general sense, settling a dispute between believers, is clear.

study.summary: ἀνακεῖμαι originally meant 'to be laid up' or 'dedicated', but in NT times it chiefly means 'to recline', especially at a meal, following the custom of lying on couches at formal dinners. The participle 'those reclining' therefore means 'the guests' or 'those at table'.

senses.label: Recline at table, dine
senses.definition: To be in the reclining position used for meals, especially festive or formal ones; hence, to be dining.
senses.note: Reclining explains scenes such as the woman anointing Jesus' head or feet as he lay at table, and the beloved disciple 'reclining at Jesus' side' at the Last Supper (John 13:23).

senses.label: Those reclining: guests, fellow diners
senses.definition: As a substantive participle, the people at a meal, the guests.
senses.note: In the wedding parable the king comes in 'to see the guests' (Matthew 22:11); Herod would not break his oath 'because of his guests' (Mark 6:26).

senses.label: Seated (of a crowd at a meal)
senses.definition: Of the crowd fed in the wilderness, those seated or reclining on the ground to eat.
senses.note: The posture of a meal is applied to an outdoor crowd.

senses.label: Lie, be laid
senses.definition: To lie, of a body or person laid down.
senses.note: In many manuscripts of Mark 5:40 Jesus goes in where the dead child 'was lying'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the dining posture to make a point about rank: the one reclining at table is normally the greater, yet Jesus says he is among them as the one who serves.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's picture of the beloved disciple reclining close to Jesus at the Last Supper depends on the reclining arrangement, in which a guest lay next to, and slightly in front of, his neighbour.

study.translationNote: Many versions say 'sat at table' or 'sat at meat', which hides the custom of reclining. Translations that say 'reclined at table' make scenes like John 13:23 easier to picture.

background.note: A papyrus list of names is headed 'those reclining' (οἱ ἀνακείμενοι), i.e. the guests at a meal, showing the dining sense in everyday use.
An inscription uses the older sense, of a month 'being dedicated' to the goddess, the meaning as passive of ἀνατίθημι.

study.exegesisTip: Picture a Greco-Roman banquet: guests lying on couches, leaning on the left elbow, feet outward. This explains how a woman could stand behind Jesus at his feet (Luke 7:37) and how one disciple could lean back against Jesus.

study.summary: ἀνέχομαι, always middle in the NT, means 'to hold oneself up under' something: to put up with, bear with or endure people and hardships, and also to accept or listen patiently to words. It describes Jesus' weary forbearance with an unbelieving generation, the mutual forbearance of believers, the endurance of persecution, and (ironically in 2 Corinthians) the Corinthians' readiness to tolerate false apostles.

senses.label: Put up with, bear with (people)
senses.definition: To tolerate a person or behaviour that is wearisome or objectionable.
senses.note: 'How long must I put up with you?' expresses Jesus' grief at the disciples' and crowd's unbelief. In 2 Corinthians 11:19-20 Paul ironically notes how readily the Corinthians tolerate those who exploit them.

senses.label: Bear with one another in love
senses.definition: Christian forbearance: patiently enduring the faults and offences of fellow believers.
senses.note: In both letters the verb is paired with humility, patience and forgiveness.

senses.label: Endure hardship
senses.definition: To bear persecution or affliction without giving way or retaliating.
senses.note: 'When persecuted, we endure' (1 Corinthians 4:12).

senses.label: Accept, listen patiently to (words)
senses.definition: To give someone a hearing or to receive teaching or exhortation willingly.
senses.note: Gallio says he would have reasonably heard the Jews out; Paul warns of a time when people will not 'put up with' sound teaching; Hebrews asks readers to 'bear with' its word of exhortation; Paul asks the Corinthians to bear with his 'foolishness'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Two thirds of the uses are Pauline. In 2 Corinthians 11 the word becomes a weapon of irony: the Corinthians gladly 'put up with' a different gospel and abusive leaders, so they can surely put up with a little of Paul's 'foolish' boasting.

study.translationNote: English versions alternate between 'bear with', 'put up with', 'endure', 'forbear' and 'tolerate'. 'Bear with' suits the loving forbearance of Ephesians 4:2 and Colossians 3:13, while 'put up with' captures the exasperation of Mark 9:19 and the irony of 2 Corinthians 11.

background.note: A papyrus uses the verb negatively, 'I could not bring myself to', in a husband's statement that he refused to send his wife away.
A legal papyrus speaks of someone who kept silent and 'held back' for over ten years, so that a statute of limitations applied: the verb as patient refraining.

study.exegesisTip: Notice who is bearing with whom. When the subject is Jesus or God, the word speaks of patience under provocation; when it is believers, it is a duty of love; when it is the Corinthians, it exposes misplaced tolerance.

study.summary: ἀνομία is 'lawlessness': conduct and a disposition that disregard God's law, and, in the plural, individual lawless deeds. In the Greek OT it renders several Hebrew words for iniquity and transgression, so in the NT it is a strong general term for wickedness viewed as rebellion against God's will, from the hidden hypocrisy of the religious to the end-time 'mystery of lawlessness'.

senses.label: Lawlessness as a condition or way of life
senses.definition: Wickedness viewed as disregard of, or rebellion against, God's law; the opposite of righteousness.
senses.note: It is set directly against δικαιοσύνη, 'righteousness' (2 Corinthians 6:14; Hebrews 1:9). Christ gave himself to redeem us 'from all lawlessness' (Titus 2:14). 'Sin is lawlessness' (1 John 3:4).

senses.label: Practising lawlessness: those judged
senses.definition: The doing of lawlessness as the mark of those rejected at the final judgement, even when they appear religious.
senses.note: 'Depart from me, you workers of lawlessness' is spoken to people who prophesied and did miracles in Jesus' name.

senses.label: End-time lawlessness
senses.definition: Lawlessness as a growing force in the last days, culminating in open rebellion against God.
senses.note: Because lawlessness increases, the love of many grows cold (Matthew 24:12); 'the mystery of lawlessness is already at work' (2 Thessalonians 2:7).

senses.label: Lawless deeds (plural)
senses.definition: Individual acts of lawlessness, iniquities, especially as forgiven by God.
senses.note: Paul quotes Psalm 32 ('blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven'); Hebrews quotes the new-covenant promise that God will remember their lawless deeds no more.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew alone among the Gospels uses the word, and he aims it at the outwardly religious: scribes and Pharisees are 'full of hypocrisy and lawlessness', and miracle-workers are dismissed as 'workers of lawlessness'. For Matthew, keeping the forms while neglecting God's will is itself lawlessness.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: 1 John defines sin as lawlessness, making clear that sin is not a trivial lapse but a stance against God.

study.translationNote: Translations vary between 'lawlessness', 'iniquity' and 'wickedness'. 'Lawlessness' preserves the link to νόμος (law); 'iniquity' (KJV) and 'wickedness' reflect the Septuagint's use of the word for general Hebrew terms for sin.

background.note: Herodotus uses ἀνομία of lawless conduct as the opposite of justice (δικαιοσύνη), the same pairing found in 2 Corinthians 6:14 and Hebrews 1:9.
The plural 'lawless deeds' is the Septuagint wording of Psalm 32 (31):1, which Paul quotes in Romans 4:7.
A petitioner complains that assailants attacked him, 'carried away by intolerable lawlessness': the word for violent disregard of legal order.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who is being called lawless. In Matthew it is often people who appear devout; in Paul it is the pre-conversion life (Romans 6:19) and the powers opposing God; in Hebrews it is what the new covenant forgives. The word always places the deed in relation to God's will.
study.caution: Scholars debate whether 'sin is lawlessness' in 1 John 3:4 simply defines sin as breaking God's law or also carries the end-time sense of rebellion associated with the antichrist (as in 2 Thessalonians 2). Some manuscripts also read 'the man of lawlessness' rather than 'the man of sin' earlier in that chapter of 2 Thessalonians.

study.summary: αὔριον means 'tomorrow'; with the article (ἡ αὔριον, understood 'day') it means 'the next day'. Besides plain time references, the NT uses 'tomorrow' as a byword for the brief and uncertain future, which God controls and humans cannot presume upon.

senses.label: Tomorrow, the next day (literal)
senses.definition: The day after the present one, in ordinary narrative and plans.
senses.note: With the article, 'the morrow' or 'the next day' (Acts 4:3, 5; Luke 10:35).

senses.label: Tomorrow as the uncertain, fleeting future
senses.definition: Tomorrow as a figure for the short, unpredictable future, used to warn against anxiety, presumption or despair.
senses.note: Grass is here today and tomorrow thrown into the oven; 'do not worry about tomorrow'; 'let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die'; James rebukes those who plan 'today or tomorrow' business without saying 'if the Lord wills'.

senses.label: 'Today and tomorrow': a short, set time
senses.definition: In a fixed phrase, a brief period that God has determined.
senses.note: Jesus will work 'today and tomorrow, and on the third day' reach his goal: his mission runs on God's timetable, not Herod's.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James uses 'tomorrow' to expose arrogant planning: 'you do not know what tomorrow will bring'. Human life is a mist, and plans must be held under the Lord's will.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul quotes the slogan 'let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' (Isaiah 22:13) as the logical outlook if there is no resurrection.

background.note: Already in Homer αὔριον is the ordinary adverb 'tomorrow'.
A boy writes to his father that a beer-seller keeps telling him 'today, tomorrow' (σήμερον αὔριον) but never delivers: tomorrow as an ever-postponed promise.
Dinner invitations of the period name the day as 'tomorrow, which is the 30th'.

study.exegesisTip: Watch for 'today' and 'tomorrow' paired (Matthew 6:30; Luke 13:32; James 4:13). The pairing usually stresses either the brevity of life or the sovereignty of God over time.

study.summary: ἀφίστημι ('to stand away from') is transitive in some tenses, 'to cause to withdraw, draw away (into revolt)', but mostly intransitive, 'to go away, withdraw, leave'. It describes physical departure, keeping away from people or evil, and, most seriously, falling away from God or the faith; the related noun ἀποστασία gives English 'apostasy'.

senses.label: Draw away, incite to revolt (transitive)
senses.definition: To cause others to withdraw, especially to lead people away in rebellion.
senses.note: Judas the Galilean 'drew away people after him' in revolt.

senses.label: Depart, withdraw, leave
senses.definition: To go away from a place or person, or to stop being present.
senses.note: Anna 'never left' the temple; the devil 'departed from' Jesus until an opportune time; Mark had 'withdrawn from' Paul in Pamphylia; Paul asked that the thorn 'leave' him.

senses.label: Keep away from, leave alone
senses.definition: To stand clear of someone, to cease troubling or associating with them.
senses.note: Gamaliel: 'keep away from these men'; the soldiers about to examine Paul 'withdrew' when they learned he was a Roman; 'depart from me, all you evildoers'.

senses.label: Turn away from evil
senses.definition: To separate oneself morally from wrongdoing.
senses.note: 'Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from unrighteousness.'

senses.label: Fall away, apostatize
senses.definition: To abandon faith in God or the gospel; to desert the Lord.
senses.note: The rocky-ground hearers 'fall away' in time of testing; some 'will depart from the faith'; Hebrews warns against an evil heart of unbelief that 'falls away from the living God'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Most uses are Luke's, chiefly of physical departure, but he also uses it for falling away in the parable of the sower, where Mark and Matthew have 'stumble'.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews frames apostasy as unbelief turning away from 'the living God', echoing Israel's rebellion in the wilderness.

study.translationNote: The same verb can be rendered 'leave', 'depart', 'withdraw', 'keep away', 'turn away' or 'fall away'. The context decides between harmless departure and religious desertion, so a single English equivalent cannot carry every use.

background.note: A tenant notes that he is not permitted to 'withdraw from' (give up) his lease, a usage with the genitive like 'depart from the faith' in 1 Timothy 4:1.
An inscription speaks of the Thebaid region that had 'revolted' (ἀποστᾶσαν) and was subdued, the political sense of rebellion.
A magical exorcism commands a demon, 'come out and depart from' the person, wording close to Luke 13:27.

study.exegesisTip: Check what is being left: a place (the temple), a person (Paul, Jesus), evil (unrighteousness), or God and the faith. Only the last is apostasy; do not read the theological sense into simple narrative departures.
study.caution: Hebrews 3:12 and Luke 8:13 feature in the long debate over whether genuine believers can finally fall away. The word itself means a real departure; how it relates to the security of true faith is a theological question on which traditions differ.

study.summary: γέ is a small enclitic particle that throws emphasis on the word before it, marking it as the least or most important: 'at least', 'indeed', 'even'. It is often untranslatable alone and usually combines with other particles (ἄρα γε 'so then', ἀλλά γε 'yet at least', καί γε 'and even', εἴ γε 'if indeed').

senses.label: Emphatic or restrictive: indeed, at least, yet
senses.definition: Used alone to highlight a word, often with a sense of 'at least this' or 'precisely this'.
senses.note: In Luke 11:8 the friend will rise 'yet because of his persistence'; in Romans 8:32 ὅς γε stresses 'he who did not even spare his own Son'.

senses.label: ἄρα γε: so then; ἆρά γε: is it really?
senses.definition: Strengthening an inference ('so then') or, with the interrogative form, a question expecting surprise.
senses.note: 'So then, by their fruits you will know them'; Philip asks, 'Do you really understand what you are reading?'

senses.label: ἀλλά γε: yet at least, but surely
senses.definition: Introducing a contrasting point that holds at any rate.
senses.note: 'If I am not an apostle to others, at least I am to you.'

senses.label: καί γε: and even, and indeed
senses.definition: Adding a point with emphasis.
senses.note: 'Even on my servants, men and women, I will pour out my Spirit'; God is 'indeed not far from each one of us'.

senses.label: εἴ γε: if indeed, since
senses.definition: A conditional that assumes or tests the truth of the condition.
senses.note: Whether it implies confidence ('since') or real doubt ('if indeed') must be judged from context.

senses.label: ὄφελόν γε: would that indeed
senses.definition: Strengthening an ironic wish.
senses.note: 'Would that you did reign, so that we might reign with you!'

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke, the most literary NT writer, uses the particle most, especially in the more polished combinations such as ἆρά γε and καί γε.

study.translationNote: Because γέ adds tone rather than content, English versions often omit it or render it with 'indeed', 'at least', 'even', 'surely' or simply by word order, so different versions may sound different without disagreeing on meaning.

background.note: A wife's letter says she thought that 'now at last' (νῦν γε), on her husband's return, she would get relief: γε emphasizing the time.
The combination εἰ δὲ μή γε, 'but if not, otherwise', appears in ordinary letters just as in the Gospels.

study.exegesisTip: Identify the word γε attaches to: that word carries the emphasis. In combinations, translate the combination as a unit rather than γε separately.
study.caution: With εἴ γε commentators disagree whether Paul expresses confidence ('since you have heard', Ephesians 4:21) or a genuine condition ('if indeed you continue', Colossians 1:23); the particle alone does not settle it.

study.summary: γεύομαι means 'to taste': to sample the flavour of something, and by extension to eat. Figuratively it means 'to experience', most strikingly in 'taste death' (to die, to undergo death) and in tasting the goodness of the Lord or the gifts of the age to come.

senses.label: Taste, sample
senses.definition: To perceive the flavour of something by the mouth, sometimes without consuming it.
senses.note: The master of the feast tastes the water made wine; Jesus tastes the wine mixed with gall but will not drink it; the ascetic rule 'do not taste' is rejected by Paul as human regulation.

senses.label: Eat, take food
senses.definition: To eat or share a meal.
senses.note: Peter is hungry and wants 'to eat'; the conspirators vow not to 'taste' anything until they have killed Paul; none of those invited will 'taste' the banquet.

senses.label: Taste death: die, undergo death
senses.definition: A Semitic idiom meaning to experience death, to die.
senses.note: Some standing there will not 'taste death' before seeing the kingdom; Jesus by God's grace 'tasted death for everyone' (Hebrews 2:9), i.e. truly underwent it on others' behalf.

senses.label: Experience (spiritual realities)
senses.definition: To come to know something by personal experience, especially God's goodness or gifts.
senses.note: Those who 'tasted the heavenly gift' and 'the goodness of the word of God' (Hebrews 6:4-5); 'if you have tasted that the Lord is good' (1 Peter 2:3, echoing Psalm 34:8).

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the word only figuratively: Jesus tasting death for all, and believers tasting the heavenly gift and the powers of the age to come, which raises the stakes of the warning against falling away.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: In Acts the word is used plainly of eating, including Paul's meal after breaking bread at Troas.

study.translationNote: Where the meaning is simply 'eat' (Acts 10:10; 20:11), many versions say 'eat'; where it is the idiom 'taste death', most keep 'taste' to preserve the vivid image.

background.note: In the certificates of the Decian persecution (A.D. 250), those who sacrificed declared 'I tasted the sacred offerings', showing the verb for eating sacrificial food.
A cup inscription reads 'from this I tasted', the verb used absolutely as in Acts 10:10.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether 'taste' is literal (sampling or eating) or figurative (experiencing). In the figurative uses, 'taste' implies real experience, not a mere sip: Jesus did not merely sample death (Hebrews 2:9).
study.caution: In Hebrews 6:4-5 interpreters disagree whether those who have 'tasted' the heavenly gift are genuine believers who may fall away or people who experienced the gospel's blessings without true faith. The verb itself denotes real experience; the theological conclusion is debated.

study.summary: γνωστός is the verbal adjective of γινώσκω, "known."
