In the NT it is used chiefly by Luke in the formula "let it be known to you" or "it became known," marking public, undeniable facts; as a noun it means a person's acquaintances or friends; and in Romans 1:19 Paul uses τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ for what is known (or knowable) about God.

senses.label: known, made public
senses.definition: Of facts or events that are, or become, common knowledge, often in the solemn formula γνωστὸν ἔστω ὑμῖν, "let this be known to you," introducing a proclamation.
senses.note: Luke uses the formula to frame decisive announcements in apostolic speeches (Peter at Pentecost and before the council, Paul at Pisidian Antioch and in Rome).

senses.label: notable, evident
senses.definition: Of something so manifest that it cannot be denied: a "notable" sign that everyone in Jerusalem recognised.

senses.label: acquaintance, friend (as noun)
senses.definition: Substantival use for people known to someone: acquaintances, friends, those personally connected with a person.
senses.note: Whether the term implies close friendship ("familiar friend") or simply acquaintance is debated; in John 18:15 it explains how the other disciple could enter the high priest's courtyard.

senses.label: what is known of God
senses.definition: Neuter with article: that which is known (or can be known) about God, which Paul says is evident to all people through creation.

senses.label: known to God
senses.definition: Of God's works or purposes as known to him from eternity.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Twelve of the fifteen NT uses are Luke's. In Acts the word marks the public, verifiable character of what happened—the death of Judas, the healing of the lame man, the gospel announcement—so that hearers are without excuse.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses it only of the unnamed disciple who was "known to the high priest," a detail that explains Peter's access to the courtyard during Jesus' trial.

study.translationNote: In Romans 1:19 versions divide between "what may be known about God" (stressing knowability) and "what is known about God" (stressing actual knowledge). Ordinary Greek usage favours "known," which fits Paul's argument that people actually possess, and suppress, this knowledge.

background.note: In classical Greek γνωστός is a collateral form of γνωτός meaning simply "known," as in Sophocles' Oedipus the King.
A late papyrus uses τὸ γνωστόν for the knowledge of a mutual intimacy, supporting the sense "known" rather than "knowable" for the neuter noun.

study.exegesisTip: When γνωστόν appears with a dative and a form of εἰμί or γίνομαι in Acts, read it as a public declaration: the speaker is putting facts on the record that the audience must now reckon with.
study.caution: Do not press "acquaintances" in Luke 2:44 and 23:49 into a technical term for intimate friends; scholars disagree how close the relationship implied is.

study.summary: γράμμα, from γράφω, is "something written": a letter of the alphabet, a document such as a bill or an epistle, the sacred writings, or learning acquired from books. Paul gives it a distinctive theological sense: "the letter," the law as an external written code, set against the life-giving Spirit of the new covenant.

senses.label: letter of the alphabet
senses.definition: A written character; Paul draws attention to the large letters of his own handwriting.
senses.note: Whether the large letters reflect emphasis or simply the contrast with a scribe's neater hand is uncertain.

senses.label: written document: bill, letter
senses.definition: A piece of writing of any kind: a debtor's bond or bill, or an official letter.

senses.label: writings, Scriptures
senses.definition: The written works of an author, especially of Moses, and "the sacred writings," i.e. the Old Testament Scriptures.
senses.note: τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα was the usual name among Greek-speaking Jews for the Scriptures.

senses.label: learning, education
senses.definition: Plural: letters in the sense of literacy or formal learning.
senses.note: In John 7:15 the opponents' question implies Jesus had no formal scribal training; Festus in Acts 26:24 speaks of Paul's "great learning."

senses.label: the letter (law as written code)
senses.definition: The law viewed as an external written code that commands but cannot give life, contrasted with the inward work of the Spirit.
senses.note: "The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life" (2 Cor 3:6) is not a contrast between literal and allegorical reading, but between the old covenant engraved on stone and the new covenant written on hearts.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's γράμμα/πνεῦμα antithesis is a covenant contrast: circumcision and law as written requirements versus the Spirit who renews the heart and enables true obedience.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John links Moses' writings to faith in Jesus ("if you do not believe his writings…") and records surprise that Jesus knows letters without having studied.

study.translationNote: Modern versions often render Paul's theological use as "written code" (Rom 2:27; 7:6) to show he means the law as an external code, while "letter" is kept in 2 Corinthians 3:6. Both reflect the same Greek word and idea.

background.note: Countless papyri describe a person who cannot write as one who does "not know letters"; a scribe writes on his behalf. This illuminates the remark in John 7:15 that Jesus had never studied "letters."
A notice is to be posted on a board "in large letters," which may illustrate emphasis as the reason for the large letters of Galatians 6:11.
γράμμα is used for a bond or written claim alongside other agreements, paralleling the steward's "bill" in Luke 16:6.
In classical Greek the word could also mean a drawing or picture, as in Plato's Republic.

study.exegesisTip: In Paul, watch for the pairing with πνεῦμα (Spirit): when γράμμα stands opposite the Spirit it refers to the Mosaic law as written requirement, not to the literal sense of a text.
study.caution: Do not use 2 Corinthians 3:6 to set literal interpretation against "spiritual" interpretation of Scripture; Paul's contrast is between covenants, not hermeneutical methods. Also, the sense of "letters" in John 7:15 (illiterate vs. untrained in rabbinic study) is debated.

study.summary: δέρω originally meant to skin or flay an animal, but in colloquial Greek and in every NT occurrence it means to beat or thrash a person. It describes the abuse of God's messengers in the parable of the tenants, the beating of Jesus and his apostles, and, figuratively, Paul's boxer who does not "beat the air."

senses.label: beat, thrash (persons)
senses.definition: To strike or flog someone, especially as mistreatment or punishment: the servants in the parable, Jesus at his trial, and the apostles before councils and magistrates.

senses.label: be beaten (passive, as punishment)
senses.definition: Passive of judicial or disciplinary beating, including Jesus' warning of floggings in synagogues and the servant beaten "with many" or "few" blows.
senses.note: In Luke 12:47-48 the word πληγάς (blows) is understood with πολλάς and ὀλίγας.

senses.label: strike in the face (insult)
senses.definition: To slap or strike someone, an act of humiliation as much as pain.

senses.label: beat the air (figurative)
senses.definition: In a boxing image, to throw punches that hit nothing: purposeless effort.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word to tie the fate of the apostles to that of the prophets and of Jesus: the servants are beaten (Luke 20), Jesus is beaten (Luke 22), and the apostles are beaten in Jerusalem and Philippi. Paul himself had once beaten believers in the synagogues.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses it figuratively of disciplined effort (not beating the air) and ironically of the Corinthians' tolerance for leaders who strike them in the face.

background.note: In Homer the verb means to skin or flay animals, e.g. oxen after sacrifice.
A second-century court record shows the colloquial sense "beat, thrash": a prefect warns a creditor that unless he makes restitution he will not only be condemned but beaten.

study.exegesisTip: In Acts 16:37 note the legal force: Paul protests that Roman citizens were beaten publicly and uncondemned, an illegal act that put the magistrates in the wrong.
study.caution: A minority suggestion takes 2 Corinthians 11:20 as "upbraid to your face" by analogy with a modern Greek idiom, but the usual sense "strike in the face" fits the series of abuses Paul lists.

study.summary: διαμαρτύρομαι is an intensive form of μαρτύρομαι: to testify solemnly, to bear earnest witness, or to charge and warn someone gravely, often as if before witnesses or before God. Luke uses it for the apostles' urgent proclamation of the gospel; Paul for solemn warnings and charges.

senses.label: testify solemnly (to the gospel)
senses.definition: To bear earnest, emphatic witness to the truth of the gospel, especially to Jesus as the Christ, to repentance and faith, and to the grace of God.

senses.label: warn earnestly
senses.definition: To warn someone solemnly so that they may avoid judgment or wrongdoing.
senses.note: In Acts 20:23 it is the Holy Spirit who solemnly warns Paul that chains await him.

senses.label: charge solemnly (before God)
senses.definition: To lay a solemn charge on someone, invoking God and Christ as witnesses ("I charge you before God…").

senses.label: declare, attest
senses.definition: To affirm or declare formally, as Scripture or God's appointed judge is attested.
senses.note: In Hebrews 2:6 it introduces a quotation of Psalm 8: "someone has testified somewhere."

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Ten of fifteen uses are Luke's. The verb characterises apostolic preaching as solemn testimony: Peter at Pentecost, Peter and John in Samaria, Paul to Jews and Greeks. Paul's whole ministry is summed up as "testifying to the gospel of the grace of God."

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In the Pastoral Letters the word introduces formal charges made in the presence of God, Christ, and the angels, underlining the accountability of church leaders.

study.translationNote: English versions alternate between "testify," "warn," and "charge" depending on context. All carry the same note of solemn, emphatic utterance; the choice depends on whether the content is a truth declared or an action required.

background.note: In Demosthenes the verb means to call gods and men to witness, to protest solemnly, especially against falsehood or wrong.
In the Greek OT it chiefly renders the Hebrew for "testify against, warn," as when Moses calls heaven and earth to witness against Israel.
A third-century BC papyrus uses the verb with an accusative of person in a formal protest.

study.exegesisTip: Notice the companion verbs: in Acts 2:40 it pairs with παρακαλέω (urge), and in Acts 20:24 it describes Paul's life-purpose. The prefix διά- intensifies; the word suggests testimony given thoroughly and with full gravity.

study.summary: διατάσσω means to arrange, direct, order, or prescribe. In the NT it describes authoritative instructions: Jesus' directions to the Twelve, God's command to Moses, official orders by Roman authorities, and Paul's apostolic directives for the churches. Of the law it is said to have been "ordained through angels."

senses.label: instruct, give directions
senses.definition: To give orders or instructions to someone, by Jesus or by an apostle exercising authority.

senses.label: prescribe, ordain (as a rule)
senses.definition: To lay down a rule or arrangement that is binding, as Paul does in all the churches, or as the Lord ordained for gospel workers.
senses.note: 1 Corinthians 9:14 refers to the Lord's own ordinance that those who preach should live by the gospel.

senses.label: command (by God or by authorities)
senses.definition: To order or decree, of God's command to Moses and of imperial or military orders.

senses.label: what is ordered (passive participle)
senses.definition: τὸ διατεταγμένον / τὰ διαταχθέντα: what has been prescribed, the appointed amount or the duties commanded.

senses.label: arrange, appoint
senses.definition: To arrange matters or appoint something, including the law "ordained through angels."

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word for his apostolic rulings, applied uniformly "in all the churches," showing a concern for common practice among congregations.

background.note: Hesiod uses it of Zeus who appointed to the immortals their several portions and ordained law for humankind.
In the papyri the verb is technical for directions in a will: the twenty drachmae "bequeathed" by a deceased father.
More generally κατὰ τὰ διατεταγμένα means "in accordance with the decrees," just as Luke 3:13 speaks of what tax collectors are authorised to collect.

study.exegesisTip: In Luke 3:13 John the Baptist tells tax collectors not to exceed what is officially prescribed; the participle refers to the fixed, legal rate, not to an arbitrary amount.

study.summary: εὐσέβεια is reverent devotion toward God expressed in a life that honours him: "godliness" or "piety." A common term of Hellenistic religion and ethics, it is taken up chiefly in the Pastoral Letters and 2 Peter to describe genuine Christian faith lived out in practice, grounded in the revealed "mystery of godliness," Christ himself.

senses.label: godliness, piety toward God
senses.definition: Reverent devotion to God that shapes conduct; the whole manner of life that fittingly responds to God.

senses.label: the Christian faith as a way of life
senses.definition: The content of true religion: the teaching and truth that accord with and produce godliness; the "mystery" revealed in Christ.
senses.note: In 1 Timothy 3:16 "the mystery of godliness" is then summarised in a hymn about Christ's incarnation and exaltation.

senses.label: godliness and gain
senses.definition: Godliness misused as a means of profit, contrasted with true godliness joined to contentment.

senses.label: outward form of piety
senses.definition: An appearance of religion without its transforming power.

senses.label: piety as human achievement
senses.definition: Personal religious devotion regarded as a source of power, which Peter denies as the cause of the healing.

senses.label: acts of godliness (plural)
senses.definition: Plural for the concrete expressions of godly living in view of the coming day of God.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In the Pastoral Letters godliness is a key word for Christian maturity and the goal of sound teaching. It is trained like an athlete trains, is profitable for this life and the next, and is rooted in the truth about Christ.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 2 Peter places godliness among the virtues to be added to faith and teaches that God's power has supplied all that is needed "for life and godliness."

study.translationNote: Nearly all English versions use "godliness"; some use "piety" or "devotion." "Religion" (as in some renderings of 1 Tim 3:16) captures the word's public, cultic side but can lose its personal, ethical dimension.

background.note: Plato speaks of piety toward the gods and parents, showing the word's original range of reverent duty.
An inscription praises the people of Priene for their piety toward the divine, a standard civic-religious formula of the time.
Emperor Claudius thanks an athletic club for a golden crown as a token of their loyalty (εὐσέβεια) to him, showing the word could also mean devotion to a ruler.
In the Greek OT εὐσέβεια renders "the fear of the LORD," e.g. in Proverbs 1:7 and Isaiah 11:2; most LXX occurrences are in 4 Maccabees.

study.exegesisTip: Read εὐσέβεια in the Pastorals against its Hellenistic background: Paul claims a word his culture used for civic piety and fills it with content defined by the gospel ("the mystery of godliness").

study.summary: εὐχαριστία means gratitude or, more often in the NT, the giving of thanks, especially thanksgiving offered to God in prayer and worship. Paul makes thanksgiving a constant mark of Christian life, flowing from God's grace and returning glory to him. Its later use for the Lord's Supper ("Eucharist") is not yet found in the NT.

senses.label: gratitude, thankfulness
senses.definition: The attitude of being grateful, expressed toward a person.
senses.note: Tertullus' flattering speech to Felix is the only NT use directed toward a human.

senses.label: giving thanks to God
senses.definition: Thanksgiving offered to God, as an accompaniment of prayer and a fitting response to his grace.

senses.label: a prayer of thanksgiving
senses.definition: A spoken act of thanks in worship, to which others respond with "Amen"; plural for repeated prayers of thanks.

senses.label: thanks over food
senses.definition: Thanksgiving with which God's gifts of food are received, sanctifying them for use.

senses.label: thanksgiving in heavenly worship
senses.definition: Thanks ascribed to God by heavenly beings in doxology.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: For Paul thanksgiving is the proper human response to grace: grace multiplies, thanksgiving overflows, and God is glorified. It replaces coarse talk and anxious prayer and is to accompany all requests.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In Revelation thanksgiving is part of the heavenly liturgy offered to God by the living creatures and angels.

background.note: A letter of Emperor Claudius to a gymnastic club speaks of his gratitude toward them, showing the meaning "thankfulness."
A third-century BC inscription refers to the gratitude of the people, the common inscriptional use of the word.
An inscription of about AD 37 speaks of finding fitting returns "for thanksgiving" to a great god, illustrating religious thanksgiving.

study.exegesisTip: Notice how often Paul pairs εὐχαριστία with prayer words (προσευχή, δέησις): thanks is not a separate religious duty but the tone of every request.
study.caution: Do not read the later technical sense "Eucharist" back into NT passages; in 1 Corinthians 14:16 the word refers to a spoken prayer of thanks, not the Lord's Supper.

study.summary: θρίξ is "hair," whether of the human head or of animals. In the NT it appears in John the Baptist's camel-hair clothing, in the woman's act of wiping Jesus' feet with her hair, in Jesus' assurance that every hair is numbered, and in the vision of the risen Christ with hair white as wool.

senses.label: hair of the head
senses.definition: Human hair, often in the plural for the whole head of hair.

senses.label: a single hair (God's care)
senses.definition: A single hair as the smallest thing, used to express God's detailed care and the certainty of protection.
senses.note: "Not a hair of your head will perish" is a proverbial idiom for complete safety.

senses.label: a hair (human powerlessness)
senses.definition: A single hair as a picture of how little control a person has over his own life.

senses.label: animal hair
senses.definition: Hair of animals, such as camel's hair used for coarse clothing, or the hair of the locusts in Revelation.

senses.label: hair in visionary description
senses.definition: Hair as a feature of the glorified Christ, white like wool, recalling the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John recalls Mary wiping Jesus' feet with her hair as an act of extravagant devotion, and in Revelation describes Christ's white hair as a sign of eternal majesty.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: Peter warns against relying on elaborately braided hair as adornment, valuing instead the inner person of the heart.

background.note: Homer uses the plural of hair standing on end in fear, and the word also of sheep's wool and pig's bristles.
The word appears often in personal descriptions in legal documents, e.g. a scar on the forehead "under the hair."
In the Greek OT it chiefly translates the Hebrew for hair, including goats' hair for the tabernacle and the Nazirite's uncut hair.

study.exegesisTip: In Luke 7:38, 44 note that a respectable woman would not normally let down her hair in public; her action expresses humility and love beyond social convention.

study.summary: καταλαμβάνω is an intensive form of λαμβάνω: to seize, take hold of, obtain; to overtake or come upon (often suddenly or with hostile intent); to catch in an act; and in the middle voice, to grasp mentally, perceive, understand. Its use in John 1:5 (the darkness did not "overcome" or "comprehend" the light) is a famous interpretive crux.

senses.label: seize, take hold of
senses.definition: To lay hold of forcibly, as a demon seizes a boy.

senses.label: obtain, attain, take hold of (a goal)
senses.definition: To win or make one's own what one strives for, such as a prize or righteousness; Paul also uses the passive of being taken hold of by Christ.
senses.note: In Philippians 3:12 Paul presses on to lay hold of that for which Christ laid hold of him: the active and passive mirror each other.

senses.label: overtake, come upon
senses.definition: To overtake or come upon someone suddenly, often with hostile or threatening force, as darkness or the day of the Lord.
senses.note: In John 1:5 "overcome" or "seize" fits the parallel in John 12:35.

senses.label: catch, detect (in an act)
senses.definition: To catch someone in the act of wrongdoing.

senses.label: perceive, realize, comprehend (middle)
senses.definition: In the middle voice, to grasp mentally: to realise, understand, or come to see a truth.
senses.note: In Ephesians 3:18 Paul prays that believers may comprehend the breadth, length, height, and depth of Christ's love.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb of strenuous pursuit and attainment, drawing on athletic imagery: runners who take the prize and the apostle straining to lay hold of the goal of his calling.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses it of darkness as a hostile power that seeks to overtake; the light shines and the darkness has not mastered it.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses only the middle voice, of mental perception: the council realises the apostles are uneducated men, Peter grasps that God shows no partiality, Festus finds Paul guiltless.

study.translationNote: John 1:5 is rendered "comprehended" (KJV), "has not overcome" (ESV, NIV, MSB), or "has not understood" (NIV margin). The active voice and the parallel in John 12:35 favour hostile "overcome/overtake," though some see a deliberate double meaning.

background.note: In Homer the verb means to seize or lay hold of, as Odysseus grasps the ram's back.
A complaint records catching a man at night breaking into a farmstead, the sense "detect, catch" as in John 8:3-4.
A Christian letter speaks of recovery from the illness that "struck down" (overtook) a woman, illustrating the sense of evils overtaking someone.
A colonists' inscription records how they "appropriated" the land, matching Paul's sense of taking possession.

study.exegesisTip: Check the voice: active forms mean seize, attain, or overtake; middle forms (in Acts and Ephesians) mean perceive or comprehend.
study.caution: John 8:3-4 belongs to the passage about the woman caught in adultery, which many manuscripts lack; scholars disagree on its place in John's Gospel.

study.summary: κατεσθίω is a strengthened form of ἐσθίω, "eat up, devour completely." It is used literally of birds devouring seed and of John eating the scroll, and figuratively of consuming destruction: scribes who devour widows' houses, believers who devour one another, a son who devours his inheritance, and fire that consumes enemies.

senses.label: eat up, devour (literal)
senses.definition: To eat completely, of birds eating seed, the dragon ready to devour the child, or John eating the little scroll.

senses.label: devour property (exploit, squander)
senses.definition: To consume someone's resources: by exploitation (devouring widows' houses) or by waste (devouring one's livelihood).
senses.note: "Devouring widows' houses" likely refers to financial exploitation of vulnerable women, perhaps through the management of their estates.

senses.label: prey on, exploit people
senses.definition: To abuse or tear others apart, whether through exploitation or communal strife.
senses.note: In Galatians 5:15 the image is of wild animals biting and devouring each other until all are consumed.

senses.label: consume (as by fire or zeal)
senses.definition: To destroy utterly, of fire consuming enemies, or zeal for God's house consuming Jesus.
senses.note: John 2:17 quotes Psalm 69:9; zeal will "consume" Jesus, likely hinting at his death.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation uses the verb repeatedly for destructive powers and divine judgment by fire, and for the prophet's eating of the scroll, sweet in the mouth but bitter in the stomach.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses it figuratively of community-destroying behaviour: false apostles who prey on the Corinthians and Galatians who devour one another.

study.translationNote: In the sayings about widows' houses, some versions render "defraud" or "cheat" to make the figurative meaning plain, while others keep the vivid "devour."

background.note: In Homer the verb is used of beasts of prey, such as a lion that has devoured a bull.
A complaint describes sheep that overran, cropped, and utterly destroyed pasture, showing the verb's perfective force.
A papyrus complains of officials "devouring" the treasury's estates, a close parallel to the figurative use in Mark 12:40.

study.exegesisTip: The prefix κατά- gives a completive force: not merely eating but eating up. This intensifies the warnings in Galatians 5:15 and the woes against the scribes.
study.caution: The saying about devouring widows' houses in Matthew 23 is absent from many early manuscripts and modern critical editions, and its verse number differs between editions; it is secure in Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47.

study.summary: To break, in the NT used only of breaking bread: in Jesus' feeding miracles and meals, at the Last Supper, and in the early church's 'breaking of bread'. The action belongs to the host who gives thanks and distributes.

senses.label: Breaking bread to share a meal
senses.definition: The host's act of breaking a loaf into pieces in order to distribute it, usually right after giving thanks or blessing God; used in Jesus' feeding miracles and ordinary meals.
senses.note: In every Gospel case the sequence is the same: take, bless/give thanks, break, give.

senses.label: Breaking the bread at the Last Supper
senses.definition: Jesus breaking the bread he identifies with his body, given for his disciples.
senses.note: The breaking is part of the ordinary Jewish meal ritual, but here Jesus attaches to the bread the words 'this is my body'.

senses.label: The church's 'breaking of bread'
senses.definition: The shared meal of the believing community, including the Lord's Supper, described by the act that began it.
senses.note: In 1 Corinthians 10:16 'the bread that we break' is a participation (κοινωνία) in the body of Christ.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke links the risen Jesus' meal at Emmaus to the church's later gatherings by the same act of taking, blessing and breaking bread; in Acts 'breaking bread' becomes shorthand for the believers' communal meal, held in homes and on the first day of the week.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul treats the broken bread as a sharing in Christ's body that binds the many into one body, and grounds the practice in the words of institution he received.

study.translationNote: Some later manuscripts of 1 Corinthians 11:24 add 'broken' (κλώμενον) to 'This is my body which is for you', which the KJV follows ('broken for you'); most modern versions omit it, following the older manuscripts.

background.note: From Homer the verb means to break or break off something physical, such as Odysseus breaking a leafy branch from a thicket.
In the Greek Old Testament it appears in a mourning context, of breaking bread for those who grieve.
A fourth-century complaint of assault uses the verb of physical breaking or injury done to the complainant's body.

study.exegesisTip: Watch the four-verb pattern 'took, blessed/gave thanks, broke, gave' in the feeding miracles, the Last Supper and Emmaus; the Gospel writers use it to link these meals with each other.
study.caution: Whether every 'breaking of bread' in Acts (e.g. ACT 2:46, ACT 27:35) means the Lord's Supper rather than an ordinary shared meal is debated; the phrase itself only describes beginning a meal, and context must decide.

study.summary: To shut or lock: doors, rooms, prisons, city gates, the abyss. Figuratively the heavens are 'shut' against rain, the kingdom is shut against people, and a person can 'shut' his heart against a needy brother. In Revelation Christ alone has authority to open and shut.

senses.label: Shut a door or room
senses.definition: To close a door, often implying it is now fastened against those outside.
senses.note: In the parable of the virgins the shut door means final exclusion (MAT 25:10).

senses.label: Lock up, make secure
senses.definition: To secure a place so that nothing can get in or out: a prison, the abyss, or (negatively) the gates of the new Jerusalem that are never shut.

senses.label: Shut the sky (withhold rain)
senses.definition: Of the heavens being closed so that no rain falls, as a divine judgment.
senses.note: Echoes Elijah's drought (1 Kings 17–18).

senses.label: Shut the kingdom; authority to open and shut
senses.definition: To bar access to God's kingdom, or the sovereign right to grant or deny entry.
senses.note: Revelation 3:7 draws on Isaiah 22:22, the key of David's house.

senses.label: Shut one's heart
senses.definition: To close off compassion (literally 'the inward parts') toward someone in need.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In the Gospel the locked doors stress that the risen Jesus came among his frightened disciples despite every barrier; in Revelation the verb expresses Christ's absolute control over access, whether to the kingdom, to the abyss, or to the heavens.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses the shut door both for private prayer and for final exclusion, and charges the scribes and Pharisees with shutting the kingdom in people's faces.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'shut', 'closed' and 'locked' (JOH 20:19; ACT 5:23). The Greek word covers both; 'locked' is justified where context implies security, as with the prison in Acts 5:23. In 1 John 3:17 the KJV's 'shutteth up his bowels of compassion' renders the idiom literally.

background.note: A petitioner in 161 BC reports that he got to the temple door first and shut it.
A dreamer writes that it was as though his eyes were shut, a figurative use of the perfect passive.
A lease describes a house fitted with doors and windows and locked.

study.exegesisTip: In the Septuagint the verb chiefly renders Hebrew sagar, 'to shut', the verb used when the LORD shut Noah into the ark; the NT 'shut door' can carry that sense of a decisive act no one else can undo (MAT 25:10; REV 3:7).
study.caution: Verse numbering differs in Matthew 23: the saying about shutting the kingdom is 23:13 in most modern editions but 23:14 in some older ones, because one verse (23:14 in the KJV) is missing from the earliest manuscripts.

study.summary: An heir: one who receives an inheritance. Used literally in Jesus' parable of the vineyard and in Paul's legal analogy, but mainly of Christ as heir of all things and of believers who, as God's children, inherit what God promised to Abraham.

senses.label: Heir (ordinary legal sense)
senses.definition: The person who will receive a father's estate on his death.
senses.note: In the parable the tenants recognize the son as heir and kill him to seize the inheritance.

senses.label: Christ, heir of all things
senses.definition: The Son appointed by God as the rightful owner of the whole creation.
senses.note: Echoes Psalm 2:8, 'I will give you the nations as your inheritance'.

senses.label: Heir of the promise to Abraham
senses.definition: Abraham and his true offspring as recipients of what God promised, received by faith rather than by the law.
senses.note: Paul widens the promise of the land to 'heir of the world' (ROM 4:13).

senses.label: Believers as heirs of God
senses.definition: Those made God's children through Christ, who will share his inheritance of eternal life and the kingdom.
senses.note: 'Heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ' (ROM 8:17), on condition of sharing his sufferings.

senses.label: Possessor (of righteousness)
senses.definition: One who comes into possession of something, with the idea of inheritance in the background.
senses.note: Noah 'became heir of the righteousness that comes by faith'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Heirship is a key image for Paul: it depends on sonship and promise, not on law-keeping. The heir as a minor is no better than a slave until the father's appointed time (GAL 4:1), but in Christ believers are sons and therefore heirs.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews begins with the Son as heir of all things and then speaks of the 'heirs of the promise' whom God assures by an oath.

background.note: A will of the early second century AD reads: if I die with this will unchanged, I leave my daughter Ammonous heir.
A document of AD 125 records that Philip has died and his son Aphrodisius is heir.
In the Greek Old Testament the word occasionally renders forms of Hebrew yarash, 'take possession', of those who take over others' property.

study.exegesisTip: Inheritance in the NT is tied to sonship: trace the chain 'children, then heirs' in ROM 8:17 and GAL 4:7, and note that the inheritance is God's promise to Abraham now extended to all who belong to Christ (GAL 3:29).
study.caution: In HEB 6:17 and HEB 11:7 some lexicons give the weakened sense 'possessor' rather than strict 'heir'; others keep the inheritance idea. In the first-century world an heir could also inherit obligations, which may lie behind Paul's stress on the conditions of heirship, but this is an inference, not stated in the text.

study.summary: A robber or bandit who uses violence, distinct from a sneak thief (κλέπτης). In the Gospels it is also the term for armed brigands and insurgents, which colours Jesus' arrest, Barabbas, and the men crucified with him.

senses.label: Violent robber, highwayman
senses.definition: One who robs openly and by force, typically on roads or in remote places.
senses.note: 'A thief and a robber' (JOH 10:1) pairs the stealthy thief with the violent bandit.

senses.label: 'Den of robbers' (the temple)
senses.definition: Jesus' charge, quoting Jeremiah 7:11, that the temple had become a hideout for those who exploit others.
senses.note: In Jeremiah a den is where robbers retreat for safety after their crimes.

senses.label: Bandit, armed insurgent
senses.definition: An outlaw of the kind dealt with by armed force, including rebels against Roman rule.
senses.note: Jesus protests being arrested with swords and clubs 'as against a bandit'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John calls Barabbas a λῃστής, and in the Good Shepherd discourse contrasts the shepherd with thieves and robbers who came before him.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark sets Jesus between two λῃσταί on the cross, ironically numbering him with the kind of men he refused to be treated as at his arrest.

study.translationNote: The KJV renders it 'thieves' for the men crucified with Jesus (MAT 27:38) and 'robber' for Barabbas, which blurs the difference from κλέπτης. Modern versions vary between 'robbers', 'bandits', 'rebels' and 'insurrectionists', reflecting the view that these men were violent outlaws, possibly political, rather than petty thieves.

background.note: Herodotus uses the word of a man who turned to piracy, raiding the Carthaginians: in classical Greek it covers robbery by sea as well as by land.
Plato speaks of living a robber's life as the opposite of a life of order and justice.
Third-century BC memoranda on criminals are headed 'concerning an attack by robbers'.
A seventh-century document speaks of having harboured robbers.

study.exegesisTip: Distinguish λῃστής (violent robber) from κλέπτης (thief who steals secretly). Both appear in JOH 10:1, and the difference matters for the crucifixion scene: the men beside Jesus were not small-time thieves.
study.caution: Some historians, drawing on Josephus' use of the same word for anti-Roman rebels, take the λῃσταί of the passion narrative as insurrectionists; Mark links Barabbas with an uprising. Others think the word need mean only violent criminals. The text alone does not settle whether the two crucified men were political rebels.

study.summary: To think, suppose, consider: holding an opinion, often one that turns out mistaken. Once (in some manuscripts) it means 'to be customary'. Luke uses it most, often to show people misreading a situation.

senses.label: Suppose (wrongly)
senses.definition: To assume something to be so when, as the story shows, it is not.
senses.note: Mary and Joseph supposed Jesus was in the caravan; the jailer supposed the prisoners had escaped.

senses.label: Do not think… (correcting a misconception)
senses.definition: With a negative, Jesus heads off a false assumption about his mission.
senses.note: 'Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law' (MAT 5:17).

senses.label: Was supposed, reckoned
senses.definition: Of public opinion: what people generally assumed.
senses.note: Jesus was 'the son, as was supposed, of Joseph'.

senses.label: Think, judge, consider (an opinion)
senses.definition: To hold a considered view or judgment, sound or unsound.
senses.note: Paul gives his own judgment in 1 Corinthians 7; false teachers 'suppose godliness is a means of gain' (1TI 6:5).

senses.label: Be customary
senses.definition: In the passive, of what is usually done by custom.
senses.note: Only in the reading 'where prayer was customarily held'; other manuscripts read 'where we supposed there was a place of prayer'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke often uses νομίζω for a mistaken assumption that the narrative then corrects: Jesus' parents, Moses' brothers, the crowd at Lystra who thought Paul dead, the Philippian jailer, the Jerusalem crowd who thought Paul had brought Trophimus into the temple.

study.translationNote: In ACT 16:13 manuscripts differ: the Byzantine text reads ἐνομίζετο, 'where prayer was wont to be made' (KJV), while most modern versions follow ἐνομίζομεν, 'where we supposed there was a place of prayer'.

background.note: A third-century BC letter uses the passive of what is customary: so that the customary payments may be made to the gods.
The active 'I think' is everyday language: 'for I think that you more than the others are a follower of truth'.

study.exegesisTip: The word is related to νόμος (custom, law); its basic idea is what is held or recognized. In the NT this has become 'think, suppose', so it marks opinion, not knowledge. Note how often the opinion proves wrong, especially in Luke 3:23, where Luke signals that Joseph was not Jesus' father.

study.summary: A relative word of quality, 'such as, of what sort'. It describes what kind something is: an incomparable tribulation, garments whiter than any launderer could make them, the sort of people Paul fears to find. It also forms the idiom 'it is not as though' (ROM 9:6).

senses.label: Such as… never (unparalleled)
senses.definition: With a negative, introduces a description of something without precedent: 'such as has never been'.
senses.note: Mark 13:19 adds a redundant τοιαύτη after οἵα, a Semitic-sounding emphasis.

senses.label: As, such as (correlative)
senses.definition: Compares kinds: 'as the one is, so are the others', often paired with τοιοῦτος.
senses.note: 'As was the earthy man, so are those who are earthy' (1CO 15:48).

senses.label: What kind of (indirect question)
senses.definition: Introduces an indirect question about the character or nature of something.
senses.note: 'You know what kind of men we proved to be among you' (1TH 1:5).

senses.label: Not as though (οὐχ οἷον ὅτι)
senses.definition: An elliptical idiom denying a possible inference: 'it is not as if', 'by no means is it the case that'.
senses.note: Paul denies that Israel's unbelief means God's word has failed.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses οἷος to compare character and conduct: what he is in letters he will be in person (2CO 10:11), what the Corinthians are versus what he wishes them to be (2CO 12:20), and what persecutions he endured (2TI 3:11).

study.translationNote: Because the word describes quality rather than identity, English renders it variously: 'such as', 'as', 'what manner of', or recasts the clause ('unmatched', 'unequalled'). In LUK 9:55 the words 'you do not know what kind of spirit you are of' are absent from many early manuscripts, so many modern versions omit or footnote them.

background.note: A contract of AD 17 requires a slave to return a mill safe and undamaged, 'in the condition in which he received it' (οἷον without τοιοῦτος).
The common idiom οἷός τε 'able to' appears in a second-century letter: the official 'might even have' proscribed you.

study.exegesisTip: Ask 'what sort?' when you meet οἷος: it describes kind and character, not simply identity. In ROM 9:6 the idiom introduces Paul's whole argument in Romans 9–11 by ruling out the conclusion that God's promise has failed.

study.summary: Active, to make stop or restrain; middle, to stop, cease. Usually it is used with a participle ('stop doing'), and very often negated: the apostles 'did not stop' teaching, Paul 'does not stop' praying. In 1 Corinthians 13:8 tongues 'will cease'.

senses.label: Restrain, keep from (active)
senses.definition: To make something stop or hold it back.
senses.note: 'Let him keep his tongue from evil', quoting Psalm 34.

senses.label: Come to an end
senses.definition: Middle: of an activity or condition ceasing.
senses.note: The storm ceased; the uproar ceased; tongues will cease.

senses.label: Stop doing something
senses.definition: Middle with a participle: to finish or leave off an action.
senses.note: Hebrews argues that if sacrifices had really cleansed, they would have stopped being offered.

senses.label: Not stop (constant activity)
senses.definition: Negated with a participle: to keep doing something without letting up, sometimes for good, sometimes for evil.
senses.note: Paul's prayers 'without stopping'; Elymas 'will not stop perverting the straight paths of the Lord'.

senses.label: Be done with sin
senses.definition: To have ceased from sin, of one who has suffered in the flesh.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the negated form to portray tireless persistence, whether of the apostles in teaching, of Paul in admonishing, or of opponents in speaking against the temple and the law.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: 'I do not stop' is Paul's way of describing unceasing thanksgiving and intercession for churches.

study.translationNote: In 1 Corinthians 13:8 most versions translate 'cease' for both tongues and the other gifts, though Paul uses παύσονται for tongues and a different verb (καταργηθήσονται, 'be done away') for prophecy and knowledge. Some versions try to show the difference.

background.note: Used from Homer: Athena comes down from heaven to check (stop) Achilles' anger.
A warning of about 245 BC: if you do not cease your malpractices in the village, you will be sorry.
A fourth-century AD letter says that if a troublemaker does not desist, he will come into the official's hands again.

study.exegesisTip: Check whether the verb is negated: οὐ παύομαι with a participle is an emphatic way of saying 'keep on, constantly', not merely 'not stop'.
study.caution: Some argue from the middle voice in 1CO 13:8 that tongues will 'cease of themselves' (at an earlier point than prophecy and knowledge). Many scholars think the change of verb is stylistic, and the passage alone does not establish when the gifts cease.

study.summary: To give to drink or to water. Used of giving water to the thirsty (a mark of true discipleship), of offering sour wine to Jesus on the cross, of watering animals and plants, and figuratively of feeding new believers milk, of the Spirit given to all believers, and of Babylon's intoxicating wine.

senses.label: Give someone a drink
senses.definition: To provide drink for a thirsty person, as an act of kindness.
senses.note: Even a cup of cold water given to a disciple will be rewarded.

senses.label: Offer a drink to the crucified Jesus
senses.definition: Holding up a sponge of sour wine for Jesus to drink.

senses.label: Water an animal
senses.definition: To lead livestock to water.
senses.note: Jesus' argument: if you water an ox on the Sabbath, how much more may a woman be freed.

senses.label: Water plants (ministry as farming)
senses.definition: To irrigate a planted crop; Paul's image of the work of those who build on another's planting.
senses.note: 'I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth' (1CO 3:6).

senses.label: Make drink (figurative)
senses.definition: To give someone something to take in, whether teaching, the Spirit, or judgment.
senses.note: Milk for infants in the faith; the one Spirit; Babylon's wine of passion.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: In the judgment of the nations, giving drink to the thirsty is giving drink to the Son of Man himself; failing to do so is failing him.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the agricultural sense for ministry (planting and watering) and the drinking sense for the Spirit received by every believer.

study.translationNote: In 1CO 12:13 English versions differ: 'made to drink of one Spirit' (KJV, ESV), 'given the one Spirit to drink' (NIV); a few suggest 'drenched/saturated with one Spirit', drawing on the verb's sense of watering or irrigating land.

background.note: Plato describes the charioteer giving his horses nectar to drink, with two accusatives as in Mark 9:41.
In Genesis a spring rose and watered the whole face of the ground; the Greek Old Testament often uses the verb for watering land.
Third-century BC workers report that they are making conduits and irrigating: irrigation is the usual sense in Egyptian papyri.
A first-century letter complains that the water hardly irrigates a single plot.

study.exegesisTip: The verb is causative ('make to drink'), so the subject provides drink and the person or plant receives it. In 1CO 12:13 God is the implied giver and all believers alike are given the Spirit.
study.caution: Interpreters disagree whether 1CO 12:13 'made to drink of one Spirit' refers to conversion, baptism, the Lord's Supper, or a later experience; the parallel with 'baptized into one body' in the same verse suggests an experience common to all believers.

study.summary: To say beforehand: to predict what will happen (of prophets and Scripture), to warn in advance, or to repeat something already said earlier. In the NT it mostly appears in the forms προεῖπον and προείρηκα.

senses.label: Foretell, predict (prophecy)
senses.definition: Of Scripture, prophets or apostles announcing in advance what would come to pass.
senses.note: The Holy Spirit 'foretold through the mouth of David' (ACT 1:16).

senses.label: Tell in advance, forewarn
senses.definition: To warn people ahead of time about trouble or judgment so that it does not take them by surprise.
senses.note: 'See, I have told you in advance' (MAT 24:25).

senses.label: Say before, repeat a warning
senses.definition: To refer back to what the writer has already said, in the letter or on an earlier visit, often a solemn warning restated.
senses.note: 'As I warned you before, I warn you now' (GAL 5:21).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb to stress that his warnings are not new: what he says now he has said before, especially about judgment and false gospels.

authorNotes.author: Jude
authorNotes.note: Jude, like 2 Peter, appeals to the words foretold by the apostles, that scoffers would come in the last time.

study.translationNote: Translations vary between 'foretold', 'said before', 'warned' and 'told you in advance', because the verb covers both genuine prediction and simply 'having said earlier'.

background.note: Herodotus uses it of an oracle predicting what will happen.
In Homer the verb has a quite different sense, 'picked out, chosen', of the leading Athenians.
A marriage contract of Augustus' time speaks of terms which the parties settle with one another beforehand, showing the plain time-sense of the prefix.

study.exegesisTip: Ask what the 'before' refers to: an Old Testament prophecy (ACT 1:16; ROM 9:29), Jesus' own prediction (MAT 24:25), or the apostle's earlier preaching or visit (1TH 3:4; 2CO 13:2).
study.caution: In GAL 1:9 'as we have said before' may refer back to the previous verse or to what Paul said when he first preached in Galatia; both views are held. Some older lexicons also allowed a sense 'declare plainly' in passages such as GAL 5:21, but most take it as a time reference.

study.summary: To shake or make sway, as wind, flood or earthquake does; then figuratively to unsettle, disturb, or stir up. It describes a reed in the wind, a house in a flood, the heavenly powers at the end, a well-shaken measure of grain, and believers shaken from composure.

senses.label: Shake physically
senses.definition: Of something swayed or jolted by wind, water or earthquake.
senses.note: The house built on rock could not be shaken by the flood (LUK 6:48).

senses.label: Shaken together (a measure)
senses.definition: Of grain shaken down in a container so that it settles and more can be added.
senses.note: 'Pressed down, shaken together, running over': a generous measure.

senses.label: Cosmic shaking
senses.definition: The upheaval of the heavenly powers and of all created things in God's final judgment.
senses.note: Hebrews contrasts the things that are shaken with the unshakable kingdom.

senses.label: Unsettle, shake in confidence
senses.definition: To disturb someone's security or composure.
senses.note: 'I will not be shaken', quoting Psalm 16:8; the Thessalonians should not be quickly shaken out of their minds.

senses.label: Stir up, agitate
senses.definition: To incite crowds to unrest.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews builds an argument on the verb: God's voice once shook the earth at Sinai, and his final shaking will remove everything created so that what cannot be shaken remains.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses it for both literal shakings (the place of prayer, the Philippian prison) and for stability of faith (the house on the rock, the Messiah who is not shaken).

background.note: Sirach says that heaven, the deep and the earth will be shaken when God visits; the future passive matches the Gospels' 'will be shaken'.
A magical text invokes the one who shook the heaven, language close to the cosmic shaking of the Gospels.
A man writes to his wife that her letters would have shaken a stone, so much did her words move him: the figurative sense in everyday speech.

study.exegesisTip: The basic picture is a ship tossed at sea (from σάλος, 'swell, tossing'). Paul's warning in 2TH 2:2 that believers should not be 'shaken from their mind' draws on this: being driven from the anchor of sound judgment.
study.caution: Some interpreters see in the 'reed shaken by the wind' (MAT 11:7) an allusion to Herod Antipas, whose coins bore a reed; others take it simply as a picture of a fickle man. The text does not decide.

study.summary: The clothes moth, whose larvae eat fabric; Jesus uses it as an image of how earthly wealth wastes away.

senses.label: Moth
senses.definition: The clothes moth that ruins stored garments, which were a major form of wealth in the ancient world; a picture of the decay that threatens all earthly treasure but cannot touch treasure in heaven.

background.note: Pindar says of gold that neither moth nor worm consumes it, a striking parallel to Jesus' saying about lasting treasure.

study.exegesisTip: Garments were stored wealth, so the moth stands beside rust and thieves as a threat to possessions, not merely a household nuisance.

study.summary: Fattened, fed up for slaughter; used only of the 'fattened calf' killed for the prodigal son's return.

senses.label: Fattened (for a feast)
senses.definition: Describes an animal specially grain-fed and kept for a special occasion; the fattened calf signals the father's lavish, celebratory welcome of his returning son.

background.note: Third-century BC papyri from the Zenon archive use the word of fattened geese, showing it was ordinary farm vocabulary.

study.summary: To dig, used by Luke of digging a foundation, digging around a tree, and manual labor generally.

senses.label: Dig
senses.definition: To dig the ground, whether excavating deep for a house's foundation, loosening soil around a fruit tree to fertilize it, or doing hard manual labor.
senses.note: In LUK 16:3 'to dig' stands for the lowest kind of manual labor, which the dismissed manager feels too weak to do.

background.note: Aristophanes already has the proverbial 'I do not know how to dig,' close to the steward's complaint in Luke.
A papyrus of 218 BC speaks of digging a foundation in order to build, just as in Jesus' parable of the two builders.

study.summary: A small boat or skiff, here the ship's boat towed or carried by Paul's vessel during the storm.

senses.label: Ship's boat, skiff
senses.definition: A light boat carried or towed by a larger ship, used for landing or escape; the sailors hauled it aboard in the storm and later tried to flee in it until the soldiers cut it loose.

background.note: Originally anything hollowed out (a tub, trough or bowl), the word was used for a light boat or skiff already in classical Greek.

study.summary: The leg, mentioned only in John's account of the soldiers breaking the legs of the crucified.

senses.label: Leg
senses.definition: The human leg from the hip down; breaking the legs hastened death on the cross, and John notes that Jesus' legs were not broken because he was already dead.

background.note: A complaint of 157 BC reports an assailant drawing a knife and striking the writer in the leg.

study.exegesisTip: John goes on to link the unbroken legs to Scripture: not a bone of the Passover lamb was to be broken.

study.summary: A tent or dwelling, used of a dwelling place for God and, figuratively, of the human body as a temporary tent.

senses.label: Dwelling for God
senses.definition: A dwelling place for God, as David sought to provide for the God of Jacob, recalling the tabernacle and the planned temple.

senses.label: Body as a tent
senses.definition: Figuratively, the body as a temporary tent in which a person lives during earthly life; laying it aside means death.

background.note: Xenophon uses the word for soldiers' quarters, showing its basic sense of a temporary encampment or lodging.

study.exegesisTip: Peter's 'tent' image, like Paul's tent imagery for the body, stresses that bodily life now is temporary and that death is a departure, not an end.

study.summary: To leap or spring, used by Luke of an unborn child leaping and of leaping for joy.

senses.label: Leap in the womb
senses.definition: Of John the Baptist as an unborn child stirring and leaping in Elizabeth's womb at Mary's greeting, which Elizabeth interprets as leaping for joy.

senses.label: Leap for joy
senses.definition: To jump or skip with exuberant gladness; Jesus tells persecuted disciples to rejoice and leap for joy because of their great reward.

background.note: Homer uses the word of young horses bounding across the fields.

study.exegesisTip: The same verb describes the twins struggling in Rebekah's womb in the Greek of GEN 25:22; Luke may intend an echo.

study.summary: Hardness of heart: a stubborn, unresponsive inner disposition toward God's will.

senses.label: Stubborn hardness of heart
senses.definition: Obstinate unresponsiveness to God, whether the human stubbornness that led Moses to permit divorce or the disciples' refusal to believe the reports of the risen Jesus.
senses.note: MAR 16:14 belongs to the longer ending of Mark, which many manuscripts lack.

background.note: The Greek Old Testament uses it for the Hebrew image of an 'uncircumcised heart' that must be circumcised.

study.exegesisTip: Jesus treats the divorce concession as an accommodation to human hardness, not as God's original design (MAT 19:8).

study.summary: Dark, full of darkness; used in Jesus' saying about the eye as the lamp of the body.

senses.label: Dark, full of darkness
senses.definition: Without light, the opposite of 'full of light'; in Jesus' image, a bad (diseased or ungenerous) eye leaves the whole person in inner darkness.

background.note: A papyrus of 159 BC speaks simply of going into a dark place.

study.summary: A worm or maggot, used in Jesus' warning about the undying worm of judgment.

senses.label: Worm of judgment
senses.definition: The worm that feeds on dead bodies, used figuratively (from ISA 66:24) for the unending ruin of those condemned to Gehenna: 'their worm does not die.'
senses.note: MAR 9:44 and 9:46 repeat 9:48 and are absent from many manuscripts.

background.note: Homer compares a fallen warrior to a worm lying stretched on the ground.

study.exegesisTip: The phrase quotes ISA 66:24, where the corpses of rebels against God lie outside Jerusalem consumed by worm and fire.

study.summary: A sponge, the one soaked in sour wine and lifted to Jesus on the cross.

senses.label: Sponge
senses.definition: A natural sponge, filled with sour wine and raised on a reed or hyssop stalk to the crucified Jesus.

background.note: Homer has Hephaestus wipe his face and hands with a sponge, showing its long everyday use.

study.summary: Ashes, whether worn with sackcloth in repentance or the ashes of the red heifer used for ritual cleansing.

senses.label: Ashes of repentance
senses.definition: In the phrase 'in sackcloth and ashes,' the outward sign of mourning and repentance that Tyre and Sidon would have shown had they seen Jesus' miracles.

senses.label: Ashes of the heifer
senses.definition: The ashes of the red heifer, mixed with water and sprinkled to cleanse those ritually defiled (NUM 19), which Hebrews contrasts with Christ's cleansing blood.

background.note: Euripides speaks of pouring ashes about the head as a sign of mourning.
An inscription prescribes ash from a sacred altar mixed with holy water as a remedy, a pagan parallel to the ritual use of ashes in HEB 9:13.

study.summary: Sown; in the plural as a noun, the sown fields or grainfields through which Jesus and his disciples walked on the Sabbath.

senses.label: Grainfields
senses.definition: Fields sown with grain; the setting where the disciples plucked heads of grain on the Sabbath, provoking a dispute with the Pharisees.

background.note: A fourth-century letter asks for nets because gazelles are spoiling the sown crops, using the same plural noun.

study.summary: Grapes or a bunch of ripe grapes.

senses.label: Grapes
senses.definition: Ripe grapes, used in Jesus' proverb that good fruit like grapes is not gathered from thornbushes, so a person's character shows in what they produce.

senses.label: Ripe grape clusters
senses.definition: The ripe grapes of 'the vine of the earth,' harvested in a vision of final judgment.

background.note: Homer describes a vineyard heavily laden with bunches of grapes.

study.summary: A roof; 'to come under someone's roof' means to enter their house.

senses.label: Roof
senses.definition: The (usually flat) roof of a house, which the friends of the paralyzed man dug through to lower him to Jesus.

senses.label: Under one's roof
senses.definition: In the idiom 'to come under my roof,' to enter someone's home as a guest; the centurion felt unworthy for Jesus to do so.

background.note: A papyrus of 241 BC reports owners taking down the upper stories of their houses to avoid having officials billeted on them.

study.summary: Narrow, describing the narrow gate that leads to life.

senses.label: Narrow (gate)
senses.definition: Narrow, confined; figuratively, the narrow gate of discipleship that leads to life, entered by few and requiring earnest effort, in contrast to the wide gate leading to destruction.

background.note: An imperial decree of AD 212 warns that no one should interpret its grace 'too narrowly,' showing the word's figurative use.

study.summary: To hem in, cramp, or confine; used by Paul in the passive of being crushed by pressure or restricted in affection.

senses.label: Be crushed, cornered
senses.definition: To be hemmed in with no way out; Paul says that though pressed on every side, he is never cornered or crushed.

senses.label: Be restricted (in affection)
senses.definition: To be cramped or restricted inwardly; Paul tells the Corinthians that any narrowness lies not in his love for them but in their own affections.

background.note: A papyrus of 241 BC uses it of being short of space: 'we are cramped for billets.'

study.summary: To make firm or strong; used of a lame man's healed feet and of churches strengthened in the faith.

senses.label: Make physically strong
senses.definition: To make firm or strong, of the lame man whose feet and ankles were made strong when he was healed in the name of Jesus.

senses.label: Strengthen in faith
senses.definition: Figuratively, to be established and made firm; the churches were strengthened in the faith.

background.note: Xenophon uses it of making a horse's feet firm and hard.

study.summary: To crown, whether a victorious athlete or Christ crowned with glory and honor.

senses.label: Crown a victor
senses.definition: To award the victor's wreath; an athlete is not crowned unless he competes by the rules.

senses.label: Crown with glory
senses.definition: Figuratively, to honor or exalt; God crowned humanity, and supremely Jesus, with glory and honor (from PSA 8).

background.note: A letter of 257 BC hopes Zenon will be 'crowned' through the boy he sponsored in the games, the athletic sense of 2TI 2:5.

study.summary: Kinsfolk, relatives, one's extended family.

senses.label: Relatives, kindred
senses.definition: A person's relatives or extended family as a group, such as Elizabeth's kin, the kindred Abraham left, or Jacob's whole household that came to Egypt.

background.note: A papyrus of AD 156 notes that two minors had no one else who could act as guardian by ties of kinship.

study.summary: To share or take part in something together with others, for good or ill.

senses.label: Participate in evil
senses.definition: To take part in or become an accomplice to wrongdoing; believers are told not to share in the fruitless deeds of darkness or in Babylon's sins.

senses.label: Share another's trouble
senses.definition: To share in someone's hardship by helping; the Philippians shared Paul's affliction through their gift.

background.note: Demosthenes uses it of having a joint share of glory.

study.summary: A fellow participant or partner who shares something together with others.

senses.label: Sharer in blessing
senses.definition: One who shares jointly in something good, such as the Gentile branch sharing the olive root's richness or Paul sharing in the gospel's blessings.

senses.label: Partner with someone
senses.definition: A partner with a person in a common experience: the Philippians as Paul's partners in grace, and John as fellow sharer in tribulation, kingdom and endurance.

study.summary: To live together with someone, especially to share in Christ's resurrection life.

senses.label: Live with Christ
senses.definition: To share Christ's life, now and in the age to come, as a consequence of having died with him.

senses.label: Live together with others
senses.definition: To share life together with people one loves; Paul says the Corinthians are in his heart to die together and to live together.

background.note: An epigram on the poet Menander speaks of his living together with Eros.

study.summary: To bear witness together with, confirming or corroborating another testimony.

senses.label: Conscience bears witness
senses.definition: Of the conscience adding its testimony, whether showing the law's work written on Gentile hearts or confirming that Paul speaks the truth.

senses.label: Spirit testifies with
senses.definition: Of the Holy Spirit joining his witness to that of the believer's own spirit that they are God's children.

background.note: In a document of AD 155 each attesting witness signs with the words 'I bear witness with (them) and seal with (them).'

study.caution: In ROM 8:16 interpreters debate whether the Spirit testifies 'with' our spirit (two witnesses) or simply 'to' it; the compound favors joint witness, but both readings are held.

study.summary: To fill completely, or (of time) to be fulfilled or arrive.

senses.label: Be swamped
senses.definition: Of a boat filling with water in a storm; Luke says 'they were being swamped,' meaning the boat and those in it.

senses.label: Time be fulfilled
senses.definition: Of an appointed time arriving or being completed, such as the days before Jesus' ascension or the day of Pentecost.

background.note: Thucydides uses it of fully manning ships.
A papyrus of 13 BC uses it of a period of time being completed, as in Luke's usage.

study.exegesisTip: LUK 9:51 presents Jesus' journey to Jerusalem as the fulfilling of a divinely appointed time.

study.summary: To gather together or assemble people.

senses.label: Assemble, gather together
senses.definition: To bring people together or (passive) to be gathered, as the disciples gathered after the resurrection, believers praying at Mary's house, or Demetrius assembling the craftsmen.

background.note: A fourth-century report speaks of having assembled the leading magistrates.

study.summary: In the phrase with 'account,' to settle accounts or make a reckoning.

senses.label: Settle accounts
senses.definition: A business term for reckoning up accounts with servants or debtors; in Jesus' parables it pictures God's day of reckoning.

background.note: The phrase 'to settle an account with' appears in first-century business accounts, showing it was everyday commercial language.

study.summary: A fellow prisoner, one who shared Paul's imprisonment.

senses.label: Fellow prisoner
senses.definition: One imprisoned together with Paul; properly a fellow prisoner of war, used of co-workers like Andronicus and Junia, Aristarchus and Epaphras who shared his captivity.

study.caution: It is debated whether Paul always means literal imprisonment alongside him or sometimes speaks figuratively of being fellow 'captives' of Christ; most take it literally.

study.summary: To mix with, associate closely with; used in instructions about keeping company with unrepentant people.

senses.label: Associate with
senses.definition: To mingle socially and keep close company with someone; Paul forbids such association with a professing believer living in open sin or refusing apostolic instruction, so that he may be ashamed.

study.exegesisTip: Paul clarifies in 1CO 5:10–11 that he means church members, not unbelievers in the world; in 2 Thessalonians the aim is correction, still treating the person as a brother.

study.summary: To be carried away together with; used of being swept along by others' error, and of associating with the lowly.

senses.label: Be carried away
senses.definition: To be swept along with others, as Barnabas was carried away by hypocrisy and believers might be carried away by the error of the lawless.

senses.label: Associate with the lowly
senses.definition: To accommodate oneself to or go along with humble people (or humble things), rather than aiming at lofty matters.

study.translationNote: In ROM 12:16 'the lowly' may be people or humble tasks, so versions vary between 'associate with the lowly' and 'give yourselves to humble tasks'.

background.note: A third-century BC papyrus uses the passive of farmers 'arrested with us,' i.e., led away together.

study.summary: To die together with someone, used of loyalty unto death and of the believer's union with Christ in his death.

senses.label: Die alongside a person
senses.definition: To share another's death, as an expression of devoted loyalty or of a bond so close that life and death are shared.

senses.label: Die with Christ
senses.definition: To share in Christ's death through union with him, the ground for the assurance of also living with him.

background.note: Herodotus already uses the verb for dying together with another person.

study.exegesisTip: In 2 Corinthians 7:3 'to die together and to live together' is a set expression of unbreakable friendship; Paul applies it to his bond with the Corinthians.

study.summary: To raise up together with, used by Paul of believers being raised with Christ.

senses.label: Raised with Christ
senses.definition: God's act of raising believers to new life together with Christ, sharing his resurrection; in the passive, 'to be raised with' him.

study.exegesisTip: The verb is paired with 'buried with' (Col 2:12) and 'seated with' (Eph 2:6): Paul views the believer's new life as a present participation in Christ's resurrection, which then grounds the call to seek the things above (Col 3:1).

study.summary: To run together, of crowds rushing to a place, and figuratively of joining others in a headlong course of conduct.

senses.label: Run together, gather
senses.definition: Of a crowd hurrying from many places to assemble at one spot.

senses.label: Plunge in with others
senses.definition: Figuratively, to rush along with others into the same way of life.

background.note: In Homer the verb describes warriors running together to meet in battle.

study.summary: Slaughter, the killing of animals for food or sacrifice, used in the NT in images of helpless victims and of judgment.

senses.label: Slaughter
senses.definition: The killing of animals; used figuratively of the innocent led to death like sheep and of a day of slaughter that pictures coming judgment.

study.exegesisTip: Acts 8:32 and Romans 8:36 both quote the Greek Old Testament (Isa 53:7; Ps 44:22). In James 5:5 the rich fatten themselves 'in a day of slaughter', like animals feeding on the very day they are to be killed.

study.summary: An adverb meaning almost or nearly.

senses.label: Almost, nearly
senses.definition: Qualifying a statement of extent, especially with 'all' or 'whole': nearly the entire city, province or set of things.

background.note: In Homer the adverb is used of place, 'near, close by'; the sense 'almost' is the later and NT use.

study.summary: Soundness of mind: sanity as opposed to madness, and the self-control or moderation that flows from it.

senses.label: Sanity, sound mind
senses.definition: Rational good sense, the opposite of madness.

senses.label: Self-control, moderation
senses.definition: Discreet, modest self-restraint in conduct and desires.

background.note: Xenophon uses the word for sanity as opposed to madness, the same contrast as in Paul's reply to Festus.

study.exegesisTip: Paul answers Festus's charge 'You are mad' by claiming words 'of truth and soberness', using the classical opposite of madness.

study.summary: A tax or toll office, the booth where Matthew (Levi) sat collecting taxes when Jesus called him.

senses.label: Tax booth, toll office
senses.definition: The place where taxes, customs or tolls were collected.

background.note: An inscription from Ephesus mentions those doing business at the custom-house for fish.

study.summary: Four-footed; in the NT always as a noun for four-footed animals.

senses.label: Four-footed animals
senses.definition: Quadrupeds, land animals as one class of creature alongside wild beasts, reptiles and birds.

background.note: Used of four-footed animals, i.e. livestock, in a third-century BC papyrus.

study.summary: To be tetrarch, to rule as a subordinate prince over a region.

senses.label: Rule as tetrarch
senses.definition: To govern a territory as a tetrarch under Roman authority; said of Herod Antipas, Philip and Lysanias.

study.exegesisTip: Luke uses the verb three times in one verse to date the start of John the Baptist's ministry within the political world of the day.

study.summary: Art, skill or craft, including a person's trade.

senses.label: Skill, craftsmanship
senses.definition: The skill of a craftsman shaping material, as in idols carved by human art.

senses.label: Trade, occupation
senses.definition: A craft practised as a living.

background.note: Common for one's trade, as in 'a river fisherman by trade'.

study.summary: A watching or keeping: concretely custody or prison, and abstractly the keeping or observance of commandments.

senses.label: Custody, prison
senses.definition: Being held under guard; the place of detention.

senses.label: Keeping, observance
senses.definition: The keeping of God's commandments.

background.note: Used of handing persons over into custody, as in Acts.

study.summary: To pluck or pull off, used of the disciples picking heads of grain on the Sabbath.

senses.label: Pluck, pick
senses.definition: To pull off by hand, of heads of grain picked while passing through a field.

background.note: Used of workers plucking fodder for animals.

study.summary: An inferential particle: therefore, accordingly, well then.

senses.label: Therefore, then
senses.definition: Draws a conclusion or practical consequence from what precedes.

background.note: Found in a second-century advocate's speech, placed after the first word as in classical usage.

study.summary: On the contrary, instead, contrariwise.

senses.label: On the contrary
senses.definition: Introduces the opposite course of action or the opposite of what might be expected.

study.summary: To tremble, especially with fear or awe.

senses.label: Tremble with fear
senses.definition: To shake with fear, as the healed woman did before Jesus.

senses.label: Stand in awe, fear
senses.definition: To be afraid of or show reverent fear toward something; with a participle, to be afraid to do something.

background.note: Homer uses it of the body trembling with fear.

study.summary: A beaten track or path, used in the Isaiah quotation about John the Baptist.

senses.label: Path, beaten track
senses.definition: A worn path or way; figuratively, the road made ready for the Lord's coming.

background.note: Used in a land document of a path marking a boundary.

study.summary: To gather in a crop, especially grapes at the vintage.

senses.label: Gather grapes, harvest
senses.definition: To gather ripe fruit; used literally and in the image of the earth's vine harvested for judgment.

background.note: Used of gathering olives from the fruit crop.

study.summary: To make blind, used in the NT only figuratively of spiritual blindness.

senses.label: Blind spiritually
senses.definition: To deprive of spiritual perception so that a person cannot see or understand the truth.

background.note: Herodotus uses the verb of literally blinding someone.

study.exegesisTip: The blinding is attributed to God's judicial hardening (John 12:40, quoting Isaiah), to 'the god of this age' (2 Cor 4:4), and to the darkness of hatred (1 John 2:11).

study.summary: To be puffed up with conceit, literally to be wrapped in smoke, so that one's judgment is clouded by pride.

senses.label: Be conceited, puffed up
senses.definition: In the passive, to be blinded by pride or arrogance, losing sound judgment.

background.note: Demosthenes uses the perfect passive for being deluded or out of one's senses.

study.exegesisTip: The image is of smoke clouding the mind: pride both inflates and blinds, so the conceited person 'understands nothing' (1 Tim 6:4).

study.summary: Openly or publicly, and also clearly or distinctly.

senses.label: Openly, publicly
senses.definition: In plain view of others, as opposed to in secret.

senses.label: Clearly, distinctly
senses.definition: Plainly and unmistakably, of a vision seen clearly.

background.note: Paired with its opposite in the phrase 'neither secretly nor openly'.

study.summary: Sorcery or witchcraft, from the use of drugs, potions and spells.

senses.label: Sorcery, magic arts
senses.definition: Magic practices involving drugs, potions or spells, condemned among works of the flesh and as a means of deceiving the nations.

background.note: Earlier the word meant the use of drugs, especially medicines.
Used in a charge of poisoning, a step toward the sense of sorcery.

study.caution: In Revelation 9:21 the critical text reads a related word for drugs or magic potions, so most modern editions have this word only in Galatians 5:20 and Revelation 18:23.

study.summary: To assert, affirm or claim, often of a claim the narrator does not endorse.

senses.label: Assert, claim
senses.definition: To state something as true, whether an accusation, an affirmation, or a self-description.

background.note: Used of someone professing to be a creditor, an allegation rather than an established fact.

study.summary: Light or brightness, of the moon or a lamp.

senses.label: Light, radiance
senses.definition: The light given off by a shining body, such as the moon or a lamp.

study.caution: In Luke 11:33 several manuscripts and editions read the common word for light instead.

study.summary: To utter a sound or speak, used of speaking out, a donkey speaking, and arrogant talk.

senses.label: Speak, utter
senses.definition: To speak out or utter words, whether bold speech, a miraculous voice, or boastful words.

background.note: Herodotus uses it of speaking with a human voice, comparable to Balaam's donkey.

study.summary: Hospitable, literally 'loving strangers'.

senses.label: Hospitable
senses.definition: Ready to welcome and care for guests and travellers, a quality required of overseers and expected of all believers.

background.note: Homer uses it of people who welcome strangers.

study.summary: To make something one's ambition, to strive eagerly.

senses.label: Aspire, strive eagerly
senses.definition: To set one's heart on a goal and pursue it earnestly; in the NT the goals are preaching where Christ is unknown, pleasing the Lord, and living quietly.

background.note: In everyday letters it means little more than 'be eager', as in being eager to remain with someone.

study.exegesisTip: The word originally meant 'love honour'. Paul turns it to unexpected goals, such as making it one's ambition to live quietly (1 Thess 4:11).

study.summary: Fearful, terrible, causing fear; used in Hebrews of judgment and of the Sinai theophany.

senses.label: Terrifying, dreadful
senses.definition: Causing fear or dread, of God's judgment and of the awesome sight at Sinai.

background.note: A Christian amulet calls God's name 'the terror of thy foes'.

study.summary: To fence in, stop or shut, used of shutting mouths and silencing.

senses.label: Shut, stop up
senses.definition: To close something off, literally the mouths of lions.

senses.label: Silence
senses.definition: Figuratively, to silence speech or put a stop to boasting.

background.note: Used of a door blocked up with bricks.
