study.summary: A guard or sentry, here the guards of a prison.

senses.label: Guard, sentry
senses.definition: One posted to watch over a prison and its prisoners.

background.note: Common for guards ordered to keep watch.

study.summary: Natural, either in accordance with nature or governed by mere instinct.

senses.label: According to nature
senses.definition: In keeping with the created order, contrasted with what is 'against nature'.

senses.label: Creatures of instinct
senses.definition: Driven by mere natural instinct like animals without reason.

study.translationNote: In 2 Peter 2:12 versions vary between 'born mere animals', 'creatures of instinct' and 'natural brute beasts'; the point is that these men act like irrational animals driven by instinct.

background.note: An adoption deed speaks of a 'true and natural' son, born of oneself.

study.summary: To grow or spring up, used of seed sprouting from the ground and, figuratively, of a bitter root that springs up in a community.

senses.label: Sprout, come up (of seed)
senses.definition: Of seed in the parable of the sower: to come up out of the ground and grow, whether to wither on rock or to bear fruit in good soil.

senses.label: Spring up (figurative)
senses.definition: Of a 'root of bitterness' that grows up within the church and causes trouble, defiling many.
senses.note: The image echoes Deuteronomy's warning against a root bearing poison and wormwood.

background.note: Common in everyday documents for plants and trees growing on a property.

study.summary: The adverb 'yesterday', used literally of the previous day and, in Hebrews, of the past as a whole.

senses.label: Yesterday (the previous day)
senses.definition: The day before the present one: the hour the official's son recovered, or the day Moses killed the Egyptian.

senses.label: Yesterday (the past)
senses.definition: Paired with 'today' and 'forever' to express the unchanging identity of Jesus Christ through all time past, present and future.

background.note: Used in ordinary letters and reports to date an event to the day before, e.g. 'in the evening of yesterday'.

study.caution: Many editions spell this word ἐχθές in all three verses; the meaning is identical.

study.summary: Snow, used in the NT only as the standard of dazzling whiteness in descriptions of heavenly glory.

senses.label: Snow (image of whiteness)
senses.definition: Snow as the comparison for brilliant whiteness: the angel's clothing at the tomb, Jesus' garments at the transfiguration, and the hair of the glorified Christ.
senses.note: In MAR 9:3 the comparison 'as snow' is found in the Byzantine text but not in many critical editions.

background.note: From Homer on the ordinary word for snow, whether fallen or falling.

study.exegesisTip: REV 1:14 echoes the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:9, whose hair was white like wool; John applies this image to the risen Christ.

study.summary: An anointing, used by John of the gift believers have received from the Holy One that teaches them the truth and remains in them.

senses.label: Spiritual anointing
senses.definition: The anointing believers have received from God (the Holy One), which abides in them and teaches them, so that they know the truth and are not dependent on false teachers; generally understood of the Holy Spirit.

background.note: Used of the anointing oil with which Aaron and the priests were consecrated.

study.exegesisTip: John's word plays on 'Christ' (the Anointed One) and contrasts with the 'antichrists' mentioned just before: true believers share in the anointing of the Anointed One.
study.caution: Interpreters differ on whether the word means the act of anointing or the anointing substance itself (the 'oil', i.e. the Spirit or the word received).

study.summary: False or lying, used of perjured witnesses and, as a noun, of liars.

senses.label: False (of witnesses)
senses.definition: Untrue, lying: the witnesses put up to accuse Stephen.

senses.label: Liar, one proved false
senses.definition: Of persons who are false: self-styled apostles exposed as liars, and liars as a class excluded from the new creation.

background.note: A letter warns its reader that someone is writing him false reports.

study.summary: A false witness: one who gives untrue testimony, used of Jesus' accusers and of Paul's own position if Christ were not raised.

senses.label: Perjured witness at trial
senses.definition: People who came forward with false testimony against Jesus before the Sanhedrin.

senses.label: False witness about God
senses.definition: One who misrepresents God; Paul says that if the dead are not raised, the apostles are found to be false witnesses who testified that God raised Christ.

study.exegesisTip: In 1CO 15:15 the genitive 'of God' may mean witnesses who misrepresent God or who testify against God; either way the apostolic proclamation would be a lie about God himself.
study.caution: Critical editions spell the word ψευδόμαρτυς; the meaning is the same.

study.summary: A small smooth stone or pebble, and, from the use of pebbles in voting, a vote.

senses.label: Pebble, small stone
senses.definition: A small stone: the white stone inscribed with a new name promised to the one who overcomes.

senses.label: Vote
senses.definition: A vote cast in a decision; Paul 'cast his vote' (or gave his approval) when believers were condemned to death.

study.caution: The background of the 'white stone' in REV 2:17 is uncertain; suggestions include a juror's vote of acquittal, an admission token to a feast, and an amulet bearing a secret name.

study.summary: A crumb or small scrap of food, such as falls from a table.

senses.label: Crumb from the table
senses.definition: Tiny morsels that fall from a table: what the dogs eat in the Canaanite woman's reply to Jesus, and what poor Lazarus longed for from the rich man's table.
senses.note: In LUK 16:21 the word 'crumbs' is in the Byzantine text; many critical editions read only 'what fell'.

study.summary: Cold, used of chilly weather and of the hardship of exposure.

senses.label: Cold
senses.definition: Cold weather or the experience of being cold: the night of Jesus' arrest, the rainy cold on Malta, and the exposure Paul endured in his ministry.

background.note: Appears in a first-century acrostic poem alongside winter.

study.summary: A vessel or container, used of flasks of oil and of containers for fish.

senses.label: Vessel, container
senses.definition: A container: the flasks in which the wise virgins carried extra oil, and the vessels into which good fish were sorted.
senses.note: In MAT 13:48 many critical editions read the related word ἄγγος with the same meaning.

background.note: Used of a jar for oil, just as in the parable of the virgins.

study.summary: A message or announcement, used by John of the core message heard from Christ.

senses.label: Message proclaimed
senses.definition: The message the apostles heard from Christ and announce: that God is light, and that believers should love one another.

background.note: From Homer on, a message or tidings, covering both the news and its delivery.

study.summary: Unshrunk or undressed, describing new cloth that has not been fulled.

senses.label: Unshrunk, new (cloth)
senses.definition: Of cloth not yet processed by the fuller, so it will shrink and tear away if sewn as a patch on an old garment.

background.note: A borrower pledges a 'new white shirt' described with this word, showing it meant fresh, unworn cloth.

study.summary: Purity, especially moral and sexual purity in conduct.

senses.label: Moral purity, chastity
senses.definition: Purity of life and conduct, including chastity in dealing with others; Timothy is to model it and to treat younger women as sisters 'in all purity'.

background.note: Used of purity in words and deeds.
Often used in inscriptions of ritual purifications connected with temple service.

study.summary: Ignorance, in the NT a culpable ignorance of God or of the truth.

senses.label: Culpable ignorance
senses.definition: A lack of knowledge that brings shame: some in Corinth had no real knowledge of God, and foolish people slander believers out of ignorance.

background.note: Used of humanity's ignorance of God in the Wisdom of Solomon.

study.summary: Having to do with the marketplace: of idlers who hang about the market, and of the court sessions held in the forum.

senses.label: Market loafers, rabble
senses.definition: Men who loiter in the marketplace, readily recruited for a mob; at Thessalonica they stirred up a riot against Paul.

senses.label: Court days
senses.definition: In the phrase 'court days are held': the regular sessions of the provincial court, where the Ephesian craftsmen could bring formal charges.

background.note: Used of the market crowd, the common people who frequent the agora.

study.summary: A catching, especially of fish, and the catch that results.

senses.label: Act of catching
senses.definition: Fishing as an activity: Peter is told to let down the nets 'for a catch'.

senses.label: The catch, haul
senses.definition: The fish actually taken, whose size astonished Peter and his companions.

background.note: In Homer and later Greek, hunting or the chase.

study.summary: The wild olive tree, Paul's image for Gentile believers grafted into God's people.

senses.label: Wild olive (Gentiles)
senses.definition: An uncultivated olive tree or shoot from one; Paul pictures Gentile believers as wild olive branches grafted into the cultivated olive tree of Israel.

study.exegesisTip: Paul himself calls the grafting 'contrary to nature' (ROM 11:24): the reversal of normal practice underlines that Gentile inclusion is grace, not merit.

study.summary: Sleeplessness, the sleepless nights Paul endured in his ministry.

senses.label: Sleepless nights
senses.definition: Going without sleep, whether through toil, danger or concern; listed among Paul's hardships as a servant of God.

background.note: Used of sleeplessness from pain or illness.

study.summary: The brotherhood: the Christian community viewed as one family of brothers and sisters.

senses.label: The Christian brotherhood
senses.definition: The whole community of believers as a family, to be loved, and found throughout the world sharing the same sufferings.

background.note: Used abstractly of the bond of brotherhood between peoples.

study.summary: Not evident: unseen or unmarked, and of a sound, indistinct or uncertain.

senses.label: Unseen, unmarked
senses.definition: Not visible or noticeable: graves people walk over without realizing it, a picture of the Pharisees' hidden defilement.

senses.label: Indistinct, uncertain
senses.definition: Of a trumpet call that gives no clear signal, so no one prepares for battle.

study.summary: Unceasing or constant, without let-up.

senses.label: Unceasing, constant
senses.definition: Continuing without interruption: Paul's unceasing anguish over Israel and his constant remembrance of Timothy in prayer.

background.note: The related adverb is used in documents of zeal shown unceasingly.

study.summary: To be impossible, used to declare that nothing is beyond the power of faith or of God.

senses.label: Be impossible
senses.definition: Of things: to be beyond doing. Nothing will be impossible for those with faith, and nothing (or no word) from God will be impossible.

study.translationNote: In LUK 1:37 versions differ: 'with God nothing will be impossible' versus 'no word from God will fail'. The Greek ῥῆμα can mean 'word' or 'thing', and the verb can mean 'be impossible' or 'be powerless'; both renderings affirm that what God has said he is able to do.

background.note: Of persons the verb kept its older meaning 'be unable', e.g. of a person unable to act while confined in a temple.

study.exegesisTip: LUK 1:37 echoes GEN 18:14, where the same verb is used: 'Is anything too hard for the LORD?'

study.summary: Unlawful or forbidden, contrary to accepted custom or divine standard.

senses.label: Against custom, forbidden
senses.definition: Contrary to accepted religious rule: Peter notes it was considered unlawful for a Jew to associate with a Gentile.

senses.label: Abominable, wicked
senses.definition: Morally outrageous and offensive to God: the 'lawless idolatries' of the readers' former pagan life.

background.note: Used of dead bodies being abhorrent to certain goddesses, supporting the sense 'abominable'.

study.summary: Lawless: used in 2 Peter of people who defy moral restraint.

senses.label: Lawless, unprincipled people
senses.definition: As a noun, those who disregard the moral law: the depraved men of Sodom who distressed Lot, and false teachers whose error could carry believers away.

background.note: A father breaks off his daughter's engagement because the young man had given himself to lawless deeds.

study.summary: Setting aside or annulment, used in Hebrews of the cancelling of the old commandment and the putting away of sin.

senses.label: Annulment of a law
senses.definition: The formal setting aside of the former priestly commandment because it was weak and useless.

senses.label: Putting away of sin
senses.definition: The doing away with sin, accomplished once for all by Christ's sacrifice of himself.

background.note: A legal term in the formula 'for annulment and cancellation' of a document.

study.exegesisTip: The legal flavour of the word suggests that sin is not merely covered but cancelled like a voided contract.

study.summary: To compete in an athletic contest, used as an image of disciplined Christian service.

senses.label: Compete as an athlete
senses.definition: To take part in the games; an athlete wins the crown only if he competes according to the rules, a picture of faithful endurance in ministry.

background.note: Used more broadly of contending in battle or struggle.

study.summary: Innocent or guiltless, used of Jesus' 'innocent blood' and of Pilate's claim to be free of guilt for it.

senses.label: Innocent, guiltless
senses.definition: Free from guilt: Judas confesses he betrayed innocent blood, and Pilate declares himself innocent of Jesus' blood.

background.note: In legal texts it often means 'unpunished', as of an assailant who might escape unpunished.

study.exegesisTip: 'Innocent blood' is an Old Testament phrase for the blood of one wrongly killed, whose guilt rests on those responsible.

study.summary: Eternal or everlasting, used of God's power and of the chains holding fallen angels.

senses.label: Eternal, everlasting
senses.definition: Without end (and of God, without beginning): God's eternal power seen in creation, and the everlasting chains in which rebellious angels are kept for judgment.

background.note: Common in inscriptions for perpetual honours and gifts meant to last forever.

study.summary: Modesty or reverence: a proper sense of shame before others and awe before God.

senses.label: Modesty, decency
senses.definition: A sense of propriety that avoids drawing improper attention; paired with self-control in how women adorn themselves.

senses.label: Reverence before God
senses.definition: Reverent awe in worship, paired with godly fear.
senses.note: Found here in the Byzantine text; many critical editions read δέος (awe).

background.note: Thucydides links this sense of shame closely with self-control (σωφροσύνη), the same pairing as in 1TI 2:9.

study.summary: Praise, specifically praise given to God.

senses.label: Praise to God
senses.definition: Praise offered to God: from the mouths of children (quoting Psalm 8), and by the crowd after the healing of the blind man near Jericho.

background.note: A poetic word; in Homer it can mean a tale or story as well as praise.

study.summary: An adjective meaning sudden or unexpected, used of the end-time day and of judgment that comes upon people without warning.

senses.label: Sudden, unexpected
senses.definition: Coming without warning; used predicatively with the force of an adverb ('suddenly') for the arrival of the day of the Lord or of destruction on the unprepared.

background.note: Used in classical prose of unforeseen, sudden events.

study.exegesisTip: Both uses are warnings: the suddenness is a danger only to those who are not watchful, which is why Jesus and Paul pair it with calls to stay alert.

study.summary: Captivity, the state of being a prisoner of war; by extension a body of captives.

senses.label: Captivity
senses.definition: The condition of being taken captive, here as a destined fate in the time of persecution.

senses.label: Body of captives
senses.definition: Abstract for concrete: a company of captives, in the quotation from Psalm 68 describing the triumphant ascent of Christ who 'led captivity captive'.

study.translationNote: In EPH 4:8 older versions keep the Hebrew idiom 'led captivity captive', while modern versions render it 'led captives' or 'led a host of captives', since the abstract noun stands for the captives themselves.

background.note: Frequently used in the Greek Old Testament both for captivity and for a band of captives taken in war.

study.summary: A verb meaning to take captive or lead away as a prisoner, used literally of a conqueror and figuratively of false teachers who captivate people.

senses.label: Lead captive
senses.definition: To take prisoners as a victorious conqueror, applied to Christ's ascent in triumph.

senses.label: Captivate, gain control over
senses.definition: Figuratively, to bring people under one's influence by deceit, as impostors do with vulnerable members of households.
senses.note: Many manuscripts here read the synonym αἰχμαλωτίζω.

background.note: Common in the Greek Old Testament for carrying off people and goods as plunder in war.

study.summary: Literally 'without evil': guileless, innocent, or (less favourably) naive and unsuspecting.

senses.label: Innocent, free from evil
senses.definition: Wholly without wickedness or malice; a quality of Christ as the perfect high priest.

senses.label: Naive, unsuspecting
senses.definition: Simple-minded and unaware of evil, and so easily deceived by smooth talk.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'simple', 'naive' and 'unsuspecting' in ROM 16:18 and 'innocent' or 'harmless' in HEB 7:26, reflecting the two sides of being 'without evil'.

background.note: In business documents it is used of goods in the passive sense 'undamaged'.

study.summary: An adjective meaning made of thorns, used of the crown placed on Jesus' head before the crucifixion.

senses.label: Made of thorns
senses.definition: Woven from thorny plants; describing the mocking crown the soldiers set on Jesus as a parody of royal honour.

background.note: Could also mean made of acacia (acantha) wood, as of a ship's mast.

study.exegesisTip: The thorny crown belongs with the purple robe as part of a mock coronation, which the Gospel writers present as unwittingly true: Jesus is indeed the King.

study.summary: An adjective meaning uncovered or unveiled, used of a woman's head in public prayer and prophecy.

senses.label: Uncovered, unveiled
senses.definition: Without a covering on the head; Paul argues it is shameful for a woman to pray or prophesy with her head uncovered.

background.note: Used of the bared head of a person with a skin disease, a sign of mourning and uncleanness.

study.caution: Whether the covering in 1 Corinthians 11 is a veil, a shawl, or the woman's own hair (cf. the argument later in the chapter) is debated; the word itself means simply 'uncovered'.

study.summary: An adjective describing a person not legally condemned, used by Paul to protest the beating of Roman citizens without due process.

senses.label: Uncondemned, without trial
senses.definition: Not having been convicted or even given a proper hearing; Paul stresses that Roman citizens were punished without legal process.

study.translationNote: Older versions render 'uncondemned'; many modern versions prefer 'without a trial', since the point is that no case had been heard at all.
study.caution: The formal meaning is 'uncondemned', but the context suggests 'untried'; some scholars think Luke uses it to render the Roman legal phrase for a case not yet investigated.

study.summary: A verb meaning to ascertain exactly or inquire carefully, used of Herod finding out from the Magi when the star appeared.

senses.label: Ascertain exactly
senses.definition: To learn precisely by careful questioning; Herod fixed the exact time of the star's appearance, which then set the age limit for his massacre.

background.note: Used in classical Greek for understanding something thoroughly or investigating accurately.

study.exegesisTip: Herod's careful inquiry in MAT 2:7 explains the deliberate 'two years old and under' of MAT 2:16.

study.summary: An adjective meaning 'at the extreme corner', used as a noun for the cornerstone, applied to Christ.

senses.label: Cornerstone
senses.definition: The foundational corner stone that fixes the line of the whole building; Christ is the stone on which God's people, his temple, are built and aligned.

study.translationNote: Some prefer 'capstone' or 'keystone' (a top stone), but the Isaiah background speaks of a stone laid in the foundation, so most versions use 'cornerstone'.

background.note: Apparently first used in the Greek Isaiah for the precious stone God lays in Zion's foundation.

study.caution: Whether the stone is a foundation cornerstone or a crowning top stone is debated; the Isaiah quotation in 1 Peter favours a foundation stone.

study.summary: Arrogant boasting or pretension: the swaggering self-confidence of one who claims more than is real.

senses.label: Arrogant boasting
senses.definition: Vaunting presumption; in James, boastful plans that ignore God's control over the future (plural: arrogant schemes).

senses.label: Pretentious pride
senses.definition: Proud display and self-sufficiency grounded in one's possessions and status in this life.

study.translationNote: 'The pride of life' in 1JO 2:16 is rendered by some as 'boasting about what one has' or 'pride in possessions', since βίος here means one's livelihood or means of life.

background.note: In classical Greek the word meant false pretension or imposture, the claiming of what one does not have.

study.summary: A boaster or braggart: one who makes empty claims about himself.

senses.label: Boaster, braggart
senses.definition: A person who parades pretended merits; listed among the vices of a humanity in revolt against God.

background.note: Classically used of charlatans and quacks, especially sophists who claimed knowledge they did not possess.

study.exegesisTip: In both lists it stands next to ὑπερήφανος ('arrogant'): the boaster displays outwardly the pride the arrogant person holds within.

study.summary: A verb for raising a loud cry, used in the NT of wailing mourners and of a clanging cymbal.

senses.label: Wail loudly
senses.definition: To cry aloud in grief, as the mourners did at the house of Jairus.

senses.label: Clang, clash
senses.definition: Of a cymbal, to make a loud, harsh noise; an image of speech without love.

background.note: Originally meant to raise the war-cry 'alala'.

study.summary: Flour or meal, ground grain used for making bread.

senses.label: Flour, meal
senses.definition: Ground wheat; in the parable a woman hides leaven in a large quantity of flour until the whole is leavened.

background.note: Classically wheat-meal, as distinct from barley-meal.

study.exegesisTip: Three measures of flour is a very large amount (enough bread for a large gathering), stressing the pervasive growth of the kingdom from a small beginning.

study.summary: A verb meaning to speak the truth, or more broadly to be truthful.

senses.label: Speak the truth
senses.definition: To tell the truth honestly, even at the cost of a relationship, or to hold to and speak the truth in a loving way within the church.

study.translationNote: In EPH 4:15 some versions broaden it to 'holding to the truth' or 'living the truth', since the participle may describe a truthful life as well as truthful speech.

background.note: Standard classical verb for speaking the truth.

study.summary: A verb meaning to grind grain, as women did daily with a hand mill.

senses.label: Grind grain
senses.definition: To grind meal at a mill; the picture of two women at ordinary work when the Son of Man comes, one taken and one left.

background.note: This later form of the verb appears in everyday documents of the Roman period.

study.summary: A threshing floor, where harvested grain was beaten out and winnowed; by extension the grain lying on it.

senses.label: Threshing floor
senses.definition: The hard, open floor where grain was threshed and winnowed; John the Baptist pictures the Messiah clearing it, separating wheat from chaff in judgment.
senses.note: The floor may stand by metonymy for the threshed grain on it.

background.note: Common in farm documents, which speak of the work of the threshing floor at harvest.

study.summary: An adjective meaning not quarrelsome or peaceable, required of church leaders and of all believers.

senses.label: Peaceable, not contentious
senses.definition: Not given to fighting or quarrelling; a gentle disposition expected of overseers and of Christians toward everyone.

background.note: Used in epitaphs to praise someone who lived without quarrelling among friends and family.

study.summary: An adverb meaning blamelessly, so that no fault can be charged.

senses.label: Blamelessly
senses.definition: In a manner open to no just accusation, whether of the apostles' conduct among believers or of believers kept whole until Christ's coming.

study.summary: An adjective meaning free from anxiety or care.

senses.label: Free from worry
senses.definition: Without anxious concern; Paul wants believers free from distracting cares.

senses.label: Out of trouble
senses.definition: Secure from consequences; the chief priests promise to keep the guards safe from punishment.

background.note: Common in letters telling someone to have no anxiety about a matter.

study.summary: An adjective meaning unchangeable or irrevocable, used of God's purpose and his oath-backed promise.

senses.label: Unchangeable
senses.definition: Unalterable and fixed; as a neuter noun, the unchangeableness of God's purpose, and of the two unchangeable things (his promise and his oath).

background.note: Used of a will that remained unchanged until the testator's death, a technical sense that strengthens the picture of heirs of the promise.

study.summary: An adjective meaning not to be regretted or taken back: irrevocable.

senses.label: Irrevocable
senses.definition: Not subject to change of mind; God's gifts and calling will not be withdrawn.

senses.label: Without regret
senses.definition: Never to be regretted; repentance that leads to salvation leaves nothing to regret.

study.translationNote: In 2CO 7:10 versions differ on whether 'without regret' goes with 'repentance' or with 'salvation'; the sense is much the same.

background.note: Used of pleasure that brings no regret afterwards.

study.summary: An adjective meaning without measure; in the phrase 'into the unmeasured' it means beyond proper limits.

senses.label: Beyond limits
senses.definition: With εἰς τὰ, boasting excessively or beyond the sphere God assigned; Paul refuses such boasting, unlike his rivals.

background.note: Used in a moral sense of what is immoderate or excessive.

study.exegesisTip: The word plays on μέτρον ('measure') in the same passage: Paul boasts only within the measure God has allotted.

study.summary: A casting net, thrown out by hand from the shore or shallows.

senses.label: Casting net
senses.definition: A circular net thrown to spread over and trap fish; Simon and Andrew were casting one when Jesus called them.
senses.note: In MAR 1:16 the critical text has the related verb instead of this noun.

background.note: The ordinary word for a casting-net in classical Greek.

study.summary: An adjective meaning blameless or without fault.

senses.label: Blameless, faultless
senses.definition: Free from any defect that would bring reproach; the character God's people should show as they await the Lord.
senses.note: In PHP 2:15 the critical text reads the near-synonym ἄμωμος.

background.note: Already in Homer in the sense blameless.

study.summary: A step; in the plural, a flight of stairs.

senses.label: Steps, stairway
senses.definition: The stairs leading up from the temple court to the Roman barracks, where Paul was carried by soldiers and then addressed the crowd.

background.note: Used of a flight of steps.

study.summary: A verb meaning to cause to be born again, used of God's giving believers new spiritual life.

senses.label: Give new birth
senses.definition: To beget anew; God by his mercy gives new life into a living hope, through imperishable seed, the word of God.

study.exegesisTip: Peter grounds the new birth in two things: the resurrection of Jesus (1PE 1:3) and the living word of God (1PE 1:23).

study.summary: A verb meaning to show clearly or to appoint publicly to a task.

senses.label: Appoint
senses.definition: To designate formally for a commission, as the Lord did with the seventy (or seventy-two).

senses.label: Show, make known
senses.definition: To reveal clearly which choice has been made; the apostles ask the Lord to show whom he has chosen.

background.note: In inscriptions it could mean publicly proclaim, as in declaring war.

study.summary: A verb meaning to receive or accept, whether welcoming guests or taking up promises.

senses.label: Welcome as guest
senses.definition: To receive and entertain hospitably, as Publius did Paul's company on Malta.

senses.label: Receive, accept
senses.definition: To take up and embrace something entrusted; Abraham had received God's promises yet offered up the son through whom they were to come.

background.note: In legal documents it means to undertake or take responsibility for something.

study.summary: A verb meaning to search out or look for diligently, especially for a person who is hard to find.

senses.label: Search for diligently
senses.definition: To seek a person with effort; Jesus' parents searching among relatives, and Barnabas seeking out Saul in Tarsus.

background.note: Used in official letters for hunting down missing persons, such as runaway slaves.

study.summary: A verb meaning to look at carefully or consider attentively.

senses.label: Observe closely
senses.definition: To examine with attention, as Paul viewed the Athenians' objects of worship.

senses.label: Consider thoughtfully
senses.definition: To reflect carefully on something; believers are to consider the outcome of their leaders' lives and imitate their faith.

study.summary: σκάνδαλον was first the trigger-stick of a trap, then a snare or an obstacle that trips someone. In the NT it is always figurative: a person, a thing or a message that makes someone fall into sin or unbelief, or that offends so deeply that people reject it. The crucified Messiah is the great σκάνδαλον of the gospel.

senses.label: Trap, snare that brings ruin
senses.definition: Something set in a person's way that catches them and brings them down, often in Old Testament quotations that pair it with 'snare' or 'net'.
senses.note: In REV 2:14 Balaam 'taught Balak to put a σκάνδαλον before the Israelites': a deliberate lure into idolatry and immorality (Num 25; 31:16).

senses.label: Cause of sin, enticement to fall away
senses.definition: A person or thing that leads others into sin or makes them abandon faith.
senses.note: Jesus says such stumbling blocks are inevitable in this age, but pronounces woe on the one through whom they come (MAT 18:7; LUK 17:1).

senses.label: Hindrance to God's purpose
senses.definition: One who stands in the way of God's will and tempts another to turn from it.
senses.note: Peter, a moment after being called the rock, becomes a stumbling stone to Jesus by urging him away from the cross.

senses.label: Offense that provokes rejection
senses.definition: Something so objectionable to people that they stumble over it and refuse to believe, especially the message of a crucified Messiah.
senses.note: In ROM 9:33 and 1PE 2:8 Christ himself is the 'rock of offense' of Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16 over which unbelieving Israel stumbles.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word for the 'offense of the cross' (GAL 5:11; 1CO 1:23), which he refuses to remove by preaching circumcision, and also for needless obstacles believers put in one another's way (ROM 14:13; ROM 16:17). The gospel's own offense must stand; any other stumbling block must go.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew stresses the judgment on those who cause others to fall: the angels will gather 'all causes of sin' out of the kingdom at the end of the age.

study.translationNote: English versions vary between 'stumbling block', 'offense', 'cause of sin', 'temptation' and 'snare'. The word joins two ideas English separates: an obstacle that trips someone (leading to sin or unbelief) and something that offends. 'Offense' alone can sound like mere annoyance; in the NT the result of a σκάνδαλον is a spiritual fall.

background.note: The Law forbids putting a stumbling block before the blind, the literal image behind the later figurative use.
An eighth-century official letter pairs it with 'pretext' (πρόφασιν ἢ σκάνδαλον), showing it later meant a ground for complaint or offense.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who falls and how: is the σκάνδαλον luring someone into sin (MAT 18:7), or is the gospel itself the thing people stumble over in unbelief (1CO 1:23)? Paul treats the first as something believers must avoid and the second as something they must never remove.
study.caution: Do not reduce the word to hurt feelings. In the NT it concerns falling into sin or away from faith, not simply being displeased.

study.summary: σφραγίζω means to seal: to press a seal on something to secure it, to close it from view, to mark it as someone's property, or to certify it as genuine. The NT uses all these ideas, from the sealed tomb of Jesus to believers sealed with the Holy Spirit as God's own.

senses.label: Seal for security
senses.definition: To fasten something with a seal so that it cannot be opened or tampered with.
senses.note: The authorities seal the stone of Jesus' tomb; an angel seals the abyss over Satan.

senses.label: Seal up, keep secret
senses.definition: To close a message or book under seal so that it is not disclosed.
senses.note: John is told to seal up what the seven thunders said, but not to seal the words of the prophecy of this book, because the time is near.

senses.label: Mark as belonging and protected
senses.definition: To put a mark of ownership on someone, setting them apart under the owner's protection.
senses.note: God's servants are sealed on their foreheads before judgment falls; believers are sealed with the Holy Spirit as God's possession until the day of redemption.

senses.label: Certify, attest, authenticate
senses.definition: To confirm something as genuine or approved, as a seal certifies a document.
senses.note: The one who accepts Jesus' testimony 'sets his seal' that God is true; the Father has set his seal on the Son as his authorized giver of life.

senses.label: Secure delivery (financial)
senses.definition: To complete and secure a transfer so that it reaches its recipients properly.
senses.note: Paul's 'having sealed to them this fruit' refers to safely completing delivery of the collection for Jerusalem.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Most occurrences are in Revelation, where sealing marks God's people for protection (REV 7:3-8) in contrast to the beast's mark, and also closes or opens revelation (REV 10:4; REV 22:10). In the Gospel the word is about attestation (JOH 3:33; JOH 6:27).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul links sealing with the gift of the Spirit: God seals believers and gives the Spirit as a down payment (2CO 1:22), and the sealing lasts 'for the day of redemption' (EPH 4:30). The seal is both ownership and guarantee.

study.translationNote: Most versions keep 'seal' throughout, but in JOH 3:33 and ROM 15:28 many paraphrase: 'certified', 'attested', 'safely delivered'. These renderings bring out the specific purpose of the sealing in each context.

background.note: Euripides uses the verb of sealing and unsealing a writing tablet.
A letter tells someone to seal seed in sacks so that it is ready for delivery; sealing was the last step before handing goods over, which illuminates Romans 15:28.
An agent is told to send a donkey 'to be sealed', that is, branded as property, a parallel to marking God's servants.
A shipmaster carrying grain is to seal a sample so that the cargo cannot be tampered with in transit.

study.exegesisTip: Ask what the seal does in each passage: secures, conceals, marks ownership, or certifies. In EPH 1:13 and EPH 4:30 the Spirit's seal both marks believers as God's and guarantees that he will complete their redemption.
study.caution: Whether 'sealing' with the Spirit in Paul refers to baptism, to a distinct later experience, or simply to receiving the Spirit at conversion is debated; the texts themselves tie it to believing and to the gift of the Spirit (EPH 1:13).

study.summary: τάλαντον first meant a balance, then a standard heavy weight (roughly 26 to 36 kg), and then a sum of money equal to that weight of silver or gold. A talent of silver was worth about 6,000 denarii, around twenty years of a laborer's wages. In the NT it appears only in two parables of Jesus in Matthew.

senses.label: An unpayable debt
senses.definition: A sum of money in talents owed to a king, multiplied to an amount no servant could ever repay.
senses.note: The 'ten thousand talents' is deliberately unpayable, the largest number and the largest unit of money then in use, set beside a fellow servant's debt of a hundred denarii.

senses.label: Money entrusted by a master
senses.definition: Large sums handed to servants to manage and increase during the master's absence, each 'according to his ability'.
senses.note: Even one talent was a fortune; the third servant's fault was not having little but refusing to use what he was given.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Only Matthew uses the word. In the unforgiving servant (MAT 18:23-35) it shows how great a debt God forgives; in the parable of the talents (MAT 25:14-30) it shows how much the master entrusts to his servants to use until his return.

study.translationNote: 'Talent' is kept in most versions, but modern English 'talent' (a natural gift) comes from this parable, not the other way round. Some versions give a value, such as 'bags of gold' or a footnote about wages, so readers grasp how large the sums are.

background.note: Homer uses the plural for a pair of scales, the original sense from which the weight and the money unit derive.
A first-century business letter speaks of selling goods 'for a talent', showing the word as an everyday unit of money.

study.exegesisTip: Work out the scale before interpreting the parables: even one talent was a fortune, so the servant who buried his one talent was not given 'little', and the forgiven debt of ten thousand talents is beyond any human repaying.
study.caution: Do not read the modern idea of personal abilities into the word. In the parable the talents are money entrusted by the master; what they stand for (the gospel, gifts, opportunities, responsibilities) must be argued from the context, not from the English word.

study.summary: τράπεζα is a table: the dining table, the sacred table of the bread of the Presence, and the money-changer's table or counter, which came to mean a bank. By extension it can mean the meal or provision set on a table, and Paul uses 'the Lord's table' for fellowship in the Lord's Supper.

senses.label: Dining table
senses.definition: A table at which people eat.
senses.note: In LUK 22:30 eating and drinking 'at my table in my kingdom' is a picture of honored fellowship with the Messiah.

senses.label: Meal, food provided
senses.definition: By extension, the food set out, a meal, or the provision and fellowship of a table.
senses.note: The jailer 'set a table' (served a meal) for Paul and Silas; in 1CO 10:21 the 'table of the Lord' and the 'table of demons' are meals of fellowship with the one honored.

senses.label: Sacred table in the tabernacle
senses.definition: The table in the Holy Place on which the bread of the Presence was set.

senses.label: Money-changer's table, bank
senses.definition: The table or counter where money was changed or deposited, hence a bank.
senses.note: In LUK 19:23 the master asks why his money was not put 'on the table', that is, deposited with bankers to earn interest.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke uses the word for the money table (LUK 19:23), for table fellowship in the kingdom (LUK 22:30), and for the daily food distribution in ACT 6:2, where the apostles refuse to leave the word of God 'to serve tables'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul contrasts the 'table of the Lord' with the 'table of demons' (1CO 10:21): eating at a table means sharing fellowship with the one it honors, so believers cannot take part in both.

study.translationNote: Usually 'table', but in LUK 19:23 versions vary between 'bank' and 'money table'; in ACT 16:34 'set food before them' or 'set a meal'. 'Wait on tables' in ACT 6:2 is usually understood of food distribution, though some take it of managing money.

background.note: Homer uses it for a household dining table.
A receipt records a tax paid 'into the bank' at Crocodilopolis to the banker, showing τράπεζα as an ordinary word for a bank.
A later Christian inventory lists a marble τράπεζα, the slab of the altar, the source of the modern Greek word for the altar-table.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether the table is literal furniture, a meal, or a bank. In 1CO 10:21 'table' stands for fellowship through a sacrificial meal, which is why Paul argues from it that idol feasts are incompatible with the Lord's Supper.
study.caution: ACT 6:2 is debated: most take 'serving tables' as distributing food to widows, but some argue (from the banking sense) that it means administering the common funds. Either way the apostles set it beside the ministry of the word.

study.summary: χορτάζω originally meant to feed animals with fodder, to fatten them. In everyday Koine it came to be used of people eating until they are full. The NT uses it for the crowds fed by Jesus, for hunger relieved, and in the Beatitudes for the full satisfaction God gives those who hunger for righteousness.

senses.label: Feed (animals), gorge
senses.definition: To feed to the full, used of birds gorging on flesh.
senses.note: The birds 'were gorged' with the flesh of God's defeated enemies, the old animal sense.

senses.label: Fill, satisfy with food
senses.definition: Of people: to feed until they have eaten enough; passive, to eat one's fill.
senses.note: Used in all the feeding miracles: 'they all ate and were satisfied'.

senses.label: Have enough (in need and plenty)
senses.definition: To have enough to eat, as opposed to going hungry; used of ordinary physical need.
senses.note: James condemns saying 'be warmed and filled' without giving what the body needs.

senses.label: Be satisfied by God (figurative)
senses.definition: To receive full satisfaction of a deep spiritual longing from God.
senses.note: Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness 'will be filled', a divine passive: God himself will satisfy them.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In JOH 6:26 Jesus rebukes the crowd for seeking him because they 'ate the loaves and were filled', not because they saw signs: physical fullness is set against the bread of life.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's only use (PHP 4:12) pairs being filled with being hungry: he has learned contentment in both.

study.translationNote: Rendered 'fed', 'filled', 'satisfied' or 'had their fill'. The word suggests eating to the point of full satisfaction, not just eating; in REV 19:21 'gorged' captures its original animal flavor.

background.note: Hesiod uses the verb for feeding oxen kept indoors, its original sense of feeding livestock.
Aristophanes comically uses it of feeding a dung-beetle as if it were a horse, showing the word still sounded like stable-feeding when used of others.

study.exegesisTip: Notice the contrast with hunger (πεινάω) in MAT 5:6, LUK 6:21 and PHP 4:12: the word describes the end of hunger, and in the Beatitudes it promises complete satisfaction, not partial relief.

study.summary: χόρτος means grass or green vegetation, including the young blades of grain. In the NT it is the grass people sat on when Jesus fed the crowds, the green growth of the field, and, following Isaiah 40, a picture of how quickly human life and glory fade.

senses.label: Grass, green growth of the field
senses.definition: Wild grass or green vegetation growing on the ground.
senses.note: Mark's 'green grass' (MAR 6:39) and John's 'much grass' (JOH 6:10) suggest the spring season of the feeding of the five thousand.

senses.label: Young blade of grain
senses.definition: The first green shoot of a cereal crop before the ear forms.
senses.note: In MAR 4:28 the earth produces 'first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain'.

senses.label: Image of transience
senses.definition: Grass that flourishes briefly and then withers or is burned, picturing the brevity of human life and glory.
senses.note: 1PE 1:24 quotes Isaiah 40:6-8: all flesh is grass, but the word of the Lord endures forever.

senses.label: Hay, worthless building material
senses.definition: Dried grass, a material that burns up at once.
senses.note: Paul lists 'hay' among materials that will not survive the testing fire.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James applies the withering grass to the rich man, who will fade away in the midst of his pursuits.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In Revelation the judgments strike grass and trees (REV 8:7), but the locusts are forbidden to harm the grass (REV 9:4), so that judgment falls on people, not creation.

study.translationNote: Usually 'grass', but 'blade' or 'stalk' in MAR 4:28 and MAT 13:26, and 'hay' in 1CO 3:12. These are one word whose meaning shifts with what is said of the growth.

background.note: Pindar uses the plural for the feeding-grounds or pastures of the Nemean lion, from the older sense of a feeding place.
Herodotus uses it for fodder.
A complaint reports that five hundred bundles of hay were carried off, showing the everyday agricultural sense.

study.exegesisTip: When grass appears in a teaching passage, look for the Isaiah 40 background: in MAT 6:30 it shows God's lavish care even for what lasts a day; in JAM 1:10-11 and 1PE 1:24 it shows how fleeting human status is.

study.summary: χωλός means lame, crippled in the feet or legs so that one limps or cannot walk. In the Gospels and Acts the healing of the lame is a sign of the messianic age foretold by Isaiah; Jesus also uses lameness in a startling saying about the cost of avoiding sin, and Hebrews uses it as a picture of weak believers.

senses.label: Lame, crippled (physical)
senses.definition: Unable to walk properly because of disability in the feet or legs.
senses.note: The man at the temple gate was lame 'from his mother's womb' (ACT 3:2), so his healing was undeniable.

senses.label: The lame as recipients of the kingdom
senses.definition: Lame people as a class among the needy whom the Messiah heals and invites.
senses.note: Jesus' answer to John the Baptist echoes Isaiah 35:6: 'the lame walk'. In Luke the lame are invited to the banquet in place of those who refused.

senses.label: Maimed (in a hyperbolic saying)
senses.definition: Crippled through losing a foot, in Jesus' warning that it is better to enter life maimed than to go to hell whole.

senses.label: Weak or limping (figurative)
senses.definition: Spiritually weak or faltering members of the community.
senses.note: Straight paths are to be made so that 'what is lame' is healed rather than put out of joint.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke shows the lame both invited to the kingdom feast (LUK 14:13; LUK 14:21) and healed through the apostles in Jesus' name (ACT 3:2; ACT 8:7; ACT 14:8), continuing Jesus' work in the church.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew records Jesus healing the lame in the temple itself (MAT 21:14), people otherwise restricted from approaching the holy place in tradition (cf. 2 Sam 5:8).

study.translationNote: Older versions use 'halt' or 'cripple', modern ones 'lame' or 'crippled'. In HEB 12:13 some versions render 'what is lame' and others 'the weak', interpreting the image.

background.note: Homer describes Thersites as lame in one foot.
A description of a person in a deed of sale lists 'straight-nosed, near-sighted, lame', showing the word as a plain descriptive term.

study.exegesisTip: Read the healings of the lame against Isaiah 35:6 ('then shall the lame leap like a deer'): they show the arrival of God's promised restoration, which is why Jesus cites them as proof to John the Baptist (MAT 11:5).

study.summary: ἄκανθα is a thorny plant, a thornbush or brier. In the NT it is always plural. Thorns choke the seed in the parable of the sower, cannot bear good fruit, form the mock crown pressed on Jesus' head, and mark land under a curse.

senses.label: Thorny weeds that choke
senses.definition: Thorny plants growing in a field that crowd out and smother the crop.
senses.note: Jesus explains the thorns as the worries of life and the deceitfulness of wealth that choke the word.

senses.label: Thornbush that bears no good fruit
senses.definition: A thornbush as the opposite of a fruitful plant, used to teach that character is known by its fruit.

senses.label: Crown of thorns
senses.definition: Thorny branches woven into a mock crown for Jesus.
senses.note: Meant as mockery of his kingship and probably also painful.

senses.label: Sign of cursed, worthless land
senses.definition: Thorns as the produce of ground that rejects cultivation and is near to being cursed.
senses.note: With 'thistles', an echo of the curse on the ground in Genesis 3:18.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses thorns and thistles (HEB 6:8), recalling Genesis 3:18, to warn that those who receive God's blessing yet produce no fruit are near to a curse.

study.translationNote: Rendered 'thorns', 'thornbushes' or 'briers'. The exact plant is not identifiable; it is any of the many prickly plants of Palestine.

background.note: Aristotle uses it of a thorn or prickle.
A comic proverb 'no thistles!' meant 'an easy job', showing thorns as a byword for difficulty.
A legacy lists a couch made of acanthus (acacia) wood, a related Egyptian tree name.

study.exegesisTip: In the parable of the sower the thorns do not destroy the seed at once; they grow up alongside it and choke it. Jesus' interpretation points to slow, competing concerns (worries, riches, pleasures), not open hostility.
study.caution: The botanical species of the crown of thorns cannot be identified with certainty; any identification is speculative.

study.summary: ἀλλότριος means 'belonging to another', not one's own, and by extension 'foreign, strange, alien'. It contrasts with ἴδιος ('one's own') and with what is kin or familiar. The NT uses it for other people's property, labors and sins, for a stranger whose voice the sheep do not know, and for a foreign land.

senses.label: Belonging to another, not one's own
senses.definition: Owned by or done by someone else, as opposed to what is one's own.
senses.note: In HEB 9:25 the high priest enters with 'blood not his own', in contrast to Christ, who offered himself.

senses.label: Outsider, not of one's family
senses.definition: Those outside one's family or people, as opposed to one's own sons.
senses.note: Kings tax 'others', not their own sons; so the sons, Jesus and his disciples, are free.

senses.label: Stranger, unknown person
senses.definition: One who is not known and therefore not trusted.
senses.note: The sheep will not follow a stranger, because they do not know his voice.

senses.label: Foreign, alien (land, people)
senses.definition: Belonging to another country or nation; foreign, and sometimes hostile.
senses.note: Abraham lived in the land of promise 'as in a foreign land' (HEB 11:9); in HEB 11:34 the word means foreign armies.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word for boundaries of responsibility: not judging another's servant (ROM 14:4), not building on another's foundation (ROM 15:20), not boasting in others' labors (2CO 10:15), and not sharing in others' sins (1TI 5:22).

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses it both for the priest's 'blood not his own' (HEB 9:25) and for the foreignness of the land and armies the faithful faced (HEB 11:9; HEB 11:34).

study.translationNote: Translations vary with context: 'another's', 'others', 'someone else's', 'stranger', 'foreign', 'alien'. In LUK 16:12 'what is another's' is set against 'what is your own', and the contrast is the point.

background.note: Homer speaks of being generous with what belongs to another, the basic sense 'another's'.
Aeschylus uses it for another man's wife.
A wife who 'became estranged' (ἀλλότρια φρονήσασα) from the marriage shows the sense of alienated, hostile.

study.exegesisTip: Look for the implied contrast with 'one's own' (ἴδιος, ὑμέτερος) or with 'sons': the meaning of ἀλλότριος is usually defined by what it is set against, as in LUK 16:12 and MAT 17:25-26.

study.summary: ἀμφότεροι means 'both', referring to two persons or things taken together. Paul uses it of Jew and Gentile made one in Christ. In later Greek it could stretch to mean 'all' of more than two, and this may explain one difficult verse in Acts.

senses.label: Both (of two persons)
senses.definition: Two people considered together, often a couple or pair.
senses.note: Zechariah and Elizabeth were 'both' righteous and 'both' advanced in years.

senses.label: Both (of two things)
senses.definition: Two objects or groups of things considered together.
senses.note: New wine in new wineskins: 'both are preserved'.

senses.label: Both groups made one (Jew and Gentile)
senses.definition: In Paul, the two peoples, Jews and Gentiles, made one and reconciled to God in Christ.
senses.note: Christ 'made both one', reconciled 'both' in one body, and through him 'both' have access in one Spirit to the Father.

senses.label: Both (of two beliefs)
senses.definition: Two doctrines or matters taken together.
senses.note: The Pharisees acknowledge 'both', resurrection and angels or spirits, as opposed to the Sadducees.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: All of Paul's uses are in Ephesians 2, where 'both' is a theological keyword: Jew and Gentile, once divided by a wall of hostility, are now one new humanity with shared access to God.

background.note: Aeschylus uses the singular for what is common to either of two lands, the basic sense 'both of two'.
A second-century document applies ἀμφότεροι to five named priests, suggesting the colloquial sense 'all' already existed.
Later papyri use the word of four men, further evidence for 'all' in late Greek.

study.exegesisTip: In Ephesians 2 count the pairs: 'both' always means Jew and Gentile, and the repeated word underlines that neither group gets to God except together through Christ.
study.caution: In the story of the seven sons of Sceva (Acts 19) many manuscripts say the possessed man overpowered 'both' of them, while the Byzantine text reads 'them'. Interpreters debate whether 'both' there means 'all' (as in some papyri) or whether only two sons were present.

study.summary: A killing or putting to death; used of Stephen's murder, which Saul approved.

senses.label: Killing, murder
senses.definition: The violent taking of a life; Stephen's death is presented as a killing, not a natural death, and Saul as consenting to it.
senses.note: The word is absent from ACT 22:20 in the critical text, which reads simply that Paul was approving.

study.translationNote: Older versions render it "death"; "killing" or "murder" better conveys the violent sense of the word.
study.exegesisTip: Luke places Saul's approval of Stephen's killing (ACT 8:1) beside Paul's own later confession of it (ACT 22:20), underlining the depth of the persecutor's change.

study.summary: Guiltless or innocent; Jesus uses it of priests who work on the Sabbath and of his disciples wrongly condemned.

senses.label: Guiltless, innocent
senses.definition: Not at fault and therefore not deserving condemnation; used of the temple priests whose Sabbath duties do not make them guilty and of the disciples condemned by the Pharisees.

background.note: In the Greek Old Testament the word is used of innocent blood whose shedding brings guilt on the land.
Already in Homer it describes a person blamed though not at fault.

study.summary: To sit up; used of people raised from death sitting up on their bier or bed.

senses.label: Sit up
senses.definition: To rise from a lying to a sitting position; in both uses, a dead person restored to life sits up.

background.note: A fourth-century Christian letter uses it of a sick woman who has managed to sit up, reflecting its common use in medical contexts.

study.exegesisTip: The word was common in medical writing for a patient sitting up; Luke uses it to show the dead truly restored to bodily life.

study.summary: To renew or make new again; Paul uses it of the believer's inner self being continually renewed by God.

senses.label: Be renewed
senses.definition: Passive: to be made new, an ongoing work of God in the believer's inner life and new self, restoring it toward the image of the Creator.
senses.note: Both uses are present-tense passives, stressing a continuing process.

study.exegesisTip: In 2CO 4:16 the inner renewal "day by day" is set against the outer self wasting away; in COL 3:10 it is renewal "in knowledge" after the Creator's image.

study.summary: Renewal; the transforming renovation of mind and life that God works in believers.

senses.label: Renewal, renovation
senses.definition: A making new of a person's inner life: the renewing of the mind that transforms conduct, and the renewal brought about by the Holy Spirit in salvation.

study.exegesisTip: In TIT 3:5 renewal stands beside "new birth"; the new birth marks the beginning, while renewal describes the Spirit's ongoing work of making the person new.

study.summary: To unveil or uncover; Paul uses it of the veil over Israel's understanding and of believers' unveiled faces.

senses.label: Unveil, uncover
senses.definition: To remove a covering; used figuratively of removing what hinders spiritual perception, so that the glory of the Lord can be seen.
senses.note: Both uses draw on Moses' veil in Exodus 34.

study.translationNote: In 2CO 3:14 versions differ on whether the participle goes with the veil ("remains, not lifted") or begins a new clause ("it is not revealed that it is removed in Christ").

study.summary: To sum up or bring together under one head; used of the commandments summed up in love and of all things gathered up in Christ.

senses.label: Sum up
senses.definition: To gather many items into a single summary statement, as the commandments are summed up in "Love your neighbor as yourself."

senses.label: Bring together in one
senses.definition: To unite all things under a single head; God's purpose to gather everything in heaven and on earth together in Christ.

study.exegesisTip: The word is built on the idea of a sum or main point (as in adding up a column); EPH 1:10 presents Christ as the one in whom the whole of creation finds its coherence.
study.caution: Whether EPH 1:10 stresses "summing up" or Christ's "headship" over all things is debated; the root relates to a sum or main point rather than directly to the word for head.

study.summary: To depart or return; used of a master returning from a wedding and of Paul's desire to depart this life.

senses.label: Return
senses.definition: To leave a place and come back, as a master returning from a wedding feast.

senses.label: Depart (die)
senses.definition: To depart from this life, pictured as setting out on a journey to be with Christ.

background.note: Papyri use the verb for leaving and returning to one's station or post.
A memorial inscription uses it for dying, the same sense as in Paul.

study.exegesisTip: The verb originally meant to loosen, as of a ship's moorings or a camp's tents; in PHP 1:23 death is a departure, not an end.

study.summary: Unworthily; in a manner unworthy of the Lord, used of improper participation in the Lord's Supper.

senses.label: Unworthily
senses.definition: In an unworthy manner; eating and drinking at the Lord's Table in a way that dishonors the Lord, such as the Corinthians' disregard for one another.
senses.note: In 1CO 11:29 the word appears in the Byzantine text but not in the critical text.

study.exegesisTip: The adverb describes the manner of participation, not the worthiness of the person; Paul's concern in context is the division and contempt for poorer believers at the meal.

study.summary: Crippled or maimed; one of the disadvantaged people Jesus tells his hearers to invite to their banquets.

senses.label: Crippled, maimed
senses.definition: Physically disabled or mutilated; listed with the poor, the lame and the blind as those unable to repay hospitality.

background.note: Used in classical Greek of maimed or mutilated people, including in a speech on behalf of a disabled man.

study.summary: Without excuse; having no defense before God's judgment.

senses.label: Without excuse
senses.definition: Having no grounds for a defense; inexcusable, used of those who suppress God's revealed truth and of those who condemn others while doing the same things.

study.exegesisTip: The word has a courtroom flavor; Paul uses it to leave both pagan and moralizing hearers without a defense, setting up his argument for universal guilt.

study.summary: To stir up or incite; used of the leaders inflaming the crowd and of the charge that Jesus agitated the people.

senses.label: Stir up, incite
senses.definition: To agitate or excite people to a course of action; used of the chief priests inciting the crowd to ask for Barabbas and of the accusation that Jesus stirred up the people.

background.note: The literal sense is to shake or wave something to and fro, such as the hands.

study.summary: To pull up or draw up; used of rescuing an animal from a pit and of the sheet in Peter's vision being drawn back to heaven.

senses.label: Pull out, draw up
senses.definition: To pull something up out of a place; used of hauling a son or an ox out of a well on the Sabbath and of the vision's sheet being drawn back up into heaven.

background.note: Used of drawing a ship up onto land.
Papyri use it of pulling up barley.

study.summary: To lay a matter before someone for consideration; used of Festus presenting Paul's case and Paul setting out his gospel to the Jerusalem leaders.

senses.label: Lay before, set forth
senses.definition: Middle: to communicate or present a matter to others, usually with a view to consultation or judgment.

background.note: A third-century papyrus uses the middle for submitting a matter, consistent with the NT sense of laying something before others.

study.exegesisTip: In GAL 2:2 the verb implies consultation, not seeking permission: Paul explains his gospel to the leaders, not asking them to authorize it.

study.summary: To overturn or upset; used figuratively of false teachers who subvert faith and ruin households.

senses.label: Overturn, subvert
senses.definition: To upset or ruin something; figuratively, false teaching undermining people's faith and wrecking whole households.

background.note: A papyrus speaks of a family household utterly overturned by profligacy, a close parallel to TIT 1:11.

study.summary: To appear or come into view; used of the expected appearing of God's kingdom and, nautically, of sighting Cyprus.

senses.label: Appear
senses.definition: Passive: to be made manifest, to come into view; used of the crowd's expectation that the kingdom of God would appear at once.

senses.label: Sight (land)
senses.definition: A sailing term: to come within sight of a place, here Cyprus.

background.note: A fourth-century Christian letter says that the knowledge of God has appeared to all, echoing LUK 19:11.

study.summary: Untraceable or beyond finding out; used of God's ways and the riches of Christ.

senses.label: Untraceable, inscrutable
senses.definition: That cannot be tracked or fully searched out; God's ways and Christ's riches exceed human ability to trace them to the end.

background.note: Paul's word appears to come from Job, where God's great deeds are said to be past finding out.

study.exegesisTip: The image is of footprints that cannot be followed to their end; the point is wonder at God's greatness, not that his ways are irrational.

study.summary: To examine judicially, especially by interrogation under torture; used of the Roman commander's plan to question Paul by flogging.

senses.label: Interrogate, examine
senses.definition: To question a prisoner to extract the truth, here by means of scourging.

background.note: A second-century papyrus uses it of government clerks examining documents.

study.summary: To find by searching; used of the shepherds finding the holy family and of Paul's companions seeking out disciples at Tyre.

senses.label: Find, seek out
senses.definition: To discover after looking for someone; the search is implied by the prefix.

background.note: Used in classical Greek for finding out or discovering.

study.summary: A charcoal fire; the fire in the high priest's courtyard where Peter denied Jesus, and the fire by the lake where Jesus restored him.

senses.label: Charcoal fire
senses.definition: A heap of burning coals or embers, used for warmth or cooking.

background.note: In classical comedy a person is said to warm himself at someone's fire.

study.exegesisTip: John uses this word only in these two scenes, inviting readers to link Peter's denial at one charcoal fire with his threefold restoration at another.

study.summary: A people-pleaser; one who serves only to win human approval.

senses.label: People-pleaser
senses.definition: Someone who works to please people, especially to look good while being watched, rather than serving sincerely as for Christ.

background.note: First found in the Greek Psalms, where God scatters the bones of those who please men.

study.summary: Folly or senseless rage; lack of understanding that may show itself as fury.

senses.label: Senseless rage
senses.definition: Mindless fury, a frenzy that overrides reason, as when the opponents were filled with rage after Jesus healed on the Sabbath.

senses.label: Folly
senses.definition: Lack of understanding; the foolishness of false teachers that will become obvious to all.

study.translationNote: In LUK 6:11 versions vary between "madness," "rage" and "fury," since the word combines lack of reason with uncontrolled anger.

background.note: Plato distinguishes two kinds of this mindlessness: madness and ignorance.

study.summary: To rebuild; used of God's promise to rebuild the fallen tent of David.

senses.label: Rebuild
senses.definition: To build again what has fallen into ruin; God's restoration of David's fallen house, applied to the inclusion of the Gentiles.
senses.note: The verb occurs twice in this quotation from Amos 9:11.

background.note: Used of rebuilding a city and its walls.
A third-century BC papyrus uses it of rebuilding altars better than before.

study.summary: Without the law; describes those who sin and perish apart from the Mosaic law.

senses.label: Without law
senses.definition: Apart from the law of Moses; used of Gentiles who sin without having the written law and will perish without it.
senses.note: The adverb appears twice in this verse.

study.exegesisTip: Here the word does not mean "lawlessly" in a moral sense but "without possessing the law," contrasted with those who sin "under the law."

study.summary: Unholy or profane; describes those who disregard what is sacred and their duties to God.

senses.label: Unholy, profane
senses.definition: Lacking reverence for God and sacred obligations; listed among the vices of the lawless and of people in the last days.

background.note: In Plato the unholy is that which is hated by the gods.

study.summary: Forbearance; God's patient holding back of judgment toward sinners.

senses.label: Forbearance
senses.definition: A restraint or suspension of deserved punishment; God's tolerance that gives time for repentance and under which past sins were passed over.

background.note: In classical Greek it commonly meant a holding back of hostilities, a truce or armistice.
A papyrus uses it of a delay of some days.

study.exegesisTip: The background idea of a truce suits ROM 2:4 and ROM 3:26: God's forbearance is a temporary suspension of judgment, not indifference to sin.

study.summary: Something given in exchange; Jesus asks what a person could give in exchange for his soul.

senses.label: Exchange, price
senses.definition: That which is given in return as an equivalent; nothing a person has can buy back a forfeited life.

background.note: Euripides uses it of something given in exchange for a friend.

study.summary: A repayment or requital, whether a favor returned or a deserved retribution.

senses.label: Repayment in kind
senses.definition: A return for a kindness, as when guests invite their host back.

senses.label: Retribution
senses.definition: Requital for wrongdoing; punishment as the due return.

study.summary: To answer back or reply against; used of Jesus' critics unable to answer and of a person talking back to God.

senses.label: Answer in reply
senses.definition: To give an answer in response to an argument or question.

senses.label: Talk back, dispute
senses.definition: To answer against someone in protest; a creature arguing with its Creator.

study.summary: A recompense in return, either a fitting penalty or a fair exchange of affection.

senses.label: Due penalty
senses.definition: A requital received as the fitting result of wrongdoing.

senses.label: Fair exchange
senses.definition: A matching response in return; Paul asks the Corinthians to repay his openness by opening their hearts in turn.

study.summary: To pass by on the opposite side, used of the priest and the Levite who avoid the wounded man in the parable of the Good Samaritan.

senses.label: pass by on the other side
senses.definition: To go past someone while deliberately keeping to the opposite side of the road, avoiding contact and help.
senses.note: Repeated for both the priest and the Levite, sharpening the contrast with the Samaritan who 'came to him'.

background.note: In Wisdom the compound is used in a quite different sense, of help coming up against an enemy.

study.exegesisTip: The double prefix (anti-, 'opposite', and para-, 'past') pictures a deliberate detour: both religious figures see the man and then choose the far side of the road.

study.summary: Something that corresponds to something else as its counterpart, used of the earthly sanctuary as a copy of the heavenly and of baptism as the reality answering to the flood.

senses.label: copy, counterpart
senses.definition: A copy that answers to an original pattern, as the man-made sanctuary corresponds to the true, heavenly one.

senses.label: corresponding reality
senses.definition: That which corresponds to an earlier figure, as baptism answers to the waters of Noah's flood through which eight were brought safely.

study.translationNote: In Hebrews the antitype is the inferior copy, while in 1 Peter it is the fulfilment answering to an Old Testament figure; English versions therefore vary between 'copy', 'figure', 'symbolizes' and 'corresponds to'.
study.exegesisTip: Note the reversal: in Hebrews the earthly sanctuary is the antitype of a heavenly original, whereas in modern usage 'antitype' usually means the greater fulfilment, as in 1 Peter.

study.summary: An upper room, the large furnished room where Jesus ate the Passover with his disciples.

senses.label: upper room
senses.definition: A room on an upper floor of a house, here a large guest room prepared for the Passover meal.
senses.note: Critical editions read the spelling anagaion for the same word.

background.note: A spelling close to this form appears in a papyrus of the early second century, and the word lives on in Modern Greek for an upper storey.

study.summary: Higher or above, used in the NT only in the neuter as an adverb: 'higher up' at a table and 'above' in a written passage.

senses.label: higher, to a better place
senses.definition: Of movement to a more honoured seat at a meal.

senses.label: above, earlier in the text
senses.definition: Of a passage already quoted earlier in the same writing.

background.note: Inscriptions use the word of time, meaning 'earlier' or 'former', close to its use for an earlier passage in Hebrews.

study.summary: Useless or unprofitable; used of pointless controversies and, as a noun, of the uselessness of the former commandment.

senses.label: unprofitable, useless
senses.definition: Bringing no benefit, said of foolish disputes about the law.

senses.label: uselessness
senses.definition: The neuter used as a noun: the inability of the old priestly regulation to bring anything to perfection.

background.note: Aeschylus uses it of useless lamentations.
A legal document of AD 139 declares a memorandum invalid and useless.

study.summary: An axe, in John the Baptist's warning that the axe already lies at the root of the trees.

senses.label: axe
senses.definition: A woodcutter's axe, used as a picture of imminent judgment on those who do not bear the fruit of repentance.

background.note: In Homer the word denotes an axe-head or battle-axe.
An inventory of 218 BC values an axe at two drachmas alongside a reaping sickle.

study.summary: To demand back what belongs to one or is owed, used of not reclaiming stolen goods and of God requiring the rich fool's life.

senses.label: demand back
senses.definition: To ask for the return of what has been taken from one.

senses.label: require, reclaim
senses.definition: To call in as due, of a life that is only on loan and is now required back.
senses.note: The impersonal plural 'they demand' is a reverent way of referring to God's action.

background.note: Herodotus uses it of demanding back what was carried off by force.
Common in the papyri of demanding payments, especially those in arrears.

study.exegesisTip: In Luke 12:20 the word implies the rich man's life was never his own; it is a loan being called in.

study.summary: Tender or soft, used of a fig branch that has become tender with new growth.

senses.label: tender
senses.definition: Soft and supple with rising sap, a sign that summer is near, in Jesus' parable of the fig tree.

study.summary: To threaten, used of the Sanhedrin's warning to the apostles and of Christ who made no threats when he suffered.

senses.label: threaten, warn sternly
senses.definition: To warn someone with threats of consequences, here forbidding the apostles to speak in Jesus' name.
senses.note: The fuller reading 'threaten with a threat' gives the sense 'strictly warn'.

senses.label: make threats
senses.definition: To answer suffering with threats of retaliation, which Christ refused to do.

study.summary: To strip off, used of believers having put off the old self and of Christ stripping the hostile powers at the cross.

senses.label: put off from oneself
senses.definition: To take off like a garment, of having renounced the old way of life.

senses.label: strip, disarm
senses.definition: To strip of power or arms, of Christ's triumph over the rulers and authorities.

study.translationNote: In Colossians 2:15 some versions say Christ 'disarmed' or 'despoiled' the powers, while others render 'having stripped off' them from himself, because the middle voice can mean either.
study.caution: Whether Colossians 2:15 means Christ stripped the powers of their arms or stripped them off himself like a garment is debated; most modern versions prefer the first.

study.summary: Single or simple, used of the 'single' or sound eye that fills the whole body with light.

senses.label: single, sound, generous
senses.definition: Of an eye that is clear and undivided, a picture of an undivided, generous heart set on God rather than on wealth.

study.translationNote: Versions render 'single', 'healthy', 'good' or 'clear', since the word can mean physically sound, morally undivided, or generous.

background.note: A marriage contract uses it of a dowry repaid 'simple', that is, without interest.

study.exegesisTip: In Matthew the saying sits between teaching on treasure and on serving two masters, and the opposite 'evil eye' was a Jewish idiom for stinginess, which supports the sense of undivided generosity.

study.summary: A casting away or a loss, used of Israel's rejection and of the loss of life Paul promised would not happen in the shipwreck.

senses.label: rejection, casting away
senses.definition: A thrusting aside, set in contrast with God's future acceptance of Israel.

senses.label: loss
senses.definition: The losing of something, here of life at sea.

background.note: Plato uses it of loss, contrasted with acquisition of wealth.

study.summary: An enrollment or census, used of the registration under Quirinius at Jesus' birth and of the census in the days of Judas the Galilean.

senses.label: census, registration
senses.definition: An official enrollment of persons and property, typically for taxation.

study.translationNote: Older versions say 'taxing', reflecting the purpose of such registration; modern versions say 'census' or 'registration'.

background.note: Plato uses it of a register of lands or property.
Many census returns survive from Roman Egypt; the oldest securely dated one is from AD 34.

study.caution: The date of the census under Quirinius in Luke 2:2 is a long-standing historical question, and the word 'first' has been read in more than one way.

study.summary: Acceptable or pleasing, used of conduct that is welcome in God's sight.

senses.label: acceptable, pleasing
senses.definition: Welcome and approved before God, of prayer for all people and of children caring for widowed parents.

study.summary: Acceptance or approval, in the phrase 'worthy of full acceptance' attached to trustworthy sayings.

senses.label: acceptance, approval
senses.definition: Wholehearted welcome and approval; a saying 'worthy of all acceptance' deserves to be fully received.

background.note: Honorific inscriptions use the formula of someone deemed worthy of the finest approval, showing the phrase was a familiar expression of esteem.

study.summary: A putting away or laying aside, used of removing dirt from the body and of Peter laying aside his bodily 'tent' in death.

senses.label: removal
senses.definition: The putting away of dirt, which baptism is said not to be.

senses.label: laying aside (in death)
senses.definition: The putting off of the body pictured as a tent, a figure for dying.

background.note: An inscription uses it of laying aside the crowns when resigning a priesthood.
