study.summary: Eager expectation, like watching with outstretched head, used of creation's longing and of Paul's hope.

senses.label: eager expectation
senses.definition: Intense, confident waiting for something to come, of creation awaiting the revealing of God's children and of Paul's expectation that Christ will be honoured in him.

study.exegesisTip: The word is built from 'head' and 'watch', suggesting someone craning forward to catch the first sight of what is coming.

study.summary: To give birth to, used of sin bringing forth death and of God giving believers new birth by the word of truth.

senses.label: bring forth (death)
senses.definition: Figuratively, of full-grown sin producing death as its offspring.

senses.label: give birth (new life)
senses.definition: Of God's deliberate act of bringing believers into new life through the gospel.

background.note: A first-century letter uses it in an ordinary way of a woman about to give birth.

study.exegesisTip: James sets the two births side by side: desire gives birth to sin and sin to death, but God by his will gives birth to his people.

study.summary: Enjoyment, used of the good things God richly gives and of the fleeting pleasures of sin Moses refused.

senses.label: enjoyment
senses.definition: The experience of enjoying something, whether God's gifts or the passing pleasure of sin.

background.note: Thucydides uses it of the enjoyment of good things.
A royal inscription of Commagene calls piety the sweetest enjoyment for humankind.

study.summary: To wash away or wash oneself clean, used of sins washed away in connection with baptism.

senses.label: wash away, be washed
senses.definition: To have oneself washed clean, figuratively of cleansing from sin.
senses.note: The middle voice stresses the person's own part in being washed.

background.note: In Homer, of washing the brine from one's shoulders.

study.summary: To lead astray, used of false messiahs deceiving the elect and of those who wandered from the faith through love of money.

senses.label: lead astray, deceive
senses.definition: To cause someone to go astray from the truth.

senses.label: wander away (passive)
senses.definition: To be led astray, to stray from the faith.

background.note: Aeschines uses it of leading someone away from the matter at hand.

study.summary: Defection or apostasy, a falling away or rebellion against God and his law.

senses.label: forsaking, abandonment
senses.definition: Turning away from an established allegiance, as Paul was accused of teaching Jews to forsake Moses.

senses.label: the rebellion
senses.definition: A decisive end-time revolt against God that precedes the revealing of the man of lawlessness.

study.translationNote: Versions render 2 Thessalonians 2:3 as 'falling away', 'apostasy' or 'rebellion', reflecting whether the emphasis is on desertion from the faith or open revolt against God.

background.note: Used of rebellion against the LORD.

study.summary: To shake off, used of shaking dust from the feet and of Paul shaking a viper into the fire.

senses.label: shake off
senses.definition: To shake something off oneself, whether dust as a testimony against an unwelcoming town or a snake from the hand.

background.note: Euripides uses it in the plain sense 'shake off'.

study.summary: Severity, the sternness of God toward those who fell, set beside his kindness.

senses.label: severity
senses.definition: Unrelenting sternness in judgment, contrasted with God's kindness.
senses.note: The word appears twice in this verse.

background.note: A legal plea of AD 186 speaks of a people among whom the severity of the laws is untempered.

study.exegesisTip: The image behind the word is something cut off sharply, like a sheer cliff; Paul pairs it with kindness to show both sides of God's dealings.

study.summary: Sharply or severely, of stern apostolic correction.

senses.label: severely, sharply
senses.definition: With stern firmness, of Paul's use of authority and of Titus' rebuke of false teachers.

study.summary: To separate or part, used of Paul and Barnabas parting company and of the sky being split apart like a scroll.

senses.label: part company
senses.definition: To separate from one another after a sharp disagreement.

senses.label: be split apart
senses.definition: Of the sky being torn away and rolled up like a scroll.

background.note: Plato uses it of separating the worse from the better.

study.summary: A man who has sexual relations with men, listed among wrongdoers in Paul's vice lists.

senses.label: male homosexual offender
senses.definition: A man who lies with a male, condemned as conduct contrary to God's law.

study.translationNote: Versions differ widely ('abusers of themselves with mankind', 'sodomites', 'homosexuals', 'men who practice homosexuality'); some combine it with the preceding word in 1 Corinthians 6:9 as passive and active partners.
study.exegesisTip: The word joins 'male' and 'bed', the same two terms that stand side by side in the Greek of Leviticus' prohibition of a man lying with a male, which suggests Paul drew on that law.
study.caution: The word is rare before Paul and its precise scope is debated, some limiting it to exploitative relations; most lexicons take it of men engaging in sexual relations with men generally.

study.summary: An archangel, a chief angel, used of the archangel's voice at the Lord's return and of Michael.

senses.label: archangel
senses.definition: A chief or highest-ranking angel.
senses.note: Michael is the only archangel named in the NT.

background.note: Magical papyri later invoke the archangel Michael by this title.

study.summary: To rule over, used of Gentile rulers who lord it over their subjects and of the root of Jesse who will rule the nations.

senses.label: rule over
senses.definition: To exercise authority over others, with the genitive of those ruled.
senses.note: In Mark 10:42 'those who are regarded as ruling' the Gentiles is contrasted with service among Jesus' followers.

study.exegesisTip: The same verb in the middle voice is the very common word 'begin'; only these two passages use it in the active sense 'rule'.

study.summary: Unshaken or immovable, used of a ship's bow stuck fast and of the unshakable kingdom believers receive.

senses.label: immovable, stuck fast
senses.definition: Literally unable to be moved, of a ship's bow lodged on a sandbar.

senses.label: unshakable
senses.definition: Figuratively, firm and secure, of God's kingdom that remains when all else is shaken.

background.note: Euripides uses it of an unshaken mind.
A fourth-century petition asks that decisions remain firm and unshaken, a common legal phrase.

study.summary: To be ungodly or act impiously, living or acting in open disregard of God.

senses.label: Live ungodly
senses.definition: To lead an impious life; Sodom and Gomorrah stand as a warning example to those who would live in defiance of God.
senses.note: Many manuscripts here read the noun 'the ungodly' instead of the verb; the sense is the same.

senses.label: Commit ungodly deeds
senses.definition: With a cognate object, to commit acts of impiety; Jude piles up the word-family to stress the godlessness of the deeds to be judged.

background.note: Classical writers used the verb for impiety and sacrilege, especially offences against the gods and their sanctuaries.
Inscriptions show the same construction with an internal object found in Jude, 'to commit impiety in matters concerning the gods'.

study.exegesisTip: In JUD 1:15 the quotation from Enoch uses 'ungodly' four times (ungodly people, ungodly deeds, which they ungodly committed, ungodly sinners), making godlessness the keynote of the indictment.

study.summary: An adverb meaning 'gladly, with pleasure', describing a warm and willing reception.

senses.label: Gladly, joyfully
senses.definition: With pleasure and readiness; used of the brothers in Jerusalem welcoming Paul's company, and (in many manuscripts) of the crowd receiving Peter's message at Pentecost.

background.note: Inscriptions pair the adverb with 'willingly', 'gladly and willingly', showing its tone of ready consent.

study.summary: Implacable: unwilling to make or keep a truce, refusing reconciliation.

senses.label: Implacable, irreconcilable
senses.definition: Describing people who will not be reconciled or come to terms with others, keeping enmity alive; listed among the vices of rebellious humanity and of the last days.
senses.note: The word stands in ROM 1:31 in many manuscripts but not in the critical text.

study.translationNote: Renderings vary between 'implacable', 'irreconcilable', 'unforgiving' and 'truce-breaker'; the word properly means one who will not enter into a truce at all.

background.note: Literally 'without libation', since treaties were ratified by drink-offerings; Thucydides uses it of acting without a formal truce, and later writers of implacable hostility.

study.summary: The assarion, a small Roman copper coin used as a picture of trifling value.

senses.label: Small copper coin
senses.definition: The Roman as (assarion), worth a small fraction of a denarius, a day's wage; two sparrows sold for one, five for two, yet none is forgotten by God.

study.translationNote: English versions use 'penny' or 'farthing' as equivalents for a coin of very small value.

background.note: An inscription from Calymna fixes a payment of four assaria for each day a freed slave fails to remain in service, showing its use for small daily sums.

study.exegesisTip: Comparing MAT 10:29 and LUK 12:6, a fifth sparrow comes free when buying two coins' worth; even that throw-in bird is not forgotten by God.

study.summary: Fine, beautiful, well-favoured; used of the infant Moses.

senses.label: Beautiful, well-favoured
senses.definition: Of fine appearance, comely; used of the infant Moses, echoing the Septuagint of Exodus 2:2, and in ACT 7:20 strengthened as 'beautiful to God', that is, exceptionally fine or pleasing in God's sight.

study.translationNote: ACT 7:20 'beautiful to God' is rendered variously as 'exceedingly fair', 'beautiful in God's sight' or 'no ordinary child'; the phrase may be a Hebraic intensive or may mean that God looked on him with favour.

background.note: Originally 'of the town, urbane', by the third century BC it simply meant 'fine', as in an instruction to wear the finest clothes possible.

study.summary: Unstable, unsettled; describing people not firmly grounded in the faith.

senses.label: Unstable, unsettled
senses.definition: Lacking firm footing in truth and character, and so easily enticed by false teachers or prone to twisting difficult Scripture.

study.exegesisTip: Peter contrasts the 'unstable' with his closing call to guard against losing one's own 'stability' in the very next verse, a word from the same root.

study.summary: Without natural affection: lacking the love that binds family members together.

senses.label: Without natural affection
senses.definition: Devoid of the instinctive love owed to kin, such as parents to children; listed among the marks of humanity given over to sin and of the last days.

study.translationNote: Some versions say 'heartless' or 'unloving'; the word is built on storgē, the affection of family members, so 'without natural affection' is closer.

background.note: Used of people without natural affection, including parents without love for their offspring.

study.summary: To flash like lightning or gleam with dazzling brightness.

senses.label: Flash as lightning
senses.definition: To flash forth, of lightning lighting up the sky from end to end, a picture of the sudden and universal visibility of the Son of Man's day.

senses.label: Gleam, be dazzling
senses.definition: To shine with dazzling brightness, of the clothing of the two men at the empty tomb.

background.note: In Homer the verb is used of Zeus sending lightning as an omen.

study.summary: To behave unbecomingly or dishonourably, acting in a shameful or improper way.

senses.label: Behave rudely, unbecomingly
senses.definition: To act in an unseemly, ill-mannered way; love does not behave so.

senses.label: Act improperly toward someone
senses.definition: To treat a person in a dishonourable or improper way; used of a man's conduct toward 'his virgin'.

background.note: A petition about an assault complains that the attacker first abused and behaved disgracefully toward the writer before striking him.

study.caution: In 1CO 7:36 it is debated whether the man is a fiance, a father or guardian of an unmarried daughter, or a partner in a spiritual marriage, and so whether 'acting improperly' means unfairness to her or the risk of improper conduct.

study.summary: Shameful indecency; also, euphemistically, the shame of nakedness.

senses.label: Shameless act
senses.definition: Indecent, disgraceful conduct; used of men committing shameless acts with men.

senses.label: Shame of nakedness
senses.definition: The exposure of one's body in shame, following Septuagint usage for nakedness; the unwatchful are warned lest their shame be seen.

background.note: The Septuagint uses it as a euphemism for nakedness in the laws against uncovering a relative's nakedness.

study.summary: In a disorderly way, out of line; used of believers who refuse to work.

senses.label: Disorderly, undisciplined
senses.definition: In a manner out of step with proper order; describes church members who live idly, refusing to work, and meddle in others' affairs, contrary to apostolic teaching.

study.translationNote: Older versions have 'disorderly'; many modern ones say 'idle' or 'undisciplined', reflecting the context of refusal to work (2TH 3:10-12).
study.exegesisTip: The word-group was at home in military use for soldiers out of rank; Paul applies it to those who break ranks with the community's pattern of diligent work.

study.summary: A preposition meaning 'without' or 'apart from'.

senses.label: In the absence of
senses.definition: Apart from, without the presence of; Judas sought to betray Jesus away from the crowd.

senses.label: Without, lacking
senses.definition: Not provided with; the disciples were sent out without purse, bag or sandals.

background.note: Originally poetic, it appears in a plain letter: the cobbler will not give up the money or the cloak without Justus.

study.summary: Vapour or mist, something that appears briefly; also a column of smoke.

senses.label: Vapour of smoke
senses.definition: A rising column or cloud of smoke, among the portents of the day of the Lord quoted from Joel.

senses.label: Passing mist
senses.definition: A vapour that appears for a little while and vanishes, picturing the brevity of human life.

background.note: Peter's 'vapour of smoke' is quoted from the Septuagint of Joel.

study.summary: Self-willed, arrogant: bent on pleasing oneself regardless of others.

senses.label: Self-willed, arrogant
senses.definition: Stubbornly set on one's own way and dismissive of others; an overseer must not be so, while false teachers are bold and self-willed.

background.note: A second-century petition complains of a grasping, self-willed man whose audacity the writer can no longer endure.

study.summary: Of one's own accord, voluntarily, without being asked or compelled.

senses.label: Of one's own accord
senses.definition: Acting by free choice; the Macedonians gave beyond their means of their own accord, and Titus went to Corinth on his own initiative.

background.note: Inscriptions praise a gymnasium official who served voluntarily and at his own expense; papyri pair the adverb with 'willingly' in a stock legal phrase.

study.summary: A flute-player, whether at a funeral or as part of a city's music.

senses.label: Flute-player
senses.definition: A player of the reed pipe; at the house of the synagogue leader they were mourners hired for the funeral, and in Babylon's fall their music falls silent.

study.translationNote: KJV has 'minstrels' in MAT 9:23 and 'pipers' in REV 18:22.

background.note: A third-century BC letter asks for a flute-player with his pipes to be sent for a festival.

study.summary: To spend the night, lodge somewhere overnight.

senses.label: Spend the night
senses.definition: To lodge for the night, possibly in the open; during Passion Week Jesus went out of Jerusalem each night to Bethany or the Mount of Olives.

background.note: A travelling apostle is to take only bread until he reaches his next night's lodging.

study.summary: Growth or increase, used of the growth of Christ's body, the church.

senses.label: Growth
senses.definition: The increase of the body as each part functions in union with Christ the head; in COL 2:19 it is 'the growth that is from God'.

background.note: A common term for growth or increase, e.g. of the growing power of enemies.

study.summary: Strict, exacting, severe: a master who demands returns.

senses.label: Strict, exacting
senses.definition: Severe and demanding, expecting a return where he has not invested; the fearful servant's description of his master in the parable of the minas.

study.translationNote: KJV 'austere' suggests asceticism; the sense is 'exacting' or 'harsh' in demands.

background.note: A letter warns that the government inspector coming to check the accounts is a very strict man, a regular martinet.

study.summary: Sufficiency, having enough; also the contentment of needing nothing more.

senses.label: Sufficiency
senses.definition: Having all that is needed in every circumstance, supplied by God's grace so that one can abound in good works.

senses.label: Contentment
senses.definition: The inner state of being satisfied with what one has; godliness with contentment is great gain.

background.note: In philosophy it named the ideal of self-sufficiency, needing nothing from outside oneself.
In everyday papyri it is concrete: 'the necessary amount' of something.

study.exegesisTip: Paul uses a Stoic ideal but reframes it: sufficiency comes from God's grace (2CO 9:8) and contentment is joined to godliness (1TI 6:6), not to self-reliance.

study.summary: Of itself, spontaneously, without visible human agency.

senses.label: By itself, spontaneously
senses.definition: Acting without outside cause visible to people; the soil bears fruit by itself while the farmer sleeps, and the iron gate opened of its own accord for Peter.

background.note: Homer uses it of the gates of Olympus opening of themselves.

study.exegesisTip: In both passages 'by itself' means without human effort, not without God: the hidden growth of the kingdom and the angel-led deliverance are God's doing.

study.summary: A latrine or drain, where food that passes through the body is expelled.

senses.label: Latrine, drain
senses.definition: The privy into which digested food passes; Jesus uses it to show that food goes through the stomach and out, not into the heart, and so cannot defile a person.

study.translationNote: KJV 'draught' means a privy; modern versions paraphrase 'is eliminated' or 'passes out of the body'.

background.note: A rare word, found in a Pergamum inscription in the same sense of privy.

study.summary: A joint or ligament binding the members of the body together.

senses.label: Joint, ligament
senses.definition: A fastening that connects parts of the body and conveys supply; through these the body of Christ is held together and grows from the head.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'joint' and 'ligament'; the word stresses the fastening that binds rather than mere contact.
study.caution: The basic meaning elsewhere is 'touch'; its use in ancient physiology for a band or ligament best fits Paul, but some take it as the 'points of contact' between members.

study.summary: Not loving money, free from greed.

senses.label: Free from love of money
senses.definition: Not avaricious; a qualification for overseers and a general call to believers, joined to contentment with what one has.

background.note: Honorific inscriptions use it in praise of public servants who were free from love of money.

study.summary: To look away from other things toward one object; also simply to see how things turn out.

senses.label: Fix one's eyes on
senses.definition: To turn one's gaze away from all else and fix it on Jesus, the founder and perfecter of faith.

senses.label: See, find out
senses.definition: To see clearly how matters stand; Paul will send Timothy once he sees how his own case turns out.

background.note: 4 Maccabees uses it of martyrs looking to God in their endurance, a close parallel to Hebrews.

study.summary: To foam at the mouth, as in a seizure.

senses.label: Foam at the mouth
senses.definition: To froth at the mouth during the violent convulsions caused by the spirit afflicting the boy.

background.note: Used in tragedy for foaming, as of horses in a chariot race.

study.summary: Ungrateful, failing to give thanks for kindness received.

senses.label: Ungrateful
senses.definition: Thankless toward benefactors; God is kind even to the ungrateful, and ingratitude marks people in the last days.

background.note: Herodotus uses it of ungrateful persons, as well as the older sense 'without charm'.

study.summary: Useless, unprofitable; a servant who brings no gain.

senses.label: Useless, unprofitable
senses.definition: Of no profit to the master; the servant who buried his talent is condemned as useless.

senses.label: Claiming no merit
senses.definition: Self-deprecating: servants who have only done their duty confess they have earned no special credit.

study.translationNote: LUK 17:10 is rendered 'unprofitable', 'unworthy' or simply 'servants'; the point is not worthlessness but that duty done earns no claim on the master.

background.note: A papyrus fragment has the same phrase 'useless slaves'.

study.summary: Chaff, the husks separated from grain at threshing.

senses.label: Chaff
senses.definition: The worthless husks winnowed from the wheat; in John the Baptist's warning it pictures those who will be burned with unquenchable fire.

background.note: Chaff was commonly used as fuel; an ostracon records an account for chaff for the furnaces.

study.summary: Wormwood, a bitter plant; in Revelation the name of a star that makes the waters bitter.

senses.label: Wormwood (name of star)
senses.definition: The name given to the burning star that falls on rivers and springs, signifying bitterness and death.

senses.label: Wormwood, bitterness
senses.definition: The bitter plant itself; a third of the waters became wormwood, that is, bitter and deadly.

study.exegesisTip: In the Old Testament wormwood symbolizes the bitterness of judgment and of idolatry (Jeremiah 9:15; Deuteronomy 29:18), the background for the image here.

study.summary: An adverb meaning "heavily" or "with difficulty"; in the NT only in the quotation of Isaiah's words about a people whose ears are dull of hearing.

senses.label: Heavily, with difficulty
senses.definition: With dull, sluggish response; "hear heavily" means to hear without taking in, a picture of spiritual unresponsiveness.

background.note: Both NT uses quote the Greek Old Testament's rendering of Isaiah's commission, where the Hebrew speaks of ears made heavy.

study.summary: To loathe or detest something as foul; in the passive, to be made abominable.

senses.label: Detest, abhor
senses.definition: Middle voice: to turn away in disgust from something, as a Jew abhors idols.

senses.label: Be made abominable
senses.definition: Passive participle: those who have become detestable, defiled by abominations, listed among those excluded from the new creation.

study.exegesisTip: Paul's charge in Romans 2 is pointed: the person who shrinks from idols as loathsome is still willing to profit from temples.

study.summary: Confirmation or legal guarantee: the act of establishing something as firm and valid.

senses.label: Confirmation, guarantee
senses.definition: Establishing something as firm and binding; of Paul's confirming the gospel, and of an oath serving as a guarantee that ends dispute.
senses.note: "For confirmation" was a standard legal phrase for a guarantee in business transactions.

background.note: Used as a technical term for the legal warranty given by a seller that the sale is valid.
Land in Israel was not to be sold "for confirmation", that is, in perpetuity, because it belongs to the Lord.

study.summary: To profane: to treat something holy as common, violating its sacred character.

senses.label: Profane, desecrate
senses.definition: To violate what is holy; of priests "profaning" the Sabbath by their temple work, and of the charge that Paul tried to desecrate the temple.

background.note: The standard Greek word for profaning the Sabbath and other holy things in the Law.

study.exegesisTip: Jesus' point in Matthew 12 is that priests technically "profane" the Sabbath by required temple duties yet are guiltless.

study.summary: To use force; in the NT only in the difficult saying about the kingdom and violence.

senses.label: Suffer violence or advance forcefully
senses.definition: Of the kingdom of heaven: either it is violently attacked (passive) or it forcefully advances (middle).

senses.label: Force one's way in
senses.definition: With "into": to press violently or force one's way into the kingdom.

study.translationNote: Versions differ on Matthew 11:12: some read "suffers violence" (passive), others "has been forcefully advancing" (middle), because the Greek form can be either.

background.note: Used in Homer of being hard-pressed or overpowered.
The passive "I am being forced" appears in a private letter, showing the passive reading is natural.

study.caution: Matthew 11:12 is disputed: interpreters differ on whether the violence is hostile opposition to the kingdom or the eager, forceful pressing of people into it.

study.summary: A little scroll or booklet, the small open scroll the angel gives John to eat.

senses.label: Little scroll
senses.definition: A small book or scroll held open in the angel's hand, which John takes and eats, sweet in the mouth but bitter in the stomach.

study.summary: To harm or injure someone.

senses.label: Harm, injure
senses.definition: To do bodily hurt; of poison that will not harm believers and of a demon leaving a man without injuring him.

background.note: Common for personal injury, often of eyesight, and for loss or damage in legal documents.

study.summary: A verbal adjective meaning "must be put": new wine must be put into new wineskins.

senses.label: Must be put
senses.definition: Expresses necessity: new wine ought to be put into fresh wineskins.

study.summary: Help or aid; in a nautical context, supports such as cables for bracing a ship.

senses.label: Help
senses.definition: Assistance given in need, as the timely help found at God's throne of grace.

senses.label: Ship's supports
senses.definition: Plural, a technical sailing term for supports, probably ropes or cables passed under the hull to hold the ship together.

background.note: Very common at the end of petitions, asking an official for his help.

study.summary: To heave the lead: to take soundings of the sea's depth.

senses.label: Take soundings
senses.definition: To measure the depth of water by casting a weighted line, as the sailors did approaching Malta.

study.summary: The north (originally the north wind).

senses.label: North
senses.definition: The northern direction; people from all four quarters entering the kingdom, and the three north gates of the new Jerusalem.

background.note: The contracted form is almost universal in everyday documents describing boundaries and directions.

study.summary: A councillor; in the NT, a member of the Sanhedrin, said of Joseph of Arimathea.

senses.label: Council member
senses.definition: A member of a governing council; here of Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the Jewish council.

background.note: Standard word for a member of a council or senate.
Used of members of town councils in Roman Egypt.

study.summary: A purpose, plan or will: what someone intends.

senses.label: Plan, intention
senses.definition: A human plan or intent, such as the soldiers' plan to kill the prisoners, or what pagans like to do.

senses.label: God's will
senses.definition: The sovereign purpose of God, which no one can resist.

background.note: Used of the intent of a lawgiver.
Used of the expressed wishes of a person in a will.

study.summary: A hill.

senses.label: Hill
senses.definition: A hill or elevation; hills brought low before the Lord's coming, and hills begged to cover people in judgment.

background.note: Herodotus notes it as a word from Cyrene.
Used in documents to mark locations of land.

study.summary: A prize awarded to the victor in the games, used by Paul for the believer's reward.

senses.label: Prize
senses.definition: The award given to the winner of a race; applied to the prize of God's upward call in Christ.

background.note: Inscriptions use it for prizes awarded to victors in contests.

study.summary: To be slow, delay or tarry.

senses.label: Delay, be slow
senses.definition: To be late or delayed; of Paul's possible delay in coming, and of the Lord who is not slow about his promise.

background.note: Used intransitively for loitering or delaying, as in "do not delay".
Found in everyday documents of people delaying.

study.summary: Rain, a downpour.

senses.label: Rain
senses.definition: Heavy rain that falls on the houses built on rock and on sand.

background.note: In Egypt the word was used of the inundation that watered the land, as in a lease counted by floodings.

study.summary: To sink, cause to sink; literally of boats and figuratively of people plunged into ruin.

senses.label: Begin to sink
senses.definition: Passive: of boats so loaded with fish that they began to sink.

senses.label: Plunge into ruin
senses.definition: Figurative: desires that drown people in destruction.

background.note: A compound form is used figuratively of a city overwhelmed by continual wars.

study.summary: To laugh.

senses.label: Laugh
senses.definition: To laugh for joy; the weeping will laugh, while those who laugh now will mourn.

study.exegesisTip: In Luke's blessings and woes the laughter of the comfortable now is contrasted with the coming reversal.

study.summary: Genealogy, a pedigree or family lineage, in the NT of speculative genealogies to be avoided.

senses.label: Genealogies
senses.definition: Lists or tales of lineage that fed endless speculation and controversy rather than faith.

background.note: Used of tracing a pedigree.

study.caution: Scholars differ on what these genealogies were: Jewish speculations on Old Testament lineages, or early Gnostic-type systems.

study.summary: A birthday celebration, used of Herod's birthday feast.

senses.label: Birthday feast
senses.definition: The celebration of a birthday, at which Herod's banquet led to John the Baptist's death.

background.note: In everyday letters the word always means a birthday feast, as in a request to send fish for a birthday.

study.summary: Birth, the event of being born.

senses.label: Birth
senses.definition: The birth of a child; of Jesus' birth and of John's birth, at which many would rejoice.

study.summary: Born; in the phrase "born of women", a way of saying all human beings.

senses.label: Born of women
senses.definition: Those born of women, that is, humanity; none among them is greater than John the Baptist.

background.note: The phrase "born of woman" for mortal humanity appears in Job.

study.summary: To grow old.

senses.label: Grow old
senses.definition: To become aged; of Peter in his old age, and of the first covenant, aging and near to disappearing.

background.note: Used in a petition of an old man pleading for mercy.

study.summary: A money box or bag, the common fund that Judas kept.

senses.label: Money box
senses.definition: A box or bag for money; Judas held the disciples' common purse and stole from it.

background.note: Used of the chest set up at the temple gate for collecting money for repairs.

study.summary: An adverb meaning terribly or vehemently.

senses.label: Terribly
senses.definition: Of severe suffering: the centurion's servant terribly tormented.

senses.label: Vehemently
senses.definition: With hostile intensity: the scribes and Pharisees pressing hard against Jesus.

background.note: Used in letters of someone being seriously ill.

study.summary: Twelve (a common Koine form for the usual word).

senses.label: Twelve
senses.definition: The number twelve: about twelve disciples at Ephesus and the twelve days since Paul went up to Jerusalem.

background.note: The regular form for twelve in the papyri of the Ptolemaic period.

study.summary: To collect a tithe from someone; passive, to pay a tithe.

senses.label: Collect a tithe
senses.definition: Active: Melchizedek received a tenth from Abraham.

senses.label: Pay a tithe
senses.definition: Passive: Levi, through his ancestor Abraham, paid a tenth.

study.exegesisTip: Hebrews argues Melchizedek's superiority from the direction of the tithe: the greater receives from the lesser.

study.summary: Made of leather, describing John the Baptist's belt.

senses.label: Leather
senses.definition: Made of skin or hide; John wore a leather belt around his waist.

background.note: Elijah is described wearing a leather belt, which John's dress recalls.

study.summary: To bind: to put in chains, or to tie things together into a bundle.

senses.label: Bind, put in chains
senses.definition: To fetter a person, as the demoniac was bound and Paul once bound believers.

senses.label: Tie up loads
senses.definition: To bundle heavy burdens, a picture of the Pharisees' demands laid on others.

background.note: Used in farm accounts of workers binding sheaves.

study.summary: A prisoner held in custody; used of Paul and the other prisoners on the voyage to Rome.

senses.label: Prisoner, captive
senses.definition: A person held in chains or under guard, here prisoners being transported under military escort.

background.note: Ordinary Greek word for a prisoner or captive from Herodotus onward.
A third-century BC official letter speaks of moving out existing prisoners to make room for new prisoners being handed over.

study.summary: To affirm something confidently and insistently, stressing it as certain.

senses.label: Affirm confidently, insist on
senses.definition: To assert emphatically. Paul uses it negatively of false teachers who confidently pronounce on things they do not understand, and positively of Titus, whom he wants to insist firmly on the gospel truths just stated.

background.note: Used in legal documents of parties solemnly affirming a fact.

study.exegesisTip: The same strong verb describes both the false teachers' empty assertions (1TI 1:7) and the confident teaching Paul wants from Titus (TIT 3:8); the difference lies in whether what is asserted is understood and true.

study.summary: To see clearly, with sight fully restored or unobstructed.

senses.label: See clearly
senses.definition: To see distinctly, used in Jesus' saying about removing the beam from one's own eye before one can see clearly enough to remove the speck from another's, and of the blind man's sight fully restored.

background.note: In Plato it means to look with eyes wide open, staring intently.

study.summary: To examine thoroughly or, as a legal term, to decide a case.

senses.label: Examine more exactly
senses.definition: To investigate in order to ascertain the facts precisely; the pretext of the plotters who wanted Paul brought before the council.

senses.label: Decide a case (legal)
senses.definition: To hear and determine a legal case, as Felix promises to do once Lysias arrives.

background.note: Common in official documents of a judge or ruler taking cognisance of and deciding a matter.

study.summary: To murmur or grumble among themselves, of a group voicing discontent.

senses.label: Grumble among themselves
senses.definition: Of a crowd or party muttering complaints to one another, here at Jesus' welcome of sinners.

background.note: Used of Israel's murmuring against God and Moses in the wilderness, a background that colors the grumbling against Jesus.

study.summary: To pass one's time or life; to live in a certain way.

senses.label: Lead a life
senses.definition: To spend or pass one's life, with the manner of life described, whether peaceful godliness or the malice and envy of the old way.

background.note: Common in letters for how one is getting on in life, e.g. wishing someone health and prosperity.

study.summary: To divide and distribute something among recipients.

senses.label: Divide, distribute, apportion
senses.definition: To divide something up and give each a share: the father dividing his property between his sons, and the Spirit distributing gifts to each believer as he wills.

background.note: The ordinary word for dividing property between parties, as in an agreement of heirs who have divided among themselves the use of an estate.

study.exegesisTip: In 1CO 12:11 the Spirit is the subject who actively and personally apportions gifts 'as he wills'.

study.summary: To clean out thoroughly, of clearing a threshing floor at the harvest.

senses.label: Clear thoroughly
senses.definition: To cleanse completely, used of the coming one clearing his threshing floor, separating wheat from chaff, as a picture of final judgment.

study.summary: To talk something over with others, or (passive) to be talked about widely.

senses.label: Discuss together
senses.definition: To talk with one another about something, as the scribes and Pharisees discussed what to do to Jesus.

senses.label: Be talked about widely
senses.definition: Passive: to be discussed and spread from person to person, of the events around John's birth throughout the Judean hill country.

study.summary: In the passive, to be thoroughly troubled, annoyed or exasperated.

senses.label: Be greatly annoyed, disturbed
senses.definition: To be deeply vexed or worn out by something, of the Jewish leaders disturbed by the apostles' preaching and of Paul exasperated by the fortune-telling slave girl.

background.note: A private letter uses it of being thoroughly upset.

study.summary: Literally to saw through; in the NT figuratively, to be cut to the quick with fury.

senses.label: Be infuriated
senses.definition: Passive, figurative: to be enraged, as if sawn through inwardly, describing the council's furious response to the apostles and to Stephen.

background.note: Inscriptions use the literal sense of sawing timber.

study.exegesisTip: The image is of rage, not remorse; in ACT 7:54 it leads directly to gnashing of teeth and stoning.

study.summary: To tear apart or break in pieces.

senses.label: Tear apart, break
senses.definition: To pull or wrench something apart by force: the demoniac snapping his chains, and the danger that Paul would be torn to pieces by the crowd.

background.note: Herodotus uses it of men torn limb from limb.

study.summary: An ordinance or arrangement established by authority.

senses.label: Ordinance, appointment
senses.definition: What has been ordered or arranged by a superior. Governing authority is God's ordinance; the law was received 'by directions of angels', that is, given through angelic mediation.

study.translationNote: In ACT 7:53 versions vary between 'ordained by angels', 'delivered by angels' and 'by the disposition of angels' because the phrase is compressed; all point to angels' role in giving the law.

background.note: Far from being a purely biblical word, it is used in everyday documents for arrangements or orders, such as making arrangements for the vintage.

study.summary: To keep carefully, whether treasuring something or keeping oneself from something.

senses.label: Treasure, keep carefully
senses.definition: To hold on to something with care, as Mary kept all these things in her heart.

senses.label: Keep oneself from
senses.definition: With a reflexive pronoun and 'from': to guard oneself against, abstain from, as in the apostolic letter.

background.note: Used of maintaining friendship and peace between peoples.

study.summary: To shine through; to dawn.

senses.label: Dawn, break through
senses.definition: Of daylight breaking through the darkness: the prophetic word is a lamp until the day dawns and the morning star rises in believers' hearts.

study.summary: To lay violent hands on, to kill.

senses.label: Kill, murder
senses.definition: To lay hands on and put to death; used of the leaders' killing of Jesus and the attempt on Paul's life.

background.note: The original sense was to handle or administer, as of those who managed common funds.

study.summary: Skilled and able to teach.

senses.label: Able to teach
senses.definition: Having the ability and readiness to teach others; a qualification for overseers and for the Lord's servant correcting opponents.

study.summary: A two-drachma coin, the amount of the annual Jewish temple tax.

senses.label: Two-drachma temple tax
senses.definition: A coin worth two drachmas, about a half-shekel, the yearly tax each Jewish man paid for the temple; 'those collecting the two drachmas' asked whether Jesus paid it.

background.note: Egyptian records show a similar two-drachma tax paid for the temple of the god Suchus.

study.summary: A period of two years.

senses.label: Two years
senses.definition: A span of two years: Paul's custody in Caesarea and his house arrest in Rome.

background.note: Common in leases and other documents for a two-year term.

study.summary: To insist strongly that something is so.

senses.label: Insist, affirm firmly
senses.definition: To maintain emphatically against doubt, as the bystander insisting Peter was with Jesus and Rhoda insisting Peter was at the door.

background.note: Plato uses it for confidently maintaining a position.

study.summary: Justification: God's act of declaring the guilty righteous.

senses.label: Justification, acquittal
senses.definition: The act of pronouncing righteous; Christ was raised for our justification, and his one righteous act brings justification that leads to life.

study.exegesisTip: Unlike the more common 'righteousness' words, this noun names the act of justifying; in ROM 5:18 'justification of life' means justification that results in life.

study.summary: To travel through a region or from place to place.

senses.label: Travel through
senses.definition: To journey through towns and places, of Jesus going through cities and villages preaching, and of Paul passing through Amphipolis and Apollonia.

background.note: A cavalry officer's petition uses it of the dangers of passing through districts on a journey.

study.summary: To doubt or hesitate, wavering between two minds.

senses.label: Doubt, waver
senses.definition: To hesitate in uncertainty, as Peter sinking on the water and some disciples at the risen Jesus' appearance.

background.note: Plato uses it for being in doubt or hesitating.

study.caution: In MAT 28:17 it is debated whether 'some doubted' refers to some of the Eleven or to others present, and whether the doubt is unbelief or hesitancy amid worship.

study.summary: To cut in two; used of the severe punishment of an unfaithful servant.

senses.label: Cut in pieces, punish severely
senses.definition: Literally to cut in two; said of the master's punishment of the wicked servant, who is then assigned a place with the hypocrites or unbelievers.

study.translationNote: Versions differ between 'cut him to pieces' and 'punish him severely' (or 'cut him off'), reflecting whether the verb is taken literally or as a figure for the harshest punishment.
study.caution: Since the servant is afterward assigned a place with others, some take the verb figuratively (severe scourging or cutting off from the household) rather than literal dismemberment; interpreters differ.

study.summary: Double-minded: divided in loyalty and so unstable.

senses.label: Double-minded, wavering
senses.definition: Having a divided soul, torn between trust in God and other loyalties; such a person is unstable and must purify the heart.

background.note: James may have coined the word; it and its related verb soon became common in early Christian writers such as the Didache and Hermas.

study.summary: The testing of faith, or the tested and genuine quality that results.

senses.label: Testing; tested genuineness
senses.definition: The proving of faith through trials, which produces endurance, and the genuine, proven quality of faith that is more precious than refined gold.

study.translationNote: Some versions render 'testing' or 'trial'; others 'genuineness' or 'proven character', especially in 1PE 1:7, where the comparison with refined gold suggests the tested result.

background.note: A related adjective is used of 'standard' or genuine gold, supporting the sense 'what is genuine' in your faith.

study.summary: Giving, or a gift.

senses.label: Giving
senses.definition: The act of giving, in the commercial phrase 'giving and receiving' used of the Philippians' financial partnership with Paul.

senses.label: Gift
senses.definition: That which is given; every good gift comes from the Father above.

background.note: Very common in financial records for a payment or instalment.

study.summary: A reception or banquet for guests.

senses.label: Banquet, reception
senses.definition: A feast given to entertain guests, as Levi's great banquet for Jesus and the feast to which Jesus says the poor should be invited.

background.note: Used of the great feast Abraham made when Isaac was weaned.

study.summary: To sink or go down, of the sun setting.

senses.label: Set (of the sun)
senses.definition: Of the sun going down at evening, when the sick were brought to Jesus after the Sabbath ended.

background.note: Used in astronomical texts for the setting of stars.

study.summary: Hard to carry; oppressively burdensome.

senses.label: Hard to bear
senses.definition: Of loads too heavy to carry, describing the burdensome rules the scribes and Pharisees laid on others without lifting a finger to help.

background.note: Used of heavy sand in a proverb comparing it with a fool's provocation, which is heavier still.
